tools.description: Trims adapter sequences and low-quality bases from reads and merges overlapping read pairs.
tools.name: AdapterRemoval

outputs.description: Read pairs in, mates merged, reads discarded and sequences retained, from an AdapterRemoval .settings report. The counts balance exactly, which is what lets a read-fate flow be drawn from them without apportioning anything. One row per report, so a pipeline that trims per lane gets one row per lane.
outputs.name: Trimming and collapsing statistics
outputs.rawYaml:
id: adapterremoval_settings
name: Trimming and collapsing statistics
description: >-
  Read pairs in, mates merged, reads discarded and sequences retained, from an
  AdapterRemoval .settings report. The counts balance exactly, which is what
  lets a read-fate flow be drawn from them without apportioning anything. One
  row per report, so a pipeline that trims per lane gets one row per lane.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.settings"
recipe: adapterremoval/settings.py
fixture: settings.tsv
renders_as:
  # Coloured by report: the table has one row per report and no group column, so
  # the report id is the only pertinent split.
  - id: collapse_vs_length
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Collapse rate against retained length
    roles: {x: average_retained_length, y: collapse_rate, label: sample, color: sample, size: retained_reads}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
      x_title: Average retained length (bp)
      y_title: Share of pairs collapsed
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is one AdapterRemoval report, usually a lane or a library: the mean
      length of its retained sequences against the share of read pairs merged into a
      single sequence, sized by the sequences retained. It answers whether the
      insert sizes of a library are short enough for mates to overlap.

      How to read: short fragments make the mates overlap, so a high collapse rate
      goes with a short retained length. That is the expected shape of an ancient or
      degraded DNA library. A low collapse rate with long retained sequences means
      the inserts are longer than the reads and the mates cannot merge.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median collapse rate of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      AdapterRemoval.

      Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: retained_reads
      color: sample
      labels: {sample: Report, retained_reads: Sequences retained}
    title: Sequences retained per report
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: retained_reads}
    description: >-
      Each bar is one AdapterRemoval report: the number of sequences it wrote out,
      which is the input of the mapper. It answers how much data each report
      contributes after trimming and collapsing.

      How to read: reports of one library type should be of similar size. A very short
      bar is a report that lost most of its reads to discarding, so check its
      discard rate before pooling it.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median number of sequences retained
      per report of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of AdapterRemoval.
  - component: card
    column: total_read_pairs
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: attrition
    attrition_cols: [well_aligned_read_pairs, collapsed_pairs]
    caption: pairs, from input to overlapping to collapsed
    title: Read pairs processed
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of read pairs given to AdapterRemoval across the
      reports, and the strip steps down to the pairs whose mates overlapped and the
      pairs merged into one sequence. It answers how much of the input survives each
      step.

      How to read: a short step from overlapping to collapsed means most overlapping
      pairs were merged. A large drop from input to overlapping means long inserts,
      which is normal for modern DNA and unusual for ancient DNA.

      Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  - component: card
    column: collapse_rate
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Collapse rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median across reports of the share of read pairs merged
      into a single sequence, and the box shows the spread. It answers how often the
      mates overlap enough to merge.

      How to read: a high share is the expected shape of an ancient or degraded
      library, with short fragments. A low share on such a library suggests modern
      DNA or long inserts. A report far from the box deserves a look at its library
      preparation.

      Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  - component: card
    column: average_retained_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Retained length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median across reports of the mean length of a retained
      sequence, in base pairs, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long the
      sequences handed to the mapper are.

      How to read: short sequences map ambiguously and long ones map better. A report
      well below its peers may have been over-trimmed or be a degraded library.
  - component: card
    column: discard_rate
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Discard rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median across reports of the share of reads dropped on
      quality or length, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much data
      trimming throws away.

      How to read: a low share means the library trims cleanly. A report far above its
      peers has many reads too short or too poor to keep, which points to adapter
      dimers or degraded input.

      Source: https://adapterremoval.readthedocs.io/en/stable/manpage.html
  - component: card
    column: retained_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: reports, by sequences retained
    title: Sequences retained
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of sequences written out across the reports, and
      the histogram counts the reports by how many each retained. It answers how much
      data is left for mapping and how evenly the reports contribute.

      How to read: a tight pile means evenly sized reports. A long tail of small
      reports holds the lanes or libraries that lost most of their reads.
  - component: table
    title: Trimming and collapsing statistics
    description: >-
      One row is one AdapterRemoval report, with its read counts at each step,
      retained length, collapse rate and discard rate. It gives the exact values
      behind the tiles and answers which reports lose or merge the most reads.

      How to read: sort by discard rate to find the reports that lose the most reads,
      then by collapse rate to see how many pairs were merged. The counts balance, so
      pairs in, mates merged and reads discarded add up to the sequences retained. It
      complements the collapse rate and discard rate tiles.

tools.description: Another Gtf/Gff Analysis Toolkit: validates, fixes and summarises genome annotations; sp_statistics reports the gene, transcript, exon and intron numbers of a GFF per feature type.
tools.name: AGAT

outputs.description: One row per assembly and transcript type from AGAT's sp_statistics: genes, transcripts per gene, exons per transcript, single-exon genes, overlapping genes and the gene, transcript, exon, intron and CDS lengths. Counts read the whole annotation, the per-transcript shape its longest isoforms, so a fragmented annotation shows as short genes with few exons and a surplus of single-exon models, whatever the isoform count.
outputs.name: Gene models per annotation
outputs.rawYaml:
id: agat_gene_models
name: Gene models per annotation
version: "1.1.0"
mode: sp-statistics/gene-models
description: >-
  One row per assembly and transcript type from AGAT's sp_statistics: genes,
  transcripts per gene, exons per transcript, single-exon genes, overlapping
  genes and the gene, transcript, exon, intron and CDS lengths. Counts read the
  whole annotation, the per-transcript shape its longest isoforms, so a
  fragmented annotation shows as short genes with few exons and a surplus of
  single-exon models, whatever the isoform count.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.stats.txt"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/stats/*.stats.txt"
recipe: agat/gene_models.py
fixture: gene_models.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: genes_vs_exons
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Genes against exons per transcript
    roles: {x: genes, y: exons_per_transcript, label: genome, color: feature_type, size: mean_gene_length}
    config:
      x_title: Genes
      y_title: Exons per transcript
      log_x: true
      top_n_labels: 6
      legend_pos: bottom
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is an annotation and a transcript type, with the number of genes
      on the horizontal axis (log scale) and the exons per transcript on the
      vertical axis, sized by mean gene length and coloured by transcript type. It
      answers how complete the gene models of each annotation look.

      How to read: a fragmented annotation shows many short, few-exon models, so
      it sits low on the vertical axis. Points of one transcript type that sit
      apart from the others are the annotation to inspect first. AGAT publishes no
      cut-off for these values.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median exons per transcript of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of AGAT.

      Source: https://agat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/agat_sp_statistics.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Genes per annotation by type
    dict_kwargs:
      x: genome
      y: genes
      color: feature_type
      barmode: stack
      labels: {genome: Annotation, genes: Genes, feature_type: Transcript type}
    description: >-
      Each bar is an annotation, with its genes stacked by transcript type such as
      mRNA, lncRNA or tRNA. It answers how many genes each annotation holds and of
      what kind.

      How to read: compare annotations of related species, whose gene counts should
      be of the same order. A bar with almost no non-coding types may reflect an
      annotation that only kept protein-coding genes.

      Source: https://agat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/agat_sp_statistics.html
  - id: gene_count
    component: card
    column: genes
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: genome
    filter_expr: "col('feature_type') == 'mrna'"
    caption: protein-coding genes, by annotation
    title: Protein-coding genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of mRNA genes over the annotations, and the bar
      splits them by annotation, with the median and maximum annotation beside it.
      It answers how many protein-coding genes the annotations hold.

      How to read: a thin share is an annotation with far fewer genes than the
      others, which may be incomplete.

      Source: https://agat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/agat_sp_statistics.html
  - id: exons_per_transcript
    component: card
    column: exons_per_transcript
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('feature_type') == 'mrna'"
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Exons per transcript
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of exons per mRNA, and the box shows the
      spread between annotations. It answers how rich the gene structures are.

      How to read: a lower value than related annotations suggests fragmented gene
      models that lack exons. The report counts the longest isoform of each gene for
      the per-transcript shape.

      Source: https://agat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/agat_sp_statistics.html
  - id: single_exon_share
    component: card
    column: single_exon_gene_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('feature_type') == 'mrna'"
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Single-exon genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent of mRNA genes made of one exon, and the
      box shows the spread between annotations. It answers how many gene models are
      a single exon.

      How to read: an annotation with a share far above its peers holds many short,
      possibly fragmented, models. Check it against the exons per transcript tile.

      Source: https://agat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/agat_sp_statistics.html
  - component: table
    title: Gene models per annotation
    description: >-
      Each row is an annotation and a transcript type, with its genes, transcripts,
      exons, single-exon genes, overlapping genes and the mean lengths of genes,
      transcripts, exons, introns and CDS. It answers the exact numbers behind every
      other tile.

      How to read: filter by transcript type to compare annotations on one kind of
      model.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: agat_statistics
name: Annotation statistics
version: "1.1.0"
mode: sp-statistics/long
description: >-
  Every number of AGAT's sp_statistics report, one row per assembly, feature
  type (mRNA, lncRNA, tRNA...), isoform view and metric, in the order AGAT
  prints them. The longest-isoform view keeps one transcript per gene, so it is
  the one to compare annotations that kept different numbers of isoforms.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.stats.txt"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/stats/*.stats.txt"
recipe: agat/statistics.py
fixture: statistics.tsv
renders_as:
  # Metrics of different scales never share an axis: one small panel per metric,
  # independent value axes, so a count of genes is never stacked on a mean length.
  - component: figure
    version: "1.1.0"
    title: AGAT metrics per annotation
    code: |
      # one isoform view, so a bar is one number: the longest-isoform view when present
      view = "longest" if (df["isoforms"] == "longest").any() else "all"
      d = df.filter(pl.col("isoforms") == view).drop_nulls(["value"])
      # the first metrics in AGAT's order, unless the metric filter picked others
      keep = d.sort("metric_order")["metric"].unique(maintain_order=True).head(9).to_list()
      d = d.filter(pl.col("metric").is_in(keep)).sort(["metric_order", "genome"])
      fig = px.bar(
          d.to_pandas(),
          x="genome",
          y="value",
          color="genome",
          facet_col="metric",
          facet_col_wrap=3,
          facet_row_spacing=0.12,
          category_orders={"metric": keep},
          labels={"genome": "Annotation", "value": "Value", "metric": "Metric"},
      )
      fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=", 1)[-1]))
      fig.update_yaxes(matches=None, showticklabels=True, title_text="")
      fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False, title_text="")
      fig.update_layout(
          legend_title_text=f"Annotation ({view} isoforms)",
          margin={"t": 32, "l": 48, "r": 16, "b": 24},
      )
    description: >-
      Each panel is one sp_statistics metric, and each bar in it the value for one
      annotation in the longest-isoform view, which keeps one transcript per gene. It
      answers how annotations compare metric by metric.

      How to read: every panel has its own value axis, so compare bars within a panel,
      not across panels. Without a metric filter the first nine metrics in AGAT's order
      are shown; pick metrics and a feature type with the filters to see others.

      Lines and annotations: no reference line is drawn, because each panel holds a
      different quantity and a cohort median of a handful of annotations says little.

      Source: https://agat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/agat_sp_statistics.html
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: feature_type
    title: Feature type
    description: >-
      Filters the dashboard to the feature types picked here, such as mRNA or
      lncRNA. It answers how one kind of feature compares between annotations.
  - component: interactive
    version: "1.1.0"
    interactive_type: Select
    column_name: metric
    title: Metric
    description: >-
      Picks one sp_statistics metric so that the chart shows a single panel and
      compares that quantity between annotations. It answers how annotations differ on that
      metric.
  - component: table
    title: Annotation statistics
    description: >-
      Each row is one number of the AGAT sp_statistics report, for an annotation, a
      feature type and an isoform view, in the order AGAT prints them. It answers the
      exact value behind the bar chart.

      How to read: filter by metric to compare one quantity, or by isoform view to
      separate all isoforms from the longest one.

      Source: https://agat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/agat_sp_statistics.html

renders_as.description:
Each panel is one sp_statistics metric, and each bar in it the value for one annotation in the longest-isoform view, which keeps one transcript per gene. It answers how annotations compare metric by metric.
How to read: every panel has its own value axis, so compare bars within a panel, not across panels. Without a metric filter the first nine metrics in AGAT's order are shown; pick metrics and a feature type with the filters to see others.
Lines and annotations: no reference line is drawn, because each panel holds a different quantity and a cohort median of a handful of annotations says little.
Source: https://agat.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tools/agat_sp_statistics.html

renders_as.description: Picks one sp_statistics metric so that the chart shows a single panel and compares that quantity between annotations. It answers how annotations differ on that metric.

renders_as.description:

How to read: filter by metric to compare one quantity, or by isoform view to separate all isoforms from the longest one.

    dict_kwargs:

      Each bar counts peptide clusters by the number of sequences they hold, split by the
      sample that contributed the representative. It answers how many AMP families are

outputs.description: Two-dimensional PCA of the AMP candidates over their physicochemical descriptors (molecular weight, isoelectric point, hydrophobicity and the helix, turn and sheet fractions), standardised before the decomposition.
outputs.name: Property embedding
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ampcombi_embedding
name: Property embedding
mode: amp/embedding
description: >-
  Two-dimensional PCA of the AMP candidates over their physicochemical
  descriptors (molecular weight, isoelectric point, hydrophobicity and the
  helix, turn and sheet fractions), standardised before the decomposition.
find: { path_glob: "**/ampcombi2/Ampcombi_summary.tsv" }
recipe: ampcombi/embedding.py
fixture: embedding.tsv
renders_as:
  # One point per candidate, so the embedding's `sample_id` role carries the
  # CDS id. Charge class is the default colour because the plane is a
  # physicochemical one; the sample and the per-tool probabilities ride along in
  # the output, and the renderer's colour menu reaches them.
  - id: amp_embedding
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: Property space of the AMP candidates
    roles: {sample_id: cds_id, dim_1: dim_1, dim_2: dim_2, color: charge_class}
    config:
      axis_prefix: PC
    description: >-
      Each point is an antimicrobial-peptide candidate placed by a principal component
      analysis of its physicochemical descriptors: molecular weight, isoelectric point,
      hydrophobicity and the helix, turn and sheet fractions, standardised first. The
      colour is the charge class. It answers which candidates resemble each other and how
      the charge classes separate.

      How to read: candidates close together share properties, and a group of one colour
      is a family with a common charge profile. Use the colour menu to colour by sample or
      by tool probability and see whether groups are sample specific.

      Lines and annotations: the charge class is a bin of the isoelectric point made by
      this catalog, basic at 8 or above and acidic at 6 or below, and not a call made by
      AMPcombi.
  - component: table
    title: Embedding coordinates table
    description: >-
      Each row is an AMP candidate with its two principal components, charge class, length
      and the probabilities of the prediction tools. It answers where a given candidate sits
      in property space.

      How to read: sort by a component to find the candidates at the edge of the cloud.

outputs.name: AMP candidates
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ampcombi_summary
name: AMP candidates
mode: amp/candidates
description: >-
  One row per antimicrobial-peptide candidate, with the per-tool probabilities,
  the physicochemistry AMPcombi computes (molecular weight, isoelectric point,
  hydrophobicity, secondary-structure fractions) and the reference-database hit.
find: { path_glob: "**/ampcombi2/Ampcombi_summary.tsv" }
recipe: ampcombi/summary.py
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # The same property plane as a first-class kind rather than hand-drawn code.
  # AMPcombi computes no net charge at pH 7, so the isoelectric point is the
  # charge axis it actually reports. The charge class colour is the recipe's own
  # bin of that isoelectric point (8 or above, 6 or below); size is the peptide
  # length.
  - id: amp_property_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Hydrophobicity against isoelectric point
    roles: {x: hydrophobicity, y: isoelectric_point, label: cds_id, color: charge_class, size: aa_length}
    config:
      x_title: Hydrophobicity
      y_title: Isoelectric point (pI)
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is an antimicrobial-peptide candidate: its hydrophobicity on the horizontal
      axis and its isoelectric point on the vertical axis. The colour is the charge class and
      the size is the peptide length. It answers which candidates combine hydrophobicity with a
      positive charge.

      How to read: candidates in the upper right are hydrophobic and have a high isoelectric
      point, which means a positive net charge at neutral pH. Candidates in the lower part
      are acidic. Follow up the labelled points in the table.

      Lines and annotations: no cut-off is drawn. The charge class is a bin of the isoelectric
      point made by this catalog, basic at 8 or above and acidic at 6 or below, and not a call
      made by AMPcombi.
  # Charge against hydrophobicity is the classic AMP property plane: cationic
  # and hydrophobic peptides cluster in the upper right. Colour = best tool
  # probability, size = peptide length.
  - component: figure
    title: Candidates by best prediction probability
    code: |
      # keep the physicochemistry complete so no point is silently dropped
      df_modified = df.drop_nulls(["hydrophobicity", "isoelectric_point", "prob_max"])

      fig = px.scatter(
          df_modified.to_pandas(),
          x="hydrophobicity",
          y="isoelectric_point",
          color="prob_max",
          size="aa_length",
          size_max=18,
          opacity=0.75,
          color_continuous_scale="Tealgrn",
          hover_name="cds_id",
          custom_data=["sample"],
      )
      fig.update_layout(
          xaxis_title="Hydrophobicity",
          yaxis_title="Isoelectric point (pI)",
          coloraxis_colorbar_title="Best probability",
          margin={"t": 24, "l": 56, "r": 16, "b": 48},
      )
    description: >-
      Each point is a candidate placed by hydrophobicity and isoelectric point, coloured by
      the best probability any prediction tool gave it and sized by peptide length. It
      answers whether the candidates the tools trust most share a property profile.

      How to read: a cluster of bright points in one region means the tools agree on a
      property signature. Bright points far from the rest are confident candidates with
      unusual properties and worth checking in the table.

      Lines and annotations: no cut-off is drawn. AMPcombi sets a prediction score under its cut-off to zero, so the colour
      only grades candidates that passed at least one tool.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: charge_class
    headline: true
    caption: candidates, by charge class
    title: AMP candidates
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of candidates, and the ring splits them by charge class.
      The secondary number counts the samples that contributed one. It answers how many
      peptides the run predicts and what kind of charge they carry.

      How to read: the charge class is a bin of the isoelectric point made by this catalog,
      basic at 8 or above and acidic at 6 or below.
  - component: card
    column: prob_ampir
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: ampir probability
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median probability the ampir tool gave its candidates, and the
      box shows the quartiles. It answers how confident that tool is about what it found.

      How to read: a median near one means a strong signal. AMPcombi sets a probability under
      its cut-off to zero, so a zero means the tool did not call that candidate.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: aa_length
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: average, with its range
    title: Peptide length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average length of the candidates in amino acids, and the
      histogram shows how lengths are spread. It answers what size of peptide the run
      predicts.

      How to read: a tail of long sequences deserves a second look. The pipeline
      has a minimum length parameter for AMPcombi, so the shortest candidates reflect the
      run's settings.
  - component: card
    column: prob_max
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, median]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.6
    threshold_direction: min
    caption: against the 0.6 probability cut-off
    title: Best prediction probability
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average of the best probability any tool gave each candidate,
      shown against the prediction cut-off. It answers how confident the predictions are.

      How to read: an average above the cut-off means the typical candidate is a confident
      call. A low average with a high maximum means a few strong candidates among many weak
      ones.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-off is a probability of 0.6, the default of the
      nf-core/funcscan parameter that sets AMPcombi's amp cut-off. The run may set another
      value.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: cds_id
    title: AMP candidates table
    description: >-
      Each row is an antimicrobial-peptide candidate with its tool probabilities, its
      physicochemical properties and its reference-database hit. It answers which
      candidates to follow up and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by best probability, then filter by charge class. A database hit with
      a high identity means the peptide is a known one.

tools.description: Generally applicable transcriptome-wide analysis of translational efficiency using anota2seq.
tools.name: anota2seq

outputs.description: One row per contrast and gene with the four anota2seq analyses side by side and one regulatory mode: translation, buffering, mRNA abundance or not regulated, assigned with anota2seq's default selection thresholds.
outputs.name: Translational regulation mode per gene
outputs.rawYaml:
id: anota2seq_regulation
name: Translational regulation mode per gene
mode: translation/regulation
description: >-
  One row per contrast and gene with the four anota2seq analyses side by side
  and one regulatory mode: translation, buffering, mRNA abundance or not
  regulated, assigned with anota2seq's default selection thresholds.
find: { path_glob: "**/*.anota2seq.results.tsv" }
recipe: anota2seq/regulation.py
fixture: regulation.tsv
renders_as:
  # The anota2seq fold-change plane: total mRNA change on x, ribosome-bound
  # mRNA change on y. Translation-regulated genes leave the diagonal, buffered
  # genes lie flat along x, mRNA-abundance genes ride the diagonal.
  - id: fold_change_plane
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Ribosome-bound against total mRNA change
    roles: { x: total_mrna_lfc, y: translated_mrna_lfc, label: gene_name, color: regulation_mode }
    config:
      x_title: Total mRNA log2 fold change
      y_title: Ribosome-bound mRNA log2 fold change
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: no change in translational efficiency
      legend_pos: bottom
      top_n_labels: 8
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene in one contrast: its change in total mRNA on the horizontal
      axis and in ribosome-bound mRNA on the vertical axis, coloured by regulatory mode.
      It answers whether a gene changes by transcript level, by translation or is
      buffered.

      How to read: genes riding the diagonal change with their mRNA level
      (mRNA abundance). Genes above or below it change translation beyond their mRNA, and
      buffered genes lie flat along the horizontal axis, where mRNA moves but
      ribosome-bound mRNA does not. Open the volcano for the statistics of the
      translation calls.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, where ribosome-bound and total mRNA
      change equally, so translational efficiency is unchanged. It is a geometric
      reference. The modes follow the anota2seq default selection, an adjusted p-value
      below 0.15 and, for translation and buffering, a change of at least log2(1.2).

      Source: https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/manuals/anota2seq/man/anota2seq.pdf
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30926999/
  - id: translation_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Translation effect volcano
    roles: { feature_id: gene_name, effect_size: translation_effect, significance: translation_padj, category: regulation_mode }
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.15
      effect_threshold: 0.263
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Translation effect (log2)
      significance_label: -log10 adjusted p-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene in one contrast: its translation effect, the change in
      ribosome-bound mRNA not explained by total mRNA, against its adjusted p-value.
      Points are coloured by regulatory mode. It answers which genes change their
      translational efficiency and how confidently.

      How to read: genes in the upper corners are translationally up- or down-regulated
      with confidence. Compare with the fold-change plane to separate them from genes
      that follow their mRNA level.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an adjusted p-value of 0.15, the
      anota2seq default maxPAdj. The vertical lines mark an absolute effect of log2(1.2),
      about 0.263, the default deltaPT for the translation analysis.

      Source: https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/manuals/anota2seq/man/anota2seq.pdf
  - id: gene_record
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: record_card
    title: Gene record
    roles: { id: gene_id, title: gene_name }
    description: >-
      One gene at a time: its fold changes, effects, adjusted p-values and regulatory
      mode across the four anota2seq analyses. Select a row in the table to open it.

      How to read: compare the total and ribosome-bound changes with the translation and
      buffering effects to see why the gene got its mode.
  - component: card
    column: gene_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: regulation_mode
    headline: true
    title: Genes by regulatory mode
    caption: gene calls, by regulatory mode
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct genes, the second figure the count of
      gene and contrast rows, and the ring splits the rows by regulatory mode. It
      answers how much of the transcriptome is translationally regulated.

      How to read: a ring mostly in not regulated means a weak response. Translation and
      buffering slices are the ones that need ribosome-bound data to detect.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30926999/
  - component: card
    column: translation_effect
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Translation effect spread
    caption: effect, quartiles over genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of translation effects and the box shows their
      quartiles. It answers how large the translational changes are.

      How to read: a box tight around zero with a long range means few genes change.
      The effect is a log2 change, so a median would cancel the two directions.
  - component: card
    column: total_mrna_lfc
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Total mRNA change spread
    caption: log2 fold change, quartiles over genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of total mRNA log2 fold changes and the box shows
      their quartiles. It answers how much transcript levels move.

      How to read: compare it with the ribosome-bound card; a wider ribosome-bound range
      means translation amplifies the changes.
  - component: card
    column: translated_mrna_lfc
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Ribosome-bound change spread
    caption: log2 fold change, quartiles over genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of ribosome-bound mRNA log2 fold changes and the box
      shows their quartiles. It answers how much translation moves.

      How to read: compare it with the total mRNA card; a narrower range means
      buffering holds ribosome-bound levels steady.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: regulation_mode
    title: Regulatory mode
    description: >-
      Filters the tiles to genes in one or more regulatory modes: translation,
      buffering, mRNA abundance or not regulated.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene_id
    title: Regulation table
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene in one contrast with the four anota2seq analyses side by side
      and one regulatory mode. It answers which genes to follow up and lets a row
      selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by translation adjusted p-value, or filter by mode. The mode is
      assigned by priority: translation, then mRNA abundance, then buffering.

outputs.name: anota2seq results per analysis
outputs.rawYaml:
id: anota2seq_results
name: anota2seq results per analysis
mode: translation/differential
description: >-
  The four anota2seq analyses of every contrast stacked in one table: change in
  ribosome-bound mRNA, change in total mRNA, the translation effect (ribosome
  association not explained by mRNA level) and buffering, each with its effect,
  RVM p-value, adjusted p-value and anota2seq's default significance call.
find: { path_glob: "**/*.anota2seq.results.tsv" }
recipe: anota2seq/results.py
fixture: results.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: analysis_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Analysis volcano
    roles: { feature_id: gene_name, effect_size: effect, significance: padj, category: direction }
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.15
      effect_threshold: 0.263
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Effect (log2)
      significance_label: -log10 adjusted p-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene in one anota2seq analysis (ribosome-bound mRNA, total mRNA,
      translation or buffering): its log2 effect against its adjusted p-value, coloured by
      direction. Use the analysis selector to read one analysis at a time. It answers
      which genes change in that analysis and how confidently.

      How to read: upper corners are significant up or down changes. Mixing analyses on
      one plot hides their different meanings, so filter to one first.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an adjusted p-value of 0.15, the
      anota2seq default maxPAdj, applied to every analysis. The vertical lines mark an
      absolute effect of log2(1.2), about 0.263, the default for translation and buffering
      only; ribosome-bound and total mRNA have no minimum effect.

      Source: https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/manuals/anota2seq/man/anota2seq.pdf
  - component: card
    column: gene_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: direction
    headline: true
    title: Calls by direction
    caption: gene calls, by direction
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct genes, the second figure the count of
      gene, contrast and analysis rows, and the ring splits the rows into up, down and
      not significant. It answers how many results pass the selection.

      How to read: a ring mostly not significant means a weak response in the analyses in
      view. Filter to one analysis to read it.

      Lines and annotations: the call is an adjusted p-value below 0.15, plus an
      absolute effect of at least log2(1.2) for translation and buffering.

      Source: https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/manuals/anota2seq/man/anota2seq.pdf
  - component: card
    column: effect
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Effect spread
    caption: effect, quartiles over results
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of log2 effects over the analyses in view and the
      box shows their quartiles. It answers how large the changes are.

      How to read: effects of different analyses mean different things, so filter to one
      analysis before comparing. A median would cancel up and down, hence the range.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: Select
    column_name: analysis
    title: Analysis
    description: >-
      Selects one of the four anota2seq analyses: ribosome-bound mRNA, total mRNA,
      translation or buffering.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene_id
    title: Analysis results table
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene in one analysis and contrast with its effect, slope, p-value,
      adjusted p-value and direction. It answers the exact statistics behind the volcano
      and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by adjusted p-value and filter by analysis. The slope is the
      anota2seq analysis of partial variance slope used to filter translation and
      buffering calls.

outputs.name: Arriba breakpoint links
outputs.rawYaml:
id: arriba_fusion_links
name: Arriba breakpoint links
mode: fusion-detection
description: >-
  The same Arriba calls as the fusion table, read as pairs of genomic loci: the
  two "chr:pos" breakpoints are split into bindable chromosome and position
  columns, the read evidence is summed into one link weight, and the event class
  and confidence come through unchanged. This is the row shape a chord diagram
  binds, so a run's fusions can be read as a partner map across the genome
  instead of as a list of names.
find: { filename: "*.arriba.fusions.tsv" }
recipe: arriba/fusion_links.py
fixture: fusion_links.tsv
renders_as:
  # Colour is the event class (category), Arriba's own `type`.
  - id: partner_chords
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_chord
    roles:
      chrom_a: chrom_a
      pos_a: pos_a
      chrom_b: chrom_b
      pos_b: pos_b
      label: label
      weight: weight
      category: category
    title: Fusion partner map
    description: >-
      Each chord joins the two breakpoints of a fusion on the genome, with its width the
      read support and its colour the event class. It answers where in the genome the
      partners sit and how strongly each fusion is supported.

      How to read: chords within one chromosome arc are local events such as deletions
      and duplications, and chords between chromosomes are translocations. A thick
      chord is a well supported fusion, so hover it for its partner genes.

      Lines and annotations: chord width is the split reads on both sides plus the
      discordant mates, as defined by the recipe, and the event class is Arriba's own
      type.
  - id: class_by_confidence
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: category
      y: weight
      color: confidence
      labels: {category: Event type, weight: Supporting reads, confidence: Confidence}
    title: Support by event type and confidence
    description: >-
      Each bar stacks the fusions of one event type, with height their supporting reads
      and colour Arriba's confidence class. It answers which kinds of event are well
      supported.

      How to read: tall high-confidence segments mark reliable events. Low-confidence
      segments are the calls Arriba's authors advise treating with skepticism.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33441414/
  - component: card
    column: weight
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    caption: median, lowest and highest
    title: Link weight
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median read support of a fusion link, the split reads on
      both sides plus the discordant mates, with the lowest and highest beside it. It
      answers how thick a typical chord is.

      How to read: a low median means the map is made of weakly supported links. The
      range is wide, so a box would draw a flat line.
  - component: card
    column: label
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: category
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: fusions, by event type
    title: Fusions by event type
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct fusions drawn, and the bars rank the
      event types by how many they hold. It answers which kind of rearrangement
      dominates.

      How to read: translocations and deletions point to different mechanisms, and a
      run with mostly read-through events may reflect transcription between neighbours
      and not a true fusion.
  - component: card
    column: category
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: category
    caption: links, by event type
    title: Event type composition
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of links and the ring splits them by event type. It
      answers what share of links each kind of event holds.

      How to read: a ring with one dominant slice means one mechanism accounts for most
      of the calls. The second number is how many event types are present.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: confidence
    title: Confidence filter
    description: >-
      Pick one or more of Arriba's confidence classes to restrict the tiles of this tab to
      them. It answers what the map looks like when only the reliable calls are kept.

      How to read: choose high, or high and medium, to drop the low-confidence calls that
      Arriba's authors advise treating with skepticism.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33441414/
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: label
    title: Breakpoint links table
    description: >-
      Each row is a fusion link with its two breakpoint loci, its read support, its event
      type and its confidence. It answers the exact coordinates behind each chord and
      lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by weight to find the best supported links.

id: arriba_fusions
name: Arriba fusion calls
mode: fusion-detection
description: >-
  Fusion calls Arriba retained, one row per call. The recipe labels each fusion
  from its two partner genes, sums the split reads, discordant mates and local
  coverage into one evidence block, derives a log-scaled support and the
  fraction of local reads that support the call, and splits the contig out of
  each breakpoint so the partners can be read as a chromosome flow.
find: { filename: "*.arriba.fusions.tsv" }
recipe: arriba/fusions.py
fixture: fusions.tsv
renders_as:
  # Confidence classes (low, medium, high) are Arriba's own; the paper recommends
  # treating low-confidence calls with skepticism (PMID 33441414). No reference line
  # is drawn on any tile, since Arriba defines no numeric cut-off on read support.
  - id: evidence_dot_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    roles: {cluster: confidence, gene: fusion, mean_expression: log_support, frac_expressing: support_fraction}
    title: Evidence for each fusion
    description: >-
      Each dot is a fusion in one confidence class: its colour is the read support on a
      log scale and its size is the share of local reads that support it. It answers
      which calls rest on strong evidence and how confident Arriba is in them.

      How to read: a large, dark dot in the high-confidence column is a well supported
      call. A call with few supporting reads in the low-confidence column is weak and
      Arriba's authors advise treating such calls with skepticism unless other
      evidence corroborates them. Check the table for the breakpoints and domains of
      the calls you keep.

      Lines and annotations: the colour scale is log10 of supporting reads plus 1, a transform of this catalog's recipe,
      where supporting reads are the split reads plus the discordant mates Arriba reports. The
      confidence classes low, medium and high are assigned by Arriba.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33441414/
  # Partner chromosomes as a flow: how a fusion circos reads without an assembly
  # to lay a ring out on. Source contig on the left, partner contig on the right.
  - id: partner_chrom_sankey
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sankey
    roles: {steps: [chrom_5p, chrom_3p]}
    config:
      value_label: Fusions
    title: Partner chromosomes
    description: >-
      Each flow joins the chromosome of the 5' partner on the left to the chromosome of
      the 3' partner on the right, with its width the number of fusions. It answers
      whether the fusions are within one chromosome or between chromosomes.

      How to read: a flow that returns to the same chromosome is a local rearrangement
      such as a deletion, an inversion or a duplication. A flow to another chromosome
      is a translocation. Many flows from one chromosome may point to a hot region or
      to a recurrent artefact worth checking.
  # The two composition bars Arriba's own report leads with: what kind of event
  # each call is, and which transcript feature each breakpoint fell in.
  - id: type_bars
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: fusion_type
      y: supporting_reads
      color: confidence
      labels: {fusion_type: Event type, supporting_reads: Supporting reads, confidence: Confidence}
    title: Support by event type
    description: >-
      Each bar stacks the calls of one event type, such as a deletion, a duplication or
      a translocation, with height the supporting reads and colour the confidence
      class. It answers which kinds of event carry the evidence.

      How to read: tall bars in the high-confidence colour are well supported events.
      An event type made only of low-confidence calls is mostly noise, so filter it
      out before interpreting the run.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33441414/
  - id: site_bars
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: site_5p
      y: supporting_reads
      color: site_3p
      labels: {site_5p: Transcript feature at the 5' breakpoint, supporting_reads: Supporting reads, site_3p: Transcript feature at the 3' breakpoint}
    title: Support by breakpoint location
    description: >-
      Each bar groups calls by the transcript feature the 5' breakpoint falls in, such
      as coding sequence, splice site or intron, with colour the feature of the 3'
      breakpoint and height the supporting reads. It answers whether breakpoints land
      where a spliced fusion transcript is expected.

      How to read: breakpoints at splice sites or in coding sequence on both sides are
      the usual shape of a real fusion. Calls with a breakpoint deep in an intron or in
      an untranslated region are less likely to produce a protein, so look at them
      with the reading frame tile.
  - id: type_frame_bars
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: fusion_type
      y: supporting_reads
      color: reading_frame
      labels: {fusion_type: Event type, supporting_reads: Supporting reads, reading_frame: Reading frame}
    title: Reading frame by event type
    description: >-
      Each bar stacks the calls of one event type, with height the supporting reads and
      colour whether the fusion keeps the reading frame. It answers which events are
      predicted to encode a protein.

      How to read: an in-frame fusion can produce a chimeric protein and is the first
      to follow up. An out-of-frame call is less likely to be functional, although the
      reading frame is one of several features used to judge a driver.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33441414/
  - component: card
    column: supporting_reads
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    caption: median, lowest and highest
    title: Supporting reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of supporting reads per call, the split reads
      plus the discordant mates, with the lowest and highest beside it. It answers how
      strong the evidence is for a typical call.

      How to read: a very low median means the calls rest on a handful of reads. The
      range is wide, so a box would draw a flat line.
  - component: card
    column: fusion
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: confidence
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    caption: fusions, by confidence
    title: Fusions called
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct fusions, and the bars rank the
      confidence classes by how many they hold. It answers how many fusions Arriba
      calls and how many it trusts.

      How to read: a run dominated by high and medium confidence is cleaner than one made
      of low-confidence calls, which Arriba's authors advise treating with skepticism.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33441414/
  - component: card
    column: split_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: fusion_type
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: split reads, by event type
    title: Split reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of split reads, reads that span the breakpoint, and
      the bars rank the event types by how many they carry. It answers where the direct
      junction evidence comes from.

      How to read: split reads show the exact breakpoint, whereas discordant mates only
      show the two partners are joined. A call with discordant mates only has an
      uncertain breakpoint.
  - component: card
    column: support_fraction
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distribution across calls
    title: Share of local reads that support the fusion
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of the reads around a breakpoint that support
      the fusion, between 0 and 1, and the histogram shows its distribution over the
      calls. It answers how dominant the fusion is over the normal transcript.

      How to read: a high share means most local reads carry the fusion, as in a clonal
      driver. A tiny share means a minor or artefactual signal.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: fusion
    title: Fusion calls table
    description: >-
      Each row is a fusion call with its partners, breakpoints, event type, confidence,
      reading frame, read support and retained protein domains. It answers which fusions
      to validate and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by confidence and supporting reads, then check the reading frame
      and the retained domains of the kinase or other drivers of interest.

tools.description: Derives allele-specific copy number profiles of tumour cells, accounting for normal cell admixture and tumour aneuploidy.
tools.name: ASCAT

outputs.description: ASCAT's called segments, turned into the canonical copy-number profile contract. Per the ASCAT documentation the .cnvs.txt file carries sample, chr, startpos, endpos, nMajor and nMinor, one row per segment. The major and minor allele counts become an absolute copy number, a log2 ratio against a diploid baseline and the segment's expected B-allele frequency, so copy-neutral LOH reads as a BAF split even though the total copy number never moves.
outputs.fixtureContent:
sample	chrom	start	end	log2	baf	copy_number	segment	label	depth
TUMOUR1	chr1	1	500000	0.0	0.5	2	segment	1+1	
TUMOUR1	chr1	500001	900000	1.0	0.25	4	segment	3+1	
TUMOUR1	chr2	1	200000	0.0	0.0	2	segment	2+0	
TUMOUR1	chr2	200001	400000	-3.0		0	segment	0+0
outputs.name: Allele-specific copy-number segments
outputs.rawYaml:
# yaml-language-server: $schema=../output.schema.json
id: ascat_cnv_segments
name: Allele-specific copy-number segments
mode: ascat
description: >-
  ASCAT's called segments, turned into the canonical copy-number profile
  contract. Per the ASCAT documentation the .cnvs.txt file carries sample, chr,
  startpos, endpos, nMajor and nMinor, one row per segment. The major and minor
  allele counts become an absolute copy number, a log2 ratio against a diploid
  baseline and the segment's expected B-allele frequency, so copy-neutral LOH
  reads as a BAF split even though the total copy number never moves.
find:
  path_glob: "**/variant_calling/ascat/*/*.cnvs.txt"
recipe: ascat/cnv_segments.py
fixture: cnv_segments.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: the profile shades segments by gain, loss and neutral from their log2
  # itself, and the table has no pertinent categorical column beyond the sample.
  - id: ascat_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: cnv_profile
    title: Allele-specific copy-number profile
    roles: {sample: sample, chrom: chrom, start: start, end: end, log2: log2, baf: baf, copy_number: copy_number, segment: segment, label: label}
    config:
      gain_threshold: 0.322
      loss_threshold: -0.415
    description: >-
      Each line is a called copy-number segment: its total copy number as a log2 ratio
      against two copies on the upper panel, and its expected B-allele frequency on the
      lower one. It answers where the tumour genome gains, loses or keeps its copy
      number, and where one allele is lost.

      How to read: segments above the upper dotted line are gains and those below the
      lower one are losses. A BAF far from 0.5 at an unchanged copy number is
      copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity, which the total copy number alone never
      shows. Zoom on a chromosome to read the allele-specific counts in the label.

      Lines and annotations: the dotted lines at log2 0.322 and -0.415 are log2(2.5/2) and
      log2(1.5/2), the total copy numbers of 2.5 and 1.5 where a rounded call leaves two. They are
      an arithmetic reference defined by this catalog, not an ASCAT cut-off. The dotted line at BAF 0.5 is the balanced state.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20837533/
  - id: ascat_cn_spread
    component: card
    column: copy_number
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Copy number spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median total copy number over the called segments, and the
      box shows their quartiles. It answers whether the tumour genome sits near the
      diploid baseline or is shifted.

      How to read: a median of two with a short box means a mostly balanced genome. A
      higher median or a long box points to widespread gains or a whole-genome
      duplication. Segments differ in length, so open the profile to see how much of the
      genome each level covers.
  - component: table
    columns: [sample, chrom, start, end, copy_number, baf, label]
    title: Copy-number segments
    description: >-
      Each row is a called segment with its position, total copy number, expected
      B-allele frequency and allele-specific label. It answers the exact boundaries and
      allele counts behind the profile.

      How to read: sort by copy number to list gains and losses, or look for rows with a
      BAF away from 0.5 and a copy number of two, which are copy-neutral LOH.

outputs.description: ASCAT's fit for each tumour sample. Per the ASCAT documentation the .purityploidy.txt file carries AberrantCellFraction and Ploidy, one data row per sample. Purity is the share of sequenced cells carrying the tumour genome, ploidy the average copy number of that genome, and every log2 ratio on the copy-number profile is read against them: a low-purity sample flattens the whole track.
outputs.name: Tumour purity and ploidy
outputs.rawYaml:
# yaml-language-server: $schema=../output.schema.json
id: ascat_purity_ploidy
name: Tumour purity and ploidy
mode: ascat
description: >-
  ASCAT's fit for each tumour sample. Per the ASCAT documentation the
  .purityploidy.txt file carries AberrantCellFraction and Ploidy, one data row
  per sample. Purity is the share of sequenced cells carrying the tumour
  genome, ploidy the average copy number of that genome, and every log2 ratio
  on the copy-number profile is read against them: a low-purity sample
  flattens the whole track.
find:
  path_glob: "**/variant_calling/ascat/*/*.purityploidy.txt"
recipe: ascat/purity_ploidy.py
fixture: purity_ploidy.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: ascat_purity_card
    component: card
    column: purity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Tumour purity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of sequenced cells that carry the tumour
      genome (ASCAT's aberrant cell fraction), and the box shows the spread across
      samples. It answers how clean the tumour content is.

      How to read: values near one mean a nearly pure tumour sample. Low purity
      flattens the copy-number profile and makes calls less certain, so treat the
      profiles of the lowest samples with care.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20837533/
  - id: ascat_ploidy_card
    component: card
    column: ploidy
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Tumour ploidy
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median average copy number of the tumour genome, and the
      box shows the spread across samples. It answers whether the tumours are near
      diploid or aneuploid.

      How to read: a value near two means a near-diploid genome and values well above
      it point to whole-genome duplication. A fit that jumps to an odd ploidy with low
      purity can be wrong, so check the profile of that sample.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20837533/
  - id: ascat_fit_table
    component: table
    columns: [sample, purity, ploidy]
    title: Purity and ploidy per sample
    description: >-
      Each row is a tumour sample with ASCAT's fitted purity and ploidy. It answers the
      exact fit behind each copy-number profile.

      How to read: read purity and ploidy together, since a low purity with an unusual
      ploidy is the usual sign of an ambiguous fit.

tools.description: Assembly summary statistics: contig count and length distribution, N50 and L50, base composition and the contigs past 1 kb, 10 kb, 100 kb and 1 Mb.
tools.name: assembly-scan

outputs.description: One row per assembly from assembly-scan's JSON report: contig count, total, median, maximum and N50 contig length, L50, GC and N content, and how many contigs pass 1 kb, 10 kb, 100 kb and 1 Mb. Contiguity bounds how much of a genome can align in long collinear blocks, so these numbers are read next to the alignment coverage.
outputs.name: Assembly statistics
outputs.rawYaml:
id: assemblyscan_stats
name: Assembly statistics
mode: assembly/summary
description: >-
  One row per assembly from assembly-scan's JSON report: contig count, total,
  median, maximum and N50 contig length, L50, GC and N content, and how many
  contigs pass 1 kb, 10 kb, 100 kb and 1 Mb. Contiguity bounds how much of a
  genome can align in long collinear blocks, so these numbers are read next to
  the alignment coverage.
find:
  path_glob: "**/assemblyscan/*.json"
recipe: assemblyscan/stats.py
fixture: stats.tsv
renders_as:
  # Fragmented assemblies sit right (many sequences) and low (short N50); the
  # point size is the assembly length and the colour the share of N bases. Both
  # axes span orders of magnitude between a draft and a chromosome-level assembly,
  # so they are logarithmic.
  - id: contiguity_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Contiguity of each assembly
    roles: {x: contigs, y: n50, label: genome, size: total_length}
    config:
      color_col: n_pct
      log_x: true
      log_y: true
      x_title: Sequences in the assembly
      y_title: N50 (bp)
      top_n_labels: 8
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is an assembly: its number of sequences on the horizontal axis and its
      N50 on the vertical axis, sized by its total length and coloured by the share of
      N bases. It answers which assemblies are chromosome-level and which are
      fragmented drafts.

      How to read: the upper left corner holds few, long sequences, the signature of a
      chromosome-level assembly. Points at the lower right are fragmented, and long
      alignments between genomes cannot span their breaks. A dark point carries many N
      bases, which are gaps that cannot align.

      Note: N50 is the sequence length at which half of the assembly is reached, longest
      first, and the assembly-scan README states no quality cut-off, so none is drawn.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median N50 of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-
      off of assembly-scan.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rpetit3/assembly-scan/master/README.md
      and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N50,_L50,_and_related_statistics
  # C1 N/A: one bar per assembly, the x axis already names it and no other column splits it.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: genome
      y: gc_pct
      labels: {genome: Assembly, gc_pct: GC content (%)}
    title: GC content per assembly
    reference_lines: [{axis: y, stat: median, column: gc_pct}]
    description: >-
      Each bar is an assembly, with its GC content as a percentage of its bases. It
      answers whether the assemblies have a similar base composition.

      How to read: bars of similar height are expected for closely related genomes. An
      assembly far from the rest may be a different species, or may be contaminated
      or built from another source.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median GC content of this table,
      a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a
      cut-off of assembly-scan.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rpetit3/assembly-scan/master/README.md
  # N50 and the total length span orders of magnitude between assemblies, so a box
  # would draw a flat line: the cards show the median with the extremes.
  - id: assembly_n50
    component: card
    column: n50
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: grid
    headline: true
    caption: median, with the shortest and longest
    title: Assembly N50
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median N50 of the assemblies, the length of the sequence at
      which half of the assembly is reached when sorted longest first, with the lowest
      and highest values. It answers how contiguous the assemblies are.

      How to read: a high N50 means long sequences, up to chromosome scale. A low N50
      beside a large sequence count marks a fragmented draft.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rpetit3/assembly-scan/master/README.md
      and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N50,_L50,_and_related_statistics
  - id: assembly_length
    component: card
    column: total_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: grid
    caption: median, with the smallest and largest
    title: Assembly length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median total length of the assemblies in base pairs, runs
      of N included, with the smallest and largest. It answers how large the genomes are.

      How to read: assemblies of related species should be of similar length. A much
      smaller assembly is probably incomplete, and a larger one may hold duplicated or
      contaminating sequence.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rpetit3/assembly-scan/master/README.md
  # Chromosome-level and fragmented assemblies make two groups, so the share of
  # sequences past 1 Mb reads as a histogram rather than as one median.
  - id: assembly_large_share
    component: card
    column: contigs_over_1mb_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: share of sequences over 1 Mb, per assembly
    title: Sequences over 1 Mb
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of an assembly's sequences that are longer
      than 1 Mb, and the histogram shows how the assemblies distribute. It answers how
      many assemblies are built from megabase-scale sequences.

      How to read: chromosome-level assemblies pile near 100 percent and fragmented
      ones near 0, so two humps mean two kinds of assembly.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rpetit3/assembly-scan/master/README.md

    component: card
    column: gc_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: GC content
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median GC content of the assemblies as a percentage, and
      the box shows the spread. It answers how similar the base composition is across
      assemblies.

      How to read: a narrow box means related genomes. An outlier assembly may be a
      different organism or contaminated.

    column: contigs

    aggregations: [min, max]

    caption: median, with the fewest and the most
    title: Sequences per assembly
    description: >-

    title: Assembly statistics table
    description: >-

      length, N50 and L50, GC and N content, and the sequences past 1 kb, 10 kb, 100 kb
      and 1 Mb. It answers the exact numbers behind every tile and lets a row selection
      filter the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by N50 to rank the assemblies by contiguity.

tools.description: Ataqv is a toolkit for measuring and comparing ATAC-seq results.
tools.name: ataqv

outputs.description: How each library's reads are spread over the reference sequences ataqv counted. One sequence carrying a disproportionate share, or a library whose profile does not match its peers, shows up here before any peak is called.
outputs.name: Reads per reference sequence
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ataqv_chromosome_counts
name: Reads per reference sequence
mode: qc/read_distribution
description: >-
  How each library's reads are spread over the reference sequences ataqv
  counted. One sequence carrying a disproportionate share, or a library whose
  profile does not match its peers, shows up here before any peak is called.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.ataqv.json"
recipe: ataqv/chromosome_counts.py
fixture: chromosome_counts.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: read_distribution
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    title: Reads per reference sequence
    roles: {cluster: sample, gene: chromosome, mean_expression: log10_read_count, frac_expressing: fraction_of_reads}
    description: >-
      Each dot is a reference sequence in a library: its size is the share of the
      library's reads on that sequence and its colour the log10 read count. It
      answers whether reads spread over the genome as expected.

      How to read: dots should grow with the length of the sequence, and the
      libraries should look alike. A sequence with a disproportionate share, such as
      the mitochondrial genome, or a library whose pattern differs from its peers
      points to a problem to fix before calling peaks.

      Source: https://github.com/ParkerLab/ataqv
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: chromosome
      y: fraction_of_reads
      color: sample
      labels: {chromosome: Reference sequence, fraction_of_reads: Share of reads, sample: Library}
    title: Share of reads per reference sequence
    description: >-
      Each bar is a reference sequence in a library: the fraction of its reads that
      fall on it. It answers which sequences take the largest part of each library.

      How to read: compare the bars between libraries. Large sequences should take
      larger shares, and any sequence standing out of that order deserves a look.
      ataqv reports no cut-off for this share, so none is drawn.
  - component: card
    column: read_count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max, median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: chromosome
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Reads per reference sequence
    caption: total reads, with the busiest sequences ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total number of reads counted by ataqv, and the bars
      rank the sequences that hold most of them. It answers where the reads of the
      run go.

      How to read: the leaders should be the longest sequences. A short sequence
      among them is a sign of enrichment or contamination.
  # ataqv publishes no cut-off for the share of reads on one sequence (the old 0.12 line had
  # no source, RULES section 17), so the card shows the value alone.
  - component: card
    column: fraction_of_reads
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Largest share on one sequence
    caption: highest share of reads on a single sequence, with the libraries ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest share of a library's reads found on a single
      reference sequence, and the bars rank the libraries with the highest one. It
      answers whether a library is dominated by one sequence.

      How to read: a high value is expected for a long chromosome and is worrying
      for a short one. ataqv defines no cut-off for it, so no pass mark is drawn.
  - component: card
    column: fraction_of_reads
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Spread of read shares
    caption: median share per sequence, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of reads on a reference sequence, and the
      box shows how the shares spread. It answers how evenly the reads are shared
      out.

      How to read: a wide box with a long upper whisker means a few sequences take
      most of the reads. A tight box means an even spread over sequences of similar
      size.
  - component: table
    title: Read counts per sequence
    description: >-
      Each row is a reference sequence in a library with its read count, share of
      the reads and log10 read count. It answers the exact values behind the dot
      plot.

      How to read: sort by share to find the busiest sequences, or filter to one
      library to compare it with its peers.

outputs.description: The fragment-length histogram of every library in long form. A good ATAC library shows a peak of short fragments followed by a decaying nucleosome ladder; a flat or ladder-free profile has lost that pattern. Each length is classed on the two windows ataqv counts (50 to 100 bp and 150 to 200 bp, ataqv src/cpp/Metrics.cpp), every other length is left outside them.
outputs.name: Fragment length distribution
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ataqv_fragment_length
name: Fragment length distribution
mode: qc/fragment_length
description: >-
  The fragment-length histogram of every library in long form. A good ATAC
  library shows a peak of short fragments followed by a decaying nucleosome
  ladder; a flat or ladder-free profile has lost that pattern. Each length is
  classed on the two windows ataqv counts (50 to 100 bp and 150 to 200 bp,
  ataqv src/cpp/Metrics.cpp), every other length is left outside them.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.ataqv.json"
recipe: ataqv/fragment_length.py
fixture: fragment_length.tsv
renders_as:
  # The ladder itself, then how much of the library sits in each window. The
  # `profile` kind draws the ladder with its windows as shaded bands, which is the
  # reading; the plain line stays for
  # dashboards that only want the curve.
  - id: fragment_ladder
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Fragment length ladder
    roles: {series: sample, x: fragment_length, y: fraction_of_all_reads}
    config:
      x_title: Fragment length (bp)
      y_title: Share of all reads
      log_y: true
      shaded_bands:
        - [50, 100, Short fragments (50-100 bp)]
        - [150, 200, Mononucleosomal (150-200 bp)]
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the share of reads at each fragment length. It answers
      whether the library shows the open-chromatin peak and the nucleosome ladder
      expected of ATAC-seq.

      How to read: a good library has a peak of short fragments followed by a
      decaying ladder with a bump near one nucleosome. A flat curve with no ladder
      points to over-tagmentation or damaged chromatin. Compare libraries and open
      the quality table for the ratio between the two windows.

      Lines and annotations: the shaded bands are the two windows ataqv counts, 50 to
      100 bp for short fragments and 150 to 200 bp for mononucleosomal ones, taken
      from the ataqv source code. The ENCODE ATAC-seq standards also require a
      nucleosome-free region and a mononucleosome peak.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ParkerLab/ataqv/master/src/cpp/Metrics.cpp
      and https://www.encodeproject.org/atac-seq/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: fragment_length
      y: fraction_of_all_reads
      color: sample
      labels: {fragment_length: Fragment length (bp), fraction_of_all_reads: Share of all reads, sample: Library}
    title: Fragment length distribution
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the share of reads at each fragment length. It
      answers the same question as the ladder as a plain curve.

      How to read: look for a first peak below 100 bp and a second, lower one near
      200 bp. A library without them lost the pattern of accessible chromatin.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: read_count
      color: fragment_class
      labels: {sample: Library, read_count: Reads, fragment_class: Fragment class}
    title: Reads per fragment class
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library, split by the fragment class ataqv counts: short
      (50 to 100 bp), mononucleosomal (150 to 200 bp) or outside those windows. It
      answers how the reads of each library divide between open and nucleosomal
      fragments.

      How to read: a larger short class than mononucleosomal one is the signature
      of open chromatin. Libraries that differ in their split should not be compared
      directly.

      Lines and annotations: the class windows are ataqv's own, from its source code.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ParkerLab/ataqv/master/src/cpp/Metrics.cpp
  - component: card
    column: read_count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max, median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: fragment_class
    top_n_count: 4
    title: Reads per fragment class
    caption: total reads, with the classes ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of reads in the table, and the bars rank the
      fragment classes that hold most of them. It answers which kind of fragment
      dominates the run.

      How to read: the short and mononucleosomal classes should hold a large part of
      the reads. A large class outside the windows is a sign of fragments ataqv does
      not count in its ratio.

      Lines and annotations: the class windows are 50 to 100 bp and 150 to 200 bp, from
      the ataqv source code.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ParkerLab/ataqv/master/src/cpp/Metrics.cpp
  # No count or median card over this table: it has one row per (library,
  # length), so either measures the x axis of the ladder, not the fragments.
  # The per-library median fragment length is `ataqv/metrics.median_fragment_length`.
  - component: table
    title: Fragment length histogram
    description: >-
      Each row is a fragment length in a library with its read count, share of all
      reads and class. It answers the exact values behind the ladder.

      How to read: filter to one library and look at the lengths with the largest
      shares.
