outputs.description: One row per ATAC library: TSS enrichment, the share of high-quality autosomal alignments that fall inside peaks, mitochondrial and duplicate fractions, and the peak statistics ataqv computed. These are the numbers an ATAC library is accepted or rejected on, and MultiQC has no module that reports them.
outputs.name: ATAC quality metrics
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ataqv_metrics
name: ATAC quality metrics
mode: qc/library
description: >-
  One row per ATAC library: TSS enrichment, the share of high-quality autosomal
  alignments that fall inside peaks, mitochondrial and duplicate fractions, and
  the peak statistics ataqv computed. These are the numbers an ATAC library is
  accepted or rejected on, and MultiQC has no module that reports them.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.ataqv.json"
recipe: ataqv/metrics.py
fixture: metrics.tsv
renders_as:
  # Signal (TSS enrichment) against specificity (reads inside peaks): the two
  # axes an ATAC library is placed on.
  - component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: TSS enrichment against reads in peaks
    roles: {x: tss_enrichment, y: hqaa_overlapping_peaks_percent, color: sample, size: total_peaks}
    config:
      x_title: TSS enrichment
      y_title: High-quality alignments in peaks (%)
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_value: 30
      reference_label: ENCODE fraction of reads in peaks, 0.3
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: its TSS enrichment on the horizontal axis and the
      percentage of its high-quality autosomal alignments that fall inside peaks on
      the vertical axis, with the marker sized by the number of peaks. It answers
      whether a library has both signal and specificity.

      How to read: good libraries sit to the right and above the line. A library
      high on one axis and low on the other has a good enrichment but poor
      specificity, or the reverse, and the two cards below give the cut-offs for
      each.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is 30 percent, the ENCODE
      ATAC-seq standard of 0.3 for the fraction of reads in peaks (0.2 is
      acceptable). ataqv computes the percentage on high-quality autosomal
      alignments, so the two are close but not identical.

      Source: https://www.encodeproject.org/atac-seq/
  # Signal, then yield, then the two ways an ATAC library wastes reads.
  - component: card
    column: tss_enrichment
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 7.0
    threshold_direction: min
    threshold_warn: 5.0
    headline: true
    title: TSS enrichment
    caption: average enrichment, with the lowest and highest library
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average TSS enrichment, the signal at transcription
      start sites over the flanks of the same window. It answers whether the
      libraries show the open chromatin expected of good ATAC-seq.

      How to read: higher is better. A library under the lower line has too little
      signal to trust its peaks, so check the fragment ladder and the TSS profile.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-offs are the ENCODE values for the GRCh38 RefSeq
      TSS annotation, 7 and above is ideal, 5 to 7 acceptable and under 5
      concerning. The values depend on the annotation, so other references use
      other cut-offs (hg19 6 and 10, mm10 10 and 15).

      Source: https://www.encodeproject.org/atac-seq/
  - component: card
    column: total_peaks
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Peaks called
    caption: total peaks, with the libraries calling most ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of peaks ataqv saw in the peak files, and the
      bars rank the libraries with the most. It answers how much accessible
      chromatin each library resolves.

      How to read: a library with far fewer peaks than its peers has less usable
      signal. The count depends on depth and on the peak caller, so compare libraries
      of one run only.
  - component: card
    column: mitochondrial_fraction
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Mitochondrial reads
    caption: median fraction of reads on the mitochondrial genome, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median fraction of reads that map to the mitochondrial
      genome, and the box shows the spread between libraries. It answers how much
      sequencing was wasted on mitochondrial DNA.

      How to read: lower is better, since mitochondrial reads carry no nuclear
      signal. A library far above the box is a candidate for a cleaner preparation.
      ataqv sets no cut-off for it, so none is drawn.

      Source: https://github.com/ParkerLab/ataqv
  - component: card
    column: hqaa_overlapping_peaks_percent
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 30.0
    threshold_direction: min
    threshold_warn: 20.0
    title: Reads in peaks
    caption: average percent of alignments in peaks, with the lowest and highest library
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average percentage of high-quality autosomal
      alignments that overlap a peak. It answers how specific the signal is to
      accessible regions.

      How to read: higher is better. A low value means most reads lie in the
      background, so the library needs more depth or a cleaner preparation.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-offs are the ENCODE ATAC-seq standard for the
      fraction of reads in peaks, above 30 percent is good and above 20 percent
      acceptable. ataqv computes the percentage on high-quality autosomal alignments,
      a close but not identical quantity.

      Source: https://www.encodeproject.org/atac-seq/
  - component: card
    column: duplicate_fraction
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Duplicate reads
    caption: average duplicate fraction, with the median and the highest library
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average fraction of reads that are duplicates, and the
      histogram shows how the libraries spread. It answers how much complexity was
      lost to PCR duplication.

      How to read: lower is better. A library at the right of the histogram has

outputs.description: Aggregate read coverage in a window centred on every transcription start site, recentred so 0 is the TSS. The height of the central spike over the flanks is the TSS enrichment score; the shape says whether that enrichment is a sharp signal or a broad shoulder.
outputs.name: TSS coverage profile
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ataqv_tss_coverage
name: TSS coverage profile
mode: qc/tss_profile
description: >-
  Aggregate read coverage in a window centred on every transcription start site,
  recentred so 0 is the TSS. The height of the central spike over the flanks is
  the TSS enrichment score; the shape says whether that enrichment is a sharp
  signal or a broad shoulder.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.ataqv.json"
recipe: ataqv/tss_coverage.py
fixture: tss_coverage.tsv
renders_as:
  # The `profile` kind rather than a line figure: it puts the TSS marker at 0,
  # the log axes and the legend placement in the tile's own Settings, which is
  # what the code-mode `at-sig-fig-tss` was written by hand to get.
  - id: tss_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Coverage around transcription start sites
    roles: {series: sample, x: position, y: coverage}
    config:
      reference_x: 0
      reference_label: TSS
      x_title: Distance from the TSS (bp)
      y_title: Normalised coverage
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: its aggregate read coverage in a window centred on
      every transcription start site, scaled so the flanks of the window average 1.
      It answers whether the reads concentrate at start sites.

      How to read: a good library has a sharp spike at the TSS standing well above
      the flanks. A low or broad shoulder means weak or diffuse enrichment, so check
      the fragment ladder and the share of reads in peaks.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical marker is the TSS at position 0. The height
      of the curve at it is the TSS enrichment score, as ataqv scales the profile by
      the mean of the 100 bp at each end of the window.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ParkerLab/ataqv/master/src/cpp/Metrics.cpp
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: position
      y: coverage
      color: sample
      labels: {position: Distance from the TSS (bp), coverage: Normalised coverage, sample: Library}
    title: Coverage around transcription start sites
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the aggregate read coverage around start sites. It
      answers the same question as the profile as a plain curve.

      How to read: look for a spike at zero over a flat baseline of about one. A
      broad bump without a spike means diffuse signal.
  # The value of the curve at position 0 is the TSS enrichment score (ataqv
  # Metrics.cpp, calculate_tss_metrics). ENCODE's GRCh38 RefSeq cut-offs apply.
  - component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 7.0
    threshold_direction: min
    threshold_warn: 5.0
    filter_expr: "col('position') == 0"
    title: Enrichment at the TSS
    caption: average coverage at the TSS, with the lowest and highest library
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average normalised coverage exactly at the start site,
      which is the TSS enrichment score. It answers how strong the signal is at the
      centre of the profile.

      How to read: higher is better. A library below the lower line has weak
      enrichment.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-offs are the ENCODE values for the GRCh38 RefSeq
      TSS annotation, 7 and above is ideal, 5 to 7 acceptable and under 5
      concerning. Other annotations use other values.

      Source: https://www.encodeproject.org/atac-seq/
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ParkerLab/ataqv/master/src/cpp/Metrics.cpp
  - component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('position') == 0"
    title: Spread of TSS enrichment
    caption: median enrichment at the TSS, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median coverage at the start site over libraries, and
      the box shows how they spread. It answers whether the libraries enrich alike.

      How to read: a library far below the box has weaker signal than its peers.
      Open the profile to see whether it lacks a spike or has a high background.
  - component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Highest point of the profile
    caption: highest coverage in the window, with the libraries ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest coverage anywhere in the window, and the bars
      rank the libraries reaching the highest point. It answers which libraries
      have the sharpest peak.

      How to read: the highest point is normally at or next to the TSS. If a library
      peaks elsewhere, the profile is noisy and its enrichment score is not
      reliable.
  - component: table
    title: Coverage profile values
    description: >-
      Each row is a position in the window around start sites with the normalised
      coverage of a library. It answers the exact values behind the profile.

      How to read: filter to position 0 to read the enrichment of every library.

outputs.description: Bambu gene-level read counts, the top 50 genes by total count across samples, features x samples.
outputs.name: Gene-level quantification
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bambu_counts_gene
name: Gene-level quantification
mode: quantification/gene
description: >-
  Bambu gene-level read counts, the top 50 genes by total count across
  samples, features x samples.
find: { path_glob: "**/bambu/counts_gene.txt" }
recipe: bambu/counts_gene.py
fixture: counts_gene.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the run's samples
  - id: top_expressed_genes_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Most expressed genes by sample
    roles: {index: gene_id, row_annotation_cols: [gene_biotype]}
    config:
      normalize: row_z
    description: >-
      Each cell is the Bambu read count of one of the most highly counted genes (rows)
      in one sample (columns), scaled per gene, with the gene biotype as a row
      annotation. It answers whether the highest-count genes behave the same in every
      library.

      How to read: columns of the same condition should share a pattern. A sample that
      looks unlike its replicates, or a block of genes high in one condition only, shows
      the main expression differences before any statistics. Colour is a per-gene
      z-score, so it shows the pattern across samples and not the absolute level.

      Lines and annotations: the genes are the 50 with the highest total count across
      samples, a fixed display size of this catalog's recipe and not a significance cut-off. Counts are Bambu's
      estimated gene counts.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GoekeLab/bambu/master/README.md
  - id: top_biotypes
    component: card
    column: gene_biotype
    aggregation: mode
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: gene_biotype
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: genes, by biotype
    title: Dominant gene biotype
    description: >-
      The hero number is the most frequent biotype among the displayed genes, the compact
      line gives how many biotypes occur, and the bars rank them by gene count. It
      answers what kind of genes take the most reads.

      How to read: protein-coding genes usually dominate. A large share of mitochondrial
      or ribosomal RNA among the top genes points to a library with little mRNA
      enrichment.
  - id: biotype_count
    component: card
    column: gene_biotype
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [mode]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: gene_biotype
    caption: genes, by biotype
    title: Gene biotypes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct gene biotypes among the displayed genes
      and the ring splits the genes by biotype. It answers how varied the top genes are.

      How to read: a ring made of one large slice means the top genes are of one kind.
      Small slices are rare classes worth a look in the table.
  - component: table
    title: Top gene counts
    description: >-
      Each row is one of the highest-count genes with its biotype and the Bambu count in
      every sample. It answers the exact counts behind the heatmap.

      How to read: sort a sample column to see its top genes and compare across columns.

outputs.description: Bambu gene counts melted to one row per sample and gene, with CPM and log2(CPM + 1) normalised against the full library. The long shape is what a sample filter can reach: the wide matrix next to it carries no sample column.
outputs.name: Gene counts per sample
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bambu_counts_gene_long
name: Gene counts per sample
mode: quantification/gene-long
description: >-
  Bambu gene counts melted to one row per sample and gene, with CPM and
  log2(CPM + 1) normalised against the full library. The long shape is what a
  sample filter can reach: the wide matrix next to it carries no sample column.
find: { path_glob: "**/bambu/counts_gene.txt" }
recipe: bambu/counts_gene_long.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 1 real library of 12 genes (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several libraries and conditions.
fixture: counts_gene_long.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: gene_expression_box
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: log_cpm
      color: condition
      labels: {sample: Library, log_cpm: "Expression, log2(CPM + 1)", condition: Condition}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: log_cpm}
    title: Expression distribution per library
    description: >-
      Each box is the distribution of log2(CPM + 1) over the genes of one library,
      coloured by condition. It answers whether the libraries are comparable after
      normalising for depth.

      How to read: boxes of similar height and position mean comparable libraries. A
      library whose box sits well above or below its replicates has a composition or
      quality difference to check before comparing conditions.

      Lines and annotations: this catalog's recipe computes counts per million from the
      Bambu gene counts against the library total, then adds 1 before the log2 transform.
      The dashed line is the median log2(CPM + 1) of this table, a reference computed
      from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Bambu.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GoekeLab/bambu/master/README.md
  - id: log_cpm_spread
    component: card
    column: log_cpm
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median expression, with its spread
    title: Typical expression
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median log2(CPM + 1) over every gene and library in view, and
      the box shows the quartiles. It answers where expression typically sits.

      How to read: many genes are not detected in a library, so the median is low and the
      upper quartile is the more informative number. Filter to one condition to compare
      them.
  - id: genes_by_biotype
    component: card
    column: gene_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: gene_biotype
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: genes, by biotype
    title: Genes quantified
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct genes, the compact line gives the gene and
      library rows, and the bars rank the biotypes by their genes. It answers how much of
      the annotation is covered and by what kind of gene.

      How to read: protein-coding genes usually lead. Rows divide by genes to give the
      number of libraries in view.
  - id: reads_by_library
    component: card
    column: count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: reads, by library
    title: Reads assigned
    description: >-
      The hero number is the sum of Bambu counts over the libraries in view, and the bars
      rank the libraries by their share. It answers how deep the sequencing is and how
      evenly it is spread.

      How to read: a library far below the others carries less information and its low
      counts are noisier. The compact line gives the median and maximum count of a single
      gene and library.
  - id: biotype_rows
    component: card
    column: gene_biotype
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: gene_biotype
    caption: gene rows, by biotype
    title: Gene biotypes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct gene biotypes and the ring splits the gene
      and library rows by biotype. It answers what kinds of genes the table holds.

      How to read: one large slice is the usual protein-coding majority. The compact line
      gives the number of rows.
  - id: cpm_peak
    component: card
    column: cpm
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, q3]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: condition
    top_n_count: 2
    caption: highest CPM, by condition
    title: Highest expression
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest counts per million of any gene in a library, and the
      bars rank the conditions by their top value. It answers whether one gene takes a
      large share of a library.

      How to read: a very high maximum means one gene dominates the library, which
      compresses the rest of the distribution. The compact line gives the median and the
      upper quartile.
  - component: table
    page_size: 25
    title: Gene counts per library
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene in one library with its biotype, Bambu count, counts per million
      and log2(CPM + 1). It answers the exact values behind the plots.

      How to read: filter to one library or condition and sort by counts per million to
      list the most expressed genes.

outputs.description: Square sample-by-sample Spearman correlation of log-CPM gene expression: the plot that shows a swapped label or a replicate that did not replicate, one row and one column per sample.
outputs.name: Sample correlation matrix
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bambu_sample_correlation
name: Sample correlation matrix
mode: exploratory/correlation
description: >-
  Square sample-by-sample Spearman correlation of log-CPM gene expression: the
  plot that shows a swapped label or a replicate that did not replicate, one
  row and one column per sample.
find: { path_glob: "**/bambu/counts_gene.txt" }
recipe: bambu/sample_correlation.py
fixture: sample_correlation.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the run's samples
  - id: correlation_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Sample correlation
    roles: {index: sample_id, row_annotation_cols: [condition]}
    description: >-
      Each cell is the Spearman correlation between two samples over their log2(CPM + 1)
      gene expression, with the condition as a row annotation and rows and columns
      clustered. It answers which samples resemble each other.

      How to read: replicates should form blocks of high correlation and conditions
      should separate. A sample that correlates better with the other condition, or with
      none, is a swapped label or a replicate that did not replicate.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is 1 by construction. Genes below a minimum
      total count are left out, and no correlation cut-off is applied.
  - id: mean_correlation_spread
    component: card
    column: mean_correlation
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mean correlation, with its spread
    title: Mean correlation per sample
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average of each sample's mean correlation with the others,
      and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how similar the libraries are overall.

      How to read: a high average with a tight box means a consistent run. A sample whose
      value sits far below the box is the outlier to inspect first. Rank correlation is
      high between any two samples of the same tissue, so compare samples within a run and
      not against an absolute value.
  - id: correlation_samples_by_condition
    component: card
    column: condition
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: condition
    caption: samples, by condition
    title: Conditions and samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of conditions, the compact line gives the number of
      samples, and the ring splits the samples by condition. It answers how the run is
      balanced.

      How to read: unequal slices mean an unbalanced design, which weakens comparisons of
      the smaller group.
  - component: table
    title: Sample correlation table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its condition, its mean correlation and its correlation
      with every other sample. It answers the exact values behind the heatmap.

      How to read: sort by mean correlation to find the least typical sample.

outputs.description: One row per sample: the first three principal components of the log-CPM gene matrix, restricted to the 500 most variable genes the way DESeq2 plotPCA does, next to the library size, the number of genes detected and the share of the library its 50 top genes take.
outputs.name: Sample structure and library readings
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bambu_sample_pca
name: Sample structure and library readings
mode: exploratory/pca
description: >-
  One row per sample: the first three principal components of the log-CPM gene
  matrix, restricted to the 500 most variable genes the way DESeq2 plotPCA
  does, next to the library size, the number of genes detected and the share of
  the library its 50 top genes take.
find: { path_glob: "**/bambu/counts_gene.txt" }
recipe: bambu/sample_pca.py
fixture: sample_pca.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: pca
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: Sample structure
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, dim_1: dim_1, dim_2: dim_2, dim_3: dim_3, color: condition}
    config:
      axis_prefix: PC
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample placed by the first principal components of its log2(CPM + 1)
      gene expression, coloured by condition. It answers whether the samples group by
      condition.

      How to read: replicates of a condition should sit together and conditions should
      separate along the first component. A sample that sits with the wrong group or far
      from its replicates is an outlier or a swapped label, so check the correlation heatmap.

      Lines and annotations: the components use the 500 genes with the highest variance of
      log2(CPM + 1), the default number of genes of DESeq2 plotPCA.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thelovelab/DESeq2/devel/man/plotPCA.Rd
  - id: depth_vs_complexity
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Depth against genes detected
    roles: {x: total_counts, y: n_genes_detected, label: sample_id, color: condition, size: top50_share_pct}
    config:
      x_title: Reads assigned
      y_title: Genes detected
      top_n_labels: 6
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: the reads Bambu assigned on the horizontal axis and the
      number of genes detected on the vertical axis, sized by the share of reads the 50 top
      genes take and coloured by condition. It answers whether depth explains how many
      genes were seen.

      How to read: genes detected rises with depth and then flattens. A library below its
      replicates at the same depth is less complex, and a large point means a few genes
      take much of the library. Both point to quality problems to check before comparing
      conditions.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median number of genes detected of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of Bambu.
  - id: reads_per_library
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample_id
      y: total_counts
      color: condition
      labels: {sample_id: Library, total_counts: Reads assigned, condition: Condition}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: total_counts}
    title: Reads assigned per library
    description: >-
      Each bar is the number of reads Bambu assigned to genes in a library, coloured by
      condition. It answers how even the depth is across the run.

      How to read: bars of similar height mean comparable depth. A short bar is a library
      with little information, and counts per million correct for the difference only in
      part.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median reads assigned of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a
      cut-off of Bambu.
  - id: reads_by_condition
    component: card
    column: total_counts
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: condition
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: reads, by condition
    title: Reads assigned
    description: >-
      The hero number is the sum of reads assigned over the libraries in view, and the bars
      rank the conditions by their share. It answers how much data the run holds and how it
      splits.

      How to read: a condition with far fewer reads is less well measured. The compact line
      gives the median and the largest library.
  - id: genes_detected_spread
    component: card
    column: n_genes_detected
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median genes detected, with its spread
    title: Genes detected
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of genes with reads per library, and the box
      shows the quartiles. It answers how complex the libraries are.

      How to read: a tight box means similar complexity. A library far below it has
      lost genes to low depth or degradation.
  - id: protein_coding_spread
    component: card
    column: pct_protein_coding
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median share, with its spread
    title: Protein-coding share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of reads falling on protein-coding genes per
      library, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how clean the mRNA signal is.

      How to read: a library far below its replicates carries more ribosomal, mitochondrial
      or other RNA, which points to depletion or enrichment differences in the prep.
  - id: top50_share_spread
    component: card
    column: top50_share_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median share, with its spread
    title: Share taken by the top genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of a library taken by its 50 most counted
      genes, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how concentrated expression is.

      How to read: a high share means a few genes use up the reads and leave less depth for
      the rest. A library above its replicates is more concentrated and less complex.
  - id: samples_by_condition
    component: card
    column: condition
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: condition
    caption: samples, by condition
    title: Conditions and samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of conditions, the compact line gives the number of
      samples, and the ring splits the samples by condition. It answers how the run is
      balanced.

      How to read: unequal slices mean an unbalanced design, which weakens comparisons of
      the smaller group.
  - component: table
    title: Library readings
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its condition, the first three components, reads assigned,
      genes detected, protein-coding share and the share of the top 50 genes. It answers
      the exact values behind the plots.

      How to read: sort by reads assigned or genes detected to find the weakest libraries.

    title: Most variable genes
    roles: {index: gene_id, row_annotation_cols: [gene_biotype]}
    config:
      normalize: row_z

description: >-

  a single `section` filter drives every tile instead of five separate
  collections. `section` is one of `indel_length` (insertion and
  deletion length, deletions negative), `substitution` (the A to C, A to G,
  ... substitution spectrum), `depth` (read depth), `allele_frequency` (non-reference allele frequency) and
  `singleton_stats` (variants seen in exactly one allele copy). The key
  column differs per section, which is the price of melting: a numeric
  distribution puts its x value in `bin` and leaves `label` null, a
  categorical one puts its x value in `label` and leaves `bin` null, and
  `depth` fills both because bcftools writes its open-ended top bucket under
  a non-numeric bin name. `count` is always a count of variant records, but
  of a different kind per section (sites for indel length and depth, SNPs
  for allele frequency, substitutions or singletons for the two
  categorical ones), so summing it within a filtered section is meaningful
  and summing it across sections is not. Sample and caller are read off the
  report's own `ID` line, so any layout a pipeline publishes the reports
  under works. The quality block is left out: it is most of the rows of a
  real callset, and the VCFtools Ts/Tv-by-quality sweep answers its question.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bcftools_stats.txt"
recipe: bcftools/stats_sections.py
fixture: stats_sections.tsv
renders_as:
  # Each `section` counts a different kind of record on its own x scale, so the
  # sections never share an axis: one panel per section, independent axes.
  - component: figure
    title: Variant distributions per caller
    code: |
      # the x value of a section: its label when it has one (categorical sections and
      # the open-ended depth bucket), else its numeric bin
      d = df.with_columns(
          pl.coalesce([pl.col("label"), pl.col("bin").map_elements(lambda v: f"{v:g}", return_dtype=pl.Utf8)]).alias("key")
      ).drop_nulls(["key", "count"]).sort(["section", "bin", "label"], nulls_last=True)
      fig = px.bar(
          d.to_pandas(),
          x="key",
          y="count",
          color="caller",
          barmode="group",
          facet_col="section",
          facet_col_wrap=2,
          facet_row_spacing=0.14,
          facet_col_spacing=0.08,
          labels={"key": "Bin", "count": "Variant records", "caller": "Caller", "section": "Section"},
      )
      fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=", 1)[-1].replace("_", " ")))
      fig.update_xaxes(matches=None, showticklabels=True, title_text="", type="category")
      fig.update_yaxes(matches=None, showticklabels=True, title_text="")
      fig.update_layout(margin={"t": 32, "l": 48, "r": 16, "b": 32})
    description: >-
      Each panel is one bcftools distribution (indel length, substitution, read depth,
      allele frequency, singletons), and each bar the number of variant records in one of
      its bins, grouped by caller. It answers how the call sets of different callers are
      distributed.

      How to read: every panel has its own axes, because the sections count different
      kinds of records on different scales; compare callers within a panel. Callers that
      peak in the same bins agree, and a caller with an extra mode, for instance very low
      allele frequencies, adds calls the others do not make.

      Lines and annotations: no reference line is drawn, because a median of bin counts
      says nothing about a distribution.

      Source: https://samtools.github.io/bcftools/bcftools.html
  # Which distribution a filtered view is looking at, and how the total
  # splits across the sections still in scope.
  - component: card
    column: count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: section
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: sections with the most records
    title: Records in the distributions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the variant records counted in the distributions in view,
      and the bars rank the sections by the records they hold, with the median and
      maximum bin beside it. It answers how large the selected distributions are.

      How to read: each section counts a different kind of record, such as sites,
      SNPs or substitutions, so a sum across sections is not a variant count. Filter
      to one section for a figure that means something.
  - component: table
    title: Distribution bins
    description: >-
      Each row is a bin of one distribution for one sample and caller, with its
      section, its numeric or categorical label and the records it holds. It answers
      the exact value behind the bar chart.

      How to read: filter by section, then sort by count to find the most populated
      bins.

outputs.description: Per-sample, per-caller variant record counts (SNPs, indels, multiallelic sites) from `bcftools stats`. Pipeline-agnostic: any workflow that runs `bcftools stats` per caller per sample, with the caller and sample in the path rather than in the file, lands in the same collection.
outputs.name: Per-caller variant counts
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bcftools_stats_summary
name: Per-caller variant counts
mode: stats-summary
description: >-
  Per-sample, per-caller variant record counts (SNPs, indels, multiallelic
  sites) from `bcftools stats`. Pipeline-agnostic: any workflow that runs
  `bcftools stats` per caller per sample, with the caller and sample in the
  path rather than in the file, lands in the same collection.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bcftools_stats.txt"
recipe: bcftools/stats_summary.py
fixture: stats_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: SNPs per caller
    dict_kwargs:
      x: caller
      y: n_snps
      color: sample
      barmode: group
      labels: {caller: Caller, n_snps: SNP records, sample: Sample}
    description: >-
      Each bar is the number of SNP records one caller reports for one sample,
      coloured by sample. It answers how productive each caller is and whether the
      ranking holds across samples.

      How to read: callers on the same sample should land in the same order of
      magnitude. A caller far above the others may be calling noise, and one far
      below may be missing variants, so confirm with the Ts/Tv tile.

      Source: https://samtools.github.io/bcftools/bcftools.html
  - component: card
    column: n_snps
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: caller
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: callers with the most SNPs
    title: SNP records
    description: >-
      The hero number is the SNP records over every caller and sample, and the bars
      rank the callers by the SNPs they report. It answers which caller finds the
      most SNPs.

      How to read: more calls is not better calls. Compare with the Ts/Tv tile and
      with the indel count before preferring a caller.
  - component: card
    column: n_indels
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: caller
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: callers with the most indels
    title: Indel records
    description: >-
      The hero number is the indel records over every caller and sample, and the
      bars rank the callers by the indels they report. It answers which caller finds
      the most indels.

      How to read: callers differ more on indels than on SNPs, so a large spread here
      is common. Check the indel length distribution before trusting the largest
      count.
  - component: card
    column: n_multiallelic_sites
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: caller
    caption: multiallelic sites, by caller
    title: Multiallelic sites
    description: >-
      The hero number is the sites carrying more than one alternate allele, and the
      ring splits them by caller. It answers which callers report multiallelic
      sites.

      How to read: a caller with a large share splits sites into several alleles
      where others do not. A caller with none may not support multiallelic calls.
  - id: caller_yield_dotplot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    title: Variant yield per caller and sample
    roles: {cluster: sample, gene: caller, mean_expression: log10_n_records, frac_expressing: snp_fraction}
    description: >-
      Each dot is one caller on one sample, sized by the share of its records that
      are SNPs and coloured by the log10 of its record count. It answers how much a
      caller finds and how its calls split between SNPs and other variants.

      How to read: a big dot is a SNP dominated call set and a small one holds many

      more records than its peers on the same sample.
  - component: table
    title: Variant counts per caller
    description: >-
      Each row is one caller on one sample, with its record, SNP, MNP, indel,
      multiallelic and other counts, the SNP fraction and the log10 of the records.

outputs.description: Per-sample, per-caller transition/transversion ratio from `bcftools stats`. The ratio varies with genome region and gene function, so it is read against the other callers on the same sample; a caller with too few SNPs to score (e.g. a structural-variant caller) reads 0.0 rather than being absent.
outputs.name: Per-caller Ts/Tv ratio
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bcftools_stats_tstv
name: Per-caller Ts/Tv ratio
mode: stats-tstv
description: >-
  Per-sample, per-caller transition/transversion ratio from `bcftools stats`.
  The ratio varies with genome region and gene function, so it is read against
  the other callers on the same sample; a caller with too few SNPs to score
  (e.g. a structural-variant caller) reads 0.0 rather than being absent.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bcftools_stats.txt"
recipe: bcftools/stats_tstv.py
fixture: stats_tstv.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Ts/Tv ratio per caller
    dict_kwargs:
      x: caller
      y: ts_tv
      color: sample
      barmode: group
      labels: {caller: Caller, ts_tv: Transition/transversion ratio, sample: Sample}
    description: >-
      Each bar is the ratio of transitions to transversions among the SNPs of one
      caller on one sample, coloured by sample. It answers whether callers agree on
      the substitution balance of the SNPs they report.

      How to read: the cited study uses the ratio as a quality indicator for SNP
      calls, so callers run on the same sample are expected to land close together.
      A caller far from its peers is adding or losing SNPs of one kind, a sign of
      noise or bias. A bar of 0 is a caller with too few SNPs to score.

      Note: the ratio varies with genome region, gene function and GC content, so
      no single cut-off applies and no reference line is drawn.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25297068/
  - component: card
    column: ts_tv
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('ts_tv') > 0"
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Typical Ts/Tv ratio
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median transition/transversion ratio over the callers
      and samples that have a ratio, and the box shows the spread. It answers how
      the SNP call sets balance transitions and transversions.

      How to read: a wide box means callers disagree. Callers scored 0 for lack of
      SNPs are left out so they do not pull the median down.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25297068/
  - component: table
    title: Ts/Tv per caller
    description: >-
      Each row is one caller on one sample, with its transition and transversion
      counts and the ratio, over all alternates and over the first alternate only.
      It answers the exact numbers behind the other tiles.

      How to read: sort by ratio to find the callers that depart from the others.

outputs.description: How the reads of each lane were shared between the libraries of the sample sheet and the Undetermined reads no index matched, with the yield, base quality and index-match purity of each library, from bcl2fastq Stats.json.
outputs.name: Reads per library and lane
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bcl2fastq_demux_stats
name: Reads per library and lane
description: >-
  How the reads of each lane were shared between the libraries of the sample
  sheet and the Undetermined reads no index matched, with the yield, base
  quality and index-match purity of each library, from bcl2fastq Stats.json.
find:
  path_glob: "**/Stats/Stats.json"
recipe: bcl2fastq/demux_stats.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several lanes.
fixture: demux_stats.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: lane_composition
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: Share of each lane per library
    roles: {sample_id: lane_label, taxon: sample, rank: level, abundance: pct_of_lane}
    config:
      top_n: 8
      x_title: Lane
      value_title: Share of the lane (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each bar is a lane, split into the libraries of the sample sheet and the Undetermined
      reads, sized by their share of the lane. It answers how evenly the libraries share a
      lane and how much went unassigned.

      How to read: libraries pooled in equal amounts should take similar slices. A very large
      or very small slice points to a pooling imbalance, and a large Undetermined slice points to
      a sample sheet or index problem, so open the unknown barcodes tile next.

      Note: the eight largest libraries are drawn and the rest are grouped as Other.
  - id: lane_sunburst
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Lanes and libraries by reads
    roles: {abundance: reads, ranks: [lane_label, sample]}
    description: >-
      Each ring segment is a lane in the inner ring and a library in the outer ring, sized by
      its reads. It answers how the reads of the run split between lanes and, within a lane,
      between libraries.

      How to read: a lane with a much smaller arc than the others yielded fewer reads, and a
      library with a thin arc received little of its lane. The Undetermined reads appear as a
      segment of their own, so a large one points to a demultiplexing problem.
  - id: library_index_purity
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Index purity against reads per library
    roles: {x: reads, y: pct_perfect_index, label: sample, color: lane_label}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
      x_title: Reads
      y_title: Reads with a perfect index match (%)
      top_n_labels: 5
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: its reads on the horizontal axis and the percentage of its reads
      whose index matched perfectly on the vertical axis, coloured by lane. It answers whether
      libraries with few reads are also the ones with doubtful index matches.

      How to read: libraries high on the axis are well assigned. A library low on the axis relies
      on reads with a mismatched index, which are more likely to come from a neighbouring
      sample, so check the unknown barcodes and the sample sheet for it. A library with very few
      reads is more exposed, since a few misassigned reads weigh more.

      Note: no cut-off is drawn, because the expected share depends on the library preparation and
      the instrument.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of reads with a perfect
      index match of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows
      the filters), not a cut-off of bcl2fastq.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample

id: bcl2fastq_unknown_barcodes
name: Top unknown barcodes
description: >-
  The index sequences bcl2fastq saw most often among the reads it could not
  assign, per lane, classed by whether their i7 and i5 belong to libraries of
  the lane: a pair of indexes both in use points at an index hop or a sample
  sheet swap.
find:
  path_glob: "**/Stats/Stats.json"
recipe: bcl2fastq/unknown_barcodes.py
fixture: unknown_barcodes.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: barcode
      y: pct_of_lane
      color: swap_class
      facet_col: lane_label
      facet_col_wrap: 2
      labels: {barcode: Index pair, pct_of_lane: Share of the lane (%), swap_class: Index status, lane_label: Lane}
    title: Most frequent unknown barcodes
    description: >-
      Each bar is an index pair that bcl2fastq could not assign to a library, sized by its share
      of the lane and coloured by whether its indexes belong to libraries of the lane, one panel
      per lane. It answers what the unassigned reads are.

      How to read: a pair whose two indexes are both in use points to index hopping or a swap in
      the sample sheet, and a pair with only one index in use suggests a sequencing error or a
      mislabelled index. A pair with neither index in use suggests a library missing from the
      sheet. Index swapping is a known effect of patterned flow cells.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29739332/
  - component: card
    column: reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: swap_class
    title: Unknown reads by index status
    caption: split by status, with the median and largest per barcode
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of reads in the listed unknown barcodes, and the ring splits
      them by whether their indexes are in use. It answers which cause is behind the
      unassigned reads.

      How to read: a ring dominated by pairs with both indexes in use points to hopping or a
      sheet swap, and one dominated by pairs with no index in use points to a missing
      library. Only the most frequent barcodes of each lane are listed, so the total is a
      part of the Undetermined reads.
  - component: table
    title: Unknown barcode table
    description: >-
      Each row is an unknown index pair of a lane, with its reads, its rank, its share of the
      lane and of the Undetermined reads, and whether each index belongs to a library of the
      lane. It answers which barcodes explain the unassigned reads.

      How to read: sort by rank and filter on the index status to find a swap candidate, then
      check the sample sheet for the pair.

renders_as.description:
Each bar is an index pair that bcl2fastq could not assign to a library, sized by its share of the lane and coloured by whether its indexes belong to libraries of the lane, one panel per lane. It answers what the unassigned reads are.
How to read: a pair whose two indexes are both in use points to index hopping or a swap in the sample sheet, and a pair with only one index in use suggests a sequencing error or a mislabelled index. A pair with neither index in use suggests a library missing from the sheet. Index swapping is a known effect of patterned flow cells.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29739332/
renders_as.title: Most frequent unknown barcodes

renders_as.caption: split by status, with the median and largest per barcode
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total of reads in the listed unknown barcodes, and the ring splits them by whether their indexes are in use. It answers which cause is behind the unassigned reads.
How to read: a ring dominated by pairs with both indexes in use points to hopping or a sheet swap, and one dominated by pairs with no index in use points to a missing library. Only the most frequent barcodes of each lane are listed, so the total is a part of the Undetermined reads.
renders_as.title: Unknown reads by index status

renders_as.description:
Each row is an unknown index pair of a lane, with its reads, its rank, its share of the lane and of the Undetermined reads, and whether each index belongs to a library of the lane. It answers which barcodes explain the unassigned reads.
How to read: sort by rank and filter on the index status to find a swap candidate, then check the sample sheet for the pair.
renders_as.title: Unknown barcode table

tools.description: Illumina's successor to bcl2fastq: converts BCL base calls to demultiplexed FASTQ files.
tools.name: BCL Convert

outputs.description: How the reads of each lane were shared between the libraries of the sample sheet and the Undetermined reads no index matched, with the yield, base quality and index-match purity of each library, from BCL Convert Reports CSVs.
outputs.name: Reads per library and lane
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bclconvert_demux_stats
name: Reads per library and lane
description: >-
  How the reads of each lane were shared between the libraries of the sample
  sheet and the Undetermined reads no index matched, with the yield, base
  quality and index-match purity of each library, from BCL Convert Reports CSVs.
find:
  path_glob: "**/Reports/Demultiplex_Stats.csv"
recipe: bclconvert/demux_stats.py
fixture: demux_stats.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: lane_composition
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: Lane share per library
    roles: {sample_id: lane_label, taxon: sample, rank: level, abundance: pct_of_lane}
    config:
      value_title: Share of the lane (%)
      x_title: Lane
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each bar is a lane and each segment a library of the sample sheet, or the
      Undetermined reads, sized by its share of the lane's reads. It answers how
      evenly the lane was split between libraries and how much no index claimed.

      How to read: segments of similar size mean a balanced pool. A large
      Undetermined segment means indexes were misread, missing from the sample
      sheet or swapped, so open the unknown barcodes tile next. A library far
      smaller than its neighbours was under-pooled.

      Note: BCL Convert publishes no pass or fail cut-off for these shares, so none
      is drawn.
  - id: lane_sunburst
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Lane and library hierarchy
    roles: {abundance: reads, ranks: [lane_label, sample]}
    description: >-
      Each arc is a share of the reads of the run: the inner ring is the lane and the
      outer ring its libraries, sized by reads and coloured by lane. It answers how
      the run's reads divide between lanes and, within a lane, between libraries.

      How to read: lanes of similar width mean even loading. A library arc that is
      wide in one lane and thin in another points to uneven pooling or a lane
      problem. Use the lane composition tile to compare shares lane by lane.
  - id: library_index_purity
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Reads against index purity
    roles: {x: reads, y: pct_perfect_index, label: sample, color: lane_label}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
      log_x: true
      x_title: Reads
      y_title: Reads with a perfect index match (%)
      top_n_labels: 3
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a library in one lane: its number of reads on the horizontal axis
      and the share of those reads whose index matched exactly on the vertical axis,
      coloured by lane. It answers whether low-yield libraries are also the ones with
      poorly read indexes.

      How to read: points should sit near the top of the plot whatever their size. A
      library low on the axis, or a whole lane shifted down, has many reads that
      only matched with a mismatch, which can signal index quality problems or
      index sets that are too close. Compare the lanes of the same library.

      Note: BCL Convert publishes no pass or fail cut-off for index purity, so no
      line is drawn.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of reads with a perfect
      index match of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows
      the filters), not a cut-off of BCL Convert.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Share of the lane per library
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: pct_of_lane
      color: lane_label
      barmode: group
      labels: {sample: Library, pct_of_lane: Share of the lane (%), lane_label: Lane}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library in one lane: the percentage of that lane's reads it
      received, coloured by lane. It answers which libraries are over- or
      under-represented.

      How to read: in an evenly pooled run the bars are close in height. Very short
      bars are under-pooled libraries and very tall ones dominate the lane. Check the
      same library across lanes to tell a pooling issue from a lane issue.
  - component: card
    column: reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: lane_label
    top_n_count: 5
    filter_expr: "col('sample') != 'Undetermined'"
    caption: reads, by lane
    title: Reads assigned to libraries
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total reads assigned to a library, leaving out the
      Undetermined reads, and the bars rank the lanes by their share of it. It
      answers how much of the run produced usable data.

      How to read: lanes of similar size mean even loading, and the median and
      maximum per library row show how skewed the pooling is.
  - component: card
    column: pct_of_lane
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('sample') != 'Undetermined'"
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Library share of its lane
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of a lane's reads taken by a library,
      and the box shows the quartiles and outliers. It answers how even the pooling
      is.

      How to read: a tight box means libraries were pooled evenly. A long tail of
      high or low values marks libraries to re-pool or re-sequence.
  - component: card
    column: pct_q30
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('sample') != 'Undetermined'"
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Bases at Q30 or above per library
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of a library's bases with a quality
      score of 30 or higher, and the box shows the spread between libraries. It
      answers whether base quality is consistent across the pool.

      How to read: a tight box near the top means uniform quality. A library far
      below the others deserves a look at its lane and read in the base quality tile.

      Note: BCL Convert publishes no Q30 cut-off, since the expected value depends on
      the instrument and read length, so none is drawn.
  - component: table
    title: Demultiplexing statistics
    description: >-
      One row is one library in one lane, plus the Undetermined reads, with its
      reads, lane share, yield, base quality and index purity. It answers which
      libraries sit behind an outlier on the tiles above.

      How to read: Sort by reads or by the lane share to find the over- and
      under-represented libraries, and by the Q30 share or the perfect-index
      share to find weak ones. Look for libraries far from their lane peers and
      for a large Undetermined row. It complements the lane summary and the
      unknown barcodes tiles of the same output.

outputs.description: One row per lane: clusters detected and passing filter, yield, base quality, the Undetermined share and how evenly the libraries split the lane, from BCL Convert Reports CSVs.
outputs.name: Lane run health
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bclconvert_lane_summary
name: Lane run health
description: >-
  One row per lane: clusters detected and passing filter, yield, base quality,
  the Undetermined share and how evenly the libraries split the lane, from
  BCL Convert Reports CSVs.
find:
  path_glob: "**/Reports/Demultiplex_Stats.csv"
recipe: bclconvert/lane_summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 4 real lanes (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several flowcells.
fixture: lane_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: lane_health
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Lane quality against Undetermined share
    roles: {x: pct_undetermined, y: pct_q30, label: lane_label, size: yield_gb, color: flowcell}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
      x_title: Undetermined reads (% of the lane)
      y_title: Bases at Q30 or above (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a lane: the share of its reads that no index claimed on the
      horizontal axis, the share of its bases at Q30 or above on the vertical axis,
      sized by yield and coloured by flowcell. It answers which lanes underperform
      and whether the cause is quality or demultiplexing.

      How to read: healthy lanes sit at the left (little Undetermined) and high on
      the plot (high quality). A lane pushed to the right lost reads to indexes
      that matched no library, and a lane pushed down has weak base quality. Compare
      each lane with the others of the same flowcell.

      Note: BCL Convert publishes no pass or fail cut-off for either measure, since
      expected values depend on the instrument and the kit, so no line is drawn.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of bases at Q30 or above
      of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of BCL Convert.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Yield per lane
    dict_kwargs:
      x: lane_label
      y: yield_gb
      color: flowcell
      barmode: group
      labels: {lane_label: Lane, yield_gb: Yield (Gb), flowcell: Flowcell}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: yield_gb}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a lane: its total yield in gigabases, coloured by flowcell. It
      answers whether the lanes produced a similar amount of data.

      How to read: lanes of a flowcell should be close in height. A short bar is a
      lane that lost clusters or was loaded lightly, so look at its pass-filter
      clusters and Undetermined share.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median yield per lane of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      BCL Convert.
  - component: card
    column: yield_gb
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: lane_label
    top_n_count: 5
    caption: yield, by lane
    title: Total yield
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total yield of the run in gigabases and the bars rank
      the lanes by their yield. It answers how much data the run produced and which
      lanes carry it.

      How to read: lanes of similar size mean even loading. The median and maximum
      per lane show how far apart the lanes are.
  - component: card
    column: clusters_pf
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: lane_label
    top_n_count: 5
    caption: passing-filter clusters, by lane
    title: Clusters passing filter
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of clusters that passed the instrument's
      chastity filter, and the bars rank the lanes. It answers how many reads the
      run could produce.

      How to read: lanes with far fewer clusters than the median were under-clustered
      or lost clusters to the filter.
  - component: card
    column: pct_q30
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: lowest lane, with the spread
    title: Lowest Q30 across lanes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest share of bases at Q30 or above of any lane, and
      the box shows the spread across lanes. It answers whether every lane reached
      good quality.

      How to read: a box that is tight and near the top means uniform quality. The
      hero value points at the weakest lane, which is where to look first.

      Note: BCL Convert publishes no Q30 cut-off, since the expected value depends
      on the instrument and read length, so none is drawn.
  - component: card
    column: pct_undetermined
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: highest lane, with the spread
    title: Highest Undetermined share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest share of reads no index claimed in any lane, and
      the box shows the spread across lanes. It answers whether a lane lost an
      unusual part of its reads to demultiplexing.

      How to read: a high hero value with a tight box means every lane shares the
      problem, usually a sample sheet or index issue. A single high lane points at
      that lane. Open the unknown barcodes tile to see which indexes are involved.
  - component: table
    title: Lane summary
    description: >-
      One row is one lane, with its clusters, yield, base quality, Undetermined
      share and the evenness of its libraries. It answers which lane is weak or
      unbalanced.

      How to read: Sort by the Undetermined share or the Q30 share to find the
      lanes that stand apart, and by the spread of library reads to find uneven
      pooling. Look for a lane that differs from the others on any of these. It
      complements the per-library demultiplexing table, which shows the
      libraries inside a lane.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: bclconvert_unknown_barcodes
name: Top unknown barcodes
description: >-
  The index sequences BCL Convert saw most often among the reads it could not
  assign, per lane, classed by whether their i7 and i5 belong to libraries of
  the lane: a pair of indexes both in use points at an index hop or a sample
  sheet swap.
find:
  path_glob: "**/Reports/Top_Unknown_Barcodes.csv"
recipe: bclconvert/unknown_barcodes.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows, with index status reassigned on some (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several index statuses.
fixture: unknown_barcodes.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Most frequent unknown barcodes
    dict_kwargs:
      x: barcode
      y: pct_of_lane
      color: swap_class
      facet_col: lane_label
      facet_col_wrap: 2
      labels: {barcode: Index pair, pct_of_lane: Share of the lane (%), swap_class: Index status, lane_label: Lane}
    description: >-
      Each bar is an index pair BCL Convert saw among reads it could not assign: its
      share of the lane's reads, coloured by whether the i7 and i5 indexes belong to
      libraries of the lane, one panel per lane. It answers why reads were left undetermined.

      How to read: a tall bar whose two indexes are both in use is an index hop or a
      sample sheet swap between those libraries. One index in use points to a
      mistyped index, and neither in use means a library missing from the sample
      sheet or a contaminant.
  - component: card
    column: reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [count, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: swap_class
    caption: reads, by index status
    title: Reads of the top unknown barcodes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total reads of the listed unknown barcodes and the ring
      splits them by whether their indexes belong to libraries of the lane. It
      answers what kind of problem the unassigned reads come from.

      How to read: a large share where both indexes are in use points to index
      hopping or a sample sheet swap. A large share where neither is in use points to
      missing libraries or contamination.
  - component: table
    title: Top unknown barcodes
    description: >-

      in-use status. It answers which indexes are in the Undetermined reads and
      why.

      an index pair with a swapped or in-use half, which points to a sample
      sheet error, and for a high-count pair that is in no sheet, which points
      to a missing library. It complements the lane summary, which gives the
      Undetermined share of each lane.

tools.description: A set of tools for genomic analysis tasks, specifically enabling genome arithmetic (merge, count, complement) on various file types. Here, genomecov computes the per-base coverage of a set of alignments, one strand at a time.
tools.name: bedtools genomecov

outputs.description: Read bases of the plus and minus strand coverage bedGraphs in 250 kb windows, one row per library per window, in parts per million of the library's signal, streamed out of files of several million intervals without holding one. Every library gets every window of the chromosomes, a window without reads at 0, so libraries and time points compare on one complete matrix.
outputs.name: Strand coverage in genomic windows
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bedtools_strand_bins
name: Strand coverage in genomic windows
mode: coverage/strand-bins
description: >-
  Read bases of the plus and minus strand coverage bedGraphs in 250 kb windows,
  one row per library per window, in parts per million of the library's signal,
  streamed out of files of several million intervals without holding one. Every
  library gets every window of the chromosomes, a window without reads at 0, so
  libraries and time points compare on one complete matrix.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.plus.bedGraph"
recipe: bedtools/strand_bins.py
fixture: strand_bins.tsv
renders_as:
  # The libraries stacked on one genome axis, one lane each, coloured by library
  # (the sample colour the rest of the dashboard uses). No cut-off is drawn:
  # bedtools publishes none for a coverage value.
  - id: strand_signal_genome_view
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Strand signal along the genome
    roles: {chr: chromosome, pos: start, end: end, score: log2_signal, sample: sample}
    config:
      facet_by_sample: true
      score_title: Signal (log2 of parts per million + 1)
      score_threshold_stat: p95
    description: >-
      Each bar is a 250 kb window of the genome, drawn from its start to its end,
      with the height of the combined plus and minus strand signal of one library
      and one lane per library. It answers where along the genome a library holds
      its reads.

      How to read: lanes that follow one another peak at the same windows when
      libraries capture the same transcription. A window that towers over its
      neighbours in one lane only is a hotspot of that library, for instance a
      repeat array, so compare the lanes before reading it as biology.

      Note: the signal is scaled to parts per million of each library, so lanes
      compare in shape and not in depth. bedtools genomecov defines no cut-off for
      coverage.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the 95th percentile of the window signal
      of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of bedtools. Windows above it are the hottest of the rows on show.

      Source: https://bedtools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/tools/genomecov.html
  - id: strand_signal_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Strand signal per chromosome
    roles: {chromosome: chromosome, position: position, end: end, value: signal_rpm, sample: sample}
    config:
      color_by: sample
    description: >-
      Each point on a line is a 250 kb window, placed at its centre, with the
      combined plus and minus strand signal of one library in parts per million.
      It answers how the signal varies along one chromosome and between libraries.

      How to read: parallel lines mean libraries read the chromosome the same way.
      A line that departs from the others over a region marks a library with a
      local gain or loss of signal, worth a look in the genome view or the browser.

      Note: bedtools genomecov defines no cut-off for coverage, so no line or band
      is drawn.

      Source: https://bedtools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/tools/genomecov.html
  - component: card
    column: log2_signal
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Typical window signal
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median signal of a 250 kb window, as log2 of parts per
      million plus one, and the box shows the spread over windows. It answers how
      much signal a typical window of the genome holds.

      How to read: a wide box with a long upper whisker means a few windows hold
      much more than the rest, which is the pattern of a hotspot or a poorly
      depleted library. The log scale is used because window signal spans orders
      of magnitude.
  - component: card
    column: plus_share_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 100
    caption: median plus-strand share, of 100
    title: Plus-strand share of a window
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent of a window's signal that falls on the
      plus strand, shown against 100 percent. It answers whether the two strands
      are read evenly along the genome.

      How to read: a value far from 50 means one strand dominates, which can be a
      protocol or strandedness problem, or simply the genes of a region that all
      lie on one strand. Check the per-library tile on the summary before drawing a
      conclusion.

      Note: bedtools genomecov reports one strand at a time with the -strand
      option, and publishes no balance cut-off, so none is drawn.

      Source: https://bedtools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/tools/genomecov.html
  - component: card
    column: signal_rpm
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, q3]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: median and upper quartile of a window
    title: Strongest window
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest signal of any 250 kb window, in parts per
      million of its library, and the strip gives the median and the upper
      quartile of a window. It answers how far the hottest window sits above a
      typical one.

      How to read: a maximum many times above the upper quartile marks a hotspot,
      such as a ribosomal array. Use the table to find which window and library
      hold it.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: chromosome
    title: Chromosome
    description: >-
      Filters every tile of the dashboard that reads these windows to the chromosomes
      picked here. It answers how a library behaves on one chromosome at a time.
  - component: table
    title: Strand signal per window
    description: >-
      Each row is a 250 kb window of one library, with the plus and minus strand
      signal in parts per million, their sum, its log2 and the plus-strand share.
      It answers the exact value behind every other tile.

      How to read: sort by signal to find the strongest windows, or filter by
      chromosome and library to compare the same region across libraries.
