outputs.description: Per-library totals of the plus and minus strand coverage bedGraphs: read bases per strand and their balance, the share on the mitochondrial contig and outside the chromosomes, and the share of the chromosome signal the top 1% of 250 kb windows hold, the reading of a poorly depleted library.
outputs.name: Strand coverage per library
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bedtools_strand_summary
name: Strand coverage per library
mode: coverage/strand-summary
description: >-
  Per-library totals of the plus and minus strand coverage bedGraphs: read
  bases per strand and their balance, the share on the mitochondrial contig and
  outside the chromosomes, and the share of the chromosome signal the top 1% of
  250 kb windows hold, the reading of a poorly depleted library.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.plus.bedGraph"
recipe: bedtools/strand_summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 2 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several libraries.
fixture: strand_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: card
    column: plus_share_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 100
    caption: median plus-strand share, of 100
    title: Plus-strand share per library
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent of a library's signal on the plus
      strand, shown against 100 percent, with the lowest and highest library
      beside it. It answers whether libraries read both strands evenly.

      How to read: a library far from the others, or far from 50, has one strand
      dominating, which can be a protocol or strandedness problem. Open the bar
      tile below to see which library it is.

      Note: bedtools genomecov reports one strand at a time with the -strand
      option and publishes no balance cut-off, so none is drawn.

      Source: https://bedtools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/tools/genomecov.html
  - component: card
    column: hotspot_share_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Signal held by hotspot windows
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of the chromosome signal held by the top
      1 percent of 250 kb windows of a library, and the box shows the spread across
      libraries. It answers how concentrated the signal is.

      How to read: a high share means a few windows, such as ribosomal arrays or
      very active loci, take most of the reads and the rest of the genome is read
      from what is left. A library well above the others is the one to check first.

      Note: the top 1 percent is a fixed definition of this recipe, not a cut-off
      published by bedtools.
  - component: card
    column: total_read_bases
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: sample
    caption: read bases, by library
    title: Read bases per library
    description: >-
      The hero number is the read bases summed over every library and both strands,
      and the bar splits them by library, with the median and maximum library beside
      it. It answers how evenly depth is shared between libraries.

      How to read: a library with a thin share has far less depth than the others,
      so its signal is noisier. Compare libraries in parts per million, as the
      genome tiles do, and not in raw bases.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Plus-strand share per library
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: plus_share_pct
      color: sample
      labels: {sample: Library, plus_share_pct: Plus-strand share (%)}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: plus_share_pct}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library, with the percent of its signal on the plus strand. It
      answers which library reads one strand more than the others.

      How to read: bars near one another mean a consistent protocol. A bar far from
      the rest has lost or gained a strand and deserves a check of the library
      preparation.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median plus-strand share of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a
      cut-off of bedtools. bedtools genomecov reports one strand at a time and publishes
      no balance cut-off.

      Source: https://bedtools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/tools/genomecov.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: scatter
    title: Hotspot share against signal outside the chromosomes
    dict_kwargs:
      x: hotspot_share_pct
      y: off_main_pct
      color: sample
      hover_name: sample
      labels: {hotspot_share_pct: Signal in top 1% windows (%), off_main_pct: Signal outside chromosomes (%), sample: Library}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: off_main_pct, label: Median signal outside chromosomes}
    description: >-
      Each point is a library, with the share of its chromosome signal held by the
      hottest windows on the horizontal axis and the share of reads outside the
      main chromosomes on the vertical axis. It answers which libraries are
      dominated by a few loci or by unplaced contigs.

      How to read: points toward the upper right combine a concentrated signal with
      many reads off the chromosomes, a pattern of a poorly depleted library. Points
      near the origin spread their reads over the chromosomes.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median share of signal outside
      the chromosomes of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it
      follows the filters), not a cut-off of bedtools. Both shares are defined by the
      recipe, and bedtools genomecov publishes no cut-off for either.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Strand coverage per library
    description: >-
      Each row is a library, with its read bases per strand, the covered megabases,
      the deepest base and the plus-strand, mitochondrial, off-chromosome and
      hotspot shares. It answers the exact numbers behind every other tile and lets
      a row selection filter the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by hotspot share or by mitochondrial share to find the
      libraries that need a closer look.

fixture: alignment_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # Bismark publishes no mapping-efficiency cut-off (its low-mapping FAQ gives
  # no number), so no pass mark is drawn on this tab.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: mapping_efficiency_pct
      color: sample
      labels: {sample: Library, mapping_efficiency_pct: Mapping efficiency (%)}
    title: Mapping efficiency per library
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: mapping_efficiency_pct
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: the percentage of read pairs Bismark aligned to a
      unique best position. It answers which libraries mapped poorly.

      How to read: libraries of one experiment usually sit in a narrow band. A
      library far below the others points to the wrong reference genome, untrimmed
      adapters or a poor library, so check the trimming report and the Bismark FAQ
      on low mapping before using it.

      Note: Bismark publishes no mapping-efficiency cut-off.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median mapping efficiency of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of Bismark.

      Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/low-mapping/
  - component: card
    column: mapping_efficiency_pct
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: Mapping efficiency, with its spread
    title: Average mapping efficiency
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean percentage of read pairs aligned uniquely, and
      the box shows the spread across libraries. It answers how well the run
      mapped overall.

      How to read: a tight box means libraries behaved alike. A long lower
      whisker is a library to open in the bar chart.
  # The former 60 / 70 % pass marks had no source: Bismark documents no
  # cut-off, so the card shows the weakest library with the median and best.
  - component: card
    column: mapping_efficiency_pct
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: Weakest library, with the median and the best
    title: Weakest mapping efficiency
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest mapping efficiency of any library, shown with
      the median and the highest. It answers how far the worst library is from the
      rest.

      How to read: a minimum close to the median means no library stands out. A
      wide gap marks a library to inspect.

      Note: Bismark publishes no mapping-efficiency cut-off, so no pass mark is
      drawn.

      Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/low-mapping/
  - component: card
    column: pairs_analysed
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: Read pairs per library
    title: Read pairs analysed
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of read pairs Bismark analysed, and the
      histogram shows how they spread over libraries. It answers whether
      sequencing depth is even.

      How to read: a narrow histogram means even depth. A long tail is a library
      with far more or fewer pairs than its peers.
  - component: card
    column: no_alignment
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: Unaligned pairs per library
    title: Pairs with no alignment
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of read pairs that never aligned, and the
      histogram shows the spread over libraries. It answers how much input was lost
      before methylation calling.

      How to read: a library with a far larger count than its peers has a mapping
      problem. Compare it with the mapping efficiency bar chart.
  - component: table
    title: Alignment table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with the read pairs Bismark analysed, the unique best
      hits, the mapping efficiency and the pairs that did not align or were not
      unique. It answers the exact counts behind the bar chart.

      How to read: sort by mapping efficiency to find the weakest library, then
      compare its unaligned and non-unique counts.

outputs.description: Genome-wide CpG methylation averaged into 10 kb windows, one row per library per window, streamed out of the per-CpG bedGraph without ever holding it in memory. The only coordinate-bound collection a methylseq run can produce, and the matrix every cohort-level panel downstream reads.
outputs.name: Binned CpG methylation
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bismark_binned_methylation
name: Binned CpG methylation
mode: methylation/windows
description: >-
  Genome-wide CpG methylation averaged into 10 kb windows, one row per library
  per window, streamed out of the per-CpG bedGraph without ever holding it in
  memory. The only coordinate-bound collection a methylseq run can produce, and
  the matrix every cohort-level panel downstream reads.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bedGraph.gz"
recipe: bismark/binned_methylation.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several libraries.
fixture: binned_methylation.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: methylation_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    roles: {chromosome: chromosome, position: position, value: methylation_pct, end: end, sample: sample}
    config:
      color_by: sample
    title: Methylation along the genome
    description: >-
      Each trace is a library: the mean CpG methylation of every 10 kb window
      along a chromosome. It answers where methylation rises or drops, and whether
      libraries share the pattern.

      How to read: traces that move together show a shared methylome. A library
      that departs over a long stretch is a candidate for a copy-number change, a
      sex or cell-type difference, or a technical problem. Zoom to a chromosome to
      read the detail.

      Note: windows with too few CpGs in a library are dropped, so gaps are
      expected in CpG-poor regions.
  - id: methylation_genome_view
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    roles: {chr: chromosome, pos: position, score: methylation_pct, end: end, sample: sample}
    config:
      score_title: Methylation (%)
    title: Methylation genome view
    description: >-
      Each mark is a 10 kb window of a library, placed on the genome and coloured by
      library, with its mean CpG methylation as the height. It answers where along
      the genome methylation is high or low.

      How to read: compare libraries on the same region to spot a difference. Drag
      to select a region and open the windows in the table to read the exact values.

      Note: the window size is fixed at 10 kb, so smaller features, such as a single
      CpG island, are averaged out.
  - component: card
    column: methylation_pct
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: Window methylation, with its spread
    title: Average window methylation
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean CpG methylation over all 10 kb windows, and the
      box shows how windows differ. It answers the overall methylation level and
      its spread.

      How to read: a box that reaches from low to high values is normal, since
      methylation varies by region. A shift of the whole box between libraries is a
      global difference.
  - component: card
    column: methylation_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 100
    caption: Median window methylation, out of 100%
    title: Median window methylation
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median CpG methylation of a window, drawn against the
      full 0 to 100 percent scale, with the lowest and highest window. It answers
      where the typical window sits.

      How to read: a median near the top is typical of mammalian somatic cells. A
      low median is typical of a hypomethylated sample or a conversion problem.
  - component: card
    column: n_cpg
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: cpg_density_class
    caption: CpGs, by density class
    title: CpGs by density class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of CpGs behind all windows, and the bar splits it
      by CpG density class. It answers how many CpGs sit in sparse and dense
      regions.

      How to read: the classes are tertiles of the CpG count per window, an
      annotation-free stand-in for CpG islands. Dense windows hold most of the CpGs.
  - component: card
    column: n_cpg
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: CpGs per window, with their spread
    title: CpGs per window
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean number of CpGs in a window, and the box shows the
      spread. It answers how much evidence sits behind each window mean.

      How to read: a window with few CpGs has a noisier methylation value. A wide
      box means windows differ strongly in density.
  # CpG density is what a CGI is defined by, so its tertiles stand in for the
  # island annotation nf-core/methylseq bundles at no version. The tertiles hold
  # equal shares by design, so the former donut over them is replaced by a
  # count of windows with their methylation range.
  - component: card
    column: methylation_pct
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: Windows, with the methylation spread
    title: Windows in the matrix
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of library windows kept, and the histogram shows
      how their methylation spreads. It answers how many windows the genome view
      rests on and how bimodal they are.

      How to read: a histogram with peaks near the two ends is typical of
      methylation. A single peak in the middle suggests noise or poor conversion.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: cpg_density_class
      y: methylation_pct
      color: cpg_density_class
      labels: {cpg_density_class: CpG density class, methylation_pct: Window methylation (%)}
    title: Methylation by CpG density
    description: >-
      Each box is the distribution of window methylation within one CpG density
      class. It answers whether CpG-dense windows are less methylated than sparse
      ones.

      How to read: methylation is typically lower in CpG-dense, island-like regions
      and higher in CpG-poor regions. A box that departs from this pattern points to
      a conversion problem or an unusual sample.

      Note: the classes are tertiles of the CpG count per window, not an island
      annotation.
  - component: table
    title: Binned methylation table
    description: >-
      Each row is a 10 kb window of a library, with its mean CpG methylation, the
      number of CpGs and the density class. It answers the exact value of a window.

      How to read: filter on a chromosome and sort by methylation to list extreme
      windows.

outputs.description: Per-sample Bismark PCR-duplicate removal: alignments examined, duplicates removed and the leftover count carried into methylation extraction. A duplication rate far above the run's median is the usual sign of a library that was oversequenced relative to its complexity.
outputs.name: Deduplication summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bismark_deduplication_summary
name: Deduplication summary
mode: deduplication
description: >-
  Per-sample Bismark PCR-duplicate removal: alignments examined, duplicates
  removed and the leftover count carried into methylation extraction. A
  duplication rate far above the run's median is the usual sign of a library
  that was oversequenced relative to its complexity.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.deduplication_report.txt"
recipe: bismark/deduplication_summary.py
fixture: deduplication_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # Bismark documents no duplication cut-off, so the former 20 / 10 % pass marks
  # (no source) are gone: the cards show the spread and the worst library.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: pct_duplication
      color: sample
      labels: {sample: Library, pct_duplication: PCR duplication (%)}
    title: PCR duplication per library
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: pct_duplication
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: the percentage of aligned reads removed as PCR
      duplicates. It answers which libraries were over-amplified relative to their
      complexity.

      How to read: libraries prepared alike should have similar rates. A library
      well above the others carries less unique information than its read count
      suggests, so weigh its methylation calls with care.

      Note: Bismark publishes no duplication cut-off. Deduplication is not
      recommended for RRBS, amplicon or other target-enrichment libraries, where
      duplicates are expected.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median PCR duplication of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of Bismark.

      Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/usage/deduplication/
  - component: card
    column: pct_duplication
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: Duplication rate, with its spread
    title: Average PCR duplication
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean duplication percentage, and the box shows the
      spread across libraries. It answers how redundant the run is overall.

      How to read: a tight box means libraries share a similar complexity. A long
      upper whisker is a library to open in the bar chart.
  - component: card
    column: pct_duplication
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: Highest library, with the median and the lowest
    title: Highest PCR duplication
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest duplication percentage of any library, shown
      with the median and the lowest. It answers how far the worst library is from
      the rest.

      How to read: a maximum close to the median means no library stands out. A
      wide gap marks a library that was over-amplified.

      Note: Bismark publishes no duplication cut-off, so no pass mark is drawn.

      Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/usage/deduplication/
  - component: card
    column: leftover_sequences
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: Alignments kept per library
    title: Alignments kept after deduplication
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of alignments carried into methylation
      extraction, and the histogram shows how they spread over libraries. It
      answers how much usable depth remains.

      How to read: a library with far fewer kept alignments than its peers will
      contribute little to window-level methylation. Compare it with the
      duplication bar chart.
  - component: table
    title: Deduplication table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with the alignments examined, the duplicates removed,
      the duplication percentage and the alignments left. It answers the exact
      counts behind the bar chart.

      How to read: sort by duplication to find the most redundant library.

renders_as.description:
Each bar is a library: the percentage of aligned reads removed as PCR duplicates. It answers which libraries were over-amplified relative to their complexity.
How to read: libraries prepared alike should have similar rates. A library well above the others carries less unique information than its read count suggests, so weigh its methylation calls with care.
Note: Bismark publishes no duplication cut-off. Deduplication is not recommended for RRBS, amplicon or other target-enrichment libraries, where duplicates are expected.
Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median PCR duplication of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Bismark.
Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/usage/deduplication/

recipe: bismark/mbias_all_contexts.py
fixture: mbias_all_contexts.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: mbias_context_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    roles: {series: series, x: position, y: pct_methylation}
    config:
      x_title: Position in read (bp)
      y_title: Methylation (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    title: M-bias in every cytosine context
    description: >-
      Each line is one read of one library in one cytosine context (CpG, CHG or
      CHH): the percentage of methylated calls at each position along the read. It
      answers whether any part of a read is biased, and whether conversion fails at
      the read ends.

      How to read: CpG sits high and CHG and CHH sit near zero in most mammalian
      data. A line that bends at the read ends, such as the start of PBAT reads or the
      first bases of read 2 after end repair, shows a methylation bias at those
      positions, so ignore them during methylation extraction.

      Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/usage/methylation-extraction/
      and https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  # Pooled over contexts the percentage mixes CpG (high) with CHG and CHH
  # (near zero), so the box is read on CHH, the conversion read-out.
  - component: card
    column: pct_methylation
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "pl.col('context') == 'CHH'"
    caption: CHH methylation along reads, with its spread
    title: CHH methylation along reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean methylation in the CHH context over all read
      positions, and the box shows how much positions differ. It answers how
      completely unmethylated cytosines were converted.

      How to read: values near zero mean good conversion. A high mean or a wide box
      points to non-conversion, often at the read start, so check the curve.

      Note: this reading assumes non-CG methylation is near zero, as in mammals.
      Other organisms can show real non-CG methylation.

      Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  - component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: context
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: Calls, by context
    title: Methylation calls by context
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of methylation calls counted in the M-bias
      tables, and the bars split it by cytosine context. It answers how much data
      sits behind each context.

      How to read: CHH and CHG usually hold far more calls than CpG because those
      contexts are more frequent in the genome.
  - component: table
    title: M-bias table, all contexts
    description: >-
      Each row is a read position of one read of one library in one context, with
      its methylation percentage and the number of calls. It answers the exact value
      and the depth at each position.

      How to read: filter on a context and a read to follow one curve. A low call
      count at a position gives a noisy percentage.

outputs.description: Post-deduplication, post-extraction methylation level in each cytosine context (CpG, CHG, CHH), one row per sample per context. CpG is where mammalian methylation concentrates; CHG and CHH sitting near zero is the usual bisulfite-conversion sanity check, not signal.
outputs.name: Methylation by context
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bismark_methylation_context_summary
name: Methylation by context
mode: methylation/context
description: >-
  Post-deduplication, post-extraction methylation level in each cytosine
  context (CpG, CHG, CHH), one row per sample per context. CpG is where
  mammalian methylation concentrates; CHG and CHH sitting near zero is the
  usual bisulfite-conversion sanity check, not signal.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_splitting_report.txt"
recipe: bismark/methylation_context_summary.py
fixture: methylation_context_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: pct_methylated
      color: context
      barmode: group
      labels: {sample: Library, pct_methylated: Methylated cytosines (%), context: Context}
    title: Methylation by cytosine context
    description: >-
      Each bar is the percentage of methylated cytosines of one library in one
      context (CpG, CHG or CHH). It answers whether CpG methylation is high and
      non-CpG methylation low, as bisulfite conversion should leave it.

      How to read: CpG methylation is high in most mammalian cells while CHG and CHH
      sit close to zero. A raised CHG or CHH bar means non-conversion, or real
      non-CG methylation in organisms that have it.

      Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  # Pooled over contexts the percentage mixes CpG with CHG and CHH, so each card
  # reads one context.
  - component: card
    column: pct_methylated
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "pl.col('context') == 'CpG'"
    caption: CpG methylation, with its spread
    title: Average CpG methylation
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean percentage of methylated cytosines in the CpG
      context, and the box shows the spread across libraries. It answers how
      methylated the libraries are overall.

      How to read: a tight box means comparable libraries. A library far from the
      others differs in biology, cell composition or conversion, so compare it with
      the PCA before drawing a conclusion.
  - component: card
    column: pct_methylated
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: compact
    filter_expr: "pl.col('context') == 'CHH'"
    caption: Highest library, with the median and the lowest
    title: Highest CHH methylation
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest CHH methylation percentage of any library,
      shown with the median and the lowest. It answers how incomplete bisulfite
      conversion could be at worst.

      How to read: a value of 0.3 percent means conversion was at least 99.7
      percent efficient, so values near zero are good. A library well above its
      peers is the one to check first.

      Note: this reading assumes non-CG methylation is near zero, as in mammals.
      Bismark publishes no cut-off for it.

      Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  - component: card
    column: methylated_c
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: context
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: Methylated calls, by context
    title: Methylated calls by context
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of methylated cytosine calls, and the bars split
      it by context. It answers where the methylated calls come from.

      How to read: CpG should carry most of the methylated calls in a mammalian
      library. A large CHH or CHG share would raise a conversion question.
  - component: table
    title: Methylation by context table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library in one context, with the methylated and unmethylated
      cytosine counts and the methylation percentage. It answers the exact counts
      behind the bar chart.

      How to read: filter on a context to compare libraries.

outputs.description: Distribution of per-CpG methylation, one curve per library, binned to 2 % buckets out of the full bedGraph. A healthy mammalian methylome is sharply bimodal at 0 % and 100 %; a curve that has lost the bimodality, or whose 0 % peak has drifted up, is reporting incomplete conversion or a depth too low for a site call.
outputs.name: Per-CpG methylation density
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bismark_methylation_density
name: Per-CpG methylation density
mode: methylation/density
description: >-
  Distribution of per-CpG methylation, one curve per library, binned to 2 %
  buckets out of the full bedGraph. A healthy mammalian methylome is sharply
  bimodal at 0 % and 100 %; a curve that has lost the bimodality, or whose 0 %
  peak has drifted up, is reporting incomplete conversion or a depth too low
  for a site call.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bedGraph.gz"
recipe: bismark/methylation_density.py
fixture: methylation_density.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: density_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    roles: {series: series, x: methylation_bin, y: fraction_of_cpgs}
    config:
      x_title: CpG methylation (%)
      y_title: Share of CpGs (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    title: Distribution of per-CpG methylation
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the share of its CpGs that fall in each 2 percent
      methylation bin. It answers how methylation is distributed across individual
      CpGs.

      How to read: in most human cell types 70 to 80 percent of CpGs are methylated,
      so a main peak near 100 percent with a smaller one near 0 percent is expected. A library whose curve is flat, or whose peak near zero has
      drifted up, suggests incomplete conversion or too little depth for site calls.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23925113/
  - component: card
    column: fraction_of_cpgs
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, q3]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: Fullest bin, with the median and upper quartile bin
    title: Tallest methylation peak
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest share of CpGs found in a single bin of any
      library, shown with the median and upper quartile bin share. It answers how
      sharp the methylation peaks are.

      How to read: a tall peak means most CpGs of a library share one methylation
      level. Low peaks mean the methylation is spread out.
  - component: card
    column: n_cpgs
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: CpGs counted, with the median and fullest bin
    title: CpGs counted
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of CpGs counted in the density bins, shown with
      the median and the largest bin. It answers how much data the densities rest
      on.

      How to read: a total far lower for one library means its density is noisier
      than the others.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: methylation_bin
      y: fraction_of_cpgs
      color: sample
      labels: {methylation_bin: CpG methylation (%), fraction_of_cpgs: Share of CpGs (%), sample: Library}
    title: Per-CpG methylation density
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the share of its CpGs in each 2 percent methylation
      bin. It answers how methylation is distributed across CpGs.

      How to read: compare the height of the peaks near 0 and near 100 percent
      between libraries. A library that departs from the others has a different
      methylome or a conversion problem.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23925113/
  - component: table
    title: Methylation density table
    description: >-
      Each row is a methylation bin of one library, with the CpG count and the share
      of its CpGs. It answers the exact counts behind the density curves.

      How to read: filter on a library and sort by bin to follow its curve.

outputs.description: Bismark's own run-level table (bismark2summary), one row per library, the only file a methylseq run publishes that puts the read funnel and the cytosine counts side by side. Adds the ratios a reader asks of those counts: alignment and duplication yields, methylation level per context, and the bisulfite conversion efficiency read off the CHH calls.
outputs.name: Run summary report
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bismark_summary_report
name: Run summary report
mode: summary
description: >-
  Bismark's own run-level table (bismark2summary), one row per library, the only
  file a methylseq run publishes that puts the read funnel and the cytosine
  counts side by side. Adds the ratios a reader asks of those counts: alignment
  and duplication yields, methylation level per context, and the bisulfite
  conversion efficiency read off the CHH calls.
find:
  path_glob: "**/bismark_summary_report.txt"
recipe: bismark/summary_report.py
fixture: summary_report.tsv
renders_as:
  # Reads to methylome in one card: what was sequenced, what aligned, what
  # survived deduplication. The CpG calls are not reads (one read holds several
  # CpGs), so they are not a funnel stage and have their own card.
  - component: card
    column: total_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: attrition
    attrition_cols: [aligned_reads, unique_reads]
    caption: Reads, from sequenced to aligned and unique
    title: Reads through alignment
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of reads sequenced, and the funnel shows how many
      aligned and how many remained after deduplication. It answers how much of the
      input became usable alignments.

      How to read: a narrow drop at each step is healthy. A large drop at alignment
      points to mapping problems, and a large drop at deduplication to
      over-amplification.
  # Bismark publishes no conversion cut-off. Its FAQ reads conversion off the
  # lowest non-CG methylation (0.3 % means at least 99.7 % converted), which is
  # what this column does with CHH, so the gauge shows the value on 0 to 100.
  - component: card
    column: conversion_efficiency_pct
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 100
    caption: Weakest library, out of 100%
    title: Lowest bisulfite conversion
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest bisulfite conversion efficiency of any library,
      read as 100 percent minus its CHH methylation, with the median and the best.
      It answers how complete the conversion was in the worst library.

      How to read: values near 100 percent are good, since few unmethylated
      cytosines remain unconverted. A library that stands out below the others
      inherits false methylation calls.

      Note: this reading assumes CHH methylation is near zero, as in mammals, and
      Bismark publishes no cut-off.

      Source: https://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/faq/conversion-efficiency/
  - component: card
    column: pct_aligned
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: Alignment yield, with its spread
    title: Average alignment yield
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean percentage of reads that aligned, and the box
      shows the spread across libraries. It answers how well the run mapped.

      How to read: a tight box means libraries mapped alike. A long lower whisker is
      a library to check against the trimming and genome choice.
  - component: card
    column: pct_duplicate
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: Duplication rate, with its spread

outputs.description: The 150 windows whose methylation moves most across the cohort, wide (windows x libraries). The region-level equivalent of a top-variable-gene heatmap: a correlation matrix says the libraries differ, this says where. A ranking, not a test; significance is the group comparison's job.
outputs.name: Most variable methylation windows
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bismark_top_variable_windows
name: Most variable methylation windows
mode: exploratory/variable-windows
description: >-
  The 150 windows whose methylation moves most across the cohort, wide (windows
  x libraries). The region-level equivalent of a top-variable-gene heatmap: a
  correlation matrix says the libraries differ, this says where. A ranking, not
  a test; significance is the group comparison's job.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bedGraph.gz"
recipe: bismark/top_variable_windows.py
fixture: top_variable_windows.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the run's samples, known only at ingest. The
  # variance and the chromosome ride as row annotations so they stay out of the
  # colour scale.
  - id: variable_windows_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    roles: {index: window_id}
    config:
      row_annotation_cols: [chromosome, window_variance]
    title: Most variable methylation windows
    description: >-
      Each cell is the mean CpG methylation of one of the most variable 10 kb
      windows (rows) in one library (columns), with the chromosome and the variance
      of each window as side annotations. It answers which regions differ most
      between libraries.

      How to read: libraries of one condition should share a colour pattern across
      the rows. A block of windows that flips between groups is a candidate region,
      and a library that follows the wrong group is an outlier to check.

      Note: this is a ranking by variance, not a test. The group comparison tab holds
      the statistics.
  - component: card
    column: window_variance
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: Window variance, with its spread
    title: Variance of the top windows
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest methylation variance across libraries of any
      listed window, and the box shows the spread among them. It answers how strongly
      the top windows differ between libraries.

      How to read: a high maximum with a low median means a few windows dominate. A
      flat box means the ranking has no standout region.
  - component: card
    column: chromosome
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: chromosome
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: Chromosomes with the most variable windows
    title: Chromosomes of the top windows
    description: >-
      The hero number is how many chromosomes carry a listed window, with the count
      of windows beside it, and the bars rank the chromosomes by windows. It answers
      whether variable windows cluster on a few chromosomes.

      How to read: a chromosome far ahead of the others can mean a copy-number or
      sex difference between libraries rather than regulated methylation.
  - component: table
    title: Most variable windows table
    description: >-
      Each row is a window with its chromosome, its variance and its methylation in
      every library. It answers the exact values behind the heatmap.

      How to read: sort by variance and compare the library columns.

outputs.description: Pairwise Pearson correlation of the libraries over their shared 10 kb windows, square (libraries x libraries). Replicates of a condition correlate with each other and less with everything else; a library that sits in the wrong block is a swap, a mislabelled sheet, or a conversion failure that flattened its methylome.
outputs.name: Library methylation correlation
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bismark_window_correlation
name: Library methylation correlation
mode: exploratory/correlation
description: >-
  Pairwise Pearson correlation of the libraries over their shared 10 kb
  windows, square (libraries x libraries). Replicates of a condition correlate
  with each other and less with everything else; a library that sits in the
  wrong block is a swap, a mislabelled sheet, or a conversion failure that
  flattened its methylome.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bedGraph.gz"
recipe: bismark/window_correlation.py
fixture: window_correlation.tsv
renders_as:
  # `index` is not optional in practice: ComplexHeatmapConfig.index_column
  # falls back to the literal "sample_id", which this matrix does not have.
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the run's samples, known only at ingest.
  - id: correlation_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    roles: {index: sample}
    title: Library methylation correlation
    description: >-
      Each cell is the Pearson correlation between the window methylation of two
      libraries, computed over their shared 10 kb windows, with rows and columns
      clustered. It answers which libraries have the most similar methylomes.

      How to read: replicates of one condition should form blocks of high
      correlation. A library that clusters with the wrong block can be a sample swap,
      a mislabelled sheet or a conversion failure, so check the sample sheet and the
      conversion cards.

      Note: the diagonal is 1 by construction.
  - component: table
    title: Library correlation table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with its correlation to every other library. It answers
      the exact value behind a cell of the heatmap.

      How to read: sort a column to find the library closest to or furthest from
      another.

renders_as.description:
Each cell is the Pearson correlation between the window methylation of two libraries, computed over their shared 10 kb windows, with rows and columns clustered. It answers which libraries have the most similar methylomes.
How to read: replicates of one condition should form blocks of high correlation. A library that clusters with the wrong block can be a sample swap, a mislabelled sheet or a conversion failure, so check the sample sheet and the conversion cards.
Note: the diagonal is 1 by construction.
renders_as.title: Library methylation correlation

renders_as.description:
Each row is a library with its correlation to every other library. It answers the exact value behind a cell of the heatmap.

outputs.description: Every eligible 10 kb window (enough CpGs in every library, re-binned from the per-CpG bedGraphs without the drawing stride) tested between the two levels of the first two-level factor of the run's design table, on the arcsine square-root transform of its methylation proportion, corrected with Benjamini-Hochberg over all tested windows. nf-core/methylseq ships no differential-methylation caller at any version, so this is the screen the published files support: a region ranking on library-level replication, not a called DMR set.
outputs.name: Window methylation group comparison
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bismark_window_group_compare
name: Window methylation group comparison
mode: differential/windows
description: >-
  Every eligible 10 kb window (enough CpGs in every library, re-binned from the
  per-CpG bedGraphs without the drawing stride) tested between the two levels
  of the first two-level factor of the run's design table, on the arcsine
  square-root transform of its methylation proportion, corrected with
  Benjamini-Hochberg over all tested windows. nf-core/methylseq ships no differential-methylation
  caller at any version, so this is the screen the published files support: a
  region ranking on library-level replication, not a called DMR set.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bedGraph.gz"
recipe: bismark/window_group_compare.py
fixture: window_group_compare.tsv
renders_as:
  # Bismark and nf-core/methylseq define no differential-methylation cut-off
  # (the pipeline ships no caller). The lines below are this table's own call
  # rule from the recipe (padj below 0.05 and at least 10 points), stated as
  # such in the descriptions, not a published standard.
  - id: window_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    roles: {feature_id: window_id, effect_size: delta_methylation, significance: padj, label: window_id, category: direction}
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 10.0
      top_n_labels: 8
      effect_label: Methylation difference (points)
      significance_label: -log10 adjusted p-value
    title: Window methylation volcano
    description: >-
      Each point is a 10 kb window: the methylation difference between the two
      groups on the horizontal axis and its adjusted p-value on the vertical axis.
      It answers which regions differ most, in which direction and how confidently.

      How to read: windows in the upper left and right corners lose or gain
      methylation with the highest confidence. With only a handful of libraries per
      group this is a screen, so confirm any region in the genome view before
      acting.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an adjusted p-value of 0.05
      (Benjamini-Hochberg) and the vertical lines are a difference of 10 percentage
      points. Both are the call rule of this table, set by the recipe, and not a
      published standard.

      Note: Bismark and nf-core/methylseq define no differential-methylation
      cut-off.
  - id: window_manhattan
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: manhattan
    roles: {chr: chromosome, pos: position, score: neg_log10_padj, feature: window_id, effect: delta_methylation}
    config:
      score_threshold: 1.30103
      color_by_columns: [direction]
      default_color_by: direction
      top_n_labels: 8
    title: Window methylation Manhattan plot
    description: >-
      Each point is a 10 kb window along the genome, with the significance of its
      group difference (minus log10 of the adjusted p-value) as height and the call
      as colour. It answers where on the genome the differences concentrate.

      How to read: a cluster of tall points on one chromosome marks a region that
      loses or gains methylation as a block. Isolated points are weaker evidence,
      so check neighbouring windows.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is minus log10 of 0.05, an adjusted
      p-value of 0.05. It is the call rule of this table, set by the recipe, and not
      a published standard.
  - component: card
    column: delta_methylation
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: direction
    caption: Windows, by call
    title: Windows tested, by call
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of windows tested, shown with the largest loss
      and gain in percentage points, and the ring splits them by call. It answers
      how many windows differ and in which direction.

      How to read: a ring almost entirely not significant means little difference
      between the groups. A lopsided ring shows a global shift in one direction.

      Note: the calls follow the recipe rule of an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and
      a difference of at least 10 percentage points, not a published standard.
  # A median over both directions of the difference cancels to about zero, so
  # each direction gets its own card.
  - component: card
    column: delta_methylation
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "pl.col('direction') == 'Hypermethylated'"
    caption: Gains, with their spread
    title: Methylation gains
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest methylation gain among the hypermethylated
      windows, and the box shows the spread of the gains. It answers how large the
      gains are.

      How to read: a box close to the 10 point rule means gains are modest. A long
      upper whisker marks a few windows with a large change.

      Note: the 10 point rule is the call rule of this table, not a published
      standard.
  - component: card
    column: delta_methylation
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "pl.col('direction') == 'Hypomethylated'"
    caption: Losses, with their spread
    title: Methylation losses
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest methylation loss among the hypomethylated
      windows, and the box shows the spread of the losses. It answers how large the
      losses are.

      How to read: a box close to the 10 point rule means losses are modest. A long
      lower whisker marks a few windows with a large change.

      Note: the 10 point rule is the call rule of this table, not a published
      standard.
  - component: card
    column: chromosome
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: chromosome
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "pl.col('direction') != 'Not significant'"
    caption: Chromosomes with the most calls
    title: Chromosomes carrying calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is how many chromosomes carry a called window, with the count
      of called windows beside it, and the bars rank the chromosomes. It answers
      whether the calls cluster on a few chromosomes.

      How to read: a chromosome far ahead of the others can reflect a copy-number or
      sex difference between the groups rather than regulated methylation.
  - component: card
    column: neg_log10_padj
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, q3]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: Significance, window by window
    title: Strongest window significance
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest minus log10 adjusted p-value, and the histogram
      shows how significance spreads over windows. It answers how strong the best
      window is and how many windows stand out.

      How to read: a histogram piled near zero with a thin tail is a screen with few
      real differences. Open the volcano to see the tail windows.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: delta_methylation
      color: direction
      labels: {delta_methylation: Methylation difference (percentage points), direction: Call}
    title: Distribution of methylation differences
    description: >-
      Each bar counts windows in a bin of methylation difference between the two
      groups, split by call. It answers how the called windows sit in the overall
      distribution.

      How to read: a distribution centred on zero is expected when the groups are
      alike. A shifted centre suggests a global difference or a batch effect.

      Lines and annotations: the call colours use an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and
      a difference of at least 10 percentage points, the call rule of this table and
      not a published standard.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: window_id
    title: Window comparison table
    description: >-
      Each row is a 10 kb window with the two group means, the difference, the test
      statistic, the adjusted p-value and the call. It answers the exact statistics
      of any window.

      How to read: sort by adjusted p-value to list the best windows, then select a
      row to inspect it in the other tiles.

outputs.description: The first components of a PCA over the binned methylome, one point per library. Answers what no per-sample QC number can: whether the libraries separate by the design the sheet declares or by depth, batch and conversion rate. Decomposed with a plain numpy SVD inside the recipe.
outputs.name: Library PCA over binned methylation
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bismark_window_pca
name: Library PCA over binned methylation
mode: exploratory/pca
description: >-
  The first components of a PCA over the binned methylome, one point per
  library. Answers what no per-sample QC number can: whether the libraries
  separate by the design the sheet declares or by depth, batch and conversion
  rate. Decomposed with a plain numpy SVD inside the recipe.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bedGraph.gz"
recipe: bismark/window_pca.py
fixture: window_pca.tsv
renders_as:
  # The design columns (the sample hub's factors) are run-dependent, so no role
  # binds one here: a dashboard colours by its own `{GROUP_COL}` via config.
  # C1 N/A: the design column is not in the recipe's OUTPUT_SCHEMA, so no role
  # can bind it; the dashboard colours by its group.
  - id: pca_embedding
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, dim_1: dim_1, dim_2: dim_2, dim_3: dim_3}
    config:
      axis_prefix: PC
    title: Libraries on the binned methylome
    description: >-
      Each point is a library, placed by its methylation over the 10 kb windows on
      the first principal components. It answers whether libraries separate by the
      design of the experiment or by depth, batch or conversion.

      How to read: replicates should sit close together and conditions apart. A
      library that sits alone, or a split that follows a technical factor, is a
      batch or quality effect to investigate before any comparison.

      Note: the components are computed on the run's windows only, so axes have no
      absolute meaning across runs.
  # C1 N/A: same reason as the embedding above, the design columns are run-dependent.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: scatter
    dict_kwargs:
      x: dim_1
      y: dim_2
      hover_name: sample_id
      labels: {dim_1: PC1, dim_2: PC2}
    title: First two components
    description: >-
      Each point is a library on the first two principal components of its binned
      methylome. It answers how libraries relate on the two axes of largest
      variation.

      How to read: neighbouring points are similar libraries. Hover a point to read
      the library, and compare with the correlation heatmap for the same structure.

outputs.description: The two Bowtie 2 alignments of a spike-in normalised run, side by side: how much of each library reached the target genome, how much reached the carrier spike-in genome, and the scale factor the pipeline divides the coverage by before two samples are compared.
outputs.name: Spike-in normalisation factors
outputs.rawYaml:
id: bowtie2_spikein_factors
name: Spike-in normalisation factors
mode: alignment/normalisation
description: >-
  The two Bowtie 2 alignments of a spike-in normalised run, side by side: how
  much of each library reached the target genome, how much reached the carrier
  spike-in genome, and the scale factor the pipeline divides the coverage by
  before two samples are compared.
# The CUT&RUN family aligns every library twice and names the second log
# `<sample>.spikein.bowtie2.log`, so one glob on the file name collects both
# sets and the infix separates them. The factor itself is
# `normalisation_c / spikein_aligned_pairs` (nf-core/cutandrun's default
# normalisation_c is 10000); a run that publishes its own scale-factor table
# should be read from that table instead.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bowtie2.log"
recipe: bowtie2/spikein_factors.py
fixture: spikein_factors.tsv
renders_as:
  # A library sequenced deeper for the same chromatin carries more spike-in, so
  # the factor is the first thing to read, and the target-against-spike-in
  # scatter says whether the two depths moved together at all.
  - id: spikein_factor_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: scale_factor
      color: sample
      labels: {sample: Library, scale_factor: Scale factor}
    title: Spike-in scale factor per sample
    reference_lines: [{axis: y, stat: median, column: scale_factor}]
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: the factor its coverage is multiplied by, the
      normalisation constant divided by the pairs aligned to the spike-in genome. It
      answers how much each library is scaled before samples are compared.

      How to read: a larger factor means fewer spike-in pairs, so the library is
      scaled up. Factors that differ widely between replicates of one condition
      point to uneven spike-in addition, so consider another normalisation.

      Lines and annotations: the constant is 10000, the default normalisation_c of
      nf-core/cutandrun, and no cut-off is drawn.
       The dashed line is the median scale factor of this table, a reference
      computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      Bowtie 2.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: spikein_depth_scatter
    component: figure
    visu_type: scatter
    dict_kwargs:
      x: spikein_aligned
      y: target_aligned
      color: sample
      labels: {spikein_aligned: Pairs aligned to the spike-in genome, target_aligned: Pairs aligned to the target genome, sample: Library}
    title: Target depth against spike-in depth
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: the pairs aligned to the spike-in genome on the
      horizontal axis and to the target genome on the vertical axis. It answers
      whether the two depths move together, as they do when the spike-in amount is
      constant.

      How to read: libraries of one antibody should lie along a rising band. A point
      off the band has an unusual amount of spike-in for its depth. With few
      libraries the pattern is weak, so read it with the scale factor bars.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: scale_factor
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Scale factor
    caption: median scale factor, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median spike-in scale factor, and the box shows how the
      libraries spread. It answers how large the normalisation adjustment is.

      How to read: a tight box means the libraries hold similar spike-in amounts. A
      long whisker marks a library that will be scaled far more than the others.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: spikein_aligned
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Spike-in pairs
    caption: total pairs aligned to the spike-in, with the richest libraries ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of pairs aligned to the spike-in genome, and the
      bars rank the libraries with most. It answers how much spike-in material the
      run holds.

      How to read: a library with far fewer pairs than the others will get a large
      scale factor. The nf-core/cutandrun documentation asks for more than 1000
      spike-in reads per sample to rise above noise, so use the next card to check.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  # nf-core/cutandrun: target samples usually carry under 1% spike-in alignment but
  # still more than 1000 reads, IgG more (2 to 5%). The old fixed 0.05 fraction line
  # mixed both, so the card checks the sourced read floor instead.
  - component: card
    column: spikein_aligned
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 1000
    threshold_direction: min
    title: Lowest spike-in depth
    caption: lowest spike-in pair count, with the median and highest
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest number of pairs aligned to the spike-in genome
      in any library. It answers whether every library holds enough spike-in to be
      normalised.

      How to read: higher is better. A library under the line has spike-in too low
      to separate from noise, so another normalisation, such as the read count, is
      safer.

      Lines and annotations: the line is 1000 spike-in reads, the level the
      nf-core/cutandrun documentation gives for a spike-in signal above noise. The
      table counts pairs, so it is a close approximation.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: target_align_rate
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 100.0
    title: Target alignment rate
    caption: average percent aligned to the target genome, with the lowest and highest
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average of Bowtie 2's overall alignment rate against the target genome,
      in percent and shown against 100. It answers how much of each library maps to
      the genome of interest.

      How to read: a low rate points to contamination, a wrong reference or poor
      reads. Bowtie 2 reports the rate but defines no pass level, so none is drawn.

      Source: https://bowtie-bio.sourceforge.net/bowtie2/manual.shtml
  - component: table
    title: Spike-in factors per library
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with its read pairs, pairs aligned to the target and
      spike-in genomes with their rates, the spike-in fraction and the scale factor.
      It answers the exact numbers behind the normalisation.

      How to read: sort by scale factor to find the libraries scaled most.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: busco_batch_summary
name: BUSCO completeness per assembly
mode: batch-summary
description: >-
  One row per assessed assembly from BUSCO's batch summary: the complete,
  single-copy, duplicated, fragmented and missing percentages against the lineage
  dataset, plus the contiguity BUSCO measures on the way. Complete single-copy is
  the headline; a high duplicated share on a haploid target points at retained
  haplotigs, a high fragmented share at a base-level error rate high enough to
  break gene models. A pipeline that runs BUSCO on both the assembly and its
  annotated proteins (nf-core/genomeqc) names the mode in the run, read into
  busco_mode, so the two scores of one assembly stay two rows.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*-busco.batch_summary.txt"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*-busco/batch_summary.txt"
    - "**/*batch_summary.txt"
recipe: busco/batch_summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 3 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several assemblies and lineages.
fixture: batch_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: completeness_vs_duplication
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Completeness against duplication
    roles: {x: complete_pct, y: duplicated_pct, label: assembly_id, color: lineage, size: contig_n50}
    config:
      x_title: Complete BUSCOs (%)
      y_title: Duplicated BUSCOs (%)
      top_n_labels: 5
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is an assessed assembly, with the percent of complete BUSCOs on the
      horizontal axis and the percent of duplicated BUSCOs on the vertical axis,
      sized by contig N50 and coloured by lineage dataset. It answers which
      assemblies are both complete and free of duplication.

      How to read: the best assemblies sit far right and low. Points high on the
      vertical axis hold the same marker genes twice, which BUSCO explains by a
      recent genome duplication or by a chimeric assembly of haplotypes. A larger
      point is a more contiguous assembly.

      Note: BUSCO publishes no pass mark and asks that results be read in the
      biology of the organism, so no reference line is drawn.

      Source: https://busco.ezlab.org/busco_userguide.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Complete BUSCOs per assembly
    dict_kwargs:
      x: assembly_id
      y: complete_pct
      color: lineage
      labels: {assembly_id: Assembly, complete_pct: Complete BUSCOs (%), lineage: Lineage dataset}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: complete_pct}
    description: >-
      Each bar is an assessed assembly, with the percent of its BUSCO markers found
      complete, coloured by the lineage dataset used. It answers which assemblies
      recover the most expected genes.

      How to read: a taller bar is a more complete assembly. Assemblies are only
      comparable when scored against the same lineage dataset, which the colour
      shows.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median percent of complete BUSCOs of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not
      a cut-off of BUSCO. BUSCO publishes no completeness cut-off.

      Source: https://busco.ezlab.org/busco_userguide.html
  - component: card
    column: complete_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Complete BUSCOs
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent of complete BUSCOs over the assessed
      assemblies, and the box shows the spread. It answers how complete the
      assemblies are overall.

      How to read: a high median with a narrow box means a consistent set. A long
      lower whisker is an assembly that lost marker genes and deserves a look.

      Source: https://busco.ezlab.org/busco_userguide.html
  - component: card
    column: duplicated_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Duplicated BUSCOs
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent of BUSCOs found more than once, and the
      box shows the spread. It answers how much redundancy the assemblies carry.

      How to read: BUSCO explains a high duplication by a recent genome duplication
      or by a chimeric assembly of haplotypes, and an unfiltered transcriptome or
      protein set also inflates it. Check the ploidy and the isoform handling of the
      input.

      Source: https://busco.ezlab.org/busco_userguide.html
  - component: card
    column: missing_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Missing BUSCOs
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent of BUSCOs not found, and the box shows
      the spread. It answers how many expected genes the assemblies lack.

      How to read: BUSCO notes that missing genes may be of biological or technical
      origin. A tissue limited transcriptome is not expected to be BUSCO complete,
      so compare consistency across samples there.

      Source: https://busco.ezlab.org/busco_userguide.html
  - component: card
    column: assembly_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    caption: BUSCO runs behind it
    title: Assemblies assessed
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct assemblies scored, and the strip
      gives the count of BUSCO runs. It answers how many assemblies the other tiles
      summarise.

      How to read: runs exceed assemblies when one assembly is scored in more than
      one mode, for example as a genome and as its annotated proteins.
  - component: table

      single-copy, duplicated, fragmented and missing percentages, the number of
      markers and the contiguity BUSCO measures. It answers the exact scores behind
      every other tile.

      How to read: sort by complete or by duplicated to rank assemblies, and read
      the lineage and mode columns before comparing two rows.

      Source: https://busco.ezlab.org/busco_userguide.html

outputs.fixtureContent:
sample	total_raw_counts	total_output_counts	total_counts_removed	fraction_counts_removed	expected_cells	found_cells	ratio_of_found_cells_to_expected_cells	target_fpr

outputs.rawYaml:
id: cellbender_metrics
name: Ambient-RNA removal metrics
mode: removebackground/metrics
description: >-
  CellBender's per-sample accounting of ambient-RNA removal: counts removed,
  cells found against the expected count, and the training convergence
  parameters.
find:
  path_glob: "**/cellbender_removebackground/*_metrics.csv"
recipe: cellbender/metrics.py
fixture: metrics.tsv
renders_as:
  # CellBender's docs give no cut-off for the removed fraction, so the card shows
  # the measure and its spread and draws no pass mark. A fraction between 0 and
  # 1 is also not a gauge (RULES section 5).
  - component: card
    column: fraction_counts_removed
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: median, with the lowest and highest sample
    title: Share of counts removed as ambient
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median fraction of all counts that CellBender called
      ambient RNA and removed, over the samples in view. It answers how much of the
      signal was background.

      How to read: a small fraction means a clean sample and little change to the
      matrix. A large one means heavy ambient contamination, so compare samples
      and look at the CellBender report of the outlier before using its matrix.

      Note: CellBender documents no cut-off for this fraction, so no pass mark is
      drawn. It depends on the target false-positive rate the run used.

      Source: https://cellbender.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage/index.html
  - component: card
    column: found_cells
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Cells found per sample
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of barcodes CellBender kept as cells, and
      the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how many cells each
      sample yielded after background removal.

      How to read: samples of the same design should give similar counts. A sample
      far below or above its peers was either filtered hard or called many empty
      droplets, so check it against its UMI curve.

      Source: https://cellbender.readthedocs.io/en/latest/usage/index.html
  # The ratio of found to expected cells is 1 when CellBender agrees with the prior
  # it started from. CellBender defines no pass range for it, so the layout is a
  # spread, not a threshold.
  - component: card
    column: ratio_of_found_cells_to_expected_cells
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: median, with the lowest and highest sample
    title: Found against expected cells
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median ratio of cells CellBender found to cells it
      expected, over the samples in view. It answers whether the called cell count
      matches the prior the run started from.

      How to read: a ratio near 1 means the call agrees with the expectation, and
      CellBender asks only for an expected-cells value within a factor of 2. A ratio far
      outside that means the setting did not match the data or the cell call went wrong,
      so compare it with the UMI curve as the CellBender troubleshooting guide advises.

      Note: CellBender defines no acceptable range for this ratio, so no pass mark
      is drawn.

      Sources: https://cellbender.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/index.html and
      https://cellbender.readthedocs.io/en/latest/troubleshooting/index.html
  - component: table
    title: Ambient-RNA removal per sample
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample, with the counts before and after removal, the fraction
      removed, the expected and found cell counts and the target false-positive
      rate. It answers the exact numbers behind the cards.

      How to read: sort by the fraction removed to find the most contaminated
      samples, then check the found-to-expected ratio of the same row.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: cellranger_aligner_summary
name: Aligner route summary
mode: analysis/aligner_summary
description: >-
  One row per nf-core/scrnaseq --aligner route: the cells it called, the
  cells CellBender kept on that route, its median UMI per cell and its
  mapping rate. Each route reports those through a different tool, so the
  table is the translation layer a comparison needs.
find:
  path_glob: "**/metrics_summary.csv"
recipe: cellranger/aligner_summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 3 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several aligner routes.
fixture: aligner_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # Calls from different routes against each other: the diagonal is "both counted
  # the same number of cells", a data-defined reference, not a quality cut-off.
  - id: aligner_agreement
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Cells called against cells kept by CellBender
    roles: {x: cells_called, y: cellbender_cells, label: aligner, color: aligner}
    config:
      x_title: Cells called by the aligner route
      y_title: Cells kept by CellBender
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: equal counts
    description: >-
      Each point is one aligner route: the cells it called on the horizontal axis and
      the cells CellBender kept on that route on the vertical axis. It answers whether
      the routes agree on how many cells the library holds.

      How to read: points on the diagonal mean CellBender kept about as many cells as
      the aligner called. A point far from the diagonal, or a route far from the others,
      means that route calls cells differently, so compare its barcode overlap in the
      cell-call UpSet before trusting its counts.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, where both counts are equal. It is a
      reference defined by the data, not a quality cut-off.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/scrnaseq/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: aligner_cells_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Cells called per aligner route
    dict_kwargs:
      x: aligner
      y: cells_called
      color: aligner
      labels: {aligner: Aligner route, cells_called: Cells called}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: cells_called
    description: >-
      Each bar is an aligner route, as nf-core/scrnaseq runs them with its
      --aligner option, and its height is the number of cells that route called.
      It answers which route finds more or fewer cells.

      How to read: similar bar heights mean the routes agree on the library. A
      route far below the rest may have mapped fewer reads to cells, so check its
      mapping rate and its barcode overlap with the others.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median number of cells called
      of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of Cell Ranger.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/scrnaseq/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: aligner_picker
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: Select
    column_name: aligner
    title: Aligner route
    description: >-
      Picks one aligner route and filters every tile of the tab to it. It answers how a
      single route behaves on its own.

      How to read: clear the selection to compare all routes again.
  - component: card
    column: cells_called
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: aligner
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: cells called, by route
    title: Cells called
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of cells called across the shown routes, and the bars
      rank the routes that called most. It answers how large the called population is
      and which route drives it.

      How to read: the minimum and maximum give the range between routes. A wide range
      means the routes disagree on what counts as a cell.
  - component: card
    column: mapping_rate
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mapping rate, with its spread
    title: Mapping rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average fraction of reads each route maps to the
      transcriptome, and the box shows the spread between routes. It answers how well
      reads land on the reference.

      How to read: a route far below the others lost reads at alignment, so check the
      reference and the library chemistry. Each tool defines its mapping rate in its own
      way, so compare routes with care.

      Note: 10x gives an expected value of more than 30 percent for the confidently
      mapped transcriptome fraction of Cell Ranger only, so no pass mark is drawn here.

      Source: https://assets.ctfassets.net/an68im79xiti/163qWiQBTVi2YLbskJphQX/e90bb82151b1cdab6d7e9b6c845e6130/CG000329_TechnicalNote_InterpretingCellRangerWebSummaryFiles_RevA.pdf
  - component: table
    title: Aligner routes
    description: >-
      Each row is an aligner route with its cells called, cells kept by CellBender,
      median UMI per cell and mapping rate. It answers the exact numbers behind the other
      tiles.

      How to read: sort a column to rank the routes. An empty cell means that route does
      not report that metric.

id: cellranger_barcode_rank
name: Barcode-rank curve
mode: count/barcode_rank
description: >-
  UMI count per barcode against its rank, summed from the raw
  feature-barcode matrix (background droplets included) and flagged against
  the barcodes Cell Ranger kept as cells, the knee that separates real
  cells from ambient noise.
find:
