recipe: cellranger/barcode_rank.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: barcode_rank.tsv
renders_as:
  # Coloured by sample (one curve each); the called cells are drawn by the knee itself.
  - id: barcode_rank_knee
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: knee_plot
    title: Barcode rank plot
    roles: {sample: sample, rank: rank, umi_count: umi_count, is_cell: is_cell}
    description: >-
      Each point is a barcode ranked by its UMI count, from the richest droplet down, on
      log axes, with one curve per sample. It answers where real cells stop and empty
      droplets start.

      How to read: a good library has a plateau of cells with high counts, a steep drop,
      then a long tail of background. A curve with no clear drop means the cells are not
      well separated from ambient RNA, so check the cell calls and the aligner summary.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-off marks the barcodes the pipeline called as cells.
      It is the call made by the cell-calling step of the run, not a fixed UMI value.
  - id: barcode_rank_curve
    component: figure
    visu_type: line
    title: Barcode rank curve
    dict_kwargs:
      x: rank
      y: umi_count
      color: sample
      log_x: "true"
      log_y: "true"
      labels: {rank: Barcode rank, umi_count: UMI count, sample: Sample}
    description: >-
      Each point is a barcode: its rank by UMI count on the horizontal axis and its UMI
      count on the vertical axis, one line per sample. It answers how deep the counts of
      the best barcodes are and how fast they fall.

      How to read: compare the plateau height and the position of the drop between
      samples. A lower plateau or an earlier drop means fewer or poorer cells in that
      library.
  - component: card
    column: umi_count
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: UMI counts of ranked barcodes
    title: Deepest barcode
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest UMI count of any barcode, and the histogram shows
      the distribution of the ranked barcodes. It answers how rich the best droplet is.

      How to read: a very high maximum next to a modest median points to a few
      outlier droplets such as doublets or debris. Open the rank plot to see where they
      sit.
  - id: barcode_umi_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: umi_count
    title: UMI count range
    description: >-
      Restricts the tab to barcodes whose UMI count falls inside the range. It answers
      which barcodes lie in a chosen depth window.

      How to read: drag the handles to keep only the cell plateau or only the background.
  - component: table
    title: Ranked barcodes
    description: >-
      Each row is a barcode with its rank, UMI count and whether the run called it a
      cell. It answers the exact values behind the curve.

renders_as:
  - id: phase_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: S and G2/M scores per cell
    roles: {x: s_score, y: g2m_score, color: phase, label: barcode}
    config:
      x_title: S-phase score
      y_title: G2/M-phase score
      quadrants:
        x: 0
        y: 0
        labels: [G2M, "S or G2M", G1, S]
    description: >-
      Each point is a cell: its S-phase score on the horizontal axis and its G2/M score on
      the vertical axis, coloured by the phase assigned. It answers which cells are
      cycling and in which phase.

      How to read: a large cloud in the lower left corner is G1 or resting cells, the
      normal majority of a tissue sample. Arms toward the upper or right regions are
      cycling cells, so check whether a cluster is mostly cycling before treating it as a
      distinct cell type.

      Lines and annotations: the two lines sit at a score of 0 on each axis. A cell with
      both scores negative is called G1, otherwise the higher score gives S or G2M, the
      rule of scanpy's score_genes_cell_cycle. The gene sets are the S and G2/M sets of
      Tirosh et al.; the scores here subtract the cell's mean expression instead of
      expression-matched control genes.

      Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scverse/scanpy/main/src/scanpy/tools/_score_genes.py
      and https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/cell_cycle_vignette
  - id: phase_by_cluster
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Cell-cycle phase per cluster
    dict_kwargs:
      x: cluster_label
      color: phase
      labels: {cluster_label: Cluster, phase: Phase}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a cluster and its segments count the cells in each cell-cycle phase. It
      answers which clusters are made of cycling cells.

      How to read: a cluster dominated by S and G2M cells is a proliferating population, and
      its markers may reflect the cycle rather than a cell type. A cluster of mostly G1 cells
      is resting.

      Source: https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/generated/scanpy.tl.score_genes_cell_cycle.html

    component: interactive

    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: phase
    top_n_count: 3

    title: Cells per phase
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of cells scored and the ring splits them by phase. It
      answers what share of the cells is cycling.

      spread. It answers how strongly S-phase genes are expressed overall.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: cellranger_cell_expression_long
name: Marker expression per cell, long
mode: analysis/cell_expression_long
description: >-
  The marker-panel slice of the cell x gene matrix (MARKER_PANEL when set, else
  the top markers of each cluster), melted to one row per
  (cell, gene), so a distribution plot can show the spread of one marker
  across clusters rather than the cluster mean a dot plot draws.
find:
  path_glob: "**/filtered_feature_bc_matrix/matrix.mtx.gz"
recipe: cellranger/cell_expression_long.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several marker genes.
fixture: cell_expression_long.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: marker_by_cluster
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Marker expression per cluster
    dict_kwargs:
      x: cluster_label
      y: expression
      color: cluster_label
      labels: {cluster_label: Cluster, expression: Expression (log1p CP10k)}
    description: >-
      Each box is a cluster and shows the expression of the selected marker genes over its
      cells. It answers which clusters express a marker.

      How to read: a high box in one cluster and low boxes elsewhere marks a cluster-specific
      gene. Boxes pinned at zero mean the gene is rarely detected there, which is common for
      lowly expressed genes.
  - id: marker_by_gene
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Marker expression per gene
    dict_kwargs:
      x: gene
      y: expression
      color: gene
      labels: {gene: Gene, expression: Expression (log1p CP10k)}
    description: >-
      Each box is a marker gene and shows its expression over the cells in view. It answers
      which markers are expressed strongly and how widely.

      How to read: a wide box with a high median is a robust marker. A box squeezed at zero
      with a few high points is detected in only a small fraction of cells.
  - id: marker_gene_picker
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: Select
    column_name: gene
    title: Marker gene
    description: >-
      Shows one marker gene on every tile of the tab. It answers how a single gene behaves.

      How to read: clear the selection to show all markers again.
  - id: marker_expression_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: expression
    title: Expression range
    description: >-
      Keeps the cells whose expression falls inside the range. It answers which cells express
      a gene above a level.

      How to read: raise the lower handle above zero to keep only the cells where the gene is
      detected.
  - component: card
    column: expression
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats, max]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: expression, with its spread
    title: Marker expression
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median expression of the marker genes over the cells in view,
      and the box shows its spread. It answers how strongly the markers are expressed.

      How to read: a median at zero is normal for sparse single-cell data, so read the upper
      whisker and the maximum for signal.
  - component: table
    title: Marker expression per cell
    description: >-
      Each row is one gene in one cell with its cluster, QC status and expression. It answers
      the exact values behind the box plots.

      How to read: filter on a gene and sort by expression to find the cells that express it
      most.

outputs.name: Cell-calling funnel
outputs.rawYaml:
id: cellranger_cell_funnel
name: Cell-calling funnel
mode: analysis/cell_funnel
description: >-
  One row per sample with the four stages of barcode filtering as four
  columns, in pipeline order: barcodes observed, cells called, cells
  CellBender also kept, cells no MAD rule flagged. The retention chain that
  is otherwise spread over four tiles in three sections.
find:
  path_glob: "**/raw_feature_bc_matrix/barcodes.tsv.gz"
recipe: cellranger/cell_funnel.py
fixture: cell_funnel.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: cell_waterfall
    component: card
    column: barcodes_observed
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: attrition
    attrition_cols: [cells_called, cellbender_cells, cells_qc_pass]
    caption: barcodes down to cells passing QC
    title: From barcodes to cells
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of barcodes observed, and the waterfall steps down to the
      cells called, the cells CellBender kept and the cells that pass the quality filter. It
      answers how many droplets end up as usable cells.

      How to read: a large first step is normal, since most barcodes are empty droplets. A
      big loss at a later step means cell calling or the quality filter removed many cells.
  - component: card
    column: barcodes_observed
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats, count]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: barcodes per sample, with their spread
    title: Barcodes observed
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of barcodes seen across samples, and the box shows
      how that varies per sample. It answers how deeply each library was sampled.

      How to read: a sample far from the others was loaded or sequenced differently, so check
      its sequencing depth before comparing it.
  - component: card
    column: cells_called
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: cells called per sample
    title: Cells called
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of cells called across samples, and the histogram shows
      the distribution per sample. It answers how many cells each library yields.

      How to read: a sample with few cells has less power in every downstream tile.
  - component: card
    column: pct_qc_pass
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 100.0
    caption: cells passing QC, of 100%
    title: Cells passing QC
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average share of called cells that pass the quality filter, and
      the gauge shows it out of 100 percent. It answers how clean the called cells are.

      How to read: the minimum shows the worst sample. A low value points to many cells with
      few genes, few UMIs or a high mitochondrial share.

      Note: the filter uses median absolute deviation limits computed per sample, see the
      description of the cell QC tab for the rules.
  - component: card
    column: pct_called
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: share of barcodes called, with its spread
    title: Share of barcodes called as cells
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent of observed barcodes called a cell, and the box
      shows its spread across samples. It answers how selective cell calling is.

      How to read: the value depends on loading and ambient RNA, so compare samples of one
      experiment, not absolute levels. An outlier sample deserves a look at its barcode rank
      plot.
  - component: table
    title: Cell counts per sample
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its barcodes, cells called, cells kept by CellBender, cells
      passing QC and the two shares. It answers the exact counts behind the cards.

      How to read: follow a row left to right to see where a sample loses cells.

  other cell-level cellranger output joins to.
find:
  path_glob: "**/filtered_feature_bc_matrix/matrix.mtx.gz"
recipe: cellranger/cell_qc.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 25 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several QC outcomes.
fixture: cell_qc.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: umap_qc
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: UMAP coloured by genes detected
    roles: {sample_id: barcode, dim_1: umap_1, dim_2: umap_2, color: log10_n_genes, cluster: graphclust}
    config:
      axis_prefix: UMAP
    description: >-
      Each point is a cell on the UMAP, coloured by the log10 of the genes it detects. It
      answers whether depth or quality follows the cell groups.

      How to read: a smooth colour within each island is expected. A whole island of low
      values is a cluster of poor cells or a low-RNA cell type, so check the mitochondrial
      and UMI tiles before trusting it.
  - id: umap_label
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: UMAP coloured by cluster
    roles: {sample_id: barcode, dim_1: umap_1, dim_2: umap_2, cluster: cluster_label, color: cluster_label}
    config:
      axis_prefix: UMAP
    description: >-
      Each point is a cell on the UMAP, coloured by its graph-based cluster and named by its
      top two marker genes. It answers how the cells group by expression.

      How to read: compact, separated islands are distinct populations. A cluster split across
      the map, or mixed with another, is weakly defined, so compare it with the k-means
      resolutions in the stability tile.
  - id: tsne_label
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: t-SNE coloured by cluster
    roles: {sample_id: barcode, dim_1: tsne_1, dim_2: tsne_2, cluster: cluster_label, color: cluster_label}
    config:
      axis_prefix: t-SNE
    description: >-
      Each point is a cell on the t-SNE map, coloured by its graph-based cluster. It answers
      whether the grouping seen on the UMAP also holds on a second embedding.

      How to read: clusters that stay compact on both maps are robust. Distances between
      islands are not meaningful on a t-SNE, so judge membership, not proximity.
  - id: umi_vs_genes
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Genes detected against UMI counts
    roles: {x: n_umi, y: n_genes, color: qc_status}
    config:
      log_x: true
      x_title: UMI counts per cell
      y_title: Genes detected per cell
    description: >-
      Each point is a cell: its total UMI count on the horizontal axis and the number of genes
      it detects on the vertical axis, coloured by its QC status. It answers whether cells
      follow the expected relation between depth and complexity.

      How to read: genes detected rise with UMIs and flatten at high depth. Cells that sit far
      below the cloud have many UMIs from few genes, which points to low-complexity cells or
      doublets, and flagged cells should lie at the edges.

      Lines and annotations: no cut-off is drawn. The QC flags come from limits of 5 median
      absolute deviations on log counts and genes, set per sample.

      Source: https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  - id: cluster_stability
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sankey
    title: Cluster stability across resolutions
    roles: {steps: [graphclust, kmeans_6, kmeans_10]}
    config:
      color_mode: source
    description: >-
      Each band is a group of cells that moves from a graph-based cluster to a k-means cluster
      with 6 groups and then one with 10, sized by cell count. It answers how stable the
      clusters are when the method and the resolution change.

      How to read: a cluster that flows into one group at every step is stable. A cluster that
      splits evenly across several groups is weakly defined, so treat its identity with care.
  - id: umi_histogram
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: UMI counts per cell
    dict_kwargs:
      x: n_umi
      color: qc_status
      labels: {n_umi: UMI counts per cell, qc_status: QC status}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: x
        stat: median
        column: n_umi
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the cells with a total UMI count in a range, split by QC
      status. It answers how deep the cells are and where the low-depth tail lies.

      How to read: a single peak with a short left tail is a healthy library. A
      second peak at low counts is empty droplets or debris that the filter
      flagged.

      The QC filter flags cells below 5 median absolute deviations under the
      median of log counts, computed per sample.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median UMI count per cell of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of the QC filter.

      Source:
      https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  - id: genes_histogram
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Genes detected per cell
    dict_kwargs:
      x: n_genes
      color: qc_status
      labels: {n_genes: Genes detected per cell, qc_status: QC status}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: x
        stat: median
        column: n_genes
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the cells with a number of detected genes in a range, split
      by QC status. It answers how complex the cells are.

      How to read: one peak is a healthy library, and a tail of few genes marks
      poor cells. Complexity depends on the cell type, so compare it across
      clusters before filtering.

      The QC filter flags cells below 5 median absolute deviations under the
      median of log genes, computed per sample.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median number of genes
      detected per cell of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show
      (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of the QC filter.

      Source:
      https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  - id: mito_box
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Mitochondrial fraction by cluster
    dict_kwargs:
      x: cluster_label
      y: pct_mito
      color: cluster_label
      labels: {cluster_label: Cluster, pct_mito: Mitochondrial UMIs (%)}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: pct_mito
    description: >-
      Each box is a cluster and shows the percent of UMIs from mitochondrial genes
      in its cells. It answers which clusters carry stressed or dying cells.

      How to read: a cluster with a high box is a candidate for broken cells, but
      some cell types are naturally rich in mitochondria. Check its markers before
      removing it.

      The QC filter flags a cell when it exceeds 3 median absolute deviations and
      a fixed 8 percent, a limit the source calls not universal.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median mitochondrial fraction
      of a cell of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it
      follows the filters), not a cut-off of the QC filter.

      Source:
      https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  - id: ribo_box
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Ribosomal fraction by cluster
    dict_kwargs:
      x: cluster_label
      y: pct_ribo
      color: cluster_label
      labels: {cluster_label: Cluster, pct_ribo: Ribosomal UMIs (%)}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: pct_ribo
    description: >-
      Each box is a cluster and shows the percent of UMIs from ribosomal genes in
      its cells. It answers which clusters are dominated by ribosomal transcripts.

      How to read: ribosomal content varies a lot between cell types, such as T
      cells against myeloid cells. A cluster far above the rest is worth a look at
      its markers, since it may reflect cell type and not quality.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median ribosomal fraction of a
      cell of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows
      the filters), not a cut-off of the QC filter.
  - id: umi_box
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: UMI counts by cluster
    dict_kwargs:
      x: cluster_label
      y: log10_n_umi
      color: cluster_label
      labels: {cluster_label: Cluster, log10_n_umi: UMI counts (log10)}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: log10_n_umi
    description: >-
      Each box is a cluster and shows the log10 of the UMI counts of its cells. It
      answers whether any cluster is much shallower than the others.

      How to read: a cluster well below the rest is either a low-RNA cell type or
      poor cells. Compare it with the genes detected and the mitochondrial
      fraction.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median log10 UMI count per
      cell of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows
      the filters), not a cut-off of the QC filter.
  - id: qc_status_by_cluster
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: QC status per cluster
    dict_kwargs:
      x: cluster_label
      color: qc_status
      labels: {cluster_label: Cluster, qc_status: QC status}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a cluster and its segments count the cells that pass or that the filter
      flagged. It answers whether flagged cells concentrate in some clusters.

      How to read: a cluster made mostly of flagged cells is probably an artefact and not a
      cell type. Open the table to see which rule flagged them.

      Source: https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  - id: qc_reason_picker
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: qc_reason
    title: QC reason
    description: >-
      Keeps the cells flagged for the chosen reason, or those that pass. It answers which rule
      removes which cells.

      How to read: select one reason to see where those cells sit on the maps.
  - id: cluster_picker
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: cluster_label
    title: Cluster
    description: >-
      Keeps only the cells of the chosen clusters. It answers how the QC metrics look in one
      population.

      How to read: clear the selection to show every cluster again.
  - id: qc_status_picker
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: SegmentedControl
    column_name: qc_status
    title: QC status
    description: >-
      Switches between the cells that pass the quality filter and the cells it flagged. It
      answers where the flagged cells lie.

      How to read: choose flagged to inspect them on the maps and in the table.
  - id: n_umi_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: n_umi
    title: UMI counts range
    description: >-
      Keeps the cells whose total UMI count falls in the range. It answers how the tab changes
      when shallow or very deep cells are left out.

      How to read: drag the lower handle to hide the shallow cells.
  - id: n_genes_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: n_genes
    title: Genes detected range
    description: >-
      Keeps the cells whose number of detected genes falls in the range. It answers how the
      tab changes when low-complexity cells are left out.

      How to read: drag the lower handle to hide cells with few genes.
  - id: top20_share_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: pct_top20
    title: Top 20 gene share range
    description: >-
      Keeps the cells whose top 20 genes hold a share of UMIs inside the range. It answers
      which cells are dominated by a few genes.

      How to read: drag the upper handle down to hide cells that few genes dominate.
  - component: card
    column: n_umi
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: UMI counts, with their spread
    title: UMI counts per cell
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median UMI count of a cell, and the histogram shows the
      distribution. It answers how deeply the cells are sequenced.

      How to read: a median in the thousands is typical for droplet data. A long left tail or a
      minimum near zero shows cells the filter should remove.
  - component: card
    column: n_genes
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: genes detected, with their spread
    title: Genes detected per cell
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of genes detected in a cell, and the histogram
      shows the distribution. It answers how complex the cells are.

      How to read: low values point to poor cells or low-RNA cell types. Compare with the UMI
      card, since the two rise together.
  - component: card
    column: pct_mito
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 8.0
    threshold_direction: max
    caption: median against the 8% mitochondrial limit
    title: Mitochondrial fraction
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent of UMIs from mitochondrial genes, shown against
      the fixed limit of 8 percent. It answers whether the typical cell is stressed.

      How to read: a median under the limit passes. A high maximum is a cell the filter flags,
      together with the median absolute deviation rule.

      Lines and annotations: the 8 percent limit is the fixed cut-off a cell must also exceed
      to be flagged, besides 3 median absolute deviations. The source states it is not
      universal because mitochondrial content differs between cell types and tissues.

      Source: https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  - component: card
    column: qc_flagged
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [average]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: qc_status
    caption: cells passing and flagged
    title: Cells flagged by QC
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of cells the quality filter flags, and the bar splits the
      cells into passing and flagged. It answers how much of the library the filter removes.

      How to read: the average is the flagged fraction. A small fraction is typical, and a
      large one means the library or the filter settings need a closer look.

      Source: https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  - component: card
    column: pct_top20
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: top 20 gene share, with its spread
    title: Top 20 gene share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent of UMIs held by a cell's 20 most expressed genes,
      and the box shows its spread. It answers how concentrated the expression is.

      How to read: a high share means a few genes dominate the cell, which is typical of low
      complexity or damaged cells. Cells above 5 median absolute deviations are flagged.

      Source: https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  - component: card
    column: pct_ribo
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: ribosomal share, with its spread
    title: Ribosomal fraction
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent of UMIs from ribosomal genes, and the box shows its
      spread. It answers how much of the signal is ribosomal.

      How to read: the level depends on the cell types in the sample. No cut-off is drawn
      because the QC rules use no ribosomal limit.
  - component: card
    column: log10_n_umi
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: UMI counts (log10), with their spread
    title: UMI counts, log scale
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median log10 of the UMI counts of a cell, and the box shows its
      spread. It answers the depth of the cells on the scale the QC rule uses.

      How to read: a narrow box means even depth. A long lower whisker holds the shallow cells.
  - component: card
    column: log10_n_genes
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: genes detected (log10), with their spread
    title: Genes detected, log scale
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median log10 of the genes detected in a cell, and the box shows
      its spread. It answers the complexity of the cells on the scale the QC rule uses.

      How to read: a narrow box means even complexity. A long lower whisker holds the
      low-complexity cells.
  - component: card
    column: cellbender_cell
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: cellbender_cell
    caption: cells kept and dropped by CellBender
    title: CellBender cell calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of cells in view and the bar splits them by whether
      CellBender also kept them. It answers how much the ambient-RNA correction agrees with the
      cell calls.

      How to read: a bar that is almost entirely kept means the two calls agree. A sizeable
      dropped share means many called cells are mostly ambient RNA.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: barcode
    title: Cell quality control
    description: >-
      Each row is a cell with its counts, mitochondrial, ribosomal and haemoglobin shares,
      embedding coordinates, clusters and QC flags. It answers the exact values behind every
      tile and lets a row selection filter the others.

      How to read: sort by a metric to find the extreme cells, and read the reason column to
      see which rule flagged a cell.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: cellranger_cluster_summary
name: Cluster summary
mode: analysis/cluster_summary
description: >-
  One row per graph-based cluster: size, QC medians and the share of cells
  CellBender also called, aggregated from the per-cell QC hub.
find:
  path_glob: "**/filtered_feature_bc_matrix/matrix.mtx.gz"
recipe: cellranger/cluster_summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 14 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: cluster_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: cluster_sizes
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Cells per cluster
    dict_kwargs:
      x: cluster_label
      y: n_cells
      color: cluster_label
      labels: {cluster_label: Cluster, n_cells: Cells}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a graph-based cluster and its height is the number of cells in it. It
      answers how the cells divide between clusters.

      How to read: a few large clusters with a tail of small ones is typical. A very small
      cluster can be a rare population or a quality artefact, so check its QC tile.
  # C6: the QC medians are numeric and named; sample is the only categorical column.
  - id: cluster_qc_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Quality profile per cluster
    roles:
      index: cluster_label
      value_columns: [median_n_umi, median_n_genes, median_pct_mito, pct_flagged, pct_cellbender_cell]
      row_annotation_cols: [sample]
    config:
      normalize: col_z
    description: >-
      Each row is a cluster and each column a quality measure: median UMIs, median genes,
      median mitochondrial share, share of flagged cells and share kept by CellBender. It
      answers which clusters differ in quality from the rest.

      How to read: colours are standardised per column, so a cluster that is dark in the UMI
      and gene columns and in the flagged column is a poor one. A cluster that stands out only
      on one measure usually reflects its cell type.

      Lines and annotations: no cut-off is drawn. Each column is scaled to a z-score over the
      clusters shown, so colours compare clusters and not absolute values.
  - id: cluster_composition
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Cluster composition per sample
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: pct_cells
      color: cluster_label
      barmode: stack
      labels: {sample: Sample, pct_cells: Cells (%), cluster_label: Cluster}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample and its segments are the share of its cells in each cluster. It
      answers whether the samples contribute evenly to every cluster.

      How to read: similar stacks mean the samples have the same composition. A cluster
      present in only one sample may be a batch effect or real biology, so check the sample
      metadata.
  - id: cluster_size_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: n_cells
    title: Cluster size range
    description: >-
      Keeps the clusters whose cell count falls inside the range. It answers how the tab looks
      without very small or very large clusters.

      How to read: raise the lower handle to hide the smallest clusters.
  - component: card
    column: n_cells
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: cluster_label
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: cells, in the largest clusters
    title: Cells in clusters
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of cells over all clusters and the bars rank the largest
      clusters. It answers where most of the cells sit.

      How to read: the median gives the size of a typical cluster, and a maximum far above it
      shows a dominant one.
  - component: card
    column: median_n_umi
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: cluster UMI medians, with their spread
    title: UMI counts per cluster
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of the clusters' median UMI counts, and the box shows
      their spread. It answers whether the clusters have similar depth.

      How to read: a cluster far below the rest is shallower, either by cell type or by poor
      quality. Compare it with the mitochondrial and flagged shares.
  - component: card
    column: pct_flagged
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 100.0
    caption: cells flagged, of 100%
    title: Flagged cells
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average percent of cells per cluster that the quality filter
      flags, shown out of 100 percent. It answers how many cells the filter would remove.

      How to read: the maximum is the worst cluster. A cluster with a high share is a candidate
      artefact, and the rule is the median absolute deviation limit set per sample.

      Source: https://www.sc-best-practices.org/preprocessing-visualization/quality-control/
  - component: card
    column: pct_cellbender_cell
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 100.0
    caption: cells kept by CellBender, of 100%
    title: Cells kept by CellBender
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average percent of a cluster's cells that CellBender also calls
      cells, shown out of 100 percent. It answers how well the ambient-RNA correction agrees
      with the called cells.

      How to read: values near 100 mean agreement. The minimum names the cluster that loses
      most cells, which may be mostly ambient RNA.
  - component: table
    title: Cluster summary
    description: >-
      Each row is a cluster with its cell count, share of the sample, median counts and genes,
      median mitochondrial share, flagged share and share kept by CellBender. It answers the
      exact values behind the tiles.

      How to read: sort by a column to rank the clusters on that measure.

id: cellranger_diffexp
name: Cluster marker genes
mode: analysis/diffexp
description: >-
  Top marker genes per graph-based cluster (cluster vs every other cell),
  ranked by adjusted p-value: log2 fold change, mean counts and
  significance.
find:
  path_glob: "**/analysis/diffexp/gene_expression_graphclust/differential_expression.csv"
recipe: cellranger/diffexp.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 18 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several clusters.
fixture: diffexp.tsv
renders_as:
  # Cell Ranger publishes no cut-off for its marker tests. The lines below are the
  # recipe's own labelling cut-off (`_LABEL_PADJ_MAX = 0.05` in diffexp.py, no
  # fold-change line), not a Cell Ranger call, and the descriptions say so.
  - id: cluster_markers
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: da_barplot
    title: Top markers per cluster
    roles: {feature_id: gene, contrast: cluster, lfc: log2fc, significance: adjusted_pvalue, label: gene}
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_label: Log2 fold change
      top_n: 10
    description: >-
      Each bar is a gene: its log2 fold change in one cluster against all other cells, for the
      genes with the largest change. It answers which genes characterise each cluster.

      How to read: long bars to the right are markers of that cluster. Bars are marked when
      their adjusted p-value passes the display limit, and a strong change without it usually
      comes from very few cells.

      Lines and annotations: the limit is an adjusted p-value of 0.05, the cut-off this
      module's recipe uses to label marker genes, not read from the run. Cell Ranger defines
      no cut-off for its marker tests.
  - id: cluster_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Marker volcano per cluster
    roles: {feature_id: gene, effect_size: log2fc, significance: adjusted_pvalue, category: cluster_label, label: gene}
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 0.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Log2 fold change
      significance_label: -log10 adjusted p-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene tested in one cluster against all other cells: its log2 fold change
      on the horizontal axis and its adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers which
      genes separate a cluster and how confidently.

      How to read: genes in the upper right are strong, confident markers of the cluster, and
      genes in the upper left are depleted in it. Only the most significant genes per cluster
      are kept, so the lower part of the plot is truncated.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an adjusted p-value of 0.05, the cut-off
      this module's recipe uses to label marker genes, not read from the run. No fold-change
      line is drawn, because Cell Ranger defines no cut-off for its marker tests.
  - component: card
    column: log2fc
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: cluster
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: strongest marker fold change, by cluster
    title: Strongest marker per cluster
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest log2 fold change among the marker genes, and the bars
      rank the clusters with the strongest marker. It answers which clusters are most clearly
      defined.

      How to read: a cluster with a high top marker is well separated from the others. A low
      value means its markers are weak, so its identity is less clear.
  - id: diffexp_resolution_picker
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: Select
    column_name: resolution
    title: Clustering resolution
    description: >-
      Switches between the graph-based clustering and the k-means clusterings Cell Ranger
      ran. It answers how the markers change with the number of clusters.

      How to read: pick one clustering at a time, since a cluster name belongs to one of them.
  - component: card
    column: log2fc
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "pl.col('log2fc') > 0"
    caption: fold change of up-regulated markers, with its spread
    title: Fold change of up markers
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median log2 fold change of the marker genes that are higher in
      their cluster, and the box shows its spread. It answers how strong the up-regulated
      markers are.

      How to read: the card keeps only positive changes, because a median over both
      directions cancels to about zero. A high median means sharply defined clusters.
  - component: card
    column: mean_counts
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: mean counts of markers, with their spread
    title: Expression of markers
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of the mean UMI counts of the marker genes in their
      cluster, and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers whether the markers are
      expressed at a usable level.

      How to read: a pile near zero means markers detected in few counts, which are less
      reliable for annotating a cluster.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene
    title: Cluster marker genes
    description: >-
      Each row is a marker gene of one cluster with its rank, mean counts, log2 fold change
      and adjusted p-value. It answers the exact statistics behind the plots and lets a row
      selection filter the others.

      How to read: sort by rank within a cluster to read its best markers first.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: cellranger_embedding
name: Cell embeddings and clusters
mode: analysis/embedding
description: >-
  UMAP, t-SNE and the first 3 principal components of every cell, coloured
  by Cell Ranger's graph-based cluster.
find:
  path_glob: "**/analysis/clustering/gene_expression_graphclust/clusters.csv"
recipe: cellranger/embedding.py
fixture: embedding.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: umap_clusters
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: UMAP of the cells
    roles: {sample_id: barcode, dim_1: umap_1, dim_2: umap_2, cluster: cluster, color: cluster}
    config:
      axis_prefix: UMAP
    description: >-
      Each point is a cell placed by UMAP and coloured by its graph-based cluster. It answers
      how the cells group by expression.

      How to read: separate islands are distinct populations and touching islands are related
      states. Distances between far islands are not reliable, so judge membership and not
      distance.
  - id: tsne_clusters
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: t-SNE of the cells

outputs.description: Mean expression against normalised dispersion for every gene Cell Ranger measured, flagged with whether it kept the gene for the PCA. The feature selection step behind every embedding on the dashboard, and the answer to why a gene is missing from one.
outputs.name: Highly variable genes
outputs.rawYaml:
id: cellranger_hvg_dispersion
name: Highly variable genes
mode: analysis/hvg_dispersion
description: >-
  Mean expression against normalised dispersion for every gene Cell Ranger
  measured, flagged with whether it kept the gene for the PCA. The feature
  selection step behind every embedding on the dashboard, and the answer to
  why a gene is missing from one.
find:
  path_glob: "**/analysis/pca/*/dispersion.csv"
recipe: cellranger/hvg_dispersion.py
fixture: hvg_dispersion.tsv
renders_as:
  # Cell Ranger keeps the top genes by normalised dispersion for the PCA, a rule of
  # its own; the colour shows that selection and no line is drawn for it.
  - id: hvg_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Gene dispersion against mean expression
    roles: {x: mean_expression, y: normalized_dispersion, color: selection, label: gene}
    config:
      x_title: Mean expression (log1p CP10k)
      y_title: Normalised dispersion
      top_n_labels: 10
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene: its mean expression over the cells on the horizontal axis and its
      normalised dispersion on the vertical axis, coloured by whether it was kept for the PCA.
      It answers which genes vary more than expected for their level of expression.

      How to read: the selected genes should sit high above the cloud, since they carry the
      variation between cell types. Selected genes at very low expression may add noise, and
      known markers missing from the selection are worth a look.

      Lines and annotations: no line is drawn. The selection is the set Cell Ranger kept
      for its PCA, and normalised dispersion scales each gene's dispersion by that of genes
      with similar mean expression.

      Source: https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/generated/scanpy.pp.highly_variable_genes.html
  - id: hvg_selection_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: Select
    column_name: selection
    title: Selection status
    description: >-
      Keeps the genes selected for the PCA or the ones left out. It answers what the selection
      kept and dropped.

      How to read: choose selected to list the genes that shaped the embedding.
  - id: hvg_dispersion_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: normalized_dispersion
    title: Normalised dispersion range
    description: >-
      Keeps the genes whose normalised dispersion falls inside the range. It answers which
      genes vary most.

      How to read: raise the lower handle to keep only the most variable genes.
  - component: card
    column: gene
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: selection
    top_n_count: 2
    caption: genes, by selection status
    title: Genes by selection
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct genes measured and the bars compare the selected
      and the other genes. It answers how many genes shaped the embedding.

      How to read: a small selected set against a large rest is the usual design. A very small
      set means few genes carry the variation.
  - component: card
    column: normalized_dispersion
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats, max]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: normalised dispersion, with its spread
    title: Normalised dispersion
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median normalised dispersion of the genes, and the box shows its
      spread. It answers how variable the typical gene is.

      How to read: dispersion is scaled so a typical gene sits near zero and variable genes lie
      far above it. The maximum names the most variable gene.

      Source: https://scanpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/generated/scanpy.pp.highly_variable_genes.html
  - component: card
    column: detection_rate
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: share of cells detecting a gene
    title: Detection rate of genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average share of cells in which a gene has at least one UMI, and
      the histogram shows the distribution over genes. It answers how widely genes are
      detected.

      How to read: most genes are detected in few cells, which is normal for sparse
      single-cell data. A selected gene with a very low rate drives variation from a few
      cells.
  - component: table
    title: Gene dispersion table
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene with its normalised dispersion, mean expression, detection rate and
      whether it was selected. It answers the exact values behind the plot.

      How to read: sort by dispersion to list the most variable genes.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: cellranger_library_metrics_long
name: Library QC metrics, thresholded
mode: count/library_metrics_long
description: >-
  The 4 headline Cell Ranger metrics for which 10x's QC guidance (technical
  note CG000329) gives an expected value, one row per (sample, metric), with
  the threshold and the status it crosses. Sequencing saturation has no 10x
  expected value and is not thresholded.
find:
  path_glob: "**/metrics_summary.csv"
recipe: cellranger/library_metrics_long.py
fixture: library_metrics_long.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: library_metric_picker
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: Select
    column_name: metric
    title: Library metric
    description: >-
      Shows one library quality metric at a time. It answers how every sample does on that
      metric.

      How to read: clear the selection to list the four metrics again.
  - id: library_status_picker
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: SegmentedControl
    column_name: status
    title: Metric status
    description: >-
      Keeps the metrics that pass or the ones that fall below their expected value. It
      answers which samples need attention.

      How to read: choose warn or fail to list only the metrics below their limit.
  - component: card
    column: metric
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: status
    caption: metrics, by status
    title: Library metrics by status
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of metric values checked and the bar splits them into pass,
      warn and fail. It answers how many checks the libraries meet.

      How to read: a bar that is mostly pass means healthy libraries. Open the table to see
      which sample and metric fell below its limit.

      Lines and annotations: each status compares a value with the expected value 10x gives for
      that metric: reads in cells above 70 percent, valid barcodes above 75 percent, Q30 of RNA
      reads above 65 percent and confidently mapped reads above 30 percent. The split between
      warn and fail is chosen by this catalogue, since the note states one expected value.

      Source: https://assets.ctfassets.net/an68im79xiti/163qWiQBTVi2YLbskJphQX/e90bb82151b1cdab6d7e9b6c845e6130/CG000329_TechnicalNote_InterpretingCellRangerWebSummaryFiles_RevA.pdf
  - component: card
    column: value
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.7
    threshold_direction: min
    filter_expr: "pl.col('metric') == 'fraction_reads_in_cells'"
    caption: reads in cells against the 70% expectation
    title: Reads in cells
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average fraction of reads that fall in called cells, shown against
      the expected minimum. It answers whether the library is rich in cells and poor in ambient
      RNA.

      How to read: a value below the line means many reads come from empty droplets. Check the
      barcode rank plot and the ambient RNA before trusting the counts.

      Lines and annotations: the line is 0.7, the value 10x lists as expected for the fraction
      of reads in cells.

      Source: https://assets.ctfassets.net/an68im79xiti/163qWiQBTVi2YLbskJphQX/e90bb82151b1cdab6d7e9b6c845e6130/CG000329_TechnicalNote_InterpretingCellRangerWebSummaryFiles_RevA.pdf
  - component: card
    column: value
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.75
    threshold_direction: min
    filter_expr: "pl.col('metric') == 'valid_barcodes'"
    caption: valid barcodes against the 75% expectation
    title: Valid barcodes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average fraction of reads whose barcode matches the whitelist,
      shown against the expected minimum. It answers whether the barcode reads are of good
      quality.

      How to read: a value below the line points to a sequencing or chemistry problem with the
      barcode read. Look at the Q30 of the barcode in the summary table.

      Lines and annotations: the line is 0.75, the value 10x lists as expected for valid
      barcodes.

      Source: https://assets.ctfassets.net/an68im79xiti/163qWiQBTVi2YLbskJphQX/e90bb82151b1cdab6d7e9b6c845e6130/CG000329_TechnicalNote_InterpretingCellRangerWebSummaryFiles_RevA.pdf
  - component: table
    title: Library metrics against expectations
    description: >-
      Each row is one metric of one sample with its value, the expected limit and a pass, warn
      or fail status. It answers which sample falls short on which metric.

      How to read: filter on status to list the metrics below their limit.

      Source: https://assets.ctfassets.net/an68im79xiti/163qWiQBTVi2YLbskJphQX/e90bb82151b1cdab6d7e9b6c845e6130/CG000329_TechnicalNote_InterpretingCellRangerWebSummaryFiles_RevA.pdf

outputs.rawYaml:
id: checkm2_quality_report
name: Bin completeness and contamination
mode: quality-report
description: >-
  How much of a genome each bin holds and how much of it belongs to something
  else. Completeness against contamination is the plot metagenome binning is
  read on: the top-left corner holds the bins worth naming, the right-hand side
  holds chimeras, and the spread between binners on the same assembly says which
  binner to trust for this sample.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_checkm2_report.tsv"
  path_glob_alt:
    # CheckM2's own output name, kept when a pipeline publishes the run
    # directory instead of the renamed copy.
    - "**/CheckM2/**/quality_report.tsv"
    - "**/checkm2/**/quality_report.tsv"
recipe: checkm2/quality_report.py
fixture: quality_report.tsv
renders_as:
  # The canonical MAG plot. Size by genome_size so a complete-looking 300 kb bin
  # cannot pass for a complete-looking 3 Mb one. The quadrant lines are the MIMAG
  # completeness (50%) and contamination (10%) limits of a medium-quality draft
  # (Bowers et al. 2017, checked in the full text on Europe PMC).
  - id: completeness_contamination
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Completeness against contamination
    roles: {x: completeness, y: contamination, label: bin_id, color: binner, size: genome_size}
    config:
      x_title: Completeness (%)
      y_title: Contamination (%)
      top_n_labels: 5
      quadrants:
        x: 50
        y: 10
        labels: [Incomplete and contaminated, Contaminated, Low quality, Medium quality or better]
    description: >-
      Each point is a bin: its predicted completeness on the horizontal axis and its
      predicted contamination on the vertical axis, coloured by binner and sized by
      genome size. It answers which bins are worth keeping and which binner delivers
      them.

      How to read: the bottom right corner holds the bins worth naming, and the top
      half holds chimeric bins with sequences from more than one organism. Compare the
      colours to see which binner produces more bins in the good corner for this
      assembly. A large point is a bin with a genome-sized sequence, so a small
      complete-looking point deserves a second look.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical line is a completeness of 50% and the
      horizontal line a contamination of 10%, the limits of a medium-quality draft in
      the MIMAG standard. A high-quality draft needs over 90% completeness and under 5%
      contamination plus rRNA and tRNA genes that CheckM2 does not count. CheckM2
      predicts both values with machine-learning models, so they are estimates.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/ and
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chklovski/CheckM2/main/README.md
  # Assembly statistics behind the verdict: a bin with a good score and a tiny
  # N50 is a collection of fragments that happen to carry the right genes.
  - id: n50_completeness
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Contiguity against completeness
    roles: {x: contig_n50, y: completeness, label: bin_id, color: assembler, size: genome_size}
    config:
      x_title: Contig N50 (bp)
      y_title: Completeness (%)
      log_x: true
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_value: 50
      reference_label: 50% complete (MIMAG medium)
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a bin: the N50 of its contigs on a logarithmic horizontal axis and
      its predicted completeness on the vertical axis, coloured by assembler and sized
      by genome size. It answers whether a bin that looks complete is also contiguous.

      How to read: points at the top right are complete and made of long contigs. A
      complete bin with a small N50 is a collection of fragments that happen to carry
      the right genes, so it is a weaker genome. Compare the colours to see which
      assembler gives longer contigs.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a completeness of 50%, the lower
      limit of a medium-quality draft in the MIMAG standard. No N50 cut-off is drawn,
      because the standard sets none.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: completeness
      color: binner
      labels: {completeness: Completeness (%), binner: Binner}
    title: Completeness distribution per binner
    reference_lines: [{axis: x, stat: median, column: completeness}]
    description: >-
      Each bar counts bins in a completeness band, split by binner. It answers whether
      a binner returns mostly complete bins or mostly fragments.

      How to read: a binner with its bars at the right produces more complete bins. A
      pile at low completeness is many partial bins. The MIMAG limit of 50% for a
      medium-quality draft is drawn on the scatter tile, not here.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median completeness of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of CheckM2.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: binner
      y: quality_score
      color: assembler
      labels: {binner: Binner, quality_score: Bin quality score, assembler: Assembler}
    title: Bin quality score by binner and assembler
    reference_lines: [{axis: y, stat: median, column: quality_score}]
    description: >-
      Each box is the spread of bin quality scores for one binner and assembler. The
      score is completeness minus five times contamination, defined by this catalog
      module. It answers which binner and assembler combination yields the best bins.

      How to read: a higher box means better bins, and a box reaching below zero holds
      bins whose contamination outweighs their completeness. With few bins per group
      the boxes are only indicative, so open the table for the individual values.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median bin quality score of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of CheckM2.
  # One row per bin: the count is the number of bins, the ring splits them by tier.
  - id: tier_donut
    component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: quality_tier
    caption: bins, by quality tier
    title: Bins by quality tier
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of bins, the second number counts the samples they
      come from, and the ring splits the bins by quality tier. It answers how many
      bins reach each tier.

      How to read: a ring dominated by high and medium quality means a good binning
      run. Contaminated is this catalog's label for bins with 10% contamination or
      more.

      Lines and annotations: the tiers use the MIMAG completeness and contamination
      limits: high is over 90% complete and under 5% contaminated, medium at least 50%
      and under 10%, and low under 50% and under 10%. The rRNA and tRNA requirements
      of a full high-quality draft are not checked here.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: card
    column: completeness
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Completeness
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median predicted completeness of the bins, and the box
      shows the spread. It answers how much of a genome a typical bin holds.

      How to read: a median near 100% means the bins are nearly whole genomes. A wide
      box means some bins are fragments, so open the scatter to see them. The MIMAG
      limits of 50% and 90% are drawn on the scatter tile.
  # MIMAG allows under 10% contamination in a medium-quality draft; the pass band
  # counts bins on each side of it.
  - component: card
    column: contamination
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 10
    threshold_direction: max
    caption: bins under and over 10% contamination
    title: Contamination
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median predicted contamination of the bins, with the
      highest bin below it, and the strip counts the bins under and over the limit. It
      answers how many bins stay clean enough to use.

      How to read: a low median with a high maximum means most bins are clean and a few
      are chimeras, which should be removed or refined. Contamination is the share of
      marker-like content found more than once.

      Lines and annotations: the limit is a contamination of 10%, the upper bound of a
      medium-quality draft in the MIMAG standard, which asks for under 5% for a
      high-quality one.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: card
    column: quality_score
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: best bin, with the spread of all bins
    title: Best bin score
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest quality score of any bin, and the box shows the
      spread over all bins. The score is completeness minus five times contamination,
      defined by this catalog module. It answers how good the best bin is and how far
      the others lag.

      How to read: a best score far above the median means a few good bins among many
      poor ones. A score below zero means contamination outweighs completeness.
  - component: card
    column: genome_size
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: genome size of every bin
    title: Genome size
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median bin genome size in base pairs, with the smallest
      and largest below it, and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how
      large the recovered genomes are.

      How to read: sizes cover a wide range because bins can be fragments or whole
      genomes. A bin far larger than its neighbours may merge several organisms, so
      compare it with its contamination.
  - component: card
    column: coding_density
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: coding density of every bin
    title: Coding density
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean coding density, the fraction of the genome that
      codes for proteins, with the lowest and highest bin below it, and the histogram
      shows the distribution. It answers whether the bins look like typical genomes.

      How to read: prokaryotic genomes are usually densely coding, so a low value
      suggests fragmented or non-coding content. No cut-off is drawn, because
      CheckM2 and the MIMAG standard set none for it.
  - component: table
    title: Bin quality table
    description: >-
      Each row is a bin with its predicted completeness and contamination, quality
      score and tier, and the assembly statistics CheckM2 reports: coding density,
      contig N50, genome size, GC content and gene count. It answers the exact values
      behind every tile of this view.

      How to read: sort by quality score to rank the bins, or filter by binner to
      compare methods.

renders_as.description:
Each point is a bin: its predicted completeness on the horizontal axis and its predicted contamination on the vertical axis, coloured by binner and sized by genome size. It answers which bins are worth keeping and which binner delivers them.
How to read: the bottom right corner holds the bins worth naming, and the top half holds chimeric bins with sequences from more than one organism. Compare the colours to see which binner produces more bins in the good corner for this assembly. A large point is a bin with a genome-sized sequence, so a small complete-looking point deserves a second look.
Lines and annotations: the vertical line is a completeness of 50% and the horizontal line a contamination of 10%, the limits of a medium-quality draft in the MIMAG standard. A high-quality draft needs over 90% completeness and under 5% contamination plus rRNA and tRNA genes that CheckM2 does not count. CheckM2 predicts both values with machine-learning models, so they are estimates.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/ and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chklovski/CheckM2/main/README.md
renders_as.title: Completeness against contamination

renders_as.description:
Each point is a bin: the N50 of its contigs on a logarithmic horizontal axis and its predicted completeness on the vertical axis, coloured by assembler and sized by genome size. It answers whether a bin that looks complete is also contiguous.
How to read: points at the top right are complete and made of long contigs. A complete bin with a small N50 is a collection of fragments that happen to carry the right genes, so it is a weaker genome. Compare the colours to see which assembler gives longer contigs.
Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a completeness of 50%, the lower limit of a medium-quality draft in the MIMAG standard. No N50 cut-off is drawn, because the standard sets none.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
renders_as.title: Contiguity against completeness

renders_as.description:
Each bar counts bins in a completeness band, split by binner. It answers whether a binner returns mostly complete bins or mostly fragments.
How to read: a binner with its bars at the right produces more complete bins. A pile at low completeness is many partial bins. The MIMAG limit of 50% for a medium-quality draft is drawn on the scatter tile, not here.
Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median completeness of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of CheckM2.
renders_as.title: Completeness distribution per binner

renders_as.description:
Each box is the spread of bin quality scores for one binner and assembler. The score is completeness minus five times contamination, defined by this catalog module. It answers which binner and assembler combination yields the best bins.
How to read: a higher box means better bins, and a box reaching below zero holds bins whose contamination outweighs their completeness. With few bins per group the boxes are only indicative, so open the table for the individual values.
Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median bin quality score of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of CheckM2.
renders_as.title: Bin quality score by binner and assembler

renders_as.caption: bins, by quality tier
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the count of bins, the second number counts the samples they come from, and the ring splits the bins by quality tier. It answers how many bins reach each tier.
How to read: a ring dominated by high and medium quality means a good binning run. Contaminated is this catalog's label for bins with 10% contamination or more.
Lines and annotations: the tiers use the MIMAG completeness and contamination limits: high is over 90% complete and under 5% contaminated, medium at least 50% and under 10%, and low under 50% and under 10%. The rRNA and tRNA requirements of a full high-quality draft are not checked here.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
renders_as.title: Bins by quality tier

renders_as.caption: median, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median predicted completeness of the bins, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much of a genome a typical bin holds.
How to read: a median near 100% means the bins are nearly whole genomes. A wide box means some bins are fragments, so open the scatter to see them. The MIMAG limits of 50% and 90% are drawn on the scatter tile.
renders_as.title: Completeness

renders_as.caption: bins under and over 10% contamination
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median predicted contamination of the bins, with the highest bin below it, and the strip counts the bins under and over the limit. It answers how many bins stay clean enough to use.
How to read: a low median with a high maximum means most bins are clean and a few are chimeras, which should be removed or refined. Contamination is the share of marker-like content found more than once.
Lines and annotations: the limit is a contamination of 10%, the upper bound of a medium-quality draft in the MIMAG standard, which asks for under 5% for a high-quality one.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
renders_as.title: Contamination

renders_as.caption: best bin, with the spread of all bins
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the highest quality score of any bin, and the box shows the spread over all bins. The score is completeness minus five times contamination, defined by this catalog module. It answers how good the best bin is and how far the others lag.
How to read: a best score far above the median means a few good bins among many poor ones. A score below zero means contamination outweighs completeness.
renders_as.title: Best bin score

renders_as.caption: genome size of every bin
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median bin genome size in base pairs, with the smallest and largest below it, and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how large the recovered genomes are.
How to read: sizes cover a wide range because bins can be fragments or whole genomes. A bin far larger than its neighbours may merge several organisms, so compare it with its contamination.
renders_as.title: Genome size

renders_as.caption: coding density of every bin
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the mean coding density, the fraction of the genome that codes for proteins, with the lowest and highest bin below it, and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers whether the bins look like typical genomes.
How to read: prokaryotic genomes are usually densely coding, so a low value suggests fragmented or non-coding content. No cut-off is drawn, because CheckM2 and the MIMAG standard set none for it.
renders_as.title: Coding density

renders_as.description:
Each row is a bin with its predicted completeness and contamination, quality score and tier, and the assembly statistics CheckM2 reports: coding density, contig N50, genome size, GC content and gene count. It answers the exact values behind every tile of this view.
How to read: sort by quality score to rank the bins, or filter by binner to compare methods.
renders_as.title: Bin quality table

id: checkv_quality_summary

renders_as:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=../output.schema.json
id: cnvkit_cnv_profile
name: Copy-number profile
mode: batch
description: >-
  CNVkit's bin-level copy ratios and its called segments in one long table.
  Per CNVkit's file-format documentation the .cnr file carries chromosome,
  start, end, gene, depth, log2 and weight, one row per bin, and the .cns file
  carries chromosome, start, end, gene, log2, depth, probes and weight, one row
  per segment, with cn and baf added when cnvkit call has run. The two are
  folded together and told apart by the segment column, so one component draws
  the evidence and the call on the same axis.
find:
  path_glob: "**/variant_calling/cnvkit/*/*.cnr"
recipe: cnvkit/cnv_profile.py
fixture: cnv_profile.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: cnvkit_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: cnv_profile
    title: Copy-number profile
    roles: {sample: sample, chrom: chrom, start: start, end: end, log2: log2, baf: baf, copy_number: copy_number, segment: segment, label: label}
    config:
      gain_threshold: 0.2
      loss_threshold: -0.25
      y_range: 3.0
    description: >-
      Each dot is a genomic bin: its log2 copy ratio against the reference along the chromosomes, with the
      called segments drawn over the bins and coloured by their integer copy number, and the B-allele
      frequency of each segment underneath when it is known. It answers which regions of the genome are
      gained or lost in a sample.

      How to read: a log2 ratio near zero is a neutral, two-copy region. Segments above the gain line are
      gains and segments below the loss line are losses, and a deep drop is a possible homozygous deletion.
      Bins scattered widely around a segment mean a noisy sample, so check the bin depth card before
      trusting small segments.

      Lines and annotations: the gain line at a log2 ratio of 0.2 and the loss line at -0.25 are the inner
      cut-offs of the default thresholds of cnvkit call, chosen to detect a single-copy change in a diploid
      tumour at a purity as low as 30%. They assume a diploid genome and are rescaled by purity when it is
      given.

      Sources: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/pipeline.html and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27100738/
  - id: cnvkit_log2_spread
    component: card
    column: log2
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('segment') == 'bin'"
    caption: bin log2 ratio, with its spread
    title: Copy-ratio spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of the bin-level log2 copy ratios, and the box shows their quartiles. It
      answers how far the bins stray from a neutral ratio.

      How to read: a box tight around zero with a few extreme bins means a mostly neutral genome with a few
      alterations. A wide box means a noisy sample or many copy-number changes. The range is shown instead of
      a median, because gains and losses cancel to about zero.

      Lines and annotations: bins are the rows of the copy ratio file, one per genomic bin, with segments
      left out.

      Source: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/fileformats.html
  - id: cnvkit_bin_depth
    component: card
    column: depth
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [q1, q3]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    filter_expr: "col('segment') == 'bin'"
    caption: bin depth, with its distribution
    title: Bin depth
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median read depth of the bins, with the quartiles beside it and the histogram of
      the depths below. It answers whether the sample is covered deeply enough for reliable calls.

      How to read: a narrow histogram of depths means even coverage. CNVkit documentation notes that larger
      alterations are called reliably down to about 10x on-target coverage, with more spurious segments
      below that. A long tail of low-depth bins is noisy.

      Lines and annotations: the 10x figure in the documentation concerns on-target coverage, and no line is
      drawn for it here.

      Source: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/pipeline.html
  - component: table
    columns: [sample, chrom, start, end, log2, copy_number, segment, label]
    title: Bins and segments table
    description: >-
      Each row is a bin or a called segment with its position, log2 copy ratio, integer copy number and the
      gene label CNVkit gives it. It answers the exact values behind the profile.

      How to read: filter the segment column to segments to list the calls, then sort by log2 to find the strongest gains and losses.

      Source: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/fileformats.html and
      https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/pipeline.html
