id: combgc_region_track
name: BGC region coordinates
mode: bgc/track
description: >-
  The comBGC regions as coordinates rather than counts: contig, interval,
  product class and region length in kilobases, one row per predicted cluster.
  Three tracks read the same rows, so a run whose genome renderer is
  unavailable still has the lane view and the density profile.
find: { path_glob: "**/combgc/combgc_complete_summary.tsv" }
recipe: combgc/region_track.py
fixture: region_track.tsv
renders_as:
  # The regions on a genome axis, as intervals rather than points: `rect`
  # needs `end_col`, which is what turns each row into the cluster's real
  # footprint on the contig instead of a tick at its start.
  # C3 N/A: no caller or consensus defines a cut-off on region length.
  - id: bgc_genome_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Cluster regions on the contigs
    roles: {chr: contig, pos: start, score: length_kb, feature: region_id, end: end, category: product_class}
    config:
      score_title: Region length (kb)
    description: >-
      Each interval is a predicted biosynthetic gene cluster placed on its contig, with its height giving the region length in kilobases and its colour the product class. It answers where on the assembly the clusters sit and which kinds they are.

      How to read: several clusters on one contig suggest a biosynthetic locus, and a cluster covering a whole short contig is probably truncated by the contig edge. Compare the classes: a contig that carries several different ones is a promising place to look first.

      Note: callers disagree on region boundaries by design, so the same locus can appear as differently sized intervals. No cut-off on region length is published, so no line is drawn.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  # The same intervals as arrows in one lane per contig, re-parameterising the
  # pattern the ARG island track uses: several clusters packed onto one contig
  # is a biosynthetic locus, which an aggregate over product classes hides.
  - id: bgc_region_arrows
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: gene_arrow_track
    title: Clusters as lanes per contig
    roles: {contig: contig, feature_id: region_id, start: start, end: end, strand: strand, class: product_class, label: product_class}
    description: >-
      Each arrow is a predicted cluster drawn along its contig, one lane per contig and coloured by product class. It answers how clusters are arranged along a contig.

      How to read: arrows packed next to each other mark a dense biosynthetic locus, and different colours in one lane mean a contig with several kinds of cluster. Overlapping arrows on a locus are usually the same cluster called by different tools.

      Note: comBGC does not report a strand, so arrows carry no direction.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  # Fallback on the same collection: a plain coordinate profile that needs no
  # genome renderer, so the tab is never empty.
  - id: bgc_region_coverage
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Region length along the contigs
    roles: {chromosome: contig, position: start, value: length_kb, end: end, sample: sample, category: product_class}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a predicted cluster on a contig, as tall as the region is long in kilobases and coloured by product class, with samples shown separately. It answers how long the predicted clusters are and where they fall.

      How to read: very short regions sitting at the start of a contig are often fragments cut by the contig edge, while long ones are more likely to be full clusters. Use it where the genome tracks are unavailable.

      Note: no cut-off on region length is published, so no line is drawn.
  - id: region_length
    component: card
    column: length_kb
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: product_class
    top_n_count: 4
    title: Typical cluster length
    caption: median length (kb), by product class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median region length in kilobases, and the bars rank the product classes by their own median. It answers how long clusters are and which classes are the longest.

      How to read: the minimum and maximum show how much lengths vary, which is wide because regions run from a few genes to whole megacomplexes. Regions cut by a contig edge pull the median down.
  - id: region_count
    component: card
    column: cds_count
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: product_class
    top_n_count: 4
    title: Predicted clusters
    caption: clusters, by product class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the number of predicted clusters, the bars rank the product classes by how many clusters each has, and the line below gives the typical and largest gene count. It answers which kinds of cluster dominate.

      How to read: a leading class is the main biosynthetic potential of the sample. Classes named Unknown or with a generic label come from callers that do not type every region.
  - component: table
    title: Cluster coordinates
    description: >-
      One row per predicted cluster with its contig, interval, product class and length. Selecting rows filters the tab to that contig.

      How to read: sort by length to find the largest clusters.
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: contig

outputs.name: BGC regions
outputs.rawYaml:
id: combgc_summary
name: BGC regions
mode: bgc/regions
description: >-
  One row per predicted biosynthetic gene cluster, with the caller, product
  class, region coordinates, CDS count and PFAM domain richness normalised
  across antiSMASH, DeepBGC and GECCO.
find: { path_glob: "**/combgc/combgc_complete_summary.tsv" }
recipe: combgc/summary.py
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: bgc_hierarchy
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Callers and product classes
    roles: {ranks: [tool, product_class], abundance: regions}
    config:
      colour_by_rank: tool
    description: >-
      Each arc is a group of predicted clusters: the inner ring is the prediction tool and the outer ring the product class, sized by the number of clusters and coloured by tool. It answers which caller contributes which kinds of cluster.

      How to read: a wide arc under one caller only means that caller alone detects the class. Class names are not shared between callers, so the same kind of cluster can appear under different names. Click an arc to zoom in on it.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  - id: regions_per_sample
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Clusters per sample
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: regions
      color: product_class
      labels:
        sample: Sample
        regions: Predicted clusters
        product_class: Product class
    description: >-
      Each bar is the number of predicted clusters in one sample, split by product class. It answers how rich each sample is in biosynthetic gene clusters and of which kinds.

      How to read: a tall bar with several classes means a sample with diverse potential. Differences between samples may follow assembly size and caller sensitivity as much as biology, so compare with care.
  - id: cluster_count
    component: card
    column: product_class
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: product_class
    top_n_count: 4
    headline: true
    title: Predicted clusters
    caption: clusters, by product class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the number of predicted clusters, the bars rank the product classes by how many clusters each has, and the line below gives the number of distinct classes. It answers how many clusters were found and which kinds lead.

      How to read: a leading class is the main biosynthetic potential. Many distinct classes with a few clusters each mean a diverse but shallow profile.
  - id: contigs_with_clusters
    component: card
    column: contig
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: tool
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Contigs with clusters
    caption: contigs, by prediction tool
    description: >-
      The hero number is the number of distinct contigs holding at least one predicted cluster, the bars rank the callers by how many contigs each reports, and the line below gives the cluster count. It answers how widely clusters are spread over the assembly.

      How to read: more clusters than contigs means several clusters share a contig. A caller reporting far fewer contigs than the others is more conservative.
  - id: cluster_length
    component: card
    column: length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: tool
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Typical cluster length
    caption: median length (bp), by prediction tool
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median cluster length in base pairs, and the bars rank the callers by their own median. It answers how long the predicted regions are and whether callers draw them alike.

      How to read: callers disagree on region boundaries by design, so a systematically longer median for one tool reflects how it sets edges. Lengths span orders of magnitude, so read the minimum and maximum beside the median.
  - id: cds_per_cluster
    component: card
    column: cds_count
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Genes per cluster
    caption: distribution of gene counts
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average number of coding sequences in a predicted cluster, and the histogram shows how the counts are distributed. It answers how large clusters are in genes.

      How to read: a pile of single-gene clusters means short or truncated regions. A long tail marks large, multi-gene biosynthetic clusters.
  - component: table
    title: Predicted clusters
    description: >-
      One row per predicted cluster with its caller, product class, coordinates, gene count and domain richness. Selecting rows filters the tab to that contig.

      How to read: sort by gene count or domain richness to find the most complex clusters.
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: contig

id: combgc_tool_overlap
name: Caller concordance
mode: bgc/concordance
description: >-
  Contig by caller membership matrix, one 0/1 column per BGC prediction tool.
  Agreement is scored on the contig: the callers disagree on region boundaries
  by design, so a coordinate join would report no overlap at all.

  - id: bgc_upset
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: upset_plot
    title: Caller concordance
    config:
      color_intersections_by: set
    description: >-
      Each bar is the number of contigs predicted to hold a cluster by one combination of callers, and the dots below show which callers. It answers which callers agree on a contig and which find clusters alone.

      How to read: tall bars of one caller alone mean clusters only that caller finds, and bars shared by all callers mark the most reliable calls. Little overlap is normal because callers use different methods.

      Note: agreement is scored on the contig, because callers set region boundaries differently and a coordinate join would report no overlap.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md

tools.description: Copy number and genotype annotation from whole genome and whole exome sequencing data.
tools.name: Control-FREEC

outputs.description: Control-FREEC's per-window copy ratios and the segments they encode. Per the Control-FREEC documentation the _ratio.txt file carries Chromosome, Start, Ratio, MedianRatio and CopyNumber, plus BAF, estimatedBAF, Genotype and UncertaintyOfGT when a SNV file was supplied. MedianRatio is the segment value written on every window the segment covers, so a run of identical values is one segment: the windows and the recovered segments land in the same table, told apart by the segment column.
outputs.name: Copy-number ratio windows
outputs.rawYaml:
# yaml-language-server: $schema=../output.schema.json
id: controlfreec_cnv_ratio
name: Copy-number ratio windows
mode: freec
description: >-
  Control-FREEC's per-window copy ratios and the segments they encode. Per the
  Control-FREEC documentation the _ratio.txt file carries Chromosome, Start,
  Ratio, MedianRatio and CopyNumber, plus BAF, estimatedBAF, Genotype and
  UncertaintyOfGT when a SNV file was supplied. MedianRatio is the segment
  value written on every window the segment covers, so a run of identical
  values is one segment: the windows and the recovered segments land in the
  same table, told apart by the segment column.
find:
  path_glob: "**/variant_calling/controlfreec/*/*_ratio.txt"
recipe: controlfreec/cnv_ratio.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 9 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: cnv_ratio.tsv
renders_as:
  # Control-FREEC gives copy number as ratio x ploidy, so for a diploid sample a
  # gain to 3 copies sits at ratio 1.5 and a loss to 1 copy at ratio 0.5. The tile
  # marks the log2 of the midpoints between neighbouring states (2.5/2 and 1.5/2),
  # derived for ploidy 2, in place of the tile's default of 0.3.
  - id: controlfreec_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: cnv_profile
    title: Copy number profile
    roles: {sample: sample, chrom: chrom, start: start, end: end, log2: log2, baf: baf, copy_number: copy_number, segment: segment, label: label}
    config:
      gain_threshold: 0.32
      loss_threshold: -0.42
    description: >-
      Each point is a genomic window: its log2 copy ratio along the chromosomes, with the
      called segments drawn over it and the B-allele frequency underneath. It answers
      where the genome has gained or lost copies.

      How to read: windows around zero are copy neutral, and a run of windows shifted
      up or down forms a gain or a loss. Segments are coloured by the predicted copy
      number. A BAF split away from 0.5 on a shifted segment supports a real alteration
      and marks loss of heterozygosity.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed lines mark log2 ratios of 0.32 and -0.42, the
      midpoints between 2 and 3 copies and between 2 and 1 copies. They are an arithmetic
      reference from Control-FREEC's copy number as ratio times ploidy, taken at ploidy
      2, and not thresholds the tool uses to call.

      Note: Control-FREEC calls copy number from the ratio and the ploidy of the run,
      so for another ploidy or a subclonal sample these lines move.

      Source: http://boevalab.inf.ethz.ch/FREEC/tutorial.html
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22155870/
  # The windows only: the segment rows repeat the same ratio, and a spread over both
  # kinds would count the genome twice. A range is the hero because the median of a
  # log ratio over gains and losses cancels towards zero.
  - id: controlfreec_log2_spread
    component: card
    column: log2
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('segment') == 'bin'"
    caption: range, with the spread
    title: Log2 ratio spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of window log2 copy ratios, and the box shows their
      quartiles. It answers how far the genome departs from copy neutral.

      How to read: a box tight around zero with a long range means a mostly neutral
      genome with a few alterations. A box shifted off zero points to a wrong ploidy or
      normalisation, so check the profile.

      Source: http://boevalab.inf.ethz.ch/FREEC/tutorial.html
  - id: controlfreec_cn_mix
    component: card
    column: copy_number
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: copy_number
    filter_expr: "col('segment') == 'bin'"
    caption: windows, by predicted copy number
    title: Windows by copy number
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of windows, the bar splits them by the copy number
      Control-FREEC predicted, and the strip gives the median and highest copy number.
      It answers how much of the genome is neutral, gained or lost.

      How to read: a bar dominated by the neutral state means a quiet genome. Large shares
      of other copy numbers mean wide alterations or aneuploidy.

      Source: http://boevalab.inf.ethz.ch/FREEC/tutorial.html
  - component: table
    columns: [sample, chrom, start, end, log2, baf, copy_number, segment]
    title: Copy number windows
    description: >-
      Each row is a genomic window or a called segment, with its sample, chromosome,
      start and end, log2 ratio, B-allele frequency and predicted copy number. It
      answers the exact values behind the profile.

      How to read: filter by the segment column to list the called segments, or by
      chromosome to read one region window by window.

      Source: http://boevalab.inf.ethz.ch/FREEC/tutorial.html

renders_as.description:
Each point is a genomic window: its log2 copy ratio along the chromosomes, with the called segments drawn over it and the B-allele frequency underneath. It answers where the genome has gained or lost copies.
How to read: windows around zero are copy neutral, and a run of windows shifted up or down forms a gain or a loss. Segments are coloured by the predicted copy number. A BAF split away from 0.5 on a shifted segment supports a real alteration and marks loss of heterozygosity.
Lines and annotations: the dashed lines mark log2 ratios of 0.32 and -0.42, the midpoints between 2 and 3 copies and between 2 and 1 copies. They are an arithmetic reference from Control-FREEC's copy number as ratio times ploidy, taken at ploidy 2, and not thresholds the tool uses to call.
Note: Control-FREEC calls copy number from the ratio and the ploidy of the run, so for another ploidy or a subclonal sample these lines move.
Source: http://boevalab.inf.ethz.ch/FREEC/tutorial.html and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22155870/
renders_as.title: Copy number profile

renders_as.caption: range, with the spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the range of window log2 copy ratios, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how far the genome departs from copy neutral.
How to read: a box tight around zero with a long range means a mostly neutral genome with a few alterations. A box shifted off zero points to a wrong ploidy or normalisation, so check the profile.
Source: http://boevalab.inf.ethz.ch/FREEC/tutorial.html
renders_as.title: Log2 ratio spread

renders_as.caption: windows, by predicted copy number
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the count of windows, the bar splits them by the copy number Control-FREEC predicted, and the strip gives the median and highest copy number. It answers how much of the genome is neutral, gained or lost.
How to read: a bar dominated by the neutral state means a quiet genome. Large shares of other copy numbers mean wide alterations or aneuploidy.
Source: http://boevalab.inf.ethz.ch/FREEC/tutorial.html
renders_as.title: Windows by copy number

renders_as.description:
Each row is a genomic window or a called segment, with its sample, chromosome, start and end, log2 ratio, B-allele frequency and predicted copy number. It answers the exact values behind the profile.
How to read: filter by the segment column to list the called segments, or by chromosome to read one region window by window.
Source: http://boevalab.inf.ethz.ch/FREEC/tutorial.html
renders_as.title: Copy number windows

outputs.description: Binned, ICE-balanced intra-chromosomal contact matrix from a cooler dump, joined to its bins. One partition per resolution, keyed by the resolution column, so a tile re-bins itself as the reader zooms; coarser levels are derived by merging bins when the run dumped a single resolution.
outputs.name: Binned contact matrix
outputs.rawYaml:
id: cooler_contact_matrix
name: Binned contact matrix
mode: dump+balance
description: >-
  Binned, ICE-balanced intra-chromosomal contact matrix from a cooler dump,
  joined to its bins. One partition per resolution, keyed by the resolution
  column, so a tile re-bins itself as the reader zooms; coarser levels are
  derived by merging bins when the run dumped a single resolution.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_balanced.txt"
recipe: cooler/contact_matrix.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 25 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: contact_matrix.tsv
renders_as:
  # The colour is the balanced contact value itself on a continuous scale, so the
  # C1 colour rule is met by the matrix.
  - id: binned_contact_map
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: contact_map
    title: Chromosome contact map
    roles: {chrom1: chrom1, start1: start1, chrom2: chrom2, start2: start2, count: count, resolution: resolution, sample: sample}
    config:
      log_scale: true
    description: >-
      Each cell is a pair of genomic bins on one chromosome, coloured by the balanced
      contact frequency between them, with position on both axes. It answers how the
      chromosome folds: which regions touch each other more than their distance
      predicts.

      How to read: the diagonal is always brightest because neighbouring bins contact
      most, and contact falls away with distance. Squares along the diagonal are
      self-interacting domains, and bright spots off the diagonal are loops or
      long-range contacts. The map re-bins to a finer resolution as you zoom in.

      Lines and annotations: the colour scale is logarithmic, since contact frequency
      spans several orders of magnitude. The values are balanced with the ICE method,
      which removes per-bin coverage biases, so a bin is comparable with another.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22941365/
  - component: card
    column: chrom1
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: contacts measured
    title: Chromosomes and contacts
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of chromosomes in view, with the number of bin pairs
      measured next to it. It answers how much of the genome the matrix covers.

      How to read: a coarser resolution has fewer bin pairs. The number of pairs
      grows as the bins get finer, so compare resolutions with this in mind.
  - component: card
    column: count
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: balanced contact, lowest to highest
    title: Balanced contact frequency
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median balanced contact frequency over the bin pairs in
      view, with the lowest and highest values next to it. It answers the typical
      strength of a contact and how far it spans.

      How to read: contact values span several orders of magnitude, from strong
      neighbour contacts to faint long-range ones, so the median sits far below the
      maximum. Compare samples at the same resolution only.

      Note: balanced values are relative contact frequencies and not read counts, so
      their scale depends on the resolution.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22941365/
  - component: table
    title: Contact table
    description: >-
      Each row is a pair of bins with its sample, resolution, coordinates and balanced
      contact frequency. It answers the exact value of any contact on the map.

      How to read: filter to one sample, resolution and chromosome, and sort by
      contact to list the strongest pairs.

tools.description: Analysis tools for genomic interaction data stored in .cool format.
tools.name: cooltools

outputs.description: Contact probability against genomic distance, recomputed from the balanced cooler dump over log-spaced distance bins, one curve per chromosome plus the genome-wide pooled curve, with the log-log slope alongside it.
outputs.name: Contact probability P(s)
outputs.rawYaml:
id: cooltools_distance_profile
name: Contact probability P(s)
mode: expected-cis
description: >-
  Contact probability against genomic distance, recomputed from the balanced
  cooler dump over log-spaced distance bins, one curve per chromosome plus the
  genome-wide pooled curve, with the log-log slope alongside it.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_balanced.txt"
recipe: cooltools/distance_profile.py
fixture: distance_profile.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: ps_curve
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Contact probability against distance
    roles: {series: chrom, x: distance, y: contact_probability}
    config:
      log_x: true
      log_y: true
      x_title: Genomic distance (bp)
      y_title: Contact probability
    description: >-
      Each line is a chromosome, plus the genome-wide pooled curve: the probability
      that two loci a given distance apart are in contact, on log axes. It answers
      how fast contacts decay with genomic distance.

      How to read: contacts fall steadily with distance. Chromosomes whose curve
      departs from the pooled one carry a different folding or a technical bias, and
      a plateau or bump at long range can point to translocations or poor
      balancing. Open the slope view for the local decay rate.

      Note: this is the tool's expected contact table re-binned over log-spaced
      distances, with no cut-off drawn.
  # The derivative of the same curve. Read on its own axis, because a slope
  # near -1 and a probability near 0.1 share no scale.
  - id: ps_slope
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Slope of the contact decay
    roles: {series: chrom, x: distance, y: log10_slope}
    config:
      log_x: true
      x_title: Genomic distance (bp)
      y_title: Log-log slope of the contact probability
    description: >-
      Each line is a chromosome, plus the genome-wide pooled curve: the local slope
      of the contact probability against distance, on log axes. It answers at which
      distance scales the decay changes.

      How to read: a steady slope means a single regime of folding. A change of
      slope marks a scale where the organisation changes, such as the footprint of
      loop extrusion, and a chromosome off the others needs a closer look.

      Note: the slope is a derivative of a noisy curve, so it is unreliable at the
      largest distances where few pairs of bins are left. No cut-off is drawn.
  # The pooled curve only: a median over it and the per-chromosome curves
  # counts the genome twice.
  - component: card
    column: log10_slope
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('chrom') == 'all'"
    title: Decay slope of the pooled curve
    caption: median log-log slope of the pooled curve, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median log-log slope of the genome-wide contact curve,
      and the box shows how the slope varies across distances. It answers how steeply
      contacts fall off overall.

      How to read: a more negative slope means contacts are lost faster with
      distance. Compare samples or resolutions, as the value shifts with both.
  # Contact probability spans orders of magnitude over the curve, so a box plot
  # would be squashed against zero: a stat strip is used instead.
  - component: card
    column: contact_probability
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    filter_expr: "col('chrom') == 'all'"
    title: Short-range contact probability
    caption: highest contact probability of the pooled curve, with its median and lowest
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest contact probability of the genome-wide curve,
      found at the shortest distance, and the strip shows its median and lowest
      value. It answers how strong the contacts are at short range and how far they
      fall.

      How to read: the maximum and the minimum differ by orders of magnitude on
      every Hi-C map. A change of the maximum between samples points to a different
      sequencing depth or resolution rather than to biology.
  - component: table
    title: Contact probability per distance
    description: >-
      Each row is a distance bin of a chromosome with its contact probability, log
      slope, observed contacts and number of possible bin pairs. It answers the
      exact values behind the curves.

      How to read: filter the chromosome column to one chromosome or to the pooled
      curve and sort by distance.

renders_as.description:
Each line is a chromosome, plus the genome-wide pooled curve: the probability that two loci a given distance apart are in contact, on log axes. It answers how fast contacts decay with genomic distance.
How to read: contacts fall steadily with distance. Chromosomes whose curve departs from the pooled one carry a different folding or a technical bias, and a plateau or bump at long range can point to translocations or poor balancing. Open the slope view for the local decay rate.

outputs.description: TAD intervals derived from the insulation track's boundary calls, one row per domain per window size, with its span, the bins it covers and the boundary strength at each edge.
outputs.name: TAD domains
outputs.rawYaml:
id: cooltools_domains
name: TAD domains
mode: insulation
description: >-
  TAD intervals derived from the insulation track's boundary calls, one row per
  domain per window size, with its span, the bins it covers and the boundary
  strength at each edge.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_balanced_insulation.tsv"
recipe: cooltools/domains.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 18 real domains (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: domains.tsv
renders_as:
  # Intervals on a chromosome-aware axis: one rectangle per domain.
  - id: domain_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: TAD domains along the genome
    roles: {chr: chrom, pos: start, score: size_kb, end: end, sample: sample}
    config:
      mark: rect
      score_title: Domain size (kb)
    description: >-
      Each rectangle is a domain, drawn from its start to its end on a
      chromosome-aware axis, at a height equal to its size in kilobases. It answers
      how the genome is partitioned into topological domains and how large they are.

      How to read: neighbouring rectangles of similar height are a regular
      partition. Very large domains often span poorly mappable regions or
      centromeres, and a run of very small ones suggests noise in the boundary
      calls.

      Note: domains are derived from the insulation boundary calls, so they change
      with the window size and the boundary threshold.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  # Same intervals on the Plotly track, so a tab still reads if the GenomeSpy
  # renderer is unavailable.
  - id: domain_size_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: TAD domain size track
    roles: {chromosome: chrom, position: start, value: size_kb, end: end, sample: sample}
    config:
      color_by: sample
    description: >-
      Each segment is a domain on its chromosome, with its size in kilobases on the
      vertical axis. It answers the same question as the domain track with a
      Plotly renderer.

      How to read: compare the sizes along a chromosome and between samples. A
      consistent size range means a stable partition, and isolated very tall
      segments mark unusually large domains.
  - component: card
    column: size_kb
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Domain size
    caption: median domain size in kilobases, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median size of a domain in kilobases, and the box shows
      how sizes spread. It answers how large the topological domains are.

      How to read: the median depends on the window size and on the resolution, so
      compare samples at the same settings. A long upper whisker means a few very
      large domains.
  - component: card
    column: size_kb
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: chrom
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Domains per chromosome
    caption: domains in view, with the chromosomes holding most ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of domains, and the bars rank the chromosomes
      that hold most of them. It answers how the domains are spread over the
      genome.

      How to read: the leaders should be the longest chromosomes. A short one among
      them means smaller domains or noisier boundary calls there.
  # valid_fraction is a 0-1 share, so a gauge would draw it on a fixed scale
  # (RULES section 5); the histogram shows how the domains spread.
  - component: card
    column: valid_fraction
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, median]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Mappable share of a domain
    caption: average share of valid bins, with the lowest and the median
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average share of a domain's bins that hold usable
      data, and the histogram shows how the domains spread. It answers how much of
      the domain calls rest on mappable sequence.

      How to read: values close to one are well supported. A pile at low values means
      many domains sit across unmappable regions, so their edges are less reliable.
  - component: table
    title: TAD domains
    description: >-
      Each row is a domain with its chromosome, start, end, size, number of bins,
      valid fraction and the boundary strength at its two edges. It answers the
      exact coordinates and support of every domain.

      How to read: sort by size or by edge strength to find the largest and the
      best supported domains.

id: cooltools_eigenvalues
name: Compartment eigenvalues
mode: eigs-cis
description: Per-chromosome eigenvalues behind the A/B compartment track, how much of the intra-chromosomal structure each eigenvector explains.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.cis.lam.txt"
recipe: cooltools/eigenvalues.py
fixture: eigenvalues.tsv

  # The second eigenvalue can be negative, so the hero is
  # the range, not an average that would cancel the signs.
  - component: card
    column: eigval1
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: First eigenvalue
    caption: average first eigenvalue, with its spread over chromosomes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average first eigenvalue, the amount of the
      intra-chromosomal structure the first eigenvector explains, and the box shows
      how chromosomes spread. It answers how strongly each chromosome separates
      into two compartments.

      How to read: a chromosome with a much lower value than the others has a weak
      compartment signal, so its compartment track is less reliable.

outputs.description: Per-bin first eigenvector (E1) of the intra-chromosomal correlation matrix, the A/B compartment track. Sign marks the compartment, zero-crossings are compartment boundaries. The recipe phases E1 per sample, resolution and chromosome so it correlates positively with bin coverage (1 / balancing weight): the better-covered compartment is A, the same way at every resolution, without a GC or gene track.
outputs.name: A/B compartment track
outputs.rawYaml:
id: cooltools_eigenvector
name: A/B compartment track
mode: eigs-cis
description: >-
  Per-bin first eigenvector (E1) of the intra-chromosomal correlation matrix,
  the A/B compartment track. Sign marks the compartment, zero-crossings are
  compartment boundaries. The recipe phases E1 per sample, resolution and
  chromosome so it correlates positively with bin coverage (1 / balancing
  weight): the better-covered compartment is A, the same way at every
  resolution, without a GC or gene track.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.cis.vecs.tsv"
recipe: cooltools/eigenvector.py
fixture: eigenvector.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: compartment_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: A/B compartment track
    roles: {chromosome: chrom, position: start, value: E1, category: compartment}
    config:
      color_by: category
    description: >-
      Each point is a bin of a chromosome with its first eigenvector value, coloured
      by compartment. It answers which parts of the genome are in the active A
      compartment and which in the inactive B compartment.

      How to read: positive values are A and negative values are B, and the
      zero-crossings are compartment boundaries. Long alternating stretches that
      match the expected pattern mean a clean decomposition, and an inverted
      chromosome arm is worth a check.

      Lines and annotations: the compartment labels are this catalog's convention, A for positive E1
      and B for negative. The recipe phases each chromosome so that E1 correlates positively with
      bin coverage, the better-covered compartment being A, the same way at every resolution. The
      cooltools documentation instead orients E1 to correlate positively with GC content, the usual
      convention for Hi-C.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/eigdecomp.py
      and https://cooltools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notebooks/compartments_and_saddles.html
  # The same track on a chromosome-aware locus axis, so it lines up with the
  # insulation and domain tracks stacked under the contact map.
  - id: compartment_locus_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: A/B compartments on the genome axis
    roles: {chr: chrom, pos: start, score: E1, end: end, sample: sample, category: compartment}
    config:
      score_title: First eigenvector (E1)
    description: >-
      Each mark is a bin with its E1 value, coloured by compartment on a
      chromosome-aware axis. It answers the same question as the track with a view
      that lines up with the insulation and domain tracks.

      other tracks. Compartment boundaries often coincide with domain boundaries.

      Lines and annotations: the compartment labels are this catalog's convention, A for positive E1
      and B for negative.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/eigdecomp.py

  - component: card
    column: E1
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Compartment signal
    caption: range of E1, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of the first eigenvector over all bins, and the
      box shows how its values spread. It answers how strong the compartment signal
      is.

      balanced A and B pattern. A box shifted to one side means an unbalanced
      decomposition or a poorly phased chromosome.

  # share is B, which a continuous E1 column cannot answer.
  - component: card
    column: E1
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: compartment
    title: Share of A and B bins
    caption: bins with an E1 value, split by compartment
    description: >-

      compartments. It answers what share of the mappable genome is active.

      sign problem in one chromosome, so check the track.

    title: Eigenvector values per bin

      eigenvector values and compartment. It answers the exact value behind every
      track.

outputs.description: Per-bin insulation score and cooltools' own boundary calls at every window size the run scanned, low insulation marks a TAD boundary.
outputs.name: TAD insulation score
outputs.rawYaml:
id: cooltools_insulation
name: TAD insulation score
mode: insulation
description: >-
  Per-bin insulation score and cooltools' own boundary calls at every window
  size the run scanned, low insulation marks a TAD boundary.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_balanced_insulation.tsv"
recipe: cooltools/insulation.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real bins (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: insulation.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: insulation_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Insulation score track
    roles: {chromosome: chrom, position: start, value: log2_insulation_score, sample: sample}
    config:
      color_by: sample
    description: >-
      Each point is a bin of a chromosome with its log2 insulation score, one line
      per sample. It answers where the local contact structure is broken into
      domains.

      How to read: dips of the score mark TAD boundaries, where contacts across the
      bin are depleted. Sharp, deep dips are strong boundaries and shallow ones are
      weak.

      Lines and annotations: boundaries are called by cooltools on the boundary
      strength, with the Li threshold by default. They are listed in the table and in
      the boundary card.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  # The same score on a chromosome-aware locus axis, so it stacks under the
  # contact map on the same x as the compartment and domain tracks.
  - id: insulation_locus_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Insulation on the genome axis
    roles: {chr: chrom, pos: start, score: log2_insulation_score, end: end, sample: sample}
    config:
      score_title: Log2 insulation score
    description: >-
      Each mark is a bin with its log2 insulation score on a chromosome-aware axis.
      It answers the same question as the track with a view that stacks under the
      contact map.

      How to read: zoom into a dip and compare it with the compartment and domain
      tracks. A boundary shared between tracks is a robust one.

      Lines and annotations: no score line is drawn, as boundaries are called on
      the boundary strength and not on this score.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  # The log2 score is centred on zero, so a median would hide the two signs: the hero is its range.
  - component: card
    column: log2_insulation_score
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Insulation score
    caption: range of the log2 insulation score, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of the log2 insulation score over all bins, and
      the box shows how it spreads. It answers how deep the dips are compared with
      the rest of the genome.

      How to read: a wide range with a box close to zero is a track with clear
      boundaries. A narrow range means weak insulation or a window that is too wide
      for the resolution.
  # Boundary strength spans orders of magnitude, so a stat strip replaces the box.
  - component: card
    column: boundary_strength
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    title: Boundary strength
    caption: median strength of the called boundaries, with the weakest and strongest
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median strength of the boundaries cooltools called, and
      the strip shows the weakest and the strongest. It answers how well defined the
      boundaries are.

      How to read: a few very strong boundaries over many weak ones is the usual
      shape. Compare the strongest ones between samples to see changes of domain
      organisation.

      Lines and annotations: cooltools keeps the boundaries above a threshold on
      their strength, Li by default or Otsu or a fixed value on request.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  - component: card
    column: log2_insulation_score
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: is_boundary
    title: Boundary bins
    caption: bins with a score, split by boundary call
    description: >-
      Each unit is a bin with an insulation score and the ring splits them into
      called boundaries and the rest. It answers what share of the genome sits on a
      boundary.

      How to read: boundaries should be a small share of the bins. A large share
      means a permissive threshold or a window too small for the resolution.

      Lines and annotations: a bin is a boundary when its strength passes the
      threshold cooltools applies, Li by default.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open2c/cooltools/master/cooltools/api/insulation.py
  - component: table
    title: Insulation per bin
    description: >-
      Each row is a bin at one window size with its insulation score, boundary
      strength and boundary call. It answers the exact values behind the tracks.

      How to read: filter to called boundaries and sort by strength to list the best
      defined ones.

tools.description: Gene editing outcome tables of the nf-core/crisprseq targeted analysis: per library read accounting, edit outcome counts (wild type, template-based repair, insertions and deletions split by frame), every indel allele with its position relative to the cut site, per-position substitution rates and the clonality call.

outputs.description: The crisprseq clonality classifier's verdict per library: a zygosity class (homozygous wild type, heterozygous or homozygous edited, ambiguous) with its confidence, a clonality label from the indel peak structure, the outcome shares it was based on and the peak statistics.
outputs.name: Clonality call per library
outputs.rawYaml:
id: crisprseq_clonality
name: Clonality call per library
mode: gene-editing/clonality
description: >-
  The crisprseq clonality classifier's verdict per library: a zygosity class
  (homozygous wild type, heterozygous or homozygous edited, ambiguous) with its
  confidence, a clonality label from the indel peak structure, the outcome shares it
  was based on and the peak statistics.
find: { path_glob: "**/*_edits_classified.csv" }
recipe: crisprseq/clonality.py
fixture: clonality.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: classification_mix
    component: card
    column: classification
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [mode]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: classification
    headline: true
    caption: libraries, by zygosity class
    title: Libraries by zygosity class
    description: >-
      Each unit is one library and the ring splits them by the classifier's zygosity
      class: homozygous wild type, heterozygous, homozygous edited or ambiguous. It
      answers how many libraries carry the edit on both, one or no allele.

      How to read: a ring dominated by one class is a uniform experiment. A large
      ambiguous share means the wild type fraction sits between the classifier's bands, so
      check the outcome composition and the clonality call before trusting the library.

      Lines and annotations: the class comes from the share of wild type reads. Above 80%
      is homozygous wild type, 40 to 60% heterozygous, below 20% homozygous edited, and
      anything between is ambiguous. These are the classifier's own constants in the
      pipeline script.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/templates/clonality_classifier.py
  - id: clonality_mix
    component: card
    column: clonality
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: clonality
    caption: libraries, by clonality label
    title: Libraries by clonality label
    description: >-
      Each unit is one library and the ring splits them by the clonality label the indel
      peak structure gives them. It answers whether the edited reads come from one clone
      or from a mixed population.

      How to read: clonal and likely clonal libraries carry one or two dominant indels,
      which is what a single edited clone looks like. Polyclonal and ambiguous libraries
      mix many alleles, and low editing activity means too few edited reads to call a
      clone.

      Lines and annotations: an indel counts as a peak when it holds more than 5% of the
      classified reads, and a library is clonal when one peak holds more than 85%.
      Libraries with too few reads are labelled insufficient data. Both rules are
      constants of the classifier script.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/templates/clonality_classifier.py
  - id: class_confidence
    component: card
    column: class_confidence
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Confidence of the zygosity call
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median confidence the classifier gives its zygosity class,
      from 0 to 1, and the box shows the quartiles over libraries. It answers how firmly
      the classes can be trusted.

      How to read: values close to 1 mean the wild type share sits on the class target.
      Low values point to libraries between classes or with few reads, so open the table
      and look at those first.

      Lines and annotations: confidence is one minus the distance of the wild type share
      from its class target (relaxed by half for heterozygous), with a penalty of up to
      10% for libraries under 3000 reads. The formula is the classifier script's own.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/templates/clonality_classifier.py
  - id: peak_share
    component: card
    column: max_peak_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.85
    threshold_direction: min
    caption: median share of the dominant indel, against the clonal line
    title: Dominant indel share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over libraries of the share of classified reads held
      by the largest indel peak, as a fraction from 0 to 1. It answers how dominant the
      main edit is.

      How to read: a value near 1 means a single edit explains the library, as in a clonal
      line. Low values mean the edited reads are spread over many alleles. Filter by
      clonality label to compare the groups.

      Lines and annotations: the threshold of 0.85 is the share above which the classifier
      calls a library clonal on the dominant peak alone.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/templates/clonality_classifier.py
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: classification
    title: Zygosity class
    description: >-
      Keeps the libraries of the chosen zygosity classes and filters every tile of the tab
      with them.

      How to read: pick the ambiguous class to review the libraries the classifier could
      not place.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: clonality
    title: Clonality label
    description: >-
      Keeps the libraries with the chosen clonality labels and filters every tile of the
      tab with them.

      How to read: pick polyclonal or ambiguous to review the libraries whose edited reads
      do not come from one clone.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Clonality call per library
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with its zygosity class, confidence, clonality label, outcome
      shares and indel peak statistics. It answers how the classifier called each library
      and why.

      How to read: sort by confidence to find the weakest calls, and compare the wild type
      share with the class. Peak shares are fractions of the classified reads from 0 to 1.
      Selecting a row filters the rest of the tab to that library.

outputs.description: At every position within the profile window of the cut site, the share of each library's classified reads whose deletion covers it and the share with an insertion starting there. A Cas9 cut shows as a deletion peak straddling offset 0.
outputs.name: Indel position around the cut site
outputs.rawYaml:
id: crisprseq_cut_site_profile
name: Indel position around the cut site
mode: gene-editing/cut-site-profile
description: >-
  At every position within the profile window of the cut site, the share of
  each library's classified reads whose deletion covers it and the share with
  an insertion starting there. A Cas9 cut shows as a deletion peak straddling
  offset 0.
find: { path_glob: "**/*_indels.csv" }
recipe: crisprseq/cut_site_profile.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 11 real offsets (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: cut_site_profile.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: deletion_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Deletion coverage around the cut site
    roles: { series: sample, x: offset, y: deletion_pct }
    config:
      reference_x: 0
      reference_label: Cut site
      x_title: Offset from the cut site (bp)
      y_title: Reads with a deletion (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a library: at every offset from the cut site, the share of its
      classified reads whose deletion covers that position. It answers where the deletions
      fall and how wide the damaged stretch is.

      How to read: an efficient nuclease edit gives a hump centred on the cut site that
      falls off within a few tens of bases. A hump displaced from the marker points to a
      misplaced cut site or a second target, and a curve flat near zero means little
      editing. Compare libraries of one guide, which should overlap.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical marker at offset 0 is the cut site the pipeline
      reports for the amplicon (the cut site file written by the CIGAR parser). It is a
      landmark, not a cut-off. This catalog's recipe leaves out positions with no indel
      and keeps a fixed window of 100 bases either side.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  - id: insertion_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Insertion starts around the cut site
    roles: { series: sample, x: offset, y: insertion_pct }
    config:
      reference_x: 0
      reference_label: Cut site
      x_title: Offset from the cut site (bp)
      y_title: Reads with an insertion (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a library: at every offset from the cut site, the share of its
      classified reads with an insertion starting there. It answers whether insertions are
      placed at the cut.

      How to read: insertions that peak at the cut site are the expected product of a
      blunt cut, usually one or a few bases. A spread-out or displaced curve is more
      likely sequencing or alignment noise than editing. A curve near zero means
      insertions are rare in this library.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical marker at offset 0 is the cut site the pipeline
      reports for the amplicon. It is a landmark, not a cut-off. This catalog's recipe
      leaves out positions with no insertion.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: offset
    title: Offset window
    description: >-
      Restricts the tiles to a range of offsets from the cut site.

      How to read: narrow it to the few bases around the cut to read the core of the
      repair, or widen it to see the amplicon ends.
  - component: table
    title: Indel position table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library and an offset from the cut site, with the share of classified
      reads whose deletion covers it and the share with an insertion starting there. It
      answers the exact values behind the curves.

      How to read: sort by deletion share to find the most damaged positions, and filter
      on a library to follow one sample.

How to read: insertions that peak at the cut site are the expected product of a blunt cut, usually one or a few bases. A spread-out or displaced curve is more likely sequencing or alignment noise than editing. A curve near zero means insertions are rare in this library.
Lines and annotations: the vertical marker at offset 0 is the cut site the pipeline reports for the amplicon. It is a landmark, not a cut-off. This catalog's recipe leaves out positions with no insertion.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
renders_as.title: Insertion starts around the cut site

renders_as.description:

How to read: narrow it to the few bases around the cut to read the core of the repair, or widen it to see the amplicon ends.
renders_as.title: Offset window

renders_as.description:
Each row is a library and an offset from the cut site, with the share of classified reads whose deletion covers it and the share with an insertion starting there. It answers the exact values behind the curves.
How to read: sort by deletion share to find the most damaged positions, and filter on a library to follow one sample.

outputs.description: One row per library: read accounting from the CIGAR parser (raw, clustered and classified reads, aligned share), reads per outcome class, the editing, frameshift, in-frame and template-based rates as shares of the classified reads, and the reads the indel filters dropped or placed outside the main indel peak.
outputs.name: Editing outcome per library
outputs.rawYaml:
id: crisprseq_edit_summary
name: Editing outcome per library
mode: gene-editing/summary
description: >-
  One row per library: read accounting from the CIGAR parser (raw, clustered and
  classified reads, aligned share), reads per outcome class, the editing, frameshift,
  in-frame and template-based rates as shares of the classified reads, and the reads
  the indel filters dropped or placed outside the main indel peak.
find: { path_glob: "**/*_edits.csv" }
recipe: crisprseq/edit_summary.py
fixture: edit_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: editing_rate
    component: card
    column: edited_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Editing rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over libraries of the share of classified reads that
      carry any edit, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how efficiently the
      guide edits.

      How to read: a higher rate means more edited reads, and replicates of one guide
      should agree. A very low rate means the cut did not take or the guide is inactive.
      Compare with the frameshift share before calling a knockout.

      Note: the rate is the share of classified reads, meaning wild type, template-based
      and indel reads. The pipeline publishes no cut-off for it.
  - id: frameshift_rate
    component: card
    column: frameshift_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Frameshift rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over libraries of the share of classified reads with
      an out-of-frame insertion or deletion, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers
      how many reads would disrupt the coding frame.

      How to read: this is the share of all reads, so it is capped by the editing rate. A
      frameshift rate close to the editing rate means almost every edit is out of frame.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  - id: inframe_rate
    component: card
    column: inframe_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: In-frame rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over libraries of the share of classified reads with
      an in-frame insertion or deletion, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how
      many edits keep the coding frame.

      How to read: in-frame edits can leave a working protein, so a high value next to a
      low frameshift rate is a weak knockout. Compare it with the frameshift rate.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  - id: template_rate
    component: card
    column: template_based_pct
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: mean and highest rate, with the spread of libraries
    title: Template-based repair rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean over libraries of the share of classified reads repaired
      from the supplied template, and the histogram shows how the libraries spread. It
      answers whether homology-directed repair happened.

      How to read: without a template the rate is zero in every library, which is
      expected. With a template, a rate above zero is precise knock-in repair, and low
      values mean most cuts are repaired by end joining.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  - id: frameshift_of_indels
    component: card
    column: frameshift_of_indels_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Frameshift share of indels
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over libraries of the out-of-frame share of the indel
      reads alone, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how often an edit breaks
      the reading frame, once editing happened.

      How to read: values close to 100% mean nearly every indel shifts the frame, which is
      what a knockout needs. Libraries with few indel reads are noisy, so check their
      depth.

      Note: a library with no indel reads has no value and is left out of the median.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  - id: aligned_rate
    component: card
    column: aligned_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Aligned reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over libraries of the share of reads that aligned to
      the amplicon, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers whether the reads belong
      to the targeted region.

      How to read: a low share means the library holds off-target or contaminating reads
      and carries less signal for the editing call. Open the table to find the libraries
      that lag.

      Note: no cut-off is drawn, because the pipeline publishes none.
  - id: raw_reads_per_library
    component: card
    column: raw_reads
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Raw reads per library
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median number of raw reads per library, and the box shows the
      quartiles. It answers how deep the sequencing is.

      How to read: rates from libraries with few reads are noisy, so read them with care.
      A box that is very uneven means some libraries are under-sequenced relative to the
      rest.

      Note: no minimum depth is drawn, because the pipeline publishes none.
  - id: raw_reads_total
    component: card
    column: raw_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: sum, with the smallest and largest library
    title: Raw reads in total
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of raw reads over all libraries in view, with the
      smallest and the largest library beside it. It answers how much data the run holds.

      How to read: a large gap between the smallest and the largest library means uneven
      loading. Open the depth scatter to see which libraries are under-sequenced.
  - id: read_attrition
    component: card
    column: raw_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: attrition
    attrition_cols: [clustered_reads, classified_reads]
    caption: reads, from raw to clustered to classified
    title: Read attrition
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of raw reads, followed by the reads left after UMI
      clustering and the reads the CIGAR parser could classify. It answers where reads are
      lost on the way to an editing call.

      How to read: a large drop at clustering means redundant or low quality reads, and a
      drop at classification means reads that did not align or failed the filters. Open
      the aligned reads and filtered indels cards to see which step lost them.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  - id: filtered_indels
    component: card
    column: indels_failing_filter
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Indel reads failing the filters
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over libraries of the indel reads that failed the
      CIGAR parser's filters, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how much of the
      indel signal is discarded as noise.

      How to read: a few discarded reads is normal. A large number means many indels sit
      below the sequencing error rate or outside the main indel peak, so the editing rate
      of that library deserves a second look.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  # Editing against depth: low-depth libraries with extreme rates are the ones
  # to distrust.
  # C1 N/A: the table has one row per library and no categorical column (no group or class) to colour by.
  - id: editing_vs_depth
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Editing rate against depth
    roles: { x: classified_reads, y: edited_pct, label: sample }
    config:
      x_title: Classified reads
      y_title: Edited reads (%)
      log_x: true
      top_n_labels: 5
      legend_pos: bottom
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: its classified reads against its editing rate. It answers whether an extreme rate comes from
      a shallow library.

      How to read: libraries at low depth with extreme rates are the ones to distrust, and
      the rates of deep libraries are reliable. Points that stay apart from the cloud at
      high depth are real outliers. Open the table for the labelled libraries.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median edited share of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      nf-core/crisprseq.

      Note: the depth axis is logarithmic.
  # Depth against alignment: libraries whose reads do not align to the
  # amplicon carry too little signal to call an editing rate.
  # C1 N/A: the table has one row per library and no categorical column (no group or class) to colour by.
  - id: depth_vs_alignment
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Alignment against depth
    roles: { x: raw_reads, y: aligned_pct, label: sample }
    config:
      x_title: Raw reads
      y_title: Aligned reads (%)
      log_x: true
      top_n_labels: 5
      legend_pos: bottom
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: its raw reads against the share that aligned to the
      amplicon. It answers whether poorly aligned libraries
      are also the shallow or the weakly edited ones.

      How to read: libraries with a low aligned share carry too little signal to call an
      editing rate, whatever their depth. A library that is both shallow and poorly
      aligned should be resequenced. Open the table for the labelled libraries.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median aligned share of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      nf-core/crisprseq.

      Note: the depth axis is logarithmic.
  # Of the edited reads, how many disrupt the reading frame: the knockout view.
  # C1 N/A: the table has one row per library and no categorical column (no group or class) to colour by.
  - id: frameshift_vs_editing
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Frameshift share against editing rate
    roles: { x: edited_pct, y: frameshift_of_indels_pct, label: sample, size: classified_reads }
    config:
      x_title: Edited reads (%)
      y_title: Out-of-frame share of indels (%)
      top_n_labels: 5
      legend_pos: bottom
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: its editing rate against the out-of-frame share of its
      indels, sized by classified reads. It answers
      whether the edits that happened are the kind that knock a gene out.

      How to read: the upper right corner holds libraries that edit often and mostly out
      of frame, the knockout view. A point high on the vertical axis but far left has few
      edits, so its frameshift share rests on few reads. Large points are the better
      supported.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median out-of-frame share of indels of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not
      a cut-off of nf-core/crisprseq.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: edited_pct
    title: Editing rate range
    description: >-
      Keeps the libraries whose editing rate falls in the chosen range and filters every
      tile of the tab with them.

      How to read: raise the lower bound to study the libraries that edited well, or lower
      the upper bound to inspect the failures.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: classified_reads
    title: Depth range
    description: >-
      Keeps the libraries whose classified reads fall in the chosen range and filters
      every tile of the tab with them.

      How to read: raise the lower bound to drop shallow libraries, whose rates are the
      least reliable.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Editing outcome table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with its read accounting, its editing, frameshift, in-frame
      and template-based rates, and the indel filter counts. It answers how each library
      fared, in numbers.

      How to read: sort by editing rate or by depth and compare the rates with the
      accounting columns. Rates are shares of the classified reads. Selecting a row
      filters the rest of the tab to that library.

      reference_value: 0
      reference_label: Cut site
      top_n_labels: 8
      legend_pos: bottom

      Each point is an indel allele of a library: where it starts relative to the cut site
      against its signed size, coloured by type and sized by its share of the classified
      reads. It answers which alleles dominate and where they sit.

      that start upstream of the cut and reach across it, and a single base insertion at
      the cut, are the usual signatures of a nuclease edit. Small points far from the cut

      them by type: deletion, insertion or deletion-insertion. It answers how many
      distinct edits were seen and which kind prevails.

outputs.description: For every amplicon position within the profile window of the cut site, the dominant base and the share of reads carrying another base (substitution) or a gap. Base editors show as a substitution peak upstream of the cut.
outputs.name: Substitution and gap rate per position
outputs.rawYaml:
id: crisprseq_substitutions
name: Substitution and gap rate per position
mode: gene-editing/substitutions
description: >-
  For every amplicon position within the profile window of the cut site, the
  dominant base and the share of reads carrying another base (substitution) or
  a gap. Base editors show as a substitution peak upstream of the cut.
find: { path_glob: "**/*_subs-perc.csv" }
recipe: crisprseq/substitutions.py
fixture: substitutions.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: substitution_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Substituted bases around the cut site
    roles: { series: sample, x: offset, y: substitution_pct }
    config:
      reference_x: 0
      reference_label: Cut site
      x_title: Offset from the cut site (bp)
      y_title: Reads with a substituted base (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a library: at every offset from the cut site, the share of aligned
      reads carrying a base other than the most common one at that position. It answers
      where bases change around the cut.

      How to read: a flat line near zero is a nuclease run with no substitution signal. A
      hump near the cut can mean base editing, and isolated spikes are usually single
      nucleotide variants of the sample or sequencing errors. Compare with the deletion
      profile to tell editing from noise.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical marker at offset 0 is the cut site the pipeline
      reports for the amplicon (the cut site file written by the CIGAR parser). This
      catalog's recipe takes the most common base of the library at each position as
      the reference, not the genome base, so a homozygous variant shows no substitution.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  - id: gap_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Gaps around the cut site
    roles: { series: sample, x: offset, y: gap_pct }
    config:
      reference_x: 0
      reference_label: Cut site
      x_title: Offset from the cut site (bp)
      y_title: Reads with a gap (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a library: at every offset from the cut site, the share of aligned
      reads with a gap, meaning a deleted base. It answers where deletions pile up around
      the cut.

      How to read: a nuclease edit shows a gap peak at the cut that decays on both sides.
      A gap level that is high everywhere points to an alignment or amplicon issue rather
      than editing. Compare with the deletion profile of the same library.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical marker at offset 0 is the cut site the pipeline
      reports for the amplicon. It is a landmark, not a cut-off.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/crisprseq/2.3.0/docs/output/targeted.md
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: offset
    title: Offset window
    description: >-
      Restricts the tiles to a range of offsets from the cut site.

      How to read: narrow it to the protospacer to read the bases the guide targets.
  - component: table
    title: Substitution rate table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library and an amplicon position, with its offset from the cut site,
      its most common base and the shares of reads with another base or a gap. It answers
      the exact values behind the curves.

      How to read: sort by substitution share to list the positions that change most, and
      filter on a library to read one sample.
