outputs.name: Cancer intron candidates
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ctatsplicing_cancer_introns
name: Cancer intron candidates
mode: cancer.introns
description: >-
  Splice junctions that matched the CTAT cancer intron reference, with their
  prevalence in TCGA tumour cohorts and GTEx normal tissues unpacked into a
  leading cohort and tissue. Empty on runs with no annotated cancer introns.
find: { path_glob: "**/ctatsplicing/*.cancer.introns" }
recipe: ctatsplicing/cancer_introns.py
fixture: cancer_introns.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: cancer_intron_manhattan
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: manhattan
    title: Cancer intron candidates along the genome
    roles: {chr: chrom, pos: start, score: score, feature: gene}
    config:
      score_kind: Uniquely mapped reads
      top_n_labels: 6
      color_by_columns: [top_tcga_cohort, strand]
      default_color_by: top_tcga_cohort
      score_threshold_stat: p95
    description: >-
      Each point is a junction that matched the CTAT cancer intron reference,
      placed at its start, with the number of uniquely mapped reads that support it,
      coloured by the TCGA cohort where it is most prevalent. It answers which
      candidate cancer introns the run holds and how strongly they are read.

      How to read: a tall point is a cancer-associated intron seen in many reads,
      the best candidate to follow up. Colour by chromosome or strand from the
      controls to see where the candidates cluster.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the 95th percentile of the
      support values of this table, a reference the data defines itself. CTAT
      requires at least 5 read alignments for an intron to enter its reference,
      which is a rule of the reference build and not of this sample, so it is not
      drawn here.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/TrinityCTAT/CTAT-SPLICING/Home.md
  - component: card
    column: uniq_mapped
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: reads per junction, distribution
    title: Reads per cancer intron
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of uniquely mapped reads supporting a
      candidate intron, and the histogram shows how the counts are distributed. It
      answers how well supported the candidates are.

      How to read: candidates resting on one or two reads are fragile and need
      confirmation in the arc view. Strongly supported ones are the leads to
      follow.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/TrinityCTAT/CTAT-SPLICING/Home.md
  - component: card
    column: intron
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: top_tcga_cohort
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    caption: TCGA cohorts holding the most candidates
    title: Cancer intron candidates
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct introns that matched the CTAT cancer
      intron reference, and the bars rank the TCGA cohorts where those introns are
      most prevalent. It answers how many cancer-associated junctions the run holds
      and in which tumour types they are common.

      How to read: a run with no candidates gives an empty tile, which is normal.
      A cohort leading the ranking hints at the tumour type the sample resembles,
      but a single intron says little on its own.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/TrinityCTAT/CTAT-SPLICING/Home.md
  - component: card
    column: top_tcga_pct
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: prevalence in the leading cohort, distribution
    title: Prevalence in the leading TCGA cohort
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest prevalence, in percent of the tumours of its
      cohort, reached by a candidate intron, and the histogram shows how the
      prevalences are distributed. It answers how common the candidates are in the
      tumours where they were seen.

      How to read: a high prevalence marks an intron frequent in a tumour type,
      which makes it a recurrent event. Low values are rare events.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/TrinityCTAT/CTAT-SPLICING/Home.md
  - component: table
    title: Cancer intron candidates
    description: >-
      Each row is a candidate intron, with its position, gene, supporting reads and
      its prevalence in TCGA tumour cohorts and GTEx normal tissues. It answers the
      exact detail behind every other tile.

      How to read: a high TCGA prevalence with a low GTEx prevalence marks an intron
      specific to tumours, the pattern CTAT-SPLICING looks for.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/TrinityCTAT/CTAT-SPLICING/Home.md

  # The junctions as arcs over the locus, arc width scaled by the reads that
  # support each one. This is the shape the file is: a junction is a span with
  # a read count, not a point, and a manhattan plot draws only where it starts.
  - id: junction_arcs
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sashimi
    title: Splice junctions as arcs
    roles: {chr: chrom, start: start, end: end, count: uniq_mapped, sample: sample}
    config:
      color_by: sample
    description: >-
      Each arc is one splice junction, from its donor to its acceptor, with the
      number of uniquely mapped reads printed at its apex, and one lane per
      sample. It answers which introns the reads of a locus use and how strongly.

      How to read: a strong arc is a well supported intron, and a weak arc beside
      it is an alternative junction worth a look when it skips or extends an exon.
      Compare lanes to see whether a junction is shared between samples.

      Note: the exon support drawn under the arcs is inferred from the junction
      ends and the reads that touch them, it is not a coverage measurement.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/TrinityCTAT/CTAT-SPLICING/Home.md
  - id: intron_manhattan
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: manhattan
    title: Junction support along the genome
    roles: {chr: chrom, pos: start, score: score, feature: gene}
    config:
      score_kind: Uniquely mapped reads
      top_n_labels: 6
      score_threshold_stat: p95
    description: >-
      Each point is a splice junction, placed at its start, with the number of
      uniquely mapped reads that support it, coloured by chromosome. It answers
      where along the genome the best supported junctions lie.

      How to read: tall points are junctions seen in many reads, usually canonical
      introns of highly expressed genes. A tall point in an unexpected gene is a
      junction to check in the arc view.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the 95th percentile of the
      support values of this table, a reference the data defines itself and not a
      cut-off published by CTAT-SPLICING. The labelled points are the strongest
      junctions.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Junction reads per gene
    dict_kwargs:
      x: gene
      y: uniq_mapped
      color: strand
      labels: {gene: Gene, uniq_mapped: Uniquely mapped reads, strand: Strand}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a gene, with the uniquely mapped reads of its splice junctions
      added up and coloured by strand. It answers which genes carry the most
      junction reads.

      How to read: a tall bar is a highly expressed gene or one with many
      junctions. Bars are split by strand, so a gene read on both strands stands
      out.
  - component: card
    column: uniq_mapped
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: reads per junction, distribution
    title: Reads per junction
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of uniquely mapped reads supporting a
      junction, and the histogram shows how the counts are distributed. It answers
      how well supported a typical junction is.

      How to read: read support is heavily skewed, with many weakly supported
      junctions and a few very strong ones. A median near the floor means most
      junctions rest on very few reads and are fragile calls.
  - component: card
    column: intron
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: gene
    top_n_count: 5
    caption: genes with the most distinct junctions
    title: Distinct junctions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct introns seen, and the bars rank the
      genes by how many distinct junctions each carries. It answers how many
      junctions the run found and where they cluster.

      How to read: a gene with many junctions is long or has many isoforms. Count
      and distinct count differ when the same intron appears in several samples.
  - component: card
    column: total_mapped
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: chrom
    caption: junction reads, by chromosome
    title: Junction reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is every read supporting a junction, unique and multi
      mapped, and the ring splits it by chromosome. It answers how the junction
      reads divide between chromosomes.

      How to read: a chromosome with a large share is gene dense or holds a very
      expressed gene. Multi mapped reads are included, so repeated loci weigh in.
  - component: card
    column: intron_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: intron length, distribution
    title: Intron length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median length of an intron in bases, and the histogram
      shows how lengths are distributed. It answers how long the spliced introns
      are.

      How to read: lengths span orders of magnitude, so the median is more telling
      than the mean. Very short introns can be spurious alignments, and a long tail
      holds the introns of large genes.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene
    title: Splice junctions
    description: >-
      Each row is a splice junction, with its position, length, strand, gene and the
      unique, multi mapped and total reads that support it. It answers the exact
      detail behind every other tile and lets a row selection filter the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by reads to find the best supported junctions, or filter by
      gene to list its introns.

name: Cancer type by classifier matrix
mode: cuppa
description: >-
  CUPPA's probabilities pivoted to one row per tumor and cancer type and one
  column per classifier, the shape a clustered heatmap reads. A row that is
  high across the DNA and RNA classifiers is a call several independent
  feature families agree on.

recipe: cuppa/classifier_matrix.py
fixture: classifier_matrix.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the classifiers present on the run (DNA and RNA ones are optional columns).
  - id: classifier_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Cancer type by classifier
    roles: {index: row_label, row_annotation_cols: [sample]}
    description: >-
      Each cell is the probability one CUPPA classifier gives to one cancer type for a tumor, with the tumor
      as a row annotation. It answers whether the classifiers agree on a tissue of origin.

      How to read: a row that is high across the DNA and RNA classifiers is a call several independent feature
      families back. A row high in the combined column but low in the others rests on one family.

  - component: table
    title: Classifier probabilities
    description: >-
      Each row is a cancer type for a tumor, with one probability column per classifier. It answers the exact
      score each classifier gave.

      How to read: sort by the combined column to see CUPPA's ranking and compare it with the feature
      classifiers.

tools.description: The run-level tables nf-core/cutandrun assembles from its own outputs: the sample hub behind every link, the peak-caller agreement between SEACR and MACS2, and the fraction of fragment coverage that falls inside the called peaks.
tools.name: nf-core/cutandrun roll-ups

outputs.description: One row per sample and peak caller: how many peaks that caller made, how wide they are, how many of them the other caller reproduced and how many it never saw. A sample a caller returned nothing for keeps a row with n_peaks 0.
outputs.name: Peak caller agreement
outputs.rawYaml:
id: cutandrun_caller_agreement
name: Peak caller agreement
mode: peaks/agreement
description: >-
  One row per sample and peak caller: how many peaks that caller made, how wide
  they are, how many of them the other caller reproduced and how many it never
  saw. A sample a caller returned nothing for keeps a row with n_peaks 0.
# nf-core/cutandrun can run SEACR and MACS2 over the same fragments. Neither is
# a subset of the other: a broad mark can be invisible to MACS2 and obvious to
# SEACR, so the disagreement is the informative part. The recipe reads both
# peak collections and the sample hub through dc_ref rather than re-parsing
# the BEDs, and counts overlap with two as-of joins instead of a cross join.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.seacr.peaks.*.bed"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*.macs2_peaks.narrowPeak"
recipe: cutandrun/caller_agreement.py
fixture: caller_agreement.tsv
renders_as:
  # Yield and agreement as one grid, then the two callers on two axes, then
  # what each of them saw alone.
  # C6: the dot plot has no axis-title option, so the description names the axes.
  - id: caller_yield_dots
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    roles: {cluster: sample, gene: caller, mean_expression: log10_n_peaks, frac_expressing: frac_shared}
    title: Peak yield and agreement by caller
    description: >-
      Each dot is a sample and peak caller: its colour is the number of peaks the
      caller made (log10) and its size is the share of those peaks the other caller
      reproduced. It answers how much each caller called and how much the two
      agree.

      How to read: large dots mean the other caller confirmed most of the peaks. A
      small dot with a dark colour is a caller that made many peaks the other did
      not. Read it with the unique peaks bars
      before trusting either caller.

      Note: neither caller is a subset of the other, so disagreement is informative
      and not an error.
  # A relation that is a diagonal by agreement is best read as departures, but
  # the points here (one per sample and caller) are drawn on log axes so the
  # orders of magnitude between SEACR and MACS2 stay visible.
  - id: caller_peak_scatter
    component: figure
    visu_type: scatter
    dict_kwargs:
      x: n_peaks_other
      y: n_peaks
      color: target
      log_x: true
      log_y: true
      hover_name: sample
      labels: {n_peaks_other: Peaks from the other caller, n_peaks: Peaks from this caller, target: Target}
    title: Peaks against the other caller
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample and peak caller: the peaks that caller made on the
      vertical axis against the peaks the other caller made on the horizontal axis,
      coloured by target. It answers which caller is more productive for each
      target.

      How to read: a point far from the equal-count diagonal means one caller
      called many more peaks than the other, so look at its unique peaks and at
      the target. Each sample appears twice, once per caller, with the axes swapped.

      Note: the equal-count diagonal is not drawn, and a caller with no peaks has no
      point on a log axis.
  - id: caller_unique_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: n_unique
      color: caller
      barmode: group
      labels: {sample: Sample, n_unique: Peaks the other caller did not make, caller: Caller}
    title: Peaks the other caller did not reproduce
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: n_unique}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample and peak caller: the number of its peaks that the other
      caller did not reproduce. It answers how much each caller sees alone.

      How to read: a tall bar means that caller made many peaks the other missed.
      Compare the two bars of a sample, and check its target, since the callers
      suit different kinds of mark.

      Note: a peak counts as reproduced when it overlaps at least one peak of the
      other caller on the same chromosome.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median number of peaks the other
      caller did not make of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it
      follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/cutandrun.
  - id: caller_shared_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: frac_shared
      color: caller
      barmode: group
      labels: {sample: Sample, frac_shared: Share of peaks reproduced, caller: Caller}
    title: Share of peaks the other caller reproduced
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: frac_shared}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample and peak caller: the fraction of its peaks that the other
      caller also made. It answers how reproducible each caller's peaks are across
      the two methods.

      How to read: a value near 1 means the other caller confirmed nearly all of the
      peaks. A caller that made few peaks can score high while the other scores low,
      so read this beside the peak counts.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of peaks reproduced by
      the other caller of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it
      follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/cutandrun.
  - component: card
    column: n_peaks
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: caller
    top_n_count: 2
    caption: Peaks, by caller
    title: Peaks called
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of peaks called, and the bars split it by peak
      caller. It answers how productive each caller was.

      How to read: SEACR and MACS2 differ by design, so unequal totals are common. A
      caller with almost nothing for a sample is worth checking against the signal
      tracks.
  # A sample a caller returned nothing for keeps a row with n_peaks 0 and a
  # fraction of 0, which would sink the box, so the cards below leave it out.
  - component: card
    column: frac_shared
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "pl.col('n_peaks') > 0"
    caption: Share reproduced, with its spread
    title: Average peak reproduction
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean share of peaks that the other caller reproduced,
      and the box shows the spread over samples and callers. It answers how well the
      two callers agree overall.

      How to read: a narrow box near 1 means strong agreement. A wide box mixes
      samples where the callers agree with samples where they diverge.
  # The former gauge drew a 0 to 1 fraction as "x% of 1", so the minimum is shown
  # with the median and the best instead.
  - component: card
    column: frac_shared
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    filter_expr: "pl.col('n_peaks') > 0"
    caption: Least reproduced, with the median and the best
    title: Least reproduced peak set
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest share of peaks reproduced by the other caller,
      shown with the median and the highest. It answers which peak set agrees least.

      How to read: a minimum far below the median is a caller and sample to
      inspect. Check its peak count first, since few peaks make the share unstable.

      Note: the nf-core pipeline gives no pass mark for this share, so none is drawn.
  - component: card
    column: median_width
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    filter_expr: "pl.col('n_peaks') > 0"
    caption: Median peak width, by sample and caller
    title: Median peak width
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of the per-sample median peak widths in base
      pairs, and the histogram shows how they spread. It answers how broad the peaks
      are.

      How to read: widths differ between callers and between targets, so a spread is
      expected. The pipeline advises broad peak mode for epitopes with a wide range
      such as histone marks, and narrow mode for small binding proteins.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: n_unique
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: caller
    caption: Peaks seen alone, by caller
    title: Peaks seen by one caller only
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of peaks that the other caller did not
      reproduce, and the bar splits it by caller. It answers which caller sees more
      on its own.

      How to read: a lopsided bar shows one caller finds many peaks the other does
      not. Open the unique peaks bars to see which samples drive it.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Peak caller agreement table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample and peak caller, with the peak count, total and median
      width, and how many peaks the other caller reproduced or did not. It answers
      the exact counts behind the figures.

      How to read: sort by the shared fraction to find the weakest agreement, and
      check the peak count beside it.

renders_as.description:
Each bar is a sample and peak caller: the fraction of its peaks that the other caller also made. It answers how reproducible each caller's peaks are across the two methods.
How to read: a value near 1 means the other caller confirmed nearly all of the peaks. A caller that made few peaks can score high while the other scores low, so read this beside the peak counts.
Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of peaks reproduced by the other caller of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/cutandrun.
renders_as.title: Share of peaks the other caller reproduced

renders_as.caption: Peaks, by caller
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total of peaks called, and the bars split it by peak caller. It answers how productive each caller was.
How to read: SEACR and MACS2 differ by design, so unequal totals are common. A caller with almost nothing for a sample is worth checking against the signal tracks.
renders_as.title: Peaks called

renders_as.caption: Share reproduced, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the mean share of peaks that the other caller reproduced, and the box shows the spread over samples and callers. It answers how well the two callers agree overall.
How to read: a narrow box near 1 means strong agreement. A wide box mixes samples where the callers agree with samples where they diverge.
renders_as.title: Average peak reproduction

renders_as.caption: Least reproduced, with the median and the best
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the lowest share of peaks reproduced by the other caller, shown with the median and the highest. It answers which peak set agrees least.
How to read: a minimum far below the median is a caller and sample to inspect. Check its peak count first, since few peaks make the share unstable.
Note: the nf-core pipeline gives no pass mark for this share, so none is drawn.
renders_as.title: Least reproduced peak set

renders_as.caption: Median peak width, by sample and caller
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median of the per-sample median peak widths in base pairs, and the histogram shows how they spread. It answers how broad the peaks are.
How to read: widths differ between callers and between targets, so a spread is expected. The pipeline advises broad peak mode for epitopes with a wide range such as histone marks, and narrow mode for small binding proteins.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
renders_as.title: Median peak width

renders_as.caption: Peaks seen alone, by caller
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total of peaks that the other caller did not reproduce, and the bar splits it by caller. It answers which caller sees more on its own.
How to read: a lopsided bar shows one caller finds many peaks the other does not. Open the unique peaks bars to see which samples drive it.
renders_as.title: Peaks seen by one caller only

renders_as.description:
Each row is a sample and peak caller, with the peak count, total and median width, and how many peaks the other caller reproduced or did not. It answers the exact counts behind the figures.
How to read: sort by the shared fraction to find the weakest agreement, and check the peak count beside it.
renders_as.title: Peak caller agreement table

outputs.description: Each sample's fragment coverage split into the part that falls inside its own peaks and the part that does not, in base pairs and as a fraction. SEACR reports no read count, so the numerator is the summed region signal de-scaled by the spike-in factor and the denominator is the fragment-length histogram.
outputs.name: Fraction of coverage in peaks
outputs.rawYaml:
id: cutandrun_frip
name: Fraction of coverage in peaks
mode: peaks/frip
description: >-
  Each sample's fragment coverage split into the part that falls inside its own
  peaks and the part that does not, in base pairs and as a fraction. SEACR
  reports no read count, so the numerator is the summed region signal de-scaled
  by the spike-in factor and the denominator is the fragment-length histogram.
# The table is long on purpose, two rows per sample, so a donut or a stacked
# bar reads it as a composition without any client-side pivot. The sample-level
# FRiP is repeated on both rows, which leaves its quantiles unchanged.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.frags.len.txt"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*.seacr.peaks.*.bed"
recipe: cutandrun/frip.py
fixture: frip.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: frip_composition_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: fraction
      color: signal_class
      labels: {sample: Sample, fraction: Share of fragment coverage, signal_class: Signal}
    title: Fragment coverage inside and outside peaks
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample split into the share of its fragment coverage that falls
      inside its own called peaks and the share that falls outside them. It answers
      how much of the signal the peaks capture.

      How to read: a larger in-peaks share means a better signal-to-noise ratio. The
      nf-core cutandrun documentation reads a FRiP above 0.3 as reasonable and above
      0.7 as the highest quality. Low values point to background, few peaks or a
      peak threshold set very high.

      Note: SEACR reports no read counts, so coverage is the summed region signal
      scaled by the spike-in factor. The score also depends on the peak caller
      settings.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  # The composition itself, then the spread of FRiP across samples and the
  # lowest FRiP in the run (on `frip`, one value per sample, not on `fraction`,
  # whose minimum is the smallest outside-peaks share).
  - component: card
    column: coverage_bp
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: signal_class
    caption: Coverage, inside and outside peaks
    title: Fragment coverage in and out of peaks
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total fragment coverage in base pairs, and the ring
      splits it into inside and outside the called peaks. It answers how much of
      the run falls in peaks.

      How to read: a large in-peaks share is good. A ring dominated by outside
      peaks means a noisy run or too few peaks called.
  - component: card
    column: frip
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: FRiP, with its spread
    title: Average FRiP
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean fraction of fragments in peaks, and the box shows
      the spread across samples. It answers how good the signal-to-noise ratio is
      overall.

      How to read: the nf-core cutandrun documentation reads a FRiP above 0.3 as
      reasonable and above 0.7 as the highest quality. A long lower whisker is a
      sample to open in the bar chart.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  # The former gauge drew a 0 to 1 fraction as "x% of 1". The 0.3 floor is the
  # "reasonable" level of the nf-core cutandrun output documentation.
  - component: card
    column: frip
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.3
    threshold_direction: min
    caption: Lowest sample, against the 0.3 floor
    title: Lowest FRiP
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest fraction of fragments in peaks of any sample,
      shown with the median and the highest, against a floor of 0.3. It answers
      whether every sample reaches a reasonable signal-to-noise ratio.

      How to read: a sample below the floor has a lot of background or few peaks, so
      check its peak caller settings and its IgG control before using it.

      Lines and annotations: the floor of 0.3 is the level the nf-core cutandrun
      documentation calls reasonable, after Landt et al.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  - component: table
    title: FRiP table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample and a signal class, with the coverage in base pairs, the
      fraction, the sample FRiP, the peak count and the spike-in scale factor. It
      answers the exact numbers behind the figure.

      How to read: the sample FRiP is repeated on both rows of a sample. Sort by it
      to find the weakest sample.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: cutandrun_samples
name: Sample hub
mode: design/samples
description: >-
  One row per CUT&RUN sample, collapsed from the library rows of the validated
  samplesheet: the name every output file uses, the target it profiles, its
  replicate number, whether it is an IgG control and which control it was
  called against.
# The samplesheet is library-level (`<sample>_T<n>`) and never spells out the
# `<group>_R<replicate>` name the rest of the run is keyed on, so the hub is
# derived rather than read. The IgG control rows stay in: a CUT&RUN sample is
# only interpretable next to the control it was thresholded against.
find:
  path_glob: "**/samplesheet.valid.csv"
recipe: cutandrun/samples.py
fixture: samples.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: sample_design_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: target
      y: n_libraries
      color: role
      labels: {target: Target, n_libraries: Libraries, role: Role}
    title: Libraries per target
    description: >-
      Each bar is a target of the experiment: the number of libraries sequenced for
      it, coloured by whether it is a profiled target or an IgG control. It answers
      how the design is balanced.

      How to read: targets should have comparable library counts, and an IgG control
      should be present for the peak caller. A target without a control or with a
      single library cannot be called against a background or checked for
      reproducibility.
  # The glance strip every tab opens with: the design split by role, by target,
  # the libraries behind it and the replicate depth.
  - component: card
    column: n_libraries
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [sum, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: role
    caption: Samples, by role
    title: Samples, by role
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of samples, shown with the libraries behind them
      and the largest library count of a sample, and the ring splits the samples into
      profiled targets and IgG controls. It answers how many samples the run holds.

      How to read: a ring without an IgG control share means the peak caller had no
      background to call against.
  - component: card
    column: target
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: target
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: Samples per target
    title: Targets
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct targets, shown with the count of
      samples, and the bars rank the targets by their samples. It answers which
      targets are best replicated.

      How to read: a target with a single sample has no replicate to compare.
  - component: card
    column: n_libraries
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: target
    caption: Libraries, by target
    title: Libraries per target
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of libraries, and the bar splits it by target. It
      answers where the sequencing effort went.

      How to read: an even split means a balanced design. A target with far fewer
      libraries has less power.
  - component: card
    column: replicate
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: Highest replicate, with the median and lowest
    title: Replicate depth
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest replicate number in the run, shown with the
      median and the lowest. It answers how many replicates the design has.

      How to read: two or more replicates per target allow reproducibility to be
      checked. A maximum of 1 means no replicates.
  # `replicate` is an Int64, so the categorical twin is what a MultiSelect can
  # filter on; both are declared so a template can pick either.
  - id: sample_replicate_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: replicate_label
    title: Replicate
    description: >-
      Pick one or more replicates to keep only their samples in the tiles that
      follow.
  - id: sample_target_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: target
    title: Target
    description: >-
      Pick one or more targets, including the IgG control, to keep only their
      samples in the tiles that follow.
  - component: table
    title: Sample table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its target, replicate, role, the control it was called
      against and the libraries behind it. It answers how the samples map to the
      files of the run.

      How to read: check that every target row names a control and that replicates
      are numbered as expected.

tools.description: Determines DNA damage patterns in ancient DNA reads, a Java replacement for mapDamage.
tools.name: DamageProfiler

outputs.description: One row per library pairing the two ancient-DNA authenticity signals, terminal deamination at the first base of a read and mapped fragment length, so a modern contaminant (long, undamaged), an ancient extract (short, damaged) and over-sheared modern DNA (short, undamaged) separate on one plane. Derived from the two tidied DamageProfiler collections, which a template must declare before this one.
outputs.name: Authenticity plane
outputs.rawYaml:
id: damageprofiler_authenticity
name: Authenticity plane
description: >-
  One row per library pairing the two ancient-DNA authenticity signals, terminal
  deamination at the first base of a read and mapped fragment length, so a
  modern contaminant (long, undamaged), an ancient extract (short, damaged) and
  over-sheared modern DNA (short, undamaged) separate on one plane. Derived from
  the two tidied DamageProfiler collections, which a template must declare
  before this one.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_freq_misincorporations.txt"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/lgdistribution.txt"
recipe: damageprofiler/authenticity.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 2 real samples (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: authenticity.tsv
renders_as:
  # Neither DamageProfiler nor the ancient-DNA literature this view cites fixes a
  # numeric authenticity cut-off, so no zone or line is drawn (C3, RULES section 17).
  # Colour is the library, the one categorical column of this one-row-per-library table.
  - id: authenticity_plane
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    roles: {x: mean_length, y: ct_5p_first, label: sample, color: sample, size: n_reads}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
      x_title: Mean fragment length (bp)
      y_title: C to T at the first 5' base
      legend_pos: bottom
    title: Authenticity plane
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: its mean mapped fragment length on the horizontal axis and
      the C to T frequency at the first 5' base on the vertical axis, with the marker
      sized by mapped fragments. It answers whether a library carries the two signals of
      ancient DNA, short fragments and terminal deamination.

      How to read: a library high on the vertical axis and short on the horizontal one
      combines damage and fragmentation, as expected for ancient DNA. A long, undamaged
      library looks modern, which may be a contaminant, and a short but undamaged one
      may be over-sheared modern DNA. No pass mark is drawn because none is defined by
      the tool, so judge each library against the others and the extraction history.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median C to T frequency at the first
      5' base of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of DamageProfiler.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: terminal_damage
      color: sample
      labels: {sample: Library, terminal_damage: Terminal deamination (mean of 5' C to T and 3' G to A)}
    title: Terminal deamination per library
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: terminal_damage}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: the mean of its C to T frequency at the first 5' base and
      its G to A frequency at the first 3' base. It answers which libraries show the most
      damage at the read ends.

      How to read: a higher bar means stronger terminal deamination, the signature of
      ancient DNA. A bar near the background level is a library without clear damage,
      so check its fragment length too.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median terminal deamination of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a
      cut-off of DamageProfiler.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/
  - component: card
    column: ct_5p_first
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: mean, with its spread
    title: C to T at the 5' end
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean frequency of C to T substitutions at the first 5' base
      over the libraries, and the box shows the spread. It answers how damaged the
      libraries are at the 5' end.

      How to read: a higher value means stronger deamination. A library far below its
      peers has little damage, which is expected for modern or repaired libraries.

      Source: https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html
  - component: card
    column: mean_length
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mean, with its spread
    title: Mean fragment length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean mapped fragment length in bases over the libraries, and
      the box shows the spread. It answers how fragmented the DNA is.

      How to read: shorter fragments fit ancient DNA, which is fragmented by depurination.
      A library with much longer fragments than its peers may hold modern DNA.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/
  - component: card
    column: ga_3p_first
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mean, with its spread
    title: G to A at the 3' end
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean frequency of G to A substitutions at the first 3' base
      over the libraries, and the box shows the spread. It answers how damaged the
      libraries are at the 3' end.

      How to read: on a double-stranded library the 3' G to A signal reflects deamination at the 5'
      end of the complementary strand, so it should agree with the 5' C to T signal. A strong 5'
      signal with no 3' signal is not explained by that pattern, so check how the library was built.

      Source: https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html and
      https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/
  - component: card
    column: n_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distribution across libraries
    title: Mapped fragments
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of mapped fragments over the libraries, and the
      histogram shows how the libraries spread. It answers how much data backs the damage
      estimates.

      How to read: estimates from a library with few fragments are noisy, so treat its
      damage and length values with caution.
  - component: table
    title: Authenticity table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with its terminal damage at both ends, its background
      substitution rate, its fragment length and its mapped fragments. It answers the
      exact values behind the authenticity tiles.

      How to read: sort by terminal damage to rank libraries, then compare with the
      fragment length.

How to read: shorter fragments fit ancient DNA, which is fragmented by depurination. A library with much longer fragments than its peers may hold modern DNA.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/
renders_as.title: Mean fragment length

renders_as.caption: mean, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the mean frequency of G to A substitutions at the first 3' base over the libraries, and the box shows the spread. It answers how damaged the libraries are at the 3' end.
How to read: on a double-stranded library the 3' G to A signal reflects deamination at the 5' end of the complementary strand, so it should agree with the 5' C to T signal. A strong 5' signal with no 3' signal is not explained by that pattern, so check how the library was built.
Source: https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/
renders_as.title: G to A at the 3' end

renders_as.caption: distribution across libraries
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the count of mapped fragments over the libraries, and the histogram shows how the libraries spread. It answers how much data backs the damage estimates.
How to read: estimates from a library with few fragments are noisy, so treat its damage and length values with caution.
renders_as.title: Mapped fragments

renders_as.description:
Each row is a library with its terminal damage at both ends, its background substitution rate, its fragment length and its mapped fragments. It answers the exact values behind the authenticity tiles.
How to read: sort by terminal damage to rank libraries, then compare with the fragment length.
renders_as.title: Authenticity table

outputs.description: Mapped fragment length by strand, from DamageProfiler's lgdistribution table. The second authenticity signal after the misincorporation profile: ancient DNA is depurination-fragmented and rarely survives past about 100 bp, so a length distribution that looks like a modern library's is a contamination flag even when the damage curve passes.
outputs.name: Fragment length distribution
outputs.rawYaml:
id: damageprofiler_lgdistribution
name: Fragment length distribution
description: >-
  Mapped fragment length by strand, from DamageProfiler's lgdistribution table.
  The second authenticity signal after the misincorporation profile: ancient DNA
  is depurination-fragmented and rarely survives past about 100 bp, so a length
  distribution that looks like a modern library's is a contamination flag even
  when the damage curve passes.
find:
  path_glob: "**/lgdistribution.txt"
recipe: damageprofiler/lgdistribution.py
fixture: lgdistribution.tsv
renders_as:
  # DamageProfiler defines no length cut-off, so no reference line is drawn (C3).
  - id: fragment_length_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    roles: {series: series, x: length, y: fraction}
    config:
      x_title: Fragment length (bp)
      y_title: Fraction of mapped fragments
      legend_pos: bottom
    title: Fragment length distribution
    description: >-
      Each line is a library and strand: the fraction of its mapped fragments at each
      length. It answers how long the surviving DNA fragments are.

      How to read: ancient DNA is fragmented, so a curve piled at short lengths fits it.
      A curve with a wide tail towards long fragments looks like a modern library, a
      possible contamination even when the damage curve passes. The two strands of a
      library should follow each other.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22479540/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: length
      y: occurrences
      color: series
      labels: {length: Fragment length (bp), occurrences: Mapped fragments, series: Library and strand}
    title: Fragment counts by length
    description: >-
      Each line is a library and strand: the number of mapped fragments at each length.
      It answers how many fragments, not only what share, fall at each length.

      How to read: a library with far more fragments dominates the plot, so use the
      profile tile to compare shapes. A sharp drop at the shortest lengths reflects the
      minimum length kept by the mapping step.

      Source: https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html
  - component: card
    column: occurrences
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: strand
    top_n_count: 2
    caption: fragments, by strand
    title: Mapped fragments
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of mapped fragments over every library in view, and
      the bars split it by strand. It answers how many fragments the length distribution
      holds and whether the strands are balanced.

      How to read: the two strands should be of similar size. A strong imbalance points to
      a mapping or library issue.
  - component: card
    column: occurrences
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distribution across length bins
    title: Fragments at the most common length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest count of fragments at a single length, and the
      histogram shows how counts are distributed over the length bins. It answers how
      peaked the length distribution is.

      How to read: a high maximum against a low median means the fragments cluster at a
      narrow range of lengths, as in a sheared or degraded library.
  - component: card
    column: length
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [min]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    caption: longest and shortest length
    title: Fragment length range
    description: >-
      The hero number is the longest fragment length present in the table, with the
      shortest beside it. It answers how wide the length window of the run is.

      How to read: the window reflects the lengths the mapping kept, not the lengths in the
      sample. Read the profile for the shape.
  - component: table
    page_size: 25
    title: Fragment length table
    description: >-
      Each row is a length bin of one library and strand, with its fragment count and
      its fraction of the library. It answers the exact numbers behind the length curves.

      How to read: filter to one library and strand to read its distribution.

outputs.description: Substitution frequency by distance from the read end, 5' and 3', C>T and G>A deamination against every other substitution pooled, the ancient-DNA authentication read.
outputs.name: Misincorporation profile
outputs.rawYaml:
id: damageprofiler_misincorporation
name: Misincorporation profile
description: >-
  Substitution frequency by distance from the read end, 5' and 3', C>T and
  G>A deamination against every other substitution pooled, the ancient-DNA
  authentication read.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_freq_misincorporations.txt"
recipe: damageprofiler/misincorporation.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 18 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: misincorporation.tsv
renders_as:
  # New in lot 2 (depictio.models.components.advanced_viz kind damage_profile):
  # a `use:` on this id may fail model validation until that kind lands.
  # DamageProfiler sets no damage cut-off, so no reference mark is drawn (C3 N/A).
  # Colour is the substitution (base_change), set by the kind.
  - id: eager_damage_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: damage_profile
    roles: {sample: sample, end: end, position: position, base_change: base_change, frequency: frequency}
    title: Misincorporation profile
    description: >-
      Each line is a substitution type at one end of the reads: its frequency at each
      distance from the 5' or 3' end, with C to T and G to A highlighted by default and the other substitutions drawn muted. It answers whether the library carries the deamination damage
      of ancient DNA.

      How to read: ancient DNA shows C to T rising towards the 5' end and G to A towards
      the 3' end on a double-stranded library, while the other substitutions stay low and
      flat. Flat lines at both ends mean little damage. Check the fragment length profile
      before calling a library authentic.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/ and
      https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: position
      y: frequency
      color: base_change
      line_dash: end
      labels: {position: Distance from the read end (bases), frequency: Substitution frequency, base_change: Substitution, end: Read end}
    title: Misincorporation frequency by position
    description: >-
      Each line is a substitution type at the 5' or 3' end of the reads, with its
      frequency at each distance from that end. It answers how damage decays away from the
      read ends.

      How to read: a high frequency at the first base that falls within a few positions is
      the shape of terminal deamination. A line that stays high along the read points to
      chemical damage or errors in the data and not to ancient DNA damage.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17715061/
  - component: card
    column: frequency
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [average]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: base_change
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: highest frequency, by substitution
    title: Strongest substitution
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest substitution frequency in the table, and the bars
      rank the substitution types by their own maximum. It answers which substitution
      stands out and how strongly.

      How to read: C to T and G to A leading the ranking is the deamination pattern
      expected of ancient DNA. Another substitution on top is not explained by damage and
      deserves a look at the data.

      Source: https://damageprofiler.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contents/output.html
  - component: table
    title: Misincorporation table
    description: >-
      Each row is a substitution type at one position from one read end of a library, with
      its frequency. It answers the exact numbers behind the damage curves.

      How to read: filter to position 0 to compare the terminal frequency of each library.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: dbcan_overview
name: CAZyme annotations
mode: cazyme/genes
description: >-
  One row per predicted carbohydrate-active enzyme gene, with the family each
  of the three run_dbCAN tools called, how many agree, the resolved family, its
  CAZy class and the predicted substrate.
find: { path_glob: "**/dbcan/cazyme_annotation/*/*_overview.tsv" }
recipe: dbcan/overview.py
fixture: overview.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: cazyme_hierarchy
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: CAZy class, family and substrate
    roles: {ranks: [cazy_class, family, substrate], abundance: genes}
    config:
      colour_by_rank: cazy_class
    description: >-
      Each arc is a group of CAZyme genes: the inner ring is the CAZy class, the
      middle ring the family and the outer ring the predicted substrate, sized by
      the number of genes and coloured by class. It answers which enzyme classes
      and families dominate and what they are predicted to act on.

      How to read: a wide arc is a class or family that many genes carry. A large
      share of genes under an unassigned substrate means the substrate prediction
      covers little of the set. Click an arc to zoom in on it.

      Source: https://dbcan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/run_from_raw_reads.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: CAZyme classes per sample
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: genes
      color: cazy_class
      labels: {sample: Sample, genes: CAZyme genes, cazy_class: CAZy class}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample, split by the CAZy class of its CAZyme genes. It answers
      how large the CAZyme repertoire of each sample is and how it divides between
      glycoside hydrolases, glycosyltransferases and the other classes.

      How to read: a taller bar is a larger repertoire, which also follows depth and
      assembly size. Compare the colour shares between samples to see a shift in
      enzyme classes.
  - component: card
    column: genes
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: cazy_class
    caption: genes, by CAZy class
    title: CAZyme genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of predicted CAZyme genes, and the ring splits
      them by CAZy class. It answers how many carbohydrate-active enzymes were found
      and which classes they belong to.

      How to read: a class that is absent or unexpectedly large is worth checking
      against the sample type.

      Source: https://dbcan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/run_from_raw_reads.html
  - component: card
    column: family
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: cazy_class
    top_n_count: 4
    headline: true
    caption: classes with the most distinct families
    title: Distinct CAZy families
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct CAZy families found, and the bars
      rank the CAZy classes by how many families each holds. It answers how diverse
      the enzyme set is.

      How to read: a class with many families is the more diverse one.
      Compare with the gene count: many genes in few families means redundancy.
  - component: card
    column: genes
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: substrate
    filter_expr: "col('substrate') != 'unassigned'"
    caption: genes, by predicted substrate
    title: Genes with a predicted substrate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of CAZyme genes that have a predicted substrate,
      and the bar splits them by substrate. It answers which carbohydrates the
      predicted enzymes act on.

      How to read: a dominant substrate points at what the community degrades most.
      Genes without a substrate are left out, so the count is lower than the total
      number of CAZyme genes.

      Source: https://dbcan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/run_from_raw_reads.html
  # The dbCAN2 paper removes CAZymes found by only one of its tools to improve
  # accuracy; two tools is the floor that rule implies.
  - component: card
    column: n_tools
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 2
    threshold_direction: min
    caption: average tools agreeing, against 2
    title: Tools agreeing on a gene
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average count of tools, out of the three of run_dbCAN,
      that call the same gene a CAZyme, and the strip compares it with 2. It answers
      how confident the annotation is.

      How to read: genes called by all three tools are the safest. A low average
      means many calls rest on one tool and may be false.

      Lines and annotations: the threshold is 2 tools. The dbCAN2 paper combines the
      tools and removes the CAZymes found by only one of them to improve accuracy.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29771380/
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: family
    title: CAZyme genes
    description: >-
      Each row is a predicted CAZyme gene, with the family each of the three tools
      called, how many agree, the resolved family, its class, its substrate and its
      EC number. It answers the exact detail behind every other tile and lets a row
      selection filter the dashboard.

      How to read: filter by substrate or family to list the genes behind a bar, or
      sort by the tools column to inspect the weakest calls.

      Source: https://dbcan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/run_from_raw_reads.html

id: dbcan_substrates
name: CGC substrates
mode: cazyme/substrates
description: >-
  One row per CAZyme gene cluster with a predicted substrate, from homology to
  dbCAN-PUL (with its bitscore) and from the dbCAN-sub majority vote.
find: { path_glob: "**/dbcan/substrate/*/*_substrate_prediction.tsv" }
recipe: dbcan/substrates.py
fixture: substrates.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Predicted substrates per sample
    dict_kwargs:
      x: substrate
      y: clusters
      color: sample
      labels: {substrate: Predicted substrate, clusters: Gene clusters, sample: Sample}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a predicted substrate, with the number of CAZyme gene clusters
      that point at it, split by sample. It answers which carbohydrates the clusters
      of each sample are predicted to process.

      How to read: a tall bar is a substrate many clusters target. A substrate that
      one sample holds alone marks a difference in degradation potential between
      samples.

      Source: https://dbcan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/run_from_raw_reads.html
  - component: card
    column: clusters
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: substrate
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: substrates with the most clusters
    title: CAZyme gene clusters
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of CAZyme gene clusters with a predicted
      substrate, and the bars rank the substrates by the clusters that target them.
      It answers how many clusters have a substrate and which ones dominate.

      How to read: the leading substrate is what the community degrades most.
      run_dbCAN prefers the dbCAN-PUL homology call over the dbCAN-sub majority
      vote when both exist.

      Source: https://dbcan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/run_from_raw_reads.html
  - component: card
    column: bitscore
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Homology support of substrate calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of the summed bit scores of the homologous gene
      pairs between a cluster and its best dbCAN-PUL hit, and the box shows the
      spread. It answers how strong the homology behind a substrate call is.

      How to read: a high score means the cluster resembles a characterised
      polysaccharide utilization locus over several genes. A low score is a
      tentative call, to read with the majority-vote column of the table.

      Note: the run_dbCAN documentation describes this value as a sum and publishes
      no minimum score, so no cut-off is drawn.

      Source: https://dbcan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/run_from_raw_reads.html
  - component: table
    title: CAZyme gene clusters
    description: >-
      Each row is a CAZyme gene cluster, with its contig, its best dbCAN-PUL hit and
      substrate, the homology score, and the substrate and score of the dbCAN-sub
      majority vote. It answers the exact detail behind every other tile.

      How to read: compare the two substrate calls of a cluster. When they differ,
      the documentation recommends the dbCAN-PUL call first.

      Source: https://dbcan.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user_guide/run_from_raw_reads.html

id: deeptools_correlation_matrix
name: Sample correlation matrix

  samples). Replicates of one target correlate with each other and with nothing

renders_as:

outputs.description: How concentrated each library's coverage is, as the quality metrics plotFingerprint writes beside its curve: the area under the observed cumulative-coverage curve, the same area for a perfectly uniform library of that depth, and the divergence between the two. Enriched targets sit far from the uniform reference, inputs and failed enrichments sit on top of it.
outputs.name: Fingerprint metrics
outputs.rawYaml:
id: deeptools_fingerprint_metrics
name: Fingerprint metrics
mode: signal/fingerprint
description: >-
  How concentrated each library's coverage is, as the quality metrics
  plotFingerprint writes beside its curve: the area under the observed
  cumulative-coverage curve, the same area for a perfectly uniform library of
  that depth, and the divergence between the two. Enriched targets sit far from
  the uniform reference, inputs and failed enrichments sit on top of it.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.plotFingerprint.qcmetrics.txt"
recipe: deeptools/fingerprint_metrics.py
fixture: fingerprint_metrics.tsv
renders_as:
  # Enrichment against divergence from uniform: the two axes disagree only for a
  # library whose curve is odd, so a point off the trend is the one to look at.
  # MultiQC draws the fingerprint curve itself but never this table, so the
  # per-sample numbers are only readable here.
  # C1: the sample is the only categorical column, so each library gets a colour.
  - id: fingerprint_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Enrichment against divergence from uniform
    roles: {x: auc, y: synthetic_js_distance, label: sample, color: sample}
    config:
      x_title: Area under the fingerprint curve
      y_title: Jensen-Shannon distance to a uniform library
      reference_line: vertical
      reference_value: 0.5
      reference_label: Maximum area (uniform library)
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: the area under its cumulative-coverage curve on the
      horizontal axis and its synthetic Jensen-Shannon distance, the distance to a perfect input of the same depth,
      on the vertical axis, with one colour per library. It answers which libraries are enriched and how strongly.

      How to read: enriched targets sit far left, with a large distance. Inputs and
      failed enrichments sit near the maximum area with a distance close to zero. A
      point off the trend is a library whose curve is odd, so open the fingerprint in
      the MultiQC tab.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical line at 0.5 is the maximum value the area can take, as
      stated by the deepTools documentation. It is the area under the diagonal, which the
      documentation equates with a perfect input of infinite coverage.

      Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/feature/plotFingerprint_QC_metrics.html
  - id: auc_ratio_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: auc_ratio
      color: auc_ratio
      labels: {sample: Sample, auc_ratio: Area relative to a uniform library}
    title: Coverage concentration relative to a uniform library
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: the area under its fingerprint curve divided by the area
      expected for a perfectly uniform library of the same depth, coloured by the same
      ratio. It answers how concentrated each library's coverage is once depth is
      accounted for.

      How to read: lower means more focal enrichment. Inputs and failed enrichments sit
      near one and strong enrichments sit well below it. Compare targets with their
      inputs rather than reading one bar alone.

      Lines and annotations: a ratio of one means no enrichment, by this catalog's
      definition of the ratio. deepTools publishes no pass or fail cut-off for it.

      Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/feature/plotFingerprint_QC_metrics.html
  - id: auc_ratio_card
    component: card
    column: auc_ratio
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: average, with its spread
    title: Fingerprint area ratio
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average ratio of each library's fingerprint area to that of
      a uniform library, and the box shows the spread. It answers how enriched the
      libraries are overall.

      How to read: lower means more focal enrichment and one means none. A mix of
      targets and inputs gives a wide box, so filter to one kind of library.

      Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/feature/plotFingerprint_QC_metrics.html
  - id: auc_ratio_extremes
    component: card
    column: auc_ratio
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: most enriched, with the least enriched
    title: Strongest and weakest enrichment
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest area ratio, the most enriched library, and the
      second number is the highest, the least enriched. It answers how far apart the
      libraries are.

      How to read: a lowest ratio close to one means no library is enriched. deepTools
      publishes no cut-off, so judge each target against its own input.

      Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/feature/plotFingerprint_QC_metrics.html
  - id: js_distance_card
    component: card
    column: synthetic_js_distance
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: average, with the spread across libraries
    title: Distance to a uniform library
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average synthetic Jensen-Shannon distance, between each library and a
      perfect input of the same depth, and the bars show how libraries spread.
      It answers how far the coverage departs from uniform.

      How to read: the distance runs from 0 to 1 and higher means a bigger difference from a perfect input of the same depth, so enriched targets
      score high and inputs low.

      Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/feature/plotFingerprint_QC_metrics.html
  - id: x_intercept_card
    component: card
    column: x_intercept
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: average, with its spread
    title: Unsequenced fraction
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average x-intercept of the fingerprint curve, the point
      where the curve stops being zero, and the box shows the spread. It answers roughly
      how much of the genome received no reads.

      How to read: values near zero are ideal. High values come from low depth or from
      very strong enrichment that soaks up all the reads, so read it with the area ratio.

      Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/feature/plotFingerprint_QC_metrics.html
  - component: table
    title: Fingerprint metrics
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with its fingerprint quality metrics and their synthetic
      counterparts for a uniform library of the same depth. It answers the exact numbers
      behind the tiles of this tab.

      How to read: compare each metric with its synthetic value, since the expectation
      for a perfect input depends on sequencing depth.

      Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/feature/plotFingerprint_QC_metrics.html

outputs.description: The mean signal of every library across the plotted window, one row per bin. With `computeMatrix scale-regions` the window is the flanking region plus a gene body stretched to a fixed number of bins; with `reference-point` it is a window centred on one anchor. `bin_label` carries deepTools' own anchors, so the marker can be placed without hard-coding the window.
outputs.name: Metagene signal profile
outputs.rawYaml:
id: deeptools_plot_profile
name: Metagene signal profile
mode: signal/metagene
description: >-
  The mean signal of every library across the plotted window, one row per bin.
  With `computeMatrix scale-regions` the window is the flanking region plus a
  gene body stretched to a fixed number of bins; with `reference-point` it is a
  window centred on one anchor. `bin_label` carries deepTools' own anchors, so
  the marker can be placed without hard-coding the window.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.plotProfile.tab"
recipe: deeptools/plot_profile.py
fixture: plot_profile.tsv
renders_as:
  # MultiQC's deeptools module has no plot for this matrix at all: nf-core
  # publishes it as a plain table beside the PDF, and this is what reads it.
  # C3 N/A: deepTools publishes no cut-off for a metagene signal; the anchors
  # (start, end, centre) vary by run, so no fixed marker is drawn.
  - id: metagene_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Metagene signal profile
    roles: {series: sample, x: bin, y: signal}
    config: {x_title: Bin across the plotted window, y_title: Mean signal}
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: its mean signal in every bin across the plotted window.
      It answers where along genes or around an anchor the signal accumulates.

      How to read: an enriched target shows a peak at its expected position, such as
      the promoter for a promoter mark, and an input stays flat. A library with no peak
      did not enrich, and a peak in the wrong place points to a mislabelled library.

      Note: the window is a fixed number of bins, so the anchor labels of the run, such
      as the start and end of the scaled region, name the bins.

      Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/tools/plotProfile.html
  - id: signal_line
    component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: bin
      y: signal
      color: sample
      labels: {bin: Bin across the plotted window, signal: Mean signal, sample: Sample}
    title: Mean signal across the plotted window
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: its mean signal in every bin of the window. It answers the
      same question as the profile above with a plain line chart you can zoom.

      How to read: compare the height and position of the peaks between libraries.
      Libraries of one target should overlap, and inputs should stay low.

      Source: https://deeptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/content/tools/plotProfile.html
  - id: signal_peak_card
    component: card
    column: signal
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: highest bin, with the median bin
    title: Peak signal
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest mean signal of any bin, and the second number is
      the median bin. It answers how far the peak rises above the typical level.

      How to read: a peak many times the median means a clear enrichment. A peak close
      to the median means a flat profile, as expected for an input.
  - id: signal_spread_card
    component: card
    column: signal
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Signal level
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median mean signal over the bins, and the box shows their
      quartiles. It answers what level the signal sits at away from its peaks.

      How to read: a long box means a strong gradient across the window. Units follow
      the normalisation of the run, so compare libraries of the same run only.
  - id: library_count_card
    component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: libraries, with the rows behind them
    title: Libraries profiled
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of libraries in the profile, and the second number is
      the count of bin rows. It answers how many libraries the window covers.

      How to read: the row count divided by the library count is the number of bins of
      the window.
  - component: table
    title: Metagene signal table
    description: >-
      Each row is one bin of one library, with the anchor label where deepTools names
      one. It answers the exact signal behind the lines.

      How to read: filter to one library and sort by bin to follow its profile.

id: deeptools_sample_pca
name: Sample PCA
mode: exploratory/pca

  Where each library sits on the first components of a PCA over the genome-wide
  bin counts, with the share of variance each component explains. Replicates of

  # C1: each library is one point, so the sample is the only categorical column;
  # colouring by it gives every library a legend entry.
  - id: pca_embedding
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: Sample PCA
    roles: {sample_id: sample, dim_1: pc1, dim_2: pc2, dim_3: pc3, color: sample}
    config:
      axis_prefix: PC
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: its score on the first principal components of the
      genome-wide bin counts. It answers which libraries have similar signal and which
      differ.

      How to read: replicates of one target should sit together, and controls should
      sit apart from enriched targets. A library that lands with the controls did not
      enrich, and an outlier within a group points to a batch or quality problem.

      components. It answers the same question as the interactive view above in a plain
      scatter.

    title: Principal component scores

outputs.rawYaml:
id: deseq2_qc_pca
name: DESeq2 QC PCA
mode: qc/pca
description: >-
  The principal components nf-core's own deseq2_qc.r computed on the count
  matrix, read from the file the pipeline publishes rather than recomputed, so
  the dashboard and the MultiQC report show the same points. The variance each
  component explains is parsed out of the file header and kept as a column.
  A run with several count matrices (one per antibody, merge level or aligner
  route) gets one PCA per matrix, told apart by the pca_set column.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*pca.vals.txt"
  path_glob_alt: # MultiQC custom-content flavour written by chipseq and atacseq
    - "**/*pca.vals_mqc.tsv"

outputs.rawYaml:
id: deseq2_qc_sample_dists
name: DESeq2 QC sample distances
mode: qc/distance
description: >-
  The square sample-by-sample Euclidean distance matrix nf-core's own
  deseq2_qc.r clusters its QC dendrogram on, read from the file the pipeline
  publishes. Symmetric with a zero diagonal, so a clustered heatmap over it
  reproduces the dendrogram the report draws.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*sample.dists.txt"
  path_glob_alt: # MultiQC custom-content flavour written by chipseq and atacseq
    - "**/*sample.dists_mqc.tsv"
recipe: deseq2/qc_sample_dists.py
fixture: qc_sample_dists.tsv
renders_as:
  # Every numeric column of this square matrix is a sample, named at ingest, so
  # value_columns cannot be written here and the default (all numeric) is right.
  - id: qc_distance_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Sample distance heatmap
    roles: {index: sample}
    description: >-
      Each cell is the Euclidean distance between two samples, computed on the
      variance-stabilised expression the pipeline QC used, and the rows and columns
      are clustered. It answers which samples resemble each other.

      How to read: replicates should form dark blocks of small distance and
      conditions should separate. A sample that clusters with the wrong group, or sits
      far from everything, is an outlier to inspect.

      Note: the diagonal is zero by construction.
  - component: table
    title: Sample distance table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its distance to every other sample. It answers the
      exact value behind a cell of the heatmap.

      How to read: sort a column to find the samples nearest or furthest from one
      sample.
