outputs.description: Per-contrast DESeq2 statistics concatenated into one tidy table, one row per contrast and feature, with the significance call and the MA abscissa precomputed.
outputs.name: Differential results
outputs.rawYaml:
id: deseq2_results
name: Differential results
mode: differential
description: >-
  Per-contrast DESeq2 statistics concatenated into one tidy table, one row per
  contrast and feature, with the significance call and the MA abscissa
  precomputed.
# A plain run writes tables/differential/<contrast>.deseq2.results.tsv; the
# megatest adds a parameter-set directory in between, and chipseq writes
# consensus/<antibody>/deseq2/<contrast>/<contrast>.deseq2.results.txt. The
# canonical glob matches a .tsv at any depth, since `**/` spans zero or more
# directories; the alternate only adds chipseq's .txt under a deseq2/ dir.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.deseq2.results.tsv"
  path_glob_alt: ["**/deseq2/**/*.deseq2.results.txt"]
recipe: deseq2/results_long.py
fixture: results.tsv
renders_as:
  # Calls follow the nf-core/differentialabundance defaults (padj < 0.05 and
  # |log2 fold change| >= 1), the same rule the recipe applies to `direction`.
  - id: volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Differential expression volcano
    roles: {feature_id: gene_id, effect_size: log2fc, significance: padj, category: contrast}
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 1.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Log2 fold change
      significance_label: -log10 adjusted p-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene in one contrast: its log2 fold change on the horizontal
      axis and its adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers which genes
      change most, in which direction, and how confidently.

      How to read: genes in the upper left and upper right corners are strongly
      down- and up-regulated with high confidence. A cloud with almost nothing past
      the lines means little differential signal, so check the QQ view and the
      sample PCA before trusting the contrast. Open the table tile to inspect the
      labelled genes.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the adjusted p-value cut-off of
      0.05 and the vertical lines mark an absolute log2 fold change of 1 (a fold
      change of 2). Both are the nf-core/differentialabundance defaults, which also
      define the up, down and not significant calls on every tile of this tab.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: ma
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: ma
    title: Fold change against mean expression
    roles: {feature_id: gene_id, avg_log_intensity: log2_base_mean, log2_fold_change: log2fc, significance: padj}
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      fold_change_threshold: 1.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Log2 fold change
      intensity_label: Mean expression (log2)
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene in one contrast: its mean normalised expression on the
      horizontal axis (log2 of base mean plus one) and its log2 fold change on the
      vertical axis. It answers whether the fold changes are real or only come from
      weakly expressed genes.

      How to read: a healthy MA plot is a flat cloud centred on zero, with the
      significant genes spread across expression levels. A funnel that widens at
      low expression is normal noise of low counts. A cloud shifted away from zero
      points to a normalisation problem, so check the sample distributions.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal lines mark an absolute log2 fold change
      of 1 (a fold change of 2) and points are highlighted when the adjusted
      p-value is below 0.05. Both are the nf-core/differentialabundance defaults.
      DESeq2 itself colours its MA plot at an adjusted p-value of 0.1, its default
      alpha.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
      and https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html
  - id: qq
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: qq
    title: P-value QQ plot
    roles: {p_value: pvalue, category: contrast, feature_id: gene_id}
    config:
      show_ci: true
      show_identity: true
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene: its observed raw p-value, as minus log10, against the
      value expected if no gene differed between the groups. One trace is drawn per
      contrast. It answers whether the test statistics are well calibrated.

      How to read: points hugging the diagonal for most of the range and lifting off
      at the far end mean a few real signals over a calibrated null. A curve that
      leaves the diagonal early, or sits below it, points to inflation or deflation
      from batch effects, a wrong design or low counts. Compare the contrasts and
      revisit the PCA when one curve differs.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, the expectation when p-values are
      uniformly distributed under no effect. The shaded band is the 95% confidence
      interval of that null, so points inside it are consistent with chance.
  - id: da_barplot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: da_barplot
    title: Top changed genes per contrast
    roles: {feature_id: gene_id, contrast: contrast, lfc: log2fc, significance: padj}
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_label: Log2 fold change
    description: >-
      Each bar is a gene: its log2 fold change in a contrast, for the genes with the
      largest absolute change. It answers which genes drive each contrast and in
      which direction.

      How to read: long bars to the right are up-regulated and to the left
      down-regulated; bars are marked when their adjusted p-value passes the cut-off.
      A strong fold change without significance usually means low or variable
      counts, so open the MA plot and the table to check it.

      Lines and annotations: significance is marked at an adjusted p-value below 0.05,
      the nf-core/differentialabundance default.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  # Effect-size spread, then the up/down/not-significant split, then how many
  # features cleared the padj cut-off and how strong the top calls are.
  # The hero is the range, not the median: a median over both directions of a
  # fold change cancels to about zero (RULES section 5).
  - component: card
    column: log2fc
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: quartiles of the fold changes
    title: Fold change spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of log2 fold changes over every gene and contrast
      in view, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how large the
      differences are overall.

      How to read: a box tight around zero with a long range means most genes are
      unchanged and a few change a lot. A box shifted off zero points to a
      normalisation issue. Filter to one contrast to compare them.
  - component: card
    column: gene_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    caption: significant genes, by direction
    breakdown_col: direction
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "col('direction') != 'not significant'"
    title: Significant genes by direction
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct genes called significant, and the
      bars rank them by direction, up or down. It answers whether the response is
      mostly induction or repression.

      How to read: a strong imbalance between up and down is worth checking against
      the normalisation, the sample PCA and the biology. Calls use an adjusted
      p-value below 0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change of at least 1.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: direction
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [mode]
    secondary_layout: donut
    caption: calls, by direction; most frequent call
    breakdown_col: direction
    headline: true
    title: Calls by direction
    description: >-
      Each unit is one gene in one contrast, and the ring splits them into up, down
      and not significant. It answers how many genes pass the cut-offs overall.

      How to read: a ring that is mostly not significant means a weak contrast or
      too little replication. Open the volcano to see the borderline genes.

      Lines and annotations: the call is an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and an
      absolute log2 fold change of at least 1, the nf-core/differentialabundance
      defaults.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: neg_log10_padj
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, q3]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distribution, with its median and upper quartile
    title: Strength of the strongest call
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest minus log10 adjusted p-value, and the histogram
      shows the distribution of that score over all genes. It answers how strong the
      best evidence is and how much of the table carries any evidence.

      How to read: a histogram piled at zero with a long right tail is the usual
      shape. DESeq2 reports an adjusted p-value of exactly 0 for its strongest calls,
      which the score caps at 300, so the maximum is a ceiling and not a measurement.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: log2fc
      color: direction
      labels: {log2fc: Log2 fold change, direction: Call}
    title: Distribution of fold changes
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: x, stat: median, column: log2fc}
    description: >-
      Each bar counts genes in a log2 fold change bin, split by call. It answers how
      the significant genes sit in the overall fold change distribution.

      How to read: a distribution centred on zero with significant genes in both
      tails is expected. A skewed or shifted distribution suggests a composition
      effect or a normalisation problem. Open the MA plot to confirm.

      Lines and annotations: the call colours use an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and
      an absolute log2 fold change of at least 1, the nf-core/differentialabundance defaults. The dashed line is the median log2 fold
      change of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of DESeq2.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene_id
    title: Differential results table
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene in one contrast with its DESeq2 statistics: base mean, log2
      fold change, standard error, p-value, adjusted p-value and the call. It
      answers which genes to follow up and lets a row selection filter the rest of
      the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by adjusted p-value or by fold change, and filter by call.
      A missing adjusted p-value means DESeq2 filtered the gene as an outlier or as
      too low in counts.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: direction
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    caption: calls, as shares; number of call classes
    breakdown_col: direction
    title: Call composition
    description: >-
      Each unit is one gene in one contrast and the bar shows the share of each
      call. It answers what fraction of the tested genes change.

      How to read: compare the shares with the ring above; a very small significant
      share means few genes pass an adjusted p-value of 0.05 and a log2 fold change
      of 1.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  # Median adjusted p-value against the 0.05 rule; 0.1 is DESeq2's own default
  # alpha, shown as the warning band.
  - component: card
    column: padj
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    caption: median, with its smallest and largest
    threshold_value: 0.05
    threshold_direction: max
    threshold_warn: 0.1
    title: Median adjusted p-value
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median adjusted p-value over all genes and contrasts,
      compared with a cut-off. It answers whether most of the table carries
      evidence of change.

      How to read: a median below the cut-off means most genes are significant,
      which is unusual outside a strong perturbation. A median near one is the
      normal case.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-off is an adjusted p-value of 0.05, the
      nf-core/differentialabundance default, and the warning level is 0.1, the
      default alpha of DESeq2 results().

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
      and https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html

outputs.description: The same DESeq2 statistics joined to the GTF gene annotation: symbol, chromosome, coordinates and biotype, so the calls can be placed on the genome.
outputs.name: Annotated results
outputs.rawYaml:
id: deseq2_results_annotated
name: Annotated results
mode: differential/annotated
description: >-
  The same DESeq2 statistics joined to the GTF gene annotation: symbol,
  chromosome, coordinates and biotype, so the calls can be placed on the genome.
find: { path_glob: "**/*_deseq2.annotated.tsv" }
recipe: deseq2/results_annotated.py
fixture: results_annotated.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: manhattan
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: manhattan
    title: Significance along the genome
    roles: {chr: chromosome, pos: start, score: neg_log10_padj, feature: gene_name, effect: log2fc}
    config:
      score_threshold: 1.301
      score_kind: -log10 adjusted p-value
      color_by_columns: [direction, gene_biotype]
      default_color_by: direction
      top_n_labels: 8
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene placed at its start coordinate, with minus log10 of its
      adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers where on the genome the
      differentially expressed genes cluster.

      How to read: isolated tall points are single genes, while a tower of points
      over one region suggests a shared locus effect such as a copy number change or
      a cluster of related genes. Colour by direction to see whether a region moves
      one way. Several contrasts overlap here, so filter to one.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an adjusted p-value of 0.05, shown
      as 1.301 on the minus log10 axis. It is the nf-core/differentialabundance
      default cut-off. The score is capped at 300 where DESeq2 reports an adjusted
      p-value of 0.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: annotated_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Volcano with gene symbols
    roles: {feature_id: gene_name, effect_size: log2fc, significance: padj, category: contrast}
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 1.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Log2 fold change
      significance_label: -log10 adjusted p-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene in one contrast, labelled by its symbol: log2 fold change
      on the horizontal axis and adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers
      which named genes change most and how confidently.

      How to read: genes in the upper left and upper right corners are strongly down-
      and up-regulated with high confidence. Few points past the lines means little
      differential signal. Open the table tile to inspect the labelled genes.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the adjusted p-value cut-off of
      0.05 and the vertical lines mark an absolute log2 fold change of 1 (a fold
      change of 2). Both are the nf-core/differentialabundance defaults.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: annotated_da_barplot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: da_barplot
    title: Top changed genes with symbols
    roles: {feature_id: gene_name, contrast: contrast, lfc: log2fc, significance: padj}
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_label: Log2 fold change
    description: >-
      Each bar is a gene, named by its symbol, with its log2 fold change in a
      contrast, for the genes with the largest absolute change. It answers which
      named genes drive each contrast and in which direction.

      How to read: long bars to the right are up-regulated and to the left
      down-regulated; bars are marked when their adjusted p-value passes the cut-off.
      A strong fold change without significance usually means low counts, so check
      the volcano and the table.

      Lines and annotations: significance is marked at an adjusted p-value below 0.05,
      the nf-core/differentialabundance default.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: chromosome_lollipop
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: lollipop
    title: Calls along each chromosome
    roles: {feature_id: chromosome, position: start, category: direction, effect: log2fc, label: gene_name}
    config:
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each lollipop is a gene placed at its start coordinate on its chromosome, sized
      by the size of its log2 fold change and coloured by call (up, down or not
      significant). It answers how the differential calls spread along each
      chromosome.

      How to read: a run of same-coloured lollipops close together suggests a
      regional effect, such as a copy number gain or a gene cluster. Calls spread
      evenly with no pattern are the usual case. Open the Manhattan view to see the
      same genes by significance.

      Lines and annotations: the calls are an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and an
      absolute log2 fold change of at least 1, the nf-core/differentialabundance
      defaults. The labels name the most extreme genes.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: gene_name
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    caption: genes, by biotype
    breakdown_col: gene_biotype
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Genes by biotype
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct annotated genes, and the bars rank the
      biotypes that hold most of them. It answers what kind of genes the table covers.

      How to read: protein coding genes dominate most annotations. A table rich in
      non-coding biotypes points to a different assay or to an annotation that
      includes them.
  - component: card
    column: chromosome
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: composition
    caption: rows, by chromosome
    breakdown_col: chromosome
    title: Chromosome coverage
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of chromosomes with at least one gene, and the bar
      splits the rows by chromosome. It answers whether the table spans the genome or
      only part of it.

      How to read: a bar dominated by one chromosome means the table was restricted
      or a region is over-represented.
  # The median of a fold change over both directions cancels to about zero, so the
  # hero is the range; the box still shows the quartiles.
  - component: card
    column: log2fc
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: quartiles of the fold changes
    title: Fold change spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of log2 fold changes over every gene in view, and
      the box shows their quartiles. It answers how large the differences are.

      How to read: a box tight around zero with a long range means most genes are
      unchanged and a few change a lot. A box shifted off zero points to a
      normalisation issue.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: gene_biotype
      color: direction
      labels: {gene_biotype: Gene biotype, direction: Call}
    title: Calls by gene biotype
    description: >-
      Each bar counts genes of one biotype, split by call (up, down or not
      significant). It answers which kinds of genes respond.

      How to read: compare the coloured share of each biotype. A biotype with a
      larger share of up or down calls than its neighbours is enriched for change.

      Lines and annotations: the calls are an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and an
      absolute log2 fold change of at least 1, the nf-core/differentialabundance
      defaults.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene_id
    title: Annotated results table
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene in one contrast with its DESeq2 statistics and its symbol,
      chromosome, coordinates and biotype. It answers which genes to follow up and
      lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by adjusted p-value or fold change, and filter by chromosome
      or biotype to focus on a region or gene class.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: gene_biotype
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: concentration
    caption: rows, by biotype share
    breakdown_col: gene_biotype
    title: Biotype concentration
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct biotypes, and the bar shows how
      concentrated the rows are in the top ones. It answers whether one gene class
      dominates the table.

      How to read: a high concentration is normal for protein coding genes. A flat
      split means a mixed annotation.
  # Counting rows (genes per contrast) split by call: a nunique broken down by
  # another column would draw ranked bars, not a ring.
  - component: card
    column: gene_name
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    caption: calls, by direction
    breakdown_col: direction
    title: Calls by direction
    description: >-
      Each unit is one gene in one contrast, and the ring splits them into up, down
      and not significant. It answers how many genes pass the cut-offs.

      How to read: a ring that is mostly not significant means a weak contrast. Open
      the volcano to see the borderline genes.

      Lines and annotations: the call is an adjusted p-value below 0.05 and an
      absolute log2 fold change of at least 1, the nf-core/differentialabundance
      defaults.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
  # Base mean spans orders of magnitude, so a box would draw a flat line: rank the
  # biotypes by their median instead.
  - component: card
    column: base_mean
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [q1, q3]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    caption: median, with its quartiles, by biotype
    breakdown_col: gene_biotype
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Expression level by biotype
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median base mean, the average normalised count, over all
      genes, and the bars rank biotypes by their median. It answers how strongly the
      genes are expressed and which classes are highest.

      How to read: low medians mean the data is shallow and the fold changes are
      noisy, so lean on adjusted p-values. Base mean spans orders of magnitude,
      which is why it is ranked and not drawn as a box.
  - component: card
    column: neg_log10_padj
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [q3, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distribution, with its upper quartile and maximum
    title: Significance distribution
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median minus log10 adjusted p-value over all genes, and
      the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how much of the table carries
      any evidence.

      How to read: a pile at zero with a long right tail is the usual shape. DESeq2
      reports an adjusted p-value of exactly 0 for its strongest calls, which the
      score caps at 300.
  - component: card
    column: chromosome
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    caption: genes, by chromosome
    breakdown_col: chromosome
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Chromosomes with most genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of chromosomes, and the bars rank the ones with
      the most rows. It answers where the tested genes sit.

      How to read: large chromosomes lead in an unrestricted table. An unexpected
      leader points to a regional effect or a filtered table.
  - component: card
    column: neg_log10_padj
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Significance spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median minus log10 adjusted p-value, and the box shows
      its quartiles. It answers how the evidence is spread across genes.

      How to read: a median near zero with a thin upper box is the normal case. A high
      median means a strong perturbation.
  - component: card
    column: padj
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    caption: smallest, with its median
    threshold_value: 0.05
    threshold_direction: max
    threshold_warn: 0.1
    title: Smallest adjusted p-value
    description: >-
      The hero number is the smallest adjusted p-value in view, compared with a
      cut-off. It answers whether any gene reaches significance.

      How to read: a value above the cut-off means nothing is called; check replication
      and the design before tuning thresholds.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-off is an adjusted p-value of 0.05, the
      nf-core/differentialabundance default, and the warning level is 0.1, the
      default alpha of DESeq2 results().

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/differentialabundance/blob/master/nextflow_schema.json
      and https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html

id: deseq2_sample_distance
name: Sample distances
mode: exploratory/distance
description: >-
  Euclidean sample-to-sample distances over the most variable features, the
  square matrix behind the DESeq2 sample-clustering QC panel.
find: { path_glob: "**/all.vst.tsv" }
recipe: deseq2/vst_sample_distance.py
fixture: sample_distance.tsv
renders_as:
  # Sample columns are named at ingest, so value_columns cannot be written here:
  # every numeric column is a sample and the default is right.
  - id: distance_matrix
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Sample distances
    roles: {index: sample}
    description: >-
      Each cell is the Euclidean distance between two samples over the most variable
      features of the variance-stabilised matrix, with rows and columns clustered. It
      answers which samples are most alike overall.

      How to read: replicates should form blocks of small distance and conditions
      should separate. A sample that joins the wrong block, or sits far from all
      others, is an outlier or a mislabelled library.

      Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html

renders_as.description:
Each cell is the Euclidean distance between two samples over the most variable features of the variance-stabilised matrix, with rows and columns clustered. It answers which samples are most alike overall.
How to read: replicates should form blocks of small distance and conditions should separate. A sample that joins the wrong block, or sits far from all others, is an outlier or a mislabelled library.
Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html
renders_as.title: Sample distances

outputs.description: Per-sample density of the variance-stabilised expression matrix, binned on a grid shared by every sample so the curves are directly comparable, plus each sample's five-number summary. The features sitting at the matrix floor are excluded from the grid, because the spike they form is tall enough to flatten the rest of the curve, and published as a share instead. This is the panel that says whether a library is shaped like its neighbours at all, which a PCA cannot.
outputs.name: Sample expression distributions
outputs.rawYaml:
id: deseq2_vst_distribution
name: Sample expression distributions
mode: exploratory/distribution
description: >-
  Per-sample density of the variance-stabilised expression matrix, binned on a
  grid shared by every sample so the curves are directly comparable, plus each
  sample's five-number summary. The features sitting at the matrix floor are
  excluded from the grid, because the spike they form is tall enough to flatten
  the rest of the curve, and published as a share instead. This is the panel that
  says whether a library is shaped like its neighbours at all, which a PCA cannot.
find: { path_glob: "**/all.vst.tsv" }
recipe: deseq2/vst_distribution.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 12 real bins (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: vst_distribution.tsv
renders_as:
  # The profile kind has no group role, so each curve takes the series colour; the
  # group column is shown by the donut card below.
  - id: distribution_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Expression density per sample
    roles: {series: sample_id, x: bin_centre, y: density}
    config:
      x_title: Variance-stabilised expression (log2 scale)
      y_title: Share of expressed features
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is one sample: the share of its expressed features in each bin of
      variance-stabilised expression, on a grid shared by every sample. It answers
      whether the libraries have the same shape before any comparison is made.

      How to read: curves should overlay each other. A curve shifted along the axis, or
      with a shorter upper tail, is normalised differently from its neighbours and
      every contrast inherits that. Features at the matrix floor are left out of the
      curves and reported as a share on the card.

      Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html
  # The median column repeats on every bin row of a sample, so the box weights each
  # sample by its number of bins; kept because no per-sample table is published.
  - component: card
    column: median
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: quartiles of the sample medians
    title: Median expression across samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of sample medians of variance-stabilised
      expression, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how far apart the
      libraries sit.

      How to read: a narrow range means comparable libraries. One sample far from the
      rest is a candidate outlier; find it on the density tile.
  # A share between 0 and 1 under a gauge would print "x% of 1", so the card shows
  # its distribution instead.
  - component: card
    column: floor_share
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distribution, with its median and maximum
    title: Share of features at the floor
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average share of features sitting at the floor of the
      matrix, the value given to genes with no counts, and the histogram shows the
      spread over samples. It answers how many genes are effectively unexpressed.

      How to read: similar shares across samples are expected. A sample with a much
      larger share is shallower or lower in complexity than its neighbours.
  - component: card
    column: sample_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    caption: samples, by group
    breakdown_col: group
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Samples per group
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of samples, and the bars rank the groups of the
      sample sheet by their number of samples. It answers how balanced the design is.

      How to read: very uneven groups make contrasts less reliable, and a group with
      one sample cannot be tested.
  - component: table
    title: Expression summary per sample
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample and expression bin, with the sample's group and its
      five-number summary of variance-stabilised expression. It answers the exact
      numbers behind each curve.

      How to read: filter to one sample to read its quartiles and its share at the
      floor.

id: deseq2_vst_heatmap
name: Top variable features
mode: exploratory/heatmap
description: >-
  The 500 most variable features of the variance-stabilised matrix, wide
  (features x samples), with the sample sheet's factors as column annotations.
find: { path_glob: "**/all.vst.tsv" }
recipe: deseq2/vst_top_variable.py
fixture: vst_heatmap.tsv
renders_as:
  # `index` is not optional in practice: ComplexHeatmapConfig.index_column falls
  # back to the literal "sample_id", which this matrix does not have. Every numeric
  # column is a sample named at ingest, so value_columns cannot be written here.
  - id: top_variable_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Most variable features
    roles: {index: gene_id}
    description: >-
      Each cell is the variance-stabilised expression of one of the most variable
      genes (rows) in one sample (columns), with the sample sheet factors as column
      annotations. It answers which genes drive the differences between samples.

      How to read: columns of the same condition should share a pattern. A column that
      looks like the other group, or a block of genes that follows a batch factor,
      shows what structures the data before any contrast is run.

      Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html

outputs.name: Sample PCA
outputs.rawYaml:
id: deseq2_vst_pca
name: Sample PCA
mode: exploratory/pca
description: >-
  Principal components of the variance-stabilised expression matrix, one point
  per sample, computed on the most variable features the way DESeq2 plotPCA does.
find: { path_glob: "**/all.vst.tsv" }
recipe: deseq2/vst_pca.py
fixture: vst_pca.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: pca
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: Sample PCA
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, dim_1: dim_1, dim_2: dim_2, color: group}
    config:
      axis_prefix: PC
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample placed on the first principal components of the
      variance-stabilised expression of its most variable genes, coloured by group.
      It answers whether the samples separate by the factor under study.

      How to read: replicates of one group should sit together and groups apart. A
      sample away from its group, or a split along a batch factor, is an outlier or a
      confounder to deal with before differential testing. Switch the colour to a
      batch column to check it.

      Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html
  - component: card
    column: sample_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    caption: samples, by group
    breakdown_col: group
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Samples per group
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of samples, and the bars rank the groups by their
      number of samples. It answers how balanced the design is.

      How to read: very uneven groups make contrasts less reliable, and a group with
      one sample cannot be tested.
  - component: card
    column: dim_1
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: quartiles of the sample scores
    title: Spread on the first component
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of sample scores on the first principal component,
      and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how widely samples spread on the
      leading axis.

      How to read: a wide range with a clear gap suggests two clusters, usually the
      groups. Check the PCA tile to see which samples sit at each end.
  - component: table
    title: PCA coordinates and sample sheet
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its principal component scores and the factors of the
      sample sheet. It answers which factors line up with the components.

      How to read: sort by a component and look for a factor that follows it.

tools.description: Differential exon / transcript usage testing, finding genes whose exon or isoform usage shifts between conditions. nf-core/nanoseq runs it on Bambu's transcript counts; nf-core/rnasplice runs it on exon bins and on transcript-level salmon counts.
tools.name: DEXSeq

outputs.description: DEXSeq differential transcript usage (DTU) as nf-core/rnasplice's dexseq_dtu route writes it: one row per contrast and transcript with its usage log2 fold change (treatment over control), p-value, adjusted p-value and the gene-level q-value.
outputs.name: Differential transcript usage
outputs.rawYaml:
id: dexseq_dtu
name: Differential transcript usage
mode: splicing/transcript-usage
description: >-
  DEXSeq differential transcript usage (DTU) as nf-core/rnasplice's dexseq_dtu
  route writes it: one row per contrast and transcript with its usage log2 fold
  change (treatment over control), p-value, adjusted p-value and the gene-level
  q-value.
find: { path_glob: "**/DEXSeqResults.*.tsv" }
recipe: dexseq/dtu.py
fixture: dtu.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: dtu_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Transcript usage volcano
    roles: { feature_id: transcript_id, effect_size: log2fc, significance: padj, label: gene_id, category: direction }
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 0.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Usage log2 fold change
      significance_label: -log10 adjusted p-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a transcript in one contrast: the log2 fold change of its usage within its gene on the
      horizontal axis and its adjusted p-value on the vertical axis. It answers which isoforms gain or lose
      share of their gene's expression between conditions, and how confidently.

      How to read: points in the upper right gain usage in the treatment and points in the upper left lose
      it. Usage is relative to the other isoforms of the gene, so an isoform can change without any change
      in the gene's total expression. Open the table tile to see the gene behind a labelled transcript.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an adjusted p-value of 0.05, the cut-off the catalog
      recipe uses for the significant, up and down calls (its fdr parameter). The DEXSeq vignette
      illustrates a 10% false discovery rate instead, so 0.05 is the stricter choice. No fold-change line
      is drawn because the calls use none.

      Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DEXSeq/inst/doc/DEXSeq.html
  - component: card
    column: transcript_id
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: direction
    caption: transcripts, by usage call
    title: Transcripts by usage call
    description: >-
      Each unit is one transcript tested in one contrast, and the ring splits them into gain, loss and
      not significant. The second figure counts the distinct transcripts. It answers how many isoforms
      change usage overall.

      How to read: a ring that is mostly not significant means few isoform switches, or too little
      replication to detect them. Open the volcano to see the borderline transcripts.

      Lines and annotations: a transcript is called when its adjusted p-value is below 0.05, the catalog
      recipe default, and the direction is the sign of its usage log2 fold change.
  - component: card
    column: log2fc
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: usage log2 fold change, with its spread
    title: Usage change spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of usage log2 fold changes over all transcripts and contrasts in view,
      and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how large the usage shifts are.

      How to read: a box tight around zero with a long range means most isoforms keep their share and a
      few switch strongly. A median is not shown as a hero because gains and losses cancel to about zero.
      Filter to one contrast to compare them.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: direction
    title: Usage call
    description: >-
      Pick one or more usage calls (up, down, not significant) to restrict every tile of the tab to those
      transcripts. It answers which isoforms gain or lose usage when you only want one side.

      How to read: select up and down together to hide the unchanged transcripts, then read the volcano and
      the table on the significant ones only.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene_id
    title: Transcript usage table
    description: >-
      Each row is a transcript in one contrast with its mean expression, usage log2 fold change, p-value,
      adjusted p-value, the gene-level q-value and the call. It answers which transcripts and genes to
      follow up, and a row selection filters the rest of the dashboard to that gene.

      How to read: sort by adjusted p-value, then check the gene-level q-value, which controls the false
      discovery rate per gene rather than per transcript. A gene with several significant isoforms is a
      stronger candidate than a single one.

      Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DEXSeq/inst/doc/DEXSeq.html

outputs.description: DEXSeq differential exon usage as nf-core/rnasplice's dexseq_exon route writes it, summarised to one row per contrast and gene: the gene-level q-value, how many exonic bins were tested and called, and the most significant bin's log2 fold change, oriented treatment over control.
outputs.name: Differential exon usage per gene
outputs.rawYaml:
id: dexseq_exon_genes
name: Differential exon usage per gene
mode: splicing/exon-usage
description: >-
  DEXSeq differential exon usage as nf-core/rnasplice's dexseq_exon route
  writes it, summarised to one row per contrast and gene: the gene-level
  q-value, how many exonic bins were tested and called, and the most
  significant bin's log2 fold change, oriented treatment over control.
find: { path_glob: "**/DEXSeqResults.*.csv" }
recipe: dexseq/exon_genes.py
fixture: exon_genes.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: exon_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Exon usage volcano
    roles: { feature_id: gene_id, effect_size: log2fc, significance: padj, category: direction, label: gene_id }
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 0.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Top exon usage log2 fold change
      significance_label: -log10 gene-level q-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene in one contrast: the usage log2 fold change of its most significant exonic bin
      on the horizontal axis and the gene-level q-value on the vertical axis. It answers which genes use
      their exons differently between conditions.

      How to read: genes high on the plot have at least one exon used differently, and the horizontal
      position says in which direction the strongest bin moves. A gene can be significant with a small fold
      change when many bins shift a little. Open the table tile to see how many bins were tested and called.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a gene-level q-value of 0.05, the cut-off the catalog
      recipe uses for its calls (its fdr parameter). The DEXSeq vignette illustrates a 10% false discovery
      rate and describes the gene-level q-value as controlling the FDR per gene. No fold-change line is
      drawn because the calls use none.

      Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DEXSeq/inst/doc/DEXSeq.html
  - component: card
    column: gene_id
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: direction
    caption: genes, by exon usage call
    title: Genes by exon usage call
    description: >-
      Each unit is one gene in one contrast, and the ring splits them by the direction of their strongest
      exon shift, or not significant. The second figure counts the distinct genes. It answers how many
      genes change exon usage.

      How to read: a ring that is mostly not significant means little differential exon usage. A strong
      imbalance between up and down usually reflects which bin is the most significant, not a gene-wide
      trend.

      Lines and annotations: a gene is called when its gene-level q-value is below 0.05, the catalog recipe
      default.
  - component: card
    column: bins_significant
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max, median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: direction
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: significant bins, by call
    title: Significant exonic bins
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of exonic bins called significant across genes and contrasts, and the
      bars split it by the direction of each gene's strongest bin. The strip gives the largest and the
      median count per gene. It answers how widespread the exon changes are within genes.

      How to read: a high maximum points to a gene with many shifted bins, often a real isoform switch. A
      median near zero is normal, since most genes change at no bin.

      Lines and annotations: a bin is called with the adjusted p-value cut-off of 0.05 used by the catalog
      recipe.
  - component: card
    column: abs_log2fc
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: absolute log2 fold change, with its spread
    title: Size of the strongest exon shift
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median absolute usage log2 fold change of each gene's most significant bin,
      and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how large the exon shifts are, whatever their direction.

      How to read: a high median means the strongest bins move a lot. The absolute value is used so that
      gains and losses do not cancel out.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: direction
    title: Exon usage call
    description: >-
      Pick one or more calls (up, down, not significant) to restrict every tile of the tab to those genes.
      It answers which genes remain when you only want one side.

      How to read: select up and down together to hide the unchanged genes before reading the volcano and
      the table.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene_id
    title: Exon usage table
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene in one contrast: how many exonic bins were tested and called, the most
      significant bin with its usage log2 fold change, and the gene-level q-value. It answers which genes to
      follow up, and a row selection filters the rest of the dashboard to that gene.

      How to read: sort by q-value and read the bin counts beside it. A gene with several significant bins
      is a stronger candidate than one with a single bin.

      Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DEXSeq/inst/doc/DEXSeq.html

config.effect_label: Top exon usage log2 fold change

renders_as.description:
Each point is a gene in one contrast: the usage log2 fold change of its most significant exonic bin on the horizontal axis and the gene-level q-value on the vertical axis. It answers which genes use their exons differently between conditions.
How to read: genes high on the plot have at least one exon used differently, and the horizontal position says in which direction the strongest bin moves. A gene can be significant with a small fold change when many bins shift a little. Open the table tile to see how many bins were tested and called.
Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a gene-level q-value of 0.05, the cut-off the catalog recipe uses for its calls (its fdr parameter). The DEXSeq vignette illustrates a 10% false discovery rate and describes the gene-level q-value as controlling the FDR per gene. No fold-change line is drawn because the calls use none.
Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DEXSeq/inst/doc/DEXSeq.html

renders_as.caption: genes, by exon usage call
renders_as.description:
Each unit is one gene in one contrast, and the ring splits them by the direction of their strongest exon shift, or not significant. The second figure counts the distinct genes. It answers how many genes change exon usage.
How to read: a ring that is mostly not significant means little differential exon usage. A strong imbalance between up and down usually reflects which bin is the most significant, not a gene-wide trend.
Lines and annotations: a gene is called when its gene-level q-value is below 0.05, the catalog recipe default.

renders_as.caption: significant bins, by call

How to read: a high maximum points to a gene with many shifted bins, often a real isoform switch. A median near zero is normal, since most genes change at no bin.

renders_as.caption: absolute log2 fold change, with its spread

outputs.description: DEXSeq per-transcript usage statistics from nanoseq's Bambu-based differential expression subworkflow, with the significance call precomputed on the gene-level adjusted q-value.
outputs.name: Differential exon/transcript usage
outputs.rawYaml:
id: dexseq_results
name: Differential exon/transcript usage
mode: differential/usage
description: >-
  DEXSeq per-transcript usage statistics from nanoseq's Bambu-based
  differential expression subworkflow, with the significance call
  precomputed on the gene-level adjusted q-value.
find: { path_glob: "**/dexseq/*.results.txt" }
recipe: dexseq/results.py
fixture: results.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Transcript usage volcano
    roles: { feature_id: feature_id, effect_size: log2fc, significance: padj, category: direction, label: gene_id }
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 0.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Usage log2 fold change
      significance_label: -log10 gene-level adjusted q-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a transcript: its usage log2 fold change between the two conditions on the horizontal
      axis and the gene-level adjusted q-value of its gene on the vertical axis. It answers which isoforms
      change share within their gene, and how confidently.

      How to read: points in the upper right gain usage and points in the upper left lose it. Every
      transcript of a gene shares one q-value, so the points of one gene line up horizontally. Open the
      table tile to see the gene behind a labelled transcript.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a gene-level q-value of 0.05, the cut-off the catalog
      recipe uses for the significant, up and down calls. The DEXSeq vignette illustrates a 10% false
      discovery rate and describes the gene-level q-value as controlling the FDR per gene. No fold-change
      line is drawn because the calls use none.

      Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DEXSeq/inst/doc/DEXSeq.html
  # C1 N/A: the table has one contrast and no group column; the call column is derived from the p-value itself, so splitting the QQ by it would be circular.
  - id: qq
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: qq
    title: P-value QQ plot
    roles: { p_value: pvalue, feature_id: feature_id }
    config:
      show_ci: true
      show_identity: true
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a transcript: its observed raw p-value, as minus log10, against the value expected if
      no isoform changed usage. It answers whether the test statistics are well calibrated.

      How to read: points hugging the diagonal for most of the range and lifting off at the far end mean a
      few real signals over a calibrated null. A curve that leaves the diagonal early, or sits below it,
      points to inflation or deflation from a wrong design, batch effects or low counts.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, the expectation when p-values are uniformly distributed
      under no effect. The shaded band is the 95% confidence interval of that null, so points inside it are
      consistent with chance.
  - component: card
    column: feature_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: direction
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: transcripts, by usage call
    title: Transcripts tested
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct transcripts tested, and the bars rank the usage calls
      (up, down, not significant) by how many transcripts each holds. It answers how large the tested set
      is and how it splits.

      How to read: a leading not significant bar is the usual case. A strong imbalance between up and down
      is worth checking against the sample design.

      Lines and annotations: the call uses a gene-level adjusted q-value below 0.05, the catalog recipe
      default.
  - component: card
    column: direction
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [mode]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: direction
    caption: calls, by direction
    title: Calls by direction
    description: >-
      Each unit is one transcript, and the ring splits them into gain, loss and not significant. The second
      figure is the most common call. It answers how many isoforms change usage overall.

      How to read: a ring that is mostly not significant means few isoform switches, or too little
      replication to detect them. Open the volcano to see the borderline transcripts.

      Lines and annotations: the call uses a gene-level adjusted q-value below 0.05, the catalog recipe
      default.
  - component: card
    column: log2fc
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: usage log2 fold change, with its spread
    title: Usage change spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of usage log2 fold changes over all transcripts, and the box shows their
      quartiles. It answers how large the usage shifts are.

      How to read: a box tight around zero with a long range means most isoforms keep their share and a few
      switch strongly. The range is shown instead of a median because gains and losses cancel to about zero.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: feature_id
    title: Transcript usage table
    description: >-
      Each row is a transcript with its gene, usage log2 fold change, p-value, gene-level adjusted q-value
      and call. It answers which transcripts and genes to follow up, and a row selection filters the rest
      of the dashboard to that transcript.

      How to read: sort by q-value, then look at the fold change to see which isoform gains share. A gene
      with several significant isoforms is a stronger candidate than a single one.

      Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/DEXSeq/inst/doc/DEXSeq.html

tools.description: Differential exon usage with edgeR's diffSpliceDGE: an exon-level test, a gene-level F-test and a Simes-combined gene test per contrast, run by nf-core/rnasplice on featureCounts exon counts.

outputs.description: edgeR diffSpliceDGE as nf-core/rnasplice's edger_exon route writes it, one row per contrast and gene: the gene-level F-test and Simes FDRs, how many exons were tested and called, and the most significant exon's relative log2 fold change (treatment over control).

outputs.rawYaml:
id: edger_diffsplice_genes
name: Differential exon usage per gene (edgeR)
mode: splicing/exon-usage
description: >-
  edgeR diffSpliceDGE as nf-core/rnasplice's edger_exon route writes it, one
  row per contrast and gene: the gene-level F-test and Simes FDRs, how many
  exons were tested and called, and the most significant exon's relative log2
  fold change (treatment over control).
find: { path_glob: "**/contrast_*.usage.gene.csv" }
recipe: edger/diffsplice_genes.py
fixture: diffsplice_genes.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: gene_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Exon shift against significance per gene
    roles: { feature_id: gene_id, effect_size: log2fc, significance: fdr, label: gene_id, category: direction }
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 0.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Top exon log2 fold change
      significance_label: -log10 FDR of the gene test
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene in one contrast: the relative log2 fold change of its most significant exon on the
      horizontal axis and the FDR of the gene-level F-test on the vertical axis, coloured by the direction of
      the call. It answers which genes show differential exon usage and which way the top exon moves.

      How to read: genes high on the plot have at least one exon behaving differently from the rest of the
      gene. A large shift of one exon with a modest FDR can still be real, so open the table tile for the

      way they move.

      alike. A ring with only one direction points to a shared bias such as a library effect.
  - component: card
    column: exons_significant
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats, max]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Significant exons
    caption: exons called per gene, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of exons called significant across genes, and the box shows how many each
      gene contributes. It answers whether usage changes sit on a single exon or spread over the gene.

      How to read: a gene with many exons called suggests a gene-wide shift, which can reflect an isoform
      switch or a coverage artefact. A gene with one or two exons called is the typical exon-skipping pattern.

    column: abs_log2fc

    description: >-

tools.description: Immcantation R package that drives nf-core/airrflow's adaptive immune receptor repertoire (AIRR) analysis: clonal assignment, nearest-neighbour distance threshold finding, and the clonal diversity / abundance / overlap report.
tools.name: enchantR

outputs.description: alakazam rank-abundance curve per sample: the bootstrapped relative abundance of every clone against its rank within the sample, with the confidence band the bootstrap gives it. The band is what separates a genuinely expanded head from one estimated off a handful of sequences.
outputs.name: Clonal rank abundance
outputs.rawYaml:
id: enchantr_clonal_abundance
name: Clonal rank abundance
mode: repertoire-analysis/abundance
description: >-
  alakazam rank-abundance curve per sample: the bootstrapped relative abundance
  of every clone against its rank within the sample, with the confidence band
  the bootstrap gives it. The band is what separates a genuinely expanded head
  from one estimated off a handful of sequences.
find: { path_glob: "**/repertoire_analysis_report/tables/clonal_abundance.tsv" }
recipe: enchantr/clonal_abundance.py
fixture: clonal_abundance.tsv
renders_as:
  # The curve itself: one series per sample over the rank axis, with the
  # bootstrap interval drawn as a ribbon around it.
  - id: abundance_ribbon
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Clone rank abundance
    roles: { series: sample_id, x: rank, y: p, lower: lower, upper: upper }
    config:
      x_title: Clone rank
      y_title: Relative abundance
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sample: the estimated share of the repertoire held by the clone
      at each rank, with a shaded band for its uncertainty. It answers how dominant
      the largest clones are and how well the estimate is backed.

      How to read: a steep curve that starts high and falls fast is an expanded
      repertoire dominated by a few clones. A flat, low curve is polyclonal. A wide
      band means the estimate rests on few sequences, so compare samples only where
      their bands do not overlap.

      Lines and annotations: the shaded band is the confidence interval alakazam
      derives by bootstrapping the clone abundances (a 95% interval from 100
      bootstrap realizations in its vignette example). It is a property of the
      estimate and not a cut-off.

      Source: https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/Diversity-Vignette/
  # How much of the repertoire the single largest clone holds, per sample.
  - component: card
    column: p
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: largest clone share, per sample
    title: Largest clone share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest relative abundance of any clone in view, and
      the box shows its quartiles over the rows in view. It answers how much of a
      repertoire the top clone can hold.

      How to read: a high maximum points to one dominant clone, which is expected in
      an immune response and unusual in a resting repertoire. Filter to one sample to
      read its own top clone.
  # How uncertain the estimate is across clones: the bootstrap standard deviation.
  - component: card
    column: p_sd
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: bootstrap spread, lowest to highest
    title: Abundance uncertainty
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median bootstrap standard deviation of a clone's relative
      abundance, with the lowest and highest values next to it. It answers how stable
      the abundance estimates are.

      How to read: a standard deviation close to the abundance itself means the clone
      is poorly estimated, usually from a shallow sample. A low value across clones
      means the curves above can be trusted.
  - component: table
    title: Clone abundance table
    description: >-
      Each row is a clone of a sample at one rank, with its relative abundance, its
      bootstrap standard deviation and the lower and upper bounds of its band. It
      answers which clones lead each sample and by how much.

      How to read: sort by rank to see the head of each sample, or by abundance to
      compare samples of one subject.

outputs.description: alakazam Hill diversity profile per sample: the bootstrapped diversity d at every order q from richness to inverse Simpson, with its confidence band and the matching evenness.
outputs.name: Clonal diversity profile
outputs.rawYaml:
id: enchantr_clonal_diversity
name: Clonal diversity profile
mode: repertoire-analysis/diversity
description: >-
  alakazam Hill diversity profile per sample: the bootstrapped diversity d at
  every order q from richness to inverse Simpson, with its confidence band
  and the matching evenness.
find: { path_glob: "**/repertoire_analysis_report/tables/clonal_diversity.tsv" }
recipe: enchantr/clonal_diversity.py
fixture: clonal_diversity.tsv
renders_as:
  # A diversity profile is a curve per sample over an ordered x: the same shape
  # a rarefaction curve has, so the rarefaction renderer draws it directly. The
  # x axis is the diversity order q, not a subsampling depth.
  - id: diversity_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: rarefaction
    title: Diversity profile by order
    roles: { sample_id: sample_id, depth: q, metric: d, group: subject_id }
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sample: its Hill diversity at every order q, coloured by
      subject. It answers how diverse each repertoire is and how that changes as
      common clones weigh more.

      How to read: the horizontal axis is the diversity order q, not a sequencing
      depth. At q = 0 every clone counts equally (richness), at q = 1 it is the
      exponential of Shannon entropy and at q = 2 the inverse Simpson index. A curve
      that falls steeply is dominated by a few clones, a flat one is even, and
      curves that run apart at high q differ in their dominant clones.

      Sources: https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/Diversity-Vignette/ and
      https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/topics/calcDiversity/
  # Narrowed to one q, the same rows are one Hill number per sample with its
  # bootstrap confidence interval.
  - id: diversity_ci_bars
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: metric_ci_bars
    title: Diversity with confidence interval
    roles: { label: sample_id, value: d, lower: d_lower, upper: d_upper }
    config:
      metric_name: Hill diversity
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample: its Hill diversity with a whisker for the bootstrap
      confidence interval. It answers which samples differ in diversity beyond the
      uncertainty of the estimate.

      colour_by_rank: size_class
    description: >-
      Each arc is a group of sequences: the inner ring is the subject, the middle ring
      the sample and the outer ring the clone size class, sized by sequence count and
      coloured by size class. It answers how much of each repertoire sits in large
      clones.

      expanded clones. A ring spread over small classes is polyclonal. Click an arc
      to zoom in on it.

      frequency, from rare to hyperexpanded, using the default class boundaries of the
      immunarch repClonality function (1e-5, 1e-4, 1e-3 and 0.01 of the repertoire).

      and upper quartile of clone sizes. It answers how large the biggest expansion is
      against a typical clone.

      bottom. A maximum far above the upper quartile marks a clearly expanded clone.

name: Repertoire summary
mode: repertoire-analysis/summary
description: >-
  One row per sample: sequences that entered clonal assignment, the clones they
  collapsed into, the clone-size spread, and the rarefied Hill numbers with

recipe: enchantr/repertoire_summary.py
fixture: repertoire_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: card
    column: number_of_clones
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: clones per sample, with their spread
    title: Clones
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of clones across the samples in view, and the
      box shows the quartiles of clones per sample. It answers how many distinct
      lineages were recovered.

      How to read: compare samples in the box, since a low outlier is usually a
      shallow library. Clones are defined within a subject.
  - component: card
    column: sequences_per_clone
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mean clone size, with its spread
    title: Sequences per clone
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over samples of the mean clone size, the number of
      sequences per clone, and the box shows its spread. It answers how expanded the
      clones are on average.

      How to read: a value near one means almost every clone is a single sequence, as
      in a polyclonal repertoire. Higher values mean larger clones, or deeper
      sequencing of the same clones.
  - component: card
    column: shannon
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: Shannon diversity, with its spread
    title: Shannon diversity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over samples of the Hill number at q = 1, the
      exponential of Shannon entropy, and the box shows its spread. It answers how
      diverse the repertoires are while giving common clones their weight.

      How to read: compare the median with the clone counts above. A diversity far
      below the clone count means a few clones dominate.

      Sources: https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/Diversity-Vignette/ and
      https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/topics/calcDiversity/
  - component: card
    column: evenness
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: evenness, with its spread
    title: Evenness
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over samples of the evenness of the Hill profile at
      q = 1, and the box shows its spread. It answers whether clones are of similar
      size or dominated by a few.

      How to read: values near one mean clones of similar size. Lower values mean a few
      large clones carry the repertoire, so check the rank abundance curve. This
      table publishes no accepted cut-off, so compare samples with each other.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: scatter
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sequences
      y: number_of_clones
      color: subject_id
      size: sequences_per_clone
      log_x: "True"
      log_y: "True"
      labels:
        sequences: Sequences
        number_of_clones: Clones
        subject_id: Subject
        sequences_per_clone: Sequences per clone
    title: Clones against sequencing depth
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample: the sequences that entered clonal assignment on the
      horizontal axis and the clones they collapsed into on the vertical axis, sized by
      sequences per clone and coloured by subject. It answers whether the number of
      clones simply follows depth.

      How to read: points rise together because deeper samples reveal more clones. A
      sample sitting well below its neighbours at the same depth is more clonal, and a
      large marker means its clones are bigger. Both axes are logarithmic.
  # Richness against evenness: the two halves of a Hill profile on one plane, so
  # a repertoire that is large but carried by a few clones separates from one
  # that is both large and flat. Size is the sequencing depth behind the point,
  # which is what a difference in richness has to be read against.
  - id: richness_evenness
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Richness against evenness
    roles: { x: richness, y: evenness, label: sample_id, color: subject_id, size: sequences }
    config:
      x_title: Richness (Hill order 0)
      y_title: Evenness
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample: its richness on the horizontal axis and its evenness on
      the vertical axis, sized by sequencing depth and coloured by subject. It answers
      whether a rich repertoire is also flat or carried by a few clones.

      How to read: points to the upper right are both rich and even. Points to the
      lower right are rich but dominated by a few clones. Read richness against marker
      size, because a deeper sample reveals more clones.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median evenness of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      Immcantation.

      Source: https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/Diversity-Vignette/
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample_id
    title: Repertoire summary table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its sequence and clone counts, clone-size spread and
      Hill numbers with their confidence bounds. It answers which samples to inspect
      and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by clones or diversity to find outliers, then select a row to
      focus the other tiles on that sample.

Each point is a sample: its richness on the horizontal axis and its evenness on the vertical axis, sized by sequencing depth and coloured by subject. It answers whether a rich repertoire is also flat or carried by a few clones.
How to read: points to the upper right are both rich and even. Points to the lower right are rich but dominated by a few clones. Read richness against marker size, because a deeper sample reveals more clones.
Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median evenness of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Immcantation.
Source: https://alakazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/Diversity-Vignette/
renders_as.title: Richness against evenness

renders_as.description:
Each row is a sample with its sequence and clone counts, clone-size spread and Hill numbers with their confidence bounds. It answers which samples to inspect and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.
How to read: sort by clones or diversity to find outliers, then select a row to focus the other tiles on that sample.

outputs.name: Sequence processing counts
outputs.rawYaml:
id: enchantr_sequence_counts
name: Sequence processing counts
mode: parsed-logs/sequences
description: >-
  Sequences left after every pRESTO and Change-O step, one row per sample, with
  the fraction of raw reads that reach the final annotated repertoire.
find: { path_glob: "**/parsed_logs/Table_sequences_process.tsv" }
recipe: enchantr/sequence_counts.py
fixture: sequence_counts.tsv
renders_as:
  # The funnel as a single card: hero = raw reads, strip = every later stage.
  - component: card
    column: sequences
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: attrition
    attrition_cols: [quality_filtered, primers_masked, paired, consensus, assembled, representative, productive, collapsed]
    caption: reads left after each stage
    title: Read attrition
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total raw reads in view, and the strip shows how many are
      left after each pRESTO and Change-O stage. It answers where the reads are lost on
      the way to the final repertoire.

      How to read: the consensus, representative and collapse stages merge reads into
      UMI groups or unique sequences, so a large drop there is expected. A drop at
      quality filtering, primer masking or pairing points to a library problem.
  - component: card
    column: sequences
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: raw reads per sample, with their spread
    title: Raw reads per sample
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median raw read count per sample, and the box shows its
      spread. It answers how evenly the samples were sequenced.

      How to read: a sample far below the box has too little depth to compare. A
      very wide box means uneven sequencing, so use the diversity at a matched depth.
  - component: card
    column: collapsed
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: final sequences per sample, with their spread
    title: Final unique sequences
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of unique sequences left after the last stage, and
      the box shows their spread across samples. It answers how much repertoire
      remains for the analysis.

      How to read: samples with very few final sequences give wide confidence
      intervals in the diversity tiles. Compare with the raw reads to see how much
      each sample lost.
  - component: card
    column: retention
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: retention, with its spread
    title: Read retention
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median fraction of raw reads still represented at the last
      stage, and the box shows its spread. It answers how efficiently the pipeline
      turns reads into repertoire.

      How to read: retention is low by design here, since reads collapse onto UMI
      groups and unique sequences. Compare samples with each other, and investigate a
      sample whose retention is far below the rest.
  - component: table
    title: Sequence counts table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its sequence count after every pRESTO and Change-O
      stage and its overall retention. It answers where each sample lost its reads.

      How to read: read across a row to find the stage with the biggest drop, and sort
      by retention to find the outliers.

outputs.name: Sequence attrition flow
outputs.rawYaml:
id: enchantr_sequence_fates
name: Sequence attrition flow
mode: parsed-logs/fates
description: >-
  Where the reads of each sample go through the pRESTO and Change-O funnel, one
  weighted row per loss point, shaped for a Sankey.
find: { path_glob: "**/parsed_logs/Table_sequences_process.tsv" }
recipe: enchantr/sequence_fates.py
fixture: sequence_fates.tsv
renders_as:
  # Only the pRESTO milestones are bound: they exist on every fastq-mode run.
  # The two Change-O ones ride in the collection for the depth slider to reach.
  # Every flow leaves the one input node, so colour by target (RULES section 8).
  - id: attrition_sankey
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sankey
    title: Where reads are lost
    roles:
      steps: [input, quality, paired, consensus, assembled, representative]
    config:
      color_mode: target
      value_col: reads
      value_label: Reads
      value_format: count
    description: >-
      Each band is a group of reads moving from one pRESTO stage to the next, and its
      width is the number of reads. It answers at which stage reads are lost and how
      many reach the final representative sequences.

      How to read: a wide band leaving to Lost marks a stage that discards many
      reads. Stages that merge reads onto UMI groups also shed width without being a
      failure. A loss at quality filtering or pairing points to the library, so open
      the counts table.

      Note: bands are coloured by the stage they lead to, because every flow starts at
      the same input node.
  - component: table
    title: Read fate table
    description: >-
      Each row is a path through the stages for one sample, with the number of reads
      that took it. It answers how many reads follow each route.

      How to read: filter to one sample and sort by reads to see its main routes.
