outputs.description: The nearest-neighbour distance model shazam fitted per subject and the threshold it chose to separate clonally related from unrelated sequences, with the sensitivity and specificity that threshold achieves.
outputs.name: Clonal distance threshold
outputs.rawYaml:
id: enchantr_threshold_summary
name: Clonal distance threshold
mode: find-threshold/summary
description: >-
  The nearest-neighbour distance model shazam fitted per subject and the
  threshold it chose to separate clonally related from unrelated sequences,
  with the sensitivity and specificity that threshold achieves.
find: { path_glob: "**/find_threshold/*_dist_report/tables/*threshold-summary.tsv" }
recipe: enchantr/threshold_summary.py
fixture: threshold_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: card
    column: threshold
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: threshold per subject, with its spread
    title: Clonal distance threshold
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean nearest-neighbour distance threshold over the
      subjects in view, and the box shows its spread. It answers how close two
      sequences must be to be called one clone.

      How to read: the threshold is fitted per subject from a bimodal distance
      distribution, so subjects differ. A subject far from the others fitted a
      weaker separation, so check its distance histogram in the report.

      Source: https://shazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/DistToNearest-Vignette/
  - component: card
    column: sensitivity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: sensitivity per subject, with its spread
    title: Threshold sensitivity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median sensitivity the chosen threshold achieves, and the
      box shows its spread across subjects. It answers how many truly related
      sequences the threshold keeps together.

      How to read: a low value means related sequences are split into separate clones.
      Shazam publishes no minimum, so compare subjects with each other.

      Source: https://shazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/DistToNearest-Vignette/
  - component: card
    column: specificity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: lowest and highest specificity
    title: Threshold specificity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median specificity the chosen threshold achieves, with the
      lowest and highest across subjects. It answers how well unrelated sequences stay
      apart.

      How to read: when the run fixes the specificity as the selection rule, every
      subject sits at that value and the card only confirms it. Otherwise a low value
      means unrelated sequences risk being merged into one clone.

      Source: https://shazam.readthedocs.io/en/stable/vignettes/DistToNearest-Vignette/
  - component: table
    title: Threshold table
    description: >-
      Each row is a subject with its fitted model, the chosen threshold, the sensitivity
      and specificity it reaches and the mean threshold applied across subjects. It
      answers which model and threshold each subject got.

      How to read: compare the subject threshold with the mean threshold, which is the
      single value the pipeline applies.

tools.description: Computes the percentage of endogenous DNA and library clonality from samtools flagstat output.
tools.name: endorS.py

outputs.description: Share of a library's reads that map to the target reference, before and after the quality filter and deduplication, from endorS.py. The headline number of an ancient-DNA screen: it says how much of an extract is the organism rather than the soil, the excavator and the lab.
outputs.name: Endogenous DNA
outputs.rawYaml:
id: endorspy_endogenous
name: Endogenous DNA
description: >-
  Share of a library's reads that map to the target reference, before and after
  the quality filter and deduplication, from endorS.py. The headline number of
  an ancient-DNA screen: it says how much of an extract is the organism rather
  than the soil, the excavator and the lab.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_endogenous_dna_mqc.json"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*_endogenous_dna.json"
recipe: endorspy/endogenous.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 2 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: endogenous.tsv
renders_as:
  # Few points per run, so the reading is carried by the identity diagonal: it
  # is the data-defined "nothing lost" reference, not a tool cut-off.
  # C1: one colour per library, the only grouping column the table has.
  - id: endogenous_pre_post
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Endogenous DNA before and after filtering
    roles: {x: endogenous_dna, y: endogenous_dna_post, label: sample, color: sample}
    config:
      x_title: Endogenous DNA, raw alignment (%)
      y_title: Endogenous DNA, filtered and deduplicated (%)
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: No loss to filtering
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: the percentage of its reads that map to the target
      reference on the raw alignment (horizontal) and after the quality filter and
      deduplication (vertical). It answers how much of the on-target signal survives
      cleaning.

      How to read: a point near the diagonal loses little to filtering and
      deduplication. A point far below it is a library whose on-target reads were
      mostly duplicates or low quality, so its usable depth is smaller than the raw
      percentage suggests. endorS.py defines no cut-off for a good library.

    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: endogenous_dna}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: the percentage of its raw reads that map to the target
      reference. It answers which extracts are rich enough to sequence deeper.

      worth deeper sequencing. A short bar means most reads come from other sources
      and the library will need far more sequencing for the same coverage. The
      filtered percentage is on the tile that compares both.

      and the box shows how it spreads across libraries. It answers how rich the

outputs.rawYaml:
id: epitopeprediction_allele_summary
name: Binding per allele
mode: epitope/alleles
description: >-
  One row per sample and allele: distinct peptides scored, peptides at least one
  tool calls a binder, their share, and the median and best IC50 of the
  peptides. The allele is normalised to HLA-A*02:01 and carries its locus and
  MHC class, so it filters and joins like the alleles an HLA typing tool writes.
find:
  path_glob: "**/predictions/*.tsv"
recipe: epitopeprediction/allele_summary.py
fixture: allele_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # Allele by sample: colour is the median affinity score, size the binder share.
  - id: allele_dot_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    title: Binding by allele and sample
    roles: { cluster: sample, gene: allele, mean_expression: median_affinity_score, frac_expressing: binder_rate }
    description: >-
      Each dot is an HLA allele in one sample: its size is the share of peptides that
      at least one tool calls a binder and its colour is the median affinity score of
      the peptides. It answers which alleles present the most candidate peptides.

      How to read: a large, strongly coloured dot is an allele with many predicted
      binders of good affinity, so its peptides are the first to follow up. Small pale
      dots are alleles that bind few of the peptides. A column that stands apart from
      the others in size points to a sample with a different peptide set or tool mix.

      Lines and annotations: the binder call is the one the pipeline writes for each
      tool, a percentile rank of 2 or less for MHCflurry, NetMHCpan and MixMHCpred, 5
      or less for NetMHCIIpan, and an affinity score of at least 0.425 (500 nM) for
      MHCnuggets. The affinity score is 1 minus log10 of the IC50 over log10 of 50000.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - id: allele_binders
    component: card
    column: binders
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: hla_locus
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: binders, by HLA locus
    title: Predicted binders
    description: >-
      The hero number is the sum of binder peptides over every allele and sample in
      view, and the bars rank the HLA loci by their share. It answers how many
      candidate peptides the alleles present and through which locus.

      How to read: a locus that carries most binders is the one the patient's
      peptides fit best. The compact line gives the median and the largest binder count
      of one allele, so a total spread over many alleles reads differently from one
      dominant allele. Binders are the tools' own calls, see the dot plot for the rules.
  - id: allele_binder_rate
    component: card
    column: binder_rate
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: binder share, with its spread
    title: Binder share per allele
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of scored peptides that a tool calls a
      binder, over the alleles in view, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how
      selective the alleles are.

      How to read: a low median with a few high alleles is the usual pattern, since few
      peptides bind any one allele. A box shifted high means a peptide set enriched for
      binders, for example after a binder filter, or permissive tools. Filter to one
      sample to compare alleles within it.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: allele
      y: binders
      color: sample
      labels: { allele: Allele, binders: Binder peptides, sample: Sample }
    title: Binders per allele
    description: >-
      Each bar is the number of binder peptides for an allele, split by sample. It
      answers which alleles contribute the most candidates and whether samples agree.

      How to read: tall bars mark alleles that bind many peptides. An allele that is
      tall in one sample only reflects that sample's peptide set, not the allele alone.
      Pick a locus in the filter to narrow the alleles.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: hla_locus
    title: HLA locus
    description: >-
      Pick one or more HLA loci to restrict the dot plot, the cards and the table to
      them. It answers how a single locus behaves.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: allele_key
    title: Allele binding table
    description: >-
      Each row is an allele in one sample with its peptide count, binder count and
      share, and the median and best IC50. It answers the exact numbers behind the plots
      and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by binders or by best IC50 to find the alleles worth following
      up.

id: epitopeprediction_peptides
name: Predicted peptides
mode: epitope/peptides
description: >-
  One row per sample and peptide: its best prediction over all alleles and
  tools (allele, tool and IC50), how many alleles were scored and how many a
  tool calls it a binder of, whether it binds, does not, or could not be scored,
  and its source: gene, transcript, consequence, protein change, genomic anchor
  and UniProt accession for variant input, the protein records for protein
  input, the peptide id for peptide input, and the MHC class it was scored for.
find:
  path_glob: "**/predictions/*.tsv"
recipe: epitopeprediction/peptides.py
fixture: peptides.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: peptide_count
    component: card
    column: sequence
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: call
    headline: true
    caption: peptides, by call
    title: Peptides scored
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of sample and peptide rows, the compact line gives
      the distinct sequences, and the bar splits the rows into binder, non-binder and
      not scored. It answers how many peptides went through prediction and how many a
      tool could score.

      How to read: a large not-scored share means the alleles or peptide lengths are
      outside what the tools support. A binder share far above a few percent suggests a
      binder filter was applied upstream. Calls are the pipeline's own, a percentile
      rank of 2 or less for most tools and an IC50 of 500 nM or less for MHCnuggets.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - id: binder_count
    component: card
    column: sequence
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    filter_expr: "col('binder') == 1"
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: length_class
    headline: true
    caption: binders, by peptide length
    title: Binder peptides
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of peptides that at least one tool calls a binder,
      the compact line gives the distinct sequences, and the bar splits them by peptide
      length. It answers how many candidates remain and which lengths dominate.

      How to read: the lengths come from the run's minimum and maximum peptide length
      settings, so a length with no binders may simply be a length the tools score
      poorly. Binders are the pipeline's own calls, see the Peptides scored tile.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - id: binding_alleles
    component: card
    column: binding_alleles
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    filter_expr: "col('binder') == 1"
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: alleles bound, distribution
    title: Alleles bound per binder
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of alleles a binder peptide binds, and the
      histogram shows the distribution. It answers whether binders are allele-specific
      or promiscuous.

      How to read: a median of one means most peptides fit a single allele. Peptides
      that bind several alleles are more likely to be presented in the patient and are
      good candidates to prioritise.
  - id: peptide_length
    component: card
    column: length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: peptide length, distribution
    title: Peptide length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median peptide length in residues and the histogram shows
      the distribution. It answers whether the peptide set matches the MHC class that
      was scored.

      How to read: the lengths are set by the run's minimum and maximum peptide length
      options for each MHC class, and each tool has its own fixed range. A wide spread
      shows a run that scored both classes.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/usage.md
  - id: length_by_class
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: length_class
      color: call
      facet_col: mhc_class
      barmode: stack
      labels: { length_class: Peptide length, call: Call, mhc_class: MHC class, count: Peptides }
    title: Calls by peptide length
    description: >-
      Each bar counts peptides of one length, stacked by binder call and split by MHC
      class. It answers which lengths yield binders.

      How to read: a length with many peptides and no binders is mostly noise, and a
      length with a high binder share is where to look first. Lengths outside a tool's
      supported range are not scored by it.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/usage.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      color: call
      labels: { sample: Sample, call: Call, count: Peptides }
    title: Calls per sample
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the peptides of a sample, stacked by call. It answers how big
      each peptide set is and how its calls split.

      How to read: compare the binder share across samples. A sample with far more
      not-scored peptides used alleles or lengths that the tools do not support.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: call
    title: Call
    description: >-
      Pick binder, non-binder or not scored to restrict the cards, the plots and the
      table to those peptides. It answers what a single call looks like.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: length_class
    title: Peptide length
    description: >-
      Pick one or more peptide lengths to restrict the tiles to them. It answers how
      binders behave at one length.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: peptide_key
    title: Peptide table
    description: >-
      Each row is a peptide in a sample with its best prediction over all alleles and
      tools, the number of alleles it binds and its source gene and protein change for
      variant input. It answers which peptides to follow up and lets a row selection
      filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by best IC50 or by the number of binding alleles, and filter to
      mutant peptides to see the neoepitope candidates.

outputs.name: Binding predictions
outputs.rawYaml:
id: epitopeprediction_predictions
name: Binding predictions
mode: epitope/predictions
description: >-
  One row per sample, peptide, allele and prediction tool that scored it: the
  0-1 affinity score, the IC50 in nM behind it, the percentile rank, the
  pipeline's binder call and an affinity class (strong, binder, weak,
  non-binding), with the peptide's length and origin (mutant, wild type or input
  sequence) and, for variant input, its gene and consequence. Alleles are
  normalised to HLA-A*02:01 with their locus and MHC class. Mutant rows whose
  wild type was predicted carry its IC50 and the agretopicity.
find:
  path_glob: "**/predictions/*.tsv"
recipe: epitopeprediction/predictions.py
fixture: predictions.tsv
renders_as:
  # Affinity against rank, one point per prediction: the two scores agree for a
  # well-calibrated tool, and a tool's binder cut-off shows as an edge.
  - id: affinity_rank_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: IC50 against percentile rank
    roles: { x: ic50_nm, y: percentile_rank, label: sequence, color: predictor }
    config:
      x_title: Predicted IC50 (nM)
      y_title: Percentile rank
      log_x: true
      log_y: true
      reference_line: vertical
      reference_value: 500
      reference_label: 500 nM, usual binder limit
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is one prediction of a peptide against an allele: its predicted IC50
      on the horizontal axis and its percentile rank on the vertical axis, coloured by
      the tool. It answers whether a tool's affinity and rank agree and where its binder
      call falls.

      How to read: a lower IC50 and a lower rank both mean stronger binding, so
      confident binders sit at the lower left. A tool whose points form a clear edge has
      a rank cut-off that decides its binder call. A tool with no IC50 does not appear
      here.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical line is 500 nM, an IC50 below which peptides
      are usually considered binders. The binder call of each tool uses its own rank
      rule, a rank of 2 or less for MHCflurry, NetMHCpan and MixMHCpred, 5 or less for
      NetMHCIIpan.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  # Mutant against wild-type affinity: below the diagonal, the mutation
  # strengthens binding (agretopicity under 1).
  - id: mutant_wildtype_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Mutant against wild-type IC50
    roles: { x: wt_ic50_nm, y: ic50_nm, label: sequence, color: allele }
    config:
      x_title: Wild-type IC50 (nM)
      y_title: Mutant IC50 (nM)
      log_x: true
      log_y: true
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: Mutant equals wild type
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a mutant peptide predicted against an allele: the IC50 of its wild
      type on the horizontal axis and its own IC50 on the vertical axis, coloured by
      allele. It answers whether the mutation changes binding.

      How to read: points below the diagonal bind more strongly than their wild type
      and are the neoepitope candidates, especially when the wild type is above the
      binder limit. Points on the diagonal are unchanged. Only missense peptides with a
      predicted wild type appear.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is where the mutant and wild-type IC50 are
      equal, an identity line and not a cut-off. A mutant IC50 below 500 nM is usually
      considered a binder.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: log10_ic50
      color: predictor
      barmode: overlay
      labels: { log10_ic50: Log10 IC50 (nM), predictor: Tool }
    title: Distribution of predicted IC50
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: x, stat: median, column: log10_ic50}
    description: >-
      Each bar counts predictions in a log10 IC50 bin, overlaid by tool. It answers how
      the tools spread their affinities and where most peptides fall.

      How to read: most peptides are weak or non-binders, so the mass sits above 3 (1000
      nM). A value of 2.7 is 500 nM, the usual binder limit, and 1.7 is 50 nM, a strong
      binder. A tool with a very different shape scores on another scale, so compare
      calls rather than raw values.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median log10 IC50 of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      nf-core/epitopeprediction.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - id: prediction_count
    component: card
    column: sequence
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: predictor
    headline: true
    caption: predictions, by tool
    title: Predictions made
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of predictions, one per peptide, allele and tool, the
      compact line gives the distinct peptides, and the ring splits them by tool. It
      answers how much scoring was done and how it is shared between tools.

      How to read: a tool with a small share scored fewer peptides because of the
      alleles or lengths it supports. The same peptide scored by several tools counts
      once per tool.
  - id: binder_calls
    component: card
    column: sequence
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    filter_expr: "col('binder') == 1"
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: hla_locus
    caption: binder calls, by HLA locus
    title: Binder calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of predictions that a tool calls a binder, the
      compact line gives the distinct peptides, and the bar splits them by HLA locus. It
      answers how many predictions pass and through which locus.

      How to read: a peptide called a binder by several tools or alleles counts several
      times here, so the distinct count is the number of candidates. Binder calls are the
      pipeline's own, a percentile rank of 2 or less for most tools.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - id: allele_count
    component: card
    column: allele
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [mode]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: hla_locus
    top_n_count: 4
    headline: true
    caption: alleles, by HLA locus
    title: Alleles scored
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct alleles scored, the compact line gives
      the most frequent one, and the bars rank the HLA loci by how many alleles they
      have. It answers how wide the typing is.

      How to read: a lower count than expected means a homozygous or partial typing.
      A locus missing here was not scored at all.
  - id: median_ic50
    component: card
    column: ic50_nm
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 500
    threshold_direction: max
    caption: median IC50 against the 500 nM binder limit
    title: Median predicted IC50
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median predicted IC50 in nM over every prediction in view,
      compared with a cut-off. It answers whether the typical peptide is a binder.

      How to read: most peptides do not bind, so a median above the limit is the normal
      case. A median below it means a peptide set already enriched for binders. The
      compact line gives the best and worst IC50.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-off is 500 nM, an IC50 below which peptides are
      usually considered binders.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: allele
    title: Allele
    description: >-
      Pick one or more alleles to restrict the plots, the cards and the table to them. It
      answers how a single allele scores.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: predictor
    title: Prediction tool
    description: >-
      Pick one or more tools to restrict the tiles to them. It answers how one tool
      scores on its own.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: log10_ic50
    title: Log10 IC50
    description: >-
      Drag the range to keep predictions within a log10 IC50 window. It answers which
      peptides fall in a chosen affinity band, for example 1.7 to 2.7 for binders between
      50 and 500 nM.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: row_id
    title: Binding prediction table
    description: >-
      Each row is one prediction of a peptide against an allele by a tool, with its
      affinity score, IC50, percentile rank, binder call and class. It answers the exact
      values behind every tile and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by IC50 or percentile rank and filter to one allele or tool to
      follow up the strongest candidates.

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md

renders_as.description:
Each bar counts predictions in a log10 IC50 bin, overlaid by tool. It answers how the tools spread their affinities and where most peptides fall.
How to read: most peptides are weak or non-binders, so the mass sits above 3 (1000 nM). A value of 2.7 is 500 nM, the usual binder limit, and 1.7 is 50 nM, a strong binder. A tool with a very different shape scores on another scale, so compare calls rather than raw values.
Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median log10 IC50 of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/epitopeprediction.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md

renders_as.caption: predictions, by tool
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the count of predictions, one per peptide, allele and tool, the compact line gives the distinct peptides, and the ring splits them by tool. It answers how much scoring was done and how it is shared between tools.
How to read: a tool with a small share scored fewer peptides because of the alleles or lengths it supports. The same peptide scored by several tools counts once per tool.
renders_as.title: Predictions made

renders_as.caption: binder calls, by HLA locus
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the count of predictions that a tool calls a binder, the compact line gives the distinct peptides, and the bar splits them by HLA locus. It answers how many predictions pass and through which locus.
How to read: a peptide called a binder by several tools or alleles counts several times here, so the distinct count is the number of candidates. Binder calls are the pipeline's own, a percentile rank of 2 or less for most tools.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
renders_as.title: Binder calls

renders_as.caption: alleles, by HLA locus
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the count of distinct alleles scored, the compact line gives the most frequent one, and the bars rank the HLA loci by how many alleles they have. It answers how wide the typing is.
How to read: a lower count than expected means a homozygous or partial typing. A locus missing here was not scored at all.
renders_as.title: Alleles scored

renders_as.caption: median IC50 against the 500 nM binder limit
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median predicted IC50 in nM over every prediction in view, compared with a cut-off. It answers whether the typical peptide is a binder.
How to read: most peptides do not bind, so a median above the limit is the normal case. A median below it means a peptide set already enriched for binders. The compact line gives the best and worst IC50.
Lines and annotations: the cut-off is 500 nM, an IC50 below which peptides are usually considered binders.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md

outputs.rawYaml:
id: epitopeprediction_predictor_agreement
name: Agreement between tools
mode: epitope/agreement
description: >-
  One row per sample, peptide, allele and pair of tools that both scored it: the
  two IC50s, their log10 ratio, the two binder calls and the outcome (both call
  a binder, neither does, or only one of the two). A run with one tool per MHC
  class has no pair.
find:
  path_glob: "**/predictions/*.tsv"
recipe: epitopeprediction/predictor_agreement.py
fixture: predictor_agreement.tsv
renders_as:
  # One tool's IC50 against the other's: on the diagonal they agree, and the
  # colour names who calls a binder.
  - id: agreement_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: IC50 of one tool against another
    roles: { x: ic50_a_nm, y: ic50_b_nm, label: sequence, color: agreement }
    config:
      x_title: IC50 of the first tool (nM)
      y_title: IC50 of the second tool (nM)
      log_x: true
      log_y: true
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: Both tools agree
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a peptide scored against an allele by two tools: the IC50 of the
      first on the horizontal axis and of the second on the vertical axis, coloured by
      whether both, neither or only one calls a binder. It answers how consistent the
      tools are.

      How to read: points on the diagonal get the same affinity from both tools. Points
      far from it, or coloured as one tool only, are peptides whose call depends on the
      tool and should be confirmed before they are trusted.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is where the two IC50 are equal, an identity
      line and not a cut-off. Binder calls are each tool's own rule, a percentile rank
      of 2 or less for most tools and an IC50 of 500 nM or less for MHCnuggets.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - id: paired_predictions
    component: card
    column: sequence
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: agreement
    caption: pairs, by agreement
    title: Tool pairs compared
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of peptide, allele and tool-pair rows, the compact
      line gives the distinct peptides, and the bar splits them by outcome. It answers
      how often the tools agree.

      How to read: a large share where neither tool calls a binder is normal, since most
      peptides do not bind. The share where only one tool calls a binder is the part
      that needs a second opinion.
  - id: ic50_gap
    component: card
    column: abs_log10_ratio
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [q3, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: IC50 gap, distribution
    title: Typical IC50 gap
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median absolute log10 ratio between the two tools' IC50,
      and the histogram shows the distribution. A value of 1 is a ten-fold difference.
      It answers how far apart the tools are on a typical peptide.

      How to read: a median near zero means the tools agree on the scale. A median of one
      or more means they score on different scales, so compare binder calls and not raw
      IC50 values.
  - id: disputed_binders
    component: card
    column: sequence
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    filter_expr: "col('concordant') == 0"
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: agreement
    caption: disputed pairs, by who calls a binder
    title: Disputed binder calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of pairs where exactly one tool calls a binder, the
      compact line gives the distinct peptides, and the bar shows which tool is the
      caller. It answers how many candidates depend on the choice of tool.

      How to read: a disputed pair is not wrong, since the tools use different rank
      rules, but its peptide is a weaker candidate than one that every tool calls. Check
      the scatter to see how far apart the IC50 values are.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: agreement
    title: Agreement
    description: >-
      Pick an outcome, both, neither or one tool only, to restrict the scatter, the cards
      and the table to it. It answers what the disputed peptides look like.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: pair_key
    title: Tool agreement table
    description: >-
      Each row is a peptide and allele scored by two tools, with both IC50, their log10
      ratio, both binder calls and the outcome. It answers the exact values behind the
      scatter and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by the absolute log ratio to find the largest disagreements.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: epitopeprediction_predictor_summary
name: Binder calls per tool
mode: epitope/tools
description: >-
  One row per sample and prediction tool: the peptides it scored, could not
  score (allele or length unsupported) and calls a binder of at least one
  allele, the binder share, the alleles it scored and its median IC50. Wild-type
  peptides are left out, as in the pipeline's MultiQC statistics, so the two
  agree.
find:
  path_glob: "**/predictions/*.tsv"
recipe: epitopeprediction/predictor_summary.py
fixture: predictor_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: binder_rate_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: binder_rate
      color: predictor
      barmode: group
      labels: { sample: Sample, binder_rate: Binder share, predictor: Tool }
    title: Binder share per tool
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: binder_rate}
    description: >-
      Each bar is the share of a tool's scored peptides that it calls a binder, grouped by
      sample. It answers how permissive each tool is on the same peptides.

      How to read: tools use different rules, a percentile rank of 2 or less for most and
      an IC50 of 500 nM or less for MHCnuggets, so their shares are not directly
      comparable. A tool far above the others in every sample is the most permissive.
      Wild-type peptides are left out, as in the pipeline's own statistics.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median binder share of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      nf-core/epitopeprediction.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - id: tool_binders
    component: card
    column: binders
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: predictor
    caption: binders, by tool
    title: Binders per tool
    description: >-
      The hero number is the sum of binder peptides over the tools and samples in view,
      and the ring splits them by tool. It answers which tool contributes the most
      candidates.

      How to read: a tool with a large slice is permissive or scored more peptides. The
      compact line gives the median and the highest count of one tool and sample.
  - id: tool_unsupported
    component: card
    column: unsupported
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: predictor
    caption: unscored peptides, by tool
    title: Peptides a tool could not score
    description: >-
      The hero number is the sum of peptides that a tool could not score because of an
      unsupported allele or length, and the bar splits them by tool. It answers how much
      of the input each tool leaves out.

      How to read: a tool that leaves out many peptides covers less of the input, so its
      binder count understates the candidates. Check the supported alleles and lengths
      in the pipeline's usage notes.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/usage.md
  - component: card
    column: binder_rate
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: binder share, with its spread
    title: Binder share per tool and sample
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median binder share over the tool and sample rows in view,
      and the box shows the quartiles. It answers what share of scored peptides a tool
      usually calls a binder.

      How to read: a low median is expected, since few peptides bind any allele. A wide
      box shows tools or samples that differ strongly, so open the bar chart to see which.

    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: predictor
    title: Prediction tool
    description: >-

      answers how one tool behaves.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: summary_key
    title: Tool summary table
    description: >-

      score and called binders, its binder share, the alleles scored and its median IC50.
      It answers the exact numbers behind the tiles and lets a row selection filter the
      rest of the dashboard.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: epitopeprediction_variant_peptides
name: Variant peptides
mode: epitope/variant-peptides
description: >-
  The candidate peptides pVACseq cuts from the annotated variants, one row per
  sample and peptide: every peptide of each requested length that overlaps the
  mutation, with the gene, transcript, consequence (missense, in-frame indel,
  frameshift), protein change, genomic anchor and UniProt accession behind it,
  plus the wild-type peptides added by --wild_type.
find:
  path_glob: "**/variant_peptides/*_length_*.tsv"
recipe: epitopeprediction/variant_peptides.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 18 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several peptide lengths.
fixture: variant_peptides.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: consequence_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: consequence
      color: length_class
      barmode: stack
      labels: { consequence: Variant consequence, length_class: Peptide length, count: Candidate peptides }
    title: Candidate peptides by consequence
    description: >-
      Each bar counts candidate peptides for one variant consequence, stacked by peptide
      length. It answers which kinds of variant yield the peptides to score.

      How to read: a frameshift or in-frame indel produces many peptides from one variant,
      because every peptide that overlaps the changed sequence counts, so a tall bar does
      not mean many variants. Missense variants are the only ones with a wild-type
      counterpart.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - id: variant_count
    component: card
    column: genomic_anchor
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: consequence
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: variants, by consequence
    title: Variants represented
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct variant positions that yielded peptides,
      the compact line gives the number of peptide rows, and the bars rank the
      consequences by their variants. It answers how many variants feed the prediction.

      How to read: a large gap between peptide rows and variants means a few variants,
      often frameshifts, contribute most of the peptides.
  - id: candidate_count
    component: card
    column: sequence
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: consequence
    caption: peptides, by consequence
    title: Candidate peptides
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of candidate peptide rows, the compact line gives the
      distinct sequences, and the bar splits them by variant consequence. It answers how
      many peptides go to the predictors.

      How to read: the same sequence can come from several samples or variants, so the
      distinct count is the number of different peptides to score. Wild-type peptides
      added by the wild-type option are counted here as well.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: consequence
    title: Variant consequence
    description: >-
      Pick one or more consequences to restrict the bars, the cards and the table to them.
      It answers what a single kind of variant contributes.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: peptide_key
    title: Variant peptide table
    description: >-
      Each row is a candidate peptide with its gene, transcript, consequence, protein
      change, genomic position and UniProt accession. It answers which variant each peptide
      comes from and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: filter to mutant peptides of one gene to review its variants.

outputs.name: Mutant against wild type
outputs.rawYaml:
id: epitopeprediction_wildtype_pairs
name: Mutant against wild type
mode: epitope/agretopicity
description: >-
  Missense mutant peptides beside their wild-type peptide (--wild_type), one row
  per sample, mutant peptide, allele and tool: both IC50s, both binder calls,
  the agretopicity (mutant over wild-type IC50) and the outcome, a mutant binder
  whose wild type does not bind being the classic neoepitope candidate.
find:
  path_glob: "**/predictions/*.tsv"
recipe: epitopeprediction/wildtype_pairs.py
fixture: wildtype_pairs.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: wildtype_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Mutant against wild-type IC50
    roles: { x: wt_ic50_nm, y: ic50_nm, label: sequence, color: pair_call }
    config:
      x_title: Wild-type IC50 (nM)
      y_title: Mutant IC50 (nM)
      log_x: true
      log_y: true
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: Mutant equals wild type
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a missense mutant peptide against an allele and a tool: the IC50 of
      its wild type on the horizontal axis and its own IC50 on the vertical axis,
      coloured by the outcome. It answers which mutations create or strengthen binding.

      How to read: points below the diagonal bind more strongly than their wild type. The
      classic neoepitope candidate is a mutant binder whose wild type does not bind.
      Points on the diagonal are unchanged by the mutation.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is where the mutant and wild-type IC50 are
      equal, an identity line and not a cut-off. Binder calls are each tool's own rule, a
      percentile rank of 2 or less for most tools and an IC50 of 500 nM or less for
      MHCnuggets.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/epitopeprediction/master/docs/output.md
  - id: pair_outcomes
    component: card
    column: sequence
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: pair_call
    caption: pairs, by outcome
    title: Mutant and wild-type pairs
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of mutant and wild-type pairs, the compact line gives
      the distinct mutant peptides, and the bar splits them by outcome. It answers how
      many mutations change binding.

      How to read: the share where the mutant binds and the wild type does not is the
      candidate list. A large share where neither binds is common, since most peptides
      do not bind.
  - id: agretopicity_median
    component: card
    column: log10_agretopicity
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: log10 agretopicity, quartiles
    title: Change in affinity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of log10 agretopicity, which is the log10 of the
      mutant IC50 over the wild-type IC50, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how
      strongly mutations change binding.

      How to read: a value below zero means the mutant binds more strongly than its wild
      type and a value above zero less strongly. A box centred on zero means most
      mutations leave binding unchanged, and the hero is a range and not a median because
      a median over both directions cancels out.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: pair_call
    title: Outcome
    description: >-
      Pick an outcome, for example a mutant binder whose wild type does not bind, to
      restrict the scatter, the cards and the table to it. It answers what the candidates
      look like.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: pair_key
    title: Mutant and wild-type table
    description: >-
      Each row is a mutant peptide with its wild type, allele and tool, both IC50, both
      binder calls, the agretopicity and the outcome. It answers the exact values behind
      the scatter and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: filter to the outcome where only the mutant binds and sort by mutant
      IC50 to rank the candidates.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: famsa_alignment
name: Family alignment
mode: protein/msa
description: >-
  The protein module's MSA table: one row per aligned sequence of every family
  alignment, the family representative first (rank 0), with each row's
  identity to the representative and the share of the representative it
  covers. Capped at 500 rows per family in file order.
find:
  path_glob: "**/full_msa/filtered/famsa_align/*/*.aln"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/update_families/full_msa/famsa_align/*/*.aln"
    - "**/full_msa/filtered/mafft_align/*/*.fas"
recipe: famsa/alignment.py
fixture: alignment.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: family_msa
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: msa
    title: Family alignment
    roles: {msa_id: msa_id, seq_id: seq_id, sequence: aligned_sequence, rank: rank, identity: identity}
    description: >-
      Each row is a sequence of a protein family, aligned to the family representative
      on top, and each column is an alignment position coloured by residue type. It
      answers how well the members of a family line up and where they differ.

      How to read: columns of one colour are conserved positions, and a block of gaps
      marks an insertion or a member that does not cover that region. Sequences with a
      low identity to the representative are the divergent members, which may be
      fragments or distant relatives. Brush columns to follow the residues on the
      structure and the sequence track.

      Lines and annotations: this module takes the first row of each alignment file as
      the family representative and measures each row's identity against it. The
      consensus row and the conservation bars are computed from the displayed rows,
      which this module caps at 500 per family in file order, not a FAMSA setting.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27670777/
  - id: aligned_rows
    component: card
    column: seq_id
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: aligned rows, with the distinct sequences
    title: Aligned sequences

outputs.name: Residue conservation
outputs.rawYaml:
id: famsa_conservation
name: Residue conservation
mode: protein/residues
description: >-
  The protein module's residue table for every family: one row per residue of
  the family representative, numbered along its ungapped sequence, with a
  0-1 conservation score (entropy of the alignment column over the 20 amino
  acids, discounted by gaps), its class (conserved, intermediate, variable),
  the column consensus and its occupancy. The representative sequence rides on
  every row, which is what a 3D tile folds in resolve mode.
find:
  path_glob: "**/full_msa/filtered/famsa_align/*/*.aln"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/update_families/full_msa/famsa_align/*/*.aln"
    - "**/full_msa/filtered/mafft_align/*/*.fas"
recipe: famsa/conservation.py
fixture: conservation.tsv
renders_as:
  # The representative's sequence with a conservation lane and a class lane;
  # brushing it emits the residue_selection the structure and the MSA follow.
  - id: conservation_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sequence_track
    title: Conservation along the sequence
    roles: {position: position, entity: entity, residue: residue, value: value, category: category}
    config:
      value_label: Conservation score
    description: >-
      Each position is a residue of the family representative, with a lane for its
      conservation score and a lane for its conservation class. It answers which
      stretches of the protein are conserved across the family and which vary.

      How to read: runs of high scores mark constrained regions, often a fold core or
      an active site, and low runs mark loops or variable linkers. Brush a stretch to
      light up the same residues on the structure and the alignment.

      Lines and annotations: the score is one minus the normalised Shannon entropy of
      the alignment column, discounted by the share of gaps, so 1 is an invariant
      gap-free column. The classes are cut at 0.7 and 0.4 by this catalog's recipe;
      they are not published cut-offs.
  # The representative folded on demand (resolve mode, by sequence) and
  # coloured by the same score, so conserved patches read as surfaces.
  - id: conservation_structure
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: molecule_3d
    title: Conservation on the structure
    roles: {position: position, entity: entity, value: value, category: category, sequence: sequence}
    config:
      color_mode: value
    description: >-
      The 3D structure of the family representative, folded on demand from its
      sequence and coloured by the residue conservation score. It answers where the
      conserved residues sit in space.

      How to read: a conserved patch on the surface suggests a binding or catalytic
      site, while conserved residues buried in the core usually hold the fold. Variable
      residues on the surface are typical of regions free to change.

      Lines and annotations: the colour is the conservation score, the same one drawn
      along the sequence, from 0 for a diverse column to 1 for an invariant one.

      Note: the structure is a prediction made from the sequence, not an experimental
      one.
  - id: conservation_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Conservation profile
    roles: {series: entity, x: position, y: value}
    config:
      x_title: Residue position
      y_title: Conservation score
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a protein family: the conservation score at every residue position
      of its representative. It answers how conserved a family is along its length and
      how families compare.

      How to read: a curve that stays high is a tightly conserved family, and one that
      stays low is a diverse one. Peaks and valleys locate the conserved and variable
      regions.

      Lines and annotations: the score is one minus the normalised Shannon entropy of
      the alignment column, discounted by the share of gaps. Positions follow the
      numbering of the representative, without gaps.
  - id: residue_conservation
    component: card
    column: value
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Residue conservation
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median conservation score over every residue of the
      families in view, and the box shows the spread. It answers how conserved the
      families are overall.

      How to read: a high median means a tight family. A box reaching to low values
      holds many variable residues, which is normal for a divergent family.
  # Colour is the conservation class, the same classes the sequence track draws.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: value
      color: category
      labels: {value: Conservation score, category: Conservation class}
    title: Distribution of conservation scores
    reference_lines: [{axis: x, stat: median, column: value}]
    description: >-
      Each bar counts residues in a conservation score bin, split by conservation
      class. It answers how many residues are conserved, intermediate or variable.

      How to read: a pile at high scores is a conserved family, and a pile at low
      scores is a divergent one. A two-humped shape means a conserved core and variable
      loops.

      Lines and annotations: the classes are cut at 0.7 and 0.4 by this catalog's
      recipe, a fixed binning of the score and not a published threshold.
       The dashed line is the median conservation score of this table, a reference
      computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      FAMSA.
  - component: table
    title: Residue table
    description: >-
      Each row is a residue of a family representative, with its position, conservation
      score and class, the most frequent residue of its column, how many members have a
      residue there and the number of members. It answers the exact values behind the
      conservation tiles.

      How to read: filter by family and sort by score to list its most conserved
      residues.

The hero number is the total count of bases in flagged ranges, with the median and the largest range beside it, and the bars rank the taxonomic division groups of the contaminants by bases. It answers how much sequence is foreign and which kind of organism it comes from.
How to read: a division group that dominates, bacteria for instance, points to the likely source of the contamination. Compare with the number of ranges to tell a few long contaminants from many short ones.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ncbi/fcs/main/README.md
renders_as.title: Bases flagged as foreign

renders_as.description:
Each bar is the count of bases FCS-GX flags as foreign in one assembly, stacked by the taxonomic division of the contaminant. It answers which assemblies are contaminated and by what.
How to read: an assembly with no bar is clean. A tall bar of one colour is a single contaminant source, and several colours point to mixed contamination, so open the table to inspect the ranges before trimming.
renders_as.title: Foreign bases per assembly

renders_as.description:
Each row is a range FCS-GX flags as foreign, with the action it recommends, its taxonomic division, the top taxon of the contaminant, the share of the range the contaminant covers and its length. An assembly with nothing flagged keeps one row with action none. It answers exactly which sequences to exclude, trim or fix.
How to read: filter by action to plan the cleaning, and read the top taxon to confirm the contaminant is plausible for this assembly.
renders_as.title: Contamination calls

outputs.description: One row per annotated contig with how many features each nf-core/funcscan screen put on it, the contig length and coverage when the contig name carries them (SPAdes or MEGAHIT headers, null otherwise), and the feature density that follows. This is the annotation layer the four screens share: they all report the contig a feature sits on, even though the annotation step itself publishes no table.
outputs.name: Contig annotation
outputs.rawYaml:
id: funcscan_contig_annotation
name: Contig annotation
mode: screening/contigs
description: >-
  One row per annotated contig with how many features each nf-core/funcscan
  screen put on it, the contig length and coverage when the contig name
  carries them (SPAdes or MEGAHIT headers, null otherwise), and the feature
  density that follows. This is
  the annotation layer the four screens share: they all report the contig a
  feature sits on, even though the annotation step itself publishes no table.
find:
  path_glob: "**/hamronization_summarize/*combined_report.tsv"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/hamronization/*combined_report.tsv"
    - "**/ampcombi2/Ampcombi_summary.tsv"
    - "**/combgc/combgc_complete_summary.tsv"
    - "**/cazyme_annotation/*/*_overview.tsv"
recipe: funcscan/contig_annotation.py
fixture: contig_annotation.tsv
renders_as:
  # Feature count against contig length. A metagenome assembly's long contigs
  # carry more of everything, so the interesting rows are the short contigs
  # high on the y axis: dense loci rather than large ones.
  - id: contig_feature_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Features against contig length
    roles:
      {x: contig_length, y: features, label: contig, color: top_screen, size: features_per_kb}
    config:
      x_title: Contig length (bp)
      y_title: Features on the contig
      log_x: true
    description: >-
      Each point is a contig: its length on the horizontal axis and the number of
      features the four screens put on it on the vertical axis, sized by feature
      density and coloured by the screen with the most features there. It answers
      which contigs carry an unusual load of resistance genes, peptides, clusters or
      CAZymes.

      How to read: long contigs carry more of everything, so the interesting points
      are the short contigs high on the plot, which are dense loci. A contig with
      features from several screens is a candidate for a mobile or multi-function
      element, so open the screening tabs for it.

      Note: length is read from the contig name when the assembler wrote it there, so
      contigs without it are not drawn.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: features_per_kb
      color: top_screen
      labels: {features_per_kb: Features per kb, top_screen: Top screen}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: x, stat: p95, column: features_per_kb}
    title: Feature density per contig
    description: >-
      Each bar counts contigs in a bin of feature density (features per kilobase),
      split by the screen with the most features on the contig. It answers how dense
      the annotated loci are and which screen drives the dense ones.

      How to read: most contigs sit at low density, and a long right tail marks dense
      loci such as resistance islands. A tail made of one screen shows which screen
      produces the dense contigs.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the 95th percentile of the feature
      density of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of funcscan.
  - component: card
    column: features
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: top_screen
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: features, by leading screen
    title: Features by screen
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of features the four screens put on the contigs and
      the bars rank the screens by the features on the contigs they lead. It answers
      which screen annotates the most loci.

      How to read: the screens differ by orders of magnitude in what they report, so a
      screen at the top reflects its design as much as the data.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: contig
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: top_screen
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: contigs, by leading screen
    title: Contigs by leading screen
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of contigs that carry at least one feature and the
      ring splits them by the screen with the most features on each. It answers which
      screen annotates most contigs.

      How to read: a ring held by one screen means the others find little on these
      contigs. Open the screening tabs to see which tools report the features.
  - component: card
    column: contig_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: contig length across contigs
    title: Contig length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median length of the annotated contigs and the histogram
      shows the distribution. It answers how contiguous the assembly is where the
      features sit.

      How to read: a metagenome assembly is mostly short contigs with a long tail of
      long ones. Contigs without the length in their name are left out.
  - component: card
    column: screens_on_contig
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 4.0
    caption: screens per contig, out of four
    title: Screens per contig
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average number of screens (resistance genes, peptides,
      clusters and CAZymes) that put a feature on the same contig, out of the four the
      pipeline runs. It answers how often the screens find features on the same locus.

      How to read: every contig in the table carries at least one screen, so an average near 1 means
      almost every contig is annotated by one screen only.
      Higher values point to loci with several functions, which are worth a look.

      Lines and annotations: the dial maximum is four, the number of screens
      nf-core/funcscan runs.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: features_per_kb
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: density across contigs
    title: Feature density
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average number of features per kilobase on the annotated
      contigs and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how densely the
      screens annotate a contig.

      How to read: an average well above the median means a few very dense contigs
      pull it up. Open the scatter to find them.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: contig
    title: Annotated contigs table
    description: >-
      Each row is a contig that carries at least one feature, with its length and
      coverage when the name holds them, the features from each screen, the screens
      on the contig and the feature density. It answers the exact numbers behind
      every tile and lets a row selection filter the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by feature density to list the densest loci.

outputs.description: One row per sample with the headline count of every nf-core/funcscan screen that produced a result: resistance-gene hits and distinct genes, antimicrobial peptide candidates and how many reach the AMPcombi prediction score cut-off (0.6, the pipeline default), biosynthetic gene cluster regions and product classes, CAZyme genes and families. The four screens share no table of their own, so this is the collection every sample filter and every cross-screen comparison hangs off.
outputs.name: Screening hub
outputs.rawYaml:
id: funcscan_screening_summary
name: Screening hub
mode: screening/summary
description: >-
  One row per sample with the headline count of every nf-core/funcscan screen
  that produced a result: resistance-gene hits and distinct genes, antimicrobial
  peptide candidates and how many reach the AMPcombi prediction score cut-off (0.6, the pipeline default), biosynthetic gene
  cluster regions and product classes, CAZyme genes and families. The four
  screens share no table of their own, so this is the collection every sample
  filter and every cross-screen comparison hangs off.
# The hub is derived from whichever screens ran, so any one of the four
# aggregated reports is enough to recognise the run.
find:
  path_glob: "**/hamronization_summarize/*combined_report.tsv"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/hamronization/*combined_report.tsv"
    - "**/ampcombi2/Ampcombi_summary.tsv"
    - "**/combgc/combgc_complete_summary.tsv"
    - "**/cazyme_annotation/*/*_overview.tsv"
recipe: funcscan/screening_summary.py
fixture: screening_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # Resistome load against carbohydrate-degradation capacity: the two screens
  # that scale with assembly size, so a sample far off the cloud is either
  # unusually resistant or unusually poorly assembled. Size is the BGC count,
  # colour is the AMP candidate count (a numeric colour column, since every
  # string column here is the sample itself) and the lasso emits the sample the
  # rest of the dashboard filters on.
  - id: screen_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Resistance genes against CAZymes
    roles: {x: arg_hits, y: cazymes, label: sample, size: bgc_regions}
    config:
      color_col: amp_candidates
      x_title: Resistance gene hits
      y_title: CAZyme genes
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample: its resistance gene hits on the horizontal axis and its
      CAZyme genes on the vertical axis, sized by biosynthetic gene cluster regions and
      coloured by antimicrobial peptide candidates. It answers how the four screens
      compare across samples.

      How to read: both counts grow with assembly size, so a sample far from the cloud
      is either unusually resistant or unusually poorly assembled. A lasso selection
      filters the rest of the dashboard to those samples.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  # The four screens differ by two orders of magnitude, so the bars need a log
  # axis; a sample missing a colour returned nothing for that screen.
  - id: screen_composition
    component: figure
    code: |
      # The colour channel belongs to the screen here, so the dashboard's
      # analysis groups take the facet axis instead: one band of samples per
      # group. Spread into the reshape below too, or the unpivot would drop the
      # annotation column before the facet could read it.
      index_cols = ["sample"] + [c for c in depictio_group_by if c != "sample"]
      grp_col = depictio_group_by[0] if depictio_group_by else None

      # wide -> long so each screen becomes its own bar colour
      df_modified = df.unpivot(
          index=index_cols,
          on=["arg_hits", "amp_candidates", "bgc_regions", "cazymes"],
          variable_name="screen",
          value_name="findings",
      ).filter(pl.col("findings") > 0)

      labels = {
          "arg_hits": "ARG hits",
          "amp_candidates": "AMP candidates",
          "bgc_regions": "BGC regions",
          "cazymes": "CAZymes",
      }
      df_modified = df_modified.with_columns(
          pl.col("screen").replace_strict(labels, default=pl.col("screen")).alias("screen")
      )

      fig = px.bar(
          df_modified.to_pandas(),
          x="sample",
          y="findings",
          color="screen",
          barmode="group",
          log_y=True,
          facet_col=grp_col,
          category_orders={"screen": list(labels.values())},
      )
      fig.update_layout(
          yaxis_title="Findings (log scale)",
          legend_title_text="Screen",
          margin={"t": 24, "l": 56, "r": 16, "b": 80},
      )
      if grp_col:
          # Each panel keeps only its own samples, and its title is the group
          # name rather than the annotation column's name and an equals sign.
          fig.update_xaxes(matches=None, showticklabels=True, title_text="")
          fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=")[-1]))
      else:
          fig.update_layout(xaxis_title="Sample")
    title: Findings per screen and sample
    description: >-
      Each bar is the number of findings one screen (resistance genes, peptide
      candidates, cluster regions or CAZymes) made in a sample, on a log axis, grouped
      by screen. It answers how the four screens compare within and between samples.

      How to read: the screens differ by orders of magnitude, so read the log axis
      rather than the bar heights. A screen missing from a sample returned nothing
      there, which can mean it was not enabled.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: arg_hits
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: hits per sample, with their spread
    title: Resistance gene hits
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of resistance gene hits over all samples and the
      box shows their quartiles per sample. It answers how large the resistome is and
      how evenly the samples share it.

      How to read: a wide box means some samples carry far more resistance genes than
      others. Hits are counted per tool, so one gene found by several tools counts
      several times.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: arg_genes
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distinct genes per sample
    title: Distinct resistance genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of distinct resistance genes per sample and
      the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how rich a typical resistome is.

      How to read: compare it with the hits card, since many hits on few genes mean the
      same genes are found by several tools or repeated in the assembly.
  - component: card
    column: amp_candidates
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: candidates per sample, with their spread
    title: Peptide candidates
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of antimicrobial peptide candidates per
      sample and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how many candidates a typical
      sample yields.

      How to read: candidates are predictions, not validated peptides, so a high
      count calls for the confidence column in the table before follow-up.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: amp_high_confidence
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: high-confidence candidates per sample
    title: High-confidence peptide candidates
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of peptide candidates whose best prediction score
      reaches the AMPcombi cut-off, and the histogram shows how many each sample has.
      It answers how many candidates are strong enough to follow up.

      How to read: a sample with many candidates and few above the cut-off carries
      mostly weak predictions. Compare it with the candidates card.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-off is a prediction score of 0.6, the default of
      the nf-core/funcscan parameter amp_ampcombi_parsetables_cutoff, below which
      AMPcombi sets a score to 0 in its summary. The pipeline does not call this high
      confidence, so the name is the dashboard's.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: bgc_regions
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: regions, by sample
    title: Biosynthetic gene cluster regions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of biosynthetic gene cluster regions found and the
      ring splits them by sample. It answers which samples hold the secondary
      metabolite potential.

      How to read: regions are predicted from the assembly, so a poorly assembled
      sample can show fewer. A ring held by one sample points to a metagenome with a
      dominant producer.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: bgc_classes
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: product classes per sample
    title: Cluster product classes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest count of distinct biosynthetic product classes in
      a sample and the histogram shows the distribution over samples. It answers how
      diverse the cluster repertoire is.

      How to read: a sample with many classes holds a broad secondary metabolite
      repertoire. Compare it with the region count, since many regions of few classes
      mean repeated clusters.
  - component: card
    column: cazymes
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: genes per sample, with their spread
    title: CAZyme genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of carbohydrate-active enzyme genes per
      sample and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how much carbohydrate
      degradation capacity a typical sample has.

      How to read: the count grows with assembly size, so compare samples of similar
      assemblies. A sample far above the box is a candidate for a specialised
      degrader.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: cazyme_families
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: families per sample
    title: CAZyme families
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average count of distinct CAZyme families per sample and
      the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how varied the enzyme
      repertoire is.

      How to read: many genes of few families mean repeated enzymes, and many families
      mean a broad repertoire.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Screening hub table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its headline counts for every screen: resistance gene
      hits and distinct genes, peptide candidates and those at the cut-off, cluster
      regions and classes, and CAZyme genes and families. It answers the exact numbers
      behind every tile and lets a row selection filter the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by a column to rank the samples, and select a row to filter
      the other tabs.

Each point is a sample: its resistance gene hits on the horizontal axis and its CAZyme genes on the vertical axis, sized by biosynthetic gene cluster regions and coloured by antimicrobial peptide candidates. It answers how the four screens compare across samples.
How to read: both counts grow with assembly size, so a sample far from the cloud is either unusually resistant or unusually poorly assembled. A lasso selection filters the rest of the dashboard to those samples.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
