    fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=")[-1]))
else:
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_title="Sample")
renders_as.description:
Each bar is the number of findings one screen (resistance genes, peptide candidates, cluster regions or CAZymes) made in a sample, on a log axis, grouped by screen. It answers how the four screens compare within and between samples.
How to read: the screens differ by orders of magnitude, so read the log axis rather than the bar heights. A screen missing from a sample returned nothing there, which can mean it was not enabled.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
renders_as.title: Findings per screen and sample

renders_as.caption: hits per sample, with their spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total of resistance gene hits over all samples and the box shows their quartiles per sample. It answers how large the resistome is and how evenly the samples share it.
How to read: a wide box means some samples carry far more resistance genes than others. Hits are counted per tool, so one gene found by several tools counts several times.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
renders_as.title: Resistance gene hits

renders_as.caption: distinct genes per sample
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median count of distinct resistance genes per sample and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how rich a typical resistome is.
How to read: compare it with the hits card, since many hits on few genes mean the same genes are found by several tools or repeated in the assembly.
renders_as.title: Distinct resistance genes

renders_as.caption: candidates per sample, with their spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median count of antimicrobial peptide candidates per sample and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how many candidates a typical sample yields.
How to read: candidates are predictions, not validated peptides, so a high count calls for the confidence column in the table before follow-up.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
renders_as.title: Peptide candidates

renders_as.caption: high-confidence candidates per sample
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total of peptide candidates whose best prediction score reaches the AMPcombi cut-off, and the histogram shows how many each sample has. It answers how many candidates are strong enough to follow up.
How to read: a sample with many candidates and few above the cut-off carries mostly weak predictions. Compare it with the candidates card.
Lines and annotations: the cut-off is a prediction score of 0.6, the default of the nf-core/funcscan parameter amp_ampcombi_parsetables_cutoff, below which AMPcombi sets a score to 0 in its summary. The pipeline does not call this high confidence, so the name is the dashboard's.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/nextflow_schema.json
renders_as.title: High-confidence peptide candidates

renders_as.caption: regions, by sample
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total of biosynthetic gene cluster regions found and the ring splits them by sample. It answers which samples hold the secondary metabolite potential.
How to read: regions are predicted from the assembly, so a poorly assembled sample can show fewer. A ring held by one sample points to a metagenome with a dominant producer.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
renders_as.title: Biosynthetic gene cluster regions

renders_as.caption: product classes per sample
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the largest count of distinct biosynthetic product classes in a sample and the histogram shows the distribution over samples. It answers how diverse the cluster repertoire is.
How to read: a sample with many classes holds a broad secondary metabolite repertoire. Compare it with the region count, since many regions of few classes mean repeated clusters.
renders_as.title: Cluster product classes

renders_as.caption: genes per sample, with their spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median count of carbohydrate-active enzyme genes per sample and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how much carbohydrate degradation capacity a typical sample has.
How to read: the count grows with assembly size, so compare samples of similar assemblies. A sample far above the box is a candidate for a specialised degrader.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
renders_as.title: CAZyme genes

renders_as.caption: families per sample
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the average count of distinct CAZyme families per sample and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how varied the enzyme repertoire is.
How to read: many genes of few families mean repeated enzymes, and many families mean a broad repertoire.
renders_as.title: CAZyme families

renders_as.description:
Each row is a sample with its headline counts for every screen: resistance gene hits and distinct genes, peptide candidates and those at the cut-off, cluster regions and classes, and CAZyme genes and families. It answers the exact numbers behind every tile and lets a row selection filter the dashboard.
How to read: sort by a column to rank the samples, and select a row to filter the other tabs.
renders_as.title: Screening hub table

outputs.rawYaml:
id: funcscan_software_versions
name: Software versions
mode: run/versions
description: >-
  One row per process and tool with the version the run recorded, plus the
  screen the process belongs to. nf-core/funcscan feeds MultiQC nothing but
  this table, so the report has no plot to bind and the versions are read out
  of the report itself instead.
# Recognised by nf-core's canonical versions file, which is the same payload
# MultiQC embeds in its report. The recipe reads the payload back out of the
# MultiQC parquet rather than this file, because a recipe source is csv, tsv
# or parquet and the canonical file is YAML; anchoring `find` on the parquet
# instead would make this output look like one more MultiQC panel, which it
# is not.
find:
  path_glob: "**/pipeline_info/*software_versions.yml"
  path_glob_alt: ["**/pipeline_info/*software_versions.yaml"]
recipe: funcscan/software_versions.py
fixture: software_versions.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: screen
      y: tools
      color: tool
      labels: {screen: Screen, tools: Tools, tool: Tool}
    title: Tools per screen
    description: >-
      Each bar is a screen of the pipeline (resistance, peptides, clusters, CAZymes or
      shared steps), stacked by the tools the run recorded for it. It answers which
      tools each screen ran.

      How to read: a screen with a single tool is a thin check, and one with many
      tools cross-validates its calls. Compare it with the findings in the screening
      tabs.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/funcscan/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: tool
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: screen
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: tools, by screen
    title: Tools in the run
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct tools the run recorded and the bars rank
      the screens by how many each used. It answers how many tools the run drew on.

      How to read: the count depends on which screens and tools were enabled, so a
      lower number than expected points to skipped tools.
  - component: card
    column: process
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: screen
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: process records, by screen
    title: Processes by screen
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of process and tool records and the ring splits them
      by screen. It answers how the workflow is divided between the screens.

      How to read: a large share for a screen means many steps (downloads, summaries,
      conversions) beside the tool itself.
  - component: card
    column: tool
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: screen
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: tool records, by screen
    title: Tool records by screen
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of tool version records and the bar shows the share
      each screen holds. It answers which screens carry the most software.

      How to read: a tool recorded in several processes appears several times, so the
      share reflects usage as well as variety.
  - component: card
    column: version
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: tool
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: versions, by tool
    title: Versions in the run
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct version strings the run recorded and the
      bars rank the tools by how many versions each reports. It answers whether any
      tool ran in more than one version.

      How to read: one version per tool is the normal case. A tool with two versions
      means mixed containers, which hurts reproducibility, so compare it with the table.
  - component: table
    title: Software versions table
    description: >-
      Each row is a process and tool with the version the run recorded, and the screen
      the process belongs to. It answers the exact software the results came from.

      How to read: filter by screen or tool, and cite the versions in a methods
      section.

outputs.name: FusionCatcher fusion genes
outputs.rawYaml:
id: fusioncatcher_fusion_genes
name: FusionCatcher fusion genes
mode: fusion-genes
description: >-
  One row per FusionCatcher candidate fusion, with both partner genes, the
  annotation labels the pair matched, the read evidence supporting the call and
  its predicted effect on the coding sequence.
find: { filename: "*.fusion-genes.txt" }
recipe: fusioncatcher/fusion_genes.py
fixture: fusion_genes.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: the dot colour is the continuous log of the supporting reads.
  - id: evidence_dot_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    title: Evidence per fusion and predicted effect
    roles: {cluster: predicted_effect, gene: fusion, mean_expression: log_support, frac_expressing: unique_fraction}
    config:
      gene_sort: mean
    description: >-
      Each dot is a candidate fusion in one predicted effect on the coding sequence:
      its colour is the log of the supporting reads (spanning pairs plus unique
      spanning reads) and its size the share of that support that comes from unique
      reads. It answers which fusions have the strongest read evidence.

      How to read: a large, dark dot is a fusion backed by many reads that are mostly
      unique. A small, pale dot rests on few reads or on multimapping ones and needs
      scrutiny. FusionCatcher gives no single cut-off that separates true from false
      fusions.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndaniel/fusioncatcher/master/doc/manual.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Supporting reads by predicted effect
    dict_kwargs:
      x: predicted_effect
      y: supporting_reads
      color: finding_method
      labels: {predicted_effect: Predicted effect, supporting_reads: Supporting reads, finding_method: Finding method}
    description: >-
      Each segment is a candidate fusion: its supporting reads, grouped by the predicted
      effect on the coding sequence and coloured by the method that found it. It
      answers which kinds of fusion have the most read support and which aligners
      agree.

      How to read: tall bars in the in-frame group are the candidates most likely to
      produce a fusion protein. The colour shows which aligners found each
      candidate, so check candidates found by one method in the table.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndaniel/fusioncatcher/master/doc/manual.md
  - component: card
    column: supporting_reads
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with the spread
    title: Supporting reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of reads supporting a candidate fusion
      (spanning pairs plus unique spanning reads), with the spread in the box. It
      answers how strong the typical evidence is.

      How to read: a low median with a long upper whisker is the usual picture of many
      weak candidates and a few strong ones. Open the dot plot to see which fusions the
      whisker belongs to.
  - component: card
    column: fusion
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: predicted_effect
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    caption: fusions, by predicted effect
    title: Candidate fusions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct fusion gene pairs, with the number of
      breakpoint rows next to it, and the bars rank the predicted effects. It answers
      how many candidates there are and what they do to the coding sequence.

      How to read: more rows than distinct pairs means some fusions have several
      breakpoints. In-frame candidates are the ones that can make a fusion protein.
  - component: card
    column: spanning_unique_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: finding_method
    caption: unique spanning reads, by finding method
    title: Unique spanning reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of unique reads that map on a fusion junction, with
      the median and the largest per candidate next to it, and the ring splits it by the
      method that found the fusion. It answers how much junction evidence there is and
      which aligners contribute it.

      How to read: unique reads exclude PCR duplicates, so they are a conservative
      measure of evidence. A ring dominated by one method means the other methods found
      few candidates.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndaniel/fusioncatcher/master/doc/manual.md
  - component: card
    column: n_annotations
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: annotation labels per fusion
    title: Annotation labels per fusion
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean count of annotation labels FusionCatcher attached to
      a fusion pair (known fusion, oncogene, a cancer study it appeared in), with the
      median and the maximum next to it, and the histogram shows their distribution. It
      answers how well documented the candidates are.

      How to read: a fusion with many labels is a known event. A fusion with none is a
      novel candidate and needs stronger evidence. Labels such as a healthy-sample
      label can also flag likely false positives, so read them in the table.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndaniel/fusioncatcher/master/doc/manual.md
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: fusion
    title: Candidate fusion genes
    description: >-
      Each row is a candidate fusion breakpoint: both partner genes, the annotation
      labels, the read evidence, the breakpoints and the predicted effect. It answers
      which fusions to validate first.

      How to read: sort by supporting reads and read the labels, then click a row to
      filter the other tiles to that fusion.

The hero number is the count of distinct fusion gene pairs, with the number of breakpoint rows next to it, and the bars rank the predicted effects. It answers how many candidates there are and what they do to the coding sequence.
How to read: more rows than distinct pairs means some fusions have several breakpoints. In-frame candidates are the ones that can make a fusion protein.
renders_as.title: Candidate fusions

renders_as.caption: unique spanning reads, by finding method
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total of unique reads that map on a fusion junction, with the median and the largest per candidate next to it, and the ring splits it by the method that found the fusion. It answers how much junction evidence there is and which aligners contribute it.
How to read: unique reads exclude PCR duplicates, so they are a conservative measure of evidence. A ring dominated by one method means the other methods found few candidates.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndaniel/fusioncatcher/master/doc/manual.md
renders_as.title: Unique spanning reads

renders_as.caption: annotation labels per fusion
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the mean count of annotation labels FusionCatcher attached to a fusion pair (known fusion, oncogene, a cancer study it appeared in), with the median and the maximum next to it, and the histogram shows their distribution. It answers how well documented the candidates are.
How to read: a fusion with many labels is a known event. A fusion with none is a novel candidate and needs stronger evidence. Labels such as a healthy-sample label can also flag likely false positives, so read them in the table.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndaniel/fusioncatcher/master/doc/manual.md
renders_as.title: Annotation labels per fusion

renders_as.description:
Each row is a candidate fusion breakpoint: both partner genes, the annotation labels, the read evidence, the breakpoints and the predicted effect. It answers which fusions to validate first.
How to read: sort by supporting reads and read the labels, then click a row to filter the other tiles to that fusion.
renders_as.title: Candidate fusion genes

outputs.name: Validated fusions
outputs.rawYaml:
id: fusioninspector_fusions
name: Validated fusions
mode: fusions/abridged
description: >-
  One row per fusion transcript pair that survived FusionInspector's
  re-alignment, with the junction and spanning read support, the normalised
  expression (FFPM), the fusion-allele ratios against each partner, and the
  protein-level consequence of the fusion.
find: { path_glob: "**/fusioninspector/*/*.FusionInspector.fusions.abridged.tsv" }
recipe: fusioninspector/fusions.py
fixture: fusions.tsv
renders_as:
  # Expression against junction purity, one dot per fusion, grouped by the
  # protein consequence: an in-frame fusion carried by mostly junction reads
  # sits top-right, a frameshift held up by spanning fragments bottom-left.
  - id: evidence_dot_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    title: Fusion evidence by protein consequence
    roles: {cluster: prot_fusion_type, gene: fusion, mean_expression: log_ffpm, frac_expressing: junction_fraction}
    description: >-
      Each dot is a fusion call placed in the column of its predicted protein
      consequence. The colour is its expression as log10 of FFPM plus one and the size is the junction reads'
      share of its supporting reads, both computed by this catalog's recipe. It
      answers which fusions are both well expressed and backed by junction reads.

      How to read: large, bright dots in the in-frame column are the best
      candidates for a functional fusion. A small dot means most support comes from
      spanning fragments, which are weaker evidence for the exact breakpoint. Open
      the table tile to check the read counts behind a dot.

      Note: FusionInspector publishes no pass or fail cut-off on these values, so none is drawn.

      Source:
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/FusionInspector/FusionInspector/FusionInspector-Outputs-Described.md
  # The two fusion-allele ratios against each other. A fusion dominant on both
  # partners lands top-right; a ratio near the axis means the wild-type allele
  # of that partner still dominates.
  - component: figure
    title: Fusion allele ratio of each partner
    code: |
      # FAR can be reported as 0, which a log axis cannot place, so shift both.
      eps = 0.01
      df_modified = df.with_columns(
          (pl.col("far_left") + eps).alias("far_left_shift"),
          (pl.col("far_right") + eps).alias("far_right_shift"),
      )

      fig = px.scatter(
          df_modified.to_pandas(),
          x="far_left_shift", y="far_right_shift",
          color="prot_fusion_type", size="supporting_reads",
          size_max=24, opacity=0.8, log_x=True, log_y=True,
          hover_name="fusion",
      )
      fig.update_layout(
          xaxis_title="FAR 5' partner (log)",
          yaxis_title="FAR 3' partner (log)",
          legend_title_text="Protein fusion type",
          margin={"t": 24, "l": 56, "r": 16, "b": 48},
      )
    description: >-
      Each point is a fusion call: the fusion allele ratio against its 5' partner
      on the horizontal axis and against its 3' partner on the vertical axis. The
      colour is the protein consequence and the size the number of supporting reads.
      It answers how much each partner's own expression is taken up by the fusion.

      How to read: a point in the top right is a fusion that is large compared with
      both wild-type partners, which is the pattern of a driver. A point near an axis
      means one partner is still expressed mostly in its normal form. Compare with the
      read counts in the table before trusting a low-support point.

      Lines and annotations: both axes are logarithmic, and a small constant of 0.01
      is added to each ratio so that a ratio of zero can be placed. No cut-off is drawn
      because FusionInspector publishes none for these ratios.
  - component: card
    column: log_ffpm
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Fusion expression
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median expression of the fusion calls, as log10 of FFPM
      plus one, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how strongly the fusions
      are expressed overall.

      How to read: the scale is logarithmic because FFPM spans several orders of
      magnitude. Calls at the low end are easy to confuse with noise, so confirm them
      with the read support in the table.
  - component: card
    column: fusion
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: prot_fusion_type
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    caption: calls, by protein consequence
    title: Distinct fusions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct fusion gene pairs, and the bars rank
      the protein consequences of the calls. It answers how many fusions were
      validated and whether they keep the reading frame.

      How to read: in-frame calls are the ones expected to give a chimeric protein.
      Many frameshift calls usually point to junction artefacts, so check their read
      support before following them up.
  - component: card
    column: supporting_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: splice_type
    caption: reads, by splice type
    title: Supporting reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of junction reads and spanning fragments over all
      calls, and the ring splits calls by the splice type FusionInspector assigned.
      It answers how much evidence there is and where the junctions sit relative to
      known splice sites.

      How to read: a ring dominated by reference splice sites is the usual pattern of
      a real fusion. A large share of non-reference splice calls deserves a look at the
      individual junctions.
  - component: card
    column: junction_fraction
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: average, with its range
    title: Junction purity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average share of supporting reads that cross the
      breakpoint, and the histogram shows how that share is spread over the calls.
      It answers how direct the evidence is.

      How to read: values near one mean the support is carried by junction reads. Values
      near zero mean the call rests on spanning fragments only. FusionInspector gives
      no cut-off, so read the shape against the rest of the run.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: fusion
    title: Validated fusions table
    description: >-
      Each row is a fusion transcript pair with its read support, expression, allele
      ratios and protein consequence. It answers which calls to follow up and lets a
      row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by supporting reads or by expression, and filter by protein
      consequence to keep the in-frame calls.

outputs.name: Fusion protein domains
outputs.rawYaml:
id: fusioninspector_protein_domains
name: Fusion protein domains
mode: fusions/pfam
description: >-
  The Pfam domains FusionInspector annotates on the 5' and 3' partner of each
  fusion protein, unpivoted from the packed PFAM_LEFT / PFAM_RIGHT fields into
  one row per domain with its amino-acid span and e-value.
find: { path_glob: "**/fusioninspector/*/*.FusionInspector.fusions.abridged.tsv" }
recipe: fusioninspector/protein_domains.py
fixture: protein_domains.tsv
renders_as:
  # The fusion protein drawn as its two partners end to end, each annotated
  # domain placed along the partner that contributes it and the breakpoint
  # marked between them. A domain the breakpoint truncated is short where the
  # same domain kept whole on the other side is not.
  - id: fusion_domains
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: fusion_structure
    title: Domains along the fusion protein
    roles: {fusion_id: fusion, partner: partner, feature: domain, start: domain_start, end: domain_end, colour_by: partner}
    description: >-
      Each block is a Pfam domain placed along the fusion protein, one lane per
      partner, and the colour tells which partner contributes it. It answers which
      protein domains a fusion keeps from each side.

      How to read: look for a kinase or DNA-binding domain kept intact on the 3' side
      next to a dimerisation domain from the 5' side, which is the classic activating
      pattern. A domain that is cut short is probably not functional in the fusion.

      Note: FusionInspector reports Pfam domains with their e-values and applies no
      cut-off of its own to them, so weak hits can appear.

      Source: https://github.com/FusionInspector/FusionInspector
  # Domain starts along the fusion protein, one lane per fusion, split by the
  # partner that contributes the domain. Kept beside the structure view: it
  # ranks many fusions at a glance where the structure reads a handful closely.
  - id: domain_lollipop
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: lollipop
    title: Domain positions per fusion
    roles: {feature_id: fusion, position: domain_start, category: partner, label: domain}
    config:
      top_n_labels: 8
    description: >-
      Each stem is a Pfam domain at the amino-acid position where it starts, drawn on
      one lane per fusion and coloured by the partner that contributes it. It answers
      how domains are distributed across fusions.

      How to read: domains from the 5' partner cluster at the start of the protein and
      those of the 3' partner come after the breakpoint. A lane with stems from only
      one partner is a fusion whose other side adds no annotated domain.
  # Domain lengths as points (one per occurrence, never summed), so a domain the
  # breakpoint truncated sits visibly lower than the same domain kept whole.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: strip
    dict_kwargs:
      x: domain
      y: domain_length
      color: partner
      labels: {domain: Pfam domain, domain_length: Length (amino acids), partner: Partner}
    title: Domain lengths
    description: >-
      Each point is one occurrence of a Pfam domain on a fusion protein, with its length in
      amino acids and the colour of the partner that contributes it. It answers which domains
      are long and whether the two partners contribute similar ones.

      How to read: a domain shorter than its usual size in the family was probably cut
      by the breakpoint. Compare it with the same domain on the other partner.
  - component: card
    column: domain
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: partner
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: domains, by partner
    title: Distinct domains
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct Pfam domains, and the bars rank the
      partners by how many domain rows each contributes. It answers how much protein
      annotation the fusions carry.

      How to read: a large imbalance between the 5' and 3' partner means one side
      brings most of the annotated function.
  - component: card
    column: domain_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Domain length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median length of the annotated domains in amino acids, and
      the box shows their quartiles. It answers how large the typical domain is.

      How to read: a very short domain is often a truncated one, so filter by fusion and
      check it in the structure view.
  - component: card
    column: neg_log10_evalue
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: average, with its range
    title: Domain hit strength
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average minus log10 e-value of the domain hits, and the
      histogram shows how it is spread. It answers how confident the Pfam annotation
      is.

      How to read: higher values are stronger hits. Domains with a score near zero have
      an e-value close to one and should be read as weak annotations.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: fusion
    title: Fusion domains table
    description: >-
      Each row is a Pfam domain on one partner of a fusion, with its start, end, length
      and e-value. It answers which domains each fusion keeps and lets a row selection
      filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by e-value to see the strongest hits first and filter by
      partner to compare the two sides.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: fusionreport_caller_evidence
name: Caller evidence
mode: detect
description: >-
  Long form of the per-caller evidence strings fusion-report writes next to each
  fusion: one row per fusion and caller, with the read support that caller
  reported normalised to a single comparable count.
find: { path_glob: "**/fusionreport/*/*.fusions.csv" }
recipe: fusionreport/caller_evidence.py
fixture: caller_evidence.tsv
renders_as:
  # Callers on one axis, fusions on the other: colour is how much read support the
  # caller found, size is that caller's share of the fusion's total support.
  # Callers count evidence differently (split reads, spanning pairs, junction reads),
  # so supporting_reads is the recipe's normalised count; no cut-off is drawn (C3 N/A).
  - id: evidence_dot_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    roles: {cluster: caller, gene: fusion, mean_expression: log_support, frac_expressing: evidence_fraction}
    title: Evidence per caller and fusion
    description: >-
      Each dot is a fusion reported by one caller: its colour is the read support on a log
      scale and its size is the share of the fusion's total support that this caller holds. It
      answers which callers back each fusion and how strongly.

      How to read: a fusion with dots in several columns is found by several callers, which is
      the main reason to trust it. A fusion with a single dot rests on one caller. Compare
      colours within a caller, since callers count evidence differently.

      Lines and annotations: the colour scale is log10 of supporting reads plus 1, where the
      read count is normalised from each caller's own evidence fields by the recipe.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: fusion
      y: supporting_reads
      color: caller
      labels: {fusion: Fusion, supporting_reads: Supporting reads, caller: Caller}
    title: Supporting reads per fusion
    description: >-
      Each bar stacks the callers of one fusion, with height their supporting reads and colour
      the caller. It answers which fusions have the most read evidence and which callers
      provide it.

      How to read: a tall bar made of several colours is a fusion with strong, shared
      support. A bar of one colour rests on one caller. Read counts are normalised from each
      caller's evidence fields, so compare callers with care.
  - component: card
    column: supporting_reads
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    caption: median, lowest and highest
    title: Supporting reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median read support of a fusion as one caller reports it, with the
      lowest and highest beside it. It answers how strong the evidence is for a typical
      report.

      How to read: a very low median means thin evidence. The range is wide and callers count
      differently, so a box would draw a flat line.
  - component: card
    column: fusion
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: caller
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: fusions, by caller
    title: Fusions per caller
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct fusions, and the bars rank the callers by how
      many fusions each reports. It answers which caller finds the most.

      How to read: a caller far ahead of the others finds many fusions alone, which can mean
      sensitivity or noise. Compare with the agreement view.
  - component: card
    column: supporting_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: caller
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: supporting reads, by caller
    title: Supporting reads by caller
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total read support over all reports, and the bars rank the
      callers by the support they contribute. It answers which caller carries the evidence.

      How to read: callers count evidence differently, so a larger total does not make a caller
      more accurate.
  - component: card
    column: evidence_fraction
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distribution across reports
    title: Largest share held by one caller
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest share of a fusion's support held by one caller, between 0
      and 1, and the histogram shows how shares are distributed over the reports. It answers
      whether support is spread across callers or concentrated in one.

      How to read: many shares near 1 mean fusions rest on one caller. A fusion reported by
      one caller always holds all of its support.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: fusion
    title: Caller evidence table
    description: >-
      Each row is a fusion reported by one caller, with the breakpoints that caller gave, its
      supporting reads, its share of the fusion's support, the index and the caller's raw
      evidence string. It answers what each caller actually saw.

      How to read: filter on one fusion to compare its callers, and read the detail column
      for the caller's own fields.

outputs.name: Fusion consensus
outputs.rawYaml:
id: fusionreport_fusions
name: Fusion consensus
mode: detect
description: >-
  One row per fusion and sample, with the knowledge bases that already know it,
  the Fusion Indication Index fusion-report ranks by and a 0/1 flag per caller
  the run executed, named after the tool. The sample is read off the file name.
  The caller flags are the set columns a caller-concordance UpSet reads.
find: { path_glob: "**/fusionreport/*/*.fusions.csv" }
recipe: fusionreport/fusions.py
fixture: fusions.tsv
renders_as:
  # The caller flags are the binary columns the renderer picks on its own.
  # C6 N/A: the set columns are whichever callers the run executed, known only at
  # ingest. On a small run n_databases, n_tools or rank can be 0/1 too, so a
  # dashboard names the sets by exclusion: set_columns_pattern
  # "^(?!(n_databases|n_tools|rank)$)".
  # FII is fusion-report's own score: 0.5 x the tools component + 0.5 x the databases
  # component, database weights COSMIC 50, Mitelman 50, FusionGDB2 0
  # (docs/score.md of Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report). Not a probability.
  - id: caller_upset
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: upset_plot
    config:
      color_intersections_by: degree
    title: Caller agreement
    description: >-
      Each bar is a combination of callers and its height the number of fusions that exactly
      those callers reported, with the bars on the left giving each caller's total. It answers
      which callers agree on a fusion and which find calls alone.

      How to read: tall bars at high degree, where most callers agree, are the safest
      fusions to follow up. Fusions seen by one caller only are the most likely false
      positives, because the callers use different approaches. A caller with a large private
      bar adds sensitivity and noise in the same measure.

      Lines and annotations: bars are coloured by the number of callers in the combination,
      the degree of the intersection.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md
  # Rank is the position in fusion-report's own FII ordering, so the lollipop
  # reads as a ranked list of the run's fusions.
  - id: fii_lollipop
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: lollipop
    roles: {feature_id: fusion, position: rank, category: tool_support, effect: fii, label: fusion}
    config:
      top_n_labels: 10
    title: Fusions ranked by indication index
    description: >-
      Each lollipop is a fusion placed at its rank in fusion-report's ordering, coloured by how
      many callers found it and sized by its Fusion Indication Index. It answers which fusions
      fusion-report puts first and how many callers back them.

      How to read: the leftmost, large lollipops are the best candidates. A top-ranked fusion
      found by one caller only ranks high on database evidence alone, so look at the caller
      evidence tab before trusting it.

      Lines and annotations: the index is computed by fusion-report as 0.5 times the share of
      callers that found the fusion plus 0.5 times a weighted database score, with COSMIC and
      Mitelman weighted 50 each and FusionGDB2 0. It is a ranking score and not a probability.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: fusion
      y: fii
      color: tool_support
      labels: {fusion: Fusion, fii: Fusion Indication Index, tool_support: Callers}
    title: Fusion Indication Index per fusion
    reference_lines: [{axis: y, stat: median, column: fii}]
    description: >-
      Each bar is a fusion with its Fusion Indication Index, coloured by how many callers found
      it. It answers how strong the combined caller and database evidence is for each fusion.

      How to read: a high bar in the colour of several callers is a fusion both found by
      the tools and known to the databases. A short bar means few callers or no known
      database record.

      Lines and annotations: the index mixes caller agreement and database knowledge with
      equal weight, and database weights of COSMIC 50, Mitelman 50 and FusionGDB2 0.
       The dashed line is the median Fusion Indication Index of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-
      off of fusion-report.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md
  - component: card
    column: fii
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Fusion Indication Index
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median Fusion Indication Index over the fusions in view, a score
      from 0 to 1, and the box shows the spread. It answers how well supported the fusions are
      as a set.

      How to read: a high median means most calls are backed by several callers or by databases.
      The index is fusion-report's own ranking score and is not a probability.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md
      and
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/fusion_report/app.py
  - component: card
    column: fusion
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: tool_support
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    caption: fusions, by caller agreement
    title: Fusions reported
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct fusions, and the bars rank the caller agreement
      classes by how many fusions they hold. It answers how many fusions the callers report and
      how many several of them agree on.

      How to read: a large class of fusions found by one caller is the usual noisy part of a
      run. Follow up the classes with more callers first.
  - component: card
    column: tool_support
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: tool_support
    caption: fusions, by caller agreement
    title: Caller agreement composition
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of fusions and the ring splits them by how many callers
      found each. It answers what share of fusions have broad caller support.

      How to read: a big slice of single-caller fusions means a noisy run, and a big slice of
      many-caller fusions a well supported one. The second number is how many agreement levels
      appear.
  - component: card
    column: n_databases
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distribution across fusions
    title: Known to databases
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean count of fusion databases that already list a fusion, and
      the histogram shows its distribution. It answers how many of the calls are previously
      described.

      How to read: a fusion listed in several databases is known, a plus for a candidate. A
      fusion known to none may be novel or an artefact, and needs separate validation.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Clinical-Genomics/fusion-report/master/docs/score.md
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: fusion
    title: Fusion consensus table
    description: >-
      Each row is a fusion in one sample with its partner genes, the databases that know it, its
      Fusion Indication Index, the arithmetic behind it and a flag for each caller. It answers
      which fusions to validate and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by index or rank, then read the caller flags and the database list
      of the top calls.

tools.description: Genome size, heterozygosity and repeat content from a read k-mer spectrum.
tools.name: GenomeScope

outputs.description: GenomeScope's fit to the read k-mer spectrum: the haploid genome length, the share of it in repeats, the heterozygosity and the read error rate, each as a min to max range. The haploid length is the size an assembly should approach; a high heterozygosity warns that a collapsed assembly will carry duplicated haplotigs, and a poor model fit that the other numbers are not to be trusted.
outputs.name: Genome profile from reads
outputs.rawYaml:
id: genomescope_summary
name: Genome profile from reads
mode: summary
description: >-
  GenomeScope's fit to the read k-mer spectrum: the haploid genome length, the
  share of it in repeats, the heterozygosity and the read error rate, each as a
  min to max range. The haploid length is the size an assembly should approach;
  a high heterozygosity warns that a collapsed assembly will carry duplicated
  haplotigs, and a poor model fit that the other numbers are not to be trusted.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_genomescope.txt"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*summary.txt"
recipe: genomescope/summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 3 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several read sets.
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: card
    column: haploid_length_max
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Haploid genome length
    caption: upper estimate per read set, with its spread
    headline: true
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over read sets of GenomeScope's upper estimate of the haploid genome
      length, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how large the genome is expected to be before any
      assembly.

      How to read: an assembly total close to this length is complete in size. A total well above it suggests
      duplicated haplotypes, and one well below suggests missing sequence. Read sets that disagree point to
      different genomes or to poor fits.
  - component: card
    column: heterozygosity_max
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Heterozygosity
    caption: upper estimate per read set, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over read sets of GenomeScope's upper estimate of heterozygosity, as a
      percentage of the genome, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how much the two haplotypes
      differ.

      How to read: a high value warns that a collapsed assembly will carry duplicated haplotigs and may need
      purging. A value near zero means the haplotypes are almost identical.
  - component: card
    column: repeat_fraction
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Repeat content
    caption: share of the genome, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over read sets of the share of the genome that GenomeScope places in
      repeats, in percent, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how repetitive the genome is.

      How to read: a high share makes short-read assembly harder and favours long reads. Treat it as an
      estimate of the k-mer model, not a count of annotated repeats.
  - component: card
    column: model_fit_max
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Model fit
    caption: best fit per read set, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest model fit over read sets, in percent, and the box shows the spread of the
      upper fit estimates. It answers whether the numbers of this tab can be trusted.

      How to read: a high fit means the model follows the observed k-mer spectrum. A poor fit usually means
      too little coverage or too much sequencing error, and then the other estimates are unreliable.
      GenomeScope recommends at least 15x coverage of the haploid genome.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tbenavi1/genomescope2.0/master/README.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Estimated haploid genome length per read set
    dict_kwargs: { x: read_set, y: haploid_length_max, color: heterozygosity_max, labels: { read_set: Read set, haploid_length_max: Haploid genome length (bp), heterozygosity_max: Heterozygosity (%) } }
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: haploid_length_max}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a read set: GenomeScope's upper estimate of its haploid genome length, coloured by its
      estimated heterozygosity. It answers whether the read sets agree on the genome size.

      How to read: similar bars mean the reads sample the same genome. A bar that stands out, especially with
      a different heterozygosity, may come from a different organism, a contaminated library or a poor fit, so
      compare it with the model fit card.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median haploid genome length of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of GenomeScope.
  - component: table
    title: GenomeScope estimates
    description: >-
      Each row is a read set, with GenomeScope's lower and upper estimates of genome length, repeat length,
      heterozygosity, read error rate and model fit. It answers what range each number was fitted to.

      How to read: the gap between the minimum and maximum columns is the uncertainty of the fit, so a wide
      gap means the estimate is loose.

outputs.name: GSEA enrichment report
outputs.rawYaml:
id: gsea_report
name: GSEA enrichment report
mode: enrichment/gsea
description: >-
  Gene sets enriched at one pole of a contrast, from the report tables a
  pre-ranked GSEA run publishes. Neither the contrast nor the pole is a column of
  those files, so the recipe recovers both from the file name and stacks every
  report into one frame. The leading-edge percentage is parsed out of the string
  GSEA writes for a human reader, and an FDR q-value of zero, which is what GSEA
  writes below its resolution, is clipped at the run's own floor rather than sent
  to infinity.
find:
  path_glob: "**/tables/gsea/**/*.gsea_report_for_*.tsv"
recipe: gsea/report.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 12 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several contrasts.
fixture: report.tsv
renders_as:
  # The signature panel: one dot per set, placed on its normalised enrichment
  # score, sized by how many of its genes were found and coloured by
  # significance, split by the pole the set came up at.
  # 0.25 is the FDR cut-off the GSEA report itself highlights (user guide).
  - id: gsea_dotplot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: enrichment
    title: Enriched gene sets
    roles:
      { term: term, nes: nes, padj: fdr_qvalue, gene_count: size, source: phenotype }
    config:
      padj_threshold: 0.25
      top_n: 20
      default_colour_by: neg_log10_padj
    description: >-
      Each dot is a gene set: its normalised enrichment score (NES) on the horizontal
      axis, its size by the number of genes in the set and its colour by the FDR
      q-value. It answers which pathways move together at one end of the ranked gene
      list, and in which direction.

      How to read: a set far from zero with a dark colour is strongly and confidently
      enriched. A positive NES means enrichment at the top of the ranked list and a
      negative one at the bottom, so compare both poles before concluding. Sets with
      few genes can reach a high score by chance, so look at the size too.

      Lines and annotations: this plot keeps only sets with an FDR q-value up to 0.25,
      the cut-off at which the GSEA report highlights sets as most likely to give
      interesting hypotheses. The report itself still gives results for every set, and
      the table below lists them all. The user guide advises a stricter 5% when the run
      has few samples and permutes gene sets rather than phenotypes.

      Source: https://docs.gsea-msigdb.org/#GSEA/GSEA_User_Guide/
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16199517/
  # The same scores as ranked bars, which is the view that compares two
  # contrasts rather than two poles of one.
  - id: gsea_nes_bars
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: da_barplot
    title: Top gene sets by enrichment score
    roles:
      { feature_id: term, contrast: contrast, lfc: nes, significance: fdr_qvalue, label: phenotype }
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.25
      effect_label: Normalised enrichment score (NES)
    description: >-
      Each bar is a gene set: its normalised enrichment score in a contrast, for the
      sets with the largest absolute score. It answers which pathways drive each
      contrast and at which pole.

      How to read: long bars to the right are enriched in the positive pole and to
      the left in the negative one. A bar that is marked passes the FDR cut-off, while
      an unmarked long bar is a strong score that is not significant, so check the dot
      plot and the table.

      Lines and annotations: bars are marked when the FDR q-value is below 0.25, the
      cut-off the GSEA report highlights.

      Source: https://docs.gsea-msigdb.org/#GSEA/GSEA_User_Guide/
  - component: card
    column: term
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: phenotype
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: gene sets, by pole
    title: Gene sets reported
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct gene sets in the report tables, with the
      row count next to it, and the bars split them by the pole they came up at. It
      answers how many sets each end of the ranking holds.

      How to read: a very uneven split means the contrast mostly pushes expression one
      way. A set listed under both poles of different contrasts appears in each.
  # On |NES|: the strongest set can sit at the negative pole.
  - component: card
    column: abs_nes
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: strongest set, with the spread
    title: Strongest enrichment
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest absolute normalised enrichment score of any set,
      with the spread of the absolute scores in the box. It answers how strong the top
      signal is.

      How to read: the sign is dropped because the strongest set can sit at either pole.
      A box close to the maximum means many sets are strongly enriched, and a low box
      with a few outliers means a few standout sets.
  - component: card
    column: fdr_qvalue
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.05
    threshold_direction: max
    threshold_warn: 0.25
    caption: median q-value, with the best and the worst
    title: FDR q-value
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median FDR q-value over the reported sets, with the lowest
      and the highest next to it and the bar placed against the two cut-offs. It answers
      how confident the enrichment calls are overall.

      How to read: a median in the green band is a strongly supported result. A median
      between the two cut-offs is acceptable for exploration, and above them the
      reported sets are mostly noise.

      Lines and annotations: 0.25 is the cut-off the GSEA report highlights and 0.05
      the stricter one the user guide advises for few samples with gene-set
      permutation.

      Source: https://docs.gsea-msigdb.org/#GSEA/GSEA_User_Guide/
  - component: card
    column: leading_edge_percent
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with the spread
    title: Leading-edge share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of a set's genes that form its leading
      edge, the genes that drive the enrichment score, with the spread in the box. It
      answers whether enrichment comes from a few genes or from most of the set.

      How to read: a high share means most of the set moves together, and a low share
      that a few genes carry the score. Read the leading-edge genes of a set in the
      table before interpreting it.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: term
    title: Enrichment report
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene set in one contrast and pole: its size, scores, p-values, FDR
      q-value and leading edge. It answers which sets to follow up and which genes drive
      them.

      How to read: sort by FDR q-value, keep the sets below the cut-off and read their
      leading-edge genes. Click a row to filter the other tiles to that set.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: gtdbtk_rank_composition
name: Recovered community per binning run
mode: rank-composition
description: >-
  The community each binning run recovered, as bins per taxon at the rank you
  pick. Two binners on the same assembly rarely recover the same set, and this
  is where that shows: a binner that finds ten phyla where its neighbour finds
  four is either more sensitive or splitting one genome into pieces, and the
  bin quality tiles next to it say which.
find:
  path_glob: "**/classify/*.summary.tsv"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/gtdbtk*.bac*.summary.tsv"
    - "**/gtdbtk*.ar*.summary.tsv"
    - "**/*.bac*.summary.tsv"
    - "**/*.ar*.summary.tsv"
recipe: gtdbtk/rank_composition.py
fixture: rank_composition.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: recovered_community
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: Community recovered by each binning run
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, taxon: taxon, rank: rank, abundance: abundance}
    config:
      default_rank: phylum
      normalise_to_one: false
      top_n: 8
      x_title: Binning run
      value_title: Bins
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each bar is a binning run, split into the taxa of one rank and sized by the number of bins
      placed in each. It answers which organisms each combination of assembler and binner
      recovered.

      How to read: switch the rank with the control. Two binners on the same assembly rarely
      recover the same set, and a binner with many more taxa than its neighbour is either more
      sensitive or splitting one genome into pieces. The bin quality tiles say which.

      Note: the eight largest taxa are drawn and the rest are grouped as Other.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample_id
      y: abundance
      color: taxon
      labels: {sample_id: Binning run, abundance: Bins, taxon: Taxon}
    title: Bins per taxon and binning run
    description: >-
      Each bar is a binning run, stacked by taxon and sized by the number of bins. It answers how
      many bins each run recovered and from which taxa.

      How to read: taller bars are runs that recovered more bins, and a bar with many colours is
      a run that recovered diverse taxa. Pick a rank in the rank filter, since without one the
      bars add up the bins of every rank.
  - component: card
    column: taxon
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: binner
    top_n_count: 5
    filter_expr: "col('rank') == 'phylum'"
    title: Phyla recovered by binner
    caption: the binners that recovered the most phyla, with the row count
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct phyla recovered, and the bars rank the binners by
      their phyla. It answers how diverse the recovered community is and which binner found most.

      How to read: a binner far ahead of the others is more sensitive or splits genomes, so check
      the bin quality before preferring it.
  - component: card
    column: abundance
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: assembler
    filter_expr: "col('rank') == 'phylum'"
    title: Bins by assembler
    caption: split by assembler, with the median and largest count per phylum
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of bins placed at phylum rank over the rows in view,
      and the bar splits it by assembler. It answers which assembler produced most of the bins.

      How to read: a bin that stopped above phylum rank is not counted. An assembler with a
      small share recovered fewer genomes.
  - component: card
    column: abundance
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('rank') == 'phylum'"
    title: Bins per phylum
    caption: median, with its spread across phyla
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of bins per phylum in a run, and the box shows the
      quartiles. It answers how many bins a typical phylum has.

      How to read: a median of one means most taxa are found as a single bin, and larger values
      mean several bins per taxon, which can be redundant bins of one genome.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: Select
    column_name: rank
    title: Rank filter
    description: Pick one taxonomic rank to keep. The bar chart adds the bins of every rank when no rank is picked, so choose one.
  - component: table
    title: Recovered taxa table
    description: >-
      Each row is a binning run, a rank and a taxon, with the number of bins placed in it. It
      answers the exact counts behind the community views.

      How to read: filter on a rank and sort by bins to find the dominant taxa of a run.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: gtdbtk_summary
name: Bin taxonomy
mode: summary
description: >-
  Which organism each recovered bin is, placed against the Genome Taxonomy
  Database. The lineage is split into one column per rank, so a phylum becomes
  a filter that reaches every other tile and the deepest rank a bin reached
  becomes a readable number instead of a string to squint at.
find:
  path_glob: "**/classify/*.summary.tsv"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/gtdbtk*.bac*.summary.tsv"
    - "**/gtdbtk*.ar*.summary.tsv"
    - "**/*.bac*.summary.tsv"
    - "**/*.ar*.summary.tsv"
recipe: gtdbtk/summary.py
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: lineage_sunburst
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Taxonomic lineage of the bins
    roles: {ranks: [domain, phylum, class_name, order, family, genus], abundance: bin_count}
    config:
      colour_by_rank: phylum
    description: >-
      Each arc is a taxon of the GTDB lineage, from domain in the centre outwards, sized by
      the number of bins placed in it and coloured by phylum. It answers which organisms the
      recovered bins belong to.

      How to read: a wide arc is a taxon with many bins. A bin that stops at a high rank was
      placed only that far, which can mean the database holds few related genomes.
      Use the rank control to move the inner ring and open the table for the bins.
  - id: assembler_binner_phylum
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sankey
    title: Assembler, binner and phylum of the bins
    roles: {steps: [assembler, binner, phylum]}
    config:
      value_label: Bins
    description: >-
      Each flow is a group of bins that goes from an assembler through a binner to a
      phylum, with the width of the flow equal to the number of bins. It answers which
      combinations of assembler and binner recover which phyla.

      How to read: a phylum reached from every binner is recovered robustly, and a phylum
      reached from one binner only is a candidate for being missed by the others. Thick flows
      into a node mark the combinations that recover the most bins.
  - id: ani_vs_alignment
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Closest reference identity against alignment fraction
    roles: {x: closest_ani, y: closest_af, label: bin_id, color: phylum}
    config:
      x_title: Average nucleotide identity to the closest reference (%)
      y_title: Alignment fraction to the closest reference
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_value: 0.5
      reference_label: Minimum alignment fraction (0.5)
      top_n_labels: 5
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a bin: its average nucleotide identity (ANI) to the closest GTDB species
      representative on the horizontal axis and the fraction of the genome aligned to it on the
      vertical axis, coloured by phylum. It answers how confidently a bin matches a known species.

      How to read: points to the upper right, with high identity and alignment, are
      assigned to a species. A point with a low alignment fraction or low identity is a
      novel lineage or a poor bin, and may stop at a higher rank. The ANI needed is specific
      to each species, typically 95 percent, so no vertical line is drawn.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the minimum alignment fraction of 0.5,
      the GTDB-Tk default (--min_af) for assigning a genome to a species during the ANI
      screen. The species-specific ANI radius is typically 95 percent.

      Source: https://ecogenomics.github.io/GTDBTk/faq.html
      and https://ecogenomics.github.io/GTDBTk/commands/classify.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: phylum
      y: bin_count
      color: binner
      labels: {phylum: Phylum, bin_count: Bins, binner: Binner}
    title: Bins recovered per phylum
    description: >-
      Each bar is a phylum, sized by the number of bins placed in it and split by the binner
      that recovered them. It answers which phyla were recovered and by which binners.

      How to read: a phylum recovered by one binner only is a candidate for being missed by the
      others. A long tail of phyla with one bin each is typical of a diverse community.
  - component: card
    column: bin_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: phylum
    top_n_count: 5
    title: Bins by phylum
    caption: the five phyla with the most bins, with the row count
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct bins classified, and the bars rank the phyla
      that hold the most. It answers how many bins were placed in the database and in which
      phyla.

      How to read: a single phylum holding most bins points to a low diversity community or to
      bins that are fragments of the same genomes.
  - component: card
    column: species
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: genus
    top_n_count: 5
    title: Species by genus
    caption: the five genera with the most species, with the row count
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct species the bins were assigned to, and the
      bars rank the genera that hold the most. It answers how many species level identities
      the run recovered.

      How to read: the row count above the distinct count means several bins share a species,
      which is expected when binners or assemblers recover the same genome. Bins stopped at a
      higher rank have no species and are not counted.
  - component: card
    column: bin_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: rank_assigned
    title: Bins by deepest rank
    caption: split by the deepest rank reached, with the row count
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct bins, and the ring splits them by the deepest
      taxonomic rank GTDB-Tk reached. It answers how many bins are identified to species and how
      many stop earlier.

      How to read: a ring mostly at species means the community is well represented in
      the database. A large share at a higher rank marks novel lineages or bins of poor quality.
  - component: card
    column: closest_ani
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Identity to the closest reference
    caption: median, with its spread across bins
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median ANI of a bin to its closest reference genome, and the box
      shows the quartiles. It answers how close the recovered genomes are to known species.

      How to read: values near the top of the scale mean the bins are close to known species.
      Only bins classified by the ANI screen carry a value, so an empty card means the run was
      placed through the tree. The species specific radius is typically 95 percent.

      Source: https://ecogenomics.github.io/GTDBTk/faq.html
  # closest_af and not msa_percent: GTDB-Tk fills msa_percent only on the
  # pplacer path, and a run classified through ANI screening leaves it empty
  # for every bin, which makes a card over it a column of blanks.
  - component: card
    column: closest_af
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Alignment fraction to the closest reference
    caption: average and median, with the smallest and the distribution
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean fraction of a bin aligned to its closest reference genome,
      and the histogram shows how the values are distributed. It answers how much of each bin
      is covered by a known genome.

      How to read: values near 1 mean the bin and the reference share nearly all their
      sequence, and low values mean only part of the bin matches. GTDB-Tk requires an
      alignment fraction of at least 0.5 for a species assignment by ANI.

      Source: https://ecogenomics.github.io/GTDBTk/commands/classify.html
  - component: table
    title: Bin taxonomy table
    description: >-
      Each row is a bin with its assembler, binner, lineage split by rank, closest reference,
      ANI, alignment fraction and classification method. It answers which organism each bin is
      and how it was placed.

      How to read: filter by phylum or by deepest rank, and sort by ANI to find the least
      certain species assignments.

outputs.name: Transcript structures
outputs.rawYaml:
id: gtf_transcripts
name: Transcript structures
mode: exon-blocks
description: >-
  Exon and CDS blocks of every transcript in a run's GTF/GFF annotations, one
  row per block, carrying the gene, the strand, the novelty class and the
  per-transcript expression when the writer recorded one.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.gtf"
  path_glob_alt: # compressed annotations, and bambu's run-level extended one
    - "**/*.gtf.gz"
    - "**/bambu/extended_annotations.gtf"
recipe: gtf/transcripts.py
fixture: transcripts.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: transcript_structures
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: transcript_structure
    title: Transcript structures
    roles:
      transcript_id: transcript_id
      gene_id: gene_id
      chrom: chrom
      start: start
      end: end
      feature: feature
      strand: strand
      sample: sample
      gene_name: gene_name
      transcript_class: transcript_class
      expression: expression
    description: >-
      Each lane is one transcript of a gene drawn on a base-pair axis, with its exons
      as blocks and its coding sequence as taller blocks, coloured by novelty class.
      It answers how the isoforms of a gene differ in exon structure and which of
      them are known or new.

      How to read: lanes that share most blocks but differ in one are alternative
      splicing events. A novel class on a lane marks a transcript the reference
      annotation does not hold, so check its expression before trusting it.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/The-Sequence-Ontology/Specifications/master/gff3.md
  # How many isoforms the annotation carries, and which genes carry most of
  # them: the one number that says whether a run found novel structure at all.
  - component: card
    column: transcript_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: gene_name
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    title: Transcripts in the annotation
    caption: genes, by isoform count
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct transcripts, with the number of
      exon and CDS blocks beside it, and the bars rank the genes that carry the most
      isoforms. It answers how rich the annotation is and where the splicing
      complexity sits.

      How to read: genes with many isoforms are candidates for alternative splicing.
      A count close to the number of genes means one isoform per gene.
  # Expression is long-tailed across isoforms, so the histogram says more about it
  # than a box over values that span orders of magnitude.
  - component: card
    column: expression
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Transcript expression
    caption: median, with the distribution
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median expression recorded by the annotation writer for
      its transcripts, with the lowest and highest value beside it, and the
      histogram shows the spread. It answers how strongly the annotated transcripts

outputs.rawYaml:
id: hamronization_gene_presence
name: Gene support
mode: arg/support
description: >-
  One row per sample and resistance gene: how many hits were reported, how many
  of the screening tools agree on it, and the mean identity and coverage of the
  hits that carry them.
find:
  path_glob: "**/hamronization_summarize/*combined_report.tsv"
  path_glob_alt: ["**/hamronization/*combined_report.tsv"]
recipe: hamronization/gene_presence.py
fixture: gene_presence.tsv
renders_as:
  # Dot colour = mean identity of the hits, dot size = share of the screening
  # tools that called the gene in that sample.
  - id: arg_dot_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    title: Gene support per sample
    roles: {cluster: sample, gene: gene_symbol, mean_expression: mean_identity, frac_expressing: tool_frac}
    description: >-
      Each dot is a resistance gene in a sample: its size is the share of screening
      tools that called the gene and its colour is the mean identity of the hits. It
      answers how well supported each detection is.

      How to read: large, strongly coloured dots are genes called by many tools at high
      identity and are the most trustworthy. Small dots are called by one tool only
      and are worth confirming with another screen or the original reads.

      Source: https://github.com/pha4ge/hAMRonization/
  # n_tools is a count, so a gauge needs a denominator that depends on how many
  # tools were run; the histogram shows its distribution instead.
  - component: card
    column: n_tools
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distribution, with its median and maximum
    title: Tools agreeing on a gene
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average count of screening tools that report a gene in a
      sample, and the histogram shows how many genes get one, two or more tools. It
      answers how much the tools agree.

      How to read: a pile at one tool means most calls rest on a single screen. A
      large share at several tools means a consistent resistome. The number of tools
      depends on how many the pipeline ran.
  - component: card
    column: mean_identity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Identity of supported genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of the mean percent identity of the hits for each
      gene in each sample, and the box shows the spread. It answers how close the
      detected genes are to known references.

      How to read: values near 100 percent are confident matches. A tail of low
      identities holds divergent homologues to check.

      Note: tools define identity at the nucleotide or amino acid level, so values are
      not strictly comparable across tools.
  - component: table
    title: Gene support table
    description: >-
      Each row is a resistance gene in a sample with its hit count, the number of
      tools that agree and the mean identity and coverage. It answers the exact support
      behind each dot.

      How to read: sort by the number of tools to see the best supported genes first.
