outputs.name: ARG hits
outputs.rawYaml:
id: hamronization_report
name: ARG hits
mode: arg/hits
description: >-
  One row per antimicrobial-resistance gene hit, with the sample recovered from
  the per-tool input file name and the drug class, screening tool, reference
  database, identity and coverage normalised across every ARG tool.
find:
  path_glob: "**/hamronization_summarize/*combined_report.tsv"
  path_glob_alt: ["**/hamronization/*combined_report.tsv"]
recipe: hamronization/report.py
fixture: report.tsv
renders_as:
  # The resistance genes as strand-aware arrows along their contig, one lane
  # per contig. Where several ARGs sit head to tail on one contig, that is a
  # resistance island, and no aggregate over drug classes can show it.
  # Coloured by tool, not by drug class: the report holds one row per (tool,
  # hit), so a single locus called by four screens draws four stacked arrows,
  # and the tool is what tells them apart. drug_class would be the biological
  # axis but hAMRonization does not normalise it, so AMINOGLYCOSIDE,
  # aminoglycoside and "aminoglycoside antibiotic" would each take a hue of
  # their own and the island would read as more diverse than it is.
  - id: arg_island_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: gene_arrow_track
    title: Resistance genes along contigs
    roles: {contig: contig, feature_id: gene_symbol, start: start, end: stop, strand: strand, class: tool, label: gene_symbol}
    description: >-
      Each arrow is one resistance gene hit placed on its contig, pointing in the
      direction of the gene and coloured by the screening tool that reported it. It
      answers whether resistance genes sit together on the same contig.

      How to read: several arrows head to tail on one contig suggest a resistance
      island or a mobile cassette, which an aggregate over drug classes cannot show.
      Arrows of different colours on the same locus are the same gene found by
      several tools, so agreement between tools raises confidence in the call.

      Note: hAMRonization does not harmonise gene names or drug classes across tools,
      so one gene can appear under different symbols.

      Source: https://github.com/pha4ge/hAMRonization/
  # Screen -> drug class -> gene: which tool contributes which part of the
  # resistome. hAMRonization does not normalise the drug-class vocabulary
  # across tools, so the tool ring keeps the three vocabularies apart.
  - id: arg_hierarchy
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Tool, drug class and gene hierarchy
    roles: {ranks: [tool, drug_class, gene_symbol], abundance: hits}
    config:
      colour_by_rank: tool
    description: >-
      Each arc is a group of hits: the inner ring is the screening tool, the middle
      ring the drug class it reports and the outer ring the gene, sized by the number
      of hits and coloured by tool. It answers which tool contributes which part of
      the resistome.

      How to read: a wide arc in one tool and nothing in the others means that tool
      alone detects the class. Drug class names differ between tools, so the same
      class can appear as separate arcs under different tools; compare within a tool.
      Click an arc to zoom in on it.

      Source: https://github.com/pha4ge/hAMRonization/
  - component: card
    column: hits
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    caption: hits, by drug class
    breakdown_col: drug_class
    top_n_count: 4
    title: Hits by drug class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of resistance gene hits, and the bars rank
      the drug classes that account for most of them. It answers which resistance
      classes dominate.

      How to read: a class leading the ranking is the main resistance signal. Names
      come from each tool's own vocabulary and are not merged, so a class can be split
      across spellings.
  - component: card
    column: gene_symbol
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    caption: distinct genes, by tool
    breakdown_col: tool
    top_n_count: 5
    headline: true
    title: Distinct resistance genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct gene symbols found, and the bars rank
      the screening tools by how many distinct genes each reports. It answers how rich
      the resistome is and which tool contributes most.

      How to read: a tool far ahead of the others may use a broader database or looser
      cut-offs. Gene symbols are not harmonised between tools, so the same gene can be
      counted twice under different names.
  - component: card
    column: identity_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Sequence identity of hits
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percent identity between a hit and its reference
      gene, and the box shows the spread. It answers how close the detected genes are
      to known resistance genes.

      How to read: identities near 100 percent mean confident, well characterised
      matches. A tail of low identities holds divergent homologues that deserve a look
      before being counted as resistance.

      Note: tools define identity at the nucleotide or amino acid level, so values are
      not strictly comparable across tools.
  # hAMRonization defines no coverage cut-off, and each screening tool sets its own
  # default, so the card shows the distribution and draws no pass mark.
  - component: card
    column: coverage_pct
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: average, with its median and minimum
    title: Coverage of hits
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average percent of the reference gene covered by a hit,
      and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how complete the detected
      genes are.

      How to read: a pile at 100 percent means complete genes. A tail of partial hits
      holds fragments, which may be truncated genes or hits on a contig edge.

      Note: hAMRonization does not set a coverage threshold and each screening tool
      applies its own, so no pass mark is drawn here.

      Source: https://github.com/pha4ge/hAMRonization/
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene_symbol
    title: Resistance gene hits
    description: >-
      Each row is a hit reported by one screening tool, with the sample, gene, drug
      class, database, coverage, identity and position on its contig. It answers the
      exact detail behind every other tile and lets a row selection filter the
      dashboard.

      How to read: filter by tool to compare what each one found, or by gene to see
      every sample that carries it.

outputs.name: Tool concordance
outputs.rawYaml:
id: hamronization_tool_overlap
name: Tool concordance
mode: arg/concordance
description: >-
  Contig by screening-tool membership matrix, one 0/1 column per ARG tool.
  Concordance is scored on the contig because every tool has its own gene
  vocabulary while the contig id is shared.
find:
  path_glob: "**/hamronization_summarize/*combined_report.tsv"
  path_glob_alt: ["**/hamronization/*combined_report.tsv"]
recipe: hamronization/tool_overlap.py
fixture: tool_overlap.tsv
renders_as:
  # The tool columns are 0/1 flags named by the tools that ran, so set_columns is
  # left to auto-detect; colouring the intersections by degree shows how many
  # tools agree.
  - id: arg_upset
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: upset_plot
    title: Contig overlap between tools
    config:
      color_intersections_by: degree
      show_values: true
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the contigs found by one exact combination of screening tools,
      and the dots below show which tools are in it. It answers which tools agree on
      where resistance genes are, and which find hits no other tool does.

      How to read: tall bars with many dots are contigs confirmed by several tools.
      Tall bars with one dot are tool specific, which can be a database difference or
      a false positive. Colour shows how many tools agree.

      Note: agreement is scored on the contig because every tool has its own gene
      vocabulary while the contig id is shared.

      Source: https://github.com/pha4ge/hAMRonization/
  - component: table
    title: Contig by tool membership
    description: >-
      Each row is a contig with a 0 or 1 flag per screening tool. It answers which
      tools found resistance genes on a given contig.

      How to read: filter to one sample or to contigs found by a single tool to inspect
      disagreements.

outputs.name: hap.py threshold sweep
outputs.rawYaml:
id: happy_roc
name: hap.py threshold sweep
mode: roc
description: >-
  Germline hap.py SNP precision-recall sweep across quality thresholds (one row
  per QQ threshold).
find: { path_glob: "**/benchmarks/happy/*.roc.Locations.SNP.PASS.csv.gz" }
recipe: happy/roc.py
fixture: roc.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: the sweep is one pooled curve and the recipe has no column that splits
  # it (no sample, caller or variant type), so there is no pertinent colour.
  - id: pr_curve
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: roc_pr_curve
    title: Precision and recall across thresholds
    roles: {recall: recall, precision: precision, threshold: quality}
    description: >-
      Each point is the precision and recall of the SNP calls that pass one variant
      quality threshold, joined into a curve. It answers how much recall is given up
      to buy precision when the callset is filtered harder.

      How to read: a curve that stays near the top right across thresholds means the
      quality score separates true from false calls well. A curve that drops fast as
      recall falls means filtering removes true calls as readily as false ones. Pick
      the threshold where precision stops improving.

      Lines and annotations: the area under the curve is computed from the swept
      points of this table, so it is a data-defined summary and not a published
      cut-off. Recall is TP over TP plus FN and precision is TP over TP plus FP, as
      hap.py defines them.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/happy.md
  - component: table
    title: Threshold sweep
    description: >-
      Each row is a quality threshold with the recall, precision and F1 of the SNP
      calls kept at it. It answers the exact numbers behind the curve.

      How to read: find the row with the highest F1 to pick a threshold that balances
      the two, or read down the recall column to see where it starts to fall.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: happy_summary
name: hap.py pooled summary
mode: benchmark-summary
description: >-
  Germline SNP/INDEL accuracy from hap.py, pooled across samples by variant type
  and filter (ALL/PASS) with recomputed precision/recall/F1.
find: { path_glob: "**/benchmarks/happy/*.summary.csv" }
recipe: happy/summary.py
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: variant_type
      y: f1
      color: filter
      barmode: group
      labels: {variant_type: Variant type, f1: F1 score, filter: Filter}
    title: F1 by variant type
    description: >-
      Each bar is the F1 score of the callset against the truth set for one variant
      type, with all calls and passing calls side by side. It answers how accurate
      the calls are for SNPs and for indels, and what the filter changes.

      How to read: a bar near one means the callset agrees with the truth. A pass bar
      clearly above its all bar shows the filter removed false calls, and equal bars
      show it removed none.

      Note: F1 is the harmonic mean of recall and precision, and the cited hap.py
      documentation states no cut-off for it, so none is drawn.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/happy.md
  - component: table
    title: Benchmark summary
    description: >-
      Each row is a variant type and filter with the true positives, false negatives
      and false positives and the recall, precision and F1 recomputed from them. It
      answers the counts behind the F1 bars.

      How to read: a low recall with a high precision means the callset misses truth
      variants, and the reverse means it calls false ones.

id: hicexplorer_distance_decay
name: Contact probability vs distance
mode: dist-vs-counts
description: >-
  Mean contact frequency against genomic distance, hicexplorer's
  hicPlotDistVsCounts curve, a basic Hi-C library-quality readout.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_distcount.txt"
recipe: hicexplorer/distance_decay.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 13 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: distance_decay.tsv
renders_as:
  # One curve per sample: the pooled curve ("all") is the file's only series
  # unless the run was made per chromosome, so the chromosome would put every
  # sample on one line.
  # C3 N/A: HiCExplorer publishes no cut-off for the decay.
  - id: decay_curve
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Contact frequency against distance
    roles: {series: sample, x: distance, y: contacts}
    config:
      x_title: Genomic distance (bp)
      y_title: Mean contact frequency
      log_x: true
      log_y: true
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sample: the mean contact frequency between pairs of bins at each
      genomic distance, on log axes. It answers how quickly interactions fade with
      distance in the library.

      How to read: contact frequency should fall smoothly as distance grows. A plateau
      or a bump at long range may point to an artefact. HiCExplorer
      publishes no cut-off for the decay.

      Note: the first bin, at distance zero, is not shown on a log axis.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/deeptools/HiCExplorer/master/hicexplorer/hicPlotDistVsCounts.py
  - component: card
    column: contacts
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: shortest-distance bin, with the median and the lowest
    title: Contact frequency range
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest mean contact frequency of any distance bin, which
      is the shortest distance, with the median and the lowest bin next to it. It
      answers how steeply contacts fall across the distance range.

      How to read: the values span orders of magnitude, so a large gap between the
      maximum and the median is normal. Use the curve to compare samples rather than
      this number.
  - component: table
    title: Contact frequency per distance bin
    description: >-
      Each row is a distance bin of one sample: the mean contact frequency, the number
      of bins behind it and the scale factor HiCExplorer wrote. It answers the exact
      value behind each point of the curve.

      How to read: read the number of bins next to each value, since a bin with few
      bins behind it is noisier.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/deeptools/HiCExplorer/master/hicexplorer/hicPlotDistVsCounts.py

outputs.rawYaml:
id: hicpro_pair_flow
name: Read-pair fates
mode: stats
description: >-
  The same HiC-Pro statistics as one weighted row per read-pair fate, mapping
  to restriction-fragment filter to contact class, so the funnel can be drawn
  as a flow and the cis/trans split as a composition.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_allValidPairs.mergestat"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*.mpairstat"
    - "**/*.mRSstat"
recipe: hicpro/pair_flow.py
fixture: pair_flow.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: pair_flow_sankey
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sankey
    title: Fate of the read pairs
    roles:
      steps: [mapping, filtering, contacts]
    config:
      value_label: Read pairs
    description: >-
      Each band is a group of read pairs flowing from how they mapped, through the restriction-fragment
      filter, to the contact class they end in. It answers where the sequenced pairs are lost on the way to
      valid contacts.

      How to read: a thick band into Lost at an early step is the main source of loss. A large dangling end
      or religation band points to a problem in the digestion or ligation, and a thin valid pairs band means
      most of the sequencing did not yield contacts. Compare samples through the table tile.

      Lines and annotations: dangling ends are unligated fragments with both reads on the same restriction
      fragment, religation is the ligation of juxtaposed fragments, and only valid pairs between two
      different fragments become contacts. No cut-off is drawn.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  # Composition of what survives: the cis/trans split plus the duplicates
  # de-duplication removed. `filter_expr` keeps the lost paths out of the ring.
  - component: card
    column: pairs
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: contacts
    filter_expr: "col('filtering') == 'Valid pairs'"
    caption: valid pairs, by contact class
    title: Valid pairs by contact class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of valid read pairs, and the ring splits them by contact class (cis,
      trans or removed duplicates). The strip gives the smallest and largest single flow. It answers what
      the surviving pairs are made of.

      How to read: cis contacts join loci on the same chromosome and trans contacts join different
      chromosomes. A large duplicate share points to a low-complexity library, and a trans share far above
      the other samples to a noisier one.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  - component: card
    column: pairs
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: mapping
    caption: read pairs, by mapping outcome
    title: Read pairs by mapping outcome
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of read pairs, and the ring splits them by how they mapped: uniquely
      mapped, singleton, low quality or unmapped. The strip gives the smallest and largest single flow. It
      answers how much of the sequencing maps to the genome.

      How to read: a large uniquely mapped share is healthy. Large unmapped or low quality shares point to
      contamination, poor read quality or the wrong reference.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  - component: table
    title: Read-pair fates table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample and a path of mapping outcome, filter outcome and contact class with the number of
      read pairs that took it. It answers the exact counts behind the flow.

      How to read: filter on a sample and sort by pairs to list its largest fates.

outputs.name: Valid-pair funnel
outputs.rawYaml:
id: hicpro_pair_stats
name: Valid-pair funnel
mode: stats
description: >-
  HiC-Pro's own mapping, pairing, restriction-fragment and contact statistics
  pivoted into one row per sample, so the valid-pair funnel and its rates are
  filterable numbers instead of a MultiQC image.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_allValidPairs.mergestat"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*.mpairstat"
    - "**/*.mRSstat"
    - "**/*.mmapstat"
recipe: hicpro/pair_stats.py
fixture: pair_stats.tsv
renders_as:
  # The whole funnel as one card: hero = pairs sequenced, strip = every stage
  # that survives, down to the long-range cis contacts a Hi-C run is built for.
  - component: card
    column: total_pairs
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: attrition
    attrition_cols: [reported_pairs, valid_pairs, valid_pairs_rmdup, cis_pairs, cis_long_range]
    caption: pairs left at each stage
    title: Valid-pair funnel
    description: >-
      The hero number is the read pairs sequenced, and the stages below it show how many remain after
      pairing, the restriction-fragment filter, de-duplication, the cis split and the long-range cut. The
      strip gives the median and the largest sample. It answers how much of the sequencing ends as useful
      long-range contacts.

      How to read: each stage should keep a sizeable share of the one before. A sharp drop at the
      restriction-fragment filter points to the digestion or ligation, and one at de-duplication to a
      low-complexity library.

      Lines and annotations: long-range contacts are cis pairs more than 20 kb apart and short-range ones are 20 kb apart
      or less, as HiC-Pro counts them.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md and
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/scripts/merge_valid_interactions.sh
  - component: card
    column: valid_pair_rate
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: mean valid pair rate, with its lowest and highest
    title: Valid pair rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean share of processed read pairs that are valid pairs, with the lowest and
      highest sample beside it. It answers how efficient the library is at yielding contacts.

      How to read: a low rate for one sample against the others marks a failed library. Look at the funnel
      and the read-pair flow to see which step loses the pairs. HiC-Pro defines no cut-off, so judge a
      sample against its peers.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  - component: card
    column: cis_ratio
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: mean cis share, with its lowest and highest
    title: Cis contact share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean share of de-duplicated valid pairs that join loci on the same chromosome,
      with the lowest and highest sample beside it. It answers how much of the signal is intra-chromosomal.

      How to read: the cis share and the trans share add up to one. A sample whose cis share is far below
      its peers is noisier, so compare samples because HiC-Pro defines no cut-off.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  - component: card
    column: long_range_ratio
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: mean long-range share of cis pairs, with its lowest and highest
    title: Long-range share of cis contacts
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean share of cis contacts that are more than 20 kb apart, with the lowest and
      highest sample beside it. It answers how much of the signal reports distant interactions.

      How to read: long-range cis contacts are the ones a Hi-C run is built to capture, so a low share
      means the library is dominated by short-range contacts. Compare samples, since HiC-Pro defines no
      cut-off.

      Lines and annotations: HiC-Pro splits cis contacts into short range (20 kb or less) and long range (over 20 kb).

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md and
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/scripts/merge_valid_interactions.sh
  - component: card
    column: duplicate_rate
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: duplicate rate, with its spread
    title: Duplicate rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean share of valid pairs removed as duplicates, and the box shows the spread
      over samples. It answers how redundant the library is.

      How to read: a high rate means the same ligation products were sequenced many times, so the library
      has low complexity and sequencing deeper adds little. Compare samples to find the outliers.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  - component: card
    column: low_qual_rate
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: low quality rate, with its spread
    title: Low quality rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean share of processed read pairs discarded for low mapping quality, and the
      box shows the spread over samples. It answers how many pairs map ambiguously.

      How to read: a high rate points to repeats, poor read quality or a mismatched reference. Compare
      samples to find the outliers. The minimum mapping quality is a HiC-Pro setting.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  - component: card
    column: valid_pairs_rmdup
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: de-duplicated valid pairs, with their range over samples
    title: De-duplicated valid pairs
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of valid pairs left after de-duplication, with the median, lowest and
      highest sample beside it. It answers how many usable contacts the run holds.

      How to read: contact maps at fine resolution need many contacts, so a sample with far fewer pairs than
      its peers limits the resolution you can use.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  - component: card
    column: cis_long_range
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: long-range cis pairs, with their range over samples
    title: Long-range cis pairs
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of cis pairs more than 20 kb apart, with the median, lowest and highest
      sample beside it. It answers how many distant contacts the run holds.

      How to read: these are the contacts that carry domain and loop information. A sample far below its
      peers is a weak one for such analyses.

      Lines and annotations: long range means more than 20 kb between the two ends, as HiC-Pro defines it.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  - component: card
    column: trans_ratio
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: trans share, with its spread
    title: Trans contact share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean share of de-duplicated valid pairs that join different chromosomes, and
      the box shows the spread over samples. It answers how much of the signal is inter-chromosomal.

      How to read: it is the complement of the cis share. A sample whose trans share is far above its peers
      is noisier. HiC-Pro defines no cut-off, so judge a sample against its peers.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  - component: card
    column: mapping_rate_r1
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mapping rate, with its spread
    title: Mapping rate of the first mate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean share of first-mate reads that mapped to the genome, and the box shows the
      spread over samples. It answers how well the reads align before pairing.

      How to read: a low rate points to contamination, poor quality or the wrong reference. HiC-Pro maps
      reads in two steps and trims reads spanning the ligation junction, so a part of the mapped reads comes
      from the second step.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
  - component: table
    title: Valid-pair funnel table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its counts at every stage of the funnel and the rates derived from them. It
      answers the exact numbers behind each card.

      How to read: sort by valid pair rate to find the weakest libraries, then read the other columns to see
      which step lost the pairs.

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nservant/HiC-Pro/master/doc/MANUAL.md
renders_as.title: Mapping rate of the first mate

renders_as.description:
Each row is a sample with its counts at every stage of the funnel and the rates derived from them. It answers the exact numbers behind each card.
How to read: sort by valid pair rate to find the weakest libraries, then read the other columns to see which step lost the pairs.
renders_as.title: Valid-pair funnel table

outputs.description: BamTools' per-depth base counts turned into the fraction of bases covered at least each depth, one curve per DNA sample. A tumor sequenced deeper than its normal sits to the right; a curve that drops early marks a sample below the depth the somatic callers need.
outputs.name: Cumulative coverage
outputs.rawYaml:
id: hmf_bamtools_coverage_profile
name: Cumulative coverage
mode: bam_metrics
description: >-
  BamTools' per-depth base counts turned into the fraction of bases covered
  at least each depth, one curve per DNA sample. A tumor sequenced deeper than
  its normal sits to the right; a curve that drops early marks a sample below
  the depth the somatic callers need.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bam_metric.coverage.tsv"
recipe: hmf_bamtools/coverage_profile.py
fixture: coverage_profile.tsv
renders_as:
  # No cut-off drawn: BamTools (hmftools) documents no coverage floor
  # (README), so the curves stand alone (RULES section 17).
  - id: cumulative_coverage_curve
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Cumulative coverage
    roles: {series: sample, x: coverage, y: fraction_at_least}
    config:
      x_title: Coverage depth (x)
      y_title: Fraction of bases at or above depth
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a DNA sample: the fraction of bases covered at least to each depth.
      It answers how much of the target is sequenced deeply enough to call variants.

      How to read: a curve that stays high and drops late means deep, even coverage. A
      tumour sequenced deeper than its normal sits to the right. A curve that drops early
      marks a sample too shallow for the somatic callers you plan to use.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. BamTools documents no coverage floor, so
      judge the depth against the requirements of your callers.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/bam-tools/README.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: coverage
      y: fraction
      color: sample
      labels: {coverage: Coverage depth (x), fraction: Fraction of bases at this depth, sample: Sample}
    title: Coverage depth distribution
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: the fraction of bases at each exact depth, the density
      behind the cumulative curve. It answers where the bulk of the coverage sits.

      How to read: a single narrow peak is even coverage. A wide or multi-peaked line
      means uneven sequencing, and a spike at depth zero is unsequenced bases.
  - component: table
    title: Coverage table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample and a depth with the bases at that depth, their fraction and
      the cumulative fraction. It answers the exact numbers behind the curves.

      How to read: filter by sample and read the cumulative fraction at the depth your
      caller needs.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: hmf_bamtools_summary
name: Alignment and coverage summary
mode: bam_metrics
description: >-
  One row per DNA sample: total, duplicate and dual-strand reads, mean, median
  and spread of the coverage, the fractions of bases lost to low mapping or
  base quality, duplicates, unmapped reads and read overlap, and the fraction
  of the genome covered at 10x, 20x, 30x, 60x and the other depths BamTools
  reports.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bam_metric.summary.tsv"
recipe: hmf_bamtools/summary.py
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: mean_coverage_spread
    component: card
    column: mean_coverage
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    title: Mean coverage
    caption: mean coverage, quartiles over samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median mean depth over the DNA samples and the box shows
      the spread. It answers how deeply the samples are sequenced.

      How to read: a tumour is normally sequenced deeper than its normal. A sample far
      below the rest may be too shallow to call variants; BamTools documents no floor.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/bam-tools/README.md
  - id: total_reads_spread
    component: card
    column: total_reads
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Total reads
    caption: reads, quartiles over samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of reads per sample and the box shows the
      spread. It answers how much sequencing each sample received.

      How to read: read counts follow the depth, so an outlier here usually explains an
      outlier in mean coverage.
  - id: worst_duplicate_frac
    component: card
    column: duplicate_frac
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Highest duplicate fraction
    caption: duplicate fraction, quartiles over samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest fraction of duplicate reads among the samples and
      the box shows the spread. It answers whether any library is dominated by
      duplicates.

      How to read: a high maximum next to low others marks one library with low
      complexity. Duplicates add depth without adding information.
  - id: min_frac_ge_30x
    component: card
    column: frac_ge_30x
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    title: Lowest breadth at 30x
    caption: fraction at 30x, quartiles over samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the smallest fraction of bases covered at 30x or more among the
      samples and the box shows the spread. It answers whether every sample reaches a
      useful depth over most of the genome.

      How to read: a low minimum marks the sample to check first. The 30x depth is one of
      the depths BamTools reports, not a pass mark.
  - id: coverage_record
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: record_card
    title: Sample record
    roles: {id: sample}
    description: >-
      One sample at a time: its reads, duplicates, coverage statistics and the fraction of
      bases lost to each quality filter. Select a row in the table to open it.

      How to read: compare the fractions lost to low mapping or base quality with the
      other samples to spot a failing library.
  - id: bam_summary_table
    component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Alignment summary table
    description: >-
      Each row is a DNA sample with its read counts, coverage statistics, quality-loss
      fractions and the fraction of bases covered at each depth. It answers the exact
      figures behind the cards and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by mean coverage or duplicate fraction to find the weakest sample.

outputs.name: Family profile HMM
outputs.rawYaml:
id: hmmer_hmm_profile
name: Family profile HMM
mode: protein/profile
description: >-
  The profile HMM of every protein family as a long table, one row per match
  state and letter: the emission probability, the letter height in bits, the
  state's information content, insert and delete behaviour, occupancy and the
  consensus, RF and CS annotation. Where the family's hmmalign alignment and
  representative are known, each state also says which residue of the
  representative it sits on, so a state selected in the logo selects that
  residue in the family's residue table and structure.
find:
  path_glob: "**/hmm/filtered/*/*.hmm.gz"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/update_families/hmm/*/*.hmm.gz"
    - "**/hmm/raw/*/*/*.hmm.gz"
recipe: hmmer/hmm_profile.py
fixture: hmm_profile.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: family_logo
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: hmm_logo
    title: Family profile logo
    roles:
      entity: entity
      position: position
      model: hmm_name
      state: hmm_position
      letter: hmm_letter
      emission: emission
      insert_prob: insert_prob
      insert_length: insert_length
      occupancy: occupancy
      consensus: consensus
      rf: rf
      cs: cs
    config:
      height_mode: relent_abovebg
      show_consensus: true
    description: >-
      Each column is a match state of the family's profile HMM, drawn as a stack of amino acids whose height
      is the state's information content in bits. It answers which positions of the family are conserved and
      which residues are allowed there.

      How to read: tall stacks are conserved positions, often the functional or structural core of the
      family, and low flat stacks tolerate substitutions. The lanes under the logo show how often a state is
      occupied and how likely and how long insertions are, so a gappy region is a poor place to trust the
      alignment. Select a state to see the residue it matches in the representative structure.

      Lines and annotations: the total height of a stack is the state's relative entropy in bits, as in
      hmmlogo. The tile draws only residues more frequent than background, hmmlogo's above-background
      option. The
      consensus, RF and CS rows come from the profile file annotation.

      Source: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf
  - id: state_information
    component: card
    column: info_bits
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: information per state, with its spread
    title: Information per state
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean information content of the match states, in bits, and the box shows its
      quartiles. It answers how conserved the family is overall.

      How to read: a high mean means a tightly conserved family, and a low one a diverse family. A box
      with a long upper whisker means a few highly conserved positions stand out from a variable background.

      Source: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf
  - id: state_occupancy
    component: card
    column: occupancy
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: state occupancy, with its spread
    title: State occupancy
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean occupancy of the match states, the probability that a family member has a
      residue at the state, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how gap-free the alignment behind the
      model is.

      How to read: values near one mean most members cover every state. A low tail marks states often skipped
      by members, such as fragment ends or variable loops.
  - component: table
    title: Profile states table
    description: >-
      Each row is a match state and an amino acid with its emission probability, letter height in bits, the
      state's information content, insert and delete behaviour, occupancy and the consensus annotation. It
      answers the exact numbers behind the logo.

      How to read: filter on one state to see which residues the model allows there, or sort by information
      content to list the most conserved positions.

outputs.name: Family member coverage of the HMM
outputs.rawYaml:
id: hmmer_hmmalign_hits
name: Family member coverage of the HMM
mode: protein/domains
description: >-
  One row per member of every family alignment (hmmalign against the family
  HMM): the stretch of the model it covers (first and last match state, and the
  share of the model between them), the member's residues at those two states
  and its length. The columns of a domain hit table without the search
  statistics (E-value and score are null), so the lane under an HMM logo draws
  the members' coverage and a domain architecture shows which members are
  fragments.
find:
  path_glob: "**/full_msa/raw/hmmer_hmmalign/*/*.sto.gz"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/hmmalign/*/*.sto.gz"
recipe: hmmer/hmmalign_hits.py
fixture: hmmalign_hits.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: member_architecture
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: domain_architecture
    title: Family member coverage of the model
    roles:
      entity: entity
      start: ali_from
      end: ali_to
      label: label
      protein_length: protein_length
      hmm_from: hmm_from
      hmm_to: hmm_to
      hmm_length: hmm_length
      hmm_coverage: hmm_coverage
    config:
      color_by: label
    description: >-
      Each row is a member of a family alignment: a backbone for its sequence with a bar for the stretch
      that aligns to the family HMM, coloured by family. It answers whether the members cover the whole model
      or only part of it.

      How to read: members whose bar spans the whole backbone are full-length. A zigzag edge marks a member
      that starts after the first or ends before the last match state of the HMM, so it is a fragment or a
      truncated sequence. Many fragments suggest the family needs a closer look before building a structure
      or a logo from it.

      Lines and annotations: the zigzag edge is drawn from the first and last HMM state each member covers
      against the length of the model, with no score cut-off, since an hmmalign alignment carries no E-value.

      Source: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf
  - id: member_count
    component: card
    column: entity
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: label
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: members, by family
    title: Family members
    description: >-
      The hero number counts the aligned family members, and the bars rank the families with the most members.
      The second figure counts the distinct sequences. It answers how large the families are.

      How to read: a family with very few members gives a weak profile, so treat its logo with caution.
      Large families give more reliable conservation estimates.
  - id: model_coverage
    component: card
    column: hmm_coverage
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: model coverage, with its spread
    title: Share of the model covered
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of the HMM that a member's alignment covers, and the box shows its
      quartiles. It answers how complete the members are.

      How to read: a median near one means most members are full length. A low median or a long lower whisker
      means many fragments, which weaken the conservation signal at the ends of the model.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: label
      y: hmm_coverage
      color: label
      labels: {label: Family, hmm_coverage: Share of the model covered}
    title: Model coverage by family
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: hmm_coverage}
    description: >-
      Each box is a family: the spread of the share of the HMM covered by its members. It answers which
      families are made of full-length members and which of fragments.

      How to read: a box close to one is a complete family, and a box that reaches low values holds many
      fragments. Open the architecture tile for the families with a low box.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of the model covered of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not
      a cut-off of HMMER.
  - component: table
    title: Member coverage table
    description: >-
      Each row is a member of a family alignment with the first and last HMM state it covers, its length and
      the share of the model between them. It answers which sequences are fragments.

      How to read: sort by model coverage and open the lowest rows to see the truncated members.

outputs.description: One row per domain hit of an hmmsearch run: the sequence, the family HMM and the database it came from, the envelope span on the sequence, the independent E-value and bit score of the domain, and how much of the HMM the alignment covers. The envelope columns are the domain span a sequence track draws.
outputs.name: Domain hits (hmmsearch)
outputs.rawYaml:
id: hmmer_hmmsearch_domtbl
name: Domain hits (hmmsearch)
mode: protein/domains
description: >-
  One row per domain hit of an hmmsearch run: the sequence, the family HMM and
  the database it came from, the envelope span on the sequence, the
  independent E-value and bit score of the domain, and how much of the HMM the
  alignment covers. The envelope columns are the domain span a sequence track
  draws.
find:
  path_glob: "**/domain_annotation/*/*.domtbl.gz"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*.domtbl.gz"
    - "**/*.domtbl"
recipe: hmmer/hmmsearch_domtbl.py
fixture: hmmsearch_domtbl.tsv
renders_as:
  # Bit score against HMM coverage separates full-length family hits (right,
  # high) from fragments that only touch a few HMM states (left).
  - id: domain_score_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    roles: {x: hmm_coverage, y: dom_score, label: label, color: source}
    title: Domain score against model coverage
    config:
      x_title: Share of the HMM covered
      y_title: Domain bit score
      top_n_labels: 10
    description: >-
      Each point is a domain hit: the share of the family HMM its alignment covers on the horizontal axis and
      its bit score on the vertical axis, coloured by the database the family comes from. It answers which
      hits are both complete and confident.

      How to read: hits in the upper right cover the whole model with a high score, the reliable family
      assignments. Hits to the left only touch part of the model and are fragments or partial domains. A
      high score with low coverage can still be a true short match, so check the architecture tile.

      Lines and annotations: no cut-off is drawn. A score threshold is specific to each family, and Pfam
      stores gathering bit score thresholds inside each model, which hmmsearch applies only on request with
      its cut_ga option.

      Source: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf
  # One backbone per protein with its domains by family; a zigzag edge marks a partial match
  # of the HMM, drawn from hmm_from / hmm_to / hmm_length.
  - id: domain_architecture
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: domain_architecture
    title: Domain architecture per protein
    roles: {entity: entity, start: start, end: end, label: label, protein_length: protein_length, hmm_from: hmm_from, hmm_to: hmm_to, hmm_length: hmm_length, hmm_coverage: hmm_coverage, evalue: i_evalue, source: source, description: description, accession: accession}
    config:
      color_by: label
    description: >-
      Each row is a protein, drawn as a backbone with its domain hits placed along it and coloured by
      family. It answers which domains each protein carries and in what order.

      How to read: proteins with the same ordered list of families share an architecture, and the
      architectures view counts them. A zigzag edge marks a domain that matches only part of the family
      model. Hover a domain for its family, accession and independent E-value.

      Lines and annotations: the domain bar is the envelope on the sequence, the region HMMER judges the
      domain most probably lies in. The zigzag edge comes from the HMM start and end against the model
      length. No E-value cut-off is applied beyond the one set in the search.

      Source: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf
  - id: domain_hits
    component: card
    column: entity
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: source
    top_n_count: 4
    headline: true
    caption: domain hits, by database
    title: Domain hits
    description: >-
      The hero number counts the domain hits, and the bars rank the databases they come from. The second
      figure counts the distinct proteins with a hit. It answers how much of the input the search annotates.

      How to read: a protein count far below the number of sequences searched means many sequences carry no
      recognised domain. Several hits per protein are normal for multi-domain proteins.
  - id: domain_families
    component: card
    column: label
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: source
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: families, by database
    title: Distinct families
    description: >-
      The hero number counts the distinct families hit, and the bars rank the databases by how many of their
      families were found. The second figure counts all hits. It answers how diverse the annotation is.

      How to read: a high ratio of hits to families means a few families dominate. A flat ranking means the
      search reached many different families.
  - id: domain_score
    component: card
    column: dom_score
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: domain bit score, with its spread
    title: Domain bit score
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median bit score of a domain, and the box shows its quartiles. A bit score is
      the log-odds of the match against a null model of random sequence, so higher is stronger. It answers
      how strong the typical hit is.

      How to read: a high median means confident hits. A low median with a long lower whisker means many
      marginal hits, which are worth checking against their E-values.

      Source: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: source
      y: dom_score
      color: source
      labels: {source: Database, dom_score: Domain bit score}
    title: Domain score by database
    description: >-
      Each box is a database: the spread of domain bit scores of its hits. It answers whether one database
      gives stronger matches than another.

      How to read: scores of different databases are not directly comparable, because each uses its own
      models and thresholds. Compare the shapes, and look for a database whose box sits near the low end.
  - component: table
    title: Domain hits table
    description: >-
      Each row is a domain hit with its protein, family, database, envelope span, E-values, bit score and
      how much of the HMM the alignment covers. It answers the exact numbers behind every tile.

      How to read: sort by independent E-value to list the most confident hits, and filter on a family or a
      database to inspect it.

How to read: sort by independent E-value to list the most confident hits, and filter on a family or a database to inspect it.
renders_as.title: Domain hits table

outputs.name: Peak annotation
outputs.rawYaml:
id: homer_annotated_peaks
name: Peak annotation
mode: peaks/annotation
description: >-
  One row per annotated peak: the genomic feature class HOMER assigned it, the
  signed distance to the nearest transcription start site and the gene that
  start site belongs to.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_peaks.annotatePeaks.txt"
recipe: homer/annotate_peaks.py
fixture: annotate_peaks.tsv
renders_as:
  # Where the peaks land relative to genes, then how far from the TSS.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      color: annotation_class
      labels: {sample: Sample, annotation_class: Genomic feature, count: Peaks}
    title: Peak annotation per sample
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample and each segment counts its peaks by the genomic feature
      HOMER assigned (promoter-TSS, exon, intron, intergenic and so on). It answers
      where the peaks of each sample land relative to genes.

      How to read: a transcription factor or an active histone mark is expected to
      concentrate on promoters, while a repressive mark sits mostly in introns and
      intergenic space. A sample whose split differs from its replicates is worth a
      check of its quality.

      Lines and annotations: HOMER gives each peak one class by priority, TSS first,
      then TTS, exons, UTRs, introns and intergenic. The promoter-TSS window is from
      1 kb upstream to 100 bp downstream of the start site, HOMER's default.

      Source: http://homer.ucsd.edu/homer/ngs/annotation.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: distance_to_tss
      color: annotation_class
      labels: {distance_to_tss: Distance to nearest TSS (bp), annotation_class: Genomic feature}
    title: Distance to nearest TSS
    description: >-
      Each bar counts peaks in a bin of their signed distance to the nearest
      transcription start site, split by genomic feature. It answers how close the
      peaks sit to promoters.

      How to read: a tall bar around zero means promoter-bound peaks. A broad, flat
      distribution with long tails means the signal is mostly distal. Negative values
      are upstream of the start site and positive values downstream.
  - component: card
    column: chr
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: annotation_class
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: peaks, by feature class
    title: Annotated peaks
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of annotated peaks, and the bars rank the feature
      classes that hold most of them. The secondary number is the count of chromosomes
      the peaks fall on. It answers how many peaks there are and where they land.

      How to read: a class that dominates the ranking tells what kind of region the
      signal marks. Open the annotation bars to compare samples.
  - component: card
    column: annotation_class
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: annotation_class
    headline: true
    caption: peaks, by feature class
    title: Peaks by feature class
    description: >-
      Each unit is one annotated peak and the ring splits them by the genomic feature
      HOMER assigned. It answers what share of peaks sit in promoters, exons, introns
      or intergenic regions.

      How to read: compare the promoter share with what is expected for the mark or
      factor. HOMER assigns one class per peak by priority, TSS first and intergenic
      last.

      Source: http://homer.ucsd.edu/homer/ngs/annotation.html
  - component: card
    column: gene_name
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: annotation_class
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: genes, by feature class
    title: Genes with a peak
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct genes that are the nearest promoter of a
      peak, and the bars rank the feature classes by how many genes they reach. It
      answers how many genes the peaks can regulate.

      How to read: HOMER assigns the nearest start site whatever the distance, so a
      distal peak still names a gene. Filter to the promoter class for the confident
      targets.
  - component: card
    column: peak_score
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Peak score
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median peak score, with a box for the quartiles. It
      answers how strong the typical peak is.

      How to read: the score comes from the peak caller, not from HOMER, so compare it
      between samples called the same way. A sample with a much lower median has weaker
      enrichment.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: peak_id
    title: Annotated peaks table
    description: >-
      Each row is a peak with its position, score, feature class, distance to the
      nearest start site and gene. It answers which peaks and genes to follow up and
      lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by score, and filter by feature class to keep promoter peaks.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: peak_score
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, q3]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: top score, with the typical peak
    title: Peak score distribution
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest peak score, and the histogram shows how scores are
      spread over all peaks. It answers how many peaks are strong and how many are weak.

      How to read: most callers give many weak peaks and a long tail of strong ones. A
      distribution with no tail means little enrichment over background.

outputs.description: How each sample's peaks are distributed around the nearest transcription start site, counted in 250 bp bins across a 20 kb window. A sharp central spike means the peaks are promoter-bound; a flat curve means they sit across gene bodies and intergenic space.
outputs.name: Distance to nearest TSS
outputs.rawYaml:
id: homer_tss_distance_profile
name: Distance to nearest TSS
mode: peaks/tss_distance
description: >-
  How each sample's peaks are distributed around the nearest transcription start
  site, counted in 250 bp bins across a 20 kb window. A sharp central spike
  means the peaks are promoter-bound; a flat curve means they sit across gene
  bodies and intergenic space.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_peaks.annotatePeaks.txt"
recipe: homer/tss_distance_profile.py
fixture: tss_distance_profile.tsv
renders_as:
  # The `profile` kind rather than a histogram figure: it owns the marker at the
  # start site, the shaded promoter window and the log axis in the tile's own
  # Settings, which is what the code-mode TSS histograms were written to get.
  - id: tss_distance
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Peak distribution around the TSS
    roles: {series: sample, x: distance_to_tss, y: fraction}
    config:
      reference_x: 0
      reference_label: TSS
      shaded_bands:
        - [-1000, 100, Promoter-TSS window]
      x_title: Distance to nearest TSS (bp)
      y_title: Fraction of peaks
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sample: the fraction of its peaks that fall in each bin of distance to the nearest transcription start
      site, 250 bp wide as set by this catalog's recipe. It answers whether the
      peaks concentrate at promoters.

      How to read: a sharp spike at zero means promoter-bound signal, as for an active
      mark or a promoter-binding factor. A flat curve means the peaks sit across gene
      bodies and intergenic space. Curves that differ between replicates point to a
      quality problem.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical marker is the start site at zero. The shaded
      band runs from 1 kb upstream to 100 bp downstream of it, the window HOMER uses to
      call a peak promoter-TSS by default.

      Source: http://homer.ucsd.edu/homer/ngs/annotation.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: distance_to_tss
      y: fraction
      color: sample
      labels: {distance_to_tss: Distance to nearest TSS (bp), fraction: Fraction of peaks, sample: Sample}
    title: Peak distribution around the nearest TSS
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: the fraction of its peaks in each 250 bp bin around the
      nearest transcription start site. It answers how the peak positions of the
      samples compare on the same axis.

      How to read: lines that overlay each other mean consistent peak positions. A
      sample with a lower central peak has more distal signal than the others.
  - component: card
    column: peak_count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: total, with the busiest bin
    title: Peaks in the window
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of peaks counted in the 20 kb window around the
      start sites, and the histogram shows how many peaks each bin holds. It answers how
      many peaks fall near a gene.

      How to read: a distribution with one huge bin and many near-empty ones is the
      signature of promoter signal. An even spread means peaks are not tied to start
      sites.
  - component: card
    column: fraction
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, q3]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: top bin, with the typical bin
    title: Share of peaks per bin
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest share of a sample's peaks in a single bin, and the
      histogram shows how the shares are spread over bins. It answers how concentrated
      the peaks are.

      How to read: a large maximum with a median near zero means the peaks pile up at
      one distance, usually the start site. A small maximum means they are spread out.
  - component: card
    column: peak_count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: sample
    caption: peaks, by sample
    title: Peaks per sample
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of peaks in the window and the bar shows each
      sample's share of it. It answers whether the samples contribute evenly.

      How to read: a sample with a very small share has fewer peaks and its profile is
      less reliable.
  - component: table
    title: Distance profile table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample and a distance bin with its peak count and the fraction of
      that sample's peaks. It answers exactly how many peaks sit at each distance.

      How to read: sort by peak count to find the dominant bin of each sample.

id: interproscan_matches

  the signature and its description, the matched span, the match E-value or

renders_as:
  - id: signature_matches
    component: card
    column: entity
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: source
    top_n_count: 4
    headline: true
    title: Signature matches
    caption: matches, by member database
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of signature matches, with the number of distinct
      proteins that have one beside it, and the bars rank the member databases that
      report them. It answers how much of the protein set is annotated and by which
      database.

      How to read: proteins without a match write no row, so compare the protein count
      with the input size to see the unannotated share. A database that dominates may
      simply be the one with the broadest signatures.

    component: card
    column: interpro_accession
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: source
    filter_expr: "(col('interpro_accession') != '')"
    title: InterPro entries
    caption: integrated matches, by member database
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct InterPro entries the matches are
      integrated into, with the number of integrated matches beside it, and the ring
      splits those matches by member database. It answers how many distinct
      functions the proteins carry.

      How to read: only integrated matches count here, so a signature that InterPro
      has not integrated is left out. A ring led by one database shows where the
      curated entries come from.

      Source: https://interproscan-docs.readthedocs.io/en/v5/OutputFormats.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: source
      color: source
      labels: {source: Member database}
    title: Matches per member database
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the signature matches reported by one member database, such as
      Pfam, PANTHER or CDD. It answers which databases contribute annotation for these
      proteins.

      How to read: a tall bar is a database with many hits, and a missing one found
      nothing or was not run. Open the table to see the signatures and spans behind a

  - component: table
    title: Signature matches table

id: isoseq_insert_length
name: FLNC insert length distribution
mode: pacbio/read-length
description: >-
  Share of each sample's full-length non-chimeric reads per 100 bp of insert
  length, from the per-read isoseq refine report: the library's size
  selection, and the first sign of degraded RNA.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.report.csv"
recipe: isoseq/insert_length.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 20 real length bins (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: insert_length.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: insert_length_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Insert length distribution
    roles: {series: sample, x: length_bp, y: pct}
    config:
      x_title: Insert length (bp)
      y_title: Share of FLNC reads per 100 bp (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sample: the share of its full-length non-chimeric reads in each
      100 bp bin of insert length. It answers what transcript sizes the library
      captured.

      How to read: a broad curve with a main peak at the expected transcript size is
      a healthy library. A curve piled at short lengths points to degraded RNA or
      fragmentation, and a hard cut on the right to a size selection. Compare the
      samples: curves that differ in shape were not prepared the same way.

      Note: isoseq refine publishes no cut-off for the insert length.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    title: Insert length by sample
    dict_kwargs:
      x: length_bp
      y: pct
      color: sample
      labels: {length_bp: Insert length (bp), pct: Share of FLNC reads (%), sample: Sample}
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: the share of its full-length non-chimeric reads per
      length bin. It answers whether the samples share the same size profile.

      How to read: overlapping lines mean consistent library preparation. A line
      shifted to the left holds shorter inserts, which is the first thing to check
      when a sample has few long isoforms.
  - component: table
    title: Insert length bins
    description: >-
      Each row is a length bin of one sample: the read count, its share of the sample
      and the cumulative share up to that length. It answers where a given fraction of
      the reads falls.

      How to read: the cumulative column gives the length below which a given share of

renders_as.caption: median, with the spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median share of full-length reads that survive chimera removal, with the spread across libraries in the box. It answers how clean the libraries are.
How to read: a high share with a tight box means little concatemer contamination. A library far below the others had many artificial concatemers, so check its preparation. isoseq refine publishes no cut-off for this share.
renders_as.title: Non-chimeric share

renders_as.caption: median, with the spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median share of FLNC reads that still carry a poly(A) tail, with the spread across libraries in the box. It answers how many reads kept the tail the refine step looks for.
How to read: the share depends on the library preparation, so compare libraries made the same way. A library far from its peers had a different poly(A) capture. isoseq refine publishes no cut-off for this share.
renders_as.title: Poly(A) share

renders_as.description:
Each bar is a library: its count of full-length non-chimeric reads, coloured by the sample it belongs to. It answers which libraries contribute most to a sample.
How to read: a sample made of several libraries of very different size depends on its largest one. A very short bar is a library worth checking for a failed run.
Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median FLNC read count of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of Iso-Seq.
renders_as.title: Full-length non-chimeric reads per library

renders_as.description:
Each row is a library: its full-length, non-chimeric and poly(A) read counts and the two shares. It answers which libraries lost the most reads to chimera removal.
How to read: sort by the non-chimeric share to find libraries with many concatemers.
renders_as.title: Refine summary per library

outputs.rawYaml:
id: ivar_oncoplot_matrix
name: Mutation matrix
mode: variants/matrix
description: >-
  Sample by gene mutation matrix derived from the long variant table, one row
  per observed sample/gene/effect combination.
find: { filename: "variants_long_table.csv" } # same raw file as the long table
recipe: nf-core/viralrecon/oncoplot_canonical.py
fixture: oncoplot_matrix.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: mutation_matrix
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: oncoplot
    title: Mutation matrix
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, gene: gene, mutation_type: mutation_type}
    config:
      legend_position: bottom
    description: >-
      Each cell is a sample and a gene, coloured by the type of mutation observed
      there. It answers which genes are mutated in which samples and how the
      mutation types are distributed.

      How to read: a row full of cells is a gene mutated across many samples, which
      can mark a lineage-defining change or a hotspot. A column full of cells is a
      divergent sample. Rows are ordered by how often the gene is mutated.
  # Both breakdown columns are required by the recipe schema, so the strips
  # cannot fall back to an empty bar on a run that omits an optional column.
  - component: card
    column: sample_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: gene
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: mutations, by gene
    title: Samples with mutations
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct samples with at least one observed
      mutation, with the number of sample and gene combinations beside it, and the
      bars rank the genes with the most mutations. It answers how widespread the
      mutations are and where they concentrate.

      How to read: a gene that leads the ranking is a hotspot or a lineage marker.
      Open the mutation matrix to see which samples carry it.
  - component: card
    column: gene
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: mutation_type
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: genes, by mutation type
    title: Genes with mutations
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct genes carrying a mutation, and the
      bars rank the mutation types by the number of genes they touch. It answers
      which kinds of change are the most widespread across the genome.

      How to read: a ranking led by synonymous changes means mostly silent variation.
      Many stop-gained or frameshift changes in a gene deserve a look
      at the variant table.
  - component: table
    title: Mutation table
    description: >-
      One row is one sample, gene and mutation type combination, with its
      mutation label. It answers which changes sit behind each cell of the
      matrix.

      How to read: Sort by gene to see which samples carry a change in it, or by
      sample to list all of its changes. Look for genes that recur across
      samples and for rare mutation types. It complements the matrix tile of the
      same output, which shows the same cells as a grid.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: gene
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: mutation_type
    caption: mutations, by type
    title: Mutations by type
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of observed mutations, with the number of distinct
      genes beside it, and the bar splits the mutations by type. It answers what the
      mix of changes looks like.

      How to read: a bar dominated by synonymous changes means mostly silent
      variation. A visible share of stop-gained or frameshift changes points at
      changes that can disable a protein.

outputs.name: Variant calls
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ivar_variants_long
name: Variant calls
mode: variants
description: Per-sample annotated variant calls (long table).
find: { filename: "variants_long_table.csv" } # raw nf-core file
recipe: ivar/variants_long.py # owns the output columns
fixture: variants_long.tsv # co-located bindable sample
renders_as:
  - id: lollipop
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: lollipop
    title: Variants along each gene
    roles: {feature_id: GENE, position: POS, category: EFFECT, effect: AF, label: mutation_label}
    config:
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each lollipop is a variant placed at its genome position within a gene, coloured
      by its predicted effect and sized by its allele frequency. It answers where
      the variants fall in each gene and which of them change the protein.

      How to read: clusters of non-synonymous or stop-gained changes in one gene
      suggest a region under selection or a problem region. Large heads are variants
      present in most reads, small heads are minor variants. Hover a head or open the
      table tile to read the change.
  - id: oncoplot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: oncoplot
    title: Mutation matrix
    roles: {sample_id: sample, gene: GENE, mutation_type: EFFECT}
    config:
      legend_position: bottom
    description: >-
      Each cell is a sample and a gene, coloured by the predicted effect of the
      variant there. It answers which genes are mutated in which samples.

      How to read: a row full of cells is a gene mutated across many samples, such as
      a lineage marker. A column full of cells is a divergent sample. Rows are
      ordered by how often the gene is mutated.
  - id: manhattan
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: manhattan
    title: Allele frequency along the genome
    roles: {chr: CHROM, pos: POS, score: AF, feature: GENE}
    config:
      score_threshold: 0.75
      score_kind: Allele frequency
      color_by_columns: [EFFECT, sample]
      default_color_by: EFFECT
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a variant at its genome position, with its allele frequency on the
      vertical axis, coloured by its predicted effect. It answers where along the
      genome variants sit and how many are fixed rather than minor.

      How to read: points at the top are present in most reads and form the consensus
      changes, while points near the bottom are minor variants. A band of points at
      intermediate frequency can mean a mixed infection or a contaminated sample.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an allele frequency of 0.75, the
      cut-off nf-core/viralrecon documents for variants integrated into the consensus
      genome of its long variant table.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Allele frequency distribution
    dict_kwargs:
      x: AF
      color: EFFECT
      labels: {AF: Allele frequency, EFFECT: Predicted effect}
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the variants in a range of allele frequency, coloured by
      predicted effect. It answers how the variants split between minor and
      near-fixed.

      How to read: a peak at 1 holds the changes present in all reads, and a spread
      at lower frequencies holds minor variants. A peak near 0.5 can mean a mixed
      sample.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: POS
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: GENE
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    caption: variant calls, by gene
    title: Variant calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of variant calls across all samples, with the
      number of distinct genome positions beside it, and the bars rank the genes
      carrying most of them. It answers how much variation there is and where.

      How to read: a large gap between calls and positions means the same positions
      are shared by many samples, as expected for a lineage. A gene leading the
      ranking is a hotspot or a long gene.
  - component: card
    column: POS
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: concentration
    breakdown_col: GENE
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: share of positions in the top genes
    title: Distinct variant positions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct genome positions with a variant, and the
      bar shows how much of it the top genes hold. It answers whether variation is
      spread out or concentrated in a few genes.

      How to read: a large share in one or two genes marks a hotspot, or simply the
      longest genes. Compare with the lollipop tile.
  - component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    caption: samples and their variant calls
    title: Samples with variants
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of samples with at least one variant call, with the
      total number of calls beside it. It answers how many samples are in view and
      how many calls they carry.

      How to read: filter the dashboard to a group to compare how many samples and
      calls it holds.
  - component: card
    column: AA
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: EFFECT
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "col('AA') != '.'"
    caption: protein changes, by effect
    title: Protein changes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct amino acid changes, leaving out
      variants with no protein change, with the number of calls beside it, and the bar
      splits the calls by predicted effect. It answers how much of the variation
      alters proteins.

      How to read: a bar dominated by synonymous changes means mostly silent
      variation. Missense and stop-gained shares mark the changes that could alter
      protein function.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Variant table
    description: >-
      One row is one variant call, with its position, alleles, depth, allele
      frequency, gene, protein change and predicted effect. It answers which
      exact variants a sample carries.

      How to read: Sort by allele frequency to separate fixed variants from
      minor ones, and by depth to spot calls with weak support. Look for high-
      impact effects at a high frequency. Select a row to filter the rest of the
      dashboard to its sample. It complements the frequency and effect tiles of
      the same output, which summarise these rows.
