outputs.name: Raw iVar variant calls
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ivar_variants_tsv
name: Raw iVar variant calls
mode: variants
description: >-
  One row per variant from the raw iVar variants table, one table per sample
  and reference: position, alleles, allele depths and frequency, Fisher's
  p-value, iVar's PASS verdict and, with a GFF, the amino acid change. Minor
  variants under the consensus threshold are kept, so the table reads
  intra-host diversity as well as the consensus changes.
find:
  path_glob: "**/variants/ivar/**/*.tsv"
recipe: ivar/variants_tsv.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several variant types and frequency classes.
fixture: variants_tsv.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: variant_genome_view
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Variants along the genome
    roles: {chr: chrom, pos: pos, score: af, feature: variant_key, sample: genome_id, category: variant_type}
    config:
      score_title: Allele frequency
      score_threshold: 0.75
    description: >-
      Each point is a variant call at its genome position, with its allele frequency
      on the vertical axis, coloured by variant type (SNV, insertion or deletion). It
      answers where in the genome calls cluster and how many are near-fixed.

      How to read: points above the line are the high-frequency calls that would be
      integrated into a consensus, and points below it are minor variants. A stretch
      with many low-frequency calls can mean a mixed sample or a poorly covered
      region, so check the depth track.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an allele frequency of 0.75, the
      cut-off nf-core/viralrecon documents for variants integrated into the consensus
      genome. iVar's own default minimum frequency to report a variant is 0.03, and
      viralrecon runs it at 0.25.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md
  # Allele frequency against depth: fixed calls stack at 1, minor ones spread
  # low, and the low-depth corner is where a frequency means little.
  - id: af_vs_depth
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Allele frequency against depth
    roles: { x: total_dp, y: af, label: variant_key, color: frequency_class }
    config:
      log_x: true
      x_title: Total read depth at the position
      y_title: Allele frequency
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_value: 0.75
      reference_label: Consensus cut-off (0.75)
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a variant call: the read depth at its position on the horizontal
      axis and its allele frequency on the vertical axis, coloured by frequency
      class. It answers which calls rest on enough reads to be trusted.

      How to read: fixed calls sit at the top at any depth. Calls at low frequency
      and low depth, in the bottom left, are the least reliable because a handful of
      reads decides the frequency. Minor calls at high depth are credible
      intra-host variants.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an allele frequency of 0.75, the
      cut-off nf-core/viralrecon documents for variants integrated into the consensus
      genome. The Fixed, Major and Minor classes (at least 0.9, 0.5 to 0.9 and under
      0.5) are this table's own grouping, not published cut-offs. viralrecon calls
      variants from a depth of 10 reads by default, while iVar's own default minimum
      depth is 0.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md
  - id: pass_variants
    component: card
    column: variant_key
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: variant_type
    headline: true
    caption: calls, by variant type
    title: Variant calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of variant calls, with the number of distinct
      variants beside it, and the bar splits the calls by type. It answers how much
      variation was called and whether it is mostly substitutions or indels.

      How to read: a large gap between calls and distinct variants means the same
      variants recur across samples. A growing share of insertions or deletions is
      worth a look in the table, since they are more error-prone to call.
  - id: frequency_classes
    component: card
    column: variant_key
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: frequency_class
    caption: calls, by frequency class
    title: Calls by frequency class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of variant calls and the ring splits them into
      Fixed, Major and Minor by allele frequency. It answers how much of the
      variation is consensus-level and how much is intra-host diversity.

      How to read: a large Minor share means a mixed or diverse sample, or noise
      at low depth. The classes are this table's own grouping (at least 0.9, 0.5 to
      0.9 and under 0.5), not a published cut-off.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Allele frequency distribution
    dict_kwargs:
      x: af
      color: frequency_class
      labels: {af: Allele frequency, frequency_class: Frequency class}
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the variant calls in a range of allele frequency, coloured by
      frequency class. It answers how the calls divide between fixed changes and
      minor variants.

      How to read: a peak at 1 holds the consensus changes and a spread at low
      frequencies holds minor variants. A peak near 0.5 can mean a mixed sample.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: filter
    title: iVar filter verdict
    description: >-
      Filters the calls by iVar's verdict. iVar marks a call as PASS when the p-value
      of its Fisher's exact test is 0.05 or below, so the other calls are
      statistically weaker.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: genome_id
    title: iVar variant table
    description: >-
      One row is one variant call, with its position, alleles, allele depths and
      frequency, p-value, iVar's verdict and the amino acid change when a GFF
      was given. It answers which exact variants each sample carries and whether
      iVar passed them.

      How to read: Sort by the allele frequency to separate fixed from minor
      variants, and by the p-value or the filter verdict to find doubtful calls.
      Look for calls that fail the filter or rest on a low depth. Select a row
      to filter the rest of the dashboard to its sample. It complements the
      frequency and variant-type tiles of the same output, which summarise these
      rows.

tools.description: K-mer counting and the read k-mer spectrum.
tools.name: Jellyfish

outputs.description: The k-mer multiplicity histogram of each read set, cut past the main peak. The main peak sits at the k-mer depth of the sequencing; a second peak at half that depth is the heterozygous share of the genome, and a long right tail the repeats. It is the curve GenomeScope fits, so a genome size estimate can be checked against it by eye.
outputs.name: Read k-mer spectrum
outputs.rawYaml:
id: jellyfish_histogram
name: Read k-mer spectrum
mode: histo
description: >-
  The k-mer multiplicity histogram of each read set, cut past the main peak.
  The main peak sits at the k-mer depth of the sequencing; a second peak at half
  that depth is the heterozygous share of the genome, and a long right tail the
  repeats. It is the curve GenomeScope fits, so a genome size estimate can be
  checked against it by eye.
find:
  path_glob: "**/jellyfish/histo/*.tsv"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*.histo"
recipe: jellyfish/histogram.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several read sets.
fixture: histogram.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: kmer_spectrum
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Read k-mer spectrum
    roles: {series: read_set, x: multiplicity, y: kmers}
    config:
      x_title: K-mer multiplicity (times seen in the reads)
      y_title: Distinct k-mers
      log_y: true
    description: >-
      Each point is a multiplicity: how many distinct k-mers occur that many times in the reads, with one curve
      per read set on a log vertical axis. It answers what sequencing depth the reads reach and whether the
      genome is heterozygous or repetitive.

      How to read: the k-mers piled up near a multiplicity of 1 are mostly sequencing
      errors. The main peak is the depth of the genome, a smaller peak at half of it is
      the heterozygous share, and peaks at three and four times that half are repeats.

      Note: GenomeScope needs at least 15x coverage of the haploid genome to fit well.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tbenavi1/genomescope2.0/master/README.md
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32188846/
  - id: kmer_mass_spectrum
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: K-mer mass spectrum
    roles: {series: read_set, x: multiplicity, y: kmer_mass}
    config:
      x_title: K-mer multiplicity (times seen in the reads)
      y_title: Total k-mers (distinct k-mers times multiplicity)
    description: >-
      Each point is a multiplicity: the total number of k-mers in the reads that occur that many times, with
      one curve per read set. It answers where most of the sequenced bases sit.

      How to read: the mass is concentrated at the main peak for a clean genome. Mass far to the right
      comes from repeats, and mass at multiplicity one is sequencing error, which inflates a poor library.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    title: Read k-mer spectrum
    dict_kwargs: { x: multiplicity, y: kmers, color: read_set, labels: { multiplicity: K-mer multiplicity, kmers: Distinct k-mers, read_set: Read set } }
    description: >-
      Each line is a read set: the number of distinct k-mers at each multiplicity. It answers how the read sets
      compare on the same axes.

      How to read: curves with peaks at the same multiplicity were sequenced to similar depth. A shifted peak
      means a different depth or a different genome.
  - component: card
    column: peak_multiplicity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Main peak depth
    caption: peak multiplicity per read set, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median multiplicity of the main peak over read sets, and the box shows its
      quartiles. It answers the typical k-mer depth of the sequencing.

      How to read: this is the depth of the genome in k-mers, so a very shallow peak predicts a poor GenomeScope
      fit. GenomeScope recommends at least 15x coverage of the haploid genome.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tbenavi1/genomescope2.0/master/README.md
  - component: table
    title: K-mer histogram
    description: >-
      Each row is a multiplicity of a read set with its number of distinct k-mers, the k-mer mass and the peak
      multiplicity. It answers the raw numbers behind the spectrum.

      How to read: the histogram is cut past the main peak and thinned, so it is for reading the shape, not
      for exact counts.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: kallisto_run_metrics
name: Run headline numbers (kallisto | bustools)
mode: kallisto/run_metrics
description: >-
  Reads processed and pseudoaligned by kallisto bus, barcodes on the 10x
  whitelist after correction, and the cells kb count --filter called, one
  row per sample.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.count/run_info.json"
recipe: kallisto/run_metrics.py
fixture: run_metrics.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: card
    column: p_pseudoaligned
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    title: Pseudoaligned reads
    caption: average share, with quartiles
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average share of reads that kallisto pseudoaligns to the
      transcriptome, and the box shows the quartiles over samples. It answers how much
      of the sequencing the reference explains.

      How to read: a high share means the reads match the reference. A low share points
      to a wrong or incomplete reference, a wrong chemistry or poor-quality reads, so
      check the index and the technology setting first.

      Note: kallisto and bustools publish no pass mark for this share, so none is
      drawn.
  - component: card
    column: cells_called
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Cells called
    caption: median, with quartiles
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of cells called per sample after the bustools
      filter, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how many cells each sample
      yields.

      How to read: compare it with the cell count you loaded. Far fewer cells point to a
      stringent filter or a failed capture, and far more to ambient RNA called as cells.
  - component: card
    column: n_barcodes
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Barcodes on the whitelist
    caption: median, with quartiles
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of barcodes found on the technology whitelist
      after correction, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how many distinct
      barcodes the reads carry, including empty droplets.

      How to read: this is far larger than the called cells, because most barcodes are
      empty droplets or ambient RNA. A sample whose count is out of line with its peers
      deserves a look at its input reads.
  - component: table
    title: Run metrics
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with the reads processed and pseudoaligned, the pseudoaligned
      share, the barcodes on the whitelist and the cells called by the filter. It
      answers the exact numbers behind the cards.

      How to read: compare the pseudoaligned share across samples to find one that
      differs, then read its barcode and cell counts.

renders_as.caption: average share, with quartiles
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the average share of reads that kallisto pseudoaligns to the transcriptome, and the box shows the quartiles over samples. It answers how much of the sequencing the reference explains.
How to read: a high share means the reads match the reference. A low share points to a wrong or incomplete reference, a wrong chemistry or poor-quality reads, so check the index and the technology setting first.
Note: kallisto and bustools publish no pass mark for this share, so none is drawn.
renders_as.title: Pseudoaligned reads

renders_as.caption: median, with quartiles
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median count of cells called per sample after the bustools filter, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how many cells each sample yields.
How to read: compare it with the cell count you loaded. Far fewer cells point to a stringent filter or a failed capture, and far more to ambient RNA called as cells.
renders_as.title: Cells called

renders_as.caption: median, with quartiles
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median count of barcodes found on the technology whitelist after correction, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how many distinct barcodes the reads carry, including empty droplets.
How to read: this is far larger than the called cells, because most barcodes are empty droplets or ambient RNA. A sample whose count is out of line with its peers deserves a look at its input reads.
renders_as.title: Barcodes on the whitelist

renders_as.description:
Each row is a sample with the reads processed and pseudoaligned, the pseudoaligned share, the barcodes on the whitelist and the cells called by the filter. It answers the exact numbers behind the cards.
How to read: compare the pseudoaligned share across samples to find one that differs, then read its barcode and cell counts.
renders_as.title: Run metrics

tools.description: Pairwise genome alignment: how much of a target genome each query aligns to one-to-one, at what identity and divergence, with which substitution spectrum and fitted scoring parameters, and where on the target the long alignments land.
tools.name: LAST

outputs.description: One row per pairwise genome alignment from the one-line summary last-split writes for MultiQC: aligned length, percent identity with and without gap columns, and the sequence count and length of both genomes. The share of each genome the one-to-one alignment covers is derived alongside, so a distant genome (lower identity) can be told apart from a fragmented one (lower coverage at the same identity).
outputs.name: One-to-one alignment identity
outputs.rawYaml:
id: last_split_identity
name: One-to-one alignment identity
mode: genome-alignment/summary
description: >-
  One row per pairwise genome alignment from the one-line summary last-split
  writes for MultiQC: aligned length, percent identity with and without gap
  columns, and the sequence count and length of both genomes. The share of each
  genome the one-to-one alignment covers is derived alongside, so a distant
  genome (lower identity) can be told apart from a fragmented one (lower
  coverage at the same identity).
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.o2o.tsv"
recipe: last/split_identity.py
fixture: split_identity.tsv
renders_as:
  # Identity falls with divergence, coverage with divergence and assembly gaps:
  # a point left of genomes of similar identity lost coverage to its assembly.
  # Colour is the query's sequence count, which is how fragmented its assembly is.
  - id: identity_vs_coverage
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Identity against coverage of the target
    roles: {x: target_aligned_pct, y: percent_identity, label: query, size: aligned_bp}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
      color_col: query_sequences
      x_title: Target covered by the one-to-one alignment (%)
      y_title: Alignment identity (%)
    description: >-
      Each point is a query genome aligned to the target: the share of the target its
      one-to-one alignment covers on the horizontal axis and the percent identity on
      the vertical axis. Size is the aligned length and colour the number of sequences
      in the query. It answers whether a genome is distant or only fragmented.

      How to read: identity falls with divergence, so a distant genome sits low.
      Coverage also falls with divergence and with assembly gaps, so a point to the
      left of genomes of similar identity lost coverage to a fragmented assembly,
      which the colour confirms. Open the distance and parameter tiles for the same
      pairs.

      Note: there is no standard way to compute nucleotide identity, so the value here
      is the one nf-core/pairgenomealign reports (gaps counted as mismatches).

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median alignment identity of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a
      cut-off of LAST.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/pairgenomealign/master/docs/output.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: query
      y: target_aligned_pct
      color: percent_identity
      labels: {query: Query genome, target_aligned_pct: Target covered (%), percent_identity: Identity (%)}
    title: Share of the target covered
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: target_aligned_pct}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a query genome with the share of the target genome its one-to-one
      alignment covers, coloured by percent identity. It answers which genomes align
      to most of the target.

      How to read: a short bar with a high identity colour is a close genome with a
      fragmented assembly or a real loss of sequence. A short bar with a low identity
      colour is simply a distant genome.

      Note: the one-to-one alignment keeps one copy of locally duplicated regions, so
      they count as missing in the other genome.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of the target covered of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not
      a cut-off of LAST.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/pairgenomealign/master/docs/output.md
  - id: identity_median
    component: card
    column: percent_identity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: identity, with its spread
    title: Alignment identity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median nucleotide percent identity of the one-to-one
      alignments and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how close the aligned
      genomes are to the target.

      How to read: closely related genomes sit near 100 percent, and the identity
      falls as genomes diverge. A wide box means the run mixes close and distant
      genomes.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/pairgenomealign/master/docs/output.md
  - id: target_coverage
    component: card
    column: target_aligned_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    headline: true
    caption: coverage across genomes
    title: Target covered
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of the target genome covered by the
      one-to-one alignment, and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how
      much of the target the queries reach.

      How to read: coverage below 100 percent is expected, since a one-to-one alignment
      leaves out duplicated and unalignable regions. A low tail marks genomes that are
      divergent or fragmented.
  - id: genome_size
    component: card
    column: query_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: genome length, with its spread
    title: Query genome length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median total length of the query genomes, and the box
      shows its quartiles. It answers whether the queries are of a similar size to the
      target.

      How to read: a query much longer or shorter than the rest has a different
      assembly completeness or a real size difference, which also lowers coverage.
  - id: aligned_length
    component: card
    column: aligned_bp
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: aligned length, with its spread
    title: Aligned length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median number of aligned base pairs in the one-to-one
      alignments, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how much sequence each
      alignment holds.

      How to read: compare it with the genome length card. A short aligned length for
      a genome of normal size means a divergent or fragmented query.
  - id: aligned_total
    component: card
    column: aligned_bp
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: concentration
    breakdown_col: query
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: share held by the top genomes
    title: Aligned bases in total
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total aligned base pairs over all pairs, and the strip
      shows the share held by the three genomes with the longest alignments. It
      answers whether the alignment is spread evenly over the queries.

      How to read: a share close to the number of genomes shown over the total means
      the queries align alike. A higher share points to a few genomes dominating.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: percent_identity
    title: Identity range
    description: >-
      Select a range of percent identity to keep only the genome pairs inside it. It
      answers which pairs fall in a given divergence band.

      How to read: narrow the range to a band of closely related genomes, and every
      other tile follows.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: query
    title: Alignment summary table
    description: >-
      Each row is a genome pair with the aligned length, identity with and without
      gaps, sequence counts and lengths of both genomes, and the share of each genome
      covered. It answers the exact numbers behind every tile and lets a row selection
      filter the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by identity to rank the pairs by divergence.

outputs.description: The substitution table last-split counts over the one-to-one alignment, summarised per genome pair: alignment blocks, identical and substituted columns, transitions against transversions, gap columns on either side, the p-distance with its JC69, F81, K80 and T92 corrections, and the substitution spectrum (the share of each of the 12 directed substitutions). Distances rank the queries by divergence from the target; the spectrum shows whether the substitution process looks alike across them.
outputs.name: Substitution matrix and distances
outputs.rawYaml:
id: last_split_matrix
name: Substitution matrix and distances
mode: genome-alignment/divergence
description: >-
  The substitution table last-split counts over the one-to-one alignment,
  summarised per genome pair: alignment blocks, identical and substituted
  columns, transitions against transversions, gap columns on either side, the
  p-distance with its JC69, F81, K80 and T92 corrections, and the substitution
  spectrum (the share of each of the 12 directed substitutions). Distances rank
  the queries by divergence from the target; the spectrum shows whether the
  substitution process looks alike across them.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.o2o.matrix.txt"
recipe: last/split_matrix.py
fixture: split_matrix.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: substitution_spectrum
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Substitution spectrum by query
    roles: {index: query,
            value_columns: [A_to_C_pct, A_to_G_pct, A_to_T_pct, C_to_A_pct, C_to_G_pct, C_to_T_pct,
                            G_to_A_pct, G_to_C_pct, G_to_T_pct, T_to_A_pct, T_to_C_pct, T_to_G_pct]}
    description: >-
      Each cell is the share of one directed substitution (a target base aligned to a
      different query base) among all substitutions in the one-to-one alignment of a
      query genome. It answers whether the substitution process looks alike across the
      queries.

      How to read: transitions (A to G, G to A, C to T, T to C) usually hold the
      largest shares, and genomes of similar divergence cluster together. A query whose
      row differs from the rest points to a different mutation process or a lower
      quality assembly.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/pairgenomealign/master/docs/output.md
  # The ratio falls as multiple hits saturate the transitions, so distant
  # genomes sit low and right. Colour is the query's gap columns.
  - id: saturation_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Transition to transversion ratio against distance
    roles: {x: p_distance, y: ts_tv_ratio, label: query, size: blocks}
    config:
      color_col: query_gap_columns
      x_title: Substitutions per aligned column (p-distance)
      y_title: Transitions to transversions ratio
    description: >-
      Each point is a query genome: its p-distance to the target on the horizontal
      axis and its ratio of transitions to transversions on the vertical axis. Size is
      the number of alignment blocks and colour the number of gap columns on the query
      side. It answers whether the distant genomes are saturated.

      How to read: the ratio falls as multiple substitutions at one site hide the
      transitions, so distant genomes sit low and to the right. A point off that trend
      is a pair whose alignment or assembly deserves a look.

      Lines and annotations: no reference line is drawn, because the expected ratio
      depends on the species pair and the tool publishes no cut-off.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: query
      y: k80_distance
      color: k80_distance
      labels: {query: Query genome, k80_distance: K80 distance}
    title: K80 distance to the target
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: k80_distance}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a query genome with its K80 distance to the target, the p-distance
      corrected for multiple substitutions with separate rates for transitions and
      transversions. It answers how diverged each query is.

      How to read: closely related genomes have short bars and distant genomes long
      ones. The correction matters for distant genomes only, so compare it with the
      raw p-distance in the table.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median K80 distance of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      LAST.
  - id: k80_median
    component: card
    column: k80_distance
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: distance, with its spread
    title: K80 distance
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median K80 distance of the queries to the target and the
      box shows its quartiles. It answers how diverged the queries are on the whole.

      How to read: a wide box means the run mixes close and distant genomes, and a
      single distant genome pulls the upper whisker out.
  - id: ts_tv_median
    component: card
    column: ts_tv_ratio
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: ratio, with its spread
    title: Transition to transversion ratio
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median ratio of transitions to transversions over the
      alignments, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers whether the substitution
      process is similar across queries.

      How to read: a tight box means the queries mutate alike. A ratio that falls
      with distance is the sign of saturation.
  # Blocks run from thousands to hundreds of thousands, so the spread reads
  # better as a histogram than as one box.
  - id: blocks_median
    component: card
    column: blocks
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: blocks across genomes
    title: Alignment blocks
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median number of alignment blocks per genome pair, and
      the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how fragmented the alignments
      are.

      How to read: more blocks come with more divergence and more rearrangements, so a
      pair far above the rest is either distant or fragmented.
  - id: query_gap_median
    component: card
    column: query_gap_columns
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: gap columns, with their spread
    title: Gap columns on the query
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of alignment columns where the target has a
      base and the query a gap, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how much
      sequence the target holds that the query lacks.

      How to read: more gap columns come with divergence and with a more fragmented
      query assembly. Compare it with the target-side gaps in the table.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: p_distance
    title: Distance range
    description: >-
      Select a range of p-distance to keep only the genome pairs inside it. It answers
      which pairs fall in a given divergence band.

      How to read: narrow the range to a band of related genomes, and every other tile
      follows.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: query
    title: Distances and substitutions table
    description: >-
      Each row is a genome pair with its alignment blocks, counts of identical and
      substituted columns, transitions and transversions, gap columns, distances under
      four models and the substitution spectrum. It answers the exact numbers behind
      every tile and lets a row selection filter the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by distance to rank the queries by divergence.

outputs.description: The one-to-one alignment read as links between a target locus and a query locus, from the PSL export (--export_aln_to psl), which carries coordinates but no sequence. Each alignment is placed at its midpoint on both genomes, weighted by its matching bases and classed by orientation; query sequence names are prefixed so shared names such as chr1 stay two arcs. The longest alignments of each pair are kept, the collinear blocks a synteny ring shows.
outputs.name: Synteny links
outputs.rawYaml:
id: last_synteny_links
name: Synteny links
mode: genome-alignment/synteny
description: >-
  The one-to-one alignment read as links between a target locus and a query
  locus, from the PSL export (--export_aln_to psl), which carries coordinates
  but no sequence. Each alignment is placed at its midpoint on both genomes,
  weighted by its matching bases and classed by orientation; query sequence
  names are prefixed so shared names such as chr1 stay two arcs. The longest
  alignments of each pair are kept, the collinear blocks a synteny ring shows.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.psl.gz"
recipe: last/synteny_links.py
fixture: synteny_links.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: synteny_ring
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_chord
    title: Synteny between target and query
    roles: {chrom_a: chrom_a, pos_a: pos_a, chrom_b: chrom_b, pos_b: pos_b,
            label: label, weight: weight, category: category, sample: query}
    config:
      colour_by: category
    description: >-
      Each chord is one of the longest one-to-one alignments, linking its locus on a
      target chromosome to its locus on a query chromosome, coloured by orientation
      and weighted by its matching bases. It answers which chromosomes of the two
      genomes share long collinear blocks.

      How to read: bundles of chords between the same two chromosomes are conserved
      synteny. Chords that fan out from one chromosome point to rearrangements, and
      inverted chords mark blocks that are reversed in the query.

      Note: only the longest alignments of each pair are kept, so short blocks do not
      appear.
  - id: links_total
    component: card
    column: label
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: category
    headline: true
    caption: links, by orientation
    title: Synteny links
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of retained alignment links and the bar splits them
      by orientation, same strand or inverted. It answers how many long blocks are
      conserved and how many are reversed.

      How to read: most long blocks of closely related genomes keep their orientation.
      A large inverted share points to rearranged or distant genomes.
  - id: links_weight
    component: card
    column: weight
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: concentration
    breakdown_col: chrom_a
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    caption: share held by the top chromosomes
    title: Matching bases in the links
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total matching bases of the retained links and the strip
      shows the share held by the three target chromosomes with the most. It answers
      whether the conserved blocks are spread over the genome.

      How to read: a high share means a few chromosomes hold most of the long blocks,
      which is expected for the largest chromosomes.
  - id: links_identity
    component: card
    column: identity_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]

      knowledgebase. Known pairs that are in frame are the highest-confidence

outputs.rawYaml:
id: linx_svs
name: Clustered structural variants
mode: linx
description: >-
  LINX's somatic structural variants, one row per SV, joined with the event
  its cluster resolves to (simple deletion or duplication, reciprocal
  translocation, LINE insertion, complex event), the breakends split into
  chromosome, position and orientation columns, the junction copy number and
  the genes at each breakend. A single breakend has no partner locus, so a
  chord diagram skips it while counts and tables keep it.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.linx.svs.tsv"
recipe: linx/svs.py
fixture: svs.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: sv_chords
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_chord
    title: Structural variants across the genome
    roles: {chrom_a: chrom_a, pos_a: pos_a, chrom_b: chrom_b, pos_b: pos_b, label: label, weight: junction_copy_number, category: resolved_type, sample: sample}
    description: >-
      Each chord joins the two breakends of a structural variant on a ring of
      chromosomes. The colour is the event type LINX resolved its cluster to and the
      width is the junction copy number. It answers where the genome is rearranged and
      how.

      How to read: many chords between the same two chromosomes suggest a translocation
      or a complex event. A dense knot on one chromosome is a cluster of local
      rearrangements.

      Note: a single breakend has no partner locus, so it is not drawn here but it stays
      in the counts and the table.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/linx/README.md
  - id: sv_count
    component: card
    column: chrom_a
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: type
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    caption: SVs, by type
    title: Structural variants
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of structural variants, and the bars rank the
      variant types. The secondary number is the count of chromosomes carrying a first
      breakend. It answers how rearranged the genome is and by what kind of event.

      How to read: a tumor dominated by one type, such as duplications or translocations,
      points to a particular mutational process. Open the chord view to see where.
  - id: sv_cluster_count
    component: card
    column: cluster_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: cluster_category
    caption: SVs, by cluster category
    title: Clusters
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of clusters LINX groups the variants into, and the
      ring splits the variants by the category of their cluster. It answers how many
      independent events there are and whether they are simple or complex.

      How to read: LINX clusters variants whose breakends are within 5 kb of each other by
      default, so one complex event can hold many variants. A large share of complex
      clusters means a heavily rearranged genome.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/linx/README.md
  - id: junction_cn_spread
    component: card
    column: junction_copy_number
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Junction copy number
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median copy number of the rearranged junctions, and the box
      shows the quartiles. It answers how many copies of a rearrangement the tumor
      carries.

      How to read: a higher value means more copies of the rearranged junction in the
      tumor. Compare variants of the same event type to find the most amplified ones.
  - id: resolved_type_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: resolved_type
      color: type
      labels: {resolved_type: Resolved event type, type: Variant type, count: Variants}
    title: Variants by resolved event type
    description: >-
      Each bar counts structural variants by the event type LINX resolved their cluster
      to, and each segment splits them by the raw variant type. It answers what kinds of
      events the variants form.

      How to read: simple deletions and duplications are single variants. Complex or
      chained events are the ones that bring several variants together.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/linx/README.md
  - id: sv_type_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: resolved_type
    title: Resolved event type
    description: >-
      Pick one or more event types to keep. It filters every tile of the tab to the
      variants in those events.

      How to read: pick one type to see where on the genome it occurs in the chord view.
  - id: sv_table
    component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: label
    title: Structural variants table
    description: >-
      Each row is a structural variant with its breakends, event type, cluster, junction
      copy number and the genes at each end. It answers which variants hit which genes
      and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by junction copy number and filter by event type.

# The narrow twin is `macs2_peaks` (*_peaks.narrowPeak, BED6+4 with a summit
# column). A run calls one or the other, so the two globs never both match.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_peaks.broadPeak"
recipe: macs2/broad_peaks.py
fixture: broad_peaks.tsv
renders_as:
  # Significance along the genome, then how wide the regions are. The dashed line is
  # MACS2's own default q-value cut-off (0.05, which is 1.301 on the -log10 axis).
  - id: broad_peak_significance
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: manhattan
    title: Broad region significance along the genome
    roles: {chr: chr, pos: midpoint, score: neg_log10_qvalue, feature: peak_id}
    config:
      score_kind: -log10 q-value
      score_threshold: 1.30103
      color_by_columns: [sample]
      default_color_by: sample
      hover_cols: [fold_enrichment]
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a broad region at its centre: the chromosome and position on the
      horizontal axis and its mean significance, as minus log10 of the q-value, on the
      vertical axis, coloured by sample. It answers where the broad domains lie and how
      confident each call is.

      How to read: tall points are the most confident regions, and a column of points
      across samples is a domain called in several libraries. For a broad call the
      q-value is the mean over the whole region and not a value at a summit. Open the
      table to inspect a labelled region.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a q-value of 0.05, the default
      q-value cut-off of MACS2 callpeak, shown as 1.301 on this axis. MACS2 also links
      nearby regions with a separate broad cut-off, and its documentation suggests 0.01
      as the q-value for broad marks, so a run may use a stricter line.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: width
      color: sample
      log_y: "True"
      labels: {sample: Sample, width: Region width (bp)}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: width}
    title: Region width per sample
    description: >-
      Each box is a sample: the spread of the widths of its broad regions, on a
      logarithmic axis, coloured by sample. It answers how wide the called domains are
      and whether samples differ.

      How to read: broad calls are meant for histone marks, whose domains are wider than
      transcription factor peaks. Compare replicates with each other, since a sample with
      much narrower regions than its replicates was probably called differently.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median region width of this table,
      a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a
      cut-off of MACS2.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  # How many regions and where they concentrate, then the spread of width,
  # enrichment and significance behind that count.
  - component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: chr
    top_n_count: 5
    caption: regions, by chromosome
    title: Broad regions called
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of broad regions in view, with the number of samples
      that called them, and the bars rank the chromosomes holding most. It answers how
      many domains are called and where they concentrate.

      How to read: large chromosomes hold more regions simply by length. A chromosome
      far above that expectation is worth a look.
  - component: card
    column: width
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [q1, q3]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: median width, with its quartiles
    title: Region width
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median region width in base pairs, with the lower and
      upper quartiles. It answers how broad the domains are.

      How to read: widths span orders of magnitude, so the quartiles tell more than a
      single number. Compare samples of the same mark with each other.
  - component: card
    column: fold_enrichment
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: fold enrichment, distribution
    title: Fold enrichment
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean fold enrichment of the regions, with its median and
      maximum, and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how strong the
      enrichment is overall.

      How to read: for a broad call the enrichment is a mean over the region, so it is
      lower than for a narrow peak. A mean close to the median means few extreme
      regions.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  - component: card
    column: neg_log10_qvalue
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 1.30103
    threshold_direction: min
    caption: weakest region against the q-value cut-off
    title: Weakest region significance
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest minus log10 q-value of any region in view, compared
      with the cut-off, with the median and the highest alongside. It answers whether
      every region clears the standard cut-off.

      How to read: a minimum above the line means all regions pass, which is expected
      when the caller used its default. A minimum below it means the run called regions
      at a looser cut-off.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-off is a q-value of 0.05, the default of MACS2
      callpeak, shown as 1.301 on the minus log10 scale.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: peak_id
    title: Broad region table
    description: >-
      Each row is a broad region with its sample, position, width, centre, fold
      enrichment and the minus log10 p-value and q-value MACS2 reported. It answers
      which regions to follow up and lets a row selection filter the rest of the
      dashboard.

      How to read: sort by significance or by width, and filter by sample or
      chromosome.

outputs.name: Consensus peak overlap
outputs.rawYaml:
id: macs2_consensus_boolean
name: Consensus peak overlap
mode: peaks/consensus
description: >-
  Merged consensus intervals against the samples that called a peak on them,
  as one 0/1 column per sample. The intersections say how reproducible the
  peak set is between replicates and between conditions.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.consensus_peaks.boolean.txt"
recipe: macs2/consensus_boolean.py
fixture: consensus_boolean.tsv
renders_as:
  # The renderer enumerates the binary sample columns itself, so the upset
  # render binds no role. C6 N/A: the set columns are the run's samples.
  - id: consensus_upset
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: upset_plot
    title: Consensus peaks shared between samples
    config:
      color_intersections_by: degree
    description: >-
      Each bar is a combination of samples and its height is the number of consensus
      intervals called in exactly those samples. It answers how reproducible the peak
      set is between replicates and conditions.

      How to read: tall bars over all replicates of one condition are reproducible
      peaks. Tall bars over a single sample are private peaks that no other sample supports.
      Bars over samples of different conditions are shared binding sites.

      Lines and annotations: bars are coloured by the number of samples in the
      combination, so private and widely shared intervals separate at a glance.
  - component: card
    column: consensus_set
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: consensus_set
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: intervals, by consensus set
    title: Consensus intervals
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of consensus sets in view with the intervals they
      hold, and the bars rank the sets by how many intervals they contain. It answers
      how large each consensus peak set is.

      How to read: a set with few intervals has little reproducible signal. Compare
      sets of the same assay.
  - component: card
    column: num_samples
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: samples per interval, with their spread
    title: Samples per interval
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean number of samples that call a peak on an interval,
      and the box shows its spread. It answers how reproducible the intervals are.

      How to read: a mean near one means most intervals are called in one sample only.
      A mean near the number of replicates means a reproducible peak set.
  - component: card
    column: num_peaks
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [average, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: peaks merged per interval, distribution
    title: Peaks merged into intervals
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of peak calls merged into the consensus intervals,
      with the mean and the largest per interval, and the histogram shows how many
      peaks each interval merges. It answers how much the merging collapses.

      How to read: an interval that merges many peaks is either a wide enriched region
      or several nearby peaks joined, so open the interval before treating it as one
      site.
  - component: card
    column: consensus_set
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: consensus_set
    caption: intervals, by consensus set
    title: Intervals by consensus set
    description: >-
      Each unit is one consensus interval, with the number of sets as the secondary
      number, and the ring splits the intervals by set. It answers how the intervals
      divide between the sets.

      How to read: a set that takes most of the ring contributes most of the peaks to
      the consensus.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: peak_id
    title: Consensus interval table
    description: >-
      Each row is a consensus interval with its set, position, the number of peaks
      merged into it, the number of samples that call it and a 0/1 flag per sample. It
      answers which intervals are shared and by whom, and lets a row selection filter
      the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by the number of samples to list the most reproducible
      intervals.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: macs2_consensus_fc
name: Consensus fold enrichment
mode: peaks/consensus_signal
description: >-
  Fold enrichment of the most strongly bound consensus intervals, one numeric
  column per sample, ready to cluster. Intervals a sample did not call are 0,
  so blocks of contrast-specific binding stand out.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.consensus_peaks.boolean.txt"
recipe: macs2/consensus_fc.py
fixture: consensus_fc.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the run's samples, known only at ingest.
  - id: consensus_signal_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Fold enrichment of consensus peaks
    roles: {index: region, row_annotation_cols: [consensus_set, support]}
    description: >-
      Each cell is a consensus interval in a sample: the MACS2 fold enrichment of the
      peak called there, or 0 where the sample called none. Rows and columns are
      clustered. It answers which intervals are bound in which samples and how strongly.

      How to read: columns that cluster together are samples with a similar binding
      profile, such as replicates or one condition. Blocks of colour in one group of
      samples only are condition-specific sites. A sample with pale rows against its
      replicates has weaker enrichment.

      Lines and annotations: the strips beside the rows name the consensus set and the
      number of samples that call the interval. Only the intervals with the largest
      summed enrichment per set are drawn.
  - component: card
    column: consensus_set
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: consensus_set
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: strongest intervals, by consensus set
    title: Strongest consensus intervals
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of consensus sets in view with the strongest
      intervals they contribute, and the bars rank the sets. It answers which sets
      supply the most strongly bound intervals.

      How to read: a set that dominates the ranking has the strongest enrichment. Only
      the top intervals per set are kept, so the counts are not the full peak sets.
  - component: card
    column: support
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: support
    caption: intervals, by number of supporting samples
    title: Support per interval
    description: >-
      Each unit is a strongly bound interval, with the number of distinct support
      levels as the secondary number, and the ring splits the intervals by how many
      samples call them. It answers how widely the strongest intervals are supported.

      How to read: a ring dominated by the highest support means the strongest peaks
      are reproducible across samples. A large share with support of one means strong
      peaks private to a sample.
  - component: table
    title: Consensus enrichment table
    description: >-
      Each row is a consensus interval with its set, region, the number of supporting
      samples and its fold enrichment in every sample. It answers the exact values
      behind the heatmap.

      How to read: sort by a sample column to list the intervals it binds most
      strongly.

renders_as.description:
Each cell is a consensus interval in a sample: the MACS2 fold enrichment of the peak called there, or 0 where the sample called none. Rows and columns are clustered. It answers which intervals are bound in which samples and how strongly.
How to read: columns that cluster together are samples with a similar binding profile, such as replicates or one condition. Blocks of colour in one group of samples only are condition-specific sites. A sample with pale rows against its replicates has weaker enrichment.
Lines and annotations: the strips beside the rows name the consensus set and the number of samples that call the interval. Only the intervals with the largest summed enrichment per set are drawn.
renders_as.title: Fold enrichment of consensus peaks

renders_as.caption: strongest intervals, by consensus set
renders_as.description:

renders_as.description:

renders_as.description:

outputs.description: One row per sample: how many peaks MACS2 called, the FRiP score, and the median, mean and maximum of peak width, fold enrichment and significance across those peaks.
outputs.name: Peak QC summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: macs2_peak_summary
name: Peak QC summary
mode: peaks/qc
description: >-
  One row per sample: how many peaks MACS2 called, the FRiP score, and the
  median, mean and maximum of peak width, fold enrichment and significance
  across those peaks.
# The long summary table the peak-QC step writes next to the calls; the FRiP
# score is joined on from the sibling MultiQC custom-content files.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*peak.summary.txt"
recipe: macs2/peak_summary.py
fixture: peak_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # Signal-to-noise per sample, then the yield behind it. ENCODE publishes no
  # accepted floor for FRiP, so the bar carries no line.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: frip_score
      color: sample
      labels: {sample: Sample, frip_score: Fraction of reads in peaks}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: frip_score}
    title: Fraction of reads in peaks per sample
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample: the fraction of its mapped reads that fall inside the called
      peaks. It answers how much of the signal in each library is enrichment and not
      background.

      How to read: a higher bar means a better signal to noise, and replicates should
      be close. A bar far below its replicates marks a weak library. ENCODE says that
      FRiP has no defined threshold and is useful for comparing similar experiments,
      so compare samples of the same assay and antibody.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median fraction of reads in peaks
      of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of MACS2.

      Source: https://www.encodeproject.org/data-standards/chip-seq/
  - component: card
    column: num_peaks
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: peaks per sample, with their spread
    title: Peaks called
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of peaks over the samples in view, and the box
      shows the quartiles of peaks per sample. It answers how many regions the
      libraries yield.

      How to read: replicates should give similar counts. A sample far below its
      replicates has weak or shallow signal. Peak counts depend on depth, so read them
      beside the FRiP bars.
  - component: card
    column: frip_score
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: FRiP, with its spread
    title: Mean FRiP
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean fraction of reads in peaks over the samples in view,
      and the box shows its spread. It answers how enriched the libraries are on
      average.

      How to read: a wide box means the libraries differ in enrichment. ENCODE defines
      no cut-off for it, so judge a sample against its replicates and its assay.

      Source: https://www.encodeproject.org/data-standards/terms/
  - component: card
    column: width_median
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median peak width, with its spread
    title: Median peak width
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over samples of each sample's median peak width, and
      the box shows its spread. It answers how broad the called peaks are.

      How to read: replicates should have similar widths, and the expected width
      depends on the mark. A sample that differs from its replicates may be called with
      different settings.
  - component: card
    column: fold_enrichment_median

    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median fold enrichment, with its spread
    title: Median fold enrichment

      enrichment, and the box shows its spread. It answers how strong the typical peak
      is against its control.

      with their replicates. A low value with a high peak count suggests many weak
      peaks.

    title: Peak QC table

      maximum of peak width, fold enrichment and significance. It answers the exact
      quality numbers behind the bars and cards.

      How to read: sort by FRiP or by peak count to find the weak libraries.

outputs.description: Every MACS2 narrow peak of every sample in one table, with the summit position, the peak width and the fold enrichment, p-value and q-value MACS2 reported for it.
outputs.name: Peak calls
outputs.rawYaml:
id: macs2_peaks
name: Peak calls
mode: peaks/narrow
description: >-
  Every MACS2 narrow peak of every sample in one table, with the summit
  position, the peak width and the fold enrichment, p-value and q-value MACS2
  reported for it.
# `--broad` writes *_peaks.broadPeak, a BED6+3 with no summit column: a
# different schema, so it is not folded in here as an alternate glob.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_peaks.narrowPeak"
recipe: macs2/peaks.py
fixture: peaks.tsv
renders_as:
  # Significance along the genome, then how wide the calls are. The dashed line is
  # MACS2's own default q-value cut-off (0.05, which is 1.301 on the -log10 axis).
  - id: peak_significance
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: manhattan
    title: Peak significance along the genome
    roles: {chr: chr, pos: summit, score: neg_log10_qvalue, feature: peak_id}
    config:
      score_kind: -log10 q-value
      score_threshold: 1.30103
      color_by_columns: [sample]
      default_color_by: sample
      hover_cols: [fold_enrichment]
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a peak at its summit position: the chromosome and position on the
      horizontal axis and its significance, as minus log10 of the q-value, on the
      vertical axis, coloured by sample. It answers where the strongest calls lie and
      whether samples call the same regions.

      How to read: tall points are the most confident peaks, and a column of points
      across samples is a region called in several libraries. Peak calls from one
      sample sit in a dense band just above the cut-off, so read this tile for
      positions and not for the density of calls. Open the table to inspect a labelled
      peak.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a q-value of 0.05, the default
      q-value cut-off of MACS2 callpeak, shown as 1.301 on this axis. A run can set its
      own cut-off, and the line then no longer matches what the caller used.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  # The same rows on a chromosome-aware locus axis, drawn by GenomeSpy. A peak is
  # an interval and not a point, so `end` is bound and a dashboard draws it with
  # `mark: rect`; the Manhattan above keeps the summit-as-a-point reading.
  # `sample` is bound so a tile can stack one lane per library without rebinding.
  - id: peak_genome_view
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Peaks on the genome
    roles: {chr: chr, pos: start, score: neg_log10_qvalue, feature: peak_id, end: end, sample: sample, category: sample}
    config:
      score_title: -log10 q-value
      score_threshold: 1.30103
    description: >-
      Each rectangle is a peak drawn over its interval on a chromosome-aware axis,
      with its height set by significance and its colour by sample. It answers where
      peaks cluster along the chromosomes and which libraries share them.

      How to read: zoom into a region to compare libraries. Peaks stacked on the same
      interval in several samples are reproducible, and an interval called in one
      sample only is private to it. Peaks are intervals, so wide ones show as long
      blocks.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal rule is a q-value of 0.05, the default
      q-value cut-off of MACS2 callpeak, shown as 1.301 on this axis.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  # The same intervals in plain Plotly, so a section that leads with the GenomeSpy
  # track still says something if that renderer is unavailable. Enrichment rather
  # than significance on the y axis: it is the quantity a coverage-shaped reading
  # of a peak set is about.
  - id: peak_coverage_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Peak enrichment along the genome
    roles: {chromosome: chr, position: start, value: fold_enrichment, end: end, sample: sample}
    config:
      color_by: sample
      smoothing_window: 0
    description: >-
      Each mark is a peak placed on its chromosome, with its fold enrichment at the
      summit over the local background on the vertical axis, one colour per sample. It
      answers how strong the enrichment is along the genome and where libraries agree.

      How to read: higher marks are peaks with more signal over the control, and
      overlapping marks of different colours are peaks found in several samples. Pick a
      chromosome to read it in detail.

      Note: MACS2 reports the fold enrichment at the peak summit against a Poisson
      background with the local lambda, so values are comparable only within a run.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  # Enrichment against significance. MACS2 reports significance already as
  # -log10, so a tile binding this sets `significance_is_neg_log10: true`.
  - id: peak_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Enrichment against significance
    roles: {feature_id: peak_id, effect_size: fold_enrichment, significance: neg_log10_qvalue, label: peak_id, category: sample}
    config:
      significance_is_neg_log10: true
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 1.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Fold enrichment
      significance_label: -log10 q-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a peak: its fold enrichment at the summit on the horizontal axis
      and its significance, as minus log10 of the q-value, on the vertical axis,
      coloured by sample. It answers which peaks are both strongly enriched and
      confidently called.

      How to read: peaks in the upper right are strong and confident, and are the ones
      to follow up. A peak with high enrichment but low significance sits in a region
      with few reads, and the reverse is a broad, modest enrichment. Open the table for
      the labelled peaks.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a q-value of 0.05, the default
      q-value cut-off of MACS2 callpeak. The vertical line is a fold enrichment of 1,
      which means no enrichment over the local background by definition of the ratio.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: width
      color: sample
      log_y: "True"
      labels: {sample: Sample, width: Peak width (bp)}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: width}
    title: Peak width per sample
    description: >-
      Each box is a sample: the spread of the widths of its peaks, on a logarithmic
      axis, coloured by sample. It answers how wide the called regions are and whether
      samples differ.

      How to read: MACS2 calls narrow peaks for transcription factor ChIP-seq and broad
      regions for histone marks, so the expected width depends on the mark. A sample
      with a very different width than its replicates may have been called with
      different settings or has a different signal to noise.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median peak width of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off
      of MACS2.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  # How many peaks and where they concentrate, then the spread of width,
  # enrichment and significance behind that count.
  - component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: chr
    top_n_count: 5
    caption: peaks, by chromosome
    title: Peaks called
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of peaks in view, with the number of samples that
      called them, and the bars rank the chromosomes holding most. It answers how many
      regions are called and where they concentrate.

      How to read: large chromosomes hold more peaks simply by length. A chromosome that
      stands out far above that expectation is worth a look.
  - component: card
    column: width
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [q1, q3]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: median width, with its quartiles
    title: Peak width
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median peak width in base pairs, with the lower and upper
      quartiles. It answers how narrow or broad the calls are.

      How to read: the expected width depends on the mark, so compare samples of the
      same assay. Widths span orders of magnitude, so the quartiles tell more than a
      box.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  - component: card
    column: fold_enrichment
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: fold enrichment, distribution
    title: Fold enrichment
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean fold enrichment of peak summits, with its median and
      maximum, and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how strong the
      enrichment is overall.

      How to read: a distribution piled near the lower end with a long right tail is
      typical. A mean close to the median means few extreme peaks.
  - component: card
    column: neg_log10_qvalue
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 1.30103
    threshold_direction: min
    caption: weakest peak against the q-value cut-off
    title: Weakest peak significance
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest minus log10 q-value of any peak in view, compared
      with the cut-off, with the median and the highest alongside. It answers whether
      every peak clears the standard cut-off.

      How to read: a minimum above the line means all peaks pass, which is expected when
      the caller used its default. A minimum below it means the run called peaks at a
      looser cut-off.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-off is a q-value of 0.05, the default of MACS2
      callpeak, shown as 1.301 on the minus log10 scale.

      Source: https://macs3-project.github.io/MACS/docs/callpeak.html
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: peak_id
    title: Peak table
    description: >-
      Each row is a peak with its sample, position, width, summit, fold enrichment and
      the minus log10 p-value and q-value MACS2 reported. It answers which peaks to
      follow up and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by significance or by fold enrichment, and filter by sample or
      chromosome.

outputs.description: The peak calls of every sample aggregated on a 4 kb window centred on their summits, in 50 bp bins: the share of the sample's peaks still covering each offset (the average peak footprint), and how densely the other samples of the run place their own summits around this sample's summits. Derived from the narrowPeak intervals only, so it is a peak-call aggregate and not a read coverage metagene.
outputs.name: Summit-centred peak profile
outputs.rawYaml:
id: macs2_summit_profile
name: Summit-centred peak profile
mode: peaks/summit_profile
description: >-
  The peak calls of every sample aggregated on a 4 kb window centred on their
  summits, in 50 bp bins: the share of the sample's peaks still covering each
  offset (the average peak footprint), and how densely the other samples of the
  run place their own summits around this sample's summits. Derived from the
  narrowPeak intervals only, so it is a peak-call aggregate and not a read
  coverage metagene.
# Reads the macs2_peaks collection through dc_ref (the recipe never globs), so
# the find below only says which run directories the output applies to: the
# ones holding narrowPeak calls. broadPeak calls carry no summit.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_peaks.narrowPeak"
recipe: macs2/summit_profile.py
fixture: summit_profile.tsv
renders_as:
  # Cross-sample summit concordance first: a central spike is agreement between
  # libraries, a flat curve is none.
  - id: summit_concordance_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Summit agreement between samples
    roles: {series: sample, x: offset_bp, y: neighbour_summit_density}
    config:
      x_title: Distance from summit (bp)
      y_title: Other samples' summits per kb
      reference_x: 0
      reference_label: Summit
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sample: how densely the summits called in the other samples fall
      around its own summits, by distance from the summit. It answers whether
      independent libraries place their peaks on the same sites.

      How to read: a sharp spike at the centre means the other samples put their
      summits on this sample's summits, so replicates agree or factors share sites. A
      flat curve means they do not. The count is over every other sample of the run,
      so filter to a comparison of interest.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical marker at zero is the summit of each anchor
      peak, which is the centre of the window by construction. This is an aggregate of
      peak calls and not a read coverage signal.
  # The same grid, read as the average shape of one call around its summit.
  - id: summit_footprint_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Average peak footprint
    roles: {series: sample, x: offset_bp, y: peak_footprint}
    config:
      x_title: Distance from summit (bp)
      y_title: Share of peaks covering the position
      reference_x: 0
      reference_label: Summit
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sample: the share of its peaks whose called interval covers each
      position, by distance from their own summit. It answers how wide the typical
      peak is around its summit.

      How to read: the curve is one at the summit and falls as peaks end. A curve that
      drops within a few hundred base pairs is a sharp, transcription factor like
      sample, and one that stays high for kilobases is a broad mark. The distance at
      which a curve crosses one half is the median half-width of its peaks.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical marker at zero is the summit of each peak,
