outputs.name: Bin summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mag_bin_summary
name: Bin summary
mode: bin-summary
description: >-
  Everything four tools know about each recovered bin in one row: how complete
  and how clean CheckM2 thinks it is, how it is assembled, what Prokka found in
  it and what GTDB-Tk calls it. It is the table the whole binning question is
  settled on, and the only place the MIMAG tier is computed with its RNA
  criteria included rather than from completeness alone.
find:
  # Rebuilt from four per-bin collections rather than read from a file; the
  # glob matches nf-core/mag's own BIN_SUMMARY output so a run that publishes
  # it is still recognised as carrying this output.
  path_glob: "**/bin_summary.tsv"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*bin_summary*.tsv"
recipe: mag/bin_summary.py
fixture: bin_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: mimag_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Bin completeness against contamination
    roles: {x: completeness, y: contamination, label: bin_id, color: mimag_tier, size: total_length}
    config:
      x_title: Completeness (%)
      y_title: Contamination (%)
      top_n_labels: 0
      legend_pos: bottom
      quadrants:
        x: 50
        y: 10
        labels: [Contaminated, Contaminated, Low quality, Medium quality or better]
    description: >-
      Each point is a recovered bin: its completeness on the horizontal axis and its
      contamination on the vertical axis, both estimated by CheckM2, sized by
      assembly length and coloured by MIMAG tier. It answers which bins are good
      enough to report as genomes.

      How to read: the best bins sit at the bottom right, complete and clean. Bins
      above the horizontal line are too contaminated for any tier, and bins left of
      the vertical line are fragmentary. Open the bin table for the lineage and
      assembly of a bin before trusting it.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical line is 50 percent completeness and the
      horizontal line 10 percent contamination, the limits of the medium-quality
      MIMAG tier. The high-quality tier needs more than 90 percent completeness and
      under 5 percent contamination, together with the 5S, 16S and 23S rRNA genes and
      at least 18 tRNAs, so a bin can look high quality here and still be medium.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - id: quality_vs_fragmentation
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Bin quality against contiguity
    roles: {x: n50, y: quality_score, label: bin_id, color: mimag_tier, size: total_length}
    config:
      log_x: true
      x_title: N50 (bp)
      y_title: Quality score (completeness minus 5 x contamination)
      top_n_labels: 0
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a bin: the N50 of its contigs on the horizontal axis and its
      quality score on the vertical axis, sized by assembly length and coloured by
      MIMAG tier. It answers whether the best bins are also the least fragmented.

      How to read: bins in the upper right are complete, clean and contiguous.
      Bins with a high score but a low N50 are assembled in many pieces, which makes
      them harder to trust and to annotate.

      Lines and annotations: no line is drawn. The quality score is this table's own
      summary, completeness minus five times contamination, and is not a published
      standard.
  - id: binner_phylum_flow
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sankey
    title: Assembler, binner and phylum flow
    roles: {steps: [assembler, binner, phylum]}
    description: >-
      Each flow is a group of bins: the left column is the assembler, the middle the
      binning tool and the right the GTDB-Tk phylum, with the width of a flow
      showing how many bins follow that path. It answers which assembler and binner
      combinations recover which lineages.

      How to read: a binner with wide flows to many phyla recovers a diverse set of
      genomes. A phylum reached by one assembler only is a lineage the others missed.
      Bins GTDB-Tk could not classify have no phylum.
  - id: bin_lineage
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Bin lineage hierarchy
    roles: {ranks: [domain, phylum, class_name, order, family, genus], abundance: total_length}
    config:
      colour_by_rank: phylum
    description: >-
      Each arc is a taxon of the GTDB-Tk classification of the bins, sized by the
      assembled length of its bins and coloured by phylum, from domain on the inner
      ring to genus on the outer. It answers how much of the assembly belongs to
      which lineages.

      How to read: wide arcs are the lineages that hold most of the recovered
      sequence. Classification stops at the deepest rank GTDB-Tk could assign, so
      short branches mean novel or poorly characterised bins.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: strip
    title: Bin quality by binner and MIMAG tier
    dict_kwargs:
      x: binner
      y: quality_score
      color: mimag_tier
      stripmode: group
      labels: {binner: Binner, quality_score: "Quality score (completeness minus 5 x contamination)", mimag_tier: MIMAG tier}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: quality_score}
    description: >-
      Each point is a bin: its quality score, grouped by the binner that recovered it
      and coloured by MIMAG tier. It answers which binner delivers the best bins.

      How to read: a binner with many high points of a good tier is the most reliable
      for this data. A binner whose points sit low or fall in the contaminated tier
      mixes genomes together.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median quality score of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      nf-core/mag. The score is this table's own summary, completeness minus five times
      contamination, and is not a published standard.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - id: mimag_donut
    component: card
    column: bin_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: mimag_tier
    caption: bins, by MIMAG tier
    title: Bins recovered
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct bins and the ring splits them by MIMAG
      tier. It answers how many of the recovered genomes reach each quality level.

      How to read: a ring mostly in the high and medium tiers means a successful
      binning. A large contaminated share points at binners mixing organisms.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: card
    column: completeness
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Bin completeness
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median completeness of the bins, as estimated by
      CheckM2, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how much of a genome a
      typical bin holds.

      How to read: a median above 50 percent means most bins are at least medium
      quality on this criterion. A long lower tail marks fragmentary bins.

      Lines and annotations: the MIMAG standard asks for at least 50 percent
      completeness for a medium-quality bin and more than 90 percent for a
      high-quality one.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: card
    column: contamination
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Bin contamination
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median contamination of the bins, as estimated by
      CheckM2, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how much foreign
      sequence a typical bin carries.

      How to read: low medians with a short tail mean clean bins. A long upper tail
      marks bins that mix genomes.

      Lines and annotations: the MIMAG standard allows under 10 percent contamination
      for a medium-quality bin and under 5 percent for a high-quality one.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: card
    column: total_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Bin size
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median assembled length of the bins in base pairs, and
      the box shows the quartiles. It answers how large a typical recovered genome is.

      How to read: very small bins are incomplete genomes, and very large ones may
      combine several organisms. Read the length together with completeness and
      contamination.
  - component: card
    column: bin_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: phylum
    top_n_count: 5
    filter_expr: "col('phylum') != ''"
    caption: bins, by phylum
    title: Bins by phylum
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of bins with a GTDB-Tk phylum and the bars rank
      the phyla by their number of bins. It answers which lineages dominate the
      recovered genomes.

      How to read: a ranking led by one phylum means a community dominated by it.
      Bins without a phylum were not classified and are left out.
  - component: card
    column: quality_score
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: assembler
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: best score, by assembler
    title: Best bin quality score
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest quality score of any bin, completeness minus five
      times contamination, and the bars rank the assemblers by their best bin. It
      answers which assembler produced the best genome.

      How to read: a tall bar for an assembler means it recovered at least one clean,
      complete bin. The median and minimum beside it show how the typical bin
      compares. The score is this table's own summary, not a published standard.
  - component: card
    column: sources_present
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: tools that reported, per bin
    title: Evidence per bin
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average count of the four tools (CheckM2, QUAST,
      Prokka and GTDB-Tk) that reported on each bin, and the histogram shows how bins
      spread over that count. It answers how complete the evidence behind each bin
      is.

      How to read: bins reported by fewer tools have blank columns in the table, so a
      low average means the MIMAG tier or lineage may be missing for some bins.
  - component: table
    title: Bin summary
    description: >-
      One row is one recovered bin, with its completeness, contamination,
      assembly statistics, annotation counts, MIMAG tier and GTDB-Tk lineage. It
      answers whether an individual bin is good enough to use.

      How to read: Sort by completeness, highest first, then check the
      contamination and the MIMAG tier of the top rows. Look for bins with high
      completeness and low contamination, and for rows with a missing tier or
      lineage. It complements the quality and taxonomy tiles of the same output,
      which summarise these bins.

outputs.name: Contig coverage
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mag_contig_depths
name: Contig coverage
mode: contig-depths
description: >-
  How deeply each contig is covered, once per sample whose reads were mapped
  back onto the assembly. Length against depth is the plot a binner sees before
  it decides anything: contigs of one organism sit in a band, and a contig deep
  in one sample and flat in another belongs to something only one of them
  carries. Contigs under 1 kbp are left out by the recipe, below the 1500 bp nf-core/mag bins from by
  default.
find:
  path_glob: "**/depths/contigs/*-depth.txt.gz"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/depths/contigs/*-depth.txt"
    - "**/*_depth.txt.gz"
recipe: mag/contig_depths.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several read samples.
fixture: contig_depths.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: length_vs_depth
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Contig length against depth
    roles: {x: contig_length, y: depth, label: contig_id, color: read_sample, size: mean_depth}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
      log_x: true
      x_title: Contig length (bp)
      y_title: Depth in this sample (X)
      top_n_labels: 0
      density_threshold: 5000
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a contig: its length on the horizontal axis and its read depth in
      one sample on the vertical axis, sized by its mean depth over all samples and
      coloured by the sample whose reads were mapped. It answers how coverage varies
      between contigs and between samples.

      How to read: contigs of one organism sit in a band of similar depth, which is
      the signal a binner uses. A contig deep in one sample and flat in another
      belongs to an organism only the first carries. Long contigs with very low depth
      may be poorly supported.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median depth of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      nf-core/mag. This catalog's recipe leaves contigs under 1 kbp out of the table,
      below the 1500 bp nf-core/mag uses by default as its minimum contig size for
      binning.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/mag/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Contig depth distribution per sample
    dict_kwargs:
      x: depth
      color: read_sample
      barmode: overlay
      labels: {depth: Depth (X), read_sample: Sample}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: x, stat: median, column: depth}
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the contigs in a range of depth, drawn per sample whose reads
      were mapped. It answers how deeply the assembly is covered in each sample.

      How to read: a sample whose histogram sits further right is more deeply
      sequenced. A large pile at zero means many contigs are absent from that sample,
      which is the differential coverage that separates organisms.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median depth of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      nf-core/mag.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Contig depth by assembly and sample
    dict_kwargs:
      x: assembly_id
      y: depth
      color: read_sample
      labels: {assembly_id: Assembly, depth: Depth (X), read_sample: Sample}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: depth}
    description: >-
      Each box summarises the contig depths of one assembly in one sample whose
      reads were mapped. It answers how coverage compares between assemblies and
      samples.

      How to read: boxes at similar heights mean comparable coverage. An assembly
      with a much lower box in one sample is poorly represented in that sample, and
      a wide box means a mix of abundant and rare organisms.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median depth of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      nf-core/mag.
  - component: card
    column: depth
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Contig depth
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median read depth of the contigs and the box shows the
      quartiles. It answers how deeply a typical contig is covered.

      How to read: a very low median means the reads barely cover the assembly and
      binning will be unreliable. A long upper tail holds highly abundant organisms.
  - component: card
    column: contig_length
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: assembler
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: longest contig, by assembler
    title: Longest contig
    description: >-
      The hero number is the length of the longest contig and the bars rank the
      assemblers by their longest contig. It answers how contiguous each assembly is.

      How to read: a longer contig means fewer breaks, which helps binning and
      annotation. The median beside it shows the typical contig, which is usually
      much shorter.
  - component: card
    column: contig_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: assembler
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: contigs, by assembler
    title: Contigs
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct contigs above the length floor, with
      the number of contig and sample rows beside it, and the bars rank the
      assemblers by their contigs. It answers how large the assemblies are.

      How to read: many more contigs from one assembler means it split the
      assembly into more pieces, or kept more short sequences.
  - component: card
    column: mean_depth
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: mean depth, with its spread
    title: Mean depth over samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average of the contigs' mean depth over all samples,
      and the histogram shows how contigs spread over it. It answers how abundant
      contigs are overall, before the per-sample split.

      How to read: a long tail of high values means a few very abundant organisms
      hold most of the reads.
  - component: table
    title: Contig coverage
    description: >-
      One row is one contig in one sample whose reads were mapped, with the
      contig length, its mean depth, its depth in that sample and the variance.
      It answers which contigs hold the reads of which sample.

      How to read: Sort by the depth in that sample to find the contigs that
      dominate it, or by the variance to find uneven coverage. Look for long
      contigs with a low depth and short ones with a very high depth. It
      complements the depth tiles of the same output, which summarise these
      rows.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: mcquant_cell_markers
name: Marker intensity per cell
mode: imaging/markers
description: >-
  The MCQUANT cell table melted on its marker columns: one row per cell and
  marker with the cell's mean intensity in the channel and the same through
  asinh(x / 150), which puts markers of very different brightness on one axis,
  the marker's position in the panel and whether it is a nuclear stain or a
  marker. The cell key matches the cell table, so a selection of cells reaches
  their intensities.
find:
  path_glob: "**/quantification/mcquant/*/*.csv"
recipe: mcquant/cell_markers.py
fixture: cell_markers.tsv
renders_as:
  # One box per marker, split by segmenter: the panel's dynamic range at a glance.
  - id: marker_box
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Marker intensity per cell
    dict_kwargs:
      x: marker
      y: asinh_intensity
      color: segmenter
      labels:
        marker: Marker
        asinh_intensity: "Intensity, asinh(x / 150)"
        segmenter: Segmentation method
    description: >-
      Each box is the spread of the cells' mean intensity in one marker channel, one box per marker and segmentation method. It answers which markers carry signal and how bright they are against the rest of the panel.

      How to read: a marker whose box sits near zero has little signal or a failed stain, and a very wide box points to a marker expressed in only a subset of cells. Compare the segmentation methods within a marker: a shift between them means the masks capture different amounts of cytoplasm or neighbours. Open the table tile to inspect single cells.

      Note: intensities are shown on the asinh(x / 150) scale, a fixed cofactor of this catalog module and not read from the run. It keeps markers of very different brightness on one axis.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/labsyspharm/quantification/master/README.md
  - id: marker_violin
    component: figure
    visu_type: violin
    title: Marker intensity shape
    dict_kwargs:
      x: marker
      y: asinh_intensity
      color: segmenter
      labels:
        marker: Marker
        asinh_intensity: "Intensity, asinh(x / 150)"
        segmenter: Segmentation method
    description: >-
      Each violin is the full distribution of the cells' mean intensity in one marker channel, one per marker and segmentation method. It answers whether a marker is unimodal or splits cells into positive and negative populations.

      How to read: two bulges mean a marker separates two populations, which is what a good lineage marker looks like. A single bulge close to the floor means a marker that stained little. Use it next to the box view, which hides modality.

      Note: intensities are shown on the asinh(x / 150) scale, a fixed cofactor of this catalog module and not read from the run.
  - id: measurement_count
    component: card
    column: cell_key
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: marker_role
    title: Intensity measurements
    caption: measurements, by marker role
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of cell by marker measurements, and the ring splits them between nuclear stains and markers. It answers how large the quantification is and how the panel is composed.

      How to read: the figure below the ring counts distinct cells, so the ratio between the two is the panel size. A ring with a single role means the marker sheet does not flag the nuclear stain.
  - component: card
    column: asinh_intensity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Typical marker intensity
    caption: median, with its spread

outputs.description: One row per segmented cell of every image and segmentation method: MCQUANT's mean intensity of the cell in each channel of the panel (one column per marker), its centroid in pixels of the registered image (origin top-left, y down) and its regionprops morphology (area, axes, eccentricity, solidity, extent, orientation), with the image (sample), the segmenter and a run-wide cell key, since MCQUANT's CellID restarts at 1 for every image and mask.
outputs.name: Segmented cells
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mcquant_cells
name: Segmented cells
mode: imaging/cells
description: >-
  One row per segmented cell of every image and segmentation method: MCQUANT's
  mean intensity of the cell in each channel of the panel (one column per
  marker), its centroid in pixels of the registered image (origin top-left, y
  down) and its regionprops morphology (area, axes, eccentricity, solidity,
  extent, orientation), with the image (sample), the segmenter and a run-wide
  cell key, since MCQUANT's CellID restarts at 1 for every image and mask.
find:
  path_glob: "**/quantification/mcquant/*/*.csv"
recipe: mcquant/cells.py
fixture: cells.tsv
renders_as:
  # The cells where they sit in their image, coloured by a marker picked in the
  # tile (the marker columns are named by pattern at the dashboard: a panel is
  # only known at ingest) or by segmenter.
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the run's panel markers, known only at ingest.
  - id: spatial_cells
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: spatial_cells
    title: Cells in the image
    roles: { cell_id: cell_key, x: X_centroid, y: Y_centroid, category: segmenter, sample: sample, area: Area }
    description: >-
      Each point is a segmented cell placed at its centroid in the registered image, coloured by segmentation method or by the intensity of a marker chosen in the controls. It answers where cells and marker signal sit in the tissue.

      How to read: marker positive cells should form the structures the marker is known for, and a patchy or empty region may be a stitching gap or an out-of-focus tile. Compare two segmentation methods on the same image to see where one finds cells the other misses.

      Note: the origin is the top left of the image and y grows downwards, as in image coordinates.
  # Size against shape: segmentation artefacts (merged or fragmented cells) sit
  # apart from the bulk.
  # C3 N/A: neither regionprops area nor eccentricity has a published cut-off.
  - id: shape_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Cell size against shape
    roles: { x: Area, y: Eccentricity, label: cell_key, color: segmenter }
    config:
      x_title: Cell area (pixels)
      y_title: Eccentricity
      top_n_labels: 5
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a segmented cell: its area in pixels on the horizontal axis and its eccentricity on the vertical axis, coloured by segmentation method. It answers whether the masks hold cells of plausible size and shape.

      How to read: most cells form a compact cloud. Points far to the right are large objects, often merged cells, and points at the top of the axis are elongated slivers, often fragments or debris. Compare the methods: one cloud shifted from the other means different masking rules.

      Note: eccentricity is that of the ellipse with the same second moments as the mask, from 0 for a circle towards 1 for a line. Neither quantity has a published cut-off, so no reference line is drawn.

      Source: https://scikit-image.org/docs/stable/api/skimage.measure.html
  - id: cell_count
    component: card
    column: Area
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: segmenter
    headline: true
    title: Segmented cells
    caption: cells, by segmentation method
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of segmented cells in view, the bar splits them by segmentation method, and the line below gives the median and largest cell area. It answers how many cells were found and which method found them.

      How to read: a method finding many times more cells than another is usually splitting cells or segmenting nuclei rather than whole cells. Filter to one image to compare them fairly.
  - id: median_area
    component: card
    column: Area
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: segmenter
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    title: Typical cell area
    caption: median area, by segmentation method
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median cell area in pixels, and the bars rank the segmentation methods by their own median. It answers how large the segmented objects are.

      How to read: nuclear masks are smaller than whole-cell masks by design. A median far below the expected cell size points to over-segmentation, and one far above to merged cells.
  - component: card
    column: Eccentricity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Cell roundness
    caption: median eccentricity, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median eccentricity of the segmented cells, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how elongated the masks are.

      How to read: tissue cells are rarely perfect circles, so a moderate median is normal. A box pushed towards 1 means many sliver-like masks, which points to over-segmentation along cell borders.
  - id: area_box
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Cell area by method
    dict_kwargs:
      x: segmenter
      y: Area
      color: segmenter
      labels:
        segmenter: Segmentation method
        Area: Cell area (pixels)
    description: >-
      Each box is the spread of cell areas for one segmentation method. It answers whether the methods agree on how big a cell is.

      How to read: overlapping boxes mean the methods mask similar objects. A method with a much smaller box is segmenting nuclei or fragments, and a long upper whisker marks merged cells.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: segmenter
    title: Segmentation method
    description: >-
      Keep the cells of one or more segmentation methods, to read each mask set on its own.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: Area
    title: Cell area
    description: >-
      Restrict the tiles to cells within an area range, for example to drop debris or merged cells.
  - component: table
    title: Segmented cells
    description: >-
      One row per segmented cell with its marker intensities, centroid and shape measures. Selecting rows filters the tab to those cells.

      How to read: sort by area or eccentricity to inspect the outliers of the size and shape plot.
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: cell_key

Markers expressed by the same cells correlate; a marker without signal has no correlation. The marker columns are only known at ingest, so a heatmap draws every numeric column.

id: mcquant_marker_correlation
name: Marker correlation
mode: imaging/markers
description: >-
  Marker by marker Pearson correlation of the cells' asinh intensities, over
  every cell a segmentation method found in the run: one row per segmenter and
  marker, one column per marker of the panel. Markers expressed by the same
  cells correlate; a marker without signal has no correlation. The marker
  columns are only known at ingest, so a heatmap draws every numeric column.
find:

recipe: mcquant/marker_correlation.py
fixture: marker_correlation.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the run's panel markers, known only at ingest.
  - id: correlation_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Marker correlation
    roles: { index: marker_row, row_annotation_cols: [segmenter, marker_role] }
    description: >-
      Each cell of the heatmap is the Pearson correlation between two markers across all segmented cells, with the rows annotated by segmentation method and marker role. It answers which markers are expressed by the same cells.

      How to read: strong positive blocks group markers of one cell lineage or compartment, and negative values separate exclusive populations. A marker with no correlation to anything either has no signal or marks a rare population. A nuclear stain should correlate with the other nuclear signals, not with membrane markers.

      Note: correlations are computed on asinh intensities, so a few very bright cells do not dominate them. No cut-off separates strong from weak correlation, so none is drawn.

    description: >-
      One row per segmentation method and marker, with its correlation to every marker of the panel.

      How to read: sort a marker's column to list the markers that move with it.

id: melon_ranks
name: Genome-copy composition
description: >-
  Melon's marker-gene estimate of the community, as genome copies rather than
  read counts, with the seven NCBI ranks already split into their own columns.
  The rows are pooled across the long-read samples the tool ran on: the sample
  id lives only in melon's output path.

find: { path_glob: "**/melon/*/*/*.tsv" }
recipe: melon/ranks.py
fixture: ranks.tsv
renders_as:
  # wide per-rank columns -> sunburst fits; stacked_taxonomy would need the long
  # rank column, and a per-sample axis this pooled table does not carry.
  - id: sunburst
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Community composition by lineage
    roles:
      ranks: [superkingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species]
      abundance: abundance
    config:
      colour_by_rank: phylum
    description: >-
      Each arc is a taxon: the rings run from superkingdom at the centre out to species, sized by its share of
      the estimated genome copies and coloured by phylum. It answers which lineages make up the community.

      How to read: wide arcs are the dominant lineages, and an arc that fans out into many species is a diverse
      group. Taxa Melon could not name at a rank are labelled unclassified. Click an arc to zoom in on it.

      Note: abundance is a share of estimated genome copies from marker genes, not of reads, and the rows are
      pooled across samples.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xinehc/melon/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: species
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: phylum
    top_n_count: 4
    filter_expr: "col('species') != 'unclassified'"
    headline: true
    title: Species detected
    caption: species, by phylum
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct named species Melon identified, and the bars rank the phyla
      that hold most of them. It answers how rich the community is and where the diversity sits.

      How to read: a phylum with many species is a diverse group. Unclassified lineages are left out, so the
      count is a lower bound.
  - component: card
    column: copy_number
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: phylum
    top_n_count: 4
    title: Genome copies
    caption: genome copies, by phylum
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of estimated genome copies, and the bars rank the phyla by their copies. It
      answers how large the profiled community is and which phyla dominate it.

      How to read: copies are estimated from marker genes, so they count genomes rather than reads and are
      less biased by genome size. Compare with the species card: a phylum with few species but many copies is
      dominated by a few organisms.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xinehc/melon/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: identity_mean
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Identity to the reference
    caption: mean identity per lineage
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean identity of the marker-gene reads to their reference genome cluster, and the
      histogram shows its distribution over lineages. It answers how close the community is to known genomes.

      How to read: values near one mean close relatives are in the database. Low values flag novel or distant
      lineages whose assignment is less certain. Melon publishes no pass mark for it.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xinehc/melon/master/README.md
  - component: table
    title: Lineages and genome copies

      reference_stat: median
      x_title: K-mer completeness (%)
      y_title: Consensus QV

      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is an assembly: the share of solid read k-mers it recovers on the
      horizontal axis and its consensus quality value (QV) on the vertical axis,
      sized by its number of k-mers. It answers which assemblies are both complete
      and accurate.

      How to read: the best assemblies sit top right. High completeness with a low
      QV is an assembly that kept everything but was not polished; high QV with low
      completeness is an accurate assembly that lost sequence. Open the copy-number

      Merqury. QV is the Phred-scaled error rate (QV 40 is one error per 10 kb), so
      compare assemblies of the same project with each other.

id: merqury_copy_number_composition
name: Read k-mer copy number in the assembly
mode: spectra-cn/composition
description: >-
  Where the solid read k-mers ended up, per assembly: absent from it, present
  once, twice, three times, four times or more. On a haploid or collapsed
  assembly nearly all of them should be present once; a large absent share is
  lost sequence, a large two-copy share is duplicated sequence such as retained
  haplotigs. Read k-mers at or below the error trough of the read spectrum are
  left out, so sequencing errors do not count as absent sequence.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.spectra-cn.hist"
recipe: merqury/copy_number_composition.py
fixture: copy_number_composition.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: copy_number_bars
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: Read k-mer copy number per assembly
    roles: {sample_id: assembly_id, taxon: copy_class, rank: rank, abundance: percent}
    config:
      value_title: Share of solid read k-mers (%)
    description: >-
      Each bar is an assembly, split by how many times its solid read k-mers occur in
      it: absent, once, twice and so on. It answers how much sequence the assembly
      lost and how much it duplicated.

      How to read: on a haploid or collapsed assembly nearly all k-mers should be
      present once. A large absent share is lost sequence and a large two-copy share
      is duplicated sequence such as retained haplotigs.

      Note: read k-mers at or below the error trough of the read spectrum are left
      out, so sequencing errors do not count as absent sequence.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marbl/merqury/master/README.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: assembly_id
      y: percent
      color: copy_class
      barmode: stack
      labels: {assembly_id: Assembly, percent: Share of solid read k-mers (%), copy_class: Copies in the assembly}
    title: Copy number shares, stacked
    description: >-
      Each stacked bar is an assembly and each segment the share of its solid read
      k-mers at one copy number. It answers the same question as the advanced tile
      above in a fixed, printable form.

      How to read: compare the single-copy segment across assemblies; the larger it
      is, the more faithful the assembly is to the reads.
  - component: card
    column: percent
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    filter_expr: "col('copy_class') == '1 copy'"
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Single-copy k-mer share
    caption: single-copy share, distribution over assemblies
    headline: true
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of solid read k-mers present exactly once
      in an assembly, the signature of a clean haploid or collapsed assembly. The
      histogram shows how the assemblies spread.

      How to read: values near 100 are expected for a haploid assembly. A low value
      means missing or duplicated sequence, so open the stacked bars to see which.
      A diploid or polyploid assembly legitimately holds more copies.
  - component: card
    column: solid_kmers
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max, median]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: copy_class
    title: K-mers by copy number
    caption: solid read k-mers, by copy number
    description: >-
      Each unit is a solid read k-mer and the ring splits them by how often the
      assembly holds them. It answers how the k-mers of all assemblies in view are
      distributed over the copy classes.

      How to read: one dominant single-copy slice is healthy. Large absent or
      multi-copy slices mean lost or duplicated sequence.
  - component: table
    title: Copy number table
    description: >-
      Each row is an assembly and a copy class with its solid k-mer count and share.
      It answers the exact numbers behind the stacked bars.

      How to read: sort by share to find the assemblies with the largest absent or
      two-copy class.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: merqury_sequence_qv
name: Per-sequence QV
mode: sequence-qv
description: >-
  Merqury's QV for every contig or scaffold of every assembly. Errors are rarely
  spread evenly: a handful of short, low-QV sequences often carry most of an
  assembly's error k-mers, and they are the ones to inspect, polish or drop.
  Sequences with no error k-mer have no finite QV and are flagged error-free.
find:
  path_glob: "**/merqury/*.*.qv"
recipe: merqury/sequence_qv.py
fixture: sequence_qv.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: sequence_qv_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Sequence QV against size
    roles: {x: total_kmers, y: qv, label: sequence, color: assembly_id}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
      x_title: K-mers in the sequence (size)
      y_title: Consensus QV
      log_x: true
      legend_pos: bottom
      top_n_labels: 8
      label_order_col: qv
    description: >-
      Each point is a contig or scaffold: its number of k-mers, a proxy for its
      length, against its consensus QV. It answers which sequences carry the lowest
      accuracy and whether they are small or large.

      How to read: errors are rarely even, so a few short low-QV sequences often hold
      most error k-mers. The lowest points are labelled; inspect, polish or drop them.
      A low QV on a large sequence matters more than on a short one.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median consensus QV of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      Merqury. The horizontal axis is logarithmic.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/marbl/merqury/2.-Overall-k-mer-evaluation.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: qv
      color: assembly_id
      barmode: overlay
      opacity: 0.6
      labels: {qv: Consensus QV, assembly_id: Assembly}
    title: Per-sequence QV distribution
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: x, stat: median, column: qv}
    description: >-
      Each bar counts sequences in a QV bin, one overlaid histogram per assembly. It
      answers how uniform the accuracy of an assembly is.

      How to read: a narrow histogram at high QV is an evenly accurate assembly. A
      long tail to the left is a set of weak sequences, so open the scatter to see
      which. Histograms of different assemblies are overlaid, not stacked.

      Note: sequences with no error k-mer have no finite QV and are not drawn.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median consensus QV of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      Merqury.
  - component: card
    column: qv
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Lowest sequence QV
    caption: QV, distribution over sequences
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest QV over all sequences in view and the histogram
      shows the distribution. It answers how bad the worst sequence is compared with
      a typical one.

      How to read: a minimum far below the median marks a sequence worth inspecting.
      QV is logarithmic, so a few points of difference are a large error ratio.
  - component: card
    column: assembly_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: error_free
    title: Sequences with no error k-mer
    caption: sequences, by error-free status
    description: >-
      The hero number is the number of assemblies and the second figure the number of
      sequences; the ring splits the sequences into those with and without any error
      k-mer. It answers how many sequences are perfectly supported by the reads.

      How to read: error-free sequences are mostly short, so a large error-free share
      alone is not proof of a good assembly. Read it next to the QV of the large
      sequences.
  - component: card
    column: asm_only_kmers
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, sum]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Error k-mers per sequence
    caption: error k-mers, distribution over sequences
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest count of error k-mers on a single sequence, with
      the median and the total beside it. It answers whether the errors are
      concentrated on a few sequences.

      How to read: a maximum far above the median means a handful of sequences carry
      most errors and polishing them gives the biggest gain.
  - component: table
    title: Sequence QV table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sequence of an assembly with its error k-mers, total k-mers, QV
      and error rate. It answers which named sequences to inspect.

      How to read: sort by QV ascending to list the weakest sequences first, and by
      error k-mers to find where most errors sit.

id: metaphlan_profile
name: Taxonomic profile
mode: profile
description: Per-sample taxonomic relative-abundance profile.
find: { filename: "*_profile.txt" }

outputs.description: Matched fragment ions per identified peptide (b, y and other series) with the median absolute fragment mass error in ppm, summarised from the pyOpenMS ion annotation mhcquant writes with --annotate_ions.
outputs.name: Fragment-ion annotation
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mhcquant_fragment_ions
name: Fragment-ion annotation
mode: immunopeptidomics/fragment-ions
description: >-
  Matched fragment ions per identified peptide (b, y and other series) with the
  median absolute fragment mass error in ppm, summarised from the
  pyOpenMS ion annotation mhcquant writes with --annotate_ions.
find: { path_glob: "**/ion_annotations/*_matching_ions.tsv" }
recipe: mhcquant/fragment_ions.py
fixture: fragment_ions.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: card
    column: fragment_ions
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median ions per peptide, with their spread
    title: Matched fragment ions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of fragment ions matched to a peptide's
      spectrum, and the box shows the spread across peptides. It answers how well
      the spectra support their identifications.

      How to read: more matched ions mean a better-supported spectrum. A box pushed
      toward few ions holds identifications resting on little evidence, so read it
      with the score distribution.
  - component: card
    column: fragment_error_ppm
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median error, with its spread
    title: Fragment mass error
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median absolute fragment mass error in ppm of a
      peptide's matched ions, and the box shows the spread across peptides. It
      answers how accurately the fragment masses match the theory.

      How to read: a small error that is similar across samples means a well
      calibrated instrument. A sample with a larger error points to a calibration
      drift.

      Note: mhcquant sets its fragment tolerance in daltons for the search (default
      0.01), not in ppm, so no ppm cut-off is drawn.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/mhcquant/blob/3.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Fragment mass error by sample
    dict_kwargs:
      x: fragment_error_ppm
      color: sample
      labels: {fragment_error_ppm: Median absolute fragment error (ppm), sample: Sample, count: Peptides}
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the peptides whose median absolute fragment error falls in a
      range, coloured by sample. It answers how the mass accuracy is distributed
      within and between samples.

      How to read: distributions that overlap mean comparable mass accuracy. A sample
      shifted to the right has a calibration problem and less reliable matches.
  - component: table
    title: Fragment ions per peptide
    description: >-
      Each row is one identified peptide, with its matched b, y and other fragment
      ions, the median absolute fragment error in ppm and the matched intensity. It
      answers the exact figures behind every tile.

      How to read: sort by matched ions to find the best and the weakest supported
      peptides.

outputs.name: Peptide length distribution
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mhcquant_length_distribution
name: Peptide length distribution
mode: immunopeptidomics/length
description: >-
  Distinct peptide sequences per length and sample, as counts and as the share
  of the sample. The class I signature is a sharp 9-mer mode inside 8 to 12
  residues; class II peptides spread over 13 to 25.
find: { path_glob: "*.tsv" }
recipe: mhcquant/length_distribution.py
fixture: length_distribution.tsv
renders_as:
  # C3: the shaded band is mhcquant's own default peptide length window
  # (peptide_min_length 8, peptide_max_length 12), read from its schema.
  - id: length_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Peptide length profile
    roles: { series: sample, x: length, y: fraction }
    config:
      x_title: Peptide length (residues)
      y_title: Share of the sample's peptides
      shaded_bands:
        - [8, 12, "mhcquant default length window"]
    description: >-
      Each curve is one sample: the share of its distinct peptides at each length.
      It answers what the length signature of the immunopeptidome is, which tells
      the class of molecule that presented the peptides.

      How to read: a sharp peak at 9 residues inside the shaded window is the
      expected class I signature, and class II ligands peak near 15 residues in the
      HLA Ligand Atlas. A broad shoulder of longer peptides points to class II
      presentation or to contamination.

      Lines and annotations: the shaded band is the peptide length window mhcquant
      keeps by default, 8 to 12 residues. It is the pipeline's setting, so it hides
      longer peptides unless the run widened it.

      Sources: https://github.com/nf-core/mhcquant/blob/3.2.0/nextflow_schema.json and
      https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33858848/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Peptides per length class
    dict_kwargs:
      x: length_class
      y: peptides
      color: sample
      barmode: group
      labels: {length_class: Peptide length, peptides: Distinct peptides, sample: Sample}
    description: >-
      Each bar is the count of distinct peptides of one length in one sample,
      coloured by sample. It answers how many peptides each length class holds.

      How to read: the tallest bar should be the 9-mer for a class I sample. Samples
      of different depth differ in height, so use the profile above to compare
      shapes.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: length_class
    title: Peptide length
    description: >-
      Pick one or more peptide lengths to restrict the tiles to them. It answers
      what the table and the bars show for a single length.
  - component: table
    title: Peptide length counts
    description: >-
      Each row is one sample and peptide length, with the count of distinct peptides
      and their share of the sample. It answers the exact values behind the profile.

      How to read: filter by length class to compare samples at one length.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: mhcquant_motif_matrix
name: Positional amino-acid frequencies
mode: immunopeptidomics/motif
description: >-
  Frequency of every standard amino acid at every position of the distinct
  peptides of each well-supported length, per sample: the anchor positions of
  the presenting MHC alleles stand out as columns dominated by a few residues.
find: { path_glob: "*.tsv" }
recipe: mhcquant/motif_matrix.py
fixture: motif_matrix.tsv
renders_as:
  # The 20 amino-acid columns are fixed by the recipe, so they are named. Rows are
  # ordered by position within a sample, so clustering would scramble them.
  - id: motif_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Amino-acid frequency by peptide position
    roles:
      index: row_id
      value_columns: [A, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, N, P, Q, R, S, T, V, W, Y]
      row_annotation_cols: [sample, length_class]
    config:
      cluster_rows: false
      cluster_cols: false
    description: >-
      Each row is one position of the peptides of a given length in one sample, and
      each column an amino acid, coloured by the share of peptides carrying that
      residue there. It answers which residues the presented peptides favour at each
      position.

      How to read: columns that are dark at only a few positions are anchor
      residues, the signature of the presenting MHC allele. A flat, pale row has no preference, so little motif.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: length_class
    title: Peptide length
    description: >-
      Pick one or more peptide lengths to restrict the heatmap and the table to
      them. It answers what the motif looks like for a single length.
  - component: table
    title: Positional amino-acid frequencies
    description: >-
      Each row is one position of one peptide length in one sample, with the number
      of peptides and the frequency of each amino acid. It answers the exact values
      behind the heatmap.

      How to read: filter by sample and length, then sort a residue column to find

outputs.description: Every FDR-filtered peptide precursor of every sample, one row per sample, peptidoform and charge: score, PSM count, observed and predicted retention time, m/z, charge, neutral mass, hydropathy, P2 and C-terminal anchors, source proteins, consensus intensity and the number of replicates it was quantified in. Read from the per-sample tables mhcquant writes at the top of its output.
outputs.name: Identified peptides
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mhcquant_peptides
name: Identified peptides
mode: immunopeptidomics/peptides
description: >-
  Every FDR-filtered peptide precursor of every sample, one row per sample,
  peptidoform and charge: score, PSM count, observed and predicted retention
  time, m/z, charge, neutral mass, hydropathy, P2 and C-terminal anchors, source
  proteins, consensus intensity and the number of replicates it was quantified
  in. Read from the per-sample tables mhcquant writes at the top of its output.
find: { path_glob: "*.tsv" }
recipe: mhcquant/peptides.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several charge states.
fixture: peptides.tsv
renders_as:
  # Observed against DeepLC-predicted retention time. mhcquant writes the DeepLC
  # prediction beside the observed time, so the diagonal is the prediction itself.
  - id: rt_observed_predicted
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Observed against predicted retention time
    roles: { x: predicted_rt_min, y: rt_min, label: peptide, color: sample }
    config:
      x_title: Predicted retention time (min)
      y_title: Observed retention time (min)
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: Observed equals predicted
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a peptide: its retention time predicted by DeepLC on the
      horizontal axis and the time observed in the run on the vertical axis,
      coloured by sample. It answers whether identifications behave as the
      prediction expects.

      How to read: points hugging the diagonal are consistent with the prediction.
      Points far off it are less trustworthy identifications, and a whole sample off
      the diagonal has a gradient or calibration difference.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is where observed equals predicted. It is
      an identity line, not a cut-off.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/mhcquant/blob/3.2.0/docs/output.md
  - id: rt_hydropathy
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Retention time against hydropathy
    roles: { x: gravy, y: rt_min, label: peptide, color: length_class }
    config:
      x_title: Hydropathy (GRAVY)
      y_title: Observed retention time (min)
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a peptide: its hydropathy score (GRAVY, the mean hydropathy of
      its residues) on the horizontal axis and its observed retention time on the
      vertical axis, coloured by length class. It answers how retention relates to
      peptide hydrophobicity in each sample.

      How to read: compare samples and lengths. A sample whose cloud tilts
      differently from the others had a different gradient or column, so treat its
      retention times with care.
  - id: mz_retention
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Precursor m/z over the gradient
    roles: { x: rt_min, y: mz, label: peptide, color: charge_state }
    config:
      x_title: Observed retention time (min)
      y_title: Precursor m/z
      top_n_labels: 0
    description: >-
      Each point is a peptide: its observed retention time on the horizontal axis
      and its precursor m/z on the vertical axis, coloured by charge state. It
      answers how identifications spread over the gradient and the mass range.

      How to read: a gradient that is evenly populated is a healthy run. Gaps point to
      a segment of the run that identified little, and a charge state that dominates
      shows the mass range it covers.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Peptide score by sample
    dict_kwargs:
      x: score
      color: sample
      labels: {score: Search-engine score, sample: Sample, count: Peptides}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: x, stat: median, column: score}
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the peptides whose search-engine score falls in a range,
      coloured by sample. It answers how the identification scores are distributed.

      How to read: the score is the Comet XCorr in a quantified run, where higher is
      better. Samples whose distribution sits lower have weaker evidence, so read them
      with the fragment-ion tiles.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median search-engine score of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of mhcquant.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/mhcquant/blob/3.2.0/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: psms
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: modification_state
    caption: PSMs, by modification state
    title: Peptide-spectrum matches
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of PSMs behind the peptides in view, and the
      bar splits it by modification state. It answers how much spectral evidence there
      is and how much of it is for modified peptides.

      How to read: a sum mixes samples, so read the median and the maximum beside it
      for a per-peptide reading.
  - component: card
    column: sequence
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: length_class
    caption: distinct sequences, by length
    title: Distinct peptide sequences
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct peptide sequences, and the bar splits
      the rows by length class. The count of rows is also shown, since a sequence
      appears once per charge, modification and sample. It answers how many different
      peptides were found and at which lengths.

      How to read: for a class I sample the 9-mer segment should be the largest.
  - component: card
    column: rt_error_min
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: spread of the error, with its quartiles
    title: Retention-time error
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of the retention-time error (observed minus
      predicted) over the peptides in view, and the box shows its quartiles. It
      answers how far observed times stray from the DeepLC prediction.

      How to read: a box tight around zero with a short range means the prediction
      fits. A box shifted off zero is a systematic offset, so check the gradient. The
      range is shown instead of the median because errors in both directions cancel.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/mhcquant/blob/3.2.0/docs/output.md

    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: length_class
    title: Peptide length
    description: >-
      Pick one or more peptide lengths to restrict every tile to them. It answers what
      the plots show for a single length.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: score
    title: Peptide score
    description: >-
      Drag the range to keep peptides with a score inside it. It answers how the plots
      change when only the best scored, or the weakest, peptides are kept.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sequence
    title: Identified peptides
    description: >-
      Each row is a peptide precursor in one sample, with its score, PSM count,
      retention times, m/z, charge, anchors, source proteins and intensity. It answers
      the exact detail behind every tile and lets a row selection filter the dashboard.

      How to read: select a sequence to see it across samples, or sort by score to
      inspect the best supported peptides.

renders_as.description:
Each point is a peptide: its retention time predicted by DeepLC on the horizontal axis and the time observed in the run on the vertical axis, coloured by sample. It answers whether identifications behave as the prediction expects.
How to read: points hugging the diagonal are consistent with the prediction. Points far off it are less trustworthy identifications, and a whole sample off the diagonal has a gradient or calibration difference.
Lines and annotations: the diagonal is where observed equals predicted. It is an identity line, not a cut-off.
Source: https://github.com/nf-core/mhcquant/blob/3.2.0/docs/output.md

renders_as.description:
Each point is a peptide: its hydropathy score (GRAVY, the mean hydropathy of its residues) on the horizontal axis and its observed retention time on the vertical axis, coloured by length class. It answers how retention relates to peptide hydrophobicity in each sample.
How to read: compare samples and lengths. A sample whose cloud tilts differently from the others had a different gradient or column, so treat its retention times with care.

renders_as.description:

      color_intersections_by: degree

      of a sample, and the dots below show which replicates are in it. It answers how
      much of a sample is seen in every injection.

      detected, and the histogram shows how many peptidoforms are seen in each
      count. It answers how consistently peptides are re-detected.

    title: Replicate detection per peptide

      the number of replicates it was detected in. It answers which peptides are

    caption: median PSMs, with their spread
    title: Peptide-spectrum matches
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of PSMs per sample, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how much spectral evidence each sample gives.

      How to read: samples of the same design should give similar counts. A sample far below its peers had a low yield, so treat its comparisons with care.
  - id: yield_peptides
    component: card
    column: peptides
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median peptides, with their spread
    title: Distinct peptides
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of distinct peptide sequences per sample, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how deep each immunopeptidome is.

      How to read: immunopeptidomes of a similar input amount give similar depth. An outlier sample is under or over sampled.
  - id: yield_peptides_total
    component: card
    column: peptides
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: peptides per sample
    title: Total peptides
    description: >-
      The hero number is the sum of distinct peptides over the samples in view, and the histogram shows how samples distribute over peptide counts. It answers how many peptides the dataset holds and how even the samples are.

      How to read: a sum mixes samples, so read the minimum and the maximum beside it. A histogram with one far bar is a sample out of step with the rest.
  - id: yield_proteins
    component: card
    column: proteins
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median proteins, with their spread
    title: Source proteins
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of source proteins per sample, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how many proteins contribute peptides to each sample.

      How to read: a sample with many peptides but few proteins is dominated by a few abundant sources. Compare with the peptide counts.
  - id: modified_share
    component: card
    column: modified_fraction
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median share, with its spread
    title: Modified peptide share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of a sample's peptidoforms that carry a modification, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how much of the immunopeptidome is modified.

      How to read: samples prepared the same way give similar shares. A sample with a much higher share may reflect a preparation artefact such as oxidation.
  - id: ninemer_share
    component: card
    column: ninemer_fraction
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median share, with its spread
    title: 9-mer share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of a sample's peptides that are 9 residues long, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how strong the 9-mer signature is.

      How to read: a class I immunopeptidome is dominated by 9-mers, so a low share points to a mix of classes or to contamination.
  - id: class_i_share
    component: card
    column: class_i_fraction
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: lowest sample, with the median
    title: Peptides in the class I window
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest share of a sample's peptides that fall in the class I length window, 8 to 12 residues, and the median sits beside it. It answers whether any sample leaves the window.

      How to read: mhcquant keeps peptides of 8 to 12 residues by default, so the share is 1 unless the run widened the range. A lower share means the run kept longer peptides.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/mhcquant/blob/3.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: class_ii_share
    component: card
    column: class_ii_fraction
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: highest sample, with the median
    title: Peptides in the class II window
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest share of a sample's peptides that fall in the class II length window, 13 to 25 residues, and the median sits beside it. It answers whether any sample holds long peptides.

      How to read: with mhcquant's default length filter of 8 to 12 residues the share is 0, so a value above 0 means the run widened the range and the sample holds class II length peptides.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/mhcquant/blob/3.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: median_length
    component: card
    column: median_length
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: mean of sample medians, with the lowest and highest
    title: Median peptide length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean over samples of each sample's median peptide length, with the lowest and highest sample beside it. It answers how long the peptides are overall.

      How to read: samples of one class give about the same value. A sample with a clearly longer median holds longer peptides, so read it with the length profile.
  - id: replicate_correlation
    component: card
    column: replicate_median_r
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median Pearson r, with its spread
    title: Replicate correlation
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over samples of the median Pearson correlation between replicate intensities, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how reproducible the quantification is.

      How to read: values close to 1 mean replicates agree. A low value means noisy intensities, so open the replicate scatter before trusting the quantities.

      Note: the correlation needs enough peptides quantified in both replicates, and samples without replicates have none.
  - id: replicate_worst_pair
    component: card
    column: replicate_min_r
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: lowest r per sample, with its spread
    title: Weakest replicate pair
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest Pearson correlation between replicate intensities over the samples in view, and the box shows the spread of each sample's weakest pair. It answers whether any replicate disagrees with the others.

      How to read: a value much lower than the median correlation points to one bad replicate. Open its pair in the scatter.
  - id: replicate_completeness
    component: card
    column: all_replicates_fraction
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median share, with its spread
    title: Peptides in every replicate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of a sample's peptides that were quantified in every replicate, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how completely replicates agree on what is present.

      How to read: a high share means replicates detect the same peptides. A low share means many peptides are seen in one injection only.
  - id: rt_error
    component: card
    column: median_abs_rt_error_min
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median error, with its spread
    title: Retention-time error
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over samples of each sample's median absolute retention-time error between observed and DeepLC-predicted time, and the box shows the spread. It answers how well the prediction fits each run.

      How to read: a small error that is similar across samples means a consistent gradient. A sample with a larger error had a different gradient or column.
  # C1 N/A: one point per sample and the only categorical column is the sample id itself,
  # so a colour would only repeat the label.
  - id: yield_vs_ninemer
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Depth against 9-mer share
    roles: { x: peptides, y: ninemer_fraction, label: sample, size: psms }
    config:
      x_title: Distinct peptides
      y_title: Share of 9-mers
      top_n_labels: 5
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample: its distinct peptide count on the horizontal axis and
      its share of 9-mers on the vertical axis, sized by PSMs. It answers whether
      deeper samples keep the 9-mer signature.

      How to read: samples of one class cluster together. A point far from the others
      is a sample with a different depth or a different length mix, so open its
      length profile.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of 9-mers of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of mhcquant, which defines none.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Immunopeptidome summary
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample, with its PSMs, peptides, proteins, modified share, length
      signature, median score, retention-time error and replicate statistics. It
      answers the exact figures behind every card and lets a row selection filter the
      dashboard.

      How to read: sort by a column to find the outlier samples, then select one to
      open it across the tiles.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: mhcquant_source_proteins
name: Source proteins
mode: immunopeptidomics/source-proteins
description: >-
  One row per sample and source protein: distinct peptides, shared peptides,
  PSMs, best score, summed intensity and the peptides themselves. Shared
  peptides are credited to every protein they map to.
find: { path_glob: "*.tsv" }
recipe: mhcquant/source_proteins.py
fixture: source_proteins.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: card
    column: protein
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: distinct proteins, with the sample and protein pairs
    title: Source proteins
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct source proteins, and the count beside
      it is the rows, one per sample and protein. It answers how many proteins give
      rise to the presented peptides and how many are shared between samples.

      How to read: a row count much higher than the distinct count means the same
      proteins are found in several samples. Shared peptides are credited to every
      protein they map to.
  - component: card
    column: peptides
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median peptides per protein, with their spread
    title: Peptides per source protein
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of distinct peptides per source protein,
      and the box shows the spread across proteins. It answers how many peptides a
      typical protein contributes.

      How to read: a few proteins with many peptides are the dominant sources. Open
      the scatter or the table to see which.
  - id: protein_coverage
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Source protein yield and intensity
    roles: { x: peptides, y: log10_intensity, label: protein_entry, color: sample, size: psms }
    config:
      x_title: Distinct peptides
      y_title: Summed log10 intensity
      top_n_labels: 8
    description: >-
      Each point is a source protein in one sample: its distinct peptides on the
      horizontal axis and its summed log10 intensity on the vertical axis, coloured
      by sample and sized by PSMs. It answers which proteins contribute the most
      peptides and signal.

      How to read: points toward the upper right are the dominant sources of the
      immunopeptidome. Proteins that dominate every sample are abundant cellular
      proteins, while sample-specific ones may reflect the biology under study.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: protein
    title: Source proteins
    description: >-
      Each row is a source protein in one sample, with its distinct and shared
      peptides, PSMs, best score, summed intensity and the peptides themselves. It
      answers the exact detail behind every tile and lets a row selection filter the
      dashboard.

      How to read: select a protein to see its peptides, or sort by peptides to find
      the dominant sources.
