outputs.name: Novel miRNA precursors
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mirdeep2_novel_precursors
name: Novel miRNA precursors
mode: mirna/discovery
description: >-
  miRDeep2's novel precursor calls merged across samples by overlapping locus,
  one row per hairpin: how many samples report it, its best score and
  true-positive estimate, the reads on each arm summed over samples, the share
  of calls with a significant randfold test, any Rfam hit, and the sequences of
  its strongest call.
find:
  path_glob: "**/result_*.csv"
recipe: mirdeep2/novel_precursors.py
fixture: novel_precursors.tsv
renders_as:
  # miRDeep2 documents a score cut-off only as the `-b` display filter (default 0)
  # and surveys cut-offs from -10 to 10; it publishes no recommended value, so no
  # threshold line is drawn (RULES section 17).
  - id: novel_support
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Novel precursors by support
    roles: {x: samples_detected, y: max_score, label: precursor_id, color: star_support, size: total_reads}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
      x_title: Samples reporting the precursor
      y_title: Best miRDeep2 score
      legend_pos: bottom
      top_n_labels: 6
    description: >-
      Each point is a novel miRNA precursor merged across samples: the number of
      samples that report it and its best miRDeep2 score, sized by its total reads and
      coloured by whether star-arm reads were seen. It answers which candidates are
      best supported.

      How to read: candidates in the upper right are detected in many samples with a
      high score. A star-arm read pair is the signature of Dicer processing, so a
      candidate with star support is stronger than one without. Open the table to read
      the sequences of the labelled candidates.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median best miRDeep2 score of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a
      cut-off of miRDeep2. The README sets a score cut-off of 0 only for which novel
      candidates its overview table lists.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rajewsky-lab/mirdeep2/master/README.md
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21911355/
  - component: card
    column: star_support
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [mode]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: star_support
    headline: true
    title: Novel precursors
    caption: precursors, by star-arm support
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of novel precursors and the ring splits them by
      whether star-arm reads support them. It answers how many candidates carry the
      Dicer signature.

      How to read: a large share without star support means many candidates rest on
      mature-arm reads alone and need validation, for instance in more samples.
  - component: card
    column: samples_detected
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Samples per precursor
    caption: samples, quartiles over precursors
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of samples that report a precursor and the
      box shows the spread. It answers how reproducible the candidates are.

      How to read: miRDeep2 flags candidates found in multiple independent samples as
      high confidence, so a box near 1 means most calls are one-off.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21911355/
  - component: card
    column: max_score
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Best score per precursor
    caption: score, quartiles over precursors
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of the best miRDeep2 score of each precursor and
      the box shows the spread. It answers how confident the discovery is overall.

      How to read: higher scores are more probable genuine miRNAs. Scores can be
      negative, so compare the box with the score-cutoff survey tile rather than with
      zero.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: samples_detected
    title: Samples per precursor
    description: >-
      Restricts the tiles to precursors reported by a chosen range of samples. Raise
      the lower bound to keep only reproducible candidates.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: precursor_id
    title: Novel precursor table
    description: >-
      Each row is a novel precursor merged across samples, with its locus, best score,
      reads per arm, randfold share and the mature, star and precursor sequences. It
      answers which candidates to validate and lets a row selection filter the rest of
      the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by score or samples detected, and check the randfold share and
      any Rfam hit, since a hit to a known non-miRNA family argues against a call.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: mirdeep2_predictions
name: miRNA precursor predictions
mode: mirna/discovery
description: >-
  Every precursor miRDeep2 scored, one row per sample and candidate: the novel
  hairpins it proposes and the miRBase precursors it re-discovered, with the
  miRDeep2 score, the estimated true-positive probability, the read stack on
  the mature, loop and star arms, the randfold test and the precursor locus.
find:
  path_glob: "**/result_*.csv"
recipe: mirdeep2/predictions.py
fixture: predictions.tsv
renders_as:
  # No score cut-off is drawn: miRDeep2 documents none (RULES section 17).
  - id: prediction_scores
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Prediction score against read support
    roles: {x: total_reads, y: score, label: prediction_id, color: category}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
      x_title: Total reads on the precursor
      y_title: miRDeep2 score
      log_x: true
      legend_pos: bottom
      top_n_labels: 6
    description: >-
      Each point is a precursor in one sample: its total reads on a log axis and its
      miRDeep2 score, coloured by novel or known (already in miRBase). It answers how
      novel candidates compare with the known miRNAs the run re-detected.

      How to read: known miRNAs show what a confident call looks like for this
      dataset. Novel candidates scoring like them are credible; low-scoring ones on
      few reads are likely noise. Open the table to read the sequences.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median miRDeep2 score of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      miRDeep2. The README sets a score cut-off of 0 only for which novel candidates its
      overview table lists, and surveys cut-offs from -10 to 10.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rajewsky-lab/mirdeep2/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: category
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [mode]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: category
    headline: true
    title: Scored precursors
    caption: precursors, novel and known
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of precursors miRDeep2 scored and the ring splits
      them into novel candidates and known miRBase precursors. It answers how much of
      the output is discovery.

      How to read: a known share that is very low means the library missed most
      expected miRNAs, which argues for checking the library quality first.
  - component: card
    column: score
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Score of predictions
    caption: score, quartiles over predictions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median miRDeep2 score and the box shows the spread. It
      answers how strongly the predictions are supported overall.

      How to read: filter to novel or known with the category selector and compare the
      two boxes. A novel box far below the known one means weak candidates.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: category
    title: Prediction category
    description: >-
      Filters the tiles to novel candidates, known miRBase precursors or both.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: prediction_id
    title: Prediction table
    description: >-
      Each row is a precursor in one sample with its score, true-positive estimate,
      read counts per arm, randfold result and locus. It answers which predictions to
      follow up and lets a row selection filter the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by score and check the true-positive estimate and its
      standard deviation together, as a wide deviation means an uncertain estimate.

renders_as.description:
Each point is a precursor in one sample: its total reads on a log axis and its miRDeep2 score, coloured by novel or known (already in miRBase). It answers how novel candidates compare with the known miRNAs the run re-detected.

Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median miRDeep2 score of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of miRDeep2. The README sets a score cut-off of 0 only for which novel candidates its overview table lists, and surveys cut-offs from -10 to 10.

outputs.description: miRDeep2's own calibration table, one row per sample and integer score cutoff: novel candidates reported, their estimated false and true positives, known miRBase precursors recovered and the signal-to-noise ratio against permuted structures. id: mirdeep2_score_summary

description: >-

  cutoff: novel candidates reported, their estimated false and true positives,
  known miRBase precursors recovered and the signal-to-noise ratio against
  permuted structures. The curve miRDeep2's authors read to pick a cutoff.
find:
  path_glob: "**/result_*.csv"
recipe: mirdeep2/score_summary.py
fixture: score_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # The survey spans score cut-offs from -10 to 10 (miRDeep2 README, survey.pl);
  # no cut-off is marked because miRDeep2 recommends none.
  - id: signal_to_noise_curve
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Signal-to-noise by score cut-off
    roles: {series: sample, x: score_cutoff, y: signal_to_noise}
    config:
      x_title: miRDeep2 score cut-off
      y_title: Signal-to-noise ratio
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sample: the signal-to-noise ratio of novel predictions, against
      permuted structures, at each integer score cut-off. It answers how stringent the
      score cut-off must be before predictions rise above the noise.

      How to read: pick a cut-off where the curve has risen and flattened, and read the
      recovery curve beside it to see what that costs in known miRNAs. A flat curve
      near 1 means the data hold little signal over noise.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The survey covers cut-offs from -10 to 10, and
      miRDeep2's README sets a default of 0 only for which novel candidates its overview table
      lists.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rajewsky-lab/mirdeep2/master/README.md
  - id: known_recovery_curve
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Known miRNAs recovered by score cut-off
    roles: {series: sample, x: score_cutoff, y: known_detected_pct}
    config:
      x_title: miRDeep2 score cut-off
      y_title: Known miRNAs detected (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sample: the share of known miRBase miRNAs present in the data
      that miRDeep2 recovers at each integer score cut-off. It answers what a stricter
      cut-off costs in sensitivity.

      How to read: a curve that stays high up to the cut-off you choose means the
      stricter filter loses few known miRNAs. A steep fall marks the cut-off beyond
      which real miRNAs are discarded.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. miRDeep2's README sets a score cut-off of 0 only for
      which novel candidates its overview table lists.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rajewsky-lab/mirdeep2/master/README.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: score_cutoff
      y: novel_reported
      color: sample
      labels: {score_cutoff: miRDeep2 score cut-off, novel_reported: Novel precursors reported, sample: Sample}
    title: Novel precursors by score cut-off
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: the number of novel precursors reported at each score
      cut-off. It answers how many candidates survive as the filter tightens.

      How to read: a steep early drop means most candidates have low scores. Combine it
      with the signal-to-noise curve to choose a cut-off that keeps a manageable list.
  - component: table
    title: Score cut-off survey table

      Each row is a sample and an integer score cut-off with the novel predictions,

      signal-to-noise ratio. It answers the exact numbers behind the curves.

name: isomiR composition per sample
mode: mirna/isomirs
description: >-
  Each sample's miRNA reads partitioned four ways: by 3' end (reference,
  trimmed, templated extension, non-templated addition), by 5' end shift, by
  the added nucleotide, and by nucleotide change (seed, central, other). Each
  partition sums to the sample's miRNA reads.
find:
  path_glob: "**/mirtop/joined_samples_mirtop.tsv"
recipe: mirtop/isomir_composition.py
fixture: isomir_composition.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: isomir_classes
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: isomiR classes per sample
    roles: {sample_id: sample, taxon: taxon, rank: rank, abundance: abundance}
    config:
      x_title: Sample
      value_title: Share of miRNA reads
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample, split into the classes of one partition of its miRNA reads,
      such as the state of the 3' end or the 5' end. It answers how much of each
      sample's miRNA reads matches the reference sequence and how the rest differs.

      How to read: switch the partition with the rank control. A shifted 5' end moves the seed region and with it the targets. Compare samples or groups, since a class that differs
      between conditions is worth following up in the landscape tile.

      Note: a nucleotide change cannot be told from an editing event, a SNP or a
      sequencing error, and a change seen in one sample only is most likely an error.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31504201/

    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: taxon
    title: isomiR class filter
    description: Pick one or more isomiR classes to keep. It filters the tiles of the dashboard that read this table.

    title: isomiR class table

      Each row is a sample, a partition and a class, with the reads in the class and
      their percentage of the sample's miRNA reads. It answers how many reads fall
      in each isomiR class.

      classes, and compare samples of different groups.

id: mirtop_isomir_landscape
name: isomiR landscape of the top miRNAs
mode: mirna/isomirs
description: >-
  For the most expressed miRNAs, the mean share of reads in each isomiR class
  (reference, 3' trimmed or extended, 3' addition, 5' shift, seed or central
  change) and the fraction of samples where the class is a real part of the
  miRNA's reads.
find:
  path_glob: "**/mirtop/joined_samples_mirtop.tsv"
recipe: mirtop/isomir_landscape.py
fixture: isomir_landscape.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: isomir_dot_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    title: isomiR classes of the top miRNAs
    roles: {cluster: variant_class, gene: mirna, mean_expression: mean_share_pct, frac_expressing: samples_fraction}
    description: >-
      Each dot is a miRNA in one isomiR class: its colour is the mean share of the miRNA's
      reads in that class and its size is the fraction of samples where the class is a real
      part of the reads. It answers which isomiR forms each abundant miRNA carries and whether
      they are the same across samples.

      How to read: a large dark dot is a class that holds many reads in most samples, such
      as a miRNA that is mostly 3' trimmed everywhere. A small dot with a dark colour is a
      class that is common in only part of the cohort, so look at the samples behind it. The
      classes are not exclusive, since one read can be 3' trimmed and carry an addition.

      Lines and annotations: a class counts as present in a sample when it holds at least 5
      percent of that miRNA's reads there, and only samples with at least 10 reads of the miRNA
      are counted. Both are settings of the recipe, not published cut-offs.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31504201/
  - component: table
    title: isomiR landscape table
    description: >-
      Each row is a miRNA in one isomiR class, with the mean share of its reads, the
      fraction of samples where the class is present, the reads in the class and the
      miRNA's expression rank. It answers how common each class is for each miRNA.

      How to read: sort by mean share to find the dominant forms, and filter on a
      miRNA to read all its classes.

id: mirtop_mirna_counts
name: miRNA expression per sample
mode: mirna/expression
description: >-
  Reads per mature miRNA and sample, summed over all its isomiRs from the
  joined mirtop table, with counts per million miRNA-assigned reads, their
  log2, the number of distinct isomiRs and the share of reads matching the
  reference sequence. Design columns ride along when a design table is given.
find:
  path_glob: "**/mirtop/joined_samples_mirtop.tsv"

fixture: mirna_counts.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: the box is one per miRNA and the x axis already names it, no
  # pertinent column is left to colour by (design columns are not in the schema).
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: mirna
      y: log2_cpm
      points: all
      labels: {mirna: miRNA, log2_cpm: Expression (log2 CPM)}
    title: miRNA expression distribution
    reference_lines: [{axis: y, stat: median, column: log2_cpm}]
    description: >-
      Each box is a miRNA, summarising its expression across samples as log2 of counts
      per million miRNA-assigned reads, with every sample drawn as a point. It answers
      how abundant each miRNA is and how much it varies between samples.

      How to read: boxes higher up are more abundant miRNAs. A wide box or a point far
      from the rest marks a miRNA or a sample that varies, so check that sample in the
      PCA. The scale is relative, so it follows the sample's total of miRNA reads.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median expression (log2 CPM) of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of mirtop.
  - component: card
    column: reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: mirna
    top_n_count: 5
    title: Reads in the top miRNAs
    caption: the five miRNAs with the most reads, with the median and largest per sample
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of miRNA reads over the samples in view, and the bars rank
      the miRNAs that hold the most of them. It answers whether a few miRNAs dominate the
      library.

      How to read: miRNA libraries are often dominated by a handful of abundant miRNAs.
      When one miRNA holds most of the reads, the others are measured with fewer reads, so
      treat the low abundance ones with caution.
  - component: card
    column: mirna
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    title: miRNAs detected
    caption: samples with the most miRNA rows, and the total of rows
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct miRNAs seen in the samples in view, and the
      bars rank the samples that have the most. It answers how many miRNAs the data
      detects.

      How to read: a sample with far fewer miRNAs than the rest points to a shallow or
      low-quality library. Open the PCA to see whether it also separates there.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: mirna
    title: miRNA filter
    description: Pick one or more miRNAs to keep. It filters the tiles of the dashboard that read this table.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: log2_cpm
    title: Expression range filter
    description: Set a range of log2 counts per million to keep. It filters the tiles of the dashboard that read this table.
  - component: table

      Each row is a miRNA in a sample, with its reads summed over its isomiRs, counts per

      sample to follow it.

tools.description: Fast BAM/CRAM depth calculation for WGS, exome, or targeted sequencing.
tools.name: mosdepth

outputs.description: Per-amplicon coverage depth, aggregated across all samples (bindable as-is).
outputs.name: Amplicon coverage
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mosdepth_amplicon_coverage
name: Amplicon coverage
mode: amplicon
description: Per-amplicon coverage depth, aggregated across all samples (bindable as-is).
find: { path_glob: "**/mosdepth/amplicon/all_samples.mosdepth.coverage.tsv" }
# no recipe → declare the columns:
columns:
  chrom: String
  start: Int64
  end: Int64
  region: String
  coverage: Float64
  sample: String
fixture: amplicon_coverage.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: coverage_track_amplicon
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Amplicon depth along the genome
    roles: {chromosome: chrom, position: start, end: end, value: coverage, sample: sample}
    config:
      color_by: sample
    description: >-
      Each point on a line is an amplicon placed at its genome position, with its
      mean read depth on the vertical axis, one line per sample. It answers which
      amplicons are poorly covered and whether the same ones fail across samples.

      How to read: lines should stay well above zero along the genome. A dip that
      appears in every sample is a failing primer pair, and a dip in one sample is a
      sample-specific drop-out. Open the amplicon matrix to compare samples side by
      side.

      Lines and annotations: no line is drawn. A consensus needs enough depth at each
      base, and nf-core/viralrecon and iVar both call a consensus base from a depth
      of 10 reads by default, so dips towards that depth are where bases turn into Ns.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/conf/modules_illumina.config
  # Depth is the one number a coverage table is read for, and a mean alone
  # hides the drop-outs: the Tukey strip shows the spread and the outliers.
  - component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Amplicon depth
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median read depth of an amplicon over all samples, and
      the box shows the quartiles and outliers. It answers how deeply the amplicons
      are covered overall.

      How to read: a median far above 10 reads with a tight box means even, deep
      coverage. A long lower tail, or amplicons near zero, are the drop-outs that
      leave gaps in the consensus.

      Lines and annotations: no mark is drawn. nf-core/viralrecon and iVar call
      consensus bases from a depth of 10 reads by default.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/conf/modules_illumina.config
  - component: table
    title: Amplicon coverage
    description: >-
      One row is one amplicon in one sample, with its genome coordinates and
      mean depth. It answers which amplicons are poorly covered.

      How to read: Sort by coverage, lowest first, to find the dropouts, and by
      start to read them in genome order. Look for amplicons that fail in
      several samples, which suggests a primer problem rather than a sample one.
      It complements the amplicon heatmap of the same module, which shows the
      same values as a grid.

name: Amplicon coverage matrix

description: Log10 amplicon-coverage matrix (samples × amplicons).

renders_as:

  # falls back to the literal "sample_id", which this matrix does not have,

  - id: complex_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Amplicon coverage matrix
    roles: {index: sample}
    config:
      cluster_cols: false
      cluster_rows: true
    description: >-
      Each cell is an amplicon in one sample, coloured by its log10 read depth, with
      amplicons in genome order and samples clustered by similarity. It answers
      which amplicons fail and which samples fail together.

      How to read: a pale column is an amplicon with low depth in many samples, which
      points at a failing primer pair. A pale row is a poorly sequenced sample, and
      samples that cluster together share the same drop-out pattern, often from the
      same batch or primer scheme.

      Lines and annotations: no mark is drawn. Values are log10 of the mean amplicon
      depth, so 1 is 10 reads and 3 is 1000 reads.

outputs.description: Share of the reference covered at least at each depth, per mapping, from mosdepth's global distribution: every depth to 100X, then a log-spaced grid. The depth at which a curve falls off is the depth a consensus caller can rely on.
outputs.name: Cumulative coverage curve
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mosdepth_cumulative_coverage
name: Cumulative coverage curve
mode: coverage
description: >-
  Share of the reference covered at least at each depth, per mapping, from
  mosdepth's global distribution: every depth to 100X, then a log-spaced
  grid. The depth at which a curve falls off is the depth a consensus caller
  can rely on.
find:
  path_glob: "**/mosdepth/**/*.mosdepth.global.dist.txt"
recipe: mosdepth/cumulative_coverage.py
fixture: cumulative_coverage.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: cumulative_curve
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Cumulative coverage curve
    roles: {series: genome_id, x: depth, y: bases_pct}
    config:
      reference_x: 10
      reference_label: 10X, minimum depth for variant and consensus calls
      x_title: Depth (X)
      y_title: Bases covered at least this deep (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each line is a mapping: the share of the reference covered at least at each
      depth, from mosdepth's global distribution. It answers how much of the genome
      is deep enough to call variants and a consensus.

      How to read: a curve that stays near 100 percent and falls late means even deep
      coverage. A curve that drops early, or a lower plateau, means part of the genome
      is thinly covered or not covered at all. Read the value where a curve crosses the
      marked line to see the breadth at that depth.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical marker is 10X, the default minimum depth at which
      nf-core/viralrecon calls variants and consensus bases. iVar's own default is 10 reads for a
      consensus base but 0 for a variant call. mosdepth itself sets no cut-off.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/conf/modules_illumina.config
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brentp/mosdepth/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: bases_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Bases covered across depths
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median, over every depth step of every mapping, of the
      percentage of bases covered at least that deep, and the box shows the spread.
      It answers how quickly coverage falls off with depth overall.

      How to read: read it next to the curve, since it pools every depth step. A
      high median with a tight box means most of the genome stays covered as the
      depth rises.
  - component: table
    title: Cumulative coverage
    description: >-
      One row is one mapping at one depth, with the percentage of bases covered
      at least that deep. It answers how much of the genome reaches a given
      depth.

      How to read: Filter on a depth of interest and sort by the percentage to
      rank the mappings. Look for a mapping whose percentage falls early as the
      depth rises. It complements the cumulative curve tile of the same output,
      which draws these rows as lines.

outputs.name: Binned depth along the reference
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mosdepth_per_base_bins
name: Binned depth along the reference
mode: coverage
description: >-
  Read depth along each reference from mosdepth's per-base output, folded
  into bins sized to the reference (50 bp on a 30 kb viral genome) as the
  length-weighted mean depth and the lowest depth of each bin. One lane per
  mapping keeps dropouts and amplicon gaps visible without the ten thousand
  rows a per-base track would draw.
find:
  path_glob: "**/mosdepth/**/*.per-base.bed.gz"
recipe: mosdepth/per_base_bins.py
fixture: per_base_bins.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: depth_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Binned depth along the reference
    roles: {chromosome: chrom, position: position, value: mean_depth, end: end, sample: genome_id}
    config:
      color_by: sample
    description: >-
      Each point on a line is a bin of the reference at its position, with its
      length-weighted mean read depth on the vertical axis, one line per mapping. It
      answers where the depth drops, as dropouts or amplicon gaps, along the genome.

      How to read: lines should stay well above zero along the genome. A dip to zero
      is a gap that will become Ns in the consensus, and repeated dips at regular
      spacing are failing amplicons. Compare mappings to see whether a gap is shared.

      Lines and annotations: no line is drawn. nf-core/viralrecon and iVar call
      consensus bases from a depth of 10 reads by default, so bins below it are
      likely to be masked.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/conf/modules_illumina.config
  - component: card
    column: min_depth
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: genome_id
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: lowest bin depth, by mapping
    title: Lowest depth in any bin
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest depth found in any bin and the bars rank the
      mappings by their lowest bin. It answers whether any part of the genome is left
      uncovered.

      How to read: a value of zero means a gap in at least one mapping, which becomes
      Ns in a consensus. The median and maximum beside it show the typical and best
      cases.

      Lines and annotations: no mark is drawn. nf-core/viralrecon and iVar call
      consensus bases from a depth of 10 reads by default.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/docs/output.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/andersen-lab/ivar/master/docs/MANUAL.md
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/viralrecon/master/conf/modules_illumina.config
  - component: table
    title: Binned depth
    description: >-
      One row is one bin of one mapping, with its coordinates, mean depth and
      lowest depth. It answers where along the genome the depth drops.

      How to read: Sort by mean depth, lowest first, to find the weak bins, and
      by the lowest depth to find bins with a gap inside. Look for bins that are
      weak in several mappings. It complements the coverage track tile of the
      same output, which draws these bins along the genome.

outputs.description: Read depth along the genome, from mosdepth's per-target `regions.bed.gz` files. The recipe folds the targets into fixed 1 Mb windows and reports the target-length-weighted mean depth of each window, so a capture panel with a few hundred thousand unevenly spaced targets becomes a track a browser can draw and an eye can read. Only the primary contigs are kept. One lane per sample: when mosdepth ran on more than one alignment stage of a sample (duplicate-marked, then recalibrated), one pass is kept, since both measure the same alignments.
outputs.name: Coverage along the genome
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mosdepth_regions
name: Coverage along the genome
mode: regions
description: >-
  Read depth along the genome, from mosdepth's per-target
  `regions.bed.gz` files. The recipe folds the targets into fixed
  1 Mb windows and reports the target-length-weighted mean depth of each
  window, so a capture panel with a few hundred thousand unevenly spaced
  targets becomes a track a browser can draw and an eye can read. Only the
  primary contigs are kept. One lane per sample: when mosdepth ran on more
  than one alignment stage of a sample (duplicate-marked, then recalibrated),
  one pass is kept, since both measure the same alignments.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.regions.bed.gz"
recipe: mosdepth/regions.py
fixture: regions.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: coverage_track_regions
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Target depth along the genome
    roles: {chromosome: chromosome, position: position, value: value, end: end, sample: sample_stage}
    config:
      color_by: sample
    description: >-
      Each point on a line is a 1 Mb window of the genome at its position, with the
      target-length-weighted mean depth of the targets in it, one line per sample.
      It answers whether the targeted regions are covered evenly along the genome.

      How to read: lines of different samples should rise and fall together,
      scaled by sequencing depth. A window that drops in every sample is a
      difficult region or a target missing from the panel, and a window that drops
      in one sample is a local failure.

      Lines and annotations: no line is drawn, and mosdepth publishes no depth
      cut-off. Judge depth against the assay's own requirement.
  # Same rows on GenomeSpy's own locus axis: the whole genome concatenated,
  # zoomable, and brushable into a region filter the rest of the tab reads.
  - id: genomespy_regions
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Target depth on the genome axis
    roles: {chr: chromosome, pos: position, score: value, end: end, feature: sample_stage, category: sample}
    config:
      score_title: Mean target depth (X)
      score_threshold_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each bar is a 1 Mb window of the genome with its target-length-weighted mean
      depth, on one axis that concatenates every chromosome, coloured by sample. It
      answers where along the whole genome the targets are covered, and lets you
      brush a region to filter the rest of the tab.

      How to read: bars should be of similar height across windows of a sample. A
      stretch of short bars is a poorly covered region, and tall bars are
      regions with high target density or copy gain. Brush a stretch to focus the
      other tiles on it.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median window depth of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      mosdepth. mosdepth publishes no depth cut-off.
  # Depth is the one number a coverage table is read for, and a mean alone
  # hides the drop-outs: the Tukey strip shows the spread and the outliers.
  - component: card
    column: value
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Window depth
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median mean target depth of a 1 Mb window, and the box
      shows the quartiles and outliers. It answers how deeply the targets are
      covered overall.

      How to read: a tight box means even coverage along the genome. A long lower
      tail holds windows that are under-covered and may hide variants.
  - component: table
    title: Window depth
    description: >-
      One row is one 1 Mb window of one sample, with its mean target depth and
      number of targets. It answers which windows are under-covered.

      How to read: Sort by the depth, lowest first, to find the weak windows,
      and check the number of targets to see whether a window is simply sparse.
      Look for windows that are weak in many samples. It complements the genome
      coverage tiles of the same module, which draw these windows along the
      chromosomes.

renders_as.description:
Each point on a line is a 1 Mb window of the genome at its position, with the target-length-weighted mean depth of the targets in it, one line per sample. It answers whether the targeted regions are covered evenly along the genome.
How to read: lines of different samples should rise and fall together, scaled by sequencing depth. A window that drops in every sample is a difficult region or a target missing from the panel, and a window that drops in one sample is a local failure.
Lines and annotations: no line is drawn, and mosdepth publishes no depth cut-off. Judge depth against the assay's own requirement.

outputs.description: mosdepth's own headline table, one row per contig with its length, the bases of sequence that landed on it and the mean, minimum and maximum depth. When mosdepth runs against a target file it reports every contig twice, once genome-wide and once over the targets only; the recipe splits that into a `scope` column (genome or region) instead of mixing two very different depths on one axis. Sample and alignment stage come from the file name, one pass is kept per sample, and only the primary contigs and the run total are kept, which drops the thousands of ALT, decoy and HLA rows a GRCh38 run lists.
outputs.name: Per-contig coverage summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mosdepth_summary
name: Per-contig coverage summary
mode: summary
description: >-
  mosdepth's own headline table, one row per contig with its length, the
  bases of sequence that landed on it and the mean, minimum and maximum
  depth. When mosdepth runs against a target file it reports every contig
  twice, once genome-wide and once over the targets only; the recipe splits
  that into a `scope` column (genome or region) instead of mixing two very
  different depths on one axis. Sample and alignment stage come from the file
  name, one pass is kept per sample, and only the primary contigs and the run
  total are kept, which drops the thousands of ALT, decoy and HLA rows a
  GRCh38 run lists.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.mosdepth.summary.txt"
recipe: mosdepth/summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Mean depth per contig
    dict_kwargs:
      x: chrom
      y: mean_depth
      color: sample
      barmode: group
      facet_row: scope
      facet_col: stage
      labels: {chrom: Contig, mean_depth: Mean depth (X), sample: Sample, scope: Scope, stage: Alignment stage}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a contig: its mean read depth, grouped by sample and split into the
      whole contig (genome) and the targeted regions only (region) when mosdepth ran
      with a target file, with one column of panels per alignment stage (md, recal). It
      answers whether coverage is even between contigs.

      How to read: bars of similar height mean even coverage. A contig far below the
      others is under-covered, and the sex chromosomes are lower than the autosomes
      in a single-copy sample. Compare the region facet with the genome facet to see
      the enrichment of the targets.

      Lines and annotations: the last bar is the run total, a pooled row, and no line
      is drawn. mosdepth publishes no depth cut-off.
  # Mean depth per contig is read for its spread as much as its centre: the
  # Tukey strip shows the under-covered contigs the bar chart flattens.
  - component: card
    column: mean_depth
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "(col('chrom') != 'total') & (col('scope') == 'genome')"
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Contig mean depth
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median mean depth of a contig over the whole contig,
      leaving out the run total and the on-target rows, and the box shows the
      quartiles. It answers how evenly the contigs are covered.

      How to read: a tight box means even coverage. A long lower tail holds
      under-covered contigs, which are usually the sex chromosomes or small contigs.
  - component: table
    title: Coverage per contig
    description: >-
      One row is one contig of one sample, stage and scope, with its length,
      bases and mean, lowest and highest depth. It answers what the depth of
      each contig is.

      How to read: Sort by the mean depth, lowest first, to find the under-
      covered contigs, which are usually sex chromosomes or small contigs. Look
      for contigs far from the depth of the rest of the sample. It complements
      the per-sample depth tiles of the same output, which summarise these rows.

renders_as.description:
Each bar is a contig: its mean read depth, grouped by sample and split into the whole contig (genome) and the targeted regions only (region) when mosdepth ran with a target file, with one column of panels per alignment stage (md, recal). It answers whether coverage is even between contigs.
How to read: bars of similar height mean even coverage. A contig far below the others is under-covered, and the sex chromosomes are lower than the autosomes in a single-copy sample. Compare the region facet with the genome facet to see the enrichment of the targets.

outputs.description: Mean depth on chromosome X and on chromosome Y for every library, from the small per-run table MultiQC's mosdepth module writes, split per sample and alignment stage. The X/Y depth ratio separates the two common karyotypes cleanly: two X and no Y leaves almost no Y signal and a large ratio, one X and one Y sits near 1. `inferred_sex` applies a 10x cut-off in the empty band between them. It is a heuristic on two summary numbers, not a genotype call, and a sex chromosome aneuploidy, a mixed or contaminated library or a very low-depth run can all land on the wrong side of it. Read it as a check against the sex recorded in the sample sheet, and read the raw X and Y depths beside it to see how far from the cut-off a library actually sits.
outputs.name: X and Y coverage sex check
outputs.rawYaml:
id: mosdepth_xy_sex_check
name: X and Y coverage sex check
mode: xy
description: >-
  Mean depth on chromosome X and on chromosome Y for every library, from the
  small per-run table MultiQC's mosdepth module writes, split per sample and
  alignment stage. The X/Y depth ratio separates the two common karyotypes
  cleanly: two X and no Y leaves almost no Y signal and a large ratio, one X
  and one Y sits near 1. `inferred_sex` applies a 10x cut-off in the empty
  band between them. It is a heuristic on two summary numbers, not a genotype
  call, and a sex chromosome aneuploidy, a mixed or contaminated library or a
  very low-depth run can all land on the wrong side of it. Read it as a check
  against the sex recorded in the sample sheet, and read the raw X and Y
  depths beside it to see how far from the cut-off a library actually sits.
find:
  path_glob: "**/mosdepth-xy-coverage-plot.txt"
recipe: mosdepth/xy_sex_check.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 4 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples and both inferred sexes.
fixture: xy_sex_check.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: sex_check_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: X against Y chromosome depth
    roles: {x: x_coverage, y: y_coverage, label: sample, color: inferred_sex}
    config:
      x_title: Mean depth on chromosome X (reads per base)
      y_title: Mean depth on chromosome Y (reads per base)
      top_n_labels: 4
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a library at one alignment stage: its mean depth on chromosome X
      on the horizontal axis and on chromosome Y on the vertical axis, coloured by the
      inferred sex. It answers whether the sequenced sex agrees with the sex
      recorded in the sample sheet.

      How to read: libraries with two X chromosomes show strong X depth and almost
      no Y depth, and libraries with one X and one Y show both at a similar depth.
      A point that lands in the other group, or between them, can be a sample swap,
      a sex chromosome aneuploidy, a mixed library or a very low-depth run.

      Lines and annotations: no line is drawn. The inferred sex uses a cut-off of 10
      on the X to Y depth ratio, a heuristic of this table placed between the two
      common karyotypes, not a published rule or a genotype call.
  # Four lanes at most (two libraries, two stages), so the strip lists the
  # spread rather than naming them: the point is which library is the outlier.
  - component: card
    column: xy_ratio
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    caption: X to Y depth ratio, lowest and highest
    title: X to Y depth ratio
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average X to Y depth ratio over the libraries, with the
      lowest and highest ratio beside it. It answers how separated the libraries are
      into the two karyotype groups.

      How to read: a large ratio means almost no Y signal, and a ratio near 1 means
      one X and one Y. A wide gap between lowest and highest means the libraries
      belong to both groups. The ratio is read against the sample sheet, not on its
      own.
  - component: table
    title: Sex check
    description: >-
      One row is one library at one alignment stage, with its X and Y depth,
      their ratio and the inferred sex. It answers whether the sex inferred from
      the reads matches the sample sheet.

      How to read: Sort by the X to Y ratio to see the two groups, and compare
      the inferred sex with the sheet. Look for a ratio between the groups or a
      stage that changes the call. It complements the X against Y depth scatter of
      the same output, which shows these values as a plot.

config.y_title: Mean depth on chromosome Y (reads per base)

tools.description: Aggregates the logs and reports of many bioinformatics tools into one report.
tools.name: MultiQC

outputs.description: How many reads AdapterRemoval kept, discarded or collapsed into a single merged read, and the length ladder behind it, AdapterRemoval, via MultiQC.
outputs.name: Adapter trimming and read collapsing
outputs.rawYaml:
id: multiqc_adapterremoval
name: Adapter trimming and read collapsing
origin_tool: AdapterRemoval
mode: adapterremoval
description: How many reads AdapterRemoval kept, discarded or collapsed into a single merged read, and the length ladder behind it, AdapterRemoval, via MultiQC.
find:
  path_glob: "**/multiqc/multiqc_data/multiqc.parquet"
  path_glob_alt: # nested report dirs, e.g. rnaseq multiqc/star_salmon/multiqc_report_data/
    - "**/multiqc/*_data/multiqc.parquet"
    - "**/multiqc/*/*_data/multiqc.parquet"
# reuse the bundled nf-core pipeline MultiQC parquet (not a per-module copy);
# `section` selects this module's plot anchors out of the shared report.
fixture: ../../projects/init/catalog_conformance/run_1/multiqc/multiqc_data/multiqc.parquet
renders_as:
  - component: multiqc
    section: adapterremoval
    title: Adapter trimming and read collapsing
    description: >-
      AdapterRemoval's own MultiQC plot: for each sample, how many reads were kept,
      discarded or collapsed into a single merged read. It answers how much of the
      library was lost to trimming and how much of it merged.

      How to read: A high retained share means clean libraries. A large discarded
      share points to adapter dimers or very short inserts, so check the library
      preparation. A high collapsed share is expected for short inserts and is not a
      defect.

      Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/adapterremoval

renders_as.description:
AdapterRemoval's own MultiQC plot: for each sample, how many reads were kept, discarded or collapsed into a single merged read. It answers how much of the library was lost to trimming and how much of it merged.
How to read: A high retained share means clean libraries. A large discarded share points to adapter dimers or very short inserts, so check the library preparation. A high collapsed share is expected for short inserts and is not a defect.
Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/adapterremoval
renders_as.title: Adapter trimming and read collapsing

outputs.description: ATAC-specific library quality, from ataqv, via MultiQC. The fragment-length ladder, the peak-enrichment percentiles, the MAPQ spread and the per-chromosome read distribution.
outputs.name: ATAC library quality
outputs.rawYaml:
id: multiqc_ataqv
name: ATAC library quality
origin_tool: ataqv
mode: ataqv
description: ATAC-specific library quality, from ataqv, via MultiQC. The fragment-length ladder, the peak-enrichment percentiles, the MAPQ spread and the per-chromosome read distribution.
find:
  path_glob: "**/multiqc/multiqc_data/multiqc.parquet"
  path_glob_alt: # nested report dirs, e.g. rnaseq multiqc/star_salmon/multiqc_report_data/
    - "**/multiqc/*_data/multiqc.parquet"
    - "**/multiqc/*/*_data/multiqc.parquet"
# reuse the bundled nf-core pipeline MultiQC parquet (not a per-module copy);
# `section` selects this module's plot anchors out of the shared report.
fixture: ../../projects/init/catalog_conformance/run_1/multiqc/multiqc_data/multiqc.parquet
renders_as:
  - component: multiqc
    section: ataqv
    title: ATAC library quality
    description: >-
      ataqv's own MultiQC plots: the fragment-length ladder, the peak-enrichment
      percentiles, the MAPQ spread and the per-chromosome read distribution, one
      line or bar per sample. They answer whether an ATAC library shows the expected
      nucleosomal structure and signal in peaks.

      How to read: A good library shows a nucleosome-free peak followed by mono- and
      di-nucleosome peaks, and a sharp rise of reads in peaks. A flat ladder or
      reads piled on mitochondrial or unplaced contigs point to over-transposition,
      low enrichment or contamination.

      Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/ataqv

name: Variant-calling summary
mode: summary-variants-metrics
description: >-
  Per-sample variant-calling summary (reads mapped, coverage, SNP/indel/total
  variant counts, lineage) parsed from MultiQC's summary_variants_metrics table.

recipe: multiqc/summary_metrics.py
fixture: summary_metrics.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: card
    column: pct_genome_covered_10x
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    headline: true # >=10x breadth
    title: Genome covered at 10x
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median across samples of the percent of the genome
      covered by at least 10 reads, and the box shows the spread. It answers whether
      the samples were sequenced deeply enough for confident variant calls.

      How to read: values near 100 percent mean the whole genome is callable. A
      sample far below the box has gaps, so its missing positions cannot be called
      and it deserves a look before its variants are trusted.

      Note: no pass mark is drawn, because the pipeline defines no cut-off for this
      metric.
  - component: card
    column: num_variants_total
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Variants per sample
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of variants called per sample (SNPs and
      indels together), and the box shows the spread. It answers how divergent the
      samples are from the reference.

      How to read: samples of one lineage should carry similar counts. A sample far
      above its peers may be a mixed infection or a different lineage, and one far
      below may have poor coverage.
  - component: table
    title: Variant-calling summary
    description: >-
      One row is one sample: reads mapped, coverage, SNP, indel and total variant
      counts, and lineage. It gives the exact values behind the cards and answers
      which samples stand out.

      How to read: sort by genome coverage ascending to find the weakest samples, then
      by variant count to find unusual ones. Compare with the lineage composition tile
      to see whether an outlier belongs to a minority lineage.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: num_variants_total
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: lineage
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: variants, by lineage
    title: Variants by lineage
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of variants called across all samples, and
      the bars rank the lineages that account for most of them. It answers which
      lineages carry the variant load.

      How to read: a lineage leading the ranking either has many samples or many
      variants per sample, so read it with the lineage composition tile.
  - component: card
    column: pct_reads_mapped
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    headline: true
    title: Reads mapped
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median across samples of the percent of reads that
      mapped to the reference, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much of
      each library is usable for calling.

      How to read: a high value means a clean library on the right reference. A
      sample far below the box points to host or other contamination, or to a
      reference that does not match.
  # Not a pass mark: the 80 and 90 percent lines that used to sit here had no
  # source (RULES 17), so the card shows the weakest sample and the spread instead.
  - component: card
    column: pct_genome_covered_10x
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: samples, by breadth at 10x
    title: Weakest genome breadth at 10x
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest percent of the genome covered at 10x among the
      samples, and the histogram counts samples by that breadth. It answers whether
      any sample is thinly covered.

      How to read: a tight pile near 100 percent means every sample is deeply
      covered. A tail to the left holds the samples to rerun or exclude.

      Note: no pass mark is drawn, because the pipeline defines no cut-off for this
      metric.
  - component: card
    column: lineage
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: lineage
    caption: samples, by lineage
    title: Lineage composition
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of samples, and the ring splits them by assigned
      lineage. It answers which lineages the batch contains and how evenly.

      How to read: one dominant lineage is typical of an outbreak. Many small slices
      mean a diverse batch, and a sample with no lineage assigned usually had too
      little coverage to classify.
  - component: card
    column: pct_genome_covered_1x
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Genome covered at 1x
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median across samples of the percent of the genome
      covered by at least one read, and the box shows the spread. It answers whether
      the samples reach the whole genome at all, however thinly.

      How to read: a gap between this tile and the 10x tile means regions covered
      too thinly for calling. A sample low on both has large missing stretches.

    section: truvari
    title: Structural-variant benchmark (Truvari)

      Truvari's accuracy summary per callset: precision against recall and the
      true-positive, false-positive and false-negative classes. It answers how
      accurate a structural-variant caller is against a truth set.

      How to read: Values close to one are better. A low recall means missed events
      and a low precision means false calls, and the breakdown by size shows where
      it fails.

      Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/truvari

renders_as.description:

How to read: Values close to one are better. A low recall means missed events and a low precision means false calls, and the breakdown by size shows where it fails.
Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/truvari
renders_as.title: Structural-variant benchmark (Truvari)

tools.description: Quality control for long-read sequencing: read length, read quality and yield summaries computed from a FASTQ, a sequencing summary or an alignment.
tools.name: NanoPlot

outputs.description: NanoStat's per-sample long-read summary read from the report itself: number of reads, yield, mean and median read length and quality, N50, and the longest and highest-quality read the run produced.
outputs.name: Long-read summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: nanoplot_nanostats
name: Long-read summary
mode: qc/long-read-summary
description: >-
  NanoStat's per-sample long-read summary read from the report itself: number
  of reads, yield, mean and median read length and quality, N50, and the
  longest and highest-quality read the run produced.
find:
  path_glob: "**/NanoStats.txt"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*_NanoStats.txt"
recipe: nanoplot/nanostats.py
fixture: nanostats.tsv
renders_as:
  # NanoStat publishes no pass mark for any of these summaries, so none of the
  # tiles below draws a threshold (C3 N/A). Colour is the library, the only
  # categorical column the report carries.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: read_length_n50
      color: sample
      labels: {sample: Library, read_length_n50: Read length N50 (bases)}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: read_length_n50}
    title: Read length N50 per library
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: the N50 of its read lengths, the length such that half
      of the sequenced bases sit in reads at least that long. It answers which
      libraries gave the longest reads for the sequenced yield.

      How to read: a taller bar means longer reads, which resolve repeats and
      structural variants better. Compare libraries prepared the same way, since a
      fragmentation or size selection step moves the N50 as much as the run does.
      Open the length against quality view to see whether a long library is also accurate.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median read length N50 of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a
      cut-off of NanoStat.

      Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat and
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wdecoster/nanomath/master/nanomath/nanomath.py
  - component: card
    column: n_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: the libraries with most reads
    title: Total reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of reads over every library in view, and the bars
      rank the libraries that contribute most. It answers how much sequence the run
      produced and where it came from.

      How to read: a library far below its peers is under-loaded or failed early.
      Reads are not bases, so read this next to the yield card.
  - component: card
    column: total_gigabases
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: the libraries with most yield
    headline: true
    title: Total yield (Gb)
    description: >-
      The hero number is the sequenced yield in gigabases over every library in
      view, and the bars rank the libraries by yield. It answers whether the run
      produced enough data for the planned analysis.

      How to read: compare each library with the yield you planned for. NanoStat
      sets no minimum yield, so judge it against the experiment, not a fixed number.

      Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  - component: card
    column: read_length_n50
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    headline: true
    title: Read length N50
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median N50 across libraries, and the box shows how the
      libraries spread around it. It answers how long the reads are in a typical
      library and how consistent the libraries are.

      How to read: a tight box means the libraries were prepared alike. A wide box
      or a far outlier points to a library with a different size distribution, so
      open the table to find it.
  - component: card
    column: mean_read_quality
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mean, with its spread
    title: Mean read quality
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean of the libraries' mean read quality, a Phred score
      averaged over each read's bases, and the box shows the spread between
      libraries. It answers how accurate the basecalls are overall.

      How to read: higher is better and the value depends on the pore chemistry and
      the basecaller model, so compare libraries of one run. A library well below
      its peers deserves a look at the quality ladder tab before analysis.
  - component: card
    column: mean_read_length
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mean, with its spread
    title: Mean read length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean of the libraries' mean read length in bases, and the
      box shows the spread between libraries. It answers how long a read is on
      average.

      How to read: the mean is pulled up by a few very long reads, so it sits above
      the median in a typical Nanopore library. A large gap between the two cards
      means a long tail.
  - component: card
    column: median_read_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Median read length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of the libraries' median read length in bases,
      and the box shows the spread between libraries. It answers how long the middle
      read is, which a few very long reads do not move.

      How to read: compare it with the mean and the N50. A median far below the N50
      means most reads are short while the bases sit in a few long ones.
  - component: card
    column: stdev_read_length
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mean, with its spread
    title: Read length spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean standard deviation of read length, in bases, over
      the libraries, and the box shows how it varies between them. It answers how
      uneven the read lengths are.

      How to read: a large value relative to the mean length means a broad
      distribution, typical of unsheared or transposase library preparations. A
      tight value points to a size-selected library.
  - component: card
    column: longest_read_length
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: the libraries with the longest read
    title: Longest read
    description: >-
      The hero number is the longest read in any library in view, in bases, and the
      bars rank the libraries by their own longest read. It answers how far the
      length tail reaches.

      How to read: one extreme read says little on its own, since a single chimeric
      or concatenated read can dominate it. Read it with the N50.
  - component: card
    column: median_read_quality
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Median read quality
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of the libraries' median read quality, a Phred
      score, and the box shows the spread between libraries. It answers what quality
      the typical read has.

      How to read: the median sits above the mean when a tail of poor reads drags the
      mean down. A library whose median is low as well has poor basecalls overall.
  - id: length_vs_quality
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    roles: {x: mean_read_length, y: mean_read_quality, label: sample, size: total_gigabases, color: sample}
    config:
      x_title: Mean read length (bases)
      y_title: Mean read quality (Phred)
      legend_pos: bottom
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    title: Read length against quality
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: its mean read length on the horizontal axis, its mean
      read quality on the vertical axis, with the marker sized by sequenced yield. It
      answers whether the longest libraries are also the most accurate.

      How to read: libraries in the upper right give long and accurate reads. A library
      that is long but low in quality, or accurate but short, shows the trade-off of
      its preparation; with few libraries the points are best read next to the table.
      No pass mark is drawn because NanoStat defines none.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median mean read quality of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a
      cut-off of NanoStat.

      Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  - component: table
    title: Long-read summary table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with its NanoStat summary: read count, yield, read length
      mean, median, N50 and standard deviation, read quality and the longest read. It
      answers which library to inspect or exclude.

      How to read: sort by N50, quality or yield to find the weakest library, and compare
      the mean with the median to spot a long tail.

renders_as.description:

How to read: a taller bar means longer reads, which resolve repeats and structural variants better. outputs.description: How much of each library survives a quality floor: reads, percentage and megabases above each NanoStat quality cutoff, one row per sample and cutoff. A mean quality hides whether a library is tight around it or bimodal; this ladder does not.
outputs.name: Yield above quality cutoffs
outputs.rawYaml:
id: nanoplot_nanostats_quality
name: Yield above quality cutoffs
mode: qc/quality-ladder
description: >-
  How much of each library survives a quality floor: reads, percentage and
  megabases above each NanoStat quality cutoff, one row per sample and cutoff.
  A mean quality hides whether a library is tight around it or bimodal; this
  ladder does not.
find:
  path_glob: "**/NanoStats.txt"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*_NanoStats.txt"
recipe: nanoplot/nanostats_quality.py
fixture: nanostats_quality.tsv
renders_as:
  # NanoStat reports a fixed ladder of cutoffs (Q5, Q7, Q10, Q12, Q15) and sets no
  # pass mark on it, so nothing is drawn as a threshold (C3 N/A). The ladder is
  # cumulative: the cards below read the Q10 rung, never a sum or mean over rungs.
  - id: quality_ladder
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    roles: {series: sample, x: q_cutoff, y: pct_reads}
    config:
      x_title: Quality cutoff (Phred Q)
      y_title: Reads above the cutoff (%)
      legend_pos: bottom
    title: Reads kept at each quality cutoff
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the percentage of its reads whose mean quality is above
      each cutoff of the NanoStat ladder. It answers how fast a library loses reads as
      the quality floor rises.

      How to read: a line that stays high and drops late is a library tight around a
      good quality. A line that falls early is poor, and a steep drop between two
      rungs means a bimodal library that a single mean quality hides. Pick the
      cutoff for filtering from the rung where the curve starts to fall.

      Lines and annotations: no pass mark is drawn, because NanoStat defines none. The
      rungs are the fixed cutoffs of the NanoStat report.

      Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: q_cutoff
      y: megabases
      color: sample
      barmode: group
      labels: {q_cutoff: Quality cutoff (Phred Q), megabases: Yield above the cutoff (Mb), sample: Library}
    title: Yield above each quality cutoff
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library at one cutoff: the megabases carried by reads above that
      quality. It answers how much usable sequence remains after filtering at each
      rung.

      How to read: compare bars within a cutoff to rank libraries by usable yield. A
      library with a large yield at Q5 but a small one at Q10 is mostly low-quality
      sequence.

      Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  - component: card
    column: pct_reads
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('q_cutoff') == 10"
    caption: mean, with its spread
    headline: true
    title: Reads above Q10
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean percentage of reads above quality Q10 over the
      libraries, and the box shows the spread between them. It answers what share of
      reads survive a common basecall quality floor.

      How to read: a high value with a tight box means consistent libraries. Q10 is one
      rung of the ladder NanoStat reports and not a pass mark, so open the ladder
      line chart to see other rungs.

      Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
  - component: card
    column: megabases
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "col('q_cutoff') == 10"
    caption: the libraries with most yield above Q10
    title: Yield above Q10 (Mb)
    description: >-
      The hero number is the megabases carried by reads above Q10 over every library
      in view, and the bars rank the libraries by it. It answers how much sequence
      is left after filtering at that quality.

      How to read: the ladder is cumulative, so a single rung is read, not a sum across
      rungs. A library that leads on total yield but not here has lower accuracy.
  - component: card
    column: n_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "col('q_cutoff') == 10"
    caption: the libraries with most reads above Q10
    title: Reads above Q10
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of reads above Q10 over every library in view, and
      the bars rank the libraries by it. It answers how many reads pass that quality
      floor.

      How to read: compare it with the total read count of the summary tab. A large
      loss means many low-quality reads.
  - component: table
    title: Quality ladder table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library at one quality cutoff: reads, percentage of reads and
      megabases above it. It answers the exact numbers behind the ladder tiles.

      How to read: filter on one cutoff to compare libraries, or on one library to see
      its whole ladder.

renders_as.description:
Each line is a library: the percentage of its reads whose mean quality is above each cutoff of the NanoStat ladder. It answers how fast a library loses reads as the quality floor rises.
How to read: a line that stays high and drops late is a library tight around a good quality. A line that falls early is poor, and a steep drop between two rungs means a bimodal library that a single mean quality hides. Pick the cutoff for filtering from the rung where the curve starts to fall.
Lines and annotations: no pass mark is drawn, because NanoStat defines none. The rungs are the fixed cutoffs of the NanoStat report.
Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat
renders_as.title: Reads kept at each quality cutoff

renders_as.description:
Each bar is a library at one cutoff: the megabases carried by reads above that quality. It answers how much usable sequence remains after filtering at each rung.
How to read: compare bars within a cutoff to rank libraries by usable yield. A library with a large yield at Q5 but a small one at Q10 is mostly low-quality sequence.
Source: https://github.com/wdecoster/nanostat

renders_as.caption: the libraries with most reads above Q10
renders_as.description:

outputs.name: Candidate neoepitopes
outputs.rawYaml:
id: neo_neoepitopes
name: Candidate neoepitopes
mode: neo
description: >-
  Neo's scored neoepitopes, one row per tumor and candidate: the event that
  creates it (missense, frameshift, in-frame indel, fusion), the gene, the
  novel amino acids between their flanks, the peptides it yields, its RNA
  support and expected and effective expression, and the copy number of the
  variant behind it.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.neo.neoepitope.tsv"
recipe: neo/neoepitopes.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several tumors.
fixture: neoepitopes.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: neoepitope_count
    component: card
    column: gene
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: variant_type
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    title: Candidate neoepitopes
    caption: candidates, by event type
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of candidate neoepitopes Neo scored, with the
      number of distinct genes behind them, and the bars rank the event types that
      create them. It answers how large the neoepitope pool is and which kind of
      event feeds it.

      How to read: compare the event types to see which of them contribute most.
      Very few candidates point to a quiet tumor or to missing inputs, so check the
      variant calls and the HLA typing first.

      Note: Neo predicts neoepitopes from DNA events only and uses RNA to weigh
      them, not to find them.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/neo/README.md
  - id: neoepitope_tpm_spread
    component: card
    column: effective_tpm
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    title: Expression of the candidates
    caption: median, with its range
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median effective expression of the candidates, with
      the lowest and highest value beside it. It answers whether the candidates sit
      in genes that are expressed in the tumor.

      How to read: a median near zero means most candidates are silent, so few of
      them can be presented. Effective expression is long-tailed, so the range
      matters more than the centre when you pick candidates to follow up.

      Note: effective expression is estimated by Neo from the sample's RNA
      transcript expression and the cohort median expression, and is empty when no
      RNA was run.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/neo/README.md
  - id: neoepitope_source_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: variant_type
      color: sample
      labels: {variant_type: Event type, sample: Tumor}
    title: Candidates by event type
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the candidate neoepitopes created by one kind of event
      (missense, frameshift, in-frame indel or fusion), split by tumor. It answers
      which events the neoepitope pool comes from.

      How to read: a pool made almost entirely of one event type is expected when
      that event dominates the tumor's mutations. Compare tumors to spot one whose
      mix differs, then open the table to inspect its candidates.
  - id: neoepitope_expression_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    roles: {x: variant_copy_number, y: effective_tpm, label: gene, color: variant_type}
    title: Copy number against expression
    config:
      x_title: Copy number of the variant
      y_title: Effective expression (TPM)
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a candidate neoepitope: the copy number of the variant behind
      it on the horizontal axis and its effective expression on the vertical axis,
      coloured by event type. It answers which candidates come from variants that
      many tumor cells carry and that are also expressed.

      How to read: points in the upper right are the strongest candidates to follow
      up, since the variant is present in most copies and the gene is expressed.
      Points on the floor are not expressed, so their peptides are unlikely to be
      presented. Open the table to inspect the labelled genes.

      Note: Neo weighs each candidate's presentation likelihood by its expression.
      No cut-off is drawn on either axis, because none is sourced.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/neo/README.md
  - id: neoepitope_table
    component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: neoepitope_id
    title: Neoepitope candidates
    description: >-
      Each row is a candidate neoepitope: the event that creates it, its gene, the
      novel amino acids between their flanks, the number of peptides it yields, its
      RNA support, its expected and effective expression and the copy number behind
      it. It answers which candidates to follow up and lets a row selection filter
      the rest of the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by effective expression, then filter by event type. A
      candidate with RNA fragments and a high copy number is better supported than
      one found in the DNA alone.
