outputs.description: Per-sample clade assignment + sequence QC.
outputs.name: Clade assignment
outputs.rawYaml:
id: nextclade_report
name: Clade assignment
mode: run
description: Per-sample clade assignment + sequence QC.
find: { path_glob: "**/nextclade/*.csv" }
recipe: nextclade/nextclade_results.py
fixture: report.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: the clade calls are coloured by the overall QC status of each sequence.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: clade
      color: qc_overallStatus
      labels: {clade: Clade, qc_overallStatus: QC status}
    title: Clade calls by QC status
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the sequences assigned to a Nextclade clade, split by their
      overall quality status. It answers which clades the run found and whether the
      calls rest on good sequences.

      How to read: a clade made of good sequences is a call to trust. Bars that are
      mostly mediocre or bad mean the clade rests on incomplete or odd sequences, so
      check the missing bases and the coverage before reporting them.

      Lines and annotations: the colour is the overall QC status, good for a score
      from 0 to 29, mediocre from 30 to 99 and bad from 100, the bands Nextclade
      defines for its combined quality score.

      Source: https://docs.nextstrain.org/projects/nextclade/en/stable/user/algorithm/06-quality-control.html
  - component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Genome coverage
    caption: average, with quartiles
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average share of the reference genome covered by the
      sequences, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how complete the
      consensus genomes are.

      How to read: a box piled near one means complete genomes. A long tail towards
      zero marks sequences with large missing stretches, which weaken both the clade
      call and the mutation list. Open the table to see which ones.
  - component: table
    title: Clade assignment table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sequence with its clade, the Pango lineage Nextclade assigns,
      the counts of substitutions, deletions, insertions, frame shifts and missing
      or ambiguous bases, its coverage and its quality score and status. It answers
      which sequences need attention and what each one carries.

      How to read: sort by quality status to find the sequences to inspect, then
      read the missing base count to see whether coverage explains the flag.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: clade
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: clade
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    title: Clades found
    caption: sequences, by clade
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct clades, with the number of sequences
      beside it, and the bars rank the clades by how many sequences carry them. It
      answers how diverse the run is and which clades dominate.

      How to read: one dominant clade is a single outbreak lineage in circulation,
      several of similar size is a mixed collection. A clade seen once is worth
      checking for a quality problem before it is reported.
  - component: card
    column: totalMissing
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Missing bases
    caption: median, with the distribution
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of missing bases (N) per sequence, with
      the lowest and highest value beside it, and the histogram shows how they are
      spread. It answers how much of each genome the sequencing failed to call.

      How to read: a pile at low values is a clean run. A long tail of sequences with
      thousands of missing bases is expected for low viral loads or failed amplicons,
      and these sequences get a worse quality status.

      Source: https://docs.nextstrain.org/projects/nextclade/en/stable/user/output-files/04-results-tsv.html

outputs.description: The coverage each library would reach at a given sequencing effort, rebuilt from the gamma model Nonpareil publishes in its merged summary. outputs.name: Coverage curve
outputs.rawYaml:
id: nonpareil_curves
name: Coverage curve
mode: set/curve
description: >-
  The coverage each library would reach at a given sequencing effort, rebuilt from
  the gamma model Nonpareil publishes in its merged summary. One curve per
  sequencing library, decimated to 200 points, with the effort actually sequenced
  and the effort projected for 95 percent coverage carried on every row.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/nonpareil/set
find:
  path_glob: "**/nonpareil/*all_samples.tsv"
recipe: nonpareil/curves.py
fixture: curves.tsv
renders_as:
  # Long series x effort x coverage -> the `profile` kind, the same three columns
  # as a preseq complexity curve or a TSS enrichment profile.
  - id: coverage_curve
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Coverage against sequencing effort
    roles: {series: library, x: sequencing_effort, y: coverage}
    config:
      log_x: true
      x_title: Sequencing effort (bp)
      y_title: Estimated average coverage
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sequencing library: the average coverage of its metagenome that
      the reads reach (vertical axis) as the sequencing effort grows (horizontal axis,
      log scale). It answers how much more sequencing a library needs before it
      describes its community.

      How to read: a curve that flattens near the top has captured most of the
      community, and extra sequencing adds little. A curve that still climbs steeply
      is far from covered, and the projected effort in the summary tiles says how much
      deeper to go. Compare curves of the same habitat only, since diversity sets the
      slope.

      Lines and annotations: the curves are redrawn from Nonpareil's fitted model
      (a gamma distribution on the log of the effort) and not from the measured
      redundancy points, which nf-core does not publish. Nonpareil projects effort for
      95 percent coverage by default.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lmrodriguezr/nonpareil/master/utils/Nonpareil/R/Nonpareil.R
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24123672/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sequencing_effort
      y: coverage
      color: library
      log_x: true
      labels: {sequencing_effort: Sequencing effort (bp), coverage: Estimated average coverage, library: Library}
    title: Coverage curves, static view
    description: >-
      Each line is a sequencing library: the estimated average coverage against the
      sequencing effort on a log scale. It answers the same question as the interactive
      curve tile, in a plain figure that can be exported.

      How to read: lines reaching the top at a lower effort belong to simpler
      communities. A line that ends low means the run stopped well short of covering
      the community.

      Note: the lines are rebuilt from Nonpareil's fitted model, not from measured points.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lmrodriguezr/nonpareil/master/utils/Nonpareil/R/Nonpareil.R
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24123672/
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: library
    title: Library
    description: >-
      Filters the tiles to one or more sequencing libraries.
  - component: table
    title: Curve points
    description: >-
      Each row is one point of a library's rebuilt coverage curve, with the sequencing
      effort, the estimated coverage, the effort actually sequenced and the effort
      projected for 95 percent coverage. It answers the exact values behind the curves.

      How to read: filter by library and compare its observed effort with its projected
      effort to see how far the run is from the target.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lmrodriguezr/nonpareil/master/utils/Nonpareil/R/Nonpareil.R

outputs.description: Nonpareil's fitted numbers, one row per sequencing library: the share of the metagenome the reads already reach, the effort projected for 95 percent coverage, how many times deeper that is than the run went, and the Nonpareil diversity index. The card strip the coverage curve is read against.
outputs.name: Coverage and diversity per library
outputs.rawYaml:
id: nonpareil_summary
name: Coverage and diversity per library
mode: set/summary
description: >-
  Nonpareil's fitted numbers, one row per sequencing library: the share of the
  metagenome the reads already reach, the effort projected for 95 percent coverage,
  how many times deeper that is than the run went, and the Nonpareil diversity
  index. The card strip the coverage curve is read against.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/nonpareil/set
find:
  path_glob: "**/nonpareil/*all_samples.tsv"
recipe: nonpareil/summary.py
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # 95% is the coverage Nonpareil projects effort for by default (Nonpareil.R, the
  # LRstar slot), the "nearly complete coverage" the tool is run to reach. It is a
  # target of the method, not a QC pass mark, and the card says so.
  - component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.95
    threshold_direction: min
    caption: average coverage, against the 95 percent target
    title: Average coverage
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average share of the metagenome that the reads already
      reach, with the lowest and highest library. It answers how completely the
      libraries describe their communities.

      How to read: a value near 1 means more sequencing would add few new sequences. A
      low value means a large part of the community is still unseen, so check the
      effort multiple card for how much deeper to go.

      Lines and annotations: the marker is 95 percent coverage, the default coverage
      for which Nonpareil projects the effort needed. It is the target of the method
      and not a pass or fail rule.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lmrodriguezr/nonpareil/master/utils/Nonpareil/R/Nonpareil.R
  - component: card
    column: diversity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Sequence diversity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median Nonpareil diversity index (Nd) of the libraries,
      and the box shows their spread. It answers how diverse the sequenced communities
      are.

      How to read: the index is on a log scale, so a higher value means a more diverse
      community that needs more sequencing to cover. Compare libraries of the same
      habitat.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29657970/
  # The effort multiple spans orders of magnitude between a nearly covered library
  # and a very diverse one, so a box would draw a flat line: show the extremes.
  - component: card
    column: effort_multiple
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: grid
    caption: median, with the shallowest and the deepest need
    title: Effort still needed
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of how many times deeper a library must be
      sequenced to reach 95 percent coverage, with the smallest and largest multiple.
      It answers how far the run is from the projected target.

      How to read: a multiple close to 1 means the library is nearly there. A large
      multiple marks a diverse community that the current depth only samples.

      Lines and annotations: the target is the 95 percent coverage Nonpareil projects
      by default, and the multiple is its projected effort divided by the effort
      sequenced.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lmrodriguezr/nonpareil/master/utils/Nonpareil/R/Nonpareil.R
  - component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: samples, with the libraries counted
    title: Samples and libraries
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of samples with a Nonpareil fit, and the strip
      counts their sequencing libraries. It answers how many libraries the coverage
      figures are drawn from.

      How to read: more libraries than samples means a sample was sequenced in several
      runs, each with its own curve.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: scatter
    dict_kwargs:
      x: diversity
      y: coverage
      color: sample
      size: effort_multiple
      labels: {diversity: Nonpareil diversity (Nd), coverage: Estimated average coverage, sample: Sample, effort_multiple: Effort multiple}
    title: Coverage against diversity
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: coverage, label: Median coverage}
    description: >-
      Each point is a sequencing library: its diversity index on the horizontal axis,
      its estimated coverage on the vertical axis, coloured by sample and sized by the
      effort still needed. It answers whether the libraries that are least covered are
      the most diverse.

      How to read: points at the lower right are diverse communities that are far from
      covered, the ones to sequence deeper. Large points need the most extra effort.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median estimated coverage of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not
      a cut-off of Nonpareil.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29657970/
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: coverage
    title: Coverage range
    description: >-
      Filters the tiles to libraries whose estimated coverage falls inside the chosen
      range.
  - component: table
    title: Coverage and diversity table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sequencing library with its fitted model: coverage, sequencing
      effort, projected effort for 95 percent coverage, the effort multiple and the
      diversity index. It answers the exact numbers behind each card.

      How to read: sort by effort multiple to find the libraries that need the most
      extra sequencing.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29657970/

tools.description: OpenMS is an open-source software C++ library for LC-MS data management and analyses.
tools.name: OpenMS

outputs.description: Target PSMs accepted per raw file as the target-decoy q-value threshold on the raw Comet Xcorr is relaxed from 0 to 10%, with the Xcorr cut-off at each threshold. A steep early rise is a file with good spectra.
outputs.name: Identifications against FDR
outputs.rawYaml:
id: openms_comet_fdr_curve
name: Identifications against FDR
mode: search/comet-fdr-curve
description: >-
  Target PSMs accepted per raw file as the target-decoy q-value threshold on
  the raw Comet Xcorr is relaxed from 0 to 10%, with the Xcorr cut-off at each
  threshold. A steep early rise is a file with good spectra.
find: { path_glob: "**/*_pin.tsv" }
recipe: openms/comet_fdr_curve.py
fixture: comet_fdr_curve.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: fdr_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Accepted PSMs against FDR
    roles: { series: run_id, x: q_value, y: accepted_psms }
    config:
      x_title: Target-decoy q-value
      y_title: Accepted target PSMs
      reference_x: 0.01
      reference_label: 1% FDR
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a raw file: the number of target peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs)
      accepted as the target-decoy q-value threshold on the raw Comet score is
      relaxed. It answers how many identifications each file yields at a given error
      rate.

      How to read: a curve that rises steeply and early belongs to a file with good
      spectra, while a flat curve has few confident matches and points to an
      acquisition or search-space problem. Compare files: one far below its peers is
      the one to investigate.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical marker is the 1% false discovery rate, the
      nf-core/mhcquant default fdr_threshold at which peptide hits are selected. This
      curve applies it to target-decoy competition on the raw Comet score, from the
      table the pipeline hands to its rescoring engine (Percolator by default). Its
      counts therefore differ from the final peptide table, which is rescored and
      filtered at peptide level by default.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/mhcquant/master/nextflow_schema.json
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17327847/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    title: Accepted PSMs by FDR threshold
    dict_kwargs:
      x: q_value
      y: accepted_psms
      color: run_id
      labels: {q_value: Target-decoy q-value, accepted_psms: Accepted target PSMs, run_id: Raw file}
    description: >-
      Each line is a raw file: the accepted target PSMs at each q-value threshold. It
      answers how the files compare across the whole 0 to 10% range, not only at one
      cut-off.

      How to read: lines that run in parallel differ in depth but not in quality. Lines
      that cross differ in how their score distributions separate targets from
      decoys.
  - component: table
    title: Accepted PSMs per threshold
    description: >-
      Each row is a threshold on one raw file: the q-value, the number of accepted
      target PSMs and the Comet score cut-off that gives it. It answers which score
      cut-off corresponds to a given error rate.

      How to read: pick the row nearest the error rate you report at and read its
      score cut-off.

outputs.description: One row per raw file: spectra searched, target and decoy PSMs, PSMs accepted at 1% and 5% target-decoy FDR on the raw Comet Xcorr, the identification rate, median target and decoy Xcorr, and the median precursor mass error. The search's own yield, before rescoring.
outputs.name: Comet search yield per raw file
outputs.rawYaml:
id: openms_comet_psms
name: Comet search yield per raw file
mode: search/comet-psms
description: >-
  One row per raw file: spectra searched, target and decoy PSMs, PSMs accepted
  at 1% and 5% target-decoy FDR on the raw Comet Xcorr, the identification rate,
  median target and decoy Xcorr, and the median precursor mass error. The
  search's own yield, before rescoring.
find: { path_glob: "**/*_pin.tsv" }
recipe: openms/comet_psms.py
fixture: comet_psms.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: card
    column: psms_1pct_fdr
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with the spread
    title: PSMs at 1% FDR
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of target PSMs accepted at a 1% target-decoy
      false discovery rate on the raw Comet score, with the spread across raw files in
      the box. It answers how productive the search is before rescoring.

      How to read: a tight box means files of similar yield. A file far below the others
      has an acquisition or search-space problem rather than a rescoring one.

      Note: the 1% is the nf-core/mhcquant default fdr_threshold,
      applied here by this module to the raw Comet score rather than after rescoring.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/mhcquant/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: identification_rate
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with the spread
    title: Identification rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of searched spectra that give a target PSM
      passing the filter, as a fraction between 0 and 1, with the spread across raw
      files in the box. It answers how efficiently the acquired spectra are
      explained.

      How to read: a low rate with many spectra searched points to noisy spectra or a
      search space that does not fit the sample. Search engines publish no universal
      cut-off for this rate.
  - component: card
    column: median_mass_error_ppm
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with the spread
    title: Precursor mass error
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median precursor mass error in parts per million across raw
      files, with the spread in the box. It answers whether the instrument is
      calibrated.

      How to read: values close to zero with a tight spread mean good calibration. A
      file shifted away from the others needs recalibration or a wider search
      tolerance.
  # C1: each point is a raw file, coloured by its own id (no grouping column).
  - id: target_decoy_separation
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Target and decoy score separation
    roles: { x: median_xcorr_decoy, y: median_xcorr_target, label: run_id, size: spectra_searched, color: run_id }
    config:
      x_title: Median decoy Xcorr
      y_title: Median target Xcorr
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: Target = decoy
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a raw file: the median Comet score of its decoy matches
      (horizontal) against that of its target matches (vertical), sized by the number
      of spectra searched. It answers how well the search separates real matches from
      random ones.

      How to read: points well above the diagonal have target scores clearly higher
      than decoy scores, which is what a good search looks like. A point near the
      diagonal has a search that cannot tell targets from decoys, so its identifications
      are unreliable.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, where target and decoy scores are
      equal, a reference defined by the plot and not a tool cut-off. The target-decoy
      strategy it rests on is described in the source.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17327847/
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: run_id
    title: Search yield per raw file
    description: >-
      Each row is a raw file: spectra searched, target and decoy PSMs, the PSMs
      accepted at 1% and 5% FDR, the identification rate, the median scores, the mass
      error and the peptide length. It answers which files to look at first.

      How to read: sort by the 1% FDR count to rank the files, then click a row to
      filter the other tiles to that file.

How to read: sort by the 1% FDR count to rank the files, then click a row to filter the other tiles to that file.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: optitype_genotypes
name: HLA class I genotypes
mode: genotypes
description: >-
  OptiType's optimal HLA class I genotype of each sample, melted long: one row
  per sample, locus (HLA-A, -B, -C) and haplotype, with the two-field allele
  normalised to HLA-A*02:01 (the spelling of the epitopeprediction tables, so an
  allele pick selects the same string there), its allele group, the zygosity of
  the locus, and the reads and objective of the solution.
find:
  path_glob: "**/optitype/*/*_result.tsv"
recipe: optitype/genotypes.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 12 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several donors.
fixture: genotypes.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: OptiType types HLA class I only (A, B, C), so hla_class is constant by design.
  # Sample by locus, each cell split into its two haplotypes; an allele click
  # selects on the normalised allele. Coloured by allele group (a hue family per
  # first field).
  - id: genotype_grid
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: allele_grid
    title: HLA class I genotype grid
    roles: { sample_id: sample_id, locus: locus, allele: allele, haplotype: haplotype, category: hla_class, value: objective, reads: reads }
    config:
      allele_group_col: allele_group
      zygosity_col: zygosity
      value_label: Solver objective
      reads_label: Reads explained
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample and each column an HLA class I locus (A, B, C); a cell is
      split in two halves, one per haplotype, coloured by allele group. It answers
      which alleles every sample carries and which loci are homozygous.

      How to read: alleles of one group share a hue, so a family recurring across the
      cohort stands out. A merged cell with a marker is a homozygous locus; the side
      bars give the reads the genotype explains and the solver objective. A sample with
      few reads deserves a second look before its alleles are used downstream.

      Note: OptiType documents no minimum number of reads for a reliable call, so none
      is drawn.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FRED-2/OptiType/master/README.md
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25143287/
  - id: allele_count
    component: card
    column: allele
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: locus
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    title: Distinct alleles
    caption: distinct alleles, by locus
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct alleles across the samples in view, and
      the second figure the count of allele calls. The bars rank the loci by distinct
      alleles. It answers how diverse the cohort is.

      How to read: the locus with the longest bar carries the most alleles in this
      cohort. A small cohort naturally shows few alleles, so read it with the sample
      count.
  - id: homozygous_loci
    component: card
    column: locus
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [mode]
    filter_expr: "(col('zygosity') == 'Homozygous') & (col('haplotype') == 1)"
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: locus
    headline: true
    title: Homozygous loci
    caption: homozygous loci, by locus
    description: >-
      Each unit is a homozygous locus in a sample, counted once, and the bar splits
      them by locus. It answers where the cohort loses allelic diversity.

      How to read: homozygosity reduces the peptides a patient can present, so a locus
      with many homozygous calls matters for epitope prediction. A typing error also
      looks homozygous when one allele is under-covered, so check the reads in the grid.
  - id: allele_calls
    component: card
    column: zygosity
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [mode]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: zygosity
    title: Allele calls by zygosity
    caption: allele calls, by zygosity
    description: >-
      Each unit is an allele call and the bar shows the share that is homozygous or
      heterozygous. It answers how often the loci are heterozygous in this cohort.

      How to read: compare the homozygous share with what you expect of the cohort. A
      high share can be real or a typing artefact, so confirm it against the reads in
      the grid.
  # Allele frequency within each locus: one trace per locus, each normalised
  # over its own calls (two per sample).
  - id: allele_frequency
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: allele
      color: locus
      histnorm: percent
      labels: {allele: Allele, locus: Locus}
    title: Allele frequency per locus
    description: >-
      Each bar is an allele, with its share of the calls of its locus. It answers which
      alleles are common in the cohort.

      How to read: a few dominant alleles per locus are typical. The frequencies
      describe this cohort only, since a small number of samples gives coarse shares.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: allele
    title: Allele
    description: >-
      Filters the tiles to samples carrying the chosen alleles.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: locus
    title: Locus
    description: >-
      Filters the tiles to one or more HLA class I loci.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: zygosity
    title: Zygosity
    description: >-
      Filters the tiles to homozygous or heterozygous calls.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: call_id
    title: Allele call table
    description: >-
      Each row is an allele call: one sample, locus and haplotype, with the allele,
      allele group, zygosity, reads and solver objective. It answers the exact alleles
      to carry into epitope prediction and lets a row selection filter the rest of the
      dashboard.

      How to read: the allele is spelled as in the epitope prediction tables, so a
      selected allele matches the same string there.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: optitype_summary
name: HLA typing per sample
mode: summary
description: >-
  One row per sample from OptiType's optimal solution: the HLA-A, -B and -C
  allele pairs, the distinct alleles as the ;-separated list an
  epitopeprediction samplesheet takes, the loci typed and how many are
  homozygous or heterozygous, the reads the genotype explains, the objective and
  the objective per read (about 1 minus beta per heterozygous locus, so it reads
  the zygosity rather than the fit), and with --enumerations the number of
  solutions and the objective gap to the runner-up.
find:
  path_glob: "**/optitype/*/*_result.tsv"
recipe: optitype/summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 3 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several donors.
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: typing_reads
    component: card
    column: reads
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    title: Reads explained by the genotype
    caption: reads, quartiles over samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of reads that map to the HLA reference and
      support the chosen genotype, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much
      evidence each typing rests on.

      How to read: a sample far below the others has little evidence and its alleles are
      less certain. OptiType documents no minimum number of reads, so judge it against
      the rest of the cohort.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FRED-2/OptiType/master/README.md
  - id: objective_per_read
    component: card
    column: objective_per_read
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Objective per read
    caption: objective per read, quartiles over samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of the solver objective divided by the reads
      explained, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much of the read evidence
      the solution keeps at full weight.

      How to read: the ratio is lower by about the homozygosity parameter beta for each
      heterozygous locus, so it reflects zygosity more than the quality of the fit. Do
      not read a low value as a bad typing on its own.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FRED-2/OptiType/master/README.md
  - id: heterozygous_loci
    component: card
    column: heterozygous_loci
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 3
    title: Heterozygous loci per sample
    caption: median out of 3 typed loci
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of heterozygous loci among the three typed
      (A, B, C), shown against 3. It answers how heterozygous the cohort is at class I.

      How to read: three means every locus carries two different alleles. Lower values
      mean homozygous loci, which narrow the set of alleles that can present peptides.
  # The objective sits under the diagonal by beta per heterozygous locus, so
  # the points split by zygosity.
  - id: reads_objective
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Solver objective against reads
    roles: { x: reads, y: objective, label: sample_id, color: homozygous_class }
    config:
      x_title: Reads explained
      y_title: Solver objective
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: objective equals reads
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample: the reads its genotype explains against the objective
      value the solver reached, coloured by how many loci are homozygous. It answers
      whether the objective follows the read support.

      How to read: points lie close to the diagonal, a little below it for each
      heterozygous locus, so the colour groups follow the zygosity. A point far below its
      group would be unexpected and worth checking.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is the identity, where the objective equals
      the reads explained. It is a mathematical reference and not a cut-off; OptiType
      sets the gap with its homozygosity parameter beta.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FRED-2/OptiType/master/README.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample_id
      y: reads
      color: homozygous_class
      labels: {sample_id: Sample, reads: Reads explained, homozygous_class: Homozygous loci}
    title: Reads per sample
    reference_lines: [{axis: y, stat: median, column: reads}]
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample and its height the reads that support its genotype, coloured

renders_as:
  # The renderer enumerates the binary species columns itself.
  - id: orthogroup_upset
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: upset_plot
    title: Orthogroups shared between species
    config:
      color_intersections_by: degree
      show_values: true
    description: >-
      Each bar is a set of species and counts the orthogroups that contain genes from
      exactly those species, with the dots below naming the set. It answers which
      orthogroups every species shares, which a clade shares and which belong to a
      single species.

      How to read: the bar with every species joined is the core set that all genomes
      carry. Tall bars for a subset of species point to a clade-specific gene family,
      and a species with a large single bar holds many genes found nowhere else, which
      is also what a fragmented or contaminated proteome looks like.

    component: card

      and the strip gives the median and largest number of genes in an orthogroup. It
      answers how many gene families the species form and how many are single copy.

      How to read: a large single-copy share means few duplications, which suits a
      species tree. A large multi-copy share points to expanded families.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidemms/OrthoFinder/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: n_genomes
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: average, with its spread
    title: Species per orthogroup
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average count of species that hold genes of an
      orthogroup, and the box shows the spread. It answers how widely shared the gene
      families are.

      How to read: an average close to the number of species means most families are
      shared by all of them. A low average with a long tail points to many
      species-specific families.

    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: copy_class
    title: Copy class
    description: >-

id: orthofinder_species_stats
name: Orthogroup assignment per species
mode: comparative-statistics/per-species
description: >-
  One row per species from OrthoFinder's per-species statistics: genes in its
  proteome, the share placed in orthogroups, the orthogroups it takes part in
  and the ones it holds alone. A proteome whose genes stay unassigned far more

find:

renders_as:
  - id: assigned_share
    component: card
    column: genes_in_orthogroups_pct
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: lowest species, with the spread
    title: Genes placed in orthogroups
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest percentage of a species' genes that OrthoFinder
      placed in an orthogroup, and the box shows how the species spread. It answers
      whether every proteome is well represented in the orthogroups.

      How to read: values close to 100 percent mean nearly every gene has a relative.
      A species well below the others carries unassigned genes, and the OrthoFinder
      tutorial names poor species sampling around it as the most likely cause.

      Note: the tutorial likes to see at least 80 percent of all genes assigned, a
      guide for the run as a whole rather than a pass mark per species, so no line is
      drawn.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidemms/OrthoFinder/master/README.md
      and https://davidemms.github.io/orthofinder_tutorials/exploring-orthofinders-results.html

    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: grid
    caption: total, with the median and largest species
    title: Species-specific orthogroups
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of orthogroups made entirely of genes from one
      species, with the median and the largest count among species. It answers how much
      of the gene content is unique to a single genome.

      How to read: a species far above the median holds many families found nowhere
      else, which is real novelty or contamination and fragmentation. Open the table to
      see which species it is.

outputs.name: Lineage report
outputs.rawYaml:
id: pangolin_report
name: Lineage report
mode: run
description: Per-sample PANGO lineage report.
find: { filename: "*.pangolin.csv" }
recipe: pangolin/pangolin_lineages.py
fixture: report.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: the lineage calls are coloured by the QC status of each sequence.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: lineage
      color: qc_status
      labels: {lineage: Pango lineage, qc_status: QC status}
    title: Lineage calls by QC status
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the sequences assigned to a Pango lineage, split by whether they
      passed Pangolin's sequence quality check. It answers which lineages the run
      found and how many calls rest on usable sequences.

      How to read: a lineage made of passing sequences is a call to trust. Failed
      sequences get an unassigned lineage, so a large unassigned bar is a data quality
      problem and not a new variant.

      Lines and annotations: the colour is the QC status, which fails a sequence with
      more than 30 percent N or shorter than 25000 bases, the defaults of Pangolin's
      max-ambig and min-length options.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cov-lineages/pangolin/master/pangolin/command.py
  - component: table
    title: Lineage report
    description: >-
      Each row is a sequence with its Pango lineage, the conflict and ambiguity
      scores, the scorpio call and its support, the Pangolin version, a note and the
      QC status. It answers which lineage each sequence got and how reliable the call
      is.

      How to read: a high ambiguity score means few sites were imputed, so the call is
      well supported. Read the note for alternative placements when the conflict score
      is above zero.

      Source: https://cov-lineages.org/resources/pangolin/output.html
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: lineage
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: lineage
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    title: Lineages found
    caption: sequences, by lineage
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct Pango lineages, with the number of
      sequences beside it, and the bars rank the lineages by how many sequences carry
      them. It answers how diverse the run is and which lineages dominate.

      How to read: one dominant lineage is a single outbreak in circulation. Several
      lineages of similar size suggest a mixed collection, and an unassigned bar means
      sequences that failed the quality check.
  - component: card
    column: qc_status
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: qc_status
    title: Sequences by QC status
    caption: sequences, by QC status
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of sequences, with the number of distinct statuses
      beside it, and the ring splits them into those that passed and failed Pangolin's
      quality check. It answers how many sequences can be trusted for lineage calling.

      How to read: a ring that is mostly pass is a healthy run. A large failed share
      means many sequences are too short or hold too many N bases, so check the
      sequencing coverage.

      Lines and annotations: a sequence fails with more than 30 percent N or fewer than
      25000 bases, the defaults of Pangolin's max-ambig and min-length options.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cov-lineages/pangolin/master/pangolin/command.py

id: pbccs_zmw_outcomes
name: CCS outcome per library
mode: pacbio/ccs-yield
description: >-
  Where every ZMW of a library went in CCS, as a share of its input ZMWs:
  passed, or the filter that removed it (too few passes, SNR, draft
  failures, heteroduplexes). Stacks to 100 % per library.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.report.json"
recipe: pbccs/zmw_outcomes.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 12 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several libraries.
fixture: zmw_outcomes.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: ccs_outcome_bars
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: ZMW outcome per library
    roles: {sample_id: library, taxon: outcome, rank: rank, abundance: pct_of_input}
    config:
      default_rank: CCS outcome
      normalise_to_one: true
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library and each segment the outcome of its ZMWs: passed, or the
      filter that removed them, as a share of the ZMWs read. It answers where the ZMWs
      of each library went.

      How to read: a large Passed segment is a productive library. A large too-few-passes
      segment means short movies or long inserts, while a growing SNR or draft-failure
      segment points to the chemistry or the polymerase. Switch to counts to see the
      absolute numbers.

      Source: https://ccs.how/faq/fail-reads.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: ZMW outcome share per library
    dict_kwargs:
      x: library
      y: pct_of_input
      color: outcome
      labels: {library: Library, pct_of_input: Share of input ZMWs (%), outcome: Outcome}
    description: >-
      Each segment is an outcome of a library: its share of the ZMWs that went into
      CCS. It answers how the libraries compare on each filter.

      How to read: compare the same colour across libraries to see which one loses more
      ZMWs to a filter. The segments of a library add up to 100%.
  - component: table
    title: CCS outcomes per library
    description: >-
      Each row is an outcome of one library: the number of ZMWs and their share of the
      ZMWs read. It answers exactly how many ZMWs each filter removed.

id: picard_markduplicates_metrics
name: Duplication metrics
description: >-
  Reads examined, duplicates flagged and the resulting duplication rate from a
  Picard MarkDuplicates report, with the sample read off the report name because
  Picard's own LIBRARY field is whatever the read group said. Low-input ancient
  libraries run far higher duplication than a modern shotgun library at the same
  depth, which is what makes this the companion of the complexity curve.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.metrics"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*.metrics.txt"
    - "**/*.MarkDuplicates.metrics.txt"
recipe: picard/markduplicates_metrics.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 2 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several libraries.
fixture: markduplicates_metrics.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: one colour per library, the only grouping column the table has.
  - id: duplication_vs_depth
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Duplication rate against depth
    roles: {x: reads_after_dedup, y: percent_duplication, label: sample, color: sample, size: duplicate_reads}
    config:
      x_title: Reads left after duplicate removal
      y_title: Duplication rate (fraction of mapped reads)
      legend_pos: bottom
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: the reads left after duplicate removal (horizontal)
      against its duplication rate (vertical), sized by the number of duplicates. It
      answers whether a library is deep because it is rich or only because it is
      duplicated.

      How to read: a point high and to the left is a library that is mostly duplicates
      with little unique data left, so more sequencing buys little. A point low and to
      the right is a complex library. The cited Picard metric definitions state no
      cut-off for an acceptable duplication rate.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median duplication rate of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of Picard.

      Source: https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/picard-metric-definitions.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Duplication rate per library
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: percent_duplication
      color: sample
      title: Duplication rate per library
      labels: {sample: Library, percent_duplication: Duplication rate (fraction of mapped reads)}
    reference_lines: [{axis: y, stat: median, column: percent_duplication}]
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: the fraction of its mapped sequence that MarkDuplicates
      flagged as duplicate. It answers which libraries are the most duplicated.

      How to read: a tall bar is a library with low molecular complexity, common with
      low-input or ancient DNA. Compare it with the complexity curve to see whether
      deeper sequencing would add new molecules.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median duplication rate of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of Picard.

      Source: https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/picard-metric-definitions.html
  - component: card
    column: percent_duplication
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mean, with the spread
    title: Duplication rate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean duplication rate, a fraction between 0 and 1, with the
      spread across libraries in the box. It answers how much of the data is redundant.

      How to read: a wide box means libraries of very different complexity. A high
      mean means resequencing will mostly return duplicates. The cited Picard metric
      definitions state no cut-off for this rate.

      Source: https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/picard-metric-definitions.html
  - component: card
    column: duplicate_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: per library, the median and the largest
    title: Duplicate reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of reads flagged as duplicates (unpaired plus
      both reads of each duplicate pair), with the median and the largest library next
      to it. It answers how much sequencing was spent on duplicates.

      How to read: a maximum far above the median is a library that wasted most of its
      reads. Compare it with the duplication rate to separate a deep library from a
      duplicated one.
  - component: card
    column: reads_after_dedup
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: per library, the median and the smallest
    title: Reads after duplicate removal
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of examined reads left once duplicates are removed,
      with the median and the smallest library next to it. It answers how much unique
      data the downstream analysis has.

      How to read: the smallest library is the one that limits a joint analysis. Coverage
      downstream rests on this number rather than the raw depth.
  - component: card
    column: unpaired_reads_examined
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: per library, the median and the largest
    title: Single-end reads examined
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of single-end reads MarkDuplicates examined, with the
      median and the largest library next to it. It answers how much input the
      duplication rate rests on.

      How to read: collapsed or single-end libraries report their reads here, while
      paired libraries report read pairs in the table.

      Source: https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/picard-metric-definitions.html
  - component: table
    title: Duplication metrics per library
    description: >-
      Each row is a library: the reads examined, the duplicates flagged, the reads left
      after removal, the duplication rate and Picard's library size estimate. It answers
      how redundant each library is.

      How to read: the estimated library size is the number of unique molecules Picard

tools.description: Software for predicting library complexity and genome coverage in high- throughput sequencing.
tools.name: Preseq

outputs.description: How many distinct molecules each library would yield at a given sequencing depth, with the confidence interval preseq puts around that extrapolation. A curve still climbing at the depth already sequenced means resequencing buys new material; one that has flattened means the library is exhausted.
outputs.name: Library complexity curve
outputs.rawYaml:
id: preseq_complexity_curve
name: Library complexity curve
mode: complexity-curve
description: >-
  How many distinct molecules each library would yield at a given sequencing
  depth, with the confidence interval preseq puts around that extrapolation. A curve
  still climbing at the depth already sequenced means resequencing buys new
  material; one that has flattened means the library is exhausted.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.ccurve.txt"
recipe: preseq/complexity_curve.py
fixture: complexity_curve.tsv
renders_as:
  # The curve with its interval as a ribbon. This is the whole reason the tool
  # has an entry of its own: MultiQC's preseq panel plots expected_distinct
  # alone and drops the two CI columns, so the width of the extrapolation is
  # only readable here.
  # C3 N/A: preseq publishes no cut-off; the data-defined reference is the
  # identity (every read distinct), described in the text.
  - id: complexity_ribbon
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Expected distinct molecules by depth
    roles: {series: sample, x: total_reads, y: expected_distinct, lower: lower_ci, upper: upper_ci}
    config:
      x_title: Total reads sequenced
      y_title: Expected distinct molecules
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a library: the number of distinct molecules preseq expects to see
      at a given sequencing depth, with the confidence interval as a band. It answers
      whether sequencing deeper would still add new molecules.

      How to read: a curve still rising steeply means the library is far from
      exhausted and resequencing pays off. A curve that has flattened is exhausted, so
      more reads return duplicates. A wide band means the extrapolation is uncertain,
      so be careful recommending deeper sequencing from it.

      Note: preseq extrapolates from the reads already sequenced, and the further it
      goes past that depth the less reliable it is. It publishes no cut-off for a
      sufficient library.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23435259/
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/smithlabcode/preseq/master/README.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    title: Expected distinct molecules by depth
    dict_kwargs:
      x: total_reads
      y: expected_distinct
      color: sample
      title: Expected distinct molecules by sequencing depth
      labels: {total_reads: Total reads sequenced, expected_distinct: Expected distinct molecules, sample: Library}
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the expected distinct molecules at each sequencing depth,
      without the interval. It answers how the libraries compare in complexity.

      How to read: a line that stays closer to the diagonal at low depth has few
      duplicates so far. Lines that part early belong to libraries of very different
      complexity.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23435259/
  - component: card
    column: expected_distinct
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [q3, median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: deepest prediction, with the upper quartile and the median
    title: Deepest expected yield
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest expected distinct molecule count of any library at
      the deepest depth extrapolated, with the upper quartile and the median over all
      points next to it. It answers how rich the best library could become.

      How to read: the value depends on how far preseq extrapolated, so compare
      libraries only at the same depth.
  - component: card
    column: lower_ci
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: conservative yield, with the median
    title: Conservative expected yield
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest lower bound of the confidence interval, the yield
      preseq is confident the library reaches, with the median next to it. It answers
      what yield can be promised with caution.

      How to read: the gap between this and the deepest expected yield is the
      uncertainty of the extrapolation.
  - component: card
    column: ci_width
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, average]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: widest interval, with the median and the mean
    title: Interval width
    description: >-
      The hero number is the widest confidence interval of any library, in molecules,
      with the median and the mean next to it. It answers how uncertain the
      extrapolation is.

      How to read: the width grows with depth, so a very wide interval means the
      extrapolation went far past the sequenced depth. Treat those predictions as
      indicative only.
  - component: card
    column: total_reads
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: deepest depth, with the median
    title: Extrapolated depth
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest sequencing depth preseq extrapolated to, with the
      median depth of the grid next to it. It answers how far the predictions go.

      How to read: all the curve past the depth you really sequenced is a prediction.
      Read the interval width there before relying on it.
  - component: table
    title: Complexity curve points
    description: >-
      Each row is a depth of one library: the expected distinct molecules, the
      confidence interval and its width. It answers the expected yield at an exact
      depth.

      How to read: find the depth you plan to sequence to and read the interval, not
      only the expected value.

How to read: a curve still rising steeply means the library is far from exhausted and resequencing pays off. A curve that has flattened is exhausted, so more reads return duplicates. A wide band means the extrapolation is uncertain, so be careful recommending deeper sequencing from it.

outputs.name: Bin locus map
outputs.rawYaml:
id: prokka_gene_track
name: Bin locus map
mode: gene-track
description: >-
  Where the genes sit along a bin's contigs, as an arrow per coding sequence,
  transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA. Pick one bin and one contig and the tile
  becomes a locus map: operon structure, strand switches, and the ribosomal RNA
  operon whose presence decides the bin's MIMAG tier.
find:
  path_glob: "**/Prokka/**/*.gff"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/prokka/**/*.gff"
recipe: prokka/gene_track.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several feature classes.
fixture: gene_track.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: locus_map
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: gene_arrow_track
    title: Gene arrows along a contig
    roles: {contig: contig, feature_id: feature_id, start: start, end: end,
            strand: strand, class: ftype, label: gene}
    description: >-
      Each arrow is a coding sequence, transfer RNA or ribosomal RNA placed on a contig
      of one bin, pointing in the direction of the gene and coloured by feature class.
      It answers how the genes of a bin are organised.

      How to read: pick one bin and one contig. Runs of arrows on one strand are
      operons, a switch of direction marks a strand change, and a cluster of ribosomal
      RNA arrows is the rRNA operon that decides the MIMAG tier of the bin.

      Note: Prokka renames contigs to internal identifiers, so the coordinates are valid
      within a bin only.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tseemann/prokka/master/README.md
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: length_bp
      color: ftype
      barmode: overlay
      opacity: 0.7
      labels: {length_bp: Feature length (bp), ftype: Feature class}
    title: Feature length by class
    description: >-
      Each bar counts features in a length bin, one overlaid histogram per feature
      class. It answers whether the lengths of coding sequences, tRNAs and rRNAs look
      as expected.

      How to read: tRNAs are short, rRNAs long and coding sequences in between, so
      each class forms its own peak. A coding sequence peak shifted to short lengths
      points to fragmented genes in a poor assembly.
  - component: card
    column: ftype
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: ftype
    title: Annotated features
    caption: features, by class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of annotated features and the ring splits them by
      class (coding sequence, tRNA, rRNA); the second figure is the number of classes.
      It answers what the annotation is made of.

      How to read: coding sequences dominate, so look for the small RNA slices. A bin
      with no rRNA slice cannot reach the MIMAG high-quality tier.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: card
    column: length_bp
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Feature length
    caption: length, quartiles over features
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median feature length in base pairs and the box shows the
      spread. It answers how long the typical annotated feature is.

      How to read: a very short median means fragmented genes. Filter to one class to
      read it for coding sequences only.
  - component: card
    column: product
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: binner
    top_n_count: 4
    title: Distinct gene products
    caption: distinct products, by binner
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct gene product names and the second figure
      the count of features; the bars rank binners by distinct products. It answers how
      functionally diverse the annotation is.

      How to read: many features with few distinct products means mostly hypothetical
      proteins, common in uncharacterised bins.
  - component: table
    title: Annotated feature table
    description: >-
      Each row is a feature with its bin, contig, class, coordinates, strand, length,
      gene name and product. It answers which features lie where.

      How to read: filter by class or product, for example to list every tRNA of a bin.

outputs.name: Bin annotation summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: prokka_summary
name: Bin annotation summary
mode: summary
description: >-
  What Prokka found in each bin: coding sequences, transfer RNAs, ribosomal
  RNAs and the gene density that follows from them. The RNA counts are the half
  of the MIMAG high-quality standard that completeness cannot answer, so a bin
  that looks finished on the completeness axis and carries no ribosomal RNA is
  visible here and nowhere else.
find:
  path_glob: "**/Prokka/**/*.txt"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/prokka/**/*.txt"
recipe: prokka/summary.py
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: density_vs_size
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Coding density against bin size
    roles: {x: bases, y: cds_per_mbp, label: bin_id, color: binner, size: cds}
    config:
      x_title: Bin size (bp)
      y_title: Coding sequences per Mbp
      log_x: true
      legend_pos: bottom
      top_n_labels: 5
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a bin: its size in base pairs and its number of coding sequences per
      megabase, sized by total coding sequences and coloured by the binner that produced
      it. It answers which bins annotate as plausible genomes.

      How to read: bins of similar density cluster together, and outliers are worth a
      look. Very low density in a large bin suggests missed genes or non-coding content;
      compare binners by their colour groups.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median coding density of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      Prokka. Prokka and MIMAG publish no density cut-off.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tseemann/prokka/master/README.md
  - id: trna_vs_rrna
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: tRNAs against rRNAs per bin
    roles: {x: trna, y: rrna, label: bin_id, color: assembler, size: bases}
    config:
      x_title: Transfer RNAs
      y_title: Ribosomal RNAs
      reference_line: vertical
      reference_value: 18
      reference_label: MIMAG, at least 18 tRNAs
      legend_pos: bottom
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a bin: its count of transfer RNAs and of ribosomal RNAs, sized by
      bin size and coloured by the assembler. It answers which bins carry the RNA genes
      of a high-quality draft.

      How to read: the MIMAG high-quality draft needs the 5S, 16S and 23S rRNA genes
      and at least 18 tRNAs, so look right of the line and at three or more rRNAs.
      Completeness alone cannot say this.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical line is the MIMAG minimum of 18 tRNAs. The
      rRNA requirement is one gene each of 5S, 16S and 23S, so a bin needs at least
      three rRNA features; the plot cannot tell which rRNA genes they are.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: cds_per_mbp
      color: assembler
      barmode: overlay
      opacity: 0.6
      labels: {cds_per_mbp: Coding sequences per Mbp, assembler: Assembler}
    title: Gene density per assembler
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: x, stat: median, column: cds_per_mbp}
    description: >-
      Each bar counts bins in a coding density bin, one overlaid histogram per
      assembler. It answers whether an assembler yields bins with systematically fewer
      annotated genes.

      How to read: histograms centred on the same value mean comparable annotation. A
      shifted one points to fragmented genes from that assembler.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median coding density of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of
      Prokka.
  - component: card
    column: cds
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: binner
    title: Coding sequences
    caption: coding sequences, by binner
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of coding sequences over the bins in view and the
      bar splits it by binner. It answers which binner contributes most of the
      annotated genes.

      How to read: a large share is partly a matter of how many bins the binner
      produced, so read it with the bin count card.
  - component: card
    column: cds_per_mbp
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Coding density
    caption: density, quartiles over bins
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of coding sequences per megabase and the box
      shows the spread. It answers how gene-dense the bins are.

      How to read: a box far from the others, or a very low median, signals bins with
      missed genes or large non-coding content. Prokka and MIMAG publish no density
      cut-off.
  - component: card
    column: trna
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 18
    threshold_direction: min
    title: Transfer RNAs
    caption: median against the MIMAG minimum of 18
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of tRNAs per bin, compared with the MIMAG
      minimum of 18 for a high-quality draft. It answers whether bins carry enough tRNA
      genes.

      How to read: below 18 a bin cannot reach the high-quality tier. Open the scatter
      to see which bins fall short.

      Lines and annotations: the threshold is the MIMAG minimum of 18 tRNAs.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: card
    column: rrna
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, q3]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Ribosomal RNAs
    caption: rRNAs, distribution over bins
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest count of rRNA features in a bin and the histogram
      shows the distribution over bins. It answers how many bins have any rRNA at all.

      How to read: a bin with no rRNA feature cannot reach the high-quality tier. That
      tier needs the 5S, 16S and 23S genes, so a bin needs at least three rRNA
      features.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  - component: card
    column: assembler
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: assembler
    top_n_count: 4
    title: Annotated bins
    caption: bins, by assembler
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of annotated bins and the second figure the number
      of assemblers; the bars rank assemblers by bins. It answers how the bins are
      spread over assemblers.

      How to read: an assembler with few bins may simply have produced few usable
      ones, so compare with the density and RNA tiles.
  - component: table
    title: Bin annotation table
    description: >-
      Each row is a bin with its assembler, binner, contigs, bases, coding sequences,
      tRNAs, rRNAs, tmRNAs and whether it meets the MIMAG RNA criteria. It answers
      which bins pass the annotation half of the high-quality standard.

      How to read: sort by tRNA or rRNA count, and check the MIMAG column. It is empty
      when the GFF, which names the rRNA genes, was not provided.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/

outputs.description: One row per domain span from every database the run searched: the four HMM libraries through hmmsearch (domains passing HMMER's default inclusion E-value) and the InterProScan member databases. Spans follow the domain table convention (entity, start, end, label, source), so a sequence track draws them as a domain lane and a 3D structure colours by them.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: proteinannotator_domains
name: Protein domains, all databases
mode: protein/domains
description: >-
  One row per domain span from every database the run searched: the four HMM
  libraries through hmmsearch (domains passing HMMER's default inclusion
  E-value) and the InterProScan member databases. Spans follow the domain
  table convention (entity, start, end, label, source), so a sequence track
  draws them as a domain lane and a 3D structure colours by them.
find:
  path_glob: "**/domain_annotation/*/*.domtbl.gz"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/functional_annotation/interproscan/*/*.tsv"
recipe: proteinannotator/domains.py
fixture: domains.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: a record card draws one record as labelled fields, no mark to colour.
  - id: domain_record
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: record_card
    title: Domain record
    roles: {id: domain_id, title: label}
    config:
      labels:
        span: Span (residues)
        protein_length: Protein length (residues)
        evalue: E-value
        neg_log10_evalue: -log10 E-value
        hmm_coverage: Fraction of the HMM covered
        hmm_from: HMM start
        hmm_to: HMM end
        hmm_length: HMM length
    description: >-
      The card shows one domain span as labelled fields: its family, database,
      position, length, E-value and the part of the family model it matches. It
      answers what a single domain hit is.

      How to read: select a row in the table to fill it. A small fraction of the HMM
      covered means a partial match to the family, which deserves a second look in
      another database.
  # Significance against span length: long confident spans are whole-protein
  # families, short confident ones are motifs, weak ones of any length are
  # borderline calls worth checking in a second database.
  # HMMER's inclusion cut-off is an E-value of 0.01 (-log10 = 2), verified in its User Guide.
  - id: domain_significance
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Domain significance against length
    roles: {x: span, y: neg_log10_evalue, label: label, color: database}
    config:
      x_title: Domain span (residues)
      y_title: -log10 E-value
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_value: 2
      reference_label: E-value 0.01
      top_n_labels: 8
    description: >-
      Each point is a domain span: its length in residues on the horizontal axis and
      the minus log10 of its independent E-value on the vertical axis, coloured by the
      database that reports it. It answers which domains are long and confident and
      which are weak.

      How to read: points high on the plot are strong matches. Long, high spans are
      whole-protein families and short, high ones are motifs. Weak points of any
      length are borderline, so check them in a second database.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an E-value of 0.01, the default
      inclusion threshold of HMMER (per-target and per-domain). HMMER applies it to the
      full-sequence and conditional E-values, so a few points can sit just below the
      line. InterProScan matches pass the filters of their own member database, not
      one shared E-value.

      Sources: http://eddylab.org/software/hmmer/Userguide.pdf and
      https://github.com/ebi-pf-team/interproscan-docs/blob/master/docs/FAQ.rst
  # The domains of every database on one backbone per protein. The HMM span columns are null
  # for InterProScan rows, which draw as complete matches.
  - id: domain_architecture
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: domain_architecture
    title: Domain architecture
    roles: {entity: entity, start: start, end: end, label: label, protein_length: protein_length, hmm_from: hmm_from, hmm_to: hmm_to, hmm_length: hmm_length, hmm_coverage: hmm_coverage, evalue: evalue, source: source, description: description, accession: accession}
    description: >-
      Each lane is a protein drawn to scale, with one block per domain coloured by
      family and placed at its start and end. It answers which domains a protein
      carries and in what order.

      How to read: proteins with the same block order share an architecture, so they
      probably share a function. A block drawn partly filled matches only part of its
      family model, and overlapping blocks from different databases describe the same
      region. Hover a block for its database, accession and E-value.

      Lines and annotations: a partly filled block shows the fraction of the family
      HMM that the match covers, from the hmmsearch alignment. No cut-off is drawn on
      this tile.
  - id: domain_count
    component: card
    column: entity
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: database
    top_n_count: 5
    caption: domains, by database
    title: Annotated proteins
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of proteins with at least one domain, the second
      number counts every domain span, and the bars rank the databases by their domain
      spans. It answers how much annotation there is and which database provides
      most.

      How to read: a database with a long bar contributes most spans, which is not
      the same as the best coverage, so check the coverage heatmap.
  - id: domain_families
    component: card
    column: label
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: source
    top_n_count: 5
    caption: domains, by source
    title: Distinct families
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct domain families, the second number
      counts every domain span, and the bars rank the sources by their spans. It
      answers how varied the annotation is and which library or member database
      reports most.

      How to read: many spans over few families means a few families repeat across
      the proteins.
  - id: domain_span
    component: card
    column: span
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Domain length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median domain span in residues, and the box shows the
      spread. It answers how long a typical domain is.

      How to read: a short median with a long upper whisker means mostly motifs with a
      few whole-protein families. Open the significance plot to see which ones are
      confident.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: database
      y: span
      color: database
      labels: {database: Database, span: Domain span (residues)}
    title: Domain length per database
    description: >-
      Each box is the spread of domain spans in residues for one database. It answers
      whether the databases describe domains of different sizes.

      How to read: a database with longer spans describes whole families, and one with
      short spans reports motifs or fragments. Compare boxes before combining counts
      across databases.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: domain_id
    title: Domain table
    description: >-
      Each row is one domain span from one database, with its position, length, E-value
      and the part of the family model it matches. It answers the details behind every
      tile of this view, and a row selection fills the domain record.

      How to read: sort by E-value to list the strongest matches, or filter by
      database to compare sources.
