outputs.rawYaml:
id: proteinannotator_proteins
name: Protein annotation summary
mode: protein/summary
description: >-
  One row per protein of the filtered FASTA: its length, domain hits per
  database and how many databases annotate it, the share of its residues
  covered by at least one domain, the best domain by E-value, and the helix,
  strand and coil shares S4PRED predicts. Unannotated proteins keep their row.
find:
  path_glob: "**/qc/*/*.fasta"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/qc/*/*.faa"
recipe: proteinannotator/proteins.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 3 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several proteins, samples and annotation statuses.
fixture: proteins.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: a record card draws one record as labelled fields, no mark to colour.
  - id: protein_record
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: record_card
    title: Protein record
    roles: {id: entity, title: top_domain}
    config:
      labels:
        length: Length (residues)
        annotation_status: Annotation status
        domain_hits: Domain hits
        databases_hit: Databases with a hit
        annotated_residues: Residues covered by a domain
        annotated_pct: Residues covered by a domain (%)
        top_domain: Best domain
        top_domain_database: Best domain database
        top_domain_evalue: Best domain E-value
        helix_pct: Helix (%)
        strand_pct: Strand (%)
        coil_pct: Coil (%)
    description: >-
      The card shows one protein as labelled fields: its length, domain hits, how many
      databases annotate it, the share of its residues covered and the predicted
      secondary structure. It answers what is known about a single protein.

      How to read: select a row in the table or a point in the scatter to fill it. A
      protein with few databases and a low covered share is poorly described.
  # Length against annotated share: short, fully covered proteins are single
  # domain; long, poorly covered ones carry regions no database describes.
  - id: length_vs_cover
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Length against annotated share
    roles: {x: length, y: annotated_pct, label: entity, color: top_domain_database}
    config:
      x_title: Protein length (residues)
      y_title: Residues covered by a domain (%)
      top_n_labels: 8
    description: >-
      Each point is a protein: its length in residues against the percentage of its
      residues covered by at least one domain, coloured by the database of its best
      domain. It answers which proteins are well described and which carry long
      unannotated regions.

      How to read: short proteins at full coverage are single-domain proteins. Long
      proteins with low coverage carry regions no searched database describes, which
      makes them candidates for new domains or for a different database. Points
      without a best domain have no colour.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn, because no published rule defines a
      sufficient coverage.
  - id: protein_count
    component: card
    column: domain_hits
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: annotation_status
    top_n_count: 2
    caption: proteins, by annotation status
    title: Domain hits
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of domain hits over the proteins, with the
      median per protein below it, and the bars rank the proteins by annotation
      status. It answers how much annotation there is and how many proteins have
      none.

      How to read: a long unannotated bar means many proteins no database describes.
      Open the scatter to see which ones are long.
  - id: protein_length
    component: card
    column: length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Protein length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median protein length in residues, and the box shows the
      spread. It answers how long the proteins are.

      How to read: a very wide spread mixes short peptides with large multidomain
      proteins, which have different annotation rates.
  - id: annotated_cover
    component: card
    column: annotated_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Residues covered by a domain
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of a protein's residues covered by at
      least one domain, and the box shows the spread. It answers how completely the
      proteins are described.

      How to read: a high median means most of each protein is explained. A box
      reaching down to zero marks proteins with no annotation.
  - id: databases_per_protein
    component: card
    column: databases_hit
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Databases per protein
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of databases with a hit on a protein, and the
      box shows the spread. It answers how many independent sources describe a typical
      protein.

      How to read: a higher count means the annotation is corroborated. A box at one
      means most proteins rest on a single source.
  - id: helix_share
    component: card
    column: helix_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Helix content
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of residues S4PRED predicts as helix,
      and the box shows the spread. It answers how helical the proteins are.

      How to read: a wide spread mixes helical and non-helical proteins. Compare with
      the strand share to classify the fold.
  - id: strand_share
    component: card
    column: strand_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Strand content
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of residues S4PRED predicts as strand,
      and the box shows the spread. It answers how much beta structure the proteins
      carry.

      How to read: a wide spread mixes beta-rich and beta-poor proteins. Compare with
      the helix share to classify the fold.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: length
      color: annotation_status
      labels: {length: Protein length (residues), annotation_status: Annotation status}
    title: Protein length distribution
    description: >-
      Each bar counts proteins in a length bin, split by annotation status. It answers
      whether unannotated proteins differ in length from the annotated ones.

      How to read: unannotated proteins piled at short lengths are often fragments or
      small peptides with no family. Unannotated proteins spread across all lengths
      point to missing database coverage.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: entity
    title: Protein table
    description: >-
      Each row is a protein with its length, domain hits per database, annotated share,
      best domain and predicted secondary structure shares. It answers the exact values
      behind every tile of this view, and a row selection fills the protein record.

      How to read: sort by annotated share to find the poorly described proteins, or
      filter by status.

renders_as.description:

renders_as.description:
Each point is a protein: its length in residues against the percentage of its residues covered by at least one domain, coloured by the database of its best domain. It answers which proteins are well described and which carry long unannotated regions.
How to read: short proteins at full coverage are single-domain proteins. Long proteins with low coverage carry regions no searched database describes, which makes them candidates for new domains or for a different database. Points without a best domain have no colour.
Lines and annotations: none are drawn, because no published rule defines a sufficient coverage.

renders_as.caption: proteins, by annotation status
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total count of domain hits over the proteins, with the median per protein below it, and the bars rank the proteins by annotation status. It answers how much annotation there is and how many proteins have none.
How to read: a long unannotated bar means many proteins no database describes. Open the scatter to see which ones are long.

renders_as.caption: median, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median protein length in residues, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long the proteins are.
How to read: a very wide spread mixes short peptides with large multidomain proteins, which have different annotation rates.
renders_as.title: Protein length

renders_as.caption: median, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median percentage of a protein's residues covered by at least one domain, and the box shows the spread. It answers how completely the proteins are described.
How to read: a high median means most of each protein is explained. A box reaching down to zero marks proteins with no annotation.
renders_as.title: Residues covered by a domain

renders_as.caption: median, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median count of databases with a hit on a protein, and the box shows the spread. It answers how many independent sources describe a typical protein.
How to read: a higher count means the annotation is corroborated. A box at one means most proteins rest on a single source.
renders_as.title: Databases per protein

renders_as.caption: median, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median percentage of residues S4PRED predicts as helix, and the box shows the spread. It answers how helical the proteins are.
How to read: a wide spread mixes helical and non-helical proteins. Compare with the strand share to classify the fold.
renders_as.title: Helix content

renders_as.caption: median, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median percentage of residues S4PRED predicts as strand, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much beta structure the proteins carry.
How to read: a wide spread mixes beta-rich and beta-poor proteins. Compare with the helix share to classify the fold.
renders_as.title: Strand content

renders_as.description:
Each bar counts proteins in a length bin, split by annotation status. It answers whether unannotated proteins differ in length from the annotated ones.
How to read: unannotated proteins piled at short lengths are often fragments or small peptides with no family. Unannotated proteins spread across all lengths point to missing database coverage.

renders_as.description:

How to read: sort by annotated share to find the poorly described proteins, or filter by status.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: proteinannotator_residues
name: Residue table (sequence, structure, domains)
mode: protein/residues
description: >-
  One row per residue of every protein: the amino acid, the S4PRED state as
  the category and its probability as the value, the best domain covering the
  residue and how many domains overlap there, and the protein's full sequence.
  The structure tile folds the shown protein from the sequence column and
  colours it by domain; the sequence track draws the state and domain lanes.
  The structure tile (predicted_structure, kind molecule_3d, structure_source:
  resolve) makes an external call: it sends the protein sequence to a public
  service (ESMFold on ESM Atlas), and stays off unless an administrator sets
  DEPICTIO_STRUCTURE_RESOLVER_ENABLED.
find:
  path_glob: "**/qc/*/*.fasta"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/s4pred/*/ss2/*.ss2"
recipe: proteinannotator/residues.py
fixture: residues.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: residue_sequence_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sequence_track
    title: Sequence, structure and domains
    roles: {position: position, entity: entity, residue: residue, category: category, value: value}
    config:
      value_label: S4PRED probability
    description: >-
      Each position is one residue of the shown protein, with the amino acid letter,
      the secondary structure state S4PRED predicts as a coloured lane and its
      probability as a line, plus a lane for the domains. It answers where the
      helices, strands and domains lie along the sequence.

      How to read: a high probability means a confident state, and a low one marks an
      uncertain stretch. Domains that coincide with helix or strand runs point to a
      folded region, and coil over a long unannotated stretch suggests a linker or a
      disordered region. Select a residue to follow it on the structure.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The probability line is the S4PRED
      probability of the predicted state at each residue.
  # C1: the structure is coloured by domain through `category`.
  - id: predicted_structure
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: molecule_3d
    title: Predicted structure coloured by domain
    roles: {position: position, entity: entity, category: domain, sequence: sequence}
    description: >-
      The protein is folded from its sequence and each residue is coloured by the
      best domain that covers it. It answers where in three dimensions the domains
      sit.

      How to read: domains that form compact blocks are folded units. Residues without
      a domain keep the neutral colour, so a large neutral region is a part no
      database describes. The structure is a prediction, so treat it as a guide and
      not as a measurement.

      Note: the structure is resolved by an external service, ESMFold on ESM Atlas, and
      stays off unless an administrator enables the resolver.
  - id: residue_count
    component: card
    column: position
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: category
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: residues, by predicted state
    title: Residues
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of residues in view, the second number is the
      highest position and so the longest protein, and the bars rank the predicted
      secondary structure states by residue count. It answers how much sequence is
      covered and how it divides between helix, strand and coil.

      How to read: coil is usually the largest class. A balance shifted to helix or
      strand points to a structured protein.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: domains_here
      color: category
      labels: {domains_here: Overlapping domains at the residue, category: Predicted state}
    title: Domain overlap per residue
    description: >-
      Each bar counts residues by the number of domains that overlap at them, split by
      predicted structure state. It answers how crowded the annotation is.

      How to read: most residues carry zero or one domain. A tail of residues under
      many domains marks regions several databases describe, or overlapping
      annotations of one family.
  - component: table
    columns: [entity, sample, position, residue, category, value, domain, domain_database, domains_here]
    title: Residue table
    description: >-
      Each row is one residue of a protein with its amino acid, predicted structure
      state and probability, best covering domain and the number of overlapping
      domains. It answers the exact annotation of any residue.

      How to read: filter to a protein, then sort by position to read it along the
      sequence.

    aggregations: [median, max]

    headline: true
    caption: kept proteins per sample
    title: Proteins kept
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of sequences kept after the length and
      duplicate filter, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the
      histogram shows the samples. It answers how much sequence enters the annotation.

      How to read: a sample far below the others lost most of its sequences to the
      filter, so compare it with the removed count.
  - id: kept_residues
    component: card
    column: kept_residues
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: kept residues per sample
    title: Residues kept

      The hero number is the total count of residues in the kept sequences, with the
      median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It
      answers how large the annotated sequence set is.

      was kept.
  - id: removed_sequences
    component: card
    column: removed_sequences
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: removed sequences per sample
    title: Sequences removed
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of sequences the length and duplicate filter
      removed, with the median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram
      shows the samples. It answers how much input was discarded.

      How to read: a sample with many removed sequences has many duplicates or
      sequences outside the length limits. Check the pipeline's minimum and maximum
      length settings.
  - id: annotated_proteins
    component: card
    column: annotated_proteins
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: annotated proteins per sample
    title: Proteins annotated
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of proteins with at least one domain, with the
      median and largest per sample below it, and the histogram shows the samples. It
      answers how many proteins the databases describe.

      annotation.
  - id: annotated_share
    component: card
    column: annotated_protein_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Share of proteins annotated
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of a sample's proteins that carry at
      least one domain, and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how
      well the databases cover the sequences.

      databases. Samples far below the others deserve a look at the input and at the
      databases that were skipped.

    component: card
    column: mean_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Mean protein length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over the samples of their mean protein length in
      residues, and the box shows the spread. It answers how long the proteins are.

    column: domain_hits

    aggregations: [median, max]

id: proteinfamilies_family_members
name: Family members
mode: families/members
description: >-
  One row per member of every family roster: the family, the sample, whether
  the family is new or an extended existing one, whether the member is the
  representative, and from the full alignment its identity to the
  representative, the share of the representative it covers and its length.
find:
  path_glob: "**/family_reps/*/*.tsv"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/update_families/family_reps/*/*.tsv"
recipe: proteinfamilies/family_members.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several families and origins.
fixture: family_members.tsv
renders_as:
  # Fragments sit left (low coverage), divergent members low (low identity).
  - id: member_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Member coverage against identity
    roles: {x: coverage, y: identity, label: member_id, color: origin, size: length}
    config:
      x_title: Share of the representative covered
      y_title: Identity to the representative
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a member sequence of a family: the share of the representative it
      covers against its identity to the representative, coloured by whether the family is
      new or an updated existing one and sized by length. It answers which members are
      fragments and which are divergent.

      How to read: well-behaved members sit top right. Fragments sit to the left, and
      divergent members, which may be false recruits, sit low. The pipeline recruits only
      members covering at least 90% of the family model length by default, so a member
      far left deserves a look.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/proteinfamilies/2.5.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: members_count
    component: card
    column: family
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: members, with the families they belong to
    title: Family members
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of members over the families in view, and the second
      number is the count of families. It answers how many sequences the families hold.

      How to read: divide the members by the families to get the average family size.
      Filter to one family to list its members in the table.
  - id: member_identity
    component: card
    column: identity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Member identity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median identity of members to their family representative,
      and the box shows the spread. It answers how similar the members are to the
      representative.

      How to read: families built from distant homologs are expected to have a modest
      identity, since the clustering identity default is low. A long box means some
      members are far from the representative.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/proteinfamilies/2.5.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: member_coverage
    component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Member coverage
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of the representative that members cover, and
      the box shows the spread. It answers how complete the members are.

      How to read: values near one mean members span the whole family. A long lower tail
      means fragments, which the scatter shows one by one.
  - id: member_length
    component: card
    column: length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Member length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median ungapped length of members in residues, and the box
      shows the spread. It answers how long the family sequences are.

      How to read: lengths within one family should be close. Filter to a family to check
      that, since pooled families of different domains differ widely.
  - id: identity_box
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: family
      y: identity
      color: origin
      labels: {family: Family, identity: Identity to the representative, origin: Origin}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: identity}
    title: Member identity per family
    description: >-
      Each box is a family: the spread of its members' identity to the representative,
      coloured by whether the family is new or updated. It answers which families are
      tight and which are diverse.

      How to read: a high, short box is a tight family. A low or long box is a diverse
      one, a candidate for a split or a second look.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median identity to the
      representative of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it
      follows the filters), not a cut-off of the pipeline.
  - component: table
    title: Family member table
    description: >-
      Each row is a member sequence with its family, origin, identity, coverage and
      length. It answers the exact values behind the scatter and the cards.

      How to read: filter to a family and sort by coverage to list its fragments.

outputs.name: Protein families
outputs.rawYaml:
id: proteinfamilies_family_metadata
name: Protein families
mode: families/summary
description: >-
  One row per family of every sample: whether the run built it or extended an
  existing one, its member count and representative (id, length, sequence),
  the seed its HMM was built from and the members recruited beyond it, the HMM
  length and effective sequence number, and the full alignment's width, mean
  identity and coverage of the members to the representative and mean residue
  conservation.
find:
  path_glob: "**/family_reps/*/*_meta_mqc.csv"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/update_families/family_reps/*/*_meta_mqc.csv"
recipe: proteinfamilies/family_metadata.py
fixture: family_metadata.tsv
renders_as:
  # Big families spread left to right; a low point is a family whose members
  # agree on few residues, a candidate for a second look or a split.
  - id: family_landscape
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Family size against conservation
    roles: {x: size, y: mean_conservation, label: family, color: origin, size: representative_length}
    config:
      x_title: Member sequences
      y_title: Mean residue conservation
      top_n_labels: 5
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a family: its number of member sequences against the mean
      conservation of its residues, coloured by whether it is new or an updated existing
      family and sized by the representative length. It answers which families are big and
      which are well conserved.

      How to read: big families spread to the right. A low point is a family whose members
      agree on few residues, a candidate for a second look or a split. A small, highly
      conserved family is a tight group of close homologs.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median mean residue conservation of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of the pipeline.
  - id: families_total
    component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: compact
    headline: true
    caption: families, with the samples they come from
    title: Protein families
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of families built or updated, and the second number is
      the count of samples they come from. It answers how many families the run produced.

      How to read: few families from a large input usually means the minimum cluster size
      was high. Lower it to get more families.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/proteinfamilies/2.5.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: members_total
    component: card
    column: size
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    headline: true
    caption: members, with the largest family
    title: Family members
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of member sequences over all families, and the second
      number is the size of the largest family. It answers how many sequences the families
      hold and how skewed they are.

      How to read: a largest family far above the average means one family dominates.
      Open the scatter to see how the others spread.
  - id: family_size
    component: card
    column: size
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: median, with the smallest and largest
    title: Family size
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median number of member sequences per family, with the
      smallest and largest family beside it. It answers how big a typical family is and
      how wide the range is.

      How to read: sizes span a wide range, so a median close to the minimum means many
      small families and a few big ones.
  - id: representative_length
    component: card
    column: representative_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Representative length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median length of the family representatives in residues, and
      the box shows the spread. It answers how long the proteins of the families are.

      How to read: short representatives are often single domains and long ones multi-domain
      proteins or fragments. A very short value can mark fragmentary families.
  - id: family_identity
    component: card
    column: mean_identity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Family identity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of each family's mean identity of members to the
      representative, and the box shows the spread. It answers how similar the family
      members are.

      How to read: the pipeline clusters distant homologs by default, with a minimum
      identity of 0.3, so modest values are expected. A family far below its peers may
      merge unrelated sequences.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/proteinfamilies/2.5.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: family_conservation
    component: card
    column: mean_conservation
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Family conservation
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of each family's mean residue conservation along the
      representative, and the box shows the spread. It answers how well the alignments
      agree column by column.

      How to read: higher means more conserved families. Low values point to diverse or
      poorly aligned families worth a second look.
  - id: recruited_total
    component: card
    column: recruited
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: recruits, with the largest family
    title: Recruited members
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of members added beyond the seed sequences, and the
      second number is the largest recruitment into one family. It answers how much the
      family models gained after the first clustering.

      How to read: recruits are found by searching the model against the input, with a
      minimum length filter of 90% of the model by default. A family with a large
      recruitment grew far beyond its seed.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/proteinfamilies/2.5.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: family_size_box
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: size
      color: origin
      log_y: true
      labels: {sample: Sample, size: Member sequences, origin: Origin}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: size}
    title: Family size per sample
    description: >-
      Each box is a sample: the spread of its family sizes on a logarithmic scale,
      coloured by whether families are new or updated. It answers how family sizes
      compare between samples.

      How to read: compare the medians and the whiskers. A sample with only small
      families had little redundancy in its input.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median family size of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off
      of the pipeline.
  - component: table
    title: Protein family table
    description: >-
      Each row is a family with its origin, size, representative, seed, model and
      alignment statistics. It answers every number behind the tiles of this tab.

      How to read: sort by conservation or size to find families to inspect.

outputs.name: Residue confidence per engine
outputs.rawYaml:
id: proteinfold_engine_plddt
name: Residue confidence per engine
mode: protein/residues
description: >-
  The per-residue pLDDT of each engine's top-ranked structure, one curve per
  engine (and per chain on a complex), averaged over windows past 200 residues.
  Kept apart from the residue table, with the engine only in the curve label,
  so that an engine picked on the residue table leaves every engine's curve
  for the same target on screen.
find:
  path_glob: "**/top_ranked_structures/*.pdb"
recipe: proteinfold/engine_plddt.py
fixture: engine_plddt.tsv
renders_as:
  # pLDDT is bounded 0 to 100 and AlphaFold DB bands it at 90, 70 and 50.
  # Profile marks are x positions only, so the bands are explained in the
  # description rather than drawn.
  - id: plddt_by_engine
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Residue confidence along the sequence
    roles: {series: series, x: position, y: plddt}
    config:
      x_title: Residue position
      y_title: pLDDT
      legend_pos: bottom
      residue_axis: true
    description: >-
      Each curve is the per-residue pLDDT of the top-ranked structure of one engine for one target, with chains of a complex drawn separately. It answers which regions of the sequence an engine places confidently.

      How to read: stretches above 90 are very high confidence, 70 to 90 confident, 50 to 70 low and below 50 very low, which often marks intrinsically disordered regions. Dips between confident stretches usually separate domains or flexible linkers. When engines disagree on a region, treat its placement as unreliable.

      Note: the bands are AlphaFold DB's reading guide and are not drawn on the plot. Curves longer than 200 residues are averaged over windows by this catalog's recipe, a display limit and not an engine setting.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/ and https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/alphafold/inputs-and-outputs/evaluating-alphafolds-predicted-structures-using-confidence-scores/plddt-understanding-local-confidence/
  - id: plddt_box
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Residue confidence per curve
    dict_kwargs:
      x: series
      y: plddt
      color: series
      labels:
        series: Target and engine
        plddt: pLDDT
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: plddt}
    description: >-
      Each box is the spread of per-residue pLDDT over one curve of the profile tile, so one box per target and engine. It answers which engine gives the most confident structure overall.

      How to read: a box high up with a short range means a uniformly confident structure, and a long lower whisker means disordered or poorly placed regions. Compare boxes of the same target across engines, and open the profile to see where the low values sit.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median residue pLDDT of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of proteinfold.
  - component: table
    title: Residue confidence per engine
    description: >-
      One row per residue and curve with its pLDDT.

      How to read: sort by pLDDT to list the least confident residues of a target.

renders_as.description:
Each curve is the per-residue pLDDT of the top-ranked structure of one engine for one target, with chains of a complex drawn separately. It answers which regions of the sequence an engine places confidently.
How to read: stretches above 90 are very high confidence, 70 to 90 confident, 50 to 70 low and below 50 very low, which often marks intrinsically disordered regions. Dips between confident stretches usually separate domains or flexible linkers. When engines disagree on a region, treat its placement as unreliable.

outputs.description: One row per predicted model of every target and engine: its rank (1 is the top-ranked model), mean pLDDT, the share of residues placed confidently (pLDDT 70 or more) and likely disordered (under 50), and, when the engine writes them, the predicted TM score (pTM) and for a complex the interface TM score (ipTM) and ipSAE.
outputs.name: Model confidence scores
outputs.rawYaml:
id: proteinfold_models
name: Model confidence scores
mode: protein/models
description: >-
  One row per predicted model of every target and engine: its rank (1 is the
  top-ranked model), mean pLDDT, the share of residues placed confidently
  (pLDDT 70 or more) and likely disordered (under 50), and, when the engine
  writes them, the predicted TM score (pTM) and for a complex the interface TM
  score (ipTM) and ipSAE.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_plddt.tsv"
recipe: proteinfold/models.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several engines.
fixture: models.tsv
renders_as:
  # pLDDT 70 and pTM 0.5 are the published floors for a confident local
  # placement and a likely correct fold (AlphaFold DB paper, EMBL-EBI
  # AlphaFold course). Quadrants draw both as reference lines.
  - id: plddt_vs_ptm
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Local against global confidence
    roles: {x: mean_plddt, y: ptm, label: model_id, color: engine, size: n_residues}
    config:
      x_title: Mean pLDDT
      y_title: pTM
      top_n_labels: 5
      legend_pos: bottom
      quadrants:
        x: 70
        y: 0.5
        labels:
          - Weak locally, fold likely
          - Confident
          - Likely wrong
          - Placed well, fold doubtful
    description: >-
      Each point is a predicted model: its mean pLDDT on the horizontal axis and its predicted TM score on the vertical axis, coloured by engine and sized by the number of residues. It answers whether a model is trustworthy locally and as a whole.

      How to read: models in the upper right are confident on both counts. A high pLDDT with a low pTM means well folded pieces that are badly arranged, and the lower left holds models that are probably wrong. Engines that write no pTM are not drawn.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical line is a mean pLDDT of 70, the AlphaFold DB threshold for a confident residue. The horizontal line is a pTM of 0.5, above which the overall fold of the model might be similar to the true structure.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/ and https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/alphafold/inputs-and-outputs/evaluating-alphafolds-predicted-structures-using-confidence-scores/confidence-scores-in-alphafold-multimer/
  - id: model_plddt
    component: card
    column: mean_plddt
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 70
    threshold_direction: min
    threshold_warn: 50
    headline: true
    title: Model confidence
    caption: models by mean pLDDT band
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over models of the mean pLDDT, and the strip counts models by band. It answers how confident the predictions are overall.

      How to read: models at or above 70 are confident on average, those between 50 and 70 are low and those below 50 are very low. The minimum and maximum show the range across models.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-offs are 70 and 50, the AlphaFold DB confidence bands for pLDDT.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
  - id: model_confident_share
    component: card
    column: confident_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Confidently placed residues
    caption: median share, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of a model's residues at pLDDT 70 or more, and the box shows its spread. It answers how much of a typical model is placed confidently.

      How to read: a high share with a tight box means whole models are reliable. A low or wide box means disordered proteins or hard targets, so check which engine and target sit low.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
  - id: model_ptm
    component: card
    column: ptm
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.5
    threshold_direction: min
    title: Predicted TM score
    caption: models by pTM at the 0.5 floor
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median pTM over models that report one, and the strip counts models above and below 0.5. It answers how many predicted folds are likely to match the real one.

      How to read: a pTM above 0.5 means the overall predicted fold might be similar to the true structure, and below 0.5 the model is likely wrong. Engines that write no pTM are left out.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-off is 0.5, from the EMBL-EBI AlphaFold course.

      Source: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/alphafold/inputs-and-outputs/evaluating-alphafolds-predicted-structures-using-confidence-scores/confidence-scores-in-alphafold-multimer/
  - id: model_iptm
    component: card
    column: iptm
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.8
    threshold_direction: min
    threshold_warn: 0.6
    title: Interface confidence
    caption: complexes by ipTM band
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median ipTM over complexes, and the strip counts models by band. It answers how well the subunits of a complex are placed against each other.

      How to read: values above 0.8 are confident high-quality predictions, values between 0.6 and 0.8 are uncertain and values below 0.6 suggest a failed prediction. Single chains have no ipTM and are not counted.

      Lines and annotations: the cut-offs are 0.8 and 0.6, from the EMBL-EBI AlphaFold course.

      Source: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/alphafold/inputs-and-outputs/evaluating-alphafolds-predicted-structures-using-confidence-scores/confidence-scores-in-alphafold-multimer/
  - id: model_count
    component: card
    column: model_rank
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: engine
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Predicted models
    caption: models, by engine
    description: >-
      The hero number is the number of predicted models in view, the bars rank the engines by how many they wrote, and the line below gives the highest rank. It answers how many models each engine produced.

      How to read: engines write a different number of models per target. A short bar usually means an engine that returns a single model.
  - id: engine_box
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Model confidence per engine
    dict_kwargs:
      x: engine
      y: mean_plddt
      color: engine
      labels:
        engine: Engine
        mean_plddt: Mean pLDDT
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: mean_plddt}
    description: >-
      Each box is the spread of the mean pLDDT of an engine's models. It answers which engine gives the most confident predictions on these targets.

      How to read: a higher box means more confident models, but confidence is not accuracy, so a high box from an engine that disagrees with the others deserves a second look. Compare the same targets across engines before preferring one.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median mean pLDDT of a model of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of proteinfold.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
  - id: rank_line
    component: figure
    visu_type: line
    title: Confidence by model rank

renders_as.description:
Each point is a predicted model: its mean pLDDT on the horizontal axis and its predicted TM score on the vertical axis, coloured by engine and sized by the number of residues. It answers whether a model is trustworthy locally and as a whole.
How to read: models in the upper right are confident on both counts. A high pLDDT with a low pTM means well folded pieces that are badly arranged, and the lower left holds models that are probably wrong. Engines that write no pTM are not drawn.
Lines and annotations: the vertical line is a mean pLDDT of 70, the AlphaFold DB threshold for a confident residue. The horizontal line is a pTM of 0.5, above which the overall fold of the model might be similar to the true structure.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/ and https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/alphafold/inputs-and-outputs/evaluating-alphafolds-predicted-structures-using-confidence-scores/confidence-scores-in-alphafold-multimer/
renders_as.title: Local against global confidence

renders_as.caption: models by mean pLDDT band
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median over models of the mean pLDDT, and the strip counts models by band. It answers how confident the predictions are overall.
How to read: models at or above 70 are confident on average, those between 50 and 70 are low and those below 50 are very low. The minimum and maximum show the range across models.
Lines and annotations: the cut-offs are 70 and 50, the AlphaFold DB confidence bands for pLDDT.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
renders_as.title: Model confidence

renders_as.caption: median share, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median percentage of a model's residues at pLDDT 70 or more, and the box shows its spread. It answers how much of a typical model is placed confidently.
How to read: a high share with a tight box means whole models are reliable. A low or wide box means disordered proteins or hard targets, so check which engine and target sit low.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
renders_as.title: Confidently placed residues

renders_as.caption: models by pTM at the 0.5 floor
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median pTM over models that report one, and the strip counts models above and below 0.5. It answers how many predicted folds are likely to match the real one.
How to read: a pTM above 0.5 means the overall predicted fold might be similar to the true structure, and below 0.5 the model is likely wrong. Engines that write no pTM are left out.
Lines and annotations: the cut-off is 0.5, from the EMBL-EBI AlphaFold course.
Source: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/alphafold/inputs-and-outputs/evaluating-alphafolds-predicted-structures-using-confidence-scores/confidence-scores-in-alphafold-multimer/
renders_as.title: Predicted TM score

renders_as.caption: complexes by ipTM band
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median ipTM over complexes, and the strip counts models by band. It answers how well the subunits of a complex are placed against each other.
How to read: values above 0.8 are confident high-quality predictions, values between 0.6 and 0.8 are uncertain and values below 0.6 suggest a failed prediction. Single chains have no ipTM and are not counted.
Lines and annotations: the cut-offs are 0.8 and 0.6, from the EMBL-EBI AlphaFold course.
Source: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/online/courses/alphafold/inputs-and-outputs/evaluating-alphafolds-predicted-structures-using-confidence-scores/confidence-scores-in-alphafold-multimer/
renders_as.title: Interface confidence

renders_as.caption: models, by engine
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the number of predicted models in view, the bars rank the engines by how many they wrote, and the line below gives the highest rank. It answers how many models each engine produced.
How to read: engines write a different number of models per target. A short bar usually means an engine that returns a single model.
renders_as.title: Predicted models

renders_as.description:
Each box is the spread of the mean pLDDT of an engine's models. It answers which engine gives the most confident predictions on these targets.
How to read: a higher box means more confident models, but confidence is not accuracy, so a high box from an engine that disagrees with the others deserves a second look. Compare the same targets across engines before preferring one.
Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median mean pLDDT of a model of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of proteinfold.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/

outputs.rawYaml:
id: proteinfold_msa
name: Multiple sequence alignments of the MSA-based engines
mode: protein/msa
description: >-
  The alignment AlphaFold2, ColabFold and RoseTTAFold All-Atom folded each
  target from, one row per aligned sequence (the query first), decoded from
  the integer-coded tables and capped at 500 rows, with identity and coverage
  against the query. The alignment id is the id of the structure folded from
  it, so a column brush selects those residues on the structure.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_msa.tsv"
recipe: proteinfold/msa.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 12 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several engines.
fixture: msa.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: an alignment is coloured by residue with the viewer's own colour
  # scheme, there is no other column to bind.
  - id: folding_msa
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: msa
    title: Alignment behind the fold
    roles: {msa_id: msa_id, seq_id: seq_id, sequence: aligned_sequence, rank: rank, identity: identity}
    description: >-
      Each row is a homologous sequence aligned to the query, which comes first, with residues coloured by type. It answers how much evolutionary evidence the engine had for each position.

      How to read: columns that stay the same in every row are conserved, and gap-filled stretches mean few homologues cover that region. A shallow or low-identity alignment predicts a less reliable structure, so compare it with the confidence tiles. Brushing columns selects those residues on the structure.

      Note: this catalog's recipe keeps at most 500 rows per alignment, a display limit and not a limit of the engine's search.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/proteinfold/master/docs/output.md
  - id: msa_depth
    component: card
    column: depth
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Alignment depth
    caption: median depth, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median number of sequences in the alignment of a target, and the box shows its spread. It answers how many homologues the engine could draw on.

      How to read: deep alignments give the engine more co-evolution signal. Targets with very few sequences are hard cases whose confidence scores deserve caution.

      Note: depth counts the stored rows, which are capped at 500.
  - id: msa_coverage
    component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Query coverage
    caption: median coverage, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of the query covered by an aligned sequence, and the box shows its spread. It answers whether homologues span the whole query or only a part.

      How to read: coverage near full length means global homologues. Low coverage means the hits match a single domain, so the rest of the protein is predicted without evidence.
  - id: identity_histogram
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Sequence identity to the query
    dict_kwargs:
      x: identity
      color: engine
      labels:
        identity: Identity to the query
        engine: Engine
    description: >-
      Each bar counts aligned sequences in an identity bin against the query, coloured by engine. It answers how close the homologues are to the target.

      How to read: a mass of high identities means close relatives, and a spread towards low identities means distant homologues that carry the evolutionary signal. A histogram piled at the low end means the alignment adds little.
  - component: table
    title: Aligned sequences
    description: >-
      One row per aligned sequence with its identity and coverage against the query.

      How to read: sort by identity to find the closest and most distant homologues.

  at most 64 residue bins per axis: row k and column bNN with the same number

  domains, or two chains of a complex) are confidently placed relative to each

    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Predicted aligned error
    roles: {index: residue_range, row_annotation_cols: [engine]}
    description: >-
      Each cell is the predicted aligned error, in Angstrom, between a row of residues and a column of residues of the top-ranked model, averaged into bins. It answers how confidently two regions of the structure are placed relative to each other.

      How to read: low values off the diagonal mean two domains, or two chains, are confidently positioned. High values mean their relative position is uncertain even if each domain is well folded. Rows are annotated by engine.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: proteinfold_residues
name: Residue confidence of the top-ranked structures
mode: protein/residues
description: >-
  One row per residue of every top-ranked structure, one structure per engine
  and target: chain and residue number in the structure's own numbering, the
  amino acid, pLDDT (the model's per-residue confidence, 0 to 100, read from
  the B-factor column) and its AlphaFold confidence band (Very high, Confident,
  Low, Very low, as the pLDDT legend of the protein tiles). The entity is the id
  the structures collection gives the same PDB, so the 3D tile, the sequence
  track and the alignment of one structure select each other's residues.
find:
  path_glob: "**/top_ranked_structures/*.pdb"
recipe: proteinfold/residues.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several engines.
fixture: residues.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: structure_plddt
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: molecule_3d
    title: Structure coloured by confidence
    roles: {position: position, entity: entity, chain: chain, value: value, category: category}
    description: >-
      Each atom of the top-ranked structure is coloured by the pLDDT of its residue, in the four AlphaFold DB confidence bands. It answers which parts of the fold can be trusted.

      How to read: regions in the two upper bands are reliable. Well folded cores usually sit there, while loops, termini and disordered regions fall in the two lower bands. Interpret the arrangement of the low bands with caution.

      Lines and annotations: the bands are pLDDT above 90 (very high), 70 to 90 (confident), 50 to 70 (low) and below 50 (very low), as used by AlphaFold DB.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
  # No category lane: the pLDDT lane already colours each residue by its band.
  - id: plddt_sequence_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sequence_track
    title: Confidence along the sequence
    roles: {position: position, entity: entity, residue: residue, value: value}
    config:
      value_label: pLDDT
    description: >-
      Each cell is one residue of the sequence, with its amino acid and a lane coloured by its pLDDT. It answers which stretches of the sequence are confidently predicted.

      How to read: continuous high stretches are well predicted domains, and runs of low values are flexible or disordered segments. Selecting a residue highlights it on the structure.

      Lines and annotations: the lane uses the AlphaFold DB bands, above 90 very high, 70 to 90 confident, 50 to 70 low and below 50 very low.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
  - id: residue_plddt
    component: card
    column: value
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Residue confidence
    caption: median pLDDT, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median pLDDT over the residues in view, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how confident a typical residue is.

      How to read: a median above 70 means most residues are confidently placed. A long lower box points to disordered or poorly predicted regions.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
  - id: confident_share
    component: card
    column: confidently_placed
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    title: Confidently placed residues
    caption: share of residues, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the percentage of residues at pLDDT 70 or more, and the box shows its spread across structures. It answers how much of the predicted structure is reliable.

      How to read: a high percentage means a mostly confident model. A low one marks hard or disordered targets, so check the per-residue tiles.

      Lines and annotations: 70 is the lower edge of the confident band of AlphaFold DB.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
  - id: residue_bands
    component: card
    column: position
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: category
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Residues by confidence band
    caption: residues, by confidence band
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of residues in view, the bars rank the confidence bands by how many residues fall in each, and the line below gives the longest structure. It answers which band dominates.

      How to read: a leading very high or confident band means a reliable model. A leading low or very low band means most of the structure is uncertain.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
  - id: plddt_histogram
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Residue confidence distribution
    dict_kwargs:
      x: value
      color: engine
      labels:
        value: pLDDT
        engine: Engine
    description: >-
      Each bar counts residues in a pLDDT bin, coloured by engine. It answers how confidence is distributed over the residues.

      How to read: a pile near 90 to 100 means a confident model, and a second mass below 50 marks disordered residues. Compare engines to see which one is more decided.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34791371/
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: Select
    column_name: engine
    title: Engine
    description: >-
      Show the structures of one engine.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: position
    title: Residue position
    description: >-
      Restrict the tiles to a stretch of residues, for example a domain.
  - component: table
    title: Residue confidence
    description: >-
      One row per residue with its chain, amino acid, pLDDT and confidence band. Selecting rows highlights the residues on the structure.

      How to read: sort by pLDDT to list the weakest residues.
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: position

tools.description: Purity, ploidy and absolute copy-number fitting for tumor/normal or tumor-only whole-genome and panel data, with the somatic and germline driver catalog and the purity-adjusted somatic variants.
tools.name: PURPLE

outputs.description: PURPLE's fitted copy-number segments turned into the canonical copy-number profile contract. The absolute, purity-adjusted copy number becomes a log2 ratio against a diploid baseline, the fitted BAF comes through, and the major and minor allele copy numbers are kept for the allele-specific locus view, so loss of heterozygosity reads as a BAF split at unchanged total copy number.
outputs.name: Allele-specific copy-number segments
outputs.rawYaml:
id: purple_cnv_segments
name: Allele-specific copy-number segments
mode: purple
description: >-
  PURPLE's fitted copy-number segments turned into the canonical copy-number
  profile contract. The absolute, purity-adjusted copy number becomes a log2
  ratio against a diploid baseline, the fitted BAF comes through, and the major
  and minor allele copy numbers are kept for the allele-specific locus view, so
  loss of heterozygosity reads as a BAF split at unchanged total copy number.
find:
  path_glob: "**/purple/*.purple.cnv.somatic.tsv"
recipe: purple/cnv_segments.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: cnv_segments.tsv
renders_as:
  # Segments are coloured by gain, neutral or loss from their log2 against a diploid
  # baseline. PURPLE publishes no log2 cut-off (it fits absolute copy numbers), so the
  # two dotted lines are set where the rounded copy number leaves two, which is how the
  # recipe defines `copy_number`: 2.5 copies is log2(1.25) and 1.5 copies log2(0.75).
  - id: purple_cn_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: cnv_profile
    title: Copy-number profile
    roles: {sample: sample, chrom: chrom, start: start, end: end, log2: log2, baf: baf, copy_number: copy_number, segment: segment, label: label}
    config:
      gain_threshold: 0.322
      loss_threshold: -0.415
    description: >-
      Each line is a fitted copy-number segment: its purity-adjusted copy number as a log2
      ratio against two copies on the upper panel, and its fitted B-allele frequency on the
      lower one. It answers where the tumor genome gains, loses or keeps its copy number,
      and where one allele is lost.

      How to read: segments above the upper dotted line are gains and those below the lower
      one are losses. A BAF that rises towards 1 at an unchanged copy number is loss of
      heterozygosity, where one allele is gone and the other duplicated. Zoom on a
      chromosome to see the allele-specific copy numbers.

      Lines and annotations: the dotted lines at log2 0.322 and -0.415 are the copy numbers
      of 2.5 and 1.5, where the rounded copy number leaves two. They are a reference defined
      by the recipe, not a PURPLE cut-off. The dotted line at BAF 0.5 is the balanced state,
      since the BAF of a segment varies between 0.5 and 1.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: segment_cn_spread
    component: card
    column: copy_number
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Segment copy number
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median rounded copy number of the segments in view, and the
      box shows their quartiles. It answers the typical copy number of the tumor genome.

      How to read: a median of two with a tight box is a near diploid genome. A median
      above two with a wide box points to a genome with many gains. Filter to a chromosome
      to see where they sit.
  - component: table
    columns: [sample, chrom, start, end, copy_number, major_copy_number, minor_copy_number, baf, label]
    title: Copy-number segments
    description: >-
      Each row is a fitted segment with its position, rounded copy number, the copy numbers
      of the major and minor alleles and its BAF. It answers the exact fit behind each line
      of the profile.

      How to read: a minor allele copy number near zero marks loss of heterozygosity, and
      the label spells the total as the sum of the two alleles.

      drivers and not passengers.

id: purple_gene_copy_number
name: Copy number per gene
mode: purple
description: >-
  PURPLE's minimum and maximum copy number across each gene's canonical
  transcript, its minimum minor-allele copy number and its copy number relative
  to the sample ploidy, with a call derived from PURPLE's driver cut-offs:
  amplification (above 3 times ploidy), homozygous deletion (below 0.5
  copies), their partial forms, loss of heterozygosity, or neutral.
find:
  path_glob: "**/purple/*.purple.cnv.gene.tsv"
recipe: purple/gene_copy_number.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several copy-number events.
fixture: gene_copy_number.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: gene_event_count
    component: card
    column: gene
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: cn_event
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "pl.col('cn_event') != 'NEUTRAL'"
    title: Genes with a copy-number event
    caption: events, by call
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of gene calls that are not neutral, and the bars rank the
      calls (amplification, deletion, loss of heterozygosity and their partial forms) by how
      many genes they hold. The count beside it is the number of distinct genes. It answers
      how much of the gene set is altered and in which way.

      How to read: loss of heterozygosity is frequent in many tumors and is not a driver by
      itself, whereas homozygous deletions and amplifications are the strong events. Open the
      scatter to see how far each gene departs.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  # C1: coloured by the copy-number call.
  - id: gene_cn_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Minimum against maximum copy number
    roles: {x: min_copy_number, y: max_copy_number, label: gene, color: cn_event}
    config:
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: Minimum equals maximum
      x_title: Minimum copy number over the gene
      y_title: Maximum copy number over the gene
      top_n_labels: 10
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene: the lowest and the highest copy number found over its exons,
      coloured by the call derived from them. It answers which genes are altered and whether
      the change covers the whole gene or only a part.

      How to read: genes on the diagonal have one copy number over their whole length. Genes
      above it change copy number inside the gene, so only part of it is deleted or
      amplified. Genes far from the main cloud with a deletion or amplification call are the
      candidates to follow up.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is the line where the minimum equals the maximum,
      so the gene has a single copy number.

      Note: PURPLE calls an amplification above three times the sample ploidy and a deletion
      below 0.5 copies, so the call depends on the fitted ploidy and not on a fixed copy number.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: gene_cn_record
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: record_card
    title: Gene record
    roles: {id: gene}
    config:
      labels: {min_copy_number: Minimum copy number, max_copy_number: Maximum copy number, min_minor_allele_copy_number: Minimum minor allele copy number, relative_min_copy_number: Copy number relative to ploidy, somatic_regions: Copy-number regions, cn_event: Call, chromosome_band: Chromosome band, reported_status: Reported status, driver_type: Driver type}
    description: >-
      The card shows every field of one gene. It answers the details behind a row you pick
      in the table or the scatter.

      How to read: a minimum minor allele copy number near zero is loss of heterozygosity, and
      the copy number relative to ploidy tells whether the gene is high or low for this tumor.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: gene_cn_event_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: cn_event
    title: Copy-number call
    description: >-
      Choose the copy-number calls to keep. It answers which genes the other tiles show.

      How to read: select amplifications and deletions to leave out the neutral genes and the
      loss of heterozygosity.
  - id: gene_cn_table
    component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene
    title: Gene copy numbers
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene with its location, its minimum and maximum copy number, its minimum
      minor allele copy number and its call. It answers the exact copy number behind each
      point of the scatter.

      How to read: sort by minimum copy number to list the deleted genes first. Select a row to
      open its record.

id: purple_protein_changes
name: Protein changes of somatic variants
mode: purple
description: >-
  The somatic calls whose canonical HGVS protein change names a residue, in the
  protein module's variant contract: the gene as entity, the residue number,
  the one-letter reference and alternate residues, PAVE's coding effect as
  category, the purity-adjusted allele frequency as value and the short change
  as label. This is the table the lollipop and the 3D structure bind, so a
  residue picked in one moves the other.
find:
  path_glob: "**/purple/*.purple.somatic.vcf.gz"
recipe: purple/protein_changes.py
fixture: protein_changes.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: protein_change_needles
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: lollipop
    title: Protein changes along the gene
    roles: {feature_id: entity, position: position, category: category, label: label, effect: value}
    config:
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each needle is a somatic change at a residue of a gene, coloured by its coding effect
      and sized by the purity-adjusted allele frequency. It answers where along the protein
      the changes fall and how many cells carry them.

      How to read: needles that stack at one residue are a hotspot, and needles clustered in a
      region point to a functional domain. A tall needle is a change present in most tumor
      cells, which makes it an early event.

      Note: the allele frequency is adjusted for tumor purity by PURPLE, so it estimates the
      share of tumor cells and not of all cells.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: protein_change_structure
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: molecule_3d
    title: Changes on the 3D structure
    roles: {position: position, entity: entity, gene: entity, value: value, category: category, ref_aa: ref_aa, alt_aa: alt_aa, label: label}
    description: >-
      Each marked residue is a somatic change mapped onto the 3D structure of its protein,
      coloured by coding effect. It answers where in the folded protein the changes sit.

      How to read: changes that fall next to each other in space, even when far apart in the
      sequence, can act on the same site. Pick a residue on the lollipop to move to it here.
  - id: protein_change_count
    component: card
    column: label
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: category
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Protein changes by effect
    caption: changes, by coding effect
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of protein changes in view, and the bars rank the coding
      effects by how many they hold. The count beside it is the number of distinct changes.
      It answers how many residues are altered and how.

      How to read: missense changes usually lead, and a high share of nonsense or frameshift
      changes points to loss of function. Synonymous changes do not alter the protein.
  - id: protein_gene_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: Select
    column_name: entity
    title: Gene
    description: >-
      Choose one gene. It answers which protein the lollipop and the structure show.

      How to read: pick a gene to see its changes along the sequence and on the structure.
  - id: protein_category_filter
    component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: category
    title: Coding effect
    description: >-
      Choose the coding effects to keep. It answers which kinds of change the other tiles show.

      How to read: keep missense changes alone to leave out the synonymous ones.
  - id: protein_change_table
    component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: label
    title: Protein changes
    description: >-
      Each row is a somatic change with its gene, residue, amino acids, coding effect, allele
      frequency and the flags for biallelic, hotspot and reported. It answers the exact
      change behind each needle.

      How to read: sort by allele frequency to find the most clonal changes. Select a row to
      follow it on the other tiles.
