outputs.name: Tumor purity, ploidy and QC
outputs.rawYaml:
id: purple_purity
name: Tumor purity, ploidy and QC
mode: purple
description: >-
  PURPLE's fit for each tumor, one row per tumor: purity, ploidy, fit status
  and sex, the genome-wide mutational load (microsatellite indels per Mb and
  MSI status, tumor mutational burden and load, structural-variant burden,
  whole-genome duplication), joined with the checks of the .purple.qc file
  (QC status, copy-number segments, deleted genes, contamination, LOH
  fraction, TINC level). Every copy number and allele frequency downstream is
  read against this fit.
find:
  path_glob: "**/purple/*.purple.purity.tsv"
recipe: purple/purity.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 1 real row (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several tumors.
fixture: purity.tsv
renders_as:
  # Low purity is flagged by PURPLE itself (WARN_LOW_PURITY below 20%), so the card
  # shows that cut-off instead of a gauge over a 0 to 1 fraction.
  - id: purity_gauge
    component: card
    column: purity
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.2
    threshold_direction: min
    headline: true
    title: Tumor purity
    caption: median, against the 0.2 warning level
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median tumor purity, the share of tumor cells in the sample, over
      the tumors in view. It answers whether the sample holds enough tumor for a reliable fit.

      How to read: a high purity gives clean copy-number and allele-frequency signals, and a
      low one blurs them. The lowest and highest values are listed beside it.

      Lines and annotations: the marker is a purity of 0.2, below which PURPLE raises its
      low-purity warning.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: ploidy_spread
    component: card
    column: ploidy
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Tumor ploidy
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median average ploidy of the tumors in view, adjusted for purity,
      and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how many copies of the genome a typical
      tumor carries.

      How to read: a ploidy near two is a near diploid genome and a ploidy near three or more
      points to a genome that has doubled. Check it against the whole-genome duplication flag
      in the table.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: tmb_spread
    component: card
    column: tmb_per_mb
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 10
    threshold_direction: max
    headline: true
    title: Tumor mutational burden
    caption: median, against the high-burden level
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median tumor mutational burden, in passing variants per megabase,
      over the tumors in view. It answers how heavily mutated the tumors are.

      How to read: a value above the marker is a high burden, which is associated with
      mismatch repair deficiency or exposure to a mutagen. The lowest and highest values are
      listed beside it.

      Lines and annotations: the marker is 10 passing variants per megabase, above which
      PURPLE labels the tumor mutational burden as high.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: msi_spread
    component: card
    column: ms_indels_per_mb
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Microsatellite indels
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of microsatellite indels per megabase over the
      tumors in view, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how unstable the
      microsatellites are.

      How to read: a high rate points to microsatellite instability, the mark of mismatch
      repair deficiency. The call itself is made by PURPLE and sits in the MSI status column of
      the table, since the README states no rate to apply.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  # C1: coloured by the fit status, the check that says whether PURPLE trusts the fit.
  - id: purity_ploidy_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Purity against ploidy
    roles: {x: ploidy, y: purity, label: sample, color: fit_status}
    config:
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_value: 0.2
      reference_label: Low-purity warning
      reference_highlight: below
      x_title: Ploidy
      y_title: Tumor purity
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a tumor: its fitted ploidy on the horizontal axis and its purity on the
      vertical axis, coloured by the status of the fit. It answers whether the fits are
      plausible and which tumors need a second look.

      How to read: a tumor below the line has too little tumor for a reliable fit. A status
      other than the usual one means PURPLE used a fallback fit or raised a warning, so the
      copy numbers of that tumor are less certain.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a purity of 0.2, below which PURPLE raises
      its low-purity warning.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: tumor_record
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: record_card
    title: Tumor record
    roles: {id: sample}
    config:
      labels: {purity: Purity, ploidy: Ploidy, fit_status: Fit status, qc_status: QC status, tmb_per_mb: Tumor mutational burden, ms_status: Microsatellite status, whole_genome_duplication: Whole-genome duplication, loh_fraction: Fraction with LOH, contamination: Contamination}
    description: >-
      The card shows every field of one tumor fit. It answers the details behind a tumor you
      pick in the table or the scatter.

      How to read: read the QC status first, then purity and ploidy, then the mutational
      load. A fail status in QC means the fit should not be trusted.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: fit_table
    component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Purity and QC table
    description: >-
      Each row is a tumor with its purity, ploidy, fit status, mutational load and QC checks.
      It answers the exact fit and the verdict behind every tile of the tab.

      How to read: start with the QC status, which PURPLE fails for contamination above 10% and
      warns about for a low purity or a noisy copy-number profile. Select a row to open its
      record.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md

outputs.name: Somatic small variants
outputs.rawYaml:
id: purple_somatic_variants
name: Somatic small variants
mode: purple
description: >-
  Every PASS somatic SNV, MNV and indel of the purity-adjusted PURPLE VCF, one
  row per call: locus and alleles, SAGE tier, PAVE's canonical gene, effect,
  coding effect and HGVS changes, the raw and purity-adjusted allele frequency,
  the copy number at the locus and of the variant, the subclonal likelihood and
  the biallelic, hotspot, reported and kataegis flags.
find:
  path_glob: "**/purple/*.purple.somatic.vcf.gz"
recipe: purple/somatic_variants.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several variant types.
fixture: somatic_variants.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: variant_count
    component: card
    column: variant_key
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: variant_type
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Somatic variants
    caption: calls, by variant type
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of passing somatic calls, and the bars rank the variant
      types (SNV, MNV, indel) by how many they hold. The count beside it is the number of
      distinct sites. It answers how many variants the tumors carry and of which kind.

      How to read: SNVs usually lead. A high share of indels can point to a defect in
      mismatch repair. Open the genome view to see where the calls lie.
  - id: coding_variant_count
    component: card
    column: variant_key
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: coding_effect
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "pl.col('coding_effect').is_in(['MISSENSE', 'NONSENSE_OR_FRAMESHIFT', 'SPLICE', 'SYNONYMOUS'])"
    title: Coding variants
    caption: calls, by coding effect
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of calls that fall in coding sequence, and the bars rank
      them by effect (missense, nonsense or frameshift, splice, synonymous). The count beside
      it is the number of distinct sites. It answers how many variants can change a protein.

      How to read: missense calls usually lead and loss-of-function calls are the rarest. A
      synonymous call does not change the protein.
  - id: purity_adjusted_af_spread
    component: card
    column: purple_af
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Purity-adjusted allele frequency
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median purity-adjusted allele frequency of the calls in view, and
      the box shows their quartiles. It answers what share of tumor cells carry a typical
      variant.

      How to read: clonal heterozygous variants sit near 0.5 on a diploid region and higher on
      a region of higher copy number. A low box means many variants are subclonal.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: variant_cn_spread
    component: card
    column: variant_copy_number
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Variant copy number
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median copy number of the variants in view, the number of copies
      of the genome that carry each one, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how many
      copies of a locus carry a typical variant.

      How to read: a clonal variant has a copy number near one, and values well below one
      point to a subclonal variant. Higher values are variants on amplified regions.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: purity_adjusted_af_histogram
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: purple_af
      color: variant_type
      labels: {purple_af: Purity-adjusted allele frequency, variant_type: Variant type, count: Number of variants}
    title: Allele frequency distribution
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the variants in a range of purity-adjusted allele frequency, stacked by
      variant type. It answers how the variants divide between clonal and subclonal ones.

      How to read: a peak near 0.5 is the clonal heterozygous variants of a diploid tumor, and a
      second peak at lower frequency is a subclone. Peaks shift to the right on regions with
      more than two copies.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  - id: variant_cn_histogram
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: variant_copy_number
      color: variant_type
      labels: {variant_copy_number: Variant copy number, variant_type: Variant type, count: Number of variants}
    title: Variant copy-number distribution
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the variants in a range of variant copy number, stacked by variant type.
      It answers how many copies of the genome carry each variant, and how many are subclonal.

      How to read: a main peak near one is the clonal variants, and variants below it are
      subclonal. PURPLE marks a fitted peak as subclonal when its variant copy number is below
      0.85.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md
  # C1: coloured by variant type.
  - id: somatic_variant_genome
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Variants along the genome
    roles: {chr: chrom, pos: pos, score: purple_af, feature: variant_key, sample: sample, category: variant_type}
    config:
      score_title: Purity-adjusted allele frequency
    description: >-
      Each point is a somatic variant placed on its chromosome, with its purity-adjusted allele
      frequency on the vertical axis, coloured by variant type. It answers where the variants lie
      and how clonal they are.

      How to read: clusters of points in one region are a hypermutated segment, and a band at a
      higher frequency over a region is a gain of the copy carrying the variants. Zoom into a
      region and pick a point to open its row in the table.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/purple/README.md

outputs.description: Multi-metric alpha-diversity per sample (shannon, evenness, faith_pd…).
outputs.name: Alpha diversity
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_alpha_diversity
name: Alpha diversity
mode: diversity
description: Multi-metric alpha-diversity per sample (shannon, evenness, faith_pd…).
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/diversitycore
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/diversity/alpha_diversity/*_vector/metadata.tsv" }
recipe: qiime2/alpha_diversity_multi_canonical.py
# bindable sample (recipe declares only sample_id/habitat; metric cols are dynamic)
fixture: alpha_diversity.tsv
renders_as:
  # code-mode figure: 2x2 facet of the four alpha-diversity metrics by habitat,
  # each panel with its own y-scale (metrics span very different ranges).
  # Coloured by habitat (C1); the habitat column is run-dependent metadata, which
  # is why this figure is code and not a bound figure.
  - component: figure
    title: Alpha diversity by habitat
    description: >-
      Each box summarises the samples of one habitat for one alpha-diversity metric,
      and each dot is a sample. It answers whether within-sample diversity differs
      between habitats.

      How to read: boxes that do not overlap point to habitats with different
      diversity, and a wide box means the samples of that habitat are heterogeneous.
      Shannon and Faith's PD grow with richness, and evenness says how equally the
      features share the reads. Compare with the beta-diversity ordination to see
      whether the same habitats also differ in composition.

      Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
    code: |
      # reshape wide -> long so each metric becomes a facet panel (stays polars)
      df_modified = df.unpivot(
          index=["sample_id", "habitat"],
          on=["shannon", "observed_features", "faith_pd", "evenness"],
          variable_name="metric",
          value_name="value",
      )

      fig = px.box(
          df_modified,
          x="habitat", y="value", color="habitat",
          facet_col="metric", facet_col_wrap=2, points="all",
          category_orders={"metric": ["shannon", "observed_features", "faith_pd", "evenness"]},
          labels={"habitat": "Habitat", "value": "Value"},
      )

      fig.update_yaxes(matches=None)  # each panel keeps its own scale
      fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=")[-1]))
      fig.update_layout(showlegend=True, legend_title_text="Habitat", boxmode="group", margin=dict(t=10))
  # one Tukey box-plot distribution card per metric (hero average + box-plot strip)
  - component: card
    column: shannon
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    title: Shannon diversity
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median Shannon diversity over the samples in view, and
      the box shows their quartiles. It answers how diverse a typical sample is,
      counting both richness and evenness.

      How to read: a higher value means more features and a more even share of the
      reads. A long whisker means samples differ a lot, so filter by habitat to see
      where. QIIME 2 publishes no pass or fail cut-off for this index.

      Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
  - component: card
    column: observed_features
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Observed features
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of distinct features (ASVs) observed per
      sample, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how rich a typical sample
      is.

      How to read: a high count means many distinct features were detected, but it
      depends on the sequencing depth, so read it together with the rarefaction
      curves. QIIME 2 publishes no pass or fail cut-off for this index.

      Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
  - component: card
    column: faith_pd
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Faith's phylogenetic diversity
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median Faith's phylogenetic diversity per sample, and the
      box shows its quartiles. It answers how much of the phylogenetic tree a typical
      sample covers.

      How to read: a higher value means the features of the sample are spread over
      more distant lineages, not just more numerous. It needs a rooted tree, so it
      is absent from runs without one. QIIME 2 publishes no pass or fail cut-off.

      Sources: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/ and
      https://scikit.bio/docs/latest/generated/skbio.diversity.alpha.faith_pd.html
  - component: card
    column: evenness
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Evenness
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median Pielou's evenness per sample, and the box shows its
      quartiles. It answers how equally the reads are shared between the features.

      How to read: values near 1 mean an even community and values near 0 a community
      dominated by few features. QIIME 2 publishes no pass or fail cut-off.

      Sources: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/ and
      https://scikit.bio/docs/latest/generated/skbio.diversity.alpha.pielou_e.html
  - component: table
    title: Alpha-diversity table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its four alpha-diversity values and its metadata. It
      answers the exact value behind each box and dot.

      How to read: sort by a metric to find the least and most diverse samples, and
      compare outliers with their sequencing depth.

outputs.description: Alpha-rarefaction curve (sample × depth × iteration × metric).
outputs.name: Alpha rarefaction
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_alpha_rarefaction
name: Alpha rarefaction
mode: alpha-rarefaction
description: Alpha-rarefaction curve (sample × depth × iteration × metric).
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/diversityalphararefaction
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/alpha-rarefaction/*.csv" }
recipe: qiime2/alpha_rarefaction.py
fixture: alpha_rarefaction.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: the raw rarefaction table carries no metadata column (sample, depth,
  # iter, faith_pd), so there is nothing to group by; the curves take one colour
  # per sample. The iteration column is bound so the tile draws its spread band.
  - id: rarefaction_alpha
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: rarefaction
    title: Rarefaction curves
    roles: {sample_id: sample, depth: depth, metric: faith_pd, iter: iter}
    config:
      show_ci: true
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: its Faith's phylogenetic diversity as the reads are
      subsampled to a growing depth, averaged over the iterations, with the spread of
      the iterations as a band. It answers whether the sequencing depth was enough to
      capture the diversity.

      How to read: a curve that levels out (approaches a slope of zero) means more reads
      would not reveal new diversity. A curve still climbing at the deepest depth means
      the diversity was not fully observed, or that sequencing error remains in the data.
      Choose the sampling depth for diversity analyses where most curves have levelled
      out, without dropping too many samples.

      Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/

renders_as.description:
Each line is a sample: its Faith's phylogenetic diversity as the reads are subsampled to a growing depth, averaged over the iterations, with the spread of the iterations as a band. It answers whether the sequencing depth was enough to capture the diversity.
How to read: a curve that levels out (approaches a slope of zero) means more reads would not reveal new diversity. A curve still climbing at the deepest depth means the diversity was not fully observed, or that sequencing error remains in the data. Choose the sampling depth for diversity analyses where most curves have levelled out, without dropping too many samples.
Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
renders_as.title: Rarefaction curves

outputs.description: The alpha-rarefaction curves collapsed over the iteration axis: one row per sample and depth carrying the median estimate, the interquartile spread that median hides, and the sample metadata joined on. Two orders of magnitude smaller than the raw table, and groupable, which the raw table is not.
outputs.name: Rarefaction summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_alpha_rarefaction_summary
name: Rarefaction summary
mode: alpha-rarefaction
description: >-
  The alpha-rarefaction curves collapsed over the iteration axis: one row per
  sample and depth carrying the median estimate, the interquartile spread that
  median hides, and the sample metadata joined on. Two orders of magnitude
  smaller than the raw table, and groupable, which the raw table is not.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/diversityalphararefaction
# Same file the raw `qiime2_alpha_rarefaction` output reads: this is the
# collapsed view of it, computed once at ingest rather than in every render.
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/alpha-rarefaction/*.csv" }
recipe: qiime2/alpha_rarefaction_summary.py
fixture: alpha_rarefaction_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # The median curve per sample. The summary stores the interquartile width, not
  # its two edges, so the profile tile cannot draw the spread as a band.
  # Colour is one per sample (profile series); the metadata columns that would
  # group them are run-dependent and not in the recipe's OUTPUT_SCHEMA.
  - id: rarefaction_band
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Median rarefaction curves
    roles: {series: sample, x: depth, y: faith_pd}
    config:
      x_title: Sequencing depth (reads per sample)
      y_title: Faith's phylogenetic diversity
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: the median, over the iterations, of its Faith's
      phylogenetic diversity at each subsampling depth. It answers whether the
      diversity of each sample has stopped growing with depth.

      How to read: a line that levels out means more reads would not reveal new
      diversity, and a line still rising at the deepest depth means the sample was
      not sequenced deeply enough. Pick the sampling depth for diversity analyses
      where most lines have levelled out.

      Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
  # C1 N/A: same reason as above, one colour per sample and no grouping column.
  - id: rarefaction_curve
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: rarefaction
    title: Rarefaction by sample
    roles: {sample_id: sample, depth: depth, metric: faith_pd}
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: its median Faith's phylogenetic diversity at each
      subsampling depth, with the controls of the rarefaction view. It answers which
      samples are the richest and whether their curves have levelled out.

      How to read: curves that flatten show that the diversity was captured, and the
      ordering of the curves shows which samples are richer at equal depth. A curve
      that stays steep is a sample worth resequencing or dropping from depth-sensitive
      comparisons.

      Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: depth
      y: faith_pd
      color: sample
      labels: {depth: Sequencing depth (reads per sample), faith_pd: Faith's phylogenetic diversity, sample: Sample}
    title: Rarefaction curves
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: its median Faith's phylogenetic diversity at each
      subsampling depth. It answers how fast the diversity of each sample grows with
      sequencing depth.

      How to read: hover a line to read the sample, and look for curves that level out.
      A curve still rising at the right edge was not sequenced deeply enough to see its
      full diversity.

      Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
  - component: card
    column: faith_pd
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Faith's diversity along the curves
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median Faith's phylogenetic diversity over every sample
      and depth step in view, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers the
      typical diversity reached across the rarefaction series.

      How to read: it mixes shallow and deep steps, so use it as a coarse summary and
      read the curves for the plateau. Filter to one sample to see its own range.
  - component: card
    column: depth
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [min, median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    title: Subsampling depths
    caption: deepest, shallowest and median depth
    description: >-
      The hero number is the deepest subsampling depth of the series, with the
      shallowest and the median step beside it. It answers how far the rarefaction
      explored.

      a sampling depth above a library size would drop that sample.

    title: Rarefaction summary table
    description: >-

      interquartile width over the iterations and the number of iterations. It answers
      the exact value behind each point of the curves.

How to read: a line that levels out means more reads would not reveal new diversity, and a line still rising at the deepest depth means the sample was not sequenced deeply enough. Pick the sampling depth for diversity analyses where most lines have levelled out.

outputs.description: ANCOM-BC differential-abundance results. The tool writes one CSV per statistic per contrast; the recipe joins + melts them into a long table.
outputs.name: Differential abundance
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_ancombc
stage: differential
name: Differential abundance
mode: composition/ancombc
description: >-
  ANCOM-BC differential-abundance results. The tool writes one CSV per statistic
  per contrast; the recipe joins + melts them into a long table.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/ancombc
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/ancombc/differentials/*/lfc_slice.csv" }
recipe: qiime2/ancombc.py
fixture: ancombc.tsv
renders_as:
  # Calls follow the nf-core/ampliseq ANCOM-BC defaults: a q-value below 0.05
  # (--p-alpha 0.05, ancombc_significance) and an effect size of 1 for the
  # differential-abundance barplot (ancombc_effect_size). The recipe's
  # `significant` column applies the same q-value rule.
  - id: volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Differential abundance volcano
    roles: {feature_id: id, effect_size: lfc, significance: q_val, label: Phylum, category: contrast}
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 1.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Log fold change
      significance_label: -log10 q-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a taxon in one contrast: its ANCOM-BC log fold change on the
      horizontal axis and its q-value (adjusted p-value) on the vertical axis, coloured
      by contrast. It answers which taxa differ most between the groups, in which
      direction, and how confidently.

      How to read: taxa in the upper left and upper right corners are less and more
      abundant than in the reference group, with high confidence. A cloud with almost
      nothing past the lines means little differential signal. Open the table tile to
      inspect the labelled taxa.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the q-value cut-off of 0.05 and the
      vertical lines mark an absolute effect size of 1. Both are the nf-core/ampliseq
      defaults for its differential-abundance barplot.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/ampliseq/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: da_barplot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: da_barplot
    title: Top changed taxa per contrast
    roles: {feature_id: id, contrast: contrast, lfc: lfc, significance: q_val, label: Phylum}
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_label: Log fold change
    description: >-
      Each bar is a taxon: its ANCOM-BC log fold change in a contrast, for the taxa with
      the largest absolute change. It answers which taxa drive each contrast and in which
      direction.

      How to read: long bars to the right are more abundant than in the reference group
      and bars to the left less abundant; bars are marked when their q-value passes the
      cut-off. A large change without significance usually means a rare or variable
      taxon, so open the MA plot and the table to check it.

      Lines and annotations: significance is marked at a q-value below 0.05, the
      nf-core/ampliseq default.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/ampliseq/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: qq
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: qq
    title: P-value QQ plot
    roles: {p_value: p_val, category: contrast, feature_id: id}
    config:
      show_ci: true
      show_identity: true
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a taxon: its observed raw p-value, as minus log10, against the value
      expected if no taxon differed between the groups. One trace is drawn per contrast.
      It answers whether the test statistics are well calibrated.

      How to read: points hugging the diagonal for most of the range and lifting off at
      the far end mean a few real signals over a calibrated null. A curve that leaves the
      diagonal early points to strong group structure or to a model that does not fit.
      Compare the contrasts and the ordination when one curve differs.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, the expectation when p-values are
      uniformly distributed under no effect. The shaded band is the 95% confidence
      interval of that null, so points inside it are consistent with chance.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: id
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: contrast
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "pl.col('significant')"
    title: Significant taxa by contrast
    caption: calls, by contrast
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of taxon calls with a q-value below 0.05, and the bars
      rank the contrasts by how many they hold. It answers which comparison shows the
      strongest differential signal.

      How to read: a contrast with many calls separates its groups clearly, and one with
      none shows no detectable difference. The count beside the hero is the number of
      distinct taxa behind the calls.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/ampliseq/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: id
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: Kingdom
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "pl.col('significant')"
    title: Significant calls by kingdom
    caption: calls, by kingdom
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of taxon calls with a q-value below 0.05, and the ring
      splits them by kingdom. It answers whether the differential signal sits in bacteria,
      archaea or both.

      How to read: a ring dominated by one kingdom says where the groups differ. Calls are
      counted per contrast, so a taxon significant in two contrasts counts twice.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/ampliseq/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: q_val
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: threshold
    threshold_value: 0.05
    threshold_direction: max
    title: Median q-value
    caption: median, against the 0.05 cut-off
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median q-value over every taxon and contrast in view, shown
      against the 0.05 cut-off. It answers whether a typical taxon differs between the
      groups.

      How to read: a median below the cut-off means most taxa differ, which is unusual
      outside strongly structured habitats. The smallest and largest q-values are listed
      beside it.

      Lines and annotations: the marker is the q-value of 0.05 used by nf-core/ampliseq as
      the ANCOM-BC significance level.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/ampliseq/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: lfc
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Fold change spread
    caption: range, with the quartiles
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of ANCOM-BC log fold changes over every taxon and
      contrast in view, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how large the
      differences are overall.

      How to read: a box tight around zero with a long range means most taxa are unchanged
      and a few change a lot. A median would cancel the two directions, so the range is
      shown instead. Filter to one contrast to compare them.
  - component: table
    title: Differential abundance table
    description: >-
      Each row is a taxon in one contrast, with its log fold change, standard error, test
      statistic, p-value, q-value and whether the call is significant. It answers the
      exact estimate behind each point of the plots.

      How to read: sort by q-value to list the strongest calls, and filter on the
      significant column to keep the calls only.

outputs.name: Sample distance matrix
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_bray_curtis
name: Sample distance matrix
mode: diversity/beta
description: >-
  Sample by sample Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrix computed from the
  relative-abundance table.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/diversitycore
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/rel_abundance_tables/rel-table-*.tsv" }
recipe: nf-core/ampliseq/bray_curtis_canonical.py
fixture: bray_curtis.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the run's samples, known only at ingest. A matrix
  # of distances needs no row annotation: the recipe carries no metadata column.
  # C1 N/A: a heatmap colours by its value scale, which the kind draws itself.
  - id: distance_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Sample distances
    roles: {index: sample}
    config:
      cluster_rows: true
      cluster_cols: true
      normalize: none
    description: >-
      Each cell is the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between two samples, computed from their
      relative abundances. It answers which samples have similar communities and which
      groups they form.

      How to read: dark blocks along the diagonal are groups of similar samples and the
      dendrograms show how they cluster. Samples that sit far from every other sample have
      an unusual community, so check them against the ordination and the habitat metadata.

      Note: Bray-Curtis runs from 0 for identical communities to 1 for communities that
      share nothing.

      Sources: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/ and
      https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.spatial.distance.braycurtis.html
  - component: table
    title: Distance matrix
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample and each column the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity to another sample.
      It answers the exact distance between any two samples.

      How to read: read across a row to find the nearest and the most distant samples of
      the one in view.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_embedding_pcoa
name: Beta-diversity ordination
mode: diversity/beta
description: >-
  Two-dimensional PCoA ordination of the samples, computed from the
  relative-abundance table. One point per sample.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/diversitycore
# The recipe chains off the abundance matrix rather than reading a QIIME 2
# artefact directly, so `find` names the raw table at the head of that chain.
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/rel_abundance_tables/rel-table-*.tsv" }
recipe: qiime2/embedding_pcoa.py
fixture: embedding_pcoa.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: the grouping column is run-dependent (the dashboard's {GROUP_COL}) and
  # is not in the recipe's OUTPUT_SCHEMA, so no role can bind it here; the
  # dashboard colours by its group through the config.
  - id: embedding
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: Samples on the first two axes
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, dim_1: dim_1, dim_2: dim_2}
    config:
      axis_prefix: PCo
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample, placed by a principal coordinates analysis of the
      Bray-Curtis dissimilarities between samples. It answers whether samples of the same
      habitat or condition have similar communities.

      How to read: points that sit close have similar communities and points far apart
      differ. Groups that separate along the first axis carry the main source of variation.
      A sample far from its group is worth checking for a technical problem.

      Note: the axes are ordination coordinates, so their sign and scale have no absolute
      meaning.

      Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
  - component: table
    title: Ordination coordinates
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its coordinates on the first axes. It answers the exact
      position of each point.

      How to read: sort by an axis to find the samples at its two extremes.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  # A median of a centred ordination axis is about zero, so the cards show the
  # range of the samples on each axis instead.
  - component: card
    column: dim_1
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Spread on the first axis
    caption: range, with the quartiles
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of the samples along the first ordination axis, and
      the box shows their quartiles. It answers how far apart the samples are on the main
      axis of variation.

      How to read: a wide range with a box split into two clusters points to groups with
      distinct communities. The axis is centred, so its median says nothing.
  - component: card
    column: dim_2
    aggregation: range
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Spread on the second axis
    caption: range, with the quartiles
    description: >-
      The hero number is the range of the samples along the second ordination axis, and
      the box shows their quartiles. It answers how much variation the second axis adds.

      How to read: a range much narrower than the first axis means one gradient explains
      most of the difference between samples.

outputs.name: Differential-abundance MA plot
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_ma
stage: differential
name: Differential-abundance MA plot
mode: composition/ancombc
description: >-
  Mean abundance against log2 fold change per taxon, joining the ANCOM-BC
  differentials with the per-sample counts.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/ancombc
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/ancombc/differentials/*/lfc_slice.csv" }
recipe: nf-core/ampliseq/ma_canonical.py
fixture: ma.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: `significance` and `label` are optional columns of the recipe, not in its
  # OUTPUT_SCHEMA, so no role can bind them here; the dashboard binds them when present.
  # C1 N/A: the MA view colours points by its significance call; with no
  # `significance` column guaranteed by the recipe, every point draws in one colour.
  - id: ma_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: ma
    title: Fold change against mean abundance
    roles: {feature_id: feature_id, avg_log_intensity: avg_log_intensity, log2_fold_change: log2_fold_change}
    config:
      fold_change_threshold: 1.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Log fold change
      intensity_label: Mean abundance (log10 of count plus 1)
    description: >-
      Each point is a taxon in one contrast: its mean abundance across samples on the
      horizontal axis (log10 of the count plus one) and its ANCOM-BC log fold change on the
      vertical axis. It answers whether the changes are real or only come from rare taxa.

      How to read: a flat cloud centred on zero with the significant taxa spread over
      abundance levels is healthy. A funnel that widens towards low abundance is the
      normal noise of rare taxa. Open the table tile to inspect the labelled taxa.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal lines mark an absolute effect size of 1, the
      nf-core/ampliseq default for its differential-abundance barplot.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/ampliseq/master/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: table
    title: Fold change and abundance table
    description: >-
      Each row is a taxon in one contrast, with its mean abundance, log fold change and
      q-value. It answers the exact values behind each point.

      How to read: sort by q-value to list the strongest calls, then compare their
      abundance in the plot.

renders_as.description:
Each point is a taxon in one contrast: its mean abundance across samples on the horizontal axis (log10 of the count plus one) and its ANCOM-BC log fold change on the vertical axis. It answers whether the changes are real or only come from rare taxa.
How to read: a flat cloud centred on zero with the significant taxa spread over abundance levels is healthy. A funnel that widens towards low abundance is the normal noise of rare taxa. Open the table tile to inspect the labelled taxa.
Lines and annotations: the horizontal lines mark an absolute effect size of 1, the nf-core/ampliseq default for its differential-abundance barplot.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/ampliseq/master/nextflow_schema.json
renders_as.title: Fold change against mean abundance

renders_as.description:
Each row is a taxon in one contrast, with its mean abundance, log fold change and q-value. It answers the exact values behind each point.
How to read: sort by q-value to list the strongest calls, then compare their abundance in the plot.
renders_as.title: Fold change and abundance table

outputs.description: Multi-metric alpha-rarefaction curves (sample × depth × iteration; shannon, observed_features, faith_pd), fanned in from the per-metric QIIME2 rarefaction CSVs.
outputs.name: Rarefaction curves
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_rarefaction_canonical
name: Rarefaction curves
mode: rarefaction
description: Multi-metric alpha-rarefaction curves (sample × depth × iteration; shannon, observed_features, faith_pd), fanned in from the per-metric QIIME2 rarefaction CSVs.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/diversityalphararefaction
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/alpha-rarefaction/*.csv" }
recipe: qiime2/rarefaction_canonical.py
fixture: rarefaction_canonical.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: the metadata column that would group the curves is run-dependent (the
  # dashboard's {GROUP_COL}) and not in the recipe's OUTPUT_SCHEMA, so no role can
  # bind it here; the curves take one colour per sample.
  - id: rarefaction
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: rarefaction
    title: Rarefaction curves
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, depth: depth, metric: shannon, iter: iter}
    config:
      metric_options: [shannon, observed_features, faith_pd]
      show_ci: true
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: its alpha diversity as the reads are subsampled to a growing
      depth, averaged over the iterations, with their spread as a band. The tab strip
      switches between Shannon, observed features and Faith's PD. It answers whether the
      sequencing depth was enough to capture the diversity.

      How to read: a curve that levels out (approaches a slope of zero) means more reads
      would not reveal new diversity. A curve still climbing at the deepest depth means the
      diversity was not fully observed, or that sequencing error remains in the data.
      Choose the sampling depth for diversity analyses where most curves have levelled out.

      Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/

renders_as.description:
Each line is a sample: its alpha diversity as the reads are subsampled to a growing depth, averaged over the iterations, with their spread as a band. The tab strip switches between Shannon, observed features and Faith's PD. It answers whether the sequencing depth was enough to capture the diversity.
How to read: a curve that levels out (approaches a slope of zero) means more reads would not reveal new diversity. A curve still climbing at the deepest depth means the diversity was not fully observed, or that sequencing error remains in the data. Choose the sampling depth for diversity analyses where most curves have levelled out.
Source: https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/
renders_as.title: Rarefaction curves

outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_rel_abundance
name: Relative abundance
mode: rel-abundance
description: Per-sample relative-abundance table with taxonomy ranks.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/relativeabundancetables
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/rel_abundance_tables/rel-table-*.tsv" }
recipe: nf-core/ampliseq/taxonomy_rel_abundance.py
fixture: rel_abundance.tsv
renders_as:
  # wide per-rank columns (Kingdom/Phylum) → sunburst fits; stacked_taxonomy
  # needs a single long-format rank column this table lacks.
  #
  # No complex_heatmap here: this table is long (one row per sample × taxon) and
  # the server's heatmap reads a wide matrix off `index_column` with no pivot
  # step, so it can only ever plot the single `rel_abundance` column. The
  # clustered heatmap is offered by `qiime2_clustered_heatmap`, which binds the
  # canonical taxon × sample matrix the same reshape produces.
  - id: sunburst
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Kingdom and phylum composition
    roles: {ranks: [Kingdom, Phylum], abundance: rel_abundance}
    config:
      colour_by_rank: Phylum
    description: >-
      Each arc is a taxon: the inner ring is the kingdom and the outer ring the phylum,
      sized by relative abundance summed over the samples in view and coloured by phylum.
      It answers which lineages make up the communities.

      How to read: a wide arc is a dominant lineage, and a ring made of many thin arcs is a
      diverse one. Click an arc to zoom in on it, and filter by habitat to compare groups.

      Note: unclassified reads form their own arc, so a large one points to a database or
      classification limit rather than a real group.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  # The relative abundances span orders of magnitude (a box plot would draw a flat
  # line), so the card shows the dominant value with its typical and upper-quartile ones.
  - component: card
    column: rel_abundance
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, q3]
    secondary_layout: compact
    title: Dominant relative abundance
    caption: largest, median and upper quartile
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest relative abundance of any taxon in any sample in view,
      with the median and the upper quartile beside it. It answers how dominant the leading
      taxon is.

      How to read: a large maximum against a small median is the usual shape of a community
      with a few dominant taxa and a long tail. Filter by sample or habitat to see how the
      dominance changes.
  - component: card
    column: taxonomy
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: Kingdom
    top_n_count: 2
    headline: true
    title: Taxa by kingdom
    caption: detections, by kingdom
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct taxa detected, and the bars rank the kingdoms
      by how many detections they hold. The count beside it is the number of sample and taxon
      detections. It answers how many lineages the run recovered and where they come from.

      How to read: a run dominated by one kingdom is usual for a 16S survey. A high count of
      detections against a low count of taxa means the same taxa are found in many samples.
  - component: card
    column: rel_abundance
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: Phylum
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "pl.col('Phylum') != 'Unclassified'"
    title: Abundance of the leading phyla
    caption: mean abundance when detected, by phylum
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean relative abundance of a detected taxon, and the bars rank
      the phyla by their mean. The largest value is listed beside it. It answers which phyla
      are abundant when they are present.

      How to read: phyla at the top make up most of the reads where they occur. Only
      detections above zero are counted, so a phylum found in a single sample can still rank
      high. Unclassified taxa are left out.
  - component: table
    title: Relative abundance table
    description: >-
      Each row is a taxon in one sample, with its relative abundance, its kingdom and phylum
      and the sample metadata. It answers the exact abundance behind each arc and card.

      How to read: sort by abundance to find the dominant taxa of a sample, or filter on a
      phylum to follow it across samples.

id: qiime2_stacked_taxonomy_canonical
name: Taxonomic composition
mode: stacked-taxonomy
description: Long-format stacked-taxonomy abundance (sample × rank × taxon) fanned in from the per-rank QIIME2 rel-table-{2..6}.tsv collapses, with a derived Kingdom level.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/barplot
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/rel_abundance_tables/rel-table-*.tsv" }
recipe: qiime2/stacked_taxonomy_canonical.py
fixture: stacked_taxonomy_canonical.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: coloured by taxon, the column that matters for a composition.
  - id: stacked_taxonomy
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: Taxonomic composition per sample
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, taxon: taxon, rank: rank, abundance: abundance}
    config:
      default_rank: Phylum
      top_n: 12
      value_title: Relative abundance
      rank_label: Taxonomic rank
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample, split into the taxa of the chosen rank by their relative
      abundance, with the least abundant lumped into Other. It answers how the community
      composition differs between samples.

      How to read: bars with the same colour pattern are samples with similar communities,
      and a bar dominated by one colour is a sample with a dominant taxon. Switch the rank
      to move from phyla to genera, sort the samples, and hide parts from the controls.

      Note: unclassified reads form their own part, so a large one points to a database or
      classification limit.

renders_as.description:
Each bar is a sample, split into the taxa of the chosen rank by their relative abundance, with the least abundant lumped into Other. It answers how the community composition differs between samples.
How to read: bars with the same colour pattern are samples with similar communities, and a bar dominated by one colour is a sample with a dominant taxon. Switch the rank to move from phyla to genera, sort the samples, and hide parts from the controls.
Note: unclassified reads form their own part, so a large one points to a database or classification limit.
renders_as.title: Taxonomic composition per sample

outputs.name: Taxonomic hierarchy
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_sunburst_canonical
name: Taxonomic hierarchy
mode: sunburst
description: Hierarchical taxonomic composition (Kingdom→…→Genus with relative abundance) for a sunburst, collapsed per sample from the QIIME2 per-rank rel-abundance tables.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/barplot
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/rel_abundance_tables/rel-table-*.tsv" }
recipe: nf-core/ampliseq/sunburst_canonical.py
fixture: sunburst_canonical.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: only Kingdom and Phylum are in the recipe's OUTPUT_SCHEMA (Class to Genus
  # are optional), so the ranks beyond them cannot be named here; the tile reads the
  # rank columns the run holds.
  - id: sunburst_taxonomy
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Taxonomic hierarchy
    roles: {abundance: abundance}
    config:
      colour_by_rank: Phylum
    description: >-
      Each arc is a taxon: rings run from kingdom outwards through the ranks the run holds, sized by relative
      abundance summed over the samples in view and coloured by phylum. It answers which
      lineages make up the communities and how they divide into finer groups.

      How to read: a wide arc is a dominant lineage, and its outer arcs show how it splits
      into classes, orders, families and genera. Click an arc to zoom in on it, and filter
      by sample to compare communities.

      Note: unclassified reads form their own arcs at each rank, so a large one points to a
      database or classification limit rather than a real group.

renders_as.description:
Each arc is a taxon: rings run from kingdom outwards through the ranks the run holds, sized by relative abundance summed over the samples in view and coloured by phylum. It answers which lineages make up the communities and how they divide into finer groups.
How to read: a wide arc is a dominant lineage, and its outer arcs show how it splits into classes, orders, families and genera. Click an arc to zoom in on it, and filter by sample to compare communities.
Note: unclassified reads form their own arcs at each rank, so a large one points to a database or classification limit rather than a real group.
renders_as.title: Taxonomic hierarchy

outputs.name: Taxa barplot
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_taxa_barplot
name: Taxa barplot
mode: taxa-barplot
description: Relative-abundance barplot table at a taxonomic level (wide → long via recipe).
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/barplot
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/barplot/level-*.csv" }
recipe: qiime2/stacked_taxonomy_canonical.py
fixture: taxa_barplot.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: coloured by taxon, the column that matters for a composition.
  - id: stacked_taxonomy_barplot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: Taxa barplot
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, taxon: taxon, rank: rank, abundance: abundance}
    config:
      default_rank: Phylum
      top_n: 12
      value_title: Relative abundance
      rank_label: Taxonomic rank
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample, split into the taxa of the chosen rank by their relative
      abundance, with the least abundant lumped into Other. It answers how the community
      composition differs between samples.

      How to read: bars with the same colour pattern are samples with similar communities,
      and a bar dominated by one colour is a sample with a dominant taxon. Switch the rank
      to move from phyla to genera, and sort the samples from the controls.

      Note: unclassified reads form their own part, so a large one points to a database or
      classification limit.

renders_as.description:
Each bar is a sample, split into the taxa of the chosen rank by their relative abundance, with the least abundant lumped into Other. It answers how the community composition differs between samples.

Note: unclassified reads form their own part, so a large one points to a database or classification limit.
renders_as.title: Taxa barplot

outputs.name: Taxon counts per sample
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_taxonomy_composition
name: Taxon counts per sample
mode: taxa/barplot
description: >-
  Long-format taxon counts per sample, melted from the taxa barplot export, with
  the taxonomy string split back into its ranks.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/barplot
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/barplot/level-*.csv" }
recipe: qiime2/taxonomy_composition.py
fixture: taxonomy_composition.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: count
      color: Phylum
      labels: {sample: Sample, count: Read count, Phylum: Phylum}
    title: Reads per sample by phylum
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample, stacked by phylum, with its height the number of reads
      assigned to each. It answers how many reads each sample holds and which phyla they
      belong to.

      How to read: bars of very different height are samples with different sequencing
      depth, so compare compositions on the relative abundance tab rather than here. A
      phylum that fills a bar dominates that sample.
  - component: table
    title: Taxon counts table
    description: >-
      Each row is a taxon in one sample, with its read count, kingdom and phylum and the
      sample metadata. It answers the exact count behind each bar segment.

      How to read: sort by count to find the dominant taxa, or filter on a phylum to follow
      it across samples.

renders_as.description:
Each bar is a sample, stacked by phylum, with its height the number of reads assigned to each. It answers how many reads each sample holds and which phyla they belong to.
How to read: bars of very different height are samples with different sequencing depth, so compare compositions on the relative abundance tab rather than here. A phylum that fills a bar dominates that sample.
renders_as.title: Reads per sample by phylum

renders_as.description:
Each row is a taxon in one sample, with its read count, kingdom and phylum and the sample metadata. It answers the exact count behind each bar segment.

renders_as.title: Taxon counts table

outputs.description: Taxon by sample abundance matrix (one row per taxon, one column per sample), pivoted from the relative-abundance table.
outputs.name: Abundance matrix
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_taxonomy_heatmap
name: Abundance matrix
mode: rel-abundance/matrix
description: >-
  Taxon by sample abundance matrix (one row per taxon, one column per sample),
  pivoted from the relative-abundance table.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/qiime2/relativeabundancetables
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/rel_abundance_tables/rel-table-*.tsv" }
recipe: qiime2/taxonomy_heatmap.py
fixture: taxonomy_heatmap.tsv
# The clustered heatmap binds to `qiime2_clustered_heatmap`, whose recipe casts
# the index + annotation columns the renderer needs. Here the matrix is the
# output, so a table is the honest render.
renders_as:
  - component: table
    title: Abundance matrix
    description: >-
      Each row is a taxon and each column a sample, holding the relative abundance of the
      taxon in that sample. It answers the exact abundance behind the clustered heatmap.

      How to read: read across a row to follow a taxon over the samples, and down a column
      to see what a sample is made of.

renders_as.description:
Each row is a taxon and each column a sample, holding the relative abundance of the taxon in that sample. It answers the exact abundance behind the clustered heatmap.
How to read: read across a row to follow a taxon over the samples, and down a column to see what a sample is made of.
renders_as.title: Abundance matrix

outputs.name: ASV taxonomy table
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qiime2_tree_metadata
name: ASV taxonomy table
mode: taxonomy/classify
description: >-
  Per-ASV classification: the assigned taxon, its rank columns and the
  classifier confidence. Annotates the phylogenetic tree, and stands on its own
  as the taxonomy assignment table.
find: { path_glob: "**/qiime2/taxonomy/taxonomy.tsv" }
recipe: nf-core/ampliseq/tree_metadata_canonical.py
fixture: tree_metadata.tsv
renders_as:
  # `uniqueness` needs no second column, so it survives a run whose taxonomy
  # table carries no rank columns (they are optional in the recipe schema).
  - component: card
    column: taxon
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: uniqueness
    title: Classified ASVs
    caption: distinct ASVs, against all rows
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct ASVs that received a taxonomic assignment,
      and the count beside it is the number of rows. It answers how many sequence variants
      the classifier labelled.

      How to read: the two numbers match when every ASV has a single assignment, so a gap
      means some sequence variants appear in more than one row.
  - component: card
    column: confidence
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Classifier confidence
    caption: median, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median classifier confidence over the ASVs in view, and the box
      shows their quartiles. It answers how certain the taxonomic assignments are.

      How to read: values close to 1 are firm assignments, and a long lower whisker is a set
      of ASVs assigned with little support. The classifier only keeps an assignment at a
      rank when its confidence reaches the minimum set for the run, 0.7 by default, so the
      lowest values sit near that floor.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/qiime2/q2-feature-classifier/master/q2_feature_classifier/classifier.py
  - component: table
    title: ASV taxonomy table
    description: >-
      Each row is an ASV with its assigned taxon, its ranks from kingdom to species, the
      classifier confidence and the habitat where it is most abundant. It answers what
      each sequence variant was called.

      How to read: sort by confidence to find the weakest assignments, and look at empty
      rank cells to see where the classifier stopped.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: taxon
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: Phylum
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "pl.col('Phylum') != ''"
    title: ASVs by phylum
    caption: ASVs, by phylum
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct ASVs with a phylum assignment, and the bars
      rank the phyla by how many ASVs they hold. It answers which phyla are the most
      diverse.

      How to read: the leading phyla hold most of the sequence variants. ASVs without a
      phylum are left out, so the number is below the total when some stay unclassified.
  - component: card
    column: Genus
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: completeness
    title: Reached genus
    caption: ASVs classified to genus
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of ASVs with a genus assignment, shown as the share of
      all ASVs, and the count beside it is the number of distinct genera. It answers how
      deep the classification reaches.

      How to read: a low share is common for environmental samples, where many sequences have
      no close relative in the reference database. Compare with the phylum card to see
      where the classifier stops.
  - component: card
    column: Genus
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: concentration
    breakdown_col: Genus
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "pl.col('Genus') != ''"
    title: Genus concentration
    caption: ASVs held by the leading genera
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct genera, and the strip shows how much of the
      classified ASVs the leading genera hold. It answers whether a few genera dominate.

      How to read: a high share in the first genera means a narrow set of genera accounts for
      most variants, and a flat strip means a diverse set. ASVs without a genus are left out.

The hero number is the count of distinct ASVs with a phylum assignment, and the bars rank the phyla by how many ASVs they hold. It answers which phyla are the most diverse.

How to read: a low share is common for environmental samples, where many sequences have no close relative in the reference database. Compare with the phylum card to see where the classifier stops.

outputs.description: Per-sample depth, mapping quality, error rate and duplication from Qualimap's BamQC genome_results.txt summary.
outputs.name: BamQC genome coverage
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qualimap_bamqc_genome_results
name: BamQC genome coverage
description: >-
  Per-sample depth, mapping quality, error rate and duplication from
  Qualimap's BamQC genome_results.txt summary.
find:
  path_glob: "**/genome_results.txt"
recipe: qualimap/bamqc_genome_results.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 2 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several libraries.
fixture: bamqc_genome_results.tsv
renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: mean_coverage
      color: sample
      labels: {sample: Library, mean_coverage: Mean depth (X)}
    title: Mean genome coverage per library
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: mean_coverage}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: its mean read depth over the reference, as reported by
      Qualimap BamQC. It answers how deeply each library covers the genome and
      whether the libraries are comparable.

      How to read: bars of similar height mean an even sequencing effort. A very
      short bar is a library that will give few usable calls, so compare it with
      the percentage of reads mapped and the duplication rate in the table before
      deciding to resequence it.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median mean depth of a library
      of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of Qualimap, which draws no
      pass level.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: mean_coverage
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    title: Mean depth
    caption: average over libraries, with the deepest ones ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average of the per-library mean depth, and the bars
      rank the deepest libraries. It answers how much sequencing the run holds per
      base of the reference.

      How to read: a large gap between the highest and the lowest library means an
      unbalanced run. Open the coverage histogram to see whether a low mean hides
      a covered fraction that is still adequate.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: duplication_rate
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Duplication rate
    caption: average percent duplicated, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average percent of reads Qualimap estimates as
      duplicated, and the box shows how libraries spread around it. It answers
      whether the libraries lost much of their depth to duplicates.

      How to read: a library far above the box is over-amplified or low in input
      DNA, so its effective depth is lower than the mean depth suggests. The
      estimate is Qualimap's own and is not a pass or fail verdict.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: gc_percentage
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    title: GC content
    caption: average percent GC, with the highest libraries ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average GC percentage of the mapped reads, and the
      bars rank the libraries with the highest value. It answers whether the
      libraries share a base composition.

      How to read: libraries of the same species and protocol should sit close
      together. An outlier suggests contamination, a different library
      preparation or a GC bias in amplification.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: table
    title: BamQC summary per library
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with its read counts, share of reads mapped, mean
      depth, mean mapping quality, error rate, GC content and duplication rate.
      It answers the exact value behind every other tile of this output.

      How to read: sort by mean depth or by duplication rate to find the libraries
      that need attention, then compare them with the coverage tiles.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html

outputs.description: Windowed read depth along the whole reference, from Qualimap BamQC's own coverage_across_reference table. Qualimap reports the window centre on the concatenated reference, so the recipe maps each window back onto its contig using the per-contig lengths in the same run's genome_results.txt; without that file the track falls back to a single pseudo-contig.
outputs.name: Coverage across the reference
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qualimap_coverage_across_reference
name: Coverage across the reference
description: >-
  Windowed read depth along the whole reference, from Qualimap BamQC's own
  coverage_across_reference table. Qualimap reports the window centre on the
  concatenated reference, so the recipe maps each window back onto its contig
  using the per-contig lengths in the same run's genome_results.txt; without
  that file the track falls back to a single pseudo-contig.
find:
  path_glob: "**/coverage_across_reference.txt"
recipe: qualimap/coverage_across_reference.py
fixture: coverage_across_reference.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: both tracks bind the library (`sample`) to colour.
  - id: reference_coverage_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Read depth along the reference
    roles: {chromosome: chromosome, position: position, value: coverage, sample: sample}
    config:
      color_by: sample
    description: >-
      Each point is a window of the reference, drawn at its position on its contig
      with the read depth Qualimap measured there, one line per library. It answers
      where along the genome the reads pile up or thin out.

      How to read: a flat line means an even library. Spikes point to repeats,
      amplified regions or organelle contigs, and long gaps point to regions
      the reads do not reach. Compare libraries to separate a sample effect from a
      reference effect.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - id: reference_genome_view
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Read depth on the genome axis
    roles: {chr: chromosome, pos: position, score: coverage, sample: sample}
    config:
      score_title: Read depth (X)
    description: >-
      Each point is a window of the reference with its read depth, laid out on a
      chromosome-aware axis that can be zoomed. It answers the same question as the
      coverage track with a scrollable view of every contig.

      How to read: zoom into a region where the depth departs from its neighbours
      and compare libraries. Qualimap defines no depth cut-off, so no threshold line
      is drawn.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: global_position
      y: coverage
      color: sample
      labels: {global_position: Position on the concatenated reference (bp), coverage: Read depth (X), sample: Library}
    title: Depth along the concatenated reference
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the read depth in every window, with all contigs laid
      end to end on one axis. It answers how the depth profiles of the libraries
      compare along the whole reference.

      How to read: parallel lines mean the libraries react to the reference in the
      same way. A library whose line departs from the others at the same positions
      points to a library-specific bias.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Window depth
    caption: average window depth, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average read depth over all windows and libraries, and
      the box shows how the windows spread. It answers how even the depth is across
      the reference.

      How to read: a box that is narrow and close to the average means an even
      library. A long upper whisker means a few windows soak up many reads.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: coverage
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Deepest window
    caption: deepest window, with the libraries that reach it ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest window depth found, and the bars rank the
      libraries holding the deepest windows. It answers which library has the
      strongest pile-up.

      How to read: a maximum far above the median marks a collapsed region such as
      a repeat or an organelle contig. Open the track to see where it sits.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: coverage_std
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Depth variability within windows
    caption: average standard deviation of depth, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average standard deviation of the depth inside a
      window, and the box shows how it varies between windows. It answers how
      uneven the depth is at a small scale.

      How to read: windows with a large deviation compared with their depth hold
      uneven or repetitive sequence. A library with a larger value overall is less
      uniform.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: table
    page_size: 25
    title: Depth per window
    description: >-
      Each row is a window of the reference with its contig, position, mean depth
      and the standard deviation of the depth inside it. It answers the exact depth
      behind the tracks.

      How to read: sort by depth to find the extreme windows, or filter by contig
      to inspect one sequence.

      Each line is a library: the share of the reference sitting at each read depth.
      It answers how the depth is distributed over the genome, not only its mean.

      How to read: a curve with a tall left end means much of the reference is
      uncovered or shallow. A narrow peak near the mean depth means an even library
      and a long tail to the right means pile-ups on repeats. Compare libraries on
      the same curve before choosing which to resequence.

    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: coverage
      y: n_genomic_locations
      color: sample
      labels: {coverage: Read depth (X), n_genomic_locations: Bases of the reference, sample: Library}
    title: Bases of the reference at each depth
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the number of bases of the reference sitting at each
      read depth. It answers the same question as the share profile in raw base
      counts.

      How to read: raw counts depend on the reference size, so use this view for
      libraries mapped to the same reference and the share view otherwise. A large
      count at zero depth is the uncovered part of the genome.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
