  # histogram, and a sum of bases over every depth is just the reference length.
  - component: card
    column: fraction
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "col('coverage') == 0"
    title: Reference with no coverage
    caption: median share at zero depth, with the least covered libraries ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of the reference with no read at all, and
      the bars rank the libraries with the largest uncovered share. It answers how
      much of the genome a library misses.

      How to read: a share near zero is a library that reaches the whole reference.
      A large share at zero depth is expected for a shallow library and is the
      first number to check before calling variants.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: n_genomic_locations
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    filter_expr: "col('coverage') == 0"
    title: Bases with no coverage
    caption: median and lowest count of uncovered bases
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest number of reference bases with no read, taken
      over the libraries. It answers how large the uncovered part is in bases rather
      than in share.

      How to read: compare the maximum with the lowest library to see how unequal
      the libraries are. Raw counts depend on the reference size, so read the share
      card for libraries on different references.

    page_size: 25
    title: Depth histogram

      behind the histogram.

      depth that holds most of the genome.

outputs.description: Per-contig length, mapped bases and mean depth from the last block of Qualimap BamQC's genome_results.txt, plus the depth relative to the library's own genome-wide mean. The substrate of a coverage-ratio sex call and the quickest read on whether one scaffold soaked up the library.
outputs.name: Coverage per contig
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qualimap_coverage_per_contig
name: Coverage per contig
description: >-
  Per-contig length, mapped bases and mean depth from the last block of
  Qualimap BamQC's genome_results.txt, plus the depth relative to the library's
  own genome-wide mean. The substrate of a coverage-ratio sex call and the
  quickest read on whether one scaffold soaked up the library.
find:
  path_glob: "**/genome_results.txt"
recipe: qualimap/coverage_per_contig.py
fixture: coverage_per_contig.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: contig_depth_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Contig depth against contig length
    roles: {x: length, y: relative_coverage, label: chromosome, color: sample, size: mapped_bases}
    config:
      log_x: true
      x_title: Contig length (bp)
      y_title: Depth relative to the library mean
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_value: 1
      reference_label: Library mean
      top_n_labels: 8
    description: >-
      Each point is a contig in one library: its length on the horizontal axis and
      its depth relative to the library mean on the vertical axis, with the marker
      sized by the bases mapped to it. It answers whether any contig is over- or
      under-covered compared with the rest of the genome.

      How to read: most long contigs should sit near the mean. A short contig far
      above it is typically an organelle genome or a repeat, and a contig well below
      it may be a sex chromosome or a missing sequence. Compare libraries before
      reading a contig as a sex call.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a relative depth of 1, the
      library's own genome-wide mean by definition. It is a data-defined reference,
      not a cut-off.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: chromosome
      y: relative_coverage
      color: sample
      labels: {chromosome: Contig, relative_coverage: Depth relative to the library mean, sample: Library}
    title: 'Depth per contig, relative to the library mean'
    description: >-
      Each bar is a contig in a library: its depth divided by the library's
      genome-wide mean. It answers which contigs deviate from the genome-wide level.

      How to read: a bar near 1 is a contig at the library mean. A bar far above or
      below it is worth a look, and an organelle contig is expected to tower over
      the rest.

      Lines and annotations: a relative depth of 1 is the library's own mean by
      definition, no cut-off is drawn.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  # The relative depth spans orders of magnitude (organelle contigs against nuclear
  # ones), so a box plot would be squashed: a stat strip is used instead.
  - component: card
    column: relative_coverage
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    title: Relative contig depth
    caption: median relative depth, with the lowest and highest contig
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median depth of a contig relative to its library mean,
      and the strip shows the lowest and highest contig. It answers how far the
      contigs depart from the genome-wide level.

      How to read: a median near 1 is expected. A maximum far above it points to an
      organelle genome or a repeat that took many reads.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: mapped_bases
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max, median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: chromosome
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Bases mapped per contig
    caption: total bases mapped, with the largest contigs ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of bases mapped, and the bars rank the contigs
      that hold most of them. It answers whether one scaffold soaked up the library.

      How to read: the ranking should follow contig length. A contig far above its
      share of the genome holds more reads than its size explains.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: length
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max, median]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: chromosome
    title: Reference length by contig
    caption: total length, split by contig
    description: >-
      Each unit is a base of the reference and the ring splits them by contig. It
      answers how the reference is divided, to put the depth of each contig in
      context.

      How to read: a ring dominated by a few contigs means a chromosome-level
      assembly, and many thin slices mean a fragmented one.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: table
    page_size: 25
    title: Per-contig depth
    description: >-
      Each row is a contig in a library with its length, mapped bases, mean depth,
      standard deviation and depth relative to the library mean. It answers the
      exact numbers behind the contig tiles.

      How to read: sort by relative depth to find the contigs that depart from the
      library mean.

outputs.description: The share of the reference covered at least X deep, from Qualimap BamQC. The number a shallow shotgun library is judged on, because a mean depth well under 1X says nothing about whether the reads are spread over the genome or piled on a tenth of it.
outputs.name: Genome fraction by depth
outputs.rawYaml:
id: qualimap_genome_fraction_coverage
name: Genome fraction by depth
description: >-
  The share of the reference covered at least X deep, from Qualimap BamQC. The
  number a shallow shotgun library is judged on, because a mean depth well
  under 1X says nothing about whether the reads are spread over the genome or
  piled on a tenth of it.
find:
  path_glob: "**/genome_fraction_coverage.txt"
recipe: qualimap/genome_fraction_coverage.py
fixture: genome_fraction_coverage.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: genome_fraction_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Genome fraction covered at least X deep
    roles: {series: sample, x: min_coverage, y: genome_fraction_pct}
    config:
      x_title: Minimum read depth (X)
      y_title: Reference covered (%)
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the percentage of the reference covered by at least
      the read depth on the horizontal axis. It answers how much of the genome is
      usable at each depth, which a mean depth cannot tell.

      How to read: a curve that stays high as the depth rises is a library with its
      reads spread over the genome. A curve that collapses at the first depths
      means the reads are piled on a small part of it, so the mean depth overstates
      what is usable.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: min_coverage
      y: genome_fraction_pct
      color: sample
      labels: {min_coverage: Minimum read depth (X), genome_fraction_pct: Reference covered (%), sample: Library}
    title: Share of the reference covered at least X deep
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: the percentage of the reference covered at least X
      deep. It answers the same question as the profile as a plain line.

      How to read: compare where the curves reach the depth you need for your
      analysis, and read the gap between libraries as a difference in evenness.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: genome_fraction_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "col('min_coverage') == 1"
    title: Reference covered at 1X
    caption: median percent covered by one read or more, with the best libraries ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of the reference covered by at least
      one read, and the bars rank the libraries that cover most of it. It answers
      how complete a library is at the lowest depth.

      How to read: a low value means large parts of the genome are unseen. A
      library that is high here and drops quickly at higher depth is complete but
      shallow.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: card
    column: min_coverage
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "col('genome_fraction_pct') > 0"
    title: Deepest depth still reached
    caption: highest depth with any coverage, with the libraries ranked
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest depth at which some of the reference is still
      covered, and the bars rank the libraries that go deepest. It answers how far
      each library's curve extends.

      How to read: a short reach means a shallow library. The table is capped at
      the depths Qualimap reports, so a value at that cap means at least that deep.

      Source: http://qualimap.conesalab.org/doc_html/analysis.html
  - component: table
    page_size: 25
    title: Genome fraction per depth
    description: >-
      Each row is a library at one minimum depth with the percentage of the
      reference covered at least that deep. It answers the exact values behind the
      curves.

      How to read: filter to a library and read down to the depth your analysis
      needs.

tools.description: Reference-free assembly quality statistics for whole assemblies and for individual bins.
tools.name: QUAST

outputs.description: Contig counts, N50 and assembled length for each assembly, one row per assembler and sample. Total length says how much of the community was assembled at all; N50 says whether that length sits in a few long contigs a binner can work with, or in a drift of short ones it cannot.
outputs.name: Assembly statistics
outputs.rawYaml:
id: quast_assembly_report
name: Assembly statistics
mode: assembly-report
description: >-
  Contig counts, N50 and assembled length for each assembly, one row per
  assembler and sample. Total length says how much of the community was
  assembled at all; N50 says whether that length sits in a few long contigs a
  binner can work with, or in a drift of short ones it cannot.
find:
  path_glob: "**/QUAST/transposed_report.tsv"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/quast/transposed_report.tsv"
    - "**/QUAST/*/transposed_report.tsv"
recipe: quast/assembly_report.py
fixture: assembly_report.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: coloured by assembler, the comparison the tab exists for. QUAST defines no
  # cut-off for N50 or assembled length, so no reference line is drawn.
  - id: n50_vs_length
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Contiguity against assembled length
    roles: {x: total_length, y: n50, label: assembly_id, color: assembler, size: n_contigs}
    config:
      x_title: Assembled length (bp)
      y_title: Contig N50 (bp)
      log_y: true
      top_n_labels: 5
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is one assembly: its total assembled length on the horizontal
      axis and its contig N50 on the vertical axis, coloured by assembler and
      sized by the number of contigs. It answers which assembler gives the most
      contiguous assembly for the length it recovers.

      How to read: points toward the upper right assemble more of the community in
      longer contigs. A large point low on the axis is a fragmented assembly, many
      small contigs, which a binner will struggle with. Compare assemblers on the
      same sample before choosing one.

      Note: QUAST defines no pass mark for N50 or assembled length. The vertical
      axis is logarithmic.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median contig N50 of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of QUAST.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Assembled length per assembly
    dict_kwargs:
      x: assembly_id
      y: total_length
      color: assembler
      labels: {assembly_id: Assembly, total_length: Assembled length (bp), assembler: Assembler}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: total_length
    description: >-
      Each bar is one assembly, with its total assembled length in base pairs,
      coloured by assembler. It answers how much of the community each assembler
      managed to assemble.

      How to read: a short bar next to its siblings on the same sample means that
      assembler lost sequence, often the low-coverage organisms. Read it beside
      the N50 plot, since a long assembly in fragments is still hard to bin.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median assembled length of
      this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of QUAST.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Contig N50 by assembler
    dict_kwargs:
      x: assembler
      y: n50
      color: sample
      barmode: group
      labels: {assembler: Assembler, n50: Contig N50 (bp), sample: Sample}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: n50
    description: >-
      Each bar is the contig N50 of one assembly, grouped by assembler and
      coloured by sample. It answers which assembler produces the longest contigs.

      How to read: N50 is the contig length such that contigs of at least that
      length cover half of the assembly, so a higher bar means a more contiguous
      assembly. An assembler that wins on every sample is the safer choice for
      binning.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median contig N50 of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of QUAST.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: total_length
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: assembler
    caption: assembled length, split by assembler
    title: Assembled length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the summed length of every assembly in view, and the bar
      splits it by assembler. It answers how much sequence each assembler
      contributes.

      How to read: a sum mixes samples, so use the median and the maximum beside it
      for a per-assembly reading. An assembler with a thin segment recovered less of
      the community.
  - component: card
    column: n50
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: assembler
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: median N50, by assembler
    title: Contig N50
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median contig N50 over the assemblies in view, and the
      bars rank the assemblers by their median. It answers which assembler is the
      most contiguous.

      How to read: N50 is the contig length such that contigs of at least that length
      cover half of the assembly, so higher is better. Contig lengths span orders of
      magnitude, so the card ranks medians instead of drawing a box.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: n_contigs
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: assembler
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: contigs, by assembler
    title: Contigs
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of contigs over the assemblies in view, and
      the bars rank the assemblers by the contigs they produce. It answers which
      assembler fragments the community most.

      How to read: a much higher count for one assembler on the same samples means a
      more fragmented assembly, usually with a lower N50. Contigs under 500 bp are
      not counted by QUAST by default.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: largest_contig
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: assembler
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: longest contig, by assembler
    title: Longest contig
    description: >-
      The hero number is the longest contig of any assembly in view, and the bars
      rank the assemblers by their longest contig. It answers whether any assembler
      reached genome-scale contigs.

      How to read: a very long contig means part of the community assembled in one
      piece. A low maximum next to a high total length points to a fragmented
      assembly.
  - component: card
    column: gc_percent
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median GC, with its spread
    title: GC content
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median GC percentage of the assemblies in view, and the
      box shows the spread across assemblies. It answers whether assemblers agree on
      the base composition of the community.

      How to read: assemblies of the same sample should give a similar GC. A shift
      points to one assembler recovering a different part of the community.
  - component: table

    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Bin contiguity against bin length
    roles: {x: total_length, y: n50, label: bin_id, color: binner, size: n_contigs}
    config:
      x_title: Bin length (bp)
      y_title: Contig N50 of the bin (bp)
      log_y: true
      top_n_labels: 5
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a recovered bin: its total length on the horizontal axis and
      the N50 of its contigs on the vertical axis, coloured by binner and sized by
      the number of contigs. It answers which bins are a few long contigs and
      which are a pile of fragments.

      estimate for them may be carried by fragments. Compare binners on the same
      assembly.

      logarithmic.

      filters), not a cut-off of QUAST.

    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Bin GC content against length
    roles: {x: total_length, y: gc_percent, label: bin_id, color: assembler, size: n_contigs}
    config:

  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Contigs per bin by binner
    dict_kwargs:
      x: n_contigs
      color: binner
      labels: {n_contigs: Contigs in the bin, binner: Binner, count: Bins}
    reference_lines:

    description: >-

    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: binner
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: median N50, by binner
    title: Bin contig N50
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median contig N50 of the bins in view, and the bars
      rank the binners by their median. It answers which binner recovers the most
      contiguous bins.

      cover half of the bin, so higher is better. Values span orders of magnitude,
      so the card ranks medians instead of drawing a box.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: n_contigs
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: assembler

    description: >-

      least fragmented bins.

  - component: card

id: quast_length_ladder
name: Contig length ladder
mode: length-ladder
description: >-
  How much of each assembly survives a minimum contig length. A curve that
  holds its length out to 25 kbp is an assembly a binner can work with; one
  that loses most of its bases between 1 and 5 kbp is a drift of fragments
  that will bin into chimeras whatever the binner.

fixture: length_ladder.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: one curve per assembly (the series role). The ladder rungs are those QUAST
  # reports for the run, and QUAST defines no pass mark on the retained length, so
  # no reference line is drawn.
  - id: cumulative_length
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Assembled length kept at each minimum contig length
    roles: {series: assembly_id, x: min_contig_length, y: total_length}
    config:
      x_title: Minimum contig length (bp)
      y_title: Length held by contigs of at least that size (bp)
    description: >-
      Each curve is one assembly: the total length held by contigs of at least a
      given size, read at each minimum contig length QUAST reports. It answers how
      much of the assembly sits in long contigs.

      How to read: a curve that stays high toward the right keeps most of its
      sequence in long contigs, which a binner can work with. A curve that falls
      steeply between the first rungs holds its length in short fragments.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - id: retained_fraction
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Share of the assembly kept at each minimum contig length
    roles: {series: assembly_id, x: min_contig_length, y: length_fraction}
    config:
      x_title: Minimum contig length (bp)
      y_title: Share of the assembled length
    description: >-
      Each curve is one assembly: the share of its total length held by contigs of
      at least a given size. It answers how quickly an assembly loses sequence as
      short contigs are set aside, independent of its size.

      How to read: curves that stay near 1 are dominated by long contigs. Curves that
      collapse early are drifts of short fragments that will bin into chimeras, so
      compare assemblies on the same sample.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    title: Contigs surviving each minimum length
    dict_kwargs:
      x: min_contig_length

      color: assembly_id

      labels: {min_contig_length: Minimum contig length (bp), n_contigs: Contigs, assembly_id: Assembly}
    description: >-
      Each line is one assembly: the number of contigs of at least a given size at
      each minimum length QUAST reports. It answers how many contigs a size filter
      leaves.

      How to read: a line that drops by orders of magnitude after the first rung is
      mostly short contigs. A flat line is an assembly of a few long contigs. The
      vertical axis is logarithmic.

    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]

    filter_expr: "col('min_contig_length') == 5000"

outputs.rawYaml:
id: quast_reference_report
name: Assembly against a reference
mode: reference-report
description: >-
  The reference-based half of QUAST's report, written only when the run gave
  QUAST a reference: how much of the reference each assembly covers, how often
  it breaks with it (misassemblies), its mismatch and indel rates, and NGA50,
  the contiguity that is left once the assembly is cut at every misassembly. A
  high N50 with a much lower NGA50 is contiguity bought with joins the reference
  does not support.
find:
  path_glob: "**/QUAST/*/transposed_report.tsv"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/quast/*/transposed_report.tsv"
    - "**/QUAST/transposed_report.tsv"
recipe: quast/reference_report.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 3 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several assemblies.
fixture: reference_report.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: coloured by assembly report. The scatter holds one point per assembly against a
  # reference, so its size depends on the run. QUAST defines no pass mark for genome
  # fraction or misassemblies, so no reference line is drawn.
  - id: fraction_vs_misassemblies
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Reference covered against misassemblies
    roles: {x: genome_fraction, y: misassemblies, label: assembly_id, color: report_id, size: nga50}
    config:
      x_title: Genome fraction (% of the reference covered)
      y_title: Misassemblies
      top_n_labels: 5
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is one assembly aligned to the reference: the share of the
      reference it covers on the horizontal axis and the number of misassemblies
      on the vertical axis, sized by NGA50. It answers which assemblies cover the
      reference without breaking it.

      How to read: points toward the lower right cover most of the reference with
      few joins the reference does not support. A high point has a long N50 bought
      with misassemblies, so read it beside NGA50.

      Note: QUAST defines no pass mark for genome fraction or misassemblies.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median number of misassemblies
      of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of QUAST.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: NGA50 per assembly
    dict_kwargs:
      x: report_id
      y: nga50
      color: genome_fraction
      labels: {report_id: Assembly, nga50: NGA50 (bp), genome_fraction: Genome fraction (%)}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: nga50
    description: >-
      Each bar is one assembly: its NGA50, the contiguity left once the assembly
      is cut at every misassembly and unaligned region, shaded by the genome
      fraction it covers. It answers how contiguous each assembly is against the
      reference.

      How to read: NGA50 is the length of a block such that blocks of at least
      that length cover half of the reference. A bar much shorter than the
      assembly's N50 means contiguity bought with joins the reference does not
      support.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median NGA50 of this table, a
      reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a
      cut-off of QUAST.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: genome_fraction
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median coverage, with its spread
    title: Reference covered
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of the reference covered by an
      assembly, and the box shows the spread across assemblies. It answers how
      complete the assemblies are against the reference.

      How to read: a value near 100 means the reference is almost fully assembled. A
      low value means missing regions, or a reference that differs from the sample.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: misassemblies
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats, max]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: misassemblies per assembly, with their spread
    title: Misassemblies
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of misassemblies over the assemblies in
      view, and the box shows how they spread per assembly. It answers how often the
      assemblies disagree with the reference.

      How to read: fewer is better, and a few assemblies carrying most of them point
      to an assembler or a setting to revisit. Compare with N50 and NGA50 before
      trusting a long assembly.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: mismatches_per_100kbp
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median rate, with its spread
    title: Mismatches per 100 kbp
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of mismatches per 100 kbp of aligned
      sequence, and the box shows the spread across assemblies. It answers how
      accurate the assembled bases are.

      How to read: lower is better. A high rate points to a polishing or
      error-correction problem, or to a reference that differs from the sample.

      Source: https://github.com/ablab/quast/blob/master/README.md
  - component: table
    title: Assembly against the reference
    description: >-
      Each row is one assembly aligned to the reference, with its genome fraction,
      duplication ratio, misassemblies, mismatch and indel rates, NG50 and NGA50. It
      answers the exact figures behind every tile.

      How to read: sort by NGA50 to rank assemblies, then check their misassemblies
      and duplication ratio.

tools.description: Screens DNA sequences for interspersed repeats and low-complexity regions against a repeat library, and masks them.
tools.name: RepeatMasker

outputs.description: One row per assembly from the header of RepeatMasker's summary table: sequences, length with and without runs of N, GC and the bases masked, with the interspersed, retroelement, DNA transposon, unclassified and simple repeat shares. A large unclassified share is a library that could not name the repeats; a masked share far from the genome's relatives is a library that missed them or a de novo one that over-called.
outputs.name: Masking summary per assembly
outputs.rawYaml:
id: repeatmasker_masking_summary
name: Masking summary per assembly
mode: tbl/summary
description: >-
  One row per assembly from the header of RepeatMasker's summary table:
  sequences, length with and without runs of N, GC and the bases masked, with
  the interspersed, retroelement, DNA transposon, unclassified and simple
  repeat shares. A large unclassified share is a library that could not name
  the repeats; a masked share far from the genome's relatives is a library
  that missed them or a de novo one that over-called.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.tbl"
recipe: repeatmasker/masking_summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 3 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several genomes.
fixture: masking_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: masked_share
    component: card
    column: masked_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: gauge
    coverage_max: 100
    caption: median share of the assembly, with the range
    title: Masked share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of the assembly masked as repeat, with the
      lowest and the highest assembly next to it. It answers how repeat-rich the
      assemblies are.

      How to read: compare an assembly with its close relatives. A share far below them
      suggests a library that missed repeats, and a share far above a de novo library
      that over-called. RepeatMasker publishes no expected share.

      Source: https://www.repeatmasker.org/
  - id: interspersed_share
    component: card
    column: interspersed_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with the spread
    title: Interspersed repeat share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of the assembly covered by interspersed
      repeats (transposable elements), with the spread across assemblies in the box. It
      answers how much of the masking is mobile elements rather than simple sequence.

      How to read: the gap between this and the masked share is simple repeats and low
      complexity sequence. A wide box means assemblies of very different repeat content.
  # C1: colour by GC content, the continuous column that varies with repeat load.
  - id: masked_vs_length
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Masked share against assembly length
    roles: {x: total_length, y: masked_pct, label: genome, size: masked_bp}
    config:
      color_col: gc_pct
      x_title: Assembly length (bp)
      y_title: Masked share of the assembly (%)
      log_x: true
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is an assembly: its total length (horizontal) against the percentage of
      it that is masked (vertical), sized by the number of masked bases and coloured by
      its GC content. It answers whether repeat load grows with genome size.

      How to read: assemblies far above the trend are repeat-rich for their size, and
      assemblies far below it may have a library that missed repeats. RepeatMasker
      defines no cut-off here, so judge each point against related genomes.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median masked share of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of RepeatMasker.
  - component: table
    title: Masking summary per assembly
    description: >-
      Each row is an assembly: its sequences, length, GC, masked bases and the share
      masked by each repeat type. It answers how the repeat content breaks down per
      assembly.

      How to read: sort by the unclassified share to find assemblies whose library could
      not name the repeats.

tools.description: Calculation of optimal P-site offsets, diagnostic analysis and visual inspection of ribosome profiling data.
tools.name: riboWaltz

outputs.description: Share of each library's P-sites in the three reading frames, per transcript region. Footprints of translating ribosomes pile into frame 0 of the CDS; the UTRs, which ribosomes do not translate, stay close to a third per frame.
outputs.name: P-site frame distribution
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ribowaltz_frames
name: P-site frame distribution
mode: riboseq/periodicity
description: >-
  Share of each library's P-sites in the three reading frames, per transcript
  region. Footprints of translating ribosomes pile into frame 0 of the CDS; the
  UTRs, which ribosomes do not translate, stay close to a third per frame.
find: { path_glob: "**/*.ribowaltz.frames.tsv" }
recipe: ribowaltz/frames.py
fixture: frames.tsv
renders_as:
  # rank = region, so the tile opens on the CDS and the reader switches to the UTRs.
  - id: frame_composition
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: P-site reading frame per library
    roles: { sample_id: sample, taxon: frame, rank: region, abundance: pct }
    config:
      rank_label: Region
      value_title: P-sites in the frame (%)
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: the share of its P-sites that fall in each of the three
      reading frames, for one transcript region. It answers whether the footprints show
      the three-nucleotide periodicity of translating ribosomes.

      How to read: on the CDS, one frame should dominate, usually frame 0. The UTRs are
      not translated, so they stay close to a third per frame. A CDS that looks like the
      UTRs means the P-site offsets are wrong or the library lacks periodicity.

      Lines and annotations: a third per frame is the split of reads with no frame
      preference, a plain expectation of three frames and not a riboWaltz cut-off.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - id: frame_psites_card
    component: card
    column: count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: frame
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: P-sites, by frame
    title: P-sites by frame
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of P-sites, the second number is the largest single
      count, and the bars rank the three frames by P-sites. It answers which frame holds
      most of the signal.

      How to read: pooled over regions the frames are mixed, so filter to the CDS to
      read the periodicity. One frame far ahead of the others means a phased library.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - component: table
    title: P-site frame counts
    description: >-
      Each row is a library, region and frame with its P-site count and share. It
      answers the exact numbers behind the bars.

      How to read: filter the region to the CDS and compare frame 0 with the other two.

name: Ribo-seq library quality
mode: riboseq/summary
description: >-
  One row per Ribo-seq library: P-sites assigned, share of CDS P-sites in frame
  0 and its margin over the other frames, P-site share per region and the CDS
  enrichment over the length expectation, modal footprint length and its spread.
find: { path_glob: "**/*.ribowaltz.frames.tsv" }
recipe: ribowaltz/library_summary.py
fixture: library_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: the sample is the only categorical column, so each library gets a colour.
  # C3: the reference at a third is the split of the three frames with no
  # preference, a plain expectation and not a riboWaltz cut-off.
  - id: phasing_plane
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: CDS share against frame 0 share
    roles: { x: cds_pct, y: frame0_cds_pct, label: sample, size: psites, color: sample }
    config:
      x_title: P-sites in the CDS (%)
      y_title: CDS P-sites in frame 0 (%)
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_value: 33.3
      reference_label: No frame preference (one third)
    description: >-
      Each point is a library: the share of its P-sites that fall in the CDS against the
      share of CDS P-sites in frame 0, sized by the number of P-sites, with one colour per library. It answers which libraries are both
      enriched on coding sequence and phased.

      How to read: good libraries sit top right. A point near the line, or with a
      negative margin, has no clear periodicity, which usually means the P-site offsets
      are wrong for that library. A point far left of its peers is dominated by UTR
      signal, as fragmented RNA would be.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line at a third marks the frame 0 share of a
      library with no frame preference. It is an arithmetic reference, an even split over three frames, and not a riboWaltz cut-off.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - id: library_record
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: record_card
    title: Library record
    roles: { id: sample }
    config:
      labels:
        psites: P-sites assigned
        frame0_cds_pct: CDS P-sites in frame 0 (%)
        frame_bias: Frame 0 margin (points)
        cds_pct: P-sites in the CDS (%)
        utr5_pct: P-sites in the 5' UTR (%)
        utr3_pct: P-sites in the 3' UTR (%)
        cds_enrichment: CDS enrichment over length
        modal_length: Modal footprint length (nt)
        length_iqr: Footprint length spread (nt)
    description: >-
      Each record is one library with its quality readouts side by side. It answers how a
      single library scores on phasing, region share and footprint length.

      How to read: pick a library from the table or the plot to read its numbers
      together. A low frame 0 share with a negative margin and a CDS enrichment near one
      point to poor periodicity.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - id: frame0_card
    component: card
    column: frame0_cds_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: CDS P-sites in frame 0
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of CDS P-sites in the annotated reading frame,
      and the box shows the spread across libraries. It answers how well phased the
      libraries are.

      How to read: a third means no periodicity and well-phased footprints sit well above
      it. A long box means some libraries are phased and others are not.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - id: frame_bias_card
    component: card
    column: frame_bias
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: lowest margin, with the median
    title: Frame 0 margin
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest margin of frame 0 over the next frame, in percentage
      points, and the second number is the median across libraries. It answers whether
      the worst library is still phased.

      How to read: a negative margin means another frame dominates, which usually means
      the P-site offsets are wrong for that library. riboWaltz publishes no minimum
      margin, so read it against the other libraries.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - id: cds_share_card
    component: card
    column: cds_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: P-sites in the CDS
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of P-sites on coding sequence, and the box
      shows the spread. It answers how well the libraries capture translation.

      How to read: footprints of translating ribosomes pile into the CDS. A library whose
      share follows the length of the CDS looks like fragmented RNA.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - id: psites_card
    component: card
    column: psites
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: P-sites, with the median per library
    title: P-sites assigned
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of P-sites assigned over all libraries, and the second
      number is the median per library. It answers how much signal the run holds.

      How to read: libraries with far fewer P-sites than the median give noisy phasing
      and region shares, so read their numbers with care.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - id: modal_length_card
    component: card
    column: modal_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: median, with the shortest and longest
    title: Modal footprint length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of each library's most common read length, with the
      shortest and longest beside it. It answers whether libraries agree on the footprint
      length.

      How to read: libraries of one protocol should share the same mode. A library off by
      several nucleotides was digested or size-selected differently.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - component: table
    title: Library quality table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library with its P-sites, phasing, region shares and footprint length.
      It answers the exact readouts behind the tiles of this tab.

      How to read: sort by frame 0 share to find the libraries that are least phased.

outputs.description: P-site signal summed over all transcripts at each nucleotide around the annotated start codon, per library. A phased library peaks at the start codon and shows a 3-nt saw-tooth along the CDS.
outputs.name: Metagene profile at the start codon
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ribowaltz_metaprofile_start
name: Metagene profile at the start codon
mode: riboseq/metagene
description: >-
  P-site signal summed over all transcripts at each nucleotide around the
  annotated start codon, per library. A phased library peaks at the start codon
  and shows a 3-nt saw-tooth along the CDS.
find: { path_glob: "**/*.ribowaltz.metaprofile_psite.tsv" }
recipe: ribowaltz/metaprofile_start.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several libraries.
fixture: metaprofile_start.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: start_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: P-site signal around the start codon
    roles: { series: sample, x: position, y: signal }
    config:
      reference_x: 0
      reference_label: First nucleotide of the start codon
      x_title: Distance from the start codon (nt)
      y_title: Share of the window's P-site signal (%)
    description: >-
      Each line is a library: its P-site signal at every nucleotide around the annotated
      start codon, summed over all transcripts. It answers whether footprints are phased
      along the coding sequence.

      How to read: Position 0 is the first nucleotide of the start codon. A peak there and a three-nucleotide saw-tooth along the CDS show a phased library. A flat or noisy line with no pattern means the offsets are wrong
      or the library has no periodicity.

      Lines and annotations: the vertical line at 0 marks the first nucleotide of the
      start codon, the origin of the distance axis, defined by the annotation riboWaltz uses.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - component: table
    title: P-site signal around the start codon
    description: >-
      Each row is a library and a position relative to the start codon, with the share of
      the window's P-site signal. It answers the exact signal behind the lines.

      How to read: filter to one library and sort by position to follow its profile.

outputs.description: Share of each library's P-sites in the 5' UTR, CDS and 3' UTR, next to the share each region would get from its length alone. Protected footprints are enriched in the CDS; a library that follows the length expectation behaves like fragmented RNA.
outputs.name: P-sites per transcript region
outputs.rawYaml:
id: ribowaltz_psite_region
name: P-sites per transcript region
mode: riboseq/region
description: >-
  Share of each library's P-sites in the 5' UTR, CDS and 3' UTR, next to the
  share each region would get from its length alone. Protected footprints are
  enriched in the CDS; a library that follows the length expectation behaves
  like fragmented RNA.
find: { path_glob: "**/*.ribowaltz.psite_region.tsv" }
recipe: ribowaltz/psite_region.py
fixture: psite_region.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: region_composition
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: P-sites per transcript region
    roles: { sample_id: sample, taxon: region, rank: scope, abundance: pct }
    config:
      rank_label: Scope
      value_title: Share of P-sites (%)
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library: the share of its P-sites in the 5' UTR, CDS and 3' UTR. It
      answers whether the footprints accumulate on coding sequence.

      How to read: ribosome profiling data should define the CDS as the region with the
      highest share of reads. A library whose shares follow the length of each region
      behaves like fragmented RNA, not like translating ribosomes.

      Lines and annotations: where the scope also holds the share expected from random
      RNA fragmentation, it is the cumulative length of each region as a percentage, as
      defined by riboWaltz.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - id: region_enrichment_card
    component: card
    column: enrichment
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('region') == 'CDS'"
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: CDS enrichment over length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median ratio of the CDS share of P-sites to the share its
      length alone would give, and the box shows the spread across libraries. It answers
      how strongly footprints favour coding sequence.

      How to read: a ratio of one means the footprints follow length, as fragmented RNA
      would, and higher values mean the CDS is enriched. Libraries far below their peers
      deserve a look.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md
  - component: table
    title: P-site region table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library and region with its P-site count, share, expected share and
      enrichment. It answers the exact numbers behind the bars.

      How to read: sort by enrichment to find the libraries that favour the CDS least.

renders_as.description:
Each bar is a library: the share of its P-sites in the 5' UTR, CDS and 3' UTR. It answers whether the footprints accumulate on coding sequence.
How to read: ribosome profiling data should define the CDS as the region with the highest share of reads. A library whose shares follow the length of each region behaves like fragmented RNA, not like translating ribosomes.
Lines and annotations: where the scope also holds the share expected from random RNA fragmentation, it is the cumulative length of each region as a percentage, as defined by riboWaltz.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LabTranslationalArchitectomics/riboWaltz/master/README.md

tools.description: Differential alternative splicing of annotated and novel events (skipped exons, retained introns, mutually exclusive exons, alternative 3' and 5' splice sites) between two groups of replicated RNA-seq samples.
tools.name: rMATS

outputs.description: rMATS junction-and-exon-count (JCEC) results for the five event types, stacked: one row per contrast and covered event with its gene, alternative region, mean inclusion (PSI) per condition, the treatment-minus-control difference, FDR and the significance call.
outputs.name: Differential splicing events (rMATS)
outputs.rawYaml:
id: rmats_events
name: Differential splicing events (rMATS)
mode: splicing/events
description: >-
  rMATS junction-and-exon-count (JCEC) results for the five event types,
  stacked: one row per contrast and covered event with its gene, alternative
  region, mean inclusion (PSI) per condition, the treatment-minus-control
  difference, FDR and the significance call.
find: { path_glob: "**/*.MATS.JCEC.txt" }
recipe: rmats/events.py
fixture: events.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: event_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Splicing change against significance
    roles: { feature_id: event_id, effect_size: dpsi, significance: fdr, label: gene_name, category: event_type }
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 0.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Change in inclusion (delta PSI)
      significance_label: -log10 FDR
    description: >-
      Each point is a splicing event in one contrast: its change in exon inclusion (delta PSI) on the
      horizontal axis and its FDR on the vertical axis, coloured by event type. It answers which events
      change most, in which direction, and how confidently.

      How to read: events in the upper left and upper right corners lose or gain inclusion in the treatment
      with strong support. A cloud with nothing above the line means little differential splicing, so check
      the replicate coverage before trusting the contrast. Open the table tile for the labelled genes.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an FDR of 0.05, the level at which rMATS counts an event
      as significant in its summary. No delta PSI line is drawn: the rnasplice template passes its MIN_DPSI
      variable to this recipe's min_dpsi parameter with a default of 0, so the call adds no floor on the
      change. A value above 0 is the user's own working value, not an rMATS default.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Xinglab/rmats-turbo/master/README.md
  - id: event_record
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: record_card
    title: Splicing event record
    roles: { id: event_id, title: gene_name }
    description: >-
      The card shows every field of one splicing event: its gene, type, coordinates, inclusion per condition,
      change in inclusion, FDR and read support. It answers what exactly is known about the event picked in
      the table or the volcano.

      How to read: select a row in the table to fill the card. Compare the inclusion in both conditions with
      the read counts, since a large change on few reads is weak evidence.
  - id: event_types
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Events by type and direction
    dict_kwargs: { x: event_type, color: direction, barmode: stack, labels: { event_type: Event type, direction: Direction of change } }
    description: >-
      Each bar is an event type, split by whether its events gain inclusion, lose it or do not change
      significantly. It answers which kinds of splicing carry the differences between the conditions.

      How to read: a type whose bar is mostly significant is where the treatment acts. Bars that are almost
      entirely not significant point to little signal for that type.
  - component: card
    column: event_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: event_type
    title: Events tested
    caption: events, by type
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct events with enough reads to be tested, and the ring splits them
      by event type. It answers how much splicing the run covered and of what kind.

      How to read: a type that is missing may have had too few reads to pass the coverage filter, so
      check the sequencing depth.
  - component: card
    column: abs_dpsi
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Size of the inclusion change
    caption: quartiles of the absolute change
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median absolute change in exon inclusion across events, and the box shows its
      quartiles. It answers how large the splicing differences are overall.

      How to read: a box close to zero means most events are unchanged and the signal sits in a few. Filter to
      one event type or contrast to see where the larger changes are.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: event_type
    title: Event type
    description: >-
      Restricts every tile to the chosen event types, such as skipped exons or retained introns.
      It answers whether a pattern holds within one kind of splicing.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: event_id
    title: Splicing events
    description: >-
      Each row is a splicing event in one contrast, with its gene, coordinates, inclusion in both conditions,
      change in inclusion, FDR and significance call. It answers which events to follow up.

      How to read: sort by FDR or by the absolute change and select a row to fill the event record.

renders_as.description:
Each point is a splicing event in one contrast: its change in exon inclusion (delta PSI) on the horizontal axis and its FDR on the vertical axis, coloured by event type. It answers which events change most, in which direction, and how confidently.
How to read: events in the upper left and upper right corners lose or gain inclusion in the treatment with strong support. A cloud with nothing above the line means little differential splicing, so check the replicate coverage before trusting the contrast. Open the table tile for the labelled genes.
Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is an FDR of 0.05, the level at which rMATS counts an event as significant in its summary. No delta PSI line is drawn: the rnasplice template passes its MIN_DPSI variable to this recipe's min_dpsi parameter with a default of 0, so the call adds no floor on the change. A value above 0 is the user's own working value, not an rMATS default.

renders_as.title: Splicing change against significance

renders_as.description:
The card shows every field of one splicing event: its gene, type, coordinates, inclusion per condition, change in inclusion, FDR and read support. It answers what exactly is known about the event picked in the table or the volcano.
How to read: select a row in the table to fill the card. Compare the inclusion in both conditions with the read counts, since a large change on few reads is weak evidence.
renders_as.title: Splicing event record

renders_as.description:
Each bar is an event type, split by whether its events gain inclusion, lose it or do not change significantly. It answers which kinds of splicing carry the differences between the conditions.
How to read: a type whose bar is mostly significant is where the treatment acts. Bars that are almost entirely not significant point to little signal for that type.

renders_as.caption: events, by type
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the count of distinct events with enough reads to be tested, and the ring splits them by event type. It answers how much splicing the run covered and of what kind.
How to read: a type that is missing may have had too few reads to pass the coverage filter, so check the sequencing depth.
renders_as.title: Events tested

renders_as.caption: quartiles of the absolute change
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median absolute change in exon inclusion across events, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how large the splicing differences are overall.
How to read: a box close to zero means most events are unchanged and the signal sits in a few. Filter to one event type or contrast to see where the larger changes are.
renders_as.title: Size of the inclusion change

renders_as.description: Restricts every tile to the chosen event types, such as skipped exons or retained introns. It answers whether a pattern holds within one kind of splicing.
renders_as.title: Event type

renders_as.description:
Each row is a splicing event in one contrast, with its gene, coordinates, inclusion in both conditions, change in inclusion, FDR and significance call. It answers which events to follow up.
How to read: sort by FDR or by the absolute change and select a row to fill the event record.
renders_as.title: Splicing events

id: rseqc_read_distribution
name: Read distribution over the annotation
mode: qc/read-distribution
description: >-
  Where each library's reads land on the annotation: coding exons, the two UTRs,
  introns, the promoter and downstream rings, and everything intergenic. RSeQC
  publishes the upstream and downstream bands nested inside each other, so the
  recipe differences them into disjoint rings and adds the unassigned tags
  explicitly, which makes the composition sum to one.
find: { path_glob: "**/*.read_distribution.txt" }
recipe: rseqc/read_distribution.py
fixture: read_distribution.tsv
renders_as:
  # Two resolutions in one tile: the coarse region classes, or the individual
  # RSeQC features, picked with the rank filter.
  - id: distribution_composition
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: Read distribution over the annotation
    roles: { sample_id: sample_id, taxon: taxon, rank: rank, abundance: abundance }
    config:
      default_rank: Region class
      rank_label: Level
      x_title: Library
      value_title: Share of mapped tags
    description: >-
      Each bar is a library, split into the share of its mapped tags that fall on each
      part of the annotation: exons, introns, promoter and downstream bands and
      intergenic sequence. It answers where the reads of each library land.

      How to read: an RNA-seq library of mature RNA is dominated by exonic reads. A high
      intronic share points to pre-mRNA or genomic DNA contamination, and a high
      intergenic share to DNA contamination or an incomplete annotation. Switch the
      level to read the individual features.

      Note: where features overlap, RSeQC assigns a read to CDS exons first, then UTR
      exons, then introns, then intergenic regions.

      Source: https://rseqc.sourceforge.net/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22743226/
  # The frame carries both resolutions, so a card that SUMS tag_count over all rows would
  # add the region-class rows to the feature rows they are made of and report twice
  # the library. The filter keeps one resolution.
  - component: card
    column: tag_count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: region_class
    filter_expr: "col('rank') == 'Region class'"
    headline: true
    title: Mapped tags by region class
    caption: tags, by region class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of mapped tags over all libraries, with the
      median and the largest class beside it, and the bar splits them by region class.
      It answers what share of the sequencing falls on exons, introns and intergenic
      regions.

      How to read: a mostly exonic bar is the expected shape for mature RNA. A large
      intergenic or intronic share is the lead for contamination or an annotation that
      misses real transcripts.

      Source: https://rseqc.sourceforge.net/
  - component: table
    title: Read distribution table
    description: >-
      Each row is a library and an annotation class, at the region level or at the
      feature level, with its tag count and its share of the library. It answers the
      exact counts behind the composition.

      How to read: filter the rank to Region class for the coarse split, or Feature for
      the exon, UTR, promoter and downstream bands.

tools.description: Real Time Genomics utilities for accurate VCF comparison and manipulation.
tools.name: RTG Tools

outputs.description: Per-callset variant-calling accuracy (TP/FP/FN, precision, recall, F1) from rtg-tools vcfeval's aggregated summary. `label` is the callset's samplesheet id, `caller` the tool that made the calls and `truth_set` the truth set it was compared against. Serves the germline (small/) and somatic (snv/, indel/) routes with the same vocabulary.
outputs.name: vcfeval benchmark summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: rtgtools_vcfeval_summary
name: vcfeval benchmark summary
mode: benchmark-summary
description: >-
  Per-callset variant-calling accuracy (TP/FP/FN, precision, recall, F1) from
  rtg-tools vcfeval's aggregated summary. `label` is the callset's samplesheet
  id, `caller` the tool that made the calls and `truth_set` the truth set it was
  compared against. Serves the germline (small/) and somatic (snv/, indel/)
  routes with the same vocabulary.
find: { path_glob: "**/summary/tables/rtgtools/rtgtools.summary.csv" }
recipe: rtgtools/vcfeval_summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 3 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several callsets.
fixture: vcfeval_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # Each point is a callset at its (recall, precision). The default point colour
  # is the F1 scale, so the colour is already bound to the quantity that ranks
  # the callsets; the point size is the true positives it recovers.
  - id: pr_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: pr_benchmark
    title: Precision against recall per callset
    roles: {label: label, recall: recall, precision: precision, f1: f1, support: tp_comp}
    description: >-
      Each point is a callset compared with its truth set: its recall on the
      horizontal axis and its precision on the vertical axis, coloured by F1 and
      sized by the true positives it recovers. It answers which callset finds the
      most true variants without adding false ones.

      How to read: the top right corner is best, with every true variant found and
      no false call. A point far to the left misses true variants, a point low down
      adds false calls, so look at the false negative and false positive cards to see
      which one dominates.

      Lines and annotations: the curved contours are lines of equal F1, the harmonic
      mean of precision and recall, and the diagonal marks precision equal to
      recall. They are drawn from the definitions of the metrics, not from a cut-off.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30858580/
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/happy.md
  - id: confusion
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: confusion_matrix
    title: True and false calls per callset
    roles: {label: label, tp: tp_comp, fp: fp, fn: fn}
    description: >-
      Each cell is a count of variants for one callset: the true positives, the
      false positives or the false negatives of its comparison with the truth set.
      It answers how many variants stand behind each precision and recall value.

      How to read: a callset with many more false negatives than false positives
      loses recall, and the reverse loses precision. Compare cells within a callset
      first, because callsets of different size are not comparable by raw count.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30858580/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: label
      y: f1
      color: caller
      labels: {label: Callset, f1: F1 score, caller: Caller}
    title: F1 score per callset
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: f1}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a callset, with its F1 score, the harmonic mean of its precision and
      recall, and a colour for the caller that made it. It answers which callset
      scores best overall.

      How to read: a short bar means either many missed variants or many false
      calls, so open the precision-recall tile to see which. Compare bars of the same
      truth set only.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median F1 score of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of RTG Tools.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30858580/
      and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/happy.md
  # Best F1, with the spread across callsets: the one number that ranks them.
  - component: card
    column: f1
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: best callset, with the spread
    title: Best F1 score
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest F1 score among the callsets in view, and the box
      shows how all of them spread. It answers how good the best callset is and how far
      the others lag.

      How to read: a best score close to 1 means a callset that agrees with the truth
      set. A wide box means the callers differ a lot, so check which one is ahead
      before pooling them.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30858580/
  - component: table
    title: Benchmark table
    description: >-
      Each row is a callset compared with a truth set, with the caller, the true
      positives on both sides, the false positives and negatives, and the precision,
      recall and F1 derived from them. It answers the exact numbers behind every other
      tile.

      How to read: sort by F1, or filter by caller or truth set to compare like with
      like.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  # Callsets by caller always split evenly (one per caller and sample), so the
  # breakdown is a measure: the true positives each caller recovers.
  - component: card
    column: tp_comp
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: caller
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: true positives, by caller
    title: True positives by caller
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of true positives across the callsets in view, and
      the bars rank the callers by how many they recover. It answers which caller
      finds the most true variants.

      How to read: a caller far ahead recovers more of the truth set, but compare it
      with the false positive card, since a looser caller finds more of both.
  - component: card
    column: f1
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Median F1 score
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median F1 score across the callsets in view, and the box
      shows their spread. It answers how accurate the benchmark is as a whole.

      How to read: a median near 1 means most callsets reproduce the truth set. A box
      that reaches far below the median points to a few weak callsets.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30858580/
  - component: card
    column: precision
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: grid
    caption: average precision, with its range
    title: Precision
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average precision, the share of a callset's calls that
      are true, with the lowest and highest values across callsets. It answers how
      free of false calls the callsets are.

      How to read: a high average with a low minimum points to one callset adding
      false calls.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30858580/
  # vcfeval and the GA4GH benchmarking best practices define recall, but neither
  # publishes a pass mark for it, so the card shows the distribution and draws none.
  - component: card
    column: recall
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Recall
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median recall, the share of the truth set that a callset
      recovers, and the box shows the spread across callsets. It answers how much of
      the truth the callsets find.

      How to read: a low recall means missed variants, which the false negative card
      counts. The cited paper states no cut-off for recall, so none is drawn.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30858580/
  - component: card
    column: fp
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: total, with the spread across callsets
    title: False positives
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of false positive calls across the callsets,
      and the box shows how they spread. It answers how many calls have no match in
      the truth set.

      How to read: a callset far above the rest is where precision is lost. Open the
      confusion matrix to compare it with its true positives.
  - component: card
    column: fn
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: total, with the distribution across callsets
    title: False negatives
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of truth variants that no callset found, and
      the histogram shows how they distribute across callsets. It answers how many true
      variants are missed.

      How to read: a pile of callsets near zero with a few far to the right means a
      few callers lose recall. Check those against the recall card.

tools.description: Single-sequence protein secondary structure prediction: helix, strand or coil for every residue, with the probability of each state.
tools.name: S4PRED

outputs.description: One row per residue: the protein, the residue number and amino acid, the predicted state (helix, strand or coil) as the residue table category, the probability of that state as its value, and the three state probabilities. A sequence track draws it as a coloured state lane over a confidence lane.
outputs.name: Secondary structure per residue
outputs.rawYaml:
id: s4pred_secondary_structure
name: Secondary structure per residue
mode: protein/residues
description: >-
  One row per residue: the protein, the residue number and amino acid, the
  predicted state (helix, strand or coil) as the residue table category, the
  probability of that state as its value, and the three state probabilities.
  A sequence track draws it as a coloured state lane over a confidence lane.
find:
  path_glob: "**/s4pred/*/ss2/*.ss2"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*.ss2"
recipe: s4pred/secondary_structure.py
fixture: secondary_structure.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: ss_sequence_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sequence_track
    title: Predicted state along the sequence
    roles: {position: position, entity: entity, residue: residue, category: category, value: value}
    description: >-
      Each cell is a residue of the protein, coloured by its predicted state (helix, strand or coil), with a
      lane below for the probability of that state. It answers which stretches fold into which structure and
      how sure the model is.

      How to read: long helix or strand runs with high confidence are likely real elements. Short stretches
      with low confidence are uncertain and may flip with a small change in the sequence. Compare the track
      with domain and structure tiles of the same protein.

      Note: S4PRED predicts from the single sequence, with no alignment.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/psipred/s4pred/main/README.md
  # The called state as a ribbon (helix, strand arrow, coil) shaded by the state probabilities.
  - id: ss_ribbon
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: secondary_structure
    title: Secondary structure ribbon
    roles: {position: position, entity: entity, residue: residue, state: ss_code,
            p_helix: p_helix, p_strand: p_strand, p_coil: p_coil}
    description: >-
      The ribbon draws the predicted structure of the protein as helices, strand arrows and coil, shaded by how
      confident the prediction is, with the three state probabilities beneath it. It answers where the
      structural elements are and where the call is ambiguous.

      How to read: dark, clear helices and strands are confident calls. Pale stretches, or places where the
      helix and strand probabilities are close, are ambiguous. The segment list gives the span of each element
      for follow-up.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/psipred/s4pred/main/README.md
  - id: ss_confidence
    component: card
    column: value
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    title: Prediction confidence
    caption: probability of the called state, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median probability S4PRED gives to the state it called at each residue, and the
      box shows its quartiles. It answers how confident the model is over the whole protein.

      How to read: values close to one mean most residues are called with certainty. Lower values point to
      disordered or ambiguous regions, where the predicted state should not be trusted.
  - id: ss_residues
    component: card
    column: position
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: category
    top_n_count: 3
    title: Residues by state
    caption: residues, by predicted state
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of residues predicted, with the longest protein length beside it, and the
      bars rank the states by how many residues take them. It answers the helix, strand and coil composition.

renders_as:
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: group
      y: log2_tpm
      color: group
      labels: {group: Group, log2_tpm: Expression (log2 TPM + 1)}
    title: Expression by group
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: log2_tpm}
    description: >-
      Each box is a group of samples: the distribution of log2(TPM + 1) over the genes
      expressed in at least one sample. It answers whether groups share the same
      overall expression level.

      How to read: boxes at similar heights mean comparable libraries. A box shifted
      up or down points to a global difference in expression or in library
      composition, so check the sample overview before a differential analysis.
      Pick genes in the filter to see one gene across groups.

      Lines and annotations: genes are kept when at least one sample reaches 1 TPM,
      a fixed filter of this view and not a Salmon cut-off.

      expressed.

    column: gene_name

    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: group
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: genes, by group
    title: Genes in view
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct genes in view, and the bars rank the
      groups by how many genes they carry rows for. It answers how many genes the
      explorer holds.

outputs.description: One row per sample: principal components of the log2(TPM + 1) matrix over its most variable genes, plus how many genes the sample detects and expresses and the median TPM of the genes it detects.
