id: salmon_sample_pca
name: Sample overview
mode: expression/pca
description: >-
  One row per sample: principal components of the log2(TPM + 1) matrix over its
  most variable genes, plus how many genes the sample detects and expresses and
  the median TPM of the genes it detects.
find: { path_glob: "**/salmon.merged.gene_tpm.tsv" }
recipe: salmon/sample_pca.py
fixture: sample_pca.tsv
renders_as:
  # The group column is the sample's factor (sheet column or the condition read off
  # the sample name), the column the dashboard's category_colors key.
  - id: pca
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, dim_1: dim_1, dim_2: dim_2, color: group}
    config:
      axis_prefix: PC
      legend_pos: bottom
    title: Sample PCA
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample, placed by the first two principal components of its
      log2(TPM + 1) over the 500 most variable genes, and coloured by group. It
      answers whether samples of one group are alike and whether any sample is an
      outlier.

      How to read: replicates should sit next to each other and groups should separate
      along a component. A sample far from its group is a candidate outlier or a
      swap, so check its row in the table and its mapping rate before keeping it.
      Groups that overlap fully mean little signal between them.

      Lines and annotations: no reference line is drawn. The 500-gene selection is a
      fixed choice of this view.
  - component: card
    column: group
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: group
    headline: true
    caption: samples, by group
    title: Groups and samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of groups and the ring splits the samples between
      them, one row per sample. It answers how the design is balanced.

      How to read: a very small slice is a group with few replicates, which limits the
      comparisons that follow.
  - component: card
    column: median_tpm
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Median TPM of detected genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median across samples of each sample's median TPM over the
      genes it detects, and the box shows the spread. It answers whether samples have a
      similar expression profile overall.

      How to read: a sample far from the others may carry a different library
      composition, for instance a dominant transcript. Compare it with the PCA.
  # The recipe counts a gene as expressed at TPM >= 1 (EXPRESSED_TPM). That is a
  # fixed convention of this view, not a Salmon cut-off, so no pass mark is drawn
  # (RULES section 17): the previous 10k floor had no source.
  - component: card
    column: genes_expressed
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: mean, with its spread
    title: Genes expressed
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean count of genes per sample with at least 1 TPM, and the
      box shows the spread between samples. It answers how complex the transcriptome
      of each library is.

      How to read: a library that expresses far fewer genes than its peers of the same
      type is a candidate for degradation or low depth. Salmon sets no minimum, so
      compare within the run.

      Lines and annotations: a gene counts as expressed at TPM of 1 or more, a fixed
      convention of this view and not a Salmon cut-off.
  - component: card
    column: genes_detected
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: distribution across samples
    title: Genes detected
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean count of genes per sample with any signal (TPM above
      0), and the histogram shows how samples spread. It answers how many genes each
      library touches at all.

      How to read: detection grows with depth, so a low value can simply mean few
      reads. Read it next to the number of genes expressed.
  - component: table
    title: Sample overview table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its principal components, its group, the genes it
      detects and expresses and the median TPM of its detected genes. It answers which
      sample to inspect.

      How to read: sort by genes expressed to find the sparsest library.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: genes_expressed
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: vertical
    caption: lowest, median and highest
    title: Fewest genes expressed
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest count of expressed genes in any sample, with the
      median and the highest beside it. It answers how far the sparsest library is from
      the rest.

      How to read: a minimum far below the median points to an under-sequenced or
      degraded library. The gap matters more than the absolute number.

    caption: the groups with most genes detected

    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest count of detected genes in any sample, and the bars
      rank the groups by their own maximum. It answers which groups carry the richest
      libraries.

      How to read: groups that differ much in detection may differ in depth rather than
      biology.

outputs.name: Reads per contig
outputs.rawYaml:
id: samtools_idxstats
name: Reads per contig
mode: alignment/contigs
description: >-
  Mapped reads per reference contig and sample from samtools idxstats, with
  each contig classed as autosome, X, Y, mitochondrion or other (alt, unplaced,
  decoy) and its share of the sample's mapped reads. The cheapest read on the
  mitochondrial fraction, the sex chromosomes and the reads lost to alt contigs.
  When a pipeline publishes idxstats before and after MarkDuplicates, one stage
  per sample is kept.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.idxstats"
recipe: samtools/idxstats.py
fixture: idxstats.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: reads_by_contig_class
    component: card
    column: mapped_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: contig_class
    caption: reads, by contig class
    title: Mapped reads by contig class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of mapped reads, the second number is the largest
      count on a single contig, and the bar splits the reads into autosome, X, Y,
      mitochondrion and other contigs. It answers where the reads went.

      How to read: most reads should fall on autosomes. A large share on other contigs
      points to alt, unplaced or decoy sequence soaking up reads, and a large

    component: card
    column: mapped_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('contig_class') == 'mitochondrion'"
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Mitochondrial share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of mapped reads on the mitochondrial genome,
      and the box shows the spread across samples. It answers how much of each library
      is mitochondrial.

      How to read: a sample far above its peers wasted sequencing on the mitochondrion,
      often from lysis or a protocol that does not deplete it. Acceptable levels depend
      on the assay, so compare against samples of the same type.

outputs.name: Alignment distributions
outputs.rawYaml:
id: samtools_stats_sections
name: Alignment distributions
mode: alignment/distributions
description: >-
  The distribution blocks of a samtools stats report, which MultiQC never
  surfaces: the read-length histogram (RL), the coverage-depth histogram
  (COV), the indel-length spectrum (ID) and, for paired data, the insert-size
  distribution (IS), with the SN summary block on one row per sample beside
  them. Each section has its own value column, so three profile tiles read the
  same collection without a filter between them.
# `*.bam.stats` rather than `*.stats`: the latter also matches the
# `*flagstat.stats` that `flagstat.yaml` owns, and a file reached by two globs
# is recognised as two different outputs.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.bam.stats"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/samtools_stats/*.stats"
    - "**/samtools/*.stats"
    # rnavar: reports/samtools/<sample>/<sample>.md.stats (and .aligned.stats)
    - "**/samtools/*/*.md.stats"
recipe: samtools/stats_sections.py
fixture: stats_sections.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: read_length_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Read length distribution
    roles: {series: series, x: bin, y: n_reads}
    config: {x_title: Read length (bp), y_title: Reads}
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: the number of reads at every read length in the alignment.
      It answers how long the aligned reads are and whether the length is uniform.

      How to read: short-read data draws one sharp peak at the sequenced length, and
      trimmed reads draw a spread below it. A long flat tail is expected for long-read
      data. Samples with a different shape were trimmed or sequenced differently.

      Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  - id: coverage_distribution
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Coverage depth distribution
    roles: {series: series, x: bin, y: n_bases}
    config: {x_title: Coverage depth, y_title: Bases}
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: the number of bases covered at every depth. It answers
      how evenly the reads cover the reference.

      How to read: a narrow hump means even coverage and a long right tail means a few
      regions are over-covered. A tall bar at depth zero or one means much of the
      target is barely sequenced, so raise depth or check the library.

      Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  - id: indel_spectrum
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Indel length spectrum
    roles: {series: series, x: bin, y: n_indels}
    config: {x_title: Indel length (bp), y_title: Indels}
    description: >-
      Each line is the number of insertions or deletions of one length in a sample,
      drawn separately for each direction. It answers whether insertions and deletions
      are balanced.

      How to read: counts fall quickly with length. Deletions far outnumbering
      insertions, or the reverse, can point to a systematic error of the sequencing
      platform, which long-read data often shows.

      Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  - component: card
    column: reads_mapped_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Reads mapped
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of reads that are mapped, and the box shows
      the spread across samples. It answers how well the reads align.

      How to read: a high median is expected. A low value or a long box means some
      samples align poorly, from contamination or the wrong reference.

      Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  - component: card
    column: identity_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Alignment identity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of aligned bases that match the reference
      (one minus the mismatch error rate), and the box shows the spread. It answers how
      closely the reads agree with the reference.

      How to read: higher means closer agreement. Long-read data sits lower than short
      reads, so compare samples from the same platform.

      Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  - component: card
    column: average_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Average read length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of each sample's average read length, and the box
      shows the spread. It answers how long the reads are.

      How to read: samples of one run should agree. A sample far from its peers was
      trimmed or sequenced differently.

      Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  - component: card
    column: maximum_length
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: longest read, with the median of the maximums
    title: Longest read
    description: >-
      The hero number is the longest read seen in any sample, and the second number is
      the median of the per-sample maximums. It answers how far the read length tail
      extends.

      How to read: a single very long read can be a chimera or an artefact, so the
      median of the maximums is the steadier value.

      Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  - component: card
    column: supplementary_alignments
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: alignments, with the largest sample
    title: Supplementary alignments
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of supplementary alignments, which are the extra
      pieces of reads that align in several places, and the second number is the
      largest count in one sample. It answers how fragmented the alignments are.

      How to read: a high count is common in long-read data and can mark structural
      variants or chimeric reads. A sample far above the rest deserves a look.

      Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  - component: card
    column: average_quality
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Average base quality
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of each sample's average base quality, and the box
      shows the spread. It answers how reliable the base calls are.

      How to read: higher is better, and the scale depends on the sequencing platform.
      A sample well below its peers may have a failed run.

      Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  - component: card
    column: reads_mapped
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: reads, with the median per sample
    title: Mapped reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of mapped reads and the second number is the median
      per sample. It answers how much aligned data the run holds.

      How to read: a median far below the total divided by the sample count means a
      few samples hold most of the data. Open the table for the counts.

      Source: https://www.htslib.org/doc/samtools-stats.html
  - component: table
    page_size: 25
    title: Alignment statistics
    description: >-
      Each row is a histogram bin or a summary line of a sample. It answers the exact
      values behind the profiles and cards.

      How to read: filter the section column to read one distribution, or to the summary
      rows for per-sample totals.

tools.description: Calls peaks and enriched regions from sparse CUT&RUN and chromatin profiling data.
tools.name: SEACR

outputs.description: Merged consensus intervals per target against the replicates that called a peak on them, as one 0/1 column per replicate. The intersections say how reproducible the peak set is between replicates.
outputs.name: Consensus peak overlap
outputs.rawYaml:
id: seacr_consensus_peaks
name: Consensus peak overlap
mode: peaks/consensus
description: >-
  Merged consensus intervals per target against the replicates that called a peak on
  them, as one 0/1 column per replicate. The intersections say how reproducible the
  peak set is between replicates.
# The CUT&RUN-family pipelines write this table for whichever caller ran; the
# member file names carry both the replicate and the caller, which is where the
# `caller` column and the set columns come from.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.consensus.peak_counts.bed"
recipe: seacr/consensus_peaks.py
fixture: consensus_peaks.tsv
renders_as:
  # The renderer enumerates the binary replicate columns itself, so the upset
  # render binds no role.
  # C1 N/A: the sets are the replicate columns themselves, there is no other column to colour by.
  - id: seacr_consensus_upset
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: upset_plot
    title: Replicate overlap of consensus peaks
    config:
      color_intersections_by: degree
    description: >-
      Each bar is a combination of replicates and counts the merged consensus intervals
      that every replicate of the combination called a peak on. It answers how
      reproducible the peak set is between replicates.

      How to read: a tall bar for all replicates together means the peaks are
      reproducible. Tall bars for single replicates mean that replicate calls peaks the
      others miss, which is typical of a noisy or over-sensitive library. Compare the set
      sizes on the left with the intersections.

      Note: SEACR publishes no minimum number of replicates, and the pipeline decides
      which consensus peaks to keep with its own replicate threshold.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  # The merged intervals on a chromosome-aware axis, coloured by target, for a
  # locus section to stack under the per-sample calls.
  - id: seacr_consensus_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Consensus intervals along the genome
    roles: {chr: chr, pos: start, score: max_signal, feature: peak_id, end: end, category: target}
    config:
      score_title: Maximum signal
      score_threshold_stat: p95
    description: >-
      Each mark is a merged consensus interval on its chromosome, coloured by target and
      high according to the strongest maximum signal among the peaks merged into it. It
      answers where the replicates agree and how strong the signal is there.

      How to read: clusters of tall intervals are enriched domains, and an isolated tall
      interval is a candidate site. Compare targets to see which regions they share. Brush
      a region to filter the tiles of the tab.

      Lines and annotations: the line is the 95th percentile of the maximum signal
      in the table, a data-defined reference computed from the rows on show and not
      a SEACR cut-off.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  - id: seacr_consensus_width_hist
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: support
      y: width
      color: support
      labels: {support: Replicates calling the interval, width: Interval width (bp)}
    title: Consensus interval width by replicate support
    description: >-
      Each box is a replicate support level: the spread of the widths of the consensus
      intervals that this many replicates called. It answers whether intervals confirmed
      by more replicates are wider or narrower.

      How to read: a box that moves up with support means reproducible calls are broader
      domains, as expected for a broad mark. Similar boxes mean width does not depend on
      support. Very wide outliers are merged neighbouring peaks.

      Note: no width cut-off is drawn, because SEACR defines none.
  - component: card
    column: target
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: target
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: intervals, by target
    title: Consensus intervals
    description: >-
      The hero number counts the consensus intervals in view and the bars rank the targets
      by how many they hold. The extra figure is the number of targets. It answers how
      large each peak set is.

      How to read: a target with far fewer intervals than the others has a weaker or more
      selective peak set. Compare it with the peak counts of its replicates.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: num_samples
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mean, with its spread
    title: Replicates per interval
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean number of replicates that called a peak on a consensus
      interval, and the box shows its spread. It answers how reproducible the peaks are on
      average.

      How to read: a mean close to the number of replicates means most intervals are
      shared. A mean close to one means most peaks are private to one replicate.

    column: support
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: support
    caption: intervals, by replicate support
    title: Intervals by replicate support
    description: >-
      Each unit is a consensus interval and the ring splits them by how many replicates
      called a peak on it. It answers how much of the peak set is confirmed by more than
      one replicate.

      How to read: a large share at the highest support is a reproducible peak set. A ring
      dominated by single replicates means the replicates disagree.

    column: total_signal
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram

      The hero number is the mean total signal, the summed fragment coverage of the peaks
      merged into an interval, and the histogram shows how it is distributed. It answers
      how strong the consensus intervals are.

outputs.name: Nucleosome fragment classes
outputs.rawYaml:
id: seacr_fragment_classes
name: Nucleosome fragment classes
mode: qc/fragments
description: >-
  The fragment-length histogram binned into the four nucleosome classes:
  sub-nucleosomal below 120 bp, mononucleosomal to 250 bp, dinucleosomal to 450 bp and
  multi-nucleosomal above it, with the share of each per sample and the mononucleosome
  to sub-nucleosome ratio behind it.
# The raw ladder answers "does this look like chromatin"; the classes answer
# "how much of this library is nucleosome-free", which is what separates a
# sharp mark from a broad one. Every sample keeps all four classes even when a
# class is empty, because an empty class is a finding.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.frags.len.txt"
recipe: seacr/fragment_classes.py
fixture: fragment_classes.tsv
renders_as:
  # Kept a figure: cutandrun dashboards reference this id as a `figure` tile.
  # Four classes stack legibly in a plain bar (RULES.md section 8 allows a
  # stacked figure for at most four parts).
  - id: seacr_fragment_class_stack
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Nucleosome classes per sample
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: fraction
      color: fragment_class
      barmode: stack
      labels: {sample: Sample, fraction: Share of fragments, fragment_class: Fragment class}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample, split into the share of its fragments in each length class:
      sub-nucleosomal, mono-, di- and multi-nucleosomal. It answers how much of the
      library is nucleosome-free against nucleosome-bound.

      How to read: a sharp mark gives a sub-nucleosomal heavy library, and a broad mark a
      mononucleosomal heavy one, so replicates of one target should look alike. A library
      dominated by multi-nucleosomal fragments was digested too little.

      Lines and annotations: the classes are cut at 120, 250 and 450 bp. The 120 bp
      boundary follows the transcription factor sized fragments of the CUT&RUN paper,
      while 250 and 450 bp are this table's own bins and not a published cut-off.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28079019/
  - component: card
    column: n_fragments
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: target
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: fragments, by target
    title: Fragments counted
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of fragments in view and the bars rank the targets by
      how many they hold. It answers how much data each target contributes.

      How to read: targets with far fewer fragments have less depth, so their class shares
      are noisier. The extra figures are the median and largest class count.
  - component: card
    column: sample_median_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Median fragment length per sample
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over samples of each sample's median fragment length,
      and the box shows the quartiles. It answers where the typical fragment sits.

      How to read: histone marks sit near a nucleosome, about 180 bp, and a median far
      above it points to little digestion. Transcription factors push the median down with
      short fragments.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: median_length
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('fragment_class') == 'Mononucleosomal'"
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Mononucleosomal median length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over samples of the median length of the
      mononucleosomal fragments, between 120 and 250 bp (this table's own class), and the
      box shows the quartiles. It answers whether the nucleosome peak sits where it should.

      How to read: a value near 180 bp, the nucleosomal fragment length the nf-core/cutandrun
      docs give for histone marks, is a clean nucleosome peak. A value pushed to the edge
      of the class suggests the digestion is uneven.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: mono_to_sub
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Mononucleosome to sub-nucleosome ratio
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median over samples of the ratio of mononucleosomal to
      sub-nucleosomal fragments, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers whether the
      libraries are nucleosome-bound or nucleosome-free.

      How to read: a high ratio belongs to broad histone marks and a low one to sharp
      marks and transcription factors. Replicates of one target should have similar
      ratios, and a stray one is worth a look.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28079019/
  - component: table
    title: Fragment class table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample and a length class, with the fragments in it, their share, the
      median length inside the class and the sample-level ratio. It answers the exact
      numbers behind the bars.

      How to read: sort by share to find the dominant class of each sample, and filter on
      a class to compare samples.

outputs.name: Fragment length distribution
outputs.rawYaml:
id: seacr_fragment_lengths
name: Fragment length distribution
mode: qc/fragments
description: >-
  How long the sequenced fragments were, per sample: the count and the fraction of
  fragments at every length, plus the running fraction at most that long.
# The signature CUT&RUN QC figure. MNase cuts around nucleosomes, so a working
# experiment shows a sharp sub-nucleosomal peak below about 120 bp next to a
# mononucleosomal shoulder around 180 bp; a flat curve is a failed digestion.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.frags.len.txt"
recipe: seacr/fragment_lengths.py
fixture: fragment_lengths.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: seacr_fragment_curve
    component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: fragment_length
      y: fraction
      color: target
      line_group: sample
      labels: {fragment_length: Fragment length (bp), fraction: Share of fragments, target: Target}
    title: Fragment length distribution
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: the share of its fragments at every length, coloured by
      target. It answers whether the experiment cut around nucleosomes.

      How to read: a working experiment shows a nucleosome shoulder, about 150 to 180 bp,
      and for sharp marks or transcription factors a peak of short fragments below about
      120 bp. A flat, featureless curve is a failed digestion. Replicates of one target
      should overlap.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28079019/ and
      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/cutandrun/master/docs/output.md
  - id: seacr_fragment_cumulative
    component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: fragment_length
      y: cumulative_fraction
      color: target
      line_group: sample
      labels: {fragment_length: Fragment length (bp), cumulative_fraction: Cumulative share of fragments, target: Target}
    title: Cumulative fragment length
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample: the share of its fragments that are at most as long as the
      length on the horizontal axis, coloured by target. It answers how much of the
      library is short and how fast it fills up.

      How to read: a steep early rise means many short fragments and a late rise means
      long, poorly digested chromatin. Replicates that diverge differ in digestion. Read
      the value at 120 bp for the sub-nucleosomal share.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28079019/
  - component: card
    column: count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: target
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: fragments, by target
    title: Fragments counted
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of fragments in view and the bars rank the targets by
      how many they hold. The extra figure is the largest count at one length. It answers
      how much data each target contributes.

      How to read: a target with far fewer fragments has less depth, so its length curve
      is noisier.
  # No median card on `fragment_length`: the table has one row per length, so
  # a median over it is the middle of the x axis. The per-sample median is
  # `seacr/fragment_classes.sample_median_length`.
  - component: card
    column: fraction
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [q3]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: highest share at one length, with the distribution
    title: Highest share at one length
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest share of fragments at any single length and the
      histogram shows how the shares are distributed over all lengths and samples. It
      answers how sharp the length peak is.

      How to read: a high maximum means a sharp peak, as for a transcription factor. A low
      maximum with a wide spread is broad chromatin.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28079019/
  - component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: target
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: samples, by target
    title: Samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of samples with a fragment histogram and the bars rank
      the targets by how many samples they hold. The extra figure counts the length rows.

outputs.description: The sequenced fragments piled up in 100 bp bins on a 6 kb window centred on the summit of each sample's 500 strongest non-overlapping SEACR regions, per million fragments of the sample: a metagene matrix around the calls and a fragment coverage track under a locus navigator, from the same rows.
outputs.name: Fragment pile-up around the peaks
outputs.rawYaml:
id: seacr_frags_profile
name: Fragment pile-up around the peaks
mode: peaks/frags_profile
description: >-
  The sequenced fragments piled up in 100 bp bins on a 6 kb window centred on the
  summit of each sample's 500 strongest non-overlapping SEACR regions, per million
  fragments of the sample: a metagene matrix around the calls and a fragment coverage
  track under a locus navigator, from the same rows.
# Reads the fragment BEDs through a raw scan collection (the sample is in the
# file name) and the tidy SEACR calls through dc_ref; see the recipe docstring.
# Fragment BEDs are published by the pipeline but are large (tens of MB per
# library), so templates declare both collections optional.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.frags.cut.bed"
recipe: seacr/frags_profile.py
fixture: frags_profile.tsv
renders_as:
  # Regions down, offsets across, one panel per sample, the mean profile on top:
  # the deepTools plotHeatmap reading, built from fragments instead of a bigWig.
  # C1 N/A: the matrix is coloured by a continuous signal scale, one panel per sample.
  - id: frags_pileup_matrix
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: signal_matrix
    title: Fragment pile-up around peak summits
    roles: {region_id: peak_id, position: offset_bp, value: cpm, group: sample}
    config:
      reference_label: Peak summit
    description: >-
      Each row is one of the strongest SEACR regions of a sample, each column a 100 bp bin
      around its summit, and the colour is the fragment coverage per million fragments of
      the sample. It answers whether the calls stand on a clean, centred pile-up.

      How to read: a bright vertical band at the centre means the signal is centred on the
      summit. A target with sharp peaks, such as a promoter mark, gives a narrow band, and
      a broad mark a wide one. Rows that are bright everywhere are broad domains.

      Lines and annotations: the marker at offset 0 is the summit of the region, the
      midpoint of its maximum signal interval as reported by SEACR. The window, 3 kb each
      side of it, is a fixed choice of this catalog's recipe, and rows are ordered by total
      signal.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  # The same bins at their genomic coordinates: a coverage track that follows
  # the region of a locus navigator.
  - id: frags_pileup_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Fragment coverage track
    roles: {chromosome: chr, position: bin_start, value: cpm, end: bin_end, sample: sample, category: target}
    config:
      color_by: category
    description: >-
      Each bar is a 100 bp bin at its genomic position, with its fragment coverage per
      million fragments, coloured by target. It answers where along a locus the fragments
      pile up in each sample.

      How to read: peaks that are present in the replicates of one target and absent in
      the other target are specific to it. Only bins around the strongest calls are drawn,
      so empty stretches mean no strong call, not no signal.

      Note: the window around each call is the pipeline's own choice, and no signal
      threshold is drawn.
  - component: card
    column: cpm
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: target
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: highest bin, by target
    title: Highest fragment coverage
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest coverage per million fragments in any bin and the
      bars rank the targets by their highest bin. It answers which target has the sharpest
      pile-up.

      How to read: sharp marks give high, narrow maxima and broad marks give low ones, so

name: Peak QC summary

fixture: peak_summary.tsv
renders_as:

    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: num_peaks
      color: sample
      labels: {sample: Sample, num_peaks: Regions called}
    title: Regions called per sample
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: num_peaks}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample: the number of enriched regions SEACR called in it. It answers
      how many peaks each library yields.

      a sign of a depth or quality problem. A sharp mark calls few, wide regions and a
      broad mark many.

      sample of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows
      the filters), not a cut-off of SEACR. The count depends on the threshold mode

      sample. It answers how many peaks the run produced.

      target. Open the bar chart for the individual samples.

    column: width_median
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]

      bases, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how broad the calls are.

outputs.description: Every SEACR region of every sample in one table, with the total and the maximum fragment coverage over the region, its width and where inside it the maximum was reached.
outputs.name: Peak calls
outputs.rawYaml:
id: seacr_peaks
name: Peak calls
mode: peaks/seacr
description: >-
  Every SEACR region of every sample in one table, with the total and the maximum
  fragment coverage over the region, its width and where inside it the maximum was
  reached.
# SEACR reports no p-value and no fold enrichment, so significance is read off
# the coverage itself: `log10_total_signal` is the height of the genome track
# and `signal_density` the coverage per base.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.seacr.peaks.*.bed"
recipe: seacr/peaks.py
fixture: peaks.tsv
renders_as:
  # Where the signal is, then how the two coverage measures relate and how wide
  # the calls are behind them.
  - id: seacr_peak_signal
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: manhattan
    title: Peak signal along the genome
    roles: {chr: chr, pos: summit, score: log10_total_signal, feature: peak_id}
    config:
      score_kind: log10 total signal
      score_threshold_stat: p95
    description: >-
      Each point is a SEACR region at the position of its summit, with the base 10
      logarithm of its total fragment coverage on the vertical axis. It answers where in
      the genome the strongest signal sits.

      How to read: tall points mark strong enriched domains and clusters of them mark
      broad regions. A level, dense band means weak calls that all sit close to the
      threshold. Use the track view to read individual loci.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the 95th percentile of the scores in
      the table, a data-defined reference and not a SEACR cut-off. SEACR gives no
      significance for a region, since it reports coverage and not a p-value.

      Note: with tens of thousands of calls per sample the points overplot, so read the
      clusters rather than single points.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  # The same three roles on a chromosome-aware locus axis, plus `end` so a call
  # is drawn as the interval it is rather than as a point at its summit. The
  # coverage track binds the same columns through the Plotly renderer, which is
  # what a tab falls back to when the GenomeSpy canvas is unavailable.
  - id: seacr_peak_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Peak calls along the genome
    roles: {chr: chr, pos: start, score: log10_total_signal, feature: peak_id, end: end, category: sample}
    config:
      score_title: log10 total signal
      score_threshold_stat: p95
    description: >-
      Each mark is a SEACR region drawn as the interval it covers, coloured by sample and
      high according to the logarithm of its total fragment coverage. It answers where
      each sample has enriched regions and how strong they are.

      How to read: regions shared by the replicates of a target are reproducible
      candidates, and a region seen in only one sample needs checking. Brush a locus to
      filter the tiles of the tab.

      Lines and annotations: the line is the 95th percentile of the scores in the
      table, a data-defined reference computed from the rows on show and not a SEACR
      cut-off.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  - id: seacr_peak_coverage
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Peak signal track
    roles: {chromosome: chr, position: start, value: log10_total_signal, end: end, sample: sample}
    config:
      color_by: sample
    description: >-
      Each bar is a SEACR region at its coordinates, high according to the logarithm of
      its total fragment coverage and coloured by sample. It answers how the calls of the
      samples line up at a locus.

      How to read: matching bars in the replicates of a target are a reproducible peak,
      and a bar in only one sample is a private call. Compare targets to find specific
      regions.

      Note: no signal threshold is drawn, because SEACR defines none.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  - id: seacr_signal_scatter
    component: figure
    visu_type: scatter
    dict_kwargs:
      x: total_signal
      y: max_signal
      color: sample
      log_x: true
      log_y: true
      labels: {total_signal: Total signal, max_signal: Maximum signal, sample: Sample}
    title: Total against maximum signal
    description: >-
      Each point is a region: its total fragment coverage against the highest coverage
      inside it, on logarithmic axes and coloured by sample. It answers whether strong
      regions are strong because they are tall or because they are wide.

      How to read: the points rise together, and a region far below the trend is wide and
      flat, such as a broad domain. A region far above it is a narrow spike. Compare
      samples to see which has the taller peaks.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  - id: seacr_width_hist
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: width
      color: sample
      log_y: true
      labels: {sample: Sample, width: Region width (bp)}
    title: Region width per sample
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: width}
    description: >-
      Each box is a sample: the spread of the widths of its regions in bases, on a
      logarithmic axis. It answers how broad the calls of each sample are.

      How to read: sharp marks give narrow regions and broad marks wide ones, so
      replicates of one target should look alike. A sample with a very different box has a
      different threshold or depth.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median region width of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of SEACR.
  # How many regions and where they concentrate, then the spread of width,
  # total coverage and coverage per base behind that count.
  - component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: sample
    caption: regions, by sample
    title: Regions called
    description: >-
      The hero number counts the regions in view and the ring splits them by sample. The
      extra figure is the number of samples. It answers how the calls are shared between
      libraries.

      How to read: a ring dominated by one sample means that sample calls far more
      regions, usually a broad mark or a deeper library.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: width
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Median region width
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median region width in bases and the box shows the quartiles.
      It answers how broad the calls are.

      How to read: narrow regions fit sharp marks and wide ones broad marks. A long upper
      whisker is merged neighbouring signal blocks.
  - component: card
    column: total_signal
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: total, with the distribution of regions
    title: Total signal in regions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the summed fragment coverage inside all regions in view and the
      histogram shows how it is distributed over the regions. It answers how much signal
      the calls hold.

      How to read: signal is strongly skewed, so a few regions carry most of it. The extra
      figures are the median and the strongest region.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  - component: card
    column: signal_density
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: mean, with the distribution of regions
    title: Coverage per base
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean fragment coverage per base inside a region and the
      histogram shows how it is distributed. It answers how dense the signal is.

      How to read: a target that worked has much more coverage per base than an IgG
      control. Compare it between samples and replicates.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FredHutch/SEACR/master/README.md
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: peak_id
    title: Peak call table
    description: >-
      Each row is a SEACR region with its sample, coordinates, width, summit, total and
      maximum signal and coverage per base. It answers the exact numbers behind the tiles.

      How to read: sort by total signal to list the strongest regions. Selecting a row
      filters the rest of the tab to it.

tools.description: Fast processing of FASTA and FASTQ files. Here, the runs of N of an assembly (its scaffolding gaps), counted per genome and binned by length.
tools.name: seqtk

outputs.description: The length distribution of the N runs of each assembly, binned on a log10 scale (four bins per decade). Scaffolding methods leave characteristic gap sizes (a fixed filler length, estimated sizes, large reference placeholders), so the curve tells how an assembly was scaffolded, which the gap count does not. The share of each assembly's runs of N per bin is given alongside the count, which puts every assembly on one scale.
outputs.name: Assembly gap lengths
outputs.rawYaml:
id: seqtk_cutn_gap_lengths
name: Assembly gap lengths
mode: assembly/gaps
description: >-
  The length distribution of the N runs of each assembly, binned on a log10
  scale (four bins per decade). Scaffolding methods leave characteristic gap
  sizes (a fixed filler length, estimated sizes, large reference placeholders),
  so the curve tells how an assembly was scaffolded, which the gap count does
  not. The share of each assembly's runs of N per bin is given alongside the
  count, which puts every assembly on one scale.
find:
  path_glob: "**/cutn/*.bed"
recipe: seqtk/cutn_gap_lengths.py
fixture: cutn_gap_lengths.tsv
renders_as:
  # One row per assembly, log10 length bins across, the share of its runs of N
  # as colour: a fixed filler is one dark cell, estimated sizes a spread, and
  # assemblies with a handful or a hundred thousand gaps share one scale.
  # A length axis has no reference point, so the marker is set out of range.
  - id: gap_length_matrix
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: signal_matrix
    title: Gap length distribution per assembly
    roles: {region_id: genome, position: log10_gap_length, value: gaps_pct}
    config:
      reference_position: -1
    description: >-
      Each row is an assembly and each column a bin of gap length on a log10 scale,
      coloured by the share of that assembly's runs of N that fall in the bin. It
      answers how an assembly was scaffolded and whether two assemblies used the same
      gap sizes.

      How to read: a single dark cell means one fixed gap length, typical of a filler
      inserted by a scaffolder. A spread across many bins means estimated gap sizes. The
      curve on top is the mean over the assemblies shown.

      Note: seqtk cutN reports runs of N, which stand for assembly gaps. Rows are
      compared as shares, so assemblies with few and with many gaps share one scale.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lh3/seqtk/master/seqtk.c
  - id: gap_length_profile
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Gaps per length bin
    roles: {series: genome, x: gap_length_bp, y: gaps}
    config:
      log_x: true
      x_title: Gap length (bp)
      y_title: Gaps per bin
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is an assembly: the number of its gaps in each length bin, on a log
      scale of gap length. It answers which gap sizes dominate each assembly.

      How to read: a sharp peak is a fixed gap length. A broad curve means gap sizes
      were estimated. Compare the heights with care, because an assembly with many gaps
      dwarfs one with few, and the matrix tile puts them on one scale.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lh3/seqtk/master/seqtk.c
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: log10_gap_length
      y: gaps
      color: genome
      labels: {log10_gap_length: Gap length (log10 bp), gaps: Gaps per bin, genome: Assembly}
    title: Assembly gaps per log10 length bin
    description: >-
      Each line is an assembly: the number of gaps in each bin of log10 gap length. It
      answers the same question as the profile tile, in a plain figure that can be
      exported.

      How to read: peaks show the dominant gap sizes of an assembly, and lines that peak
      at the same place were scaffolded in the same way.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lh3/seqtk/master/seqtk.c
  - component: table
    title: Gap length bins
    description: >-
      Each row is an assembly and a bin of gap length, with the number of gaps, their
      share of the assembly's gaps and the bases they cover. It answers the exact counts
      behind the matrix.

      How to read: filter by assembly and sort by gap length to see its gap sizes in
      order.

outputs.description: Runs of N per assembly from seqtk cutN: how many, their total and median length, the longest, and how many sequences carry one. N runs are the scaffolding gaps an assembler leaves between contigs; they cannot align, so a gap-rich assembly covers less of the target without being more divergent.
outputs.name: Assembly gaps
outputs.rawYaml:
id: seqtk_cutn_gaps
name: Assembly gaps
mode: assembly/gaps
description: >-
  Runs of N per assembly from seqtk cutN: how many, their total and median
  length, the longest, and how many sequences carry one. N runs are the
  scaffolding gaps an assembler leaves between contigs; they cannot align, so a
  gap-rich assembly covers less of the target without being more divergent.
find:
  path_glob: "**/cutn/*.bed"
recipe: seqtk/cutn_gaps.py
fixture: cutn_gaps.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1 N/A: one bar per assembly, the x axis already names it and no other column splits it.
  # The bases in gaps span orders of magnitude between assemblies, so the axis is logarithmic.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: genome
      y: gap_bp
      log_y: true
      labels: {genome: Assembly, gap_bp: Bases in gaps}
    title: Bases in assembly gaps per genome
    reference_lines: [{axis: y, stat: median, column: gap_bp}]
    description: >-
      Each bar is an assembly, with the total bases that sit in runs of N, on a log
      scale. It answers which assemblies carry the most unresolved sequence.

      How to read: a tall bar is a gap-rich assembly, which covers less of a target
      without being more divergent. Compare it with the number of gaps in the table to
      tell a few long gaps from many short ones.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median number of bases in gaps
      of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the
      filters), not a cut-off of Seqtk.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lh3/seqtk/master/seqtk.c
  # The number of gaps spans orders of magnitude, so the card shows the extremes.
  - id: gap_runs
    component: card
    column: gaps
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: grid
    caption: median, with the fewest and the most
    title: Gaps per assembly
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of runs of N per assembly, with the smallest
      and largest count. It answers how gapped the assemblies are.

      How to read: a count near zero means a gap-free assembly. Thousands of gaps mean a
      scaffolded draft, whose gaps cannot align to a target.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lh3/seqtk/master/seqtk.c
  # Genomes are long ids, so the card gives the spread of the totals, not a ranking.
  - id: gap_bases
    component: card
    column: gap_bp
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: grid
    headline: true
    caption: total, with the median and largest assembly
    title: Bases in gaps
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of bases inside runs of N over the assemblies in view,
      with the median and the largest per assembly. It answers how much sequence is
      unresolved.

      How to read: a large maximum against a small median points to one assembly that
      is far more gapped than the rest. Open the gap table to find it.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lh3/seqtk/master/seqtk.c
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: gaps
    title: Gap count range
    description: >-
      Filters the tiles to assemblies whose number of gaps falls inside the chosen range.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: genome
    title: Assembly gaps table
    description: >-
      Each row is an assembly with its number of gaps, their total and median length,
      the longest gap and how many sequences carry one. It answers the exact numbers
      behind every tile and lets a row selection filter the dashboard.

      How to read: sort by total gap bases to rank the assemblies by unresolved sequence.

outputs.name: Reconstructed features
outputs.rawYaml:
id: sidle_reconstructed
name: Reconstructed features
mode: reconstructed
description: >-
  The cross-region reconstructed feature table melted to one row per feature
  and sample, with the Greengenes lineage split into rank columns. This is the
  community a multi-region run actually resolves, as opposed to the per-primer
  tables it starts from.
find:
  path_glob: "**/sidle/reconstructed/reconstructed_merged.tsv"
recipe: sidle/reconstructed.py
fixture: reconstructed.tsv
renders_as:
  # Wide per-rank columns, so the nested view is a sunburst; `stacked_taxonomy`
  # needs the single long rank column this table lacks.
  - id: reconstructed_sunburst
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Reconstructed community by rank
    roles: {ranks: [Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Genus], abundance: count}
    config:
      colour_by_rank: Phylum
    description: >-
      Each arc is a taxon of the reconstructed community, with kingdom in the centre and
      genus on the outside, sized by its read count and coloured by phylum. It answers
      which groups make up the community resolved across all amplified regions.

      How to read: wide arcs are the dominant taxa. A large share of arcs labelled
      Unclassified means the reference database could not name those sequences at that
      rank, so read the deeper ranks with care.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: count
      color: Phylum
      labels: {sample: Sample, count: Reads, Phylum: Phylum}
    title: Composition by phylum
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample and each segment is the read count of one phylum in the
      reconstructed table. It answers how the phylum composition differs between
      samples.

      How to read: compare the heights of the same colour across bars. A phylum that
      dominates one sample but not the others is worth a look at the sample metadata.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: count
      color: Genus
      labels: {sample: Sample, count: Reads, Genus: Genus}
    title: Composition by genus
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample and each segment is the read count of one genus in the
      reconstructed table. It answers which genera drive the differences between samples.

      How to read: the reconstruction resolves finer ranks than a single region does, so
      genus level is meaningful here. Many segments in a bar mean a diverse sample.
  # How much was reconstructed, from how many samples, across how many phyla.
  - component: card
    column: feature_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: Phylum
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    caption: features, by phylum
    title: Reconstructed features
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct reconstructed features, and the bars rank
      the phyla that hold most of them. It answers how rich the reconstructed community
      is.

      How to read: the secondary number counts feature and sample rows. A feature found in
      few samples is rare, so check its confidence in the reconstruction tab.
  - component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: rows, by sample
    title: Samples
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of samples in the table, and the bars rank the samples
      by the number of feature rows they hold. It answers how many samples were
      reconstructed and how rich each is.

      How to read: a sample with far fewer rows than the others had less depth or lost
      features during reconstruction.
  - component: card
    column: Phylum
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: Phylum
    caption: rows, by phylum
    title: Phyla
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct phyla, and the bar shows each phylum's
      share of the feature rows. It answers how broad the community is and whether a few
      phyla dominate.

      How to read: a bar mostly made of one phylum means a community with low evenness at
      this rank.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: Phylum
    title: Phylum
    description: >-
      Pick one or more phyla to keep. It filters every tile of the tab to the features of
      those phyla.

      How to read: pick one phylum to see its genera in the composition bars.
  - component: table
    title: Reconstructed features table
    description: >-
      Each row is a feature in a sample with its read count, full lineage and the rank
      columns. It answers exactly what was found and in how many reads.

      How to read: sort by count, or filter by phylum or genus to find a taxon.

How to read: wide arcs are the dominant taxa. A large share of arcs labelled Unclassified means the reference database could not name those sequences at that rank, so read the deeper ranks with care.

outputs.description: How many amplified regions mapped to each reconstructed feature and how much kmer support stood behind them. A feature carried by one region is a different claim from one carried by all of them, and this is the table that separates the two.
outputs.name: Reconstruction confidence
outputs.rawYaml:
id: sidle_reconstruction_qc
name: Reconstruction confidence
mode: reconstruction-summary
description: >-
  How many amplified regions mapped to each reconstructed feature and how much
  kmer support stood behind them. A feature carried by one region is a
  different claim from one carried by all of them, and this is the table that
  separates the two.
find:
  path_glob: "**/sidle/**/reconstruction_summary/metadata.tsv"
recipe: sidle/reconstruction_qc.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 17 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several k-mer spreads.
fixture: reconstruction_qc.tsv
renders_as:
  # Support against coverage: the two axes that qualify a reconstructed feature.
  - id: reconstruction_support
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Region coverage against kmer support
    roles: {x: num_regions, y: total_kmers_mapped, size: mean_kmer_per_region, label: feature_id}
    config:
      color_col: stdv_kmer_per_region
      x_title: Regions mapped
      y_title: Kmers mapped
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a reconstructed feature: the number of amplified regions that mapped
      to it on the horizontal axis and the kmer support summed over them on the vertical
      axis. The size is the mean support per region and the colour its spread across
      regions. It answers how well each feature is backed by the sequenced regions.

      How to read: a point to the right is carried by several regions and is a stronger
      claim than one carried by a single region. A high point with an uneven colour has
      most of its support in one region. Follow up the labelled points in the table.

      Note: q2-sidle publishes no minimum number of regions or kmers, so no cut-off is
      drawn.

      Source: https://q2-sidle.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reconstruction.html
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    # C1 N/A: every column of this table is numeric or an identifier, so no
    # category exists to split the bars by.
    dict_kwargs:
      x: num_regions
      labels: {num_regions: Regions mapped, count: Features}
    title: Features by regions mapped
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the reconstructed features that were mapped by a given number of
      amplified regions. It answers how many features rest on one region and how many
      on all of them.

      How to read: a distribution piled on the highest value means the regions agree and
      the reconstruction is well supported. A tall bar at one region means many features
      are single-region claims.
  - component: card
    column: num_regions
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: average, with its spread
    title: Regions per feature
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average count of amplified regions that mapped to a feature,
      and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how much cross-region support the
      features have.

      How to read: the closer it is to the number of regions sequenced, the more complete
      the reconstruction. A low value means most features come from a single region.
  - component: card
    column: total_kmers_mapped
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: median, with its range
    title: Kmer support
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median total kmer support per feature, and the histogram
      shows its distribution. It answers how much sequence evidence stands behind a
      typical feature.

      How to read: a long right tail is normal. Features at the lowest values are the
      weakest reconstructions, so look at them in the table first.
  - component: card
    column: mean_kmer_per_region
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: average, with its range
    title: Kmers per region
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average kmer support per mapped region, and the histogram
      shows its distribution over features. It answers how deep the support is on each
      region and not only in total.

      How to read: a value near one means each region adds little evidence by itself.
      Higher values mean regions that pin the feature down.
  - component: table
    title: Reconstruction confidence table
    description: >-
      Each row is a reconstructed feature with the number of regions mapped, the kmer
      support and the per-region ASVs behind it. It answers which features are well
      supported.

      How to read: sort by regions mapped, then by kmer support.

renders_as.description:
Each point is a reconstructed feature: the number of amplified regions that mapped to it on the horizontal axis and the kmer support summed over them on the vertical axis. The size is the mean support per region and the colour its spread across regions. It answers how well each feature is backed by the sequenced regions.
How to read: a point to the right is carried by several regions and is a stronger claim than one carried by a single region. A high point with an uneven colour has most of its support in one region. Follow up the labelled points in the table.

tools.description: Fits a tumor's 96-context SNV counts to COSMIC mutational signatures.
tools.name: SIGS

outputs.description: The number and share of the tumor's SNVs SIGS allocates to each COSMIC signature, one row per tumor and signature. Clock-like, APOBEC, homologous-recombination and mismatch-repair signatures each point at a different mutational process.
outputs.name: Mutational signature allocation
outputs.rawYaml:
id: sigs_allocation
name: Mutational signature allocation
mode: sigs
description: >-
  The number and share of the tumor's SNVs SIGS allocates to each COSMIC
  signature, one row per tumor and signature. Clock-like, APOBEC,
  homologous-recombination and mismatch-repair signatures each point at a
  different mutational process.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.sig.allocation.tsv"
recipe: sigs/allocation.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 13 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several tumors.
fixture: allocation.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: the bars are coloured by tumor, so two tumors can be compared per signature.
  - id: signature_share_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: signature
      y: percent
      color: sample
      labels: {signature: COSMIC signature, percent: Share of SNVs (%), sample: Tumor}
    title: Share of SNVs per signature
    description: >-
      Each bar is the percent of a tumor's SNVs that SIGS allocates to one COSMIC
      mutational signature. It answers which mutational processes shaped the tumor.

      How to read: tall bars are the dominant processes, for instance clock-like,
      APOBEC, homologous recombination deficiency or mismatch repair signatures, so
      read each signature's aetiology in COSMIC. The MISALLOC bar is the share the
      fitted signatures do not explain.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/sigs/README.md
  - id: signature_snv_total
    component: card
    column: allocation
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: signature
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    title: SNVs allocated to signatures
    caption: SNVs, by signature
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of SNVs allocated to signatures, with the
      median and the largest allocation beside it, and the bars rank the signatures by
      SNVs. It answers how many mutations the fit explains and which signatures carry
      most of them.

      How to read: a high total with a few dominant signatures is a clear mutational
      process. A large MISALLOC share means the signature set explains the tumor poorly.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/sigs/README.md
  - component: table
    title: Signature allocation
    description: >-
      Each row is a tumor and a signature with the SNVs allocated to it, the fraction
      and the percent of the tumor's SNVs. It answers the exact allocation behind the
      bars.

      How to read: sort by percent to list the main signatures, and compare tumors by
      filtering on the signature.

mode: simpleaf_quant/barcode_rank
description: >-
  UMI count per barcode against its rank, read from alevin-fry's per-barcode
  feature dump and flagged against CellBender's cell-barcode list for this
  route, so it can be compared to the Cell Ranger knee curve for the same
  sample.
find:
  path_glob: "**/simpleaf_quant/af_quant/featureDump.txt"
recipe: simpleaf/barcode_rank.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 16 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: barcode_rank.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: simpleaf_barcode_rank_knee
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: knee_plot
    title: Barcode rank plot
    roles: {sample: sample, rank: rank, umi_count: umi_count, is_cell: is_cell}
    description: >-
      Each point is a barcode ranked by its UMI count, from the richest droplet down, on log axes, with one
      curve per sample. It answers where real cells stop and empty droplets start.

      How to read: a good library has a plateau of cells with high counts, a steep drop and a long flat tail of
      ambient barcodes. A curve with no clear drop, or one where the called cells sit on the tail, points to a
      noisy or low-quality library. Compare it with the Cell Ranger curve of the same sample.

      Lines and annotations: the marked cut-off is where the called cells end. alevin-fry reports every barcode
      it quantified and calls no cells itself, so the cells are CellBender's cell-barcode list for this sample
      and the line is a data-defined reference, not a threshold from the tool.
  - component: card
    column: umi_count
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [sum]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: UMI count per barcode
    caption: UMI counts, per barcode
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest UMI count of any barcode, with the total UMIs beside it, and the
      histogram shows how counts are distributed over barcodes. It answers how deep the richest droplets are
      and how skewed the library is.

      How to read: a few barcodes with very high counts and a long tail of near-empty ones is the normal shape
      of droplet data. Use the knee plot to see where the cells end.
  - component: table
    title: Barcodes by rank
    description: >-
      Each row is a barcode with its rank, UMI count and whether it is in the called cell list. It answers
      which barcodes carry the library.

      How to read: sort by rank to see the richest barcodes and check that the called cells are the top ones.

    column: mapping_rate
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    title: Mapping rate
    caption: lowest and highest sample
    headline: true
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean share of reads that piscem mapped, with the lowest and highest sample beside
      it. It answers how well the reads fit the reference index.

      How to read: a sample far below the others points to a wrong reference, a poor library or contamination.
      The tool publishes no pass mark for this rate, so compare samples with each other.

    column: num_processed
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Reads processed
    caption: reads per sample, with their spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total number of reads processed across samples, and the box shows the spread per
      sample. It answers how much sequencing each sample received and how even it was.

      How to read: a sample with far fewer reads than the others may give fewer cells or a noisier profile.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: snpeff_ann_variants
name: Annotated variant calls
mode: per-variant
description: >-
  One row per annotated variant call: the locus and allele the caller reported,
  its quality, filter status, genotype, depth and allele fraction, and SnpEff's
  most severe consequence for it (gene, impact class, consequence term and
  protein change). The per-variant counterpart of the SnpEff CSV summary.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_snpEff.ann.vcf.gz"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/annotation/*/*/*_snpEff.ann.vcf.gz"
recipe: snpeff/ann_variants.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several impact classes.
fixture: ann_variants.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: impact_composition
    component: card
    column: variant_key
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: impact
    caption: calls, by impact class
    title: Calls by impact class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of annotated variant calls and the ring splits
      them by the impact class SnpEff assigned to the most severe consequence. It
      answers how many calls could change a protein.

      How to read: most calls of a typical callset are MODIFIER (non-coding or
      downstream) and only a small share is HIGH or MODERATE. A ring with an unusually
      large HIGH share is worth checking against the callers and the filter status.

      Lines and annotations: the classes are SnpEff's own. HIGH is a disruptive effect
      such as a stop gained or a frameshift, MODERATE a non-disruptive one such as a
      missense, LOW a mostly harmless one and MODIFIER a mostly non-coding one.

      Source: https://pcingola.github.io/SnpEff/snpeff/inputoutput/
  - component: card
    column: vaf
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: allele fraction, with its spread
    title: Allele fraction of calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the average variant allele fraction over the calls in view,
      and the box shows its quartiles. It answers whether the calls look heterozygous,
      homozygous or mixed.

      How to read: a box centred near 0.5 with a tail towards 1 is the shape of a
      diploid germline callset. A box pushed towards low values points to mosaic or
      low-confidence calls, so check the filter status and the read depth.
  - component: card
    column: dp
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: read depth, with its spread
    title: Read depth of calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median read depth at the called positions, and the box
      shows its quartiles. It answers how much evidence stands behind a typical call.

      How to read: a low median or a wide box means many calls rest on few reads, so
      genotypes and allele fractions are less reliable. Compare the callsets before
      trusting a difference between callers.
  - component: card
    column: variant_key
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: consequence
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: the most frequent consequences
    title: Most frequent consequences
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of annotated calls and the bars rank the
      consequence terms that account for most of them. It answers what kind of effect
      the callset mostly holds.

      How to read: terms such as downstream or intron variants lead on a whole-genome
      callset, while missense and synonymous variants lead among coding calls. A
      missing or surprising term can point to a filtered callset or a different
      annotation database.

      Source: https://pcingola.github.io/SnpEff/snpeff/inputoutput/
  - id: annotated_vaf_against_depth
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Allele fraction against read depth
    roles: {x: dp, y: vaf, label: hgvs_p, color: impact}
    config:
      x_title: Read depth
      y_title: Variant allele fraction
      legend_pos: right
    description: >-
      Each point is a variant call: its read depth on the horizontal axis and its
      variant allele fraction on the vertical axis, coloured by SnpEff impact class.
      It answers whether the damaging calls rest on enough reads.

      How to read: calls at high depth cluster near 0.5 and 1, the heterozygous and
      homozygous alternate genotypes. Scattered values at low depth are expected
      sampling noise, and a HIGH or MODERATE call there deserves a manual look before
      follow-up.

      Lines and annotations: no cut-off is drawn, because neither the callers nor
      SnpEff publish a depth or allele fraction rule for these calls.
  # Density of calls along the genome, coloured by impact class: the rainfall
  # view, drawn by the chr/pos/score kind that asks nothing of the score.
  - id: annotated_rainfall
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: manhattan
    title: Calls along the genome
    roles: {chr: chrom, pos: pos, score: vaf, feature: gene}
    config:
      score_kind: Variant allele fraction
      color_by_columns: [impact, caller]
      default_color_by: impact
      top_n_labels: 0
      score_threshold_stat: p95
    description: >-
      Each point is a variant call placed at its chromosome position, with its variant
      allele fraction on the vertical axis and its colour set by impact class. It
      answers where the calls cluster along the genome and which regions hold the
      damaging ones.

      How to read: dense bands of points mark gene-rich or highly variable regions,
      and gaps mark regions without calls (centromeres, low mappability). A tight
      cluster of HIGH calls in one region is worth a look in the gene tiles.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is the 95th percentile of the allele
      fractions in this table, a data-defined reference and not a published cut-off.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: vaf
      color: impact
      labels: {vaf: Variant allele fraction, impact: Impact class}
    title: Distribution of allele fractions
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the variant calls in an allele fraction bin, split by impact
      class. It answers how the genotypes spread and whether the damaging calls follow
      the same pattern as the rest.

      How to read: peaks near 0.5 and 1 are the heterozygous and homozygous alternate
      genotypes of a germline callset. A different shape in the HIGH class than in
      MODIFIER suggests artefacts concentrated in damaging calls.
  - component: table
    title: Annotated variant calls
    description: >-
      Each row is one annotated variant call with its locus, alleles, quality, filter
      status, genotype, depth, allele fraction, gene and SnpEff consequence. It
      answers the exact detail behind every other tile.

      How to read: sort by impact class or filter by gene to review the damaging
      calls, and check depth and filter status before relying on one.
