outputs.name: Annotation composition
outputs.rawYaml:
id: snpeff_csv_stats
name: Annotation composition
mode: summary-sections
description: >-
  What kind of variants a callset holds, as SnpEff counts them: impact classes,
  functional classes, consequence terms, genomic regions, variant types and
  zygosity. One long frame keyed by section and category, so a single section
  picker drives every tile. Percent is null in the zygosity section because
  SnpEff reports counts only there.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_snpEff.csv"
recipe: snpeff/csv_stats.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several callers.
fixture: csv_stats.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: composition_bars
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: category
      y: count
      color: caller
      barmode: group
      labels: {category: Category, count: Count, caller: Caller}
    title: Annotation counts by category
    description: >-
      Each bar is a category of the selected SnpEff summary section (an impact class,
      a consequence term, a genomic region, a variant type or a zygosity class), with
      its count, grouped by caller. It answers what kind of variants each callset
      holds.

      How to read: pick a section with the filter. Compare the callers within a
      category, and expect a few categories to dominate. A caller whose bars differ in
      shape from the others calls a different kind of variant.

      Source: https://pcingola.github.io/SnpEff/snpeff/outputsummary/
  - component: card
    column: count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: category
    caption: share of each category
    title: Total count in the section
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of the counts in the selected section and the ring
      splits it by category. It answers whether one category dominates the section.

      How to read: pick a section with the filter first, because totals of different
      sections (variants, effects, regions) are not comparable. A ring held by one or
      two categories is the normal shape of an annotation summary.

      Source: https://pcingola.github.io/SnpEff/snpeff/outputsummary/
  - component: card
    column: percent
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, min]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: share per category
    title: Largest share of a category
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest percentage any single category holds in its
      section, and the histogram shows how the percentages are distributed. It
      answers how concentrated the section is.

      How to read: a histogram piled near zero with a long tail is the usual shape,
      with many small categories and a few large ones. The zygosity section carries no
      percentage, because SnpEff reports counts only there.
  - component: table
    title: Summary sections table
    description: >-
      Each row is one category of one SnpEff summary section for a callset, with its
      count and percentage. It answers the exact numbers behind the bars and rings.

      How to read: filter by section and sort by count to list the dominant
      categories.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: snpeff_gene_heatmap
name: Gene burden heatmap
mode: matrix
description: >-
  The genes carrying the most coding variants, as a gene by callset matrix of
  variant counts. Clustering the columns says whether the callers separate more
  than the sequencing depths do.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*_snpEff.genes.txt"
recipe: snpeff/gene_heatmap.py
fixture: gene_heatmap.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the callsets (sample and caller), known only at ingest
  - id: burden_matrix
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Gene burden by callset
    roles: {index: gene_name}
    description: >-
      Each cell is the number of coding variants SnpEff assigned to a gene (row) in a
      callset (column), a sample called by one caller. It answers which genes carry
      the most variants and whether the callsets agree on them.

      How to read: columns that cluster together call similar variants, so if the
      callers separate more than the sequencing depths do, the caller matters more
      than the data. A row that is dark in every column is a robust high-burden
      gene, and a row dark in one column only is a call to inspect.

      Source: https://pcingola.github.io/SnpEff/snpeff/outputsummary/
  - component: table
    title: Gene burden table
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene with its variant count in every callset. It answers the exact
      numbers behind the heatmap cells.

      How to read: sort a callset column to rank the genes, and compare across columns
      to spot a caller that misses a gene.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: snpeff_genes
name: Per-gene variant burden
mode: gene-level
description: >-
  One row per gene and callset with the number of variants SnpEff assigned to
  it in each impact class, summed over the gene's transcripts. The cheapest
  gene-level view a variant-calling run publishes, and the input of the gene
  overlap, the burden heatmap and the oncoplot.
find:

recipe: snpeff/genes.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several callers.
fixture: genes.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: gene_burden_top
    component: card
    column: n_variants
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: concentration
    breakdown_col: gene_name
    top_n_count: 5
    caption: share held by the top genes
    title: Variants concentrated in a few genes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of variants SnpEff assigned to genes, and the strip
      shows the share held by the five genes with the most. It answers whether the
      burden is spread out or concentrated.

      How to read: large genes and repeat-rich genes lead on any callset, so a high
      concentration is normal. A single gene far above the rest on one caller only
      points to a calling artefact.
  - component: card
    column: n_high
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: caller
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: HIGH-impact variants, by caller
    title: High-impact variants by caller
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of HIGH-impact variants, such as stop gained or
      frameshift, and the bars rank the callers by how many each reports. It answers
      which caller finds the most disruptive variants.

      How to read: a caller far ahead of the rest may call more false positives, and
      one far behind may miss real ones. Open the gene overlap to see which genes they
      agree on.

      Source: https://pcingola.github.io/SnpEff/snpeff/inputoutput/
  - component: card
    column: n_coding
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: coding variants per gene, with their spread
    title: Coding variants per gene
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of coding variants per gene and callset, and
      the box shows its quartiles. It answers how many coding variants a typical gene
      carries.

      How to read: most genes carry few or none and a handful carry hundreds, so the
      median sits low and the upper whisker is long. A median that differs between
      callers means they disagree on the coding variants of a typical gene.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: biotype
      y: n_variants
      color: caller
      barmode: group
      labels: {biotype: Gene biotype, n_variants: Variants, caller: Caller}
    title: Variants by gene biotype
    description: >-
      Each bar is a gene biotype with the number of variants SnpEff assigned to its
      genes, grouped by caller. It answers which kinds of genes hold the variants.

      How to read: protein coding genes lead on most callsets. A caller with a different
      split of biotypes than the others is calling in different regions of the genome.

      Source: https://pcingola.github.io/SnpEff/snpeff/outputsummary/
  - component: table
    title: Per-gene variant burden table
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene in one callset with its variants split by impact class

outputs.rawYaml:
id: sompy_regions
name: som.py allele-fraction strata
mode: stratified
description: >-
  Somatic accuracy stratified by allele-fraction bin (caller x AF-bin recall /
  precision / F1).
find: { path_glob: "**/summary/tables/sompy/sompy.regions.csv" }
recipe: sompy/regions.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 5 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several callers.
fixture: regions.tsv
renders_as:
  # C3 N/A: som.py defines no accuracy cut-off per allele-fraction bin.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: af_bin
      y: f1
      color: caller
      barmode: group
      labels: {af_bin: Allele fraction bin, f1: F1 score, caller: Caller}
    title: F1 across allele fraction bins
    description: >-
      Each bar is the F1 score of one caller in one allele fraction bin. It answers whether a caller keeps
      its accuracy for the low-fraction variants that are hardest to call.

      How to read: a caller that holds its F1 down to the low bins detects subclonal variants, and one that
      falls off there only finds the clonal ones. A missing bar is a bin with no truth variant or no call, where the ratio divides by zero, so
      the recipe leaves it undefined rather than zero.

      Lines and annotations: no cut-off is drawn. som.py bins true positives and false negatives by the
      allele fraction of the truth set and false positives by the fraction observed in the query.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - component: table
    title: Allele fraction strata table
    description: >-
      Each row is a caller and allele fraction bin with its recall, precision, F1 and the counts of true
      positives, false positives and false negatives. It answers the exact numbers behind the bars.

      How to read: read the counts beside each ratio, because a high F1 in a bin with a handful of variants
      means little.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md

outputs.description: Somatic small-variant accuracy from som.py: precision/recall/F1 per callset with binomial confidence intervals. `caller` is the tool that made the calls, `label` the callset's samplesheet id and `truth_set` the truth set.
outputs.name: som.py benchmark summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: sompy_summary
name: som.py benchmark summary
mode: benchmark-summary
description: >-
  Somatic small-variant accuracy from som.py: precision/recall/F1 per callset
  with binomial confidence intervals. `caller` is the tool that made the calls,
  `label` the callset's samplesheet id and `truth_set` the truth set.
find: { path_glob: "**/summary/tables/sompy/sompy.summary.csv" }
recipe: sompy/summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 3 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several variant types.
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: pr_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: pr_benchmark
    roles: {label: caller, recall: recall, precision: precision, f1: f1, support: tp}
    title: Precision against recall
    config:
      show_diagonal: false
    description: >-
      Each point is a callset: its recall on the horizontal axis, its precision on the vertical axis, with
      the point coloured by its F1 score and sized by its true positives. It answers which caller finds
      the most true variants without adding false ones.

      How to read: the best callsets sit in the upper right. A callset far to the left misses variants, and
      one low on the plot adds false calls. The curves join points of equal F1, so compare callsets by which curve they sit on.

      Lines and annotations: the curves are iso-F1 contours at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 drawn by this
      chart, with F1 the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
      Recall is tp / (tp + fn) and precision is tp / (tp + fp), as som.py defines them. No cut-off is drawn.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - id: confusion
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: confusion_matrix
    roles: {label: caller, tp: tp, fp: fp, fn: fn}
    title: True and false calls per caller
    description: >-
      Each row is a callset and each cell a count of true positives, false positives or false negatives,
      shaded by its share of the row. It answers what kind of error each caller makes.

      How to read: a caller with a large false positive cell is too permissive, and one with a large false
      negative cell is too strict. Compare the rows, since the truth set is the same for every callset.

      Lines and annotations: a true positive is a variant in both the truth and the query. A query-only
      variant is a false positive and a truth-only variant a false negative.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - id: precision_ci
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: metric_ci_bars
    roles: {label: caller, value: precision, lower: precision_lower, upper: precision_upper}
    title: Precision with its interval
    config:
      metric_name: Precision
    description: >-
      Each point is a callset's precision with a bar for its confidence interval. It answers whether two
      callsets really differ in precision or only appear to.

      How to read: callsets whose intervals do not overlap differ in precision. A wide interval means few
      calls, so the value is uncertain.

      Lines and annotations: the bars are the 95% confidence interval for a binomial proportion, computed
      by the Jeffreys method (som.py default level 0.95).

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - id: recall_ci
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: metric_ci_bars
    roles: {label: caller, value: recall, lower: recall_lower, upper: recall_upper}
    title: Recall with its interval
    config:
      metric_name: Recall
    description: >-
      Each point is a callset's recall with a bar for its confidence interval. It answers whether two
      callsets really differ in the share of truth variants they find.

      How to read: callsets whose intervals do not overlap differ in recall. A wide interval means few truth
      variants were tested.

      Lines and annotations: the bars are the 95% confidence interval for a binomial proportion, computed
      by the Jeffreys method (som.py default level 0.95).

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: caller
      y: f1
      color: variant_type
      barmode: group
      labels: {caller: Caller, f1: F1 score, variant_type: Variant type}
    title: F1 by caller
    description: >-
      Each bar is the F1 score of a callset for one variant type (SNVs or indels), the harmonic mean of its
      precision and recall. It answers which caller is most accurate for each type.

      How to read: a higher bar is a better balance of finding true variants and avoiding false ones. Open
      the precision and recall views to see which side limits a low bar.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - component: card
    column: f1
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: F1 over the callsets, with its spread
    title: Best F1
    description: >-
      The hero number is the highest F1 score among the callsets and the box shows the spread of all of
      them. It answers how good the best caller is and how far the others trail.

      How to read: a best F1 far above the median means the callers differ a lot. Open the precision and
      recall views to see why.
  - component: table
    title: Benchmark summary table
    description: >-
      Each row is a callset and variant type with its true positives, false positives, false negatives,
      recall, precision, F1 and their confidence intervals. It answers the exact numbers behind every tile.

      How to read: sort by F1, then check the counts, since a high ratio on few variants is weak evidence.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: tp
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max, median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: caller
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: true positives, by caller
    title: True positives by caller
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of true positives over the callsets, and the bars rank the callers by
      how many they found. It answers which caller recovers the most truth variants.

      How to read: a caller far ahead on true positives is not necessarily best, since it may also add many
      false positives. Compare with the false positive card.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - component: card
    column: f1
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: median F1, with its spread
    title: Median F1
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median F1 score over the callsets and the box shows its quartiles. It answers
      how accurate a typical caller is on this truth set.

      How to read: a high median with a narrow box means the callers agree. A low median points to a hard
      truth set or to calls that need filtering.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - component: card
    column: recall
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: mean recall, with its lowest and highest
    title: Recall
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean recall over the callsets, the share of truth variants they find, with the
      lowest and highest beside it. It answers how complete the calls are.

      How to read: a low lowest value marks a caller that misses many truth variants. A gap between lowest
      and highest means the callers are not interchangeable.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - component: card
    column: precision
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: median precision, with its lowest and highest
    title: Precision
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median precision over the callsets, the share of calls that are true, with the
      lowest and highest beside it. It answers how clean the calls are.

      How to read: a very low lowest value marks a caller that adds many false positives and needs
      filtering. No cut-off is applied, because som.py defines none.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - component: card
    column: fp
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: caller
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: false positives, by caller
    title: False positives by caller
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of false positives over the callsets, and the bars rank the callers by
      how many they added. It answers which caller is noisiest.

      How to read: false positives often differ by orders of magnitude between callers. The caller leading
      this ranking is the first to filter.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - component: card
    column: fn
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [min, max, median]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: false negatives, with their range over callsets
    title: False negatives
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of truth variants missed over the callsets, with the lowest, highest and
      median per callset beside it. It answers how many variants the calls fail to find.

      How to read: a narrow range means every caller misses about the same variants, which points to hard
      truth variants such as low allele fraction ones.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
  - component: card
    column: f1
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [min, median, average]
    secondary_layout: grid
    caption: F1 over the callsets
    title: F1 summary
    description: >-
      The hero number is the best F1 score, with the lowest, median and mean beside it. It answers the
      range of accuracy over the callsets.

      How to read: a large gap between the lowest and the best F1 means the choice of caller matters here.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md

renders_as.description:
Each row is a callset and each cell a count of true positives, false positives or false negatives, shaded by its share of the row. It answers what kind of error each caller makes.
How to read: a caller with a large false positive cell is too permissive, and one with a large false negative cell is too strict. Compare the rows, since the truth set is the same for every callset.
Lines and annotations: a true positive is a variant in both the truth and the query. A query-only variant is a false positive and a truth-only variant a false negative.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: True and false calls per caller

renders_as.description:
Each point is a callset's precision with a bar for its confidence interval. It answers whether two callsets really differ in precision or only appear to.
How to read: callsets whose intervals do not overlap differ in precision. A wide interval means few calls, so the value is uncertain.
Lines and annotations: the bars are the 95% confidence interval for a binomial proportion, computed by the Jeffreys method (som.py default level 0.95).
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: Precision with its interval

renders_as.description:
Each point is a callset's recall with a bar for its confidence interval. It answers whether two callsets really differ in the share of truth variants they find.
How to read: callsets whose intervals do not overlap differ in recall. A wide interval means few truth variants were tested.
Lines and annotations: the bars are the 95% confidence interval for a binomial proportion, computed by the Jeffreys method (som.py default level 0.95).
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: Recall with its interval

renders_as.description:
Each bar is the F1 score of a callset for one variant type (SNVs or indels), the harmonic mean of its precision and recall. It answers which caller is most accurate for each type.
How to read: a higher bar is a better balance of finding true variants and avoiding false ones. Open the precision and recall views to see which side limits a low bar.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: F1 by caller

renders_as.caption: F1 over the callsets, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the highest F1 score among the callsets and the box shows the spread of all of them. It answers how good the best caller is and how far the others trail.
How to read: a best F1 far above the median means the callers differ a lot. Open the precision and recall views to see why.
renders_as.title: Best F1

renders_as.description:
Each row is a callset and variant type with its true positives, false positives, false negatives, recall, precision, F1 and their confidence intervals. It answers the exact numbers behind every tile.
How to read: sort by F1, then check the counts, since a high ratio on few variants is weak evidence.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: Benchmark summary table

renders_as.caption: true positives, by caller
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total of true positives over the callsets, and the bars rank the callers by how many they found. It answers which caller recovers the most truth variants.
How to read: a caller far ahead on true positives is not necessarily best, since it may also add many false positives. Compare with the false positive card.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: True positives by caller

renders_as.caption: median F1, with its spread
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median F1 score over the callsets and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how accurate a typical caller is on this truth set.
How to read: a high median with a narrow box means the callers agree. A low median points to a hard truth set or to calls that need filtering.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: Median F1

renders_as.caption: mean recall, with its lowest and highest
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the mean recall over the callsets, the share of truth variants they find, with the lowest and highest beside it. It answers how complete the calls are.
How to read: a low lowest value marks a caller that misses many truth variants. A gap between lowest and highest means the callers are not interchangeable.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: Recall

renders_as.caption: median precision, with its lowest and highest
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the median precision over the callsets, the share of calls that are true, with the lowest and highest beside it. It answers how clean the calls are.
How to read: a very low lowest value marks a caller that adds many false positives and needs filtering. No cut-off is applied, because som.py defines none.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: Precision

renders_as.caption: false positives, by caller
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total of false positives over the callsets, and the bars rank the callers by how many they added. It answers which caller is noisiest.
How to read: false positives often differ by orders of magnitude between callers. The caller leading this ranking is the first to filter.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: False positives by caller

renders_as.caption: false negatives, with their range over callsets
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the total of truth variants missed over the callsets, with the lowest, highest and median per callset beside it. It answers how many variants the calls fail to find.
How to read: a narrow range means every caller misses about the same variants, which points to hard truth variants such as low allele fraction ones.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: False negatives

renders_as.caption: F1 over the callsets
renders_as.description:
The hero number is the best F1 score, with the lowest, median and mean beside it. It answers the range of accuracy over the callsets.
How to read: a large gap between the lowest and the best F1 means the choice of caller matters here.
Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/hap.py/master/doc/sompy.md
renders_as.title: F1 summary

outputs.rawYaml:
id: stableexpression_dataset_funnel
name: Samples through the filters
mode: expression/sample-funnel
description: >-
  The samples of every downloaded dataset at each step, one row per dataset and
  step: downloaded, after the gene ID mapping, after the zero filter and after
  the missing-value filter (the samples of the merged matrix), with the samples
  lost at the step. A step a dataset never reached holds 0, so a step sums to
  the run's funnel.
find:
  path_glob: "**/statistics/zero_values_filter_stats.csv"
recipe: stableexpression/dataset_funnel.py
fixture: dataset_funnel.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: sample_funnel
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Samples at each filtering step
    dict_kwargs:
      x: step
      y: samples
      color: platform
      histfunc: sum
      labels: {step: Step, samples: Samples, platform: Platform}
    description: >-
      Each bar adds up the samples of every downloaded dataset at one step of the
      pipeline, split by the platform that measured them. It answers how many
      samples survive from download to the merged matrix.

      How to read: bars should shrink only a little from one step to the next. A
      large drop after the gene ID mapping means many datasets could not be
      mapped, and a drop after a filter means many samples were mostly zeros or
      mostly missing. Filter by step to see which datasets lose most.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The pipeline rejects a sample whose
      share of zeros or missing values is above 0.9 by default (max_zero_ratio and
      max_null_ratio), and the run may have changed them.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: samples_lost
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Samples lost at each step
    dict_kwargs:
      x: step
      y: samples_lost
      color: outcome
      histfunc: sum
      labels: {step: Step, samples_lost: Samples lost, outcome: Dataset outcome}
    description: >-
      Each bar adds up the samples lost at one step, split by the final outcome of
      their dataset. It answers where in the pipeline samples are removed and which
      kind of dataset loses them.

      How to read: losses coloured as a dataset that was never merged are expected,
      since such a dataset loses everything at the step that stopped it. Losses in
      merged datasets are partial filtering and are the ones to check against the
      zero and missing-value filters.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/docs/output.md
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: step
    title: Pipeline step
    description: >-
      Keeps only the rows of the chosen steps, so the figures and the table show
      one stage of the funnel at a time.
  - component: table
    title: Samples per dataset and step
    description: >-
      Each row is one dataset at one pipeline step, with its platform, final
      outcome, the samples it holds and the samples lost there. It answers which
      datasets lose samples and at which step.

      How to read: sort by samples lost to find the datasets that shrink most, then
      check their outcome and platform before trusting them.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: stableexpression_dataset_summary
name: Downloaded datasets
mode: expression/datasets
description: >-
  One row per public dataset the run downloaded: accession, platform,
  normalisation state and array design, the samples and conditions it came with,
  its gene ID mapping (ids in, kept, collapsed, rare, unmapped, mapped share),
  the samples each filter rejected and the samples kept in the merged matrix,
  the median zero share, missing share and skewness of its samples, and its
  outcome: merged, no gene mapped, only rare genes, or all samples filtered out.
find:
  path_glob: "**/statistics/zero_values_filter_stats.csv"
recipe: stableexpression/dataset_summary.py
fixture: dataset_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # Datasets through the pipeline's steps, as attrition: downloaded, ID-mapped,
  # merged.
  - id: dataset_attrition
    component: card
    column: downloaded
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: attrition
    attrition_cols: [id_mapped, merged]
    headline: true
    title: Datasets through the pipeline
    caption: datasets, at each step
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of datasets the run downloaded, and the bars show
      how many were mapped to Ensembl genes and how many reached the merged matrix.
      It answers how many of the public datasets end up usable.

      How to read: a large gap between downloaded and mapped means many gene ID
      schemes could not be translated, and a gap between mapped and merged means
      the sample filters or the rare-gene filter removed whole datasets. Open the
      outcome ring to see the reason for each.
  - id: sample_attrition
    component: card
    column: samples_downloaded
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: attrition
    attrition_cols: [samples_id_mapped, samples_after_zero_filter, samples_kept]
    title: Samples through the pipeline
    caption: samples, at each step
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of downloaded samples, and the bars show how many
      remain after the ID mapping, the zero filter and the missing-value filter. It
      answers how much of the downloaded data the merged matrix keeps.

      How to read: a small loss at the zero and missing-value filters is normal. A
      large loss points to datasets with many empty measurements, so check the
      per-dataset table.

      Lines and annotations: the filters reject samples with more than 0.9 zeros or
      0.9 missing values by default (max_zero_ratio and max_null_ratio), unless the
      run changed them.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: dataset_outcomes
    component: card
    column: samples_kept
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: outcome
    title: Dataset outcomes
    caption: datasets, by outcome
    description: >-
      Each unit is one downloaded dataset and the ring splits them by what happened
      to it: merged, no gene mapped, only rare genes, or all samples filtered out. It
      answers why datasets drop out.

      How to read: a ring mostly merged is the healthy case. A large share with no
      gene mapped means the dataset's gene IDs are not covered by the mapping
      service, which is a limit of the source and not of the data.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/docs/output.md
  - id: mapped_share_card
    component: card
    column: mapped_share
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Gene IDs mapped
    caption: share mapped, per dataset
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of gene IDs a dataset had that mapped to
      an Ensembl gene, and the histogram shows the share of each dataset. It answers
      how well the source gene IDs translate.

      How to read: a distribution piled near one is healthy. A low tail means
      datasets whose probes or transcript IDs are poorly annotated, and they add
      little to the merged matrix.
  - id: samples_per_dataset
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Samples kept per dataset
    dict_kwargs:
      x: samples_kept
      color: platform
      labels: {samples_kept: Samples kept, platform: Platform}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: x
        stat: median
        column: samples_kept
    description: >-
      Each bar counts datasets that kept a given number of samples in the merged
      matrix, split by platform. It answers how the cohort is spread over
      datasets.

      How to read: a few very large datasets next to many small ones mean the
      stability scores lean on those large datasets. A bar at zero lists datasets
      that did not reach the merged matrix.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median number of samples kept
      per dataset of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it
      follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/stableexpression.
  # The share of genes a dataset misses is set by what measured it: one
  # strip per array design (RNA-seq its own), one point per dataset.
  - id: missing_by_design
    component: figure
    visu_type: strip
    title: Missing values by array design
    dict_kwargs:
      x: design
      y: missing_share
      color: platform
      labels: {design: Array design, missing_share: Share of missing values, platform: Platform}
    description: >-
      Each point is a dataset: the median share of missing values over its samples,
      against the array design that measured it. It answers whether a design leaves
      many genes unmeasured.

      How to read: points near zero are complete datasets. A design with every point
      high leaves many genes unmeasured, and those genes are scored on fewer
      datasets. Compare the platforms by colour.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The pipeline's own limit is a missing
      share of 0.9 per sample (max_null_ratio), a run parameter.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: outcome
    title: Dataset outcome
    description: >-
      Keeps only datasets with the chosen outcome, for example the merged ones, so
      the tiles describe what reached the analysis.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: platform
    title: Platform
    description: >-
      Keeps only datasets measured on the chosen platform, RNA-seq or microarray.
  - id: dataset_table
    component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: dataset
    title: Downloaded datasets table
    description: >-
      Each row is a downloaded dataset with its platform, gene ID mapping counts,
      the samples each filter rejected, its outcome and the reason it failed when it
      did. It answers what happened to each dataset and lets a row selection open its
      record.

      How to read: sort by outcome to group the failures, then read the failure
      reason and the mapping note to see whether the cause is the dataset or the
      mapping service.
  - id: dataset_record
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: record_card
    roles: {id: dataset, title: accession}
    title: Dataset record
    description: >-
      One card per dataset, listing every field of its summary row. It answers what
      is known about the dataset picked in the table.

      How to read: select a row in the table to load its record, then check the
      mapping note and the samples rejected at each filter.

Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median number of samples kept per dataset of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/stableexpression.
renders_as.title: Samples kept per dataset

renders_as.description:
Each point is a dataset: the median share of missing values over its samples, against the array design that measured it. It answers whether a design leaves many genes unmeasured.
How to read: points near zero are complete datasets. A design with every point high leaves many genes unmeasured, and those genes are scored on fewer datasets. Compare the platforms by colour.
Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The pipeline's own limit is a missing share of 0.9 per sample (max_null_ratio), a run parameter.
Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/nextflow_schema.json
renders_as.title: Missing values by array design

renders_as.description: Keeps only datasets with the chosen outcome, for example the merged ones, so the tiles describe what reached the analysis.
renders_as.title: Dataset outcome

renders_as.description: Keeps only datasets measured on the chosen platform, RNA-seq or microarray.
renders_as.title: Platform

renders_as.description:
Each row is a downloaded dataset with its platform, gene ID mapping counts, the samples each filter rejected, its outcome and the reason it failed when it did. It answers what happened to each dataset and lets a row selection open its record.
How to read: sort by outcome to group the failures, then read the failure reason and the mapping note to see whether the cause is the dataset or the mapping service.
renders_as.title: Downloaded datasets table

renders_as.description:
One card per dataset, listing every field of its summary row. It answers what is known about the dataset picked in the table.
How to read: select a row in the table to load its record, then check the mapping note and the samples rejected at each filter.
renders_as.title: Dataset record

outputs.description: One row per candidate gene (the candidates of each expression section): the stability score (lower is more stable), its rank within the section and over every candidate, the four measures behind it (Normfinder stability value, geNorm M, coefficient of variation, robust MAD-based CV), each normalised to 0-1, the score split into its weighted parts plus the missing-value penalty, and the gene's expression level, measured share and platforms.
outputs.name: Candidate gene stability
outputs.rawYaml:
id: stableexpression_gene_stability
name: Candidate gene stability
mode: expression/stability
description: >-
  One row per candidate gene (the candidates of each expression section): the
  stability score (lower is more stable), its rank within the section and over
  every candidate, the four measures behind it (Normfinder stability value,
  geNorm M, coefficient of variation, robust MAD-based CV), each normalised to
  0-1, the score split into its weighted parts plus the missing-value penalty,
  and the gene's expression level, measured share and platforms.
find:
  path_glob: "**/reporting/all_genes_summary.csv"
recipe: stableexpression/gene_stability.py
fixture: gene_stability.tsv
renders_as:
  # Two of the four measures against each other, rank against rank within the
  # section: they agree for a gene stable by every account, and a gene good by
  # one only stands off the diagonal.
  - id: measure_agreement
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Normfinder against geNorm rank
    roles: {x: normfinder_rank, y: genorm_rank, label: gene_name, color: section}
    config:
      x_title: Normfinder rank within section
      y_title: geNorm rank within section
      reference_line: diagonal
      reference_label: Same rank in both methods
      top_n_labels: 8
    description: >-
      Each point is a candidate gene: its rank by Normfinder on the horizontal axis
      and its rank by geNorm M on the vertical axis, within its expression section,
      coloured by section. It answers whether two independent stability methods pick
      the same genes.

      How to read: points near the diagonal are genes both methods rank alike, and
      those at the lower left are stable by both accounts. A gene far from the
      diagonal is good by one method only, so check its distribution before using it
      as a reference.

      Lines and annotations: the diagonal is y = x, where both methods give the same
      rank. It is a reference of the plot and not a cut-off.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15289330/ and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12184808/
  - id: candidate_record
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: record_card
    roles: {id: gene_id, title: gene_name}
    title: Candidate gene record
    description: >-
      One card per candidate gene, listing its stability score, rank, the four
      measures behind it and its expression level. It answers how a single gene
      scored.

      How to read: select a row in the table to load a gene, then compare its
      measures with the section it belongs to.
  - id: candidate_count
    component: card
    column: gene_id
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: expression_level
    headline: true
    title: Candidate genes
    caption: candidates, by expression level
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of candidate genes that were scored, and the bar
      splits them by expression level. It answers how many candidates each part of
      the expression range contributes.

      How to read: candidates are shortlisted per section by their coefficient of
      variation, so every section should contribute. A level with very few
      candidates means that part of the range has little stable signal.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/README.md
  - id: best_score
    component: card
    column: stability_score
    aggregation: min
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    title: Best stability score
    caption: scores, with their spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the lowest stability score, the most stable candidate, and
      the box shows the quartiles of all scores. It answers how stable the best gene
      is and how the rest compare.

      How to read: lower is more stable. A best score far below the median means a
      clear standout, and a tight box means most candidates are alike. The score is
      relative to this run and has no absolute cut-off.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The pipeline publishes no cut-off for
      the stability score.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/README.md
  - id: candidate_measured
    component: card
    column: measured_share
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Share of samples measuring a gene
    caption: share measured, per candidate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of samples in which a candidate gene was
      measured, and the histogram shows its spread over candidates. It answers how
      complete the evidence behind each score is.

      How to read: a gene measured in few samples is scored on little evidence and
      carries a missing-value penalty. Prefer candidates with a high share.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: score_by_section
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Stability score by section
    dict_kwargs:
      x: section
      y: stability_score
      color: section
      labels: {section: Expression section, stability_score: Stability score}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: stability_score
    description: >-
      Each box is an expression section and summarises the stability scores of its
      candidates, a view of this catalog: the pipeline's report boxes the
      normalised expression of the top 25 genes per section instead. Section 1
      holds the most expressed genes, and the chart answers how stable genes are
      at each level of expression.

      How to read: lower scores are more stable. Sections whose box sits lower
      offer better reference genes, and a wide box means the choice within that
      section matters.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median stability score of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of nf-core/stableexpression.

      Source:
      https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/docs/output.md
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: section
    title: Expression section
    description: >-
      Keeps only the candidates of the chosen sections, to look for a reference gene
      at a given expression level.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: expression_level
    title: Expression level
    description: >-
      Keeps only candidates in the chosen expression level, from very high to very
      low.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: stability_score
    title: Stability score
    description: >-
      Keeps only candidates whose stability score falls in the chosen range. Lower
      scores are more stable.
  - id: candidate_table
    component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene_id
    title: Candidate genes table
    description: >-
      Each row is a candidate gene with its stability score, ranks, the four
      measures behind the score, its expression level and the platforms that measured
      it. It answers which genes to take forward as references and lets a row
      selection open the gene's record.

      How to read: sort by stability score or by section rank, and read the measured
      share beside it before trusting a low score.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: stableexpression_gene_statistics
name: Gene expression statistics
mode: expression/gene-statistics
description: >-
  One row per gene of the merged expression matrix: mean, median, standard
  deviation, MAD and both coefficients of variation over the samples that
  measured it, the share of samples that measured it and the share that read
  zero, its expression section, percentile and level, whether it was a
  candidate, which platforms measured it, the per-platform mean and CV, and how
  many source ids (probes, transcripts) map onto it.
find:
  path_glob: "**/reporting/all_genes_summary.csv"
recipe: stableexpression/gene_statistics.py
fixture: gene_statistics.tsv
renders_as:
  # Spread against level, every gene: the candidates sit on the lower edge of
  # each section's band.
  - id: expression_plane
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Variation against mean expression
    roles: {x: mean, y: cv, label: gene_name, color: candidate}
    config:
      x_title: Mean normalised expression
      y_title: Coefficient of variation
      top_n_labels: 10
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene of the merged matrix: its mean normalised expression on
      the horizontal axis and its coefficient of variation on the vertical axis,
      coloured by whether it was shortlisted as a candidate. It answers where the
      stable genes sit relative to the rest.

      How to read: stable reference genes sit low, with little variation at their
      expression level. Candidates are picked from the lower edge of each
      expression section, so a gene far above that edge is not a good reference.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median coefficient of
      variation of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it
      follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/stableexpression, which
      defines none. Candidates are the lowest-variation genes of each section.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/README.md
  - id: gene_count
    component: card
    column: gene_id
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: candidate
    headline: true
    title: Genes in the merged matrix
    caption: genes, candidate or not
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of genes in the merged matrix, and the ring
      splits them into candidates and other genes. It answers how many genes were
      scored out of all those measured.

      How to read: candidates are a small shortlist per section, so a small share is
      expected. A matrix with few genes means strict ID mapping or occurrence
      filters removed many.
  - id: gene_measured_share
    component: card
    column: measured_share
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Share of samples measuring a gene
    caption: share measured, per gene
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of samples in which a gene was measured,
      and the histogram shows how it varies between genes. It answers how complete
      the merged matrix is.

      How to read: genes measured in few samples, usually from a single platform,
      carry weaker statistics. A histogram piled to the right is a complete matrix.
  - id: level_composition
    component: card
    column: gene_id
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: expression_level
    title: Genes by expression level
    caption: genes, by expression level
    description: >-
      Each unit is one gene and the bar shows the share of genes in each expression
      level, from very high to very low. It answers how the genes are spread over
      the expression range.

      How to read: the five levels are percentile bands of expression, so a heavily
      skewed split means the dataset mix favours some levels over others.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/docs/output.md
  - id: cv_by_section
    component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Variation by expression section
    dict_kwargs:
      x: section
      y: cv
      color: candidate
      labels: {section: Expression section, cv: Coefficient of variation, candidate: Candidate}
    reference_lines:
      - axis: y
        stat: median
        column: cv
    description: >-
      Each box is the distribution of the coefficient of variation of the genes in
      one expression section, split into candidates and other genes. It answers
      whether candidates are really the least variable genes of their section.

      How to read: the candidate box should sit below the other genes in every
      section. A section where it does not has few stable genes to choose from.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median coefficient of
      variation of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it
      follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/stableexpression.
  - id: source_ids_hist
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Source IDs per gene
    dict_kwargs:
      x: source_ids
      color: platforms
      labels: {source_ids: Source IDs per gene, platforms: Platforms}
    description: >-
      Each bar counts genes by how many source IDs (probes or transcripts) map onto
      them, coloured by the platforms that measured the gene. It answers how much
      the ID collapsing merged measurements.

      How to read: most genes should map from one or a few IDs. A long tail of many
      IDs per gene is typical of microarrays with several probes per gene.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: expression_level
    title: Expression level
    description: >-
      Keeps only genes in the chosen expression levels.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: platforms
    title: Platforms
    description: >-
      Keeps only genes measured by the chosen platform combination: RNA-seq only,
      microarray only or both.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene_id
    title: Gene statistics table
    description: >-
      Each row is a gene of the merged matrix with its mean, median, spread,
      coefficients of variation, measured share, expression level and per-platform
      statistics. It answers how any gene behaves across the datasets and lets a row
      selection filter the other tiles.

      How to read: sort by coefficient of variation to find the least variable genes,
      then check the measured share and the platforms.

id: stableexpression_id_mapping
name: Gene ID mapping
mode: expression/id-mapping
description: >-
  Where the gene ids of every downloaded dataset went, one row per dataset and
  fate: kept as a gene of the merged matrix, collapsed (one of several ids of
  the same gene), dropped as a rare gene (seen in too few datasets), or not
  mapped to an Ensembl gene. The four fates add up to the ids the dataset came
  with.
find:
  path_glob: "**/statistics/id_mapping_stats.csv"
recipe: stableexpression/id_mapping.py
fixture: id_mapping.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: id_fates
    component: card
    column: gene_ids
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: fate
    title: Fate of gene IDs
    caption: gene IDs, by fate
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of gene IDs the datasets came with, and the bar
      splits them by fate: kept, collapsed, dropped as rare, or not mapped. It
      answers how much of the source identifiers reach the merged matrix.

      How to read: a large kept share is healthy. A large not-mapped share means the
      datasets use identifiers the mapping service does not know, and a large rare
      share means genes seen in too few datasets were removed.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/docs/output.md
  - id: id_fate_bars
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Gene ID fate per dataset
    dict_kwargs:
      x: dataset
      y: share
      color: fate
      labels: {dataset: Dataset, share: Share of gene IDs, fate: Fate}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a dataset and its segments are the share of its gene IDs in each
      fate: kept, collapsed, rare or not mapped. It answers which datasets map well
      and which lose their genes.

      How to read: bars mostly kept are well mapped. A bar mostly not mapped is a
      dataset the pipeline could not use, so check its platform and identifier type.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/docs/output.md
  - id: id_fate_by_platform
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Gene ID fate by platform
    dict_kwargs:
      x: platform
      y: gene_ids
      color: fate
      histfunc: sum
      labels: {platform: Platform, gene_ids: Gene IDs, fate: Fate}
    description: >-
      Each bar adds up the gene IDs of every dataset on one platform, split by fate.
      It answers whether microarray and RNA-seq datasets lose genes in the same way.

      How to read: microarray probes usually collapse onto fewer genes, while
      RNA-seq identifiers are closer to genes already. A platform with many
      unmapped IDs points to an identifier scheme the mapping does not cover.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: fate
    title: Fate
    description: >-
      Keeps only the chosen fates, for example the IDs that were not mapped.
  - component: table
    title: Gene ID mapping table
    description: >-
      Each row is a dataset and a fate, with the number of gene IDs and their share
      of the dataset. It answers exactly how many IDs each dataset lost and why.

      How to read: sort by gene IDs within a fate to find the datasets that lose
      most, then check their outcome in the dataset summary.

mode: expression/stability-components
description: >-

  gene and part: each of the four normalised measures (Normfinder, geNorm M,
  coefficient of variation, robust CV) times its weight, and the penalty for
  the samples where the gene was not measured. A gene's parts add up to its

recipe: stableexpression/score_components.py
fixture: score_components.tsv
renders_as:
  # The mean part per section, stacked: the height is the section's mean score
  # and the segments say what drives it.
  - id: components_by_section
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: What drives the score in each section
    dict_kwargs:
      x: section
      y: contribution
      color: component
      histfunc: avg
      labels: {section: Expression section, contribution: Mean contribution to the score, component: Part of the score}
    description: >-
      Each bar is an expression section and its segments are the mean weighted part
      of each measure in the stability score: Normfinder, geNorm M, the coefficient
      of variation, the robust coefficient and the missing-value penalty. It answers
      which measure drives the score of each section.

      How to read: the height is the section's mean score, where lower is more
      stable. A large penalty segment means genes were missing from many samples, and
      a large segment for one measure means that measure separates the genes most.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The weights of the four measures are a

  - component: table

    description: >-
      Each row is one part of one candidate gene's stability score, with the
      normalised measure and its weighted contribution. It answers how a gene's score
      adds up.

      How to read: a gene's parts sum to its stability score, so sort by contribution

outputs.description: The best-ranked candidates of every expression section (25 per section by default, as many as the pipeline's report draws), one row per gene: stability score, rank within the section and over every candidate, and the box statistics of its normalised expression over the samples that measured it (quartiles, Tukey whisker ends, mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, samples measured and their share of the cohort). Computed from the merged matrix before imputation, so thousands of samples ship as one row per gene.
outputs.name: Most stable genes, box statistics
outputs.rawYaml:
id: stableexpression_stable_gene_distribution
name: Most stable genes, box statistics
mode: expression/stability-distribution
description: >-
  The best-ranked candidates of every expression section (25 per section by
  default, as many as the pipeline's report draws), one row per gene: stability
  score, rank within the section and over every candidate, and the box
  statistics of its normalised expression over the samples that measured it
  (quartiles, Tukey whisker ends, mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum,
  samples measured and their share of the cohort). Computed from the merged
  matrix before imputation, so thousands of samples ship as one row per gene.
find:
  path_glob: "**/reporting/all_genes_summary.csv"
recipe: stableexpression/stable_gene_distribution.py
fixture: stable_gene_distribution.tsv
renders_as:
  # The pipeline's own view: each gene's spread across the cohort beside the
  # score that ranked it. Ranked within the section, so the first ten rows are
  # the best gene of each of ten sections, the next ten the second best.
  - id: stability_ranking
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: ranked_distribution
    title: Most stable genes and their spread
    roles: {feature_id: gene_id, score: stability_score, rank: section_rank, label: gene_name, group: section,
             q1: q1, median: median, q3: q3, lower: lower, upper: upper, mean: mean}
    config:
      score_label: Stability score (lower is more stable)
      value_label: Normalised expression
    description: >-
      Each row is one of the best-ranked candidate genes of an expression section,
      coloured by section: a box of its normalised expression over the samples that
      measured it, beside the stability score that ranked it. It answers which genes
      are the best reference candidates and how steady their expression is.

      How to read: a good reference has a short box and a low score. A long box or a
      long whisker means the gene varies between samples or datasets, whatever its
      rank. Compare genes of the same section, since sections differ in level.

      Lines and annotations: the box spans the first to the third quartile with the
      median inside, and whiskers reach the furthest values within 1.5 times the
      interquartile range (Tukey's rule, computed by this catalog's recipe). The
      pipeline's report also draws boxes of the normalised expression of the top 25 genes
      per section.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/docs/output.md
  - id: ranked_gene_count
    component: card
    column: gene_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: expression_level
    title: Top genes drawn
    caption: genes, by expression level
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct top-ranked genes, and the bar splits
      them by expression level. It answers which part of the expression range the best
      candidates come from.

      How to read: top candidates are taken per section, so each level should be
      represented. A level with none has no stable genes in this run.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/stableexpression/blob/1.1.0/docs/output.md
  - id: ranked_measured_share
    component: card
    column: measured_share
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Share of samples measuring a gene
    caption: share measured, per gene
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of samples in which a top gene was
      measured, and the histogram shows its spread. It answers how much evidence
      stands behind the box statistics.

      How to read: genes measured in only a few samples are less reliable references,
      even with a low score. Prefer genes near the right edge.
  - id: ranked_iqr_figure
    component: figure
    visu_type: scatter
    title: Stability score against median expression
    dict_kwargs:
      x: median
      y: stability_score
      color: section
      labels: {median: Median normalised expression, stability_score: Stability score, section: Expression section}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: stability_score, label: Median stability score}
    description: >-
      Each point is a top-ranked gene: its median normalised expression against its
      stability score, coloured by section. It answers whether the most stable genes
      are also the most highly expressed.

      How to read: lower scores are more stable. Points low at their level are good
      reference candidates, and a trend with expression means the score depends on
      level.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median stability score of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not
      a cut-off of the pipeline.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: section
    title: Expression section
    description: >-
      Keeps only the genes of the chosen sections.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: stability_score
    title: Stability score
    description: >-
      Keeps only genes whose stability score falls in the chosen range. Lower scores
      are more stable.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: gene_id
    title: Top genes table
    description: >-
      Each row is a top-ranked candidate gene with its stability score, ranks, box
      statistics and measured share. It answers the exact numbers behind the box
      view and lets a row selection filter the other tiles.

      How to read: sort by section rank to see the best gene of each section, and
      read the quartiles for the spread of its expression.

      section: the distribution of its normalised expression over the samples in view,
      beside its stability score. It answers how steady a gene's expression is across
      datasets, and recomputes when you filter samples.

      gene. A wide or multi-peaked shape means expression differs between datasets or

outputs.name: Splice junctions
outputs.rawYaml:
id: star_junctions
name: Splice junctions
mode: alignment/splice-junctions
description: >-
  STAR's collapsed splice junctions summed per sample into intron motif class
  (GT/AG, GC/AG, AT/AC, non-canonical) by annotated or novel, with the junctions
  and the uniquely and multi-mapping reads in each cell. A clean library spends
  nearly all its reads on annotated GT/AG junctions; novel non-canonical ones
  with few reads each are alignment noise.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.SJ.out.tab"
recipe: star/junctions.py
fixture: junctions.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: junction_motif_bars
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: junctions_pct
      color: motif_class
      labels: {sample: Sample, junctions_pct: Junctions (%), motif_class: Intron motif}
    title: Junctions by intron motif
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample and each segment is the share of its splice junctions that
      carry one intron motif class. It answers whether the junctions look like real
      splicing.

      How to read: nearly all junctions should be the canonical GT/AG motif, with a
      small share of GC/AG and AT/AC. A large share of non-canonical junctions points to
      alignment noise or a damaged library, so check them against their read counts in the
      table.

      Lines and annotations: the motif classes fold the intron motif codes STAR writes in SJ.out.tab (0 non-canonical, 1
      GT/AG and 2 CT/AC, 3 GC/AG and 4 CT/GC, 5 AT/AC and 6 GT/AT), joining each motif with its
      reverse strand reading. The folding is done by this catalog's recipe, and no cut-off is drawn.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexdobin/STAR/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf
  - id: junctions_by_annotation
    component: card
    column: junctions
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: annotation
    caption: junctions, by annotation
    title: Collapsed junctions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of collapsed splice junctions, and the bar shows the
      share that is annotated or novel. It answers how much of the splicing is known.

      How to read: a large annotated share is expected for a well-annotated organism.
      A large novel share points to unannotated isoforms or to alignment noise.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexdobin/STAR/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf
  - id: junction_reads_by_motif
    component: card
    column: unique_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: motif_class
    caption: reads, by intron motif
    title: Reads crossing junctions
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of uniquely mapped reads that cross a splice junction,
      and the ring splits them by intron motif. It answers where the spliced reads go.

      How to read: the GT/AG motif should hold almost all reads. The STAR manual advises
      removing non-canonical junctions supported by only a few reads as likely false
      positives, so a read-poor non-canonical slice is noise.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexdobin/STAR/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf
  - component: table
    title: Splice junctions table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample, an intron motif class and an annotation status, with the
      junctions and the uniquely and multi-mapping reads in it. It answers exactly how
      the junctions and reads divide up.

      How to read: filter to novel junctions and compare their reads per junction with
      the annotated ones.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: star_log_final
name: Alignment summary
mode: alignment/summary
description: >-
  One row per sample from STAR's Log.final.out: input reads, uniquely mapped,
  multi-mapped and unmapped reads with their shares, the splices STAR crossed
  (annotated, canonical motifs, non-canonical) and the per-base mismatch,
  deletion and insertion rates. The splice shares are derived, so a card can
  say how much of the splicing matches the annotation.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.Log.final.out"
recipe: star/log_final.py
fixture: log_final.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: unique_mapped
    component: card
    column: uniquely_mapped_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Uniquely mapped reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of reads that STAR mapped to a single place, and
      the box shows the spread over samples. It answers how well the libraries align.

      How to read: a high median with a tight box is good. A low value or a long lower
      whisker marks samples to inspect in the read fate bars. STAR publishes no cut-off.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexdobin/STAR/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf
  - id: input_reads
    component: card
    column: input_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: total, with the per-sample range
    title: Input reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of input reads over all samples, and the histogram shows
      how many each sample has. It answers how deep the sequencing is and how even.

      How to read: samples far below the others have less power for expression or splicing
      analysis.
  - id: multimapped
    component: card
    column: multimapped_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Multi-mapped reads
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of reads that align to several loci, and the box
      shows the spread over samples. It answers how much of the library falls in repeats or
      paralogs.

      How to read: a sample with a much higher share than the others may be contaminated or
      rich in repeat or rRNA reads.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexdobin/STAR/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf
  - id: mismatch_rate
    component: card
    column: mismatch_rate_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Mismatch rate per base
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of aligned bases that differ from the reference,
      and the box shows the spread over samples. It answers how closely the reads match the
      genome.

      How to read: a high rate points to a divergent reference, variants, or sequencing
      errors. An outlier sample deserves a look at its quality report.
  - id: annotated_splices
    component: card
    column: splices_annotated_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Annotated splices
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of splices that match an annotated junction, and
      the box shows the spread over samples. It answers how much of the splicing matches the
      gene annotation.

      How to read: values near the top mean the annotation describes the library well. A low
      share suggests unannotated transcripts or a mismatched annotation.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexdobin/STAR/master/doc/STARmanual.pdf
  - id: unique_vs_mismatch
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Unique mapping against mismatch rate
    roles: {x: mismatch_rate_pct, y: uniquely_mapped_pct, label: sample}
    config:
      color_col: multimapped_pct
      x_title: Mismatch rate (% of bases)
      y_title: Uniquely mapped reads (%)
      top_n_labels: 5
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample: its mismatch rate on the horizontal axis and the share of
      uniquely mapped reads on the vertical axis, coloured by its multi-mapped share. It
      answers whether poorly aligned samples also carry more mismatches.

      How to read: good samples sit at the top left. A sample drifting to the bottom right
      has more errors and fewer clean alignments, so open it in the read fate bars.

      Note: STAR publishes no cut-off for either measure, so none is drawn. Few samples make
      a weak trend, and the table has the exact values.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median uniquely mapped read
      share of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows
      the filters), not a cut-off of STAR.
  - component: table
    title: Alignment summary table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample with its input reads, mapped, multi-mapped and unmapped shares,
      splice counts and error rates from the STAR final log. It answers exactly how each
      sample aligned.

      How to read: sort by uniquely mapped share to find the weakest libraries.

id: star_read_fate
name: Read fate
mode: alignment/read-fate
description: >-
  Where each sample's input reads went, one row per sample and fate: uniquely
  mapped, multi-mapped, mapped to too many loci, or unmapped as too short, for
  too many mismatches or for another reason. STAR's own percentages, so the six
  fates of a sample add up to its input.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.Log.final.out"
recipe: star/read_fate.py
fixture: read_fate.tsv
renders_as:

    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: reads_pct
      color: fate
      labels: {sample: Sample, reads_pct: Reads (%), fate: Read fate}
    title: Where the reads went
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample and each segment is the share of its input reads that STAR
      uniquely mapped, multi-mapped, mapped to too many loci or left unmapped, with the
      reason. It answers how well each library aligned and why reads were lost.

      How to read: a high uniquely mapped share is good. A large unmapped too short share
      points to adapter or quality problems, and a large too many mismatches share to
      contamination or a wrong reference. Compare with the summary table.

      add up to the whole input. No cut-off is drawn because STAR publishes none.
