outputs.name: STAR-Fusion calls
outputs.rawYaml:
id: starfusion_fusions
name: STAR-Fusion calls
mode: fusion-detection
description: >-
  Fusion predictions from the abridged STAR-Fusion table, one row per call. The
  recipe strips the Ensembl id off each partner gene, sums junction reads and
  spanning fragments into one evidence count, and derives a log-scaled FFPM plus
  the fraction of the evidence that crosses the junction itself.
find: { filename: "*.starfusion.abridged.tsv" }
recipe: starfusion/fusions.py
fixture: fusions.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: evidence_dot_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    title: Fusion evidence by splice pattern
    roles: {cluster: splice_type, gene: fusion, mean_expression: log_ffpm, frac_expressing: junction_fraction}
    description: >-
      Each dot is a fusion call placed under its splice pattern, coloured by its abundance (log10 of FFPM plus
      one) and sized by the share of its evidence that crosses the junction itself. It answers which fusions
      have the strongest and most direct support.

      How to read: large, dark dots are abundant fusions backed mostly by junction reads, the most convincing
      kind. Small, pale dots rest on spanning fragments alone and deserve a second look.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Supporting reads per fusion
    dict_kwargs: { x: fusion, y: supporting_reads, color: splice_type, labels: { fusion: Fusion, supporting_reads: Supporting reads (junction reads plus spanning fragments), splice_type: Splice pattern } }
    description: >-
      Each bar is a fusion call: the sum of its junction reads and spanning fragments, coloured by splice
      pattern. It answers which fusions have the most evidence.

      How to read: tall bars are well supported. STAR-Fusion's defaults keep only calls with at least two
      supporting fragments, so the shortest bars are near the filter.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/STAR-Fusion/STAR-Fusion/master/STAR-Fusion
  - component: card
    column: log_ffpm
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Fusion abundance
    caption: log10 FFPM plus one, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median abundance of the calls on a log10 scale of fusion fragments per million
      (plus one), and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how strongly fusions are expressed.

      How to read: higher values mean more fusion fragments per million RNA-seq fragments. STAR-Fusion's
      defaults keep only calls with at least 0.1 FFPM, so every call here passed that floor.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/STAR-Fusion/STAR-Fusion/master/STAR-Fusion
  - component: card
    column: fusion
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: splice_type
    top_n_count: 3
    headline: true
    title: Fusions called
    caption: fusions, by splice pattern
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct fusions called, and the bars rank the splice patterns that
      account for most of them. It answers how many fusion candidates there are and how they splice.

      How to read: review the less common patterns against the evidence plot before reporting them.
  - component: card
    column: supporting_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: splice_type
    title: Supporting reads
    caption: reads, by splice pattern
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of junction reads and spanning fragments over all calls, and the ring
      splits it by splice pattern. It answers where the evidence comes from.

      How to read: a ring dominated by one pattern means most evidence sits on that kind of splice.
  - component: card
    column: junction_fraction
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Junction evidence share
    caption: share of evidence at the junction
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean share of each call's evidence that crosses the junction itself rather than
      spanning it, and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how direct the evidence is.

      How to read: values near one mean the call is backed by reads over the breakpoint. Calls near zero rest
      on spanning fragments only.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: fusion
    title: STAR-Fusion calls
    description: >-
      Each row is a fusion call with its partner genes, breakpoints, splice pattern, read evidence, FFPM and
      annotations. It answers which fusions to validate.

      How to read: sort by supporting reads or FFPM and check the annotations for known cancer fusions.

outputs.description: Spearman correlation of log2(cpm + 1) between every pair of libraries, over the features detected in at least half of them, square (libraries x libraries). Libraries of one condition or of neighbouring time points correlate; one that correlates with nothing is an outlier.
outputs.name: Library correlation matrix
outputs.rawYaml:
id: subread_correlation
name: Library correlation matrix
mode: exploratory/correlation
description: >-
  Spearman correlation of log2(cpm + 1) between every pair of libraries, over
  the features detected in at least half of them, square (libraries x
  libraries). Libraries of one condition or of neighbouring time points
  correlate; one that correlates with nothing is an outlier.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.featureCounts.txt"
recipe: subread/correlation.py
fixture: correlation.tsv
renders_as:
  # `index` is not optional in practice: ComplexHeatmapConfig.index_column falls
  # back to the literal "sample_id", which this matrix does not have.
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the run's libraries, known only at ingest.
  - id: correlation_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Library correlation
    roles: {index: sample}
    description: >-
      Each cell is the Spearman correlation between two libraries over the features
      detected in at least half of them, with libraries ordered by clustering. It
      answers which libraries resemble each other and which stand apart.

      How to read: blocks of high correlation are libraries of one condition or of
      neighbouring time points. A library whose row is paler than all others is an
      outlier, to check for a failed preparation or a swap before any comparison.

      Note: featureCounts publishes no correlation cut-off and no pass mark is
      drawn.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24227677/
  - component: table
    title: Library correlation matrix
    description: >-
      Each row is a library and each column the Spearman correlation of its
      log2 counts per million with another library. It answers the exact correlation
      behind every cell of the heatmap.

      How to read: read across a row to find the libraries it resembles least.

renders_as.description:
Each cell is the Spearman correlation between two libraries over the features detected in at least half of them, with libraries ordered by clustering. It answers which libraries resemble each other and which stand apart.
How to read: blocks of high correlation are libraries of one condition or of neighbouring time points. A library whose row is paler than all others is an outlier, to check for a failed preparation or a swap before any comparison.
Note: featureCounts publishes no correlation cut-off and no pass mark is drawn.
Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24227677/

renders_as.description:

id: subread_gene_counts
name: Gene counts per library
mode: quantification/gene-counts
description: >-
  The featureCounts count matrix as a long table, one row per feature per
  library, with counts per million and log2(cpm + 1). Each feature keeps its
  first contig and strand and the span of its exons, so the same rows feed a
  table, a per-gene trajectory and a genome axis. Features with no read in any
  library are dropped.

    column: gene_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: chromosome
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: chromosomes with the most features
    title: Features counted
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct features with at least one read in
      some library, and the bars rank the chromosomes by how many they hold. It
      answers how many features the count matrix covers and where they sit.

      How to read: the count is the size of the quantified annotation after features
      with no read anywhere are dropped. A chromosome that leads is gene rich.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24227677/

    column: counts
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: sample
    caption: counted reads, by library

    description: >-
      The hero number is the reads assigned to features over every library, and the
      bar splits them by library, with the median and maximum count of one feature
      in one library beside it. It answers how much of the total each library
      contributes.

      How to read: a thin share is a shallow library, whose counts are noisier.
      Libraries are compared in counts per million below, so depth differences do
      not distort the comparison.

tools.description: Fast, alignment-free differential splicing: PSI per local event and per isoform from transcript TPMs, and the delta PSI between two conditions with an empirical significance.
tools.name: SUPPA2

outputs.description: SUPPA2 diffSplice on local events, one row per contrast and event: the parsed event id (gene, type, chromosome, span, strand), the delta PSI oriented treatment minus control, its empirical p-value and the significance call.
outputs.name: Differential splicing of local events (SUPPA2)
outputs.rawYaml:
id: suppa_local_events
name: Differential splicing of local events (SUPPA2)
mode: splicing/events
description: >-
  SUPPA2 diffSplice on local events, one row per contrast and event: the
  parsed event id (gene, type, chromosome, span, strand), the delta PSI
  oriented treatment minus control, its empirical p-value and the
  significance call.
find: { path_glob: "**/*_local_diffsplice.dpsi" }
recipe: suppa/local_events.py
fixture: local_events.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: local_event_volcano
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: volcano
    title: Splicing change against significance
    roles: { feature_id: event_id, effect_size: dpsi, significance: pvalue, label: gene_id, category: event_type }
    config:
      significance_threshold: 0.05
      effect_threshold: 0.0
      top_n_labels: 10
      effect_label: Change in inclusion (delta PSI)
      significance_label: -log10 p-value
    description: >-
      Each point is a local splicing event in one contrast: its change in inclusion (delta PSI) on the
      horizontal axis and its empirical p-value on the vertical axis, coloured by event type. It answers which
      events change most, in which direction, and how confidently.

      How to read: events in the upper left and upper right corners lose or gain inclusion in the treatment
      with strong support. A p-value of exactly zero is drawn at the top of the axis. A cloud with nothing above
      the line means little differential splicing, so check the transcript quantification before trusting it.

      Lines and annotations: the horizontal line is a p-value of 0.05, the default alpha of SUPPA2 diffSplice.
      No delta PSI line is drawn: the rnasplice template passes its MIN_DPSI variable to this recipe's
      min_dpsi parameter with a default of 0, so the call adds no floor on the change. A value above 0 is the
      user's own working value, not a SUPPA2 default.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/comprna/SUPPA/master/README.md
  - id: local_event_types
    component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    title: Events by type and direction
    dict_kwargs: { x: event_type, color: direction, barmode: stack, labels: { event_type: Event type, direction: Direction of change } }
    description: >-
      Each bar is a local event type, split by whether its events gain inclusion, lose it or do not change
      significantly. It answers which kinds of splicing carry the differences between the conditions.

      How to read: a type whose bar is mostly significant is where the treatment acts. Bars that are almost
      entirely not significant point to little signal for that type.
  - component: card
    column: event_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: event_type
    title: Events tested
    caption: events, by type
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct local events SUPPA2 could quantify, and the ring splits them by
      event type. It answers how much splicing the run covers and of what kind.

      How to read: a type that is missing may have had no events in the annotation or too little expression, so
      check the transcript quantification.
  - component: card
    column: abs_dpsi
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Size of the inclusion change
    caption: quartiles of the absolute change
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median absolute change in inclusion across events, and the box shows its
      quartiles. It answers how large the splicing differences are overall.

      How to read: a box close to zero means most events are unchanged and the signal sits in a few. Filter to
      one event type or contrast to see where the larger changes are.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: event_type
    title: Event type
    description: >-
      Restricts every tile to the chosen event types, such as skipped exons or retained introns.
      It answers whether a pattern holds within one kind of splicing.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: event_id
    title: Local splicing events
    description: >-
      Each row is a local splicing event in one contrast, with its gene, type, span, change in inclusion,
      p-value and significance call. It answers which events to follow up.

      How to read: sort by p-value or by the absolute change and select a row to filter the dashboard to it.

id: svanalyzer_svbenchmark

      with the precision and recall in the table to see whether the gap is missed

      positives. The cited page states no cut-off for F1, so none is drawn.

outputs.name: Containment ANI
outputs.rawYaml:
id: sylph_ani
name: Containment ANI
mode: profile
description: >-
  One row per reference genome sylph detected in a sample: the adjusted ANI of
  the containment match next to the taxonomic and sequence abundances and the
  effective coverage. ANI against abundance separates confident calls from
  divergent relatives, which read-count profilers cannot express.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/sylph/profile
find: { filename: "*.sylph.tsv" }
recipe: sylph/ani.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 30 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples.
fixture: ani.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: ani_dot_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    title: Detected genomes per sample
    roles: {cluster: sample, gene: genome, mean_expression: adjusted_ani, frac_expressing: abundance_frac}
    description: >-
      Each dot is a reference genome that sylph detected in a sample: its colour is the
      adjusted containment ANI and its size is the taxonomic abundance as a fraction.
      It answers which genomes are present in which samples and how close each match is.

      How to read: large dark dots are abundant genomes with a close match. A small
      dot with a lower ANI is a divergent relative of the reference, so the sample holds
      a different strain or species than the database. A genome present in every
      sample is part of the shared community.

      Source: https://sylph-docs.github.io/Output-format/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: scatter
    dict_kwargs:
      x: taxonomic_abundance
      y: adjusted_ani
      color: sample
      size: eff_cov
      labels: {taxonomic_abundance: Taxonomic abundance (%), adjusted_ani: Adjusted ANI (%), sample: Sample, eff_cov: Effective coverage}
    title: ANI against abundance
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: adjusted_ani, label: Median adjusted ANI}
    description: >-
      Each point is a genome detected in a sample: its taxonomic abundance on the
      horizontal axis and its adjusted ANI on the vertical axis, coloured by sample and
      sized by effective coverage. It answers whether the abundant genomes are also the
      confident, close matches.

      How to read: points at the upper right are abundant and near identical to the
      reference. A point with low abundance and low ANI is a weak or divergent
      detection to treat with care. Large points have more coverage behind their ANI.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median adjusted ANI of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not
      a cut-off of sylph.

      Note: sylph reports a coverage-adjusted ANI only below 3x coverage and otherwise
      the naive ANI, so very deep genomes are not adjusted.

      Source: https://sylph-docs.github.io/Output-format/
  - component: card
    column: adjusted_ani
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Adjusted ANI
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median adjusted containment ANI of the detected genomes,
      and the box shows the spread. It answers how close the sample genomes are to the
      reference genomes.

      How to read: values near 100 percent mean the sample holds the reference strain.
      A lower median means divergent relatives of the references, so the database may
      lack the exact genomes.

      Note: containment ANI slightly overestimates the true ANI.

      Source: https://sylph-docs.github.io/Output-format/
  - component: card
    column: genome
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: genomes, with detections counted
    title: Detected genomes
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct reference genomes detected, and the
      strip counts detections, a genome found in two samples counting twice. It answers
      how rich the profiled communities are.

      How to read: many detections of few genomes means a shared community across
      samples. A detection count close to the genome count means each sample has its
      own genomes.

      Source: https://sylph-docs.github.io/Output-format/
  # Effective coverage spans orders of magnitude, so a box or a ranking would
  # flatten it: the card shows the extremes. sylph documents a detection limit
  # (above 0.01 to 0.05x for bacterial genomes), not a coverage pass mark, so none is drawn.
  - component: card
    column: eff_cov
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: grid
    caption: median, with the lowest and highest genome
    title: Effective coverage
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median effective coverage of the detected genomes, a
      k-mer based estimate of the sequencing depth, with the lowest and highest values.
      It answers how deeply each detected genome is covered.

      How to read: a low coverage means a thin detection whose ANI is less certain.
      High coverage detections support the ANI and the abundance.

      Note: the cited sylph page gives only a minimum of more than 0.01 to 0.05x

How to read: large dark dots are abundant genomes with a close match. A small dot with a lower ANI is a divergent relative of the reference, so the sample holds a different strain or species than the database. A genome present in every sample is part of the shared community.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: tama_category_composition
name: Structural category composition
mode: long-read/isoforms
description: >-
  Share of each sample's isoforms, and of its FLNC reads, in every structural
  category, stacked to 100 % per sample; the level switches between the two.
find:
  path_glob: "**/09_GSTAMA_MERGE/*.bed"
recipe: tama/category_composition.py
fixture: category_composition.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: category_bars
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    roles: {sample_id: sample, taxon: structural_category, rank: level, abundance: pct}
    title: Structural categories per sample
    config:
      default_rank: Isoforms
      value_title: Share of the sample (%)
      x_title: Sample
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample, split into the share of its isoforms (or of its FLNC reads, with the level
      control) in each structural category. It answers how much of a sample's transcriptome matches the
      reference annotation and how much is novel.

      How to read: a high share of full splice matches means the sample is well covered by the reference.
      Large novel categories (NIC, NNC) are either real new isoforms or artefacts, so compare the isoform
      level with the read level: novel isoforms backed by few reads are the first to doubt. Switch the
      level to see whether the novelty is in many rare isoforms or in a few abundant ones.

      Lines and annotations: the categories follow SQANTI3. FSM is a full splice match to a reference
      transcript, ISM an incomplete one, NIC a new combination of known splice sites, NNC an isoform with at least one unannotated splice site. Genic intron isoforms sit inside an
      annotated intron, genic genomic ones overlap introns and exons, antisense ones lie on the
      opposite strand of a gene and intergenic ones outside any gene.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/ConesaLab/SQANTI3/SQANTI3-isoform-classification:-categories-and-subcategories.md
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: level
    title: Isoforms or reads
    description: >-
      Choose whether the shares count isoforms or FLNC reads. It answers whether a category is large because
      it holds many distinct isoforms or because it holds many reads.

      How to read: select one level at a time. Selecting both stacks two different denominators in the same
      table.
  - component: table
    title: Category composition table
    description: >-
      Each row is a sample, a level (isoforms or reads) and a structural category with its count and its
      share of that sample and level. It answers the exact numbers behind the bars.

      How to read: sort by share to find the dominant category of each sample, and compare the two levels
      for the same category.

description: >-

renders_as:

    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy

    title: Isoforms against read support per gene
    config:
      log_x: true
      x_title: FLNC reads supporting the gene
      y_title: Isoforms per gene
      top_n_labels: 10
    description: >-
      Each point is a gene in one sample: the full-length reads behind it on the horizontal axis (log
      scale) and the number of distinct isoforms TAMA found on the vertical axis, coloured by the most
      common structural category among its isoforms. It answers which genes carry the most isoform diversity
      and whether that diversity is backed by reads.

      How to read: genes high on the plot have many isoforms. Isoform count rises with read depth, so a gene
      that sits high at low read support is the more surprising one. A gene with many isoforms that are
      mostly novel categories is a candidate for follow-up or for artefacts.
  - component: card
    column: gene_id
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: gene_status
    top_n_count: 2

    title: Genes with isoforms

      The hero number counts the gene entries (one per sample and gene) with at least one isoform, and the bars split them into
      annotated and novel genes. The second figure counts the distinct gene ids over all samples. It answers
      how many genes the long reads reach and how many are not in the reference.

      How to read: a small novel share is expected for a well annotated organism. A large one is worth
      checking against the reference GTF used for the structural categories.

      answers how many isoforms a typical gene carries.

      depth.

outputs.name: Isoforms with read support and structural category
outputs.rawYaml:
id: tama_transcripts
name: Isoforms with read support and structural category
mode: long-read/isoforms
description: >-
  One row per TAMA merge isoform: position, exon count, length, the FLNC reads
  TAMA collapsed into it and, against a reference GTF, its SQANTI-style
  structural category (FSM, ISM, NIC, NNC, genic, antisense, intergenic) and
  reference gene.
find:
  path_glob: "**/09_GSTAMA_MERGE/*.bed"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/*_merge.txt"
recipe: tama/transcripts.py
fixture: transcripts.tsv
renders_as:
  # Length against support, coloured by category: the novel isoforms worth a
  # look are the well supported ones, top of the plot.
  - id: isoform_support_plane
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    roles: {x: transcript_length, y: read_support, label: transcript_id, color: structural_category}
    title: Isoform length against read support
    config:
      log_y: true
      x_title: Isoform length (nt)
      y_title: FLNC reads supporting the isoform
      top_n_labels: 10
    description: >-
      Each point is an isoform of the merged transcriptome: its spliced length on the horizontal axis and the
      full-length reads collapsed into it on the vertical axis (log scale), coloured by structural category.
      It answers which novel isoforms are well supported.

      How to read: novel isoforms (NIC, NNC) high on the plot are the well supported ones worth following up.
      Novel isoforms at the bottom rest on one or two reads, so treat them with caution: the SQANTI study
      found that a share of novel long-read isoforms are technical artefacts.

      Lines and annotations: the colours are the structural categories of SQANTI3 (FSM full splice match,
      ISM incomplete, NIC new combination of known splice sites, NNC at least one unannotated splice site).
      No cut-off is drawn.

      Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/ConesaLab/SQANTI3/SQANTI3-isoform-classification:-categories-and-subcategories.md
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29440222/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: structural_category
      y: transcript_length
      color: structural_category
      labels: {structural_category: Structural category, transcript_length: Isoform length (nt)}
    title: Isoform length by category
    description: >-
      Each box is a structural category: the spread of isoform lengths in it. It answers whether novel
      isoforms are shorter or longer than the isoforms that match the reference.

      How to read: incomplete splice matches (ISM) lack 5' exons of their reference transcript, so they can be
      shorter than full splice matches. A category much shorter than the rest may reflect partial reads. Similar lengths across
      categories argue for real isoforms.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/ConesaLab/SQANTI3/SQANTI3-isoform-classification:-categories-and-subcategories.md
  - component: card
    column: transcript_id
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: structural_category
    top_n_count: 4
    headline: true
    caption: isoforms, by structural category
    title: Isoforms in the merge
    description: >-
      The hero number counts the isoforms of the merged transcriptome, and the bars rank the structural
      categories by how many isoforms each holds. The second figure counts the distinct isoform ids. It
      answers how large the transcriptome is and what it is made of.

      How to read: a leading full splice match bar means the data mostly confirm the annotation. A leading
      novel category means the reference is incomplete for this tissue or the data hold many artefacts.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/ConesaLab/SQANTI3/SQANTI3-isoform-classification:-categories-and-subcategories.md
  - component: card
    column: read_support
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [q1, q3, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: reads per isoform, median with its quartiles and maximum
    title: Read support per isoform
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of full-length reads behind an isoform, with the quartiles and the
      maximum beside it. It answers how well supported a typical isoform is.

      How to read: a median of one or two reads means most isoforms are singletons and the transcriptome is
      under-sampled. A maximum orders of magnitude above the median is normal, since a few abundant genes
      dominate the reads.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: structural_category
    title: Structural category
    description: >-
      Pick one or more structural categories to restrict every tile of the tab to those isoforms. It answers
      what the novel isoforms alone look like.

      How to read: select NIC and NNC to look at novel isoforms only, then read the support scatter.
  - component: table
    title: Isoforms table
    description: >-
      Each row is an isoform: its position, exon count, length, read support, structural category and the
      reference gene and transcript it matches. It answers which isoforms to follow up.

      How to read: filter to a novel category and sort by read support to list the best supported new
      isoforms.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: taxpasta_embedding
name: Profiler ordination
mode: merge/ordination
description: >-
  Bray-Curtis PCoA over every profiling run. One point per sample, profiler and
  database, so runs that agree on the community land together and the spread
  reads as profiler disagreement rather than as biological distance.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/taxpasta/merge
find: { path_glob: "**/taxpasta/*.tsv" }
recipe: taxpasta/embedding.py
fixture: embedding.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: profiler_embedding
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: embedding
    title: Profiler ordination
    roles: {sample_id: sample_id, dim_1: dim_1, dim_2: dim_2, color: profiler}
    config:
      axis_prefix: PCo
    description: >-
      Each point is one profiling run, a sample classified by one profiler and
      database, placed by the Bray-Curtis distance between taxon abundance profiles
      and coloured by profiler. It answers whether the profilers describe the same
      community or disagree.

      How to read: runs that sit together report similar communities, so a tight
      cluster of profilers agrees. A profiler that lands apart from the others
      reports a different set of taxa or names them differently, so open the
      detection overlap and the taxon by run matrix to see which taxa drive the gap.
      Runs of one profiler from different samples spread apart when the samples
      differ biologically.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The axes are principal coordinates of
      the Bray-Curtis matrix, so only distances between points carry meaning.
  - component: table
    title: Profiling run coordinates
    description: >-
      Each row is one profiling run, a sample classified by one profiler and
      database, with its two ordination coordinates and the platform it was
      sequenced on. It answers where a given run sits in the ordination.

      How to read: sort by a coordinate to find the runs at either extreme, then
      filter to a profiler to compare its runs across samples.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  # One row per run, so the count is the number of runs and the ring splits them by platform.
  - component: card
    column: profiler_db
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: platform
    caption: runs, by sequencing platform
    title: Profiling runs
    description: >-
      Each unit is one profiling run, a sample classified by one profiler and
      database, and the ring splits the runs by sequencing platform. The second
      number counts the distinct profiler and database pairs. It answers how much
      of the ordination each platform contributes.

      How to read: a ring dominated by one platform means the ordination mostly
      compares runs of that platform, so profiler differences may partly be platform
      differences.

outputs.name: Cross-profiler lineages
outputs.rawYaml:
id: taxpasta_lineage
name: Cross-profiler lineages
mode: merge/lineage
description: >-
  The same grain as the cross-profiler abundances, with the seven NCBI ranks widened
  into their own columns so a hierarchy can be drawn from them. The ancestry is read
  back out of the indented kraken-style reports the run writes, and reads no
  profiler could place keep an explicit unclassified lineage rather than dropping
  out of the rings.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/taxpasta/merge
find: { path_glob: "**/taxpasta/*.tsv" }
recipe: taxpasta/lineage.py
fixture: lineage.tsv
renders_as:
  # Wide per-rank columns -> sunburst, exactly the shape melon's pooled table has,
  # except this one keeps the profiler, database and sample it came from.
  - id: lineage_sunburst
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Taxonomic hierarchy
    roles:
      ranks: [superkingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species]
      abundance: rel_abundance
    config:
      colour_by_rank: phylum
    description: >-
      Each arc is a taxon: the rings run from superkingdom at the centre to species
      at the edge, sized by the summed relative abundance of the profiling runs in
      view and coloured by phylum. It answers which lineages dominate the community
      the profilers report.

      How to read: a wide arc at an inner ring means that lineage holds most of the
      abundance, and its children show how it splits. Reads no profiler could place
      keep their own unclassified branch, so a large one means the database misses
      much of the sample. Filter to one profiler to compare its hierarchy with
      another.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. Arc sizes add the relative abundances of
      every run in view, so filter to a single run for shares that sum to one.
  # Pavian's flow view: the root fans out into the domains, and the reads the
  # profiler could not place leave it as their own branch. `steps` is the catalog
  # spelling of the tile's `step_cols`; a dashboard widens or narrows it.
  # Every flow leaves the root, so colour by target (RULES section 8).
  - id: lineage_sankey
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sankey
    title: Taxonomic flow
    roles: {steps: [root, superkingdom, phylum, genus]}
    config:
      color_mode: target
      value_col: rel_abundance
      value_label: Summed relative abundance
    description: >-
      Each band is a group of taxa flowing from the root through superkingdom and
      phylum down to genus, sized by the summed relative abundance of the runs in
      view. It answers how the community divides at each rank and where the
      unclassified reads leave the tree.

      How to read: a thick band from the root into one superkingdom means that domain
      dominates. A band that splits into many thin ones at the genus step marks a
      diverse phylum. Compare a profiler with a large unclassified band against one
      with a small band to see how much each database covers.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. Band widths add the relative
      abundances of every run in view.
  - component: card
    column: species
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: phylum
    top_n_count: 4
    filter_expr: "(col('phylum') != 'unclassified') & (col('phylum') != 'unresolved')"
    caption: species rows, by the richest phyla
    title: Distinct species
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct species reported, the second number
      counts every species row, and the bars rank the phyla by how many rows they
      hold. It answers how rich the profiles are and which phyla contribute most.

      How to read: a few phyla holding most of the rows is the usual shape of a
      mock or low-complexity community. Rows without a placed phylum are left out
      of the ranking.
  - component: card
    column: rel_abundance
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: relative abundance of every taxon
    title: Typical taxon abundance
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median relative abundance of a taxon in a run, with the
      smallest and largest below it, and the histogram shows the distribution. It
      answers how evenly the abundance is spread over the reported taxa.

      How to read: a distribution piled near zero with a long right tail means a
      few taxa dominate over a long tail of rare ones. The values span orders of
      magnitude, so the histogram reads better filtered to one profiler.
  - component: card
    column: phylum
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: superkingdom
    top_n_count: 4
    filter_expr: "(col('phylum') != 'unclassified') & (col('phylum') != 'unresolved')"
    caption: phylum rows, by domain of life
    title: Distinct phyla
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct phyla reported, and the bars rank the
      superkingdoms by how many phylum rows they hold. It answers which domains of
      life the profilers place their taxa in.

      How to read: a ranking led by Bacteria with a short Archaea bar is typical.
      Compare profilers with the filters to see which ones reach a domain the
      others miss.
  - component: card
    column: rel_abundance
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: relative abundance of every taxon
    title: Largest taxon share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest relative abundance any taxon reaches in a run,
      with the median below it, and the histogram shows all values. It answers
      whether one taxon dominates a profile.

      How to read: a maximum far above the median means one taxon takes a large
      share of the run. It is a fraction of the run's total, so a high value also
      follows from a profile reporting few taxa.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: superkingdom
    title: Superkingdom
    description: >-
      Filters every tile of this view to the chosen superkingdoms. It answers
      whether a pattern holds within one domain of life.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: phylum
    title: Phylum
    description: >-
      Filters every tile of this view to the chosen phyla. It answers which phyla
      drive a profile.
  - component: table
    title: Lineage table
    description: >-
      Each row is a taxon reported by one profiler in one sample, with its seven
      NCBI ranks, its read count and its relative abundance. It answers which
      lineage a given taxon belongs to and how abundant it is.

      How to read: sort by relative abundance to see the leading taxa, or filter by
      rank columns. Rows labelled unclassified or unresolved are reads the profiler
      could not place at that rank.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: taxpasta_matrix
name: Taxon by run matrix
mode: merge/matrix
description: >-
  The top taxa as a wide taxon by profiling-run matrix of relative abundances,
  with the taxonomic rank as a row annotation and the profiler and platform of
  each column serialised for the heatmap's column strips.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/taxpasta/merge
find: { path_glob: "**/taxpasta/*.tsv" }
recipe: taxpasta/matrix.py
fixture: matrix.tsv
renders_as:
  # C6 N/A: value columns are the run's profiling runs, known only at ingest.
  - id: concordance_heatmap
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: complex_heatmap
    title: Taxon by run abundance heatmap
    roles: {index: taxon}
    config:
      row_annotation_cols: [rank]
    description: >-
      Each cell is the relative abundance of one taxon (row) in one profiling run
      (column), with the taxonomic rank as a row strip and the profiler and platform
      as column strips. It answers which taxa the profilers agree on and which runs
      group together.

      How to read: columns that cluster together report similar communities, and a
      profiler that falls on its own branch differs from the rest. A taxon bright in
      some columns and blank in others is detected by only some profilers, so check
      the detection overlap tile. Rows are the most abundant taxa, so rare taxa are
      not shown.

      Lines and annotations: the dendrograms come from hierarchical clustering of
      the rows and columns, and the strips label rank, profiler and platform.
  - component: table
    title: Taxon by run table
    description: >-
      Each row is a taxon with its relative abundance in every profiling run, one
      column per run. It answers the exact value behind a heatmap cell.

      How to read: sort a run column to see its leading taxa, or filter by rank. A
      zero means that profiler did not report the taxon in that run.

outputs.name: Profiler detection overlap
outputs.rawYaml:
id: taxpasta_presence
name: Profiler detection overlap
mode: merge/presence
description: >-
  Per sample and taxon, a 0/1 membership column for every profiler in the run.
  The intersections show how much of the community the classifiers agree on and
  how long each profiler's private tail is.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/taxpasta/merge
find: { path_glob: "**/taxpasta/*.tsv" }
recipe: taxpasta/presence.py
fixture: presence.tsv
renders_as:
  # upset_plot binds no canonical role: the set columns are the run's profilers,
  # so they are named in the tile's config rather than in a role.
  # C6 N/A: set columns are the run's profilers, known only at ingest.
  - id: profiler_upset
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: upset_plot
    title: Profiler detection overlap
    config:
      color_intersections_by: degree
    description: >-
      Each bar is an intersection: the number of sample and taxon detections reported
      by exactly that set of profilers, coloured by how many profilers share them. It
      answers how much of the community the profilers agree on and how long each
      one's private tail is.

      How to read: tall bars with many joined dots are detections every profiler
      makes, so they are the safest. Tall single-dot bars are taxa only one profiler
      reports, which often means a database difference or a false positive. Open the
      cross-profiler table to see which taxa sit in a private tail.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The side bars give the total detections
      of each profiler.
  - component: card
    column: n_profilers
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Profilers per detection
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of profilers that report a taxon in a
      sample, and the box shows the spread. It answers how widely a detection is
      shared.

      How to read: a median near the number of profilers means a consensus
      community. A low median with a wide box means most detections are specific to
      one or two profilers.
  - component: table
    title: Detection table
    description: >-
      Each row is a taxon detected in a sample, with the number of profilers that
      report it and a 0 or 1 for each profiler. It answers which taxa a given
      profiler misses or reports alone.

      How to read: filter to a low profiler count to list the contested taxa, or sort
      by rank to compare species with genus calls.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: taxpasta_profiles
name: Cross-profiler abundances
mode: merge
description: >-
  Every standardised taxpasta table melted into one long frame: one row per
  profiler, database, sample and taxon, with the raw count and the within-run
  relative abundance. The hub every cross-profiler comparison is computed from.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/taxpasta/merge
find: { path_glob: "**/taxpasta/*.tsv" }
recipe: taxpasta/profiles.py
fixture: profiles.tsv
renders_as:
  # long format (run x rank x taxon x abundance) -> stacked_taxonomy fits; a
  # sunburst would need the wide per-rank columns this frame does not carry.
  # One bar per profiling run (profiler x database): each bar keeps one
  # classifier's naming vocabulary, and pools only the samples in scope.
  - id: stacked_taxonomy
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: stacked_taxonomy
    title: Community composition per run
    roles: {sample_id: profiler_db, taxon: name, rank: rank, abundance: rel_abundance}
    description: >-
      Each bar is one profiler and database, split into the taxa it reports at the
      chosen rank and sized by relative abundance, pooling the samples in view. It
      answers how the community looks to each classifier.

      How to read: bars with the same colours in similar proportions agree on the
      community. A bar dominated by an unclassified segment points to a database
      that misses much of the sample, and a bar with different taxa reflects another
      naming vocabulary. Switch the rank, or filter to a sample, to compare like with
      like.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taxprofiler/taxpasta/dev/README.md
  - component: card
    column: name
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: uniqueness
    caption: distinct and repeated taxon names
    title: Distinct taxon names
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct taxon names reported, the second
      number counts every row, and the ring splits distinct from repeated names. It
      answers how much of the vocabulary is shared between runs.

      How to read: a high share of repeated names means the profilers and samples
      report the same taxa. Profilers use different naming, so one organism can
      appear under several names.
  - component: card
    column: count
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: profiler
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: assigned counts, by profiler
    title: Assigned counts
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count assigned to taxa, with the median per row
      below it, and the bars rank the profilers by total. It answers how much of the
      data each profiler assigns.

      How to read: compare profilers with care, since each one counts its own
      units. The values span orders of magnitude, so a spread is not drawn.
  - component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: profiler
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: taxon rows, by profiler
    title: Samples profiled
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct samples, the second number counts every
      row, and the bars rank the profilers by how many taxon rows they report. It
      answers how many samples the table covers and which profiler reports the
      longest list.

      How to read: a profiler with a much longer bar reports a long tail of taxa,
      which may include false positives.
  - component: card
    column: rel_abundance
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: relative abundance of every taxon
    title: Largest taxon share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest relative abundance a taxon reaches in a run,
      with the median below it, and the histogram shows all values. It answers
      whether one taxon dominates a profile.

      How to read: a maximum far above the median means one taxon takes a large
      share of a run. No cut-off is drawn, because no published rule separates a
      dominant taxon from an ordinary one.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: profiler
    title: Profiler
    description: >-
      Filters every tile of this view to the chosen profilers. It answers how one
      classifier reads the data on its own.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: sample
    title: Sample
    description: >-
      Filters every tile of this view to the chosen samples. It answers how the
      profilers behave on one sample.
  - component: table
    title: Abundance table
    description: >-
      Each row is a taxon reported by one profiler and database in one sample, with
      its rank, raw count and relative abundance. It answers the exact value behind a
      bar of the composition.

      How to read: sort by relative abundance for the leading taxa, or filter by
      rank. Relative abundance is a share of that run's total.
  # Metric cards and the row-level table behind them: the readings the
  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: rank
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: rank
    caption: rows, by taxonomic rank
    title: Rows by rank
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of rows, the second number counts the ranks
      present, and the bar shows the share of rows at each rank. It answers at which
      level the profilers report.

      How to read: a bar mostly at species means the profilers resolve to species
      level, and a large genus or domain share means some stop higher.
  - component: card
    column: rel_abundance
    aggregation: q3
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: relative abundance of every taxon
    title: Upper quartile abundance
    description: >-
      The hero number is the upper quartile of relative abundance, with the median and
      the largest value below it, and the histogram shows all values. It answers how abundant the commoner taxa are
      relative to the rarest ones.

      How to read: a quartile far below the maximum means the abundance is held by
      few taxa.

outputs.name: Per-run profile statistics
outputs.rawYaml:
id: taxpasta_sample_summary
name: Per-run profile statistics
mode: merge/summary
description: >-
  One row per sample, profiler and database: how many taxa were reported, how
  many reads were assigned, how concentrated the profile is on its top hit, and
  Shannon diversity with Pielou evenness.
nf_core_url: https://github.com/nf-core/modules/tree/master/modules/nf-core/taxpasta/merge
find: { path_glob: "**/taxpasta/*.tsv" }
recipe: taxpasta/sample_summary.py
fixture: sample_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: richness_dot_plot
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: dot_plot
    title: Diversity per sample and profiler
    roles: {cluster: sample, gene: profiler_db, mean_expression: shannon, frac_expressing: top_taxon_fraction}
    description: >-
      Each dot is one profiling run, a sample (column) classified by one profiler and
      database (row). Its colour is the Shannon diversity of the profile and its size
      is the share held by the single top taxon. It answers which runs report a
      diverse community and which report one dominated by a taxon.

      How to read: large dots mean one taxon takes a big share of the profile, and
      pale or dark colour gives the diversity. Rows of different profilers that
      disagree on a sample point to a database or method difference, so compare them
      in the ordination. No cut-off is drawn, because no published rule separates a
      diverse profile from a dominated one.
  - headline: true
    component: card
    column: taxa_observed
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median, with its spread
    title: Taxa observed per run
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of taxa a profiling run reports, and the
      box shows the spread. It answers how rich the profiles are.

      How to read: a wide box means the profilers disagree strongly on richness, so
      compare them with the bar chart below. A high count is not necessarily better,
      since a long tail of rare taxa can be false positives.
  - component: card
    column: shannon
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: Shannon diversity of every run
    title: Shannon diversity
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean Shannon diversity of the runs, with the smallest and
      largest below it, and the histogram shows the distribution. It answers how
      diverse the reported communities are.

      How to read: higher values mean more taxa and a more even spread. Compare runs of
      the same sample, since profilers that report more rare taxa score higher.
      Shannon diversity has no published pass level, so no cut-off is drawn.
  - component: card
    column: evenness
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: mean, with the spread
    title: Pielou evenness
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean Pielou evenness of the runs, and the box shows the
      spread. It answers whether the abundance is spread evenly over the taxa or held
      by a few.

      How to read: values near 1 mean an even community and values near 0 one
      dominated by a taxon. A low score points to a profiler that over-reports a few taxa. No cut-off is
      drawn, because no published rule defines a good evenness.
  - component: card
    column: profiler_db
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: profiler
    top_n_count: 4
    caption: runs, by profiler
    title: Profiler and database pairs
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct profiler and database pairs, the second
      number counts every run, and the bars rank the profilers by their runs. It
      answers how many classifiers are compared and which ones have most runs.

      How to read: a profiler with several databases has a longer bar. Interpret
      comparisons across profilers with unequal run counts with care.
  - component: card
    column: assigned_count
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    caption: assigned counts of every run
    title: Assigned counts per run
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count assigned to taxa in a run, with the smallest
      and largest below it, and the histogram shows every run. It answers how much of
      the data a typical run assigns.

      How to read: the values span orders of magnitude between profilers and
      platforms, so read the extremes as a range and not as a spread. A very small
      count against the others suggests a run with little usable data.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: scatter
    dict_kwargs:
      x: taxa_observed
      y: shannon
      color: profiler
      symbol: platform
      labels: {taxa_observed: Taxa observed, shannon: Shannon diversity, profiler: Profiler, platform: Platform}
    title: Richness against diversity
    reference_lines: [{axis: y, stat: median, column: shannon}]
    description: >-
      Each point is one profiling run: the number of taxa it reports against its
      Shannon diversity, coloured by profiler with the sequencing platform as the
      marker shape. It answers whether runs that report more taxa also report a more
      diverse community.

      How to read: points rise together because Shannon diversity grows with richness.
      A profiler whose points sit above the others for the same richness has a more
      even profile, and one below is dominated by a few taxa. No reference line is
      drawn, since no published rule defines a good value.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median Shannon diversity of this
      table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters),
      not a cut-off of taxpasta.
  # How concentrated a run's profile is: the share its single top taxon holds,
  # which separates classifiers reporting a few dominant taxa from those that
  # spread the same community over a long tail.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    dict_kwargs:
      x: profiler_db
      y: top_taxon_fraction
      color: profiler
      labels: {profiler_db: Profiler and database, top_taxon_fraction: Share of the top taxon, profiler: Profiler}
    title: Share held by the top taxon
    reference_lines: [{axis: y, stat: median, column: top_taxon_fraction}]
    description: >-
      Each box is a profiler and database: the share of each sample's profile held by
      its single most abundant taxon, coloured by profiler. It answers which classifiers
      report a few dominant taxa and which spread the community over a long tail.

      How to read: a high box means the profiles are concentrated on one taxon, and a
      low box a flatter profile. Filter to one sample to compare profilers on the same
      community, since the share depends on the community as well as on the profiler.

      Lines and annotations: The dashed line is the median share held by the top
      taxon of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows
      the filters), not a cut-off of taxpasta.
  - component: table
    title: Run statistics table
    description: >-
      Each row is one profiling run with its taxa observed, assigned count, top taxon
      and its share, Shannon diversity and evenness. It answers the exact values
      behind the tiles above.

      How to read: sort by a statistic to find the extreme runs, or filter by profiler
      to compare its runs.

id: teal_telomere_length
name: Telomere length
mode: teal
description: >-
  TEAL's telomere length estimate, one row per DNA sample (tumor and normal):
  the raw and purity-adjusted final length, the telomeric fragments behind it
  and the purity, ploidy and depth it was normalised with. A tumor far above
  its normal suggests telomerase or ALT activity.

columns:
  sampleId: String
  type: String
  rawTelomereLength: Float64
  finalTelomereLength: Float64
  fullFragments: Int64
  totalTelomericReads: Int64
  purity: Float64
  ploidy: Float64
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 2 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several samples and types.
fixture: telomere_length.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: the bars are coloured by the type of DNA sample, tumor or reference.
  - id: telomere_length_bar
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sampleId
      y: finalTelomereLength
      color: type
      labels: {sampleId: Sample, finalTelomereLength: Telomere length (bp), type: Sample type}
    title: Telomere length per sample
    description: >-
      Each bar is the telomere length TEAL estimates for a DNA sample, adjusted for
      tumor purity, coloured by sample type. It answers how long the telomeres are and
      whether the tumor differs from its normal.

      How to read: a tumor far above its normal suggests telomerase or ALT activity,
      and a tumor far below it suggests telomere attrition. Compare each tumor with its
      own reference sample.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/teal/README.md
  - id: telomere_length_spread
    component: card
    column: finalTelomereLength
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    headline: true
    title: Telomere length
    caption: median, with its range
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median final telomere length over the DNA samples, with the
      shortest and longest beside it. It answers how long the telomeres are across the
      run.

      How to read: tumor and reference samples sit in one table, so read the range
      together with the bar chart to see which sample is at each end. A tumor with a
      length far from its normal is the finding.

      Note: the final length is adjusted for purity and ploidy for tumor samples and
      equals the raw length for the reference.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/teal/README.md
  - id: telomere_table
    component: table
    title: Telomere length estimates
    description: >-
      Each row is a DNA sample with its raw and final telomere length, the telomeric
      fragments behind it and the purity, ploidy and read depth used to normalise it.
      It answers how reliable each estimate is.

      How to read: an estimate on few telomeric reads or at low purity is less certain,
      so check the fragment counts before comparing samples.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hartwigmedical/hmftools/master/teal/README.md

outputs.rawYaml:
id: tiara_classifications
name: Sequence classes
mode: tiara/classifications
description: >-
  One row per classified sequence: Tiara's first-stage class (eukarya,
  bacteria, archaea, prokarya, organelle, unknown), its organelle call, and one
  class that merges the two (mitochondrion and plastid replace organelle). In a
  eukaryotic assembly every class but eukarya, mitochondrion and plastid is a
  candidate contaminant or a sequence too short or repetitive to call.
find:
  path_glob: "**/tiara/**/*.txt"
recipe: tiara/classifications.py
fixture: classifications.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: sequence_classes
    component: card
    column: genome
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: tiara_class
    headline: true
    title: Sequences by Tiara class
    caption: sequences, by class
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of sequences Tiara classified, with the number of
      assemblies beside it, and the bar splits them by class (eukarya, bacteria,
      archaea, prokarya, mitochondrion, plastid or unknown). It answers how much of an
      assembly is the expected organism and how much is foreign or organellar.

      How to read: in a eukaryotic assembly, bacteria, archaea and prokarya are
      candidate contaminants, and unknown marks sequences Tiara could not classify
      precisely. Mitochondrion and plastid are expected organelle genomes, so they are not
      contamination.

      Note: Tiara classifies sequences of at least 3000 bases by default and advises
      against classifying those under 1000, so shorter sequences are left out.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ibe-uw/tiara/main/README.md and
      https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34570171/
  # C1: the bars are coloured by the Tiara class of each sequence.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: genome
      color: tiara_class
      labels: {genome: Assembly, tiara_class: Tiara class}
    title: Sequences per Tiara class
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the sequences of one assembly, coloured by the class Tiara gives
      them. It answers which assemblies carry sequences from other organisms.

      How to read: an assembly that is almost all eukarya is clean. A visible share of
      bacteria, archaea or prokarya sequences is a lead for decontamination, which
      FCS-GX or a BLAST check can confirm before sequences are removed.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34570171/
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: tiara_class
    title: Tiara class
    description: >-
      Pick one or more classes to filter every tile of the dashboard to the sequences
      Tiara placed in them.

      How to read: select bacteria, archaea and prokarya to list the candidate
      contaminants of the assemblies.
  - component: table
    title: Sequence classes
    description: >-
      Each row is a classified sequence with its assembly, its merged class, the stage
      of the run it came from, the first-stage class, the organelle call and whether
      it is eukaryotic. It answers which sequences carry each class.

      How to read: filter by class to list the candidate contaminants, and by stage to
      compare the raw and the cleaned assembly.

id: truvari_summary

mode: benchmark-summary

renders_as:
  - id: pr_scatter
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: pr_benchmark
    title: Precision against recall per callset
    roles: {label: label, recall: recall, precision: precision, f1: f1}
    description: >-
      Each point is a benchmarked callset: its recall on the horizontal axis and its precision on the vertical
      axis, coloured by F1. It answers which caller finds the most true structural variants without adding
      false ones.

      How to read: points in the upper right corner are both sensitive and precise. A point high but far left
      misses true variants, and one far right but low adds false calls. Compare callsets of the same truth set
      only.

      Lines and annotations: the curved lines are contours of equal F1, the harmonic mean of precision and
      recall, and the diagonal marks equal precision and recall. They are mathematical references, not
      cut-offs, and Truvari publishes no pass mark.

  # nf-core dashboards were already computing off this output by hand.
  - component: card
    column: f1

    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: compact
    title: Callsets benchmarked
    caption: lowest and highest F1
    description: >-

      answers how many callsets were compared and how far apart they are.

      How to read: a callset without calls has no defined F1 and is left out of this count.

    column: f1
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    title: F1 score

    description: >-
      The hero number is the median F1 over callsets, and the box shows its quartiles. It answers how accurate
      the structural variant calls are overall, balancing precision and recall.

      How to read: higher is better, and a wide box means the callers differ a lot. Use the precision-recall
      plot to see which side limits each caller.
  - component: card
    column: precision
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Precision
    caption: precision per callset, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median precision over callsets, the share of calls that match the truth set, and
      the box shows its quartiles. It answers how many of the reported variants are real.

      How to read: low precision means false calls, which filtering the callset can reduce.
  - component: card
    column: recall

    title: Recall
    caption: recall per callset, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median recall over callsets, the share of truth variants that were found, and the

      How to read: low recall means missed variants, which more coverage or a more sensitive caller can

outputs.description: One row per callset (sample and caller) computed from its own VCF: calls and the share the caller kept, PASS SNVs, indels and multiallelic sites, the transition/transversion ratio, the heterozygous over homozygous-alternate ratio and the median quality, depth and heterozygous allele fraction. For the pipelines that publish VCFs without a bcftools stats report.
outputs.name: Callset summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: vcf_callset_summary
name: Callset summary
mode: per-callset
description: >-
  One row per callset (sample and caller) computed from its own VCF: calls and
  the share the caller kept, PASS SNVs, indels and multiallelic sites, the
  transition/transversion ratio, the heterozygous over homozygous-alternate
  ratio and the median quality, depth and heterozygous allele fraction. For the
  pipelines that publish VCFs without a bcftools stats report.
find:
  path_glob: "**/variant_calling/**/*.vcf.gz"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/variant_calling/*/*/*.vcf.gz"
    - "**/*.filtered.vcf.gz"
recipe: vcf/callset_summary.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 4 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several callers.
fixture: callset_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: ts_tv
    component: card
    column: ts_tv
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    headline: true
    title: Transition to transversion ratio
    caption: median, with its spread across callsets
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median transition to transversion (Ts/Tv) ratio over
      the callsets in view, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers whether the
      substitutions of a callset look like real variation.

      How to read: callsets of one data type should sit close together, so a
      callset far from the others points to false calls or a different sample or
      region. No cut-off is drawn, because the expected ratio depends on the data
      type (exome, genome or RNA) and no single source gives one for every callset.
      Open the table to compare callsets, then the FILTER breakdown for the calls
      that were removed.
  - id: pass_calls
    component: card
    column: pass_calls
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: PASS calls per callset
    caption: median, with its spread across callsets
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of calls that passed every filter, over
      the callsets in view. It answers how large a typical callset is once the caller's
      own filters are applied.

      How to read: a callset with far fewer calls than the others points to low
      coverage, a failed run or an over-strict filter. Compare it with the share of
      calls kept before deciding which.

      Source: https://samtools.github.io/hts-specs/VCFv4.3.pdf
  - id: pass_share
    component: card
    column: pass_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Share of calls kept
    caption: median, with its spread across callsets
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median percentage of calls a caller kept, over the
      callsets in view. A call is kept when its FILTER field is PASS, meaning it
      passed every filter.

      How to read: a low share means the caller's hard filters removed many calls,
      which is common in noisy data such as RNA. A share that differs a lot between
      callsets of one cohort suggests a quality difference, so open the FILTER
      breakdown to see which filters removed the calls.

      Source: https://samtools.github.io/hts-specs/VCFv4.3.pdf
  - id: het_hom
    component: card
    column: het_hom_ratio
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Heterozygous to homozygous ratio
    caption: median, with its spread across callsets
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median ratio of heterozygous to homozygous-alternate
      genotype calls, over the callsets in view. It answers whether the genotype mix is
      similar from callset to callset.

      How to read: a callset whose ratio departs from the others can point to
      contamination, a sample swap, or a caller or filter difference. No cut-off is
      drawn, because the expected ratio depends on the population and the data
      type. Open the table to find the callset.
  - id: tstv_vs_hethom
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Substitution ratio against genotype ratio
    roles: {x: het_hom_ratio, y: ts_tv, label: sample, color: caller}
    config:
      x_title: Heterozygous to homozygous-alternate ratio
      y_title: Transition to transversion ratio
      top_n_labels: 10
      legend_pos: bottom
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a callset: its heterozygous to homozygous-alternate ratio on the
      horizontal axis and its transition to transversion ratio on the vertical axis,
      coloured by caller. It answers whether a callset is an outlier on either
      measure.

      How to read: callsets of one data type should form a tight group. A point apart
      from the group on one axis points to a genotype issue, on the other axis to
      noisy substitutions, and a callset of one caller that sits apart from the other
      callers points to a caller effect. With few callsets, read the table instead, since neither ratio has a cut-off that holds for every data type.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median transition to
      transversion ratio of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show
      (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of the caller.
  - component: table
    title: Callset table
    description: >-
      Each row is a callset (a sample and the caller that produced it) with its
      counts of calls, PASS calls, SNVs, indels and multiallelic sites, its
      Ts/Tv ratio, its genotype counts and its median quality, depth and

      How to read: sort by the share of calls kept, by Ts/Tv or by the genotype
      ratio to find outliers, and compare callsets of the same caller.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: vcf_variant_density
name: Variant density
mode: per-variant/density
description: >-
  Distinct PASS variants per sample in fixed windows (1 Mb by default) along
  the primary contigs, one row per sample and window: chrom, start, end, value
  and sample, the shape a genome-wide density panel reads. Alt, unplaced and
  decoy contigs are left out, since no assembly-aware panel can place them.
find:
  path_glob: "**/variant_calling/**/*.vcf.gz"

recipe: vcf/variant_density.py

renders_as:
  - id: density_windows
    component: card
    column: value
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Variants per window
    caption: the densest window, with the spread over all windows
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest count of distinct PASS variants in a single window,
      and the box shows the quartiles over all windows. It answers how dense variation is
      and how uneven it is along the genome.

      How to read: a maximum far above the box marks a hot spot, such as a region
      of high diversity or of mapping artefacts. Open the karyotype or the track to see
      where it sits.
  # The karyotype: every primary contig drawn to the assembly's length, one
  # heat band per window (the rows are their own bins).
  - id: density_karyotype
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: ideogram
    title: Variant density along chromosomes
    roles: {chrom: chrom, start: start, end: end, value: value, sample: sample}
    description: >-
      Each band is a window on a chromosome, shaded on a continuous scale by the count
      of distinct PASS variants it holds. It answers where along the genome the
      variants of each sample concentrate.

      How to read: dark bands are dense and pale bands are sparse, so a dark band
      shared by every sample suggests a region that differs from the reference
      assembly. A band dense in one sample only points to that sample. Open the track
      to read the counts.
  - id: density_track
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: coverage_track
    title: Variant density track
    roles: {chromosome: chrom, position: start, end: end, value: value, sample: sample}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a window along a chromosome, with the count of distinct PASS
      variants in it as its height, one trace per sample. It answers how density
      changes along a chromosome and whether samples agree.

      How to read: traces that rise and fall together point to regions of the genome
      that vary in every sample. A trace that departs from the others over a stretch
      points to a sample-specific event or to a coverage difference.
