outputs.name: Variant calls
outputs.rawYaml:
id: vcf_variants
name: Variant calls
mode: per-variant
description: >-
  One row per variant call, read straight out of the caller's own VCF: locus,
  allele, quality, filter status, genotype, read depth and variant allele
  fraction. Pipeline-agnostic, and the only collection in a variant-calling
  template that is granular enough for a caller-against-caller comparison at
  the variant level rather than at the summary-count level.
find:
  path_glob: "**/variant_calling/**/*.vcf.gz"
  path_glob_alt:
    - "**/variant_calling/*/*/*.vcf.gz"
    - "**/*.filtered.vcf.gz"
recipe: vcf/variants.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several callers and variant types.
fixture: variants.tsv
renders_as:
  # Depth against allele fraction is the plane a germline callset is read on:
  # a clean diploid run stacks at 0.5 and 1.0, and everything off those two
  # bands is either low coverage or a caller artefact.
  - id: vaf_against_depth
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Allele fraction against read depth
    roles: {x: dp, y: vaf, label: variant_key, color: caller}
    config:
      x_title: Read depth
      y_title: Variant allele fraction
      top_n_labels: 5
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each point is a variant call: its read depth on the horizontal axis and its
      variant allele fraction on the vertical axis, coloured by caller. It answers
      whether the calls rest on enough reads and whether their allele balance is
      plausible.

      How to read: a heterozygous germline variant sits near an allele fraction of 0.5
      and a homozygous-alternate one near 1.0, so calls scattered between the two
      bands, especially at low depth, are less reliable. Allele balance in RNA is
      often skewed by expression, so read the bands loosely there. Compare callers
      to see whether one produces more calls off the bands, and note that no cut-off is drawn, since no source gives one for every data type.
  # Rainfall / density along the genome. The manhattan kind takes chr/pos/score
  # and asks nothing of the score's meaning, so the allele fraction reads as
  # the y axis honestly once `score_kind` says so.
  - id: variant_rainfall
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: manhattan
    title: Allele fraction along the genome
    roles: {chr: chrom, pos: pos, score: vaf, feature: variant_key}
    config:
      score_kind: Variant allele fraction
      highlight: none
      score_threshold_stat: p95
      color_by_columns: [caller, sample]
      default_color_by: caller
      hover_cols: [dp, qual]
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a variant call at its position along the chromosomes, with its
      variant allele fraction as the height, coloured by caller. It answers where along
      the genome the calls cluster and whether their allele balance changes by region.

      How to read: horizontal lines of points at the same height are the usual
      genotype bands. A stretch where calls are dense and off the bands can mark a
      copy number change, a mapping problem or a hot spot of artefacts. Switch the
      colour to the sample to see whether it is shared.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the 95th percentile of the allele
      fraction in this table, a reference defined by the data and not a cut-off from
      any source.
  - id: variant_genome_view
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: genome_view
    title: Variant calls along the genome
    roles: {chr: chrom, pos: pos, score: vaf, feature: variant_key, sample: caller, category: variant_type}
    config:
      score_title: Variant allele fraction
      top_stars: 0
    description: >-
      Each point is a variant call at its position, with its allele fraction as the
      height, coloured by variant type, with one lane per caller. It answers where each
      caller makes calls and whether callers agree on a region.

      How to read: a region with calls in one lane and none in the others is a locus the
      callers disagree on. Colours separate SNPs from insertions and deletions, so a
      run of indels in one lane may be a homopolymer error. Zoom to a locus and open the
      table for the calls.
  - component: card
    column: qual
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Call quality
    caption: median, with its spread across calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median QUAL value of the calls in view, and the box shows
      their quartiles. It answers how much confidence the caller put in its calls.

      How to read: a low median or a box reaching down to small values means many weak
      calls. The scale of QUAL depends on the caller, so compare callers only against
      their own runs, and filter on PASS to see the kept calls.
  - component: card
    column: dp
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Read depth at calls
    caption: median, with its spread across calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median read depth at the calls in view, and the box shows
      their quartiles. It answers how well covered the called sites are.

      How to read: a box reaching down to a depth of a few reads means many calls rest
      on little evidence, and a very long upper whisker marks repeats or collapsed
      regions. Open the depth against allele fraction plot to see how that affects the
      allele balance.
  - component: card
    column: vaf
    aggregation: average
    aggregations: [median, box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Variant allele fraction
    caption: average and median, with the spread across calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the mean variant allele fraction of the calls in view, and the
      box shows their quartiles. It answers where the allele balance sits overall.

      How to read: a mix of heterozygous and homozygous-alternate calls pulls the mean
      between 0.5 and 1.0, so it moves with the genotype mix more than with quality.
      Use the histogram below to see the two bands.
  - component: figure
    visu_type: histogram
    dict_kwargs:
      x: vaf
      color: caller
      labels: {vaf: Variant allele fraction, caller: Caller}
    title: Allele fraction distribution
    description: >-
      Each bar counts the variant calls in a bin of allele fraction, split by caller. It
      answers whether the allele balance shows the expected genotype bands.

      How to read: peaks near 0.5 and near 1.0 are the heterozygous and
      homozygous-alternate genotypes of a diploid sample. A mass of calls at low
      fractions suggests noise, mosaicism or contamination, and callers whose
      histograms differ are making different calls on the same data.
  - component: table
    title: Variant table
    description: >-
      Each row is a variant call with its locus, alleles, quality, FILTER status,
      genotype, read depth and allele fraction. It answers which calls to inspect or
      follow up.

      How to read: filter on FILTER status or sort by depth or quality to find weak calls,
      and use the variant key to look a call up in a genome browser.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: vcftools_filter_summary
name: Filter breakdown
mode: filter-summary
description: >-
  One row per caller and FILTER value: how many calls carry it, how they split
  between transitions and transversions, and what share of the callset they
  are. The per-caller view the pooled MultiQC panel cannot give.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.FILTER.summary"
recipe: vcftools/filter_summary.py
fixture: filter_summary.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: filter_partition
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: caller
      y: n_variants
      color: filter_label
      barmode: stack
      labels: {caller: Caller, n_variants: Variants, filter_label: FILTER value}
    title: Calls by FILTER value per caller
    description: >-
      Each bar is a caller, stacked by the FILTER value its calls carry, with the number
      of variants in each. It answers what each caller keeps and what it flags as
      filtered.

      How to read: a bar that is mostly PASS means a caller that keeps most of its calls.
      A large share under another label shows what the caller's own filters remove, and
      a caller that applies no filter shows a single segment. Compare shares and not
      heights, since callers differ in the number of calls.

      Source: https://vcftools.github.io/man_latest.html
  # The ring splits the calls by FILTER value; the sum is the callset size.
  - component: card
    column: n_variants
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: filter_label
    caption: calls, by FILTER value
    title: Calls by FILTER value
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of calls across the callers in view, and the
      ring splits them by FILTER value. It answers what share of the calls pass the
      callers' own filters.

      How to read: a ring that is mostly PASS means the filters remove little. A large
      slice of another label is what the callers discard, so check its Ts/Tv in the table
      to see whether the removed calls look like noise.

      Source: https://vcftools.github.io/man_latest.html
  - component: card
    column: n_variants
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: caller
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: calls, by caller
    title: Calls by caller
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total count of calls, and the bars rank the callers by how
      many calls they made. It answers which caller is the most and the least productive.

      How to read: a caller far ahead may be more sensitive or less strict, so read the
      count with its Ts/Tv and its share of PASS calls.

      Source: https://vcftools.github.io/man_latest.html
  # The ratio is read on the calls a caller keeps: PASS, or the unfiltered "." of a
  # caller that sets no FILTER. A pooled median would mix them with the rejected calls.
  - component: card
    column: ts_tv
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('filter_label').is_in(['PASS', '.'])"
    caption: kept calls, median with its spread
    title: Ts/Tv of kept calls
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median transition to transversion ratio of the calls that
      carry PASS or no filter, and the box shows the spread across callers and samples.
      It answers whether the kept calls have the balance expected of real variants.

      How to read: false calls are spread evenly over bases, so they pull the ratio down.
      A caller whose kept calls sit below the others adds noise, and the expected value
      depends on the genome region sequenced, whole genome or exome.

      Note: the tool publishes no cut-off for the ratio, so none is drawn.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25297068/
  - component: table
    title: FILTER summary table
    description: >-
      Each row is a caller and a FILTER value, with the number of calls, how many are
      transitions and transversions, their ratio and their share of the callset. It
      answers the exact numbers behind each tile.

      How to read: compare the Ts/Tv of the rejected labels with PASS to see whether a
      filter removes noise or good calls.

      Source: https://vcftools.github.io/man_latest.html

outputs.rawYaml:
id: vcftools_tstv_qual
name: Ts/Tv by quality threshold
mode: quality-sweep
description: >-
  The transition/transversion ratio of the calls above each quality threshold,
  one curve per sample and caller. Where a curve flattens is where that
  caller's quality score stops separating real variants from noise, which
  compares callers on calibration rather than on yield.
find:
  path_glob: "**/*.TsTv.qual"
recipe: vcftools/tstv_qual.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 15 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several callers.
fixture: tstv_qual.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: tstv_quality_sweep
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Ts/Tv by quality threshold
    roles: {series: series, x: qual_threshold, y: ts_tv_above}
    config:
      x_title: Minimum quality score
      y_title: Ts/Tv of the calls above it
      legend_pos: bottom
    description: >-
      Each curve is a sample and caller: the transition to transversion ratio of the
      SNPs whose quality is above each threshold. It answers whether raising the quality
      floor makes the calls more like real variants.

      How to read: a ratio that rises with the threshold means quality separates real
      from false calls, and a curve that stays flat means the quality score carries no
      information. The level to expect depends on the genome region sequenced, so compare
      callers on the same data.

      Note: the tool publishes no ideal ratio, so no reference line is drawn. Only
      bi-allelic SNPs are counted.

      Source: https://vcftools.github.io/man_latest.html
      and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25297068/
  - component: figure
    visu_type: line
    dict_kwargs:
      x: qual_threshold
      y: ts_tv_above
      color: series
      labels: {qual_threshold: Minimum quality score, ts_tv_above: Ts/Tv of the calls above it, series: Sample and caller}
    title: Ts/Tv by quality, static view
    description: >-
      Each line is a sample and caller: the Ts/Tv ratio of the calls above each quality
      threshold. It answers the same question as the interactive sweep, in a plain figure
      that can be exported.

      How to read: a line that climbs and levels off marks the quality score from which
      extra filtering gains little.

      Source: https://vcftools.github.io/man_latest.html
  # The median runs over every threshold step and series, so the card reads the
  # typical ratio of the sweep and the box its spread.
  - component: card
    column: ts_tv_above
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    caption: median over the sweep, with its spread
    title: Ts/Tv across the sweep
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median Ts/Tv ratio over every quality threshold and series
      in view, and the box shows the spread. It answers the typical balance of
      transitions and transversions of the callsets.

      How to read: callsets with a lower box add more noise. Filter to one caller to read
      its own level.

      Note: the tool publishes no ideal ratio, which depends on the genome region.

      Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25297068/
  - component: table
    title: Ts/Tv sweep table
    description: >-
      Each row is a quality threshold of a sample and caller, with the transitions and
      transversions above it and their ratio. It answers the exact numbers behind the
      curves.

      How to read: filter by series and read down the thresholds to see where the ratio
      stops improving.

      Source: https://vcftools.github.io/man_latest.html

outputs.name: Contig clusters per sample
outputs.rawYaml:
id: viralmetagenome_clusters
name: Contig clusters per sample
mode: per-cluster/summary
description: >-
  One row per contig cluster: its taxon, its centroid and whether that
  centroid is a reference-pool sequence or one of the sample's own contigs,
  the member contigs and their summed length, the share of the sample's
  contig read depth the cluster holds, and whether a consensus was refined
  from it or it was filtered out.
find:
  path_glob: "**/polishing/intermediate/cluster/*/*.clusters.tsv"
recipe: viralmetagenome/clusters.py
fixture: clusters.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: clusters_by_status
    component: card
    column: member_bp
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: status
    title: Contig clusters
    caption: clusters, by status
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of contig clusters, and the bar splits them into
      those a consensus was refined from and those that were filtered out. It answers
      how many clusters turned into genomes.

      How to read: clusters filtered out are usually small groups of contigs holding
      few reads, which the pipeline treats as likely false positives. A sample with
      every cluster filtered out produced no de novo genome.

      Lines and annotations: a cluster is filtered out when the contigs in it hold
      less than 5 percent of the mapped reads by default (perc_reads_contig), or when
      it is a singleton and singleton filtering is on.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: card
    column: read_depth_pct
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: cluster_type
    top_n_count: 2
    title: Read depth by cluster type
    caption: depth share, by cluster type
    description: >-
      The hero number is the summed share of contig read depth held by all clusters,
      and the bars rank the cluster types, reference-anchored or contig-only. It
      answers whether the reads sit in clusters anchored on a reference sequence.

      How to read: a high share in reference-anchored clusters means the sample's
      contigs match known viruses. A high share in contig-only clusters points to
      sequence with no close reference, or to contamination.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/docs/output.md
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Read depth share per cluster
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: read_depth_pct
      color: status
      labels: {sample: Sample, read_depth_pct: Share of contig read depth (%), status: Cluster status}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample and its segments are its contig clusters, sized by the
      share of the sample's contig read depth they hold and coloured by status. It
      answers how the reads of each sample divide among clusters.

      How to read: one large refined segment is a clean single-virus sample. Many
      segments or a large filtered-out segment mean mixed or fragmented assembly, so
      check the contigs and their taxonomic calls.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The pipeline's own cut-off is 5 percent of
      mapped reads per cluster (perc_reads_contig), a run parameter.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Contig clusters table
    description: >-
      Each row is a contig cluster with its taxon, centroid, member contigs, summed
      length, read depth share and status. It answers what each cluster holds and
      whether it became a consensus, and lets a row selection filter the other tiles.

      How to read: sort by read depth share to find the dominant clusters, and read
      the status to see which were discarded.

renders_as.caption: clusters, by status

    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [nunique]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: classification
    title: Contig taxonomic calls
    caption: contigs, classified or not
    description: >-
      Each unit is one contig and the ring splits them into classified and
      unclassified by the merged Kraken2 and Kaiju call. It answers how much of the
      assembly the classifiers could place in a taxon.

      How to read: a ring mostly classified means the contigs resemble known
      viruses. A large unclassified share points to novel sequence, chimeric
      contigs or classifier databases that lack the virus.

      before clustering.

      How to read: filter to unclassified contigs to see the sequence the
      classifiers could not place.

outputs.name: De novo consensus across refinement steps
outputs.rawYaml:
id: viralmetagenome_contig_iterations
name: De novo consensus across refinement steps
mode: per-genome/refinement
description: >-
  Every de novo consensus at every step of its iterative refinement: the
  scaffold built from the contigs, each mapping iteration and the final
  variant-calling round, with the ambiguous bases, the mismatches and identity
  to the closest reference and the depth at each step. Read along a genome,
  it shows how far the refinement moved the consensus away from the scaffold.
find:
  path_glob: "**/overview-tables/*contigs_overview-with-iterations.tsv"
recipe: viralmetagenome/contig_iterations.py
fixture: contig_iterations.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: ambiguous_by_step
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Ambiguous bases across refinement
    roles: {series: genome_id, x: step_order, y: n_pct}
    config:
      x_title: Refinement step (0 is the scaffold)
      y_title: Ambiguous bases (%)
    description: >-
      Each line is a de novo consensus genome: its share of ambiguous bases at every
      step, from the scaffold built from contigs through each mapping iteration to
      the final variant-calling round. It answers whether refinement fills or
      creates gaps.

      How to read: a flat low line means refinement left the genome unambiguous. A
      line that rises means positions were masked as the reads were mapped, which
      happens where depth is too low to call a base.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. Positions covered by fewer than 5 reads
      are masked in the consensus by default (min_consensus_depth).

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: identity_by_step
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: profile
    title: Identity to the closest reference across refinement
    roles: {series: genome_id, x: step_order, y: annotation_identity_pct}
    config:
      x_title: Refinement step (0 is the scaffold)
      y_title: Identity to the closest reference (%)
    description: >-
      Each line is a de novo consensus genome: its identity to the closest sequence
      of the annotation database at every refinement step. It answers how far
      refinement moved the consensus away from the scaffold and from that reference.

      How to read: a flat line means refinement changed little. Identity falling
      across steps is expected when the sample differs from the reference, since the
      consensus follows the reads. A line low from the start is a divergent virus or
      a poor assembly.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/docs/output.md
  - component: card
    column: annotation_mismatches
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    filter_expr: "col('step') == 'itvariant-calling'"
    title: Mismatches to the closest reference
    caption: mismatches, with their spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median count of mismatches between the final consensus
      and its closest annotated reference, and the box shows their quartiles. It
      answers how far the finished genomes sit from known sequence.

      How to read: few mismatches mean a genome close to a known virus. Many
      mismatches point to a divergent virus or an unreliable consensus, so check
      the ambiguous bases and the depth.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/docs/output.md
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: genome_id
    title: Refinement steps table
    description: >-
      Each row is a consensus genome at one refinement step, with its length,
      ambiguous bases, identity and mismatches to the closest reference, depth and
      CheckV call. It answers how each metric changed between steps and lets a row
      selection filter the other tiles.

      How to read: sort by genome and step to follow one genome through the
      refinement.

Each line is a de novo consensus genome: its share of ambiguous bases at every step, from the scaffold built from contigs through each mapping iteration to the final variant-calling round. It answers whether refinement fills or creates gaps.
How to read: a flat low line means refinement left the genome unambiguous. A line that rises means positions were masked as the reads were mapped, which happens where depth is too low to call a base.
Lines and annotations: none are drawn. Positions covered by fewer than 5 reads are masked in the consensus by default (min_consensus_depth).
Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json

outputs.rawYaml:
id: viralmetagenome_contigs
name: De novo contigs
mode: per-contig/summary
description: >-
  One row per de novo contig: the assembler, its length and length band, the
  reads that map back to it and their share of the sample, the merged Kraken2
  and Kaiju call, and the cluster it ended in as centroid or member.
find:
  path_glob: "**/assembly/assemblers/*/idxstats/*.idxstats"
recipe: viralmetagenome/contigs.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 14 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several classifications.
fixture: contigs.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: contigs_by_class
    component: card
    column: length_bp
    aggregation: count
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: classification
    headline: true
    title: De novo contigs
    caption: contigs, classified or not
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of de novo contigs, and the bar splits them by the
      merged Kraken2 and Kaiju call. It answers how many contigs were assembled and
      how many could be placed in a taxon.

      How to read: a large classified share means the assembly resembles known
      viruses. A large unclassified share points to novel sequence, chimeric contigs
      or a classifier database without the virus.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/docs/output.md
  - id: assembled_bp
    component: card
    column: length_bp
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: length_class
    title: Assembled length
    caption: bases, by contig length band
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total number of assembled bases, and the bar splits it
      by contig length band. It answers how much of the assembly sits in long, usable
      contigs.

      How to read: most bases in long bands mean a contiguous assembly. Bases in short
      bands are fragments that the clustering may discard.

      Lines and annotations: contigs shorter than 500 bases are dropped by default
      (min_contig_size), so none appear in the shortest band.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: reads_on_contigs
    component: card
    column: mapped_reads
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: donut
    breakdown_col: cluster_role
    title: Reads on contigs
    caption: reads, by cluster role
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of reads that map back to the contigs, and the
      ring splits them by the role of their contig in its cluster: centroid or
      member. It answers where the sequencing effort went.

      How to read: reads concentrated on centroids and members of refined clusters
      are well used. Reads on contigs that never clustered were not carried into a
      consensus.
  # Length against reads: a long contig few reads support is a chimera or a
  # contaminant, a short one with many is a fragment of a deep genome.
  - id: length_vs_reads
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Contig length against mapped reads
    roles: {x: length_bp, y: mapped_reads, label: contig, color: classification, size: read_share_pct}
    config:
      x_title: Contig length (bp)
      y_title: Reads mapped to the contig
      log_x: true
      log_y: true
      top_n_labels: 5
    description: >-
      Each point is a de novo contig: its length on the horizontal axis and the reads
      that map back to it on the vertical axis, sized by its share of the sample's
      reads and coloured by its taxonomic call. It answers whether long contigs are
      supported by the reads.

      How to read: long contigs with many reads are well supported. A long contig
      with few reads may be a chimera or a contaminant, and a short contig with many
      reads is a fragment of a deeply covered genome. Both axes are logarithmic.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn, because the pipeline publishes no
      length-to-reads cut-off.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: classification
    title: Taxonomic call
    description: >-
      Keeps only contigs with the chosen call, classified or unclassified.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: De novo contigs table
    description: >-
      Each row is a de novo contig with its assembler, length, mapped reads, read
      share, taxonomic call and cluster. It answers how each contig was built and
      where it ended up, and lets a row selection filter the other tiles.

      How to read: sort by mapped reads to see the best supported contigs, and by
      length to see the longest.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: viralmetagenome_contigs_overview
name: Final de novo consensus genomes
mode: per-genome/consensus
description: >-
  One row per final de novo consensus genome, a sample and contig cluster
  refined to the end: its closest reference in the annotation database and
  the identity to it, the best BLAST hit in the reference pool, the ambiguous
  bases, the CheckV call, the mapping and depth of the sample's reads on it
  and the variant counts of the last round, keyed <sample>_<cluster>.
find:
  path_glob: "**/overview-tables/*contigs_overview.tsv"
recipe: viralmetagenome/contigs_overview.py
# The fixture is enriched synthetically from 4 real rows (copies with seeded noise), so the preview shows several viruses.
fixture: contigs_overview.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: denovo_genomes
    component: card
    column: genome_id
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: composition
    breakdown_col: virus
    headline: true
    title: De novo consensus genomes
    caption: genomes, by virus
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of final de novo consensus genomes, and the bar
      splits them by the virus of their closest annotated reference. It answers what
      the run reconstructed.

      How to read: genomes of the expected virus are the result, and other viruses
      may be co-infections or contamination. Genomes with no assigned virus had no
      significant hit in the annotation database.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/docs/output.md
  # No sourced cut-off for ambiguous bases of a consensus genome: the pipeline
  # only masks positions below its minimum depth, so the card shows the spread.
  - id: denovo_ambiguous
    component: card
    column: n_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Ambiguous bases per genome
    caption: ambiguous bases (%), with their spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of ambiguous bases (N) in the final
      consensus genomes, and the box shows their quartiles. It answers how complete
      the called sequence is.

      How to read: a median near zero means the genomes are fully called. A high
      median or a long upper whisker marks genomes with gaps, usually where depth was
      too low to call a base.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The pipeline masks positions covered by
      fewer than 5 reads by default (min_consensus_depth) and publishes no cut-off for
      the share of ambiguous bases of a genome.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  # Ambiguous bases against identity to the closest reference: the genomes
  # worth trusting sit top left.
  - id: denovo_identity_vs_n
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Ambiguous bases against identity
    roles: {x: n_pct, y: annotation_identity_pct, label: genome_id, color: virus, size: mean_depth}
    config:
      x_title: Ambiguous bases (%)
      y_title: Identity to the closest reference (%)
      top_n_labels: 5
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a final de novo consensus genome: its share of ambiguous bases on
      the horizontal axis and its identity to the closest annotated reference on the
      vertical axis, sized by mean depth and coloured by virus. It answers which
      genomes are both complete and close to a known sequence.

      How to read: genomes at the top left are fully called and close to a reference.
      Genomes to the right have gaps, and those low on the axis are divergent or
      poorly assembled, so check their depth before using them.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median identity to the closest
      reference of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it
      follows the filters), not a cut-off of the pipeline or the annotation
      database.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/docs/output.md
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: genome_id
    title: De novo genomes table
    description: >-
      Each row is a final de novo consensus genome with its closest reference,
      identity, ambiguous bases, best BLAST hit, CheckV call, mapping, depth and
      variant counts. It answers how good each reconstructed genome is, and lets a row
      selection filter the other tiles.

      How to read: sort by ambiguous bases or identity, and read the CheckV call and
      the depth before accepting a genome.

id: viralmetagenome_mapping_overview
name: Consensus genomes against the mapping constraints
mode: per-genome/consensus
description: >-
  One row per sample and constraint reference of the mapping constraint
  sheet: the consensus built from the reads mapped to it, with its closest
  annotated reference, ambiguous bases and CheckV call, the share of reads
  mapped and duplicated, the depth and breadth, the variant counts and, for a

renders_as:
  # No sourced breadth cut-off: the pipeline publishes none, so the card shows
  # the spread of the 10x breadth rather than a pass mark.
  - id: constraint_breadth
    component: card
    column: cov_10x_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [min, max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    headline: true
    title: Breadth at 10x depth
    caption: genome covered at 10x (%), per genome
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of the constraint genome covered by at least
      10 reads, and the histogram shows it for every sample and reference. It answers
      how completely the reads cover each reference.

      How to read: values near 100 mean a fully covered genome. A low tail marks
      references the sample barely contains, and their consensus is mostly masked.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. The pipeline masks positions covered by
      fewer than 5 reads by default (min_consensus_depth) and publishes no breadth
      cut-off.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  - id: constraint_depth
    component: card
    column: mean_depth
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Mean depth
    caption: mean depth, with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median of the mean read depth over the constraint
      genomes, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how deeply the reads cover
      the references.

      How to read: higher depth supports a confident consensus. A low box means many
      positions fall under the minimum depth and are masked.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/nextflow_schema.json
  # Depth against breadth: a deep but narrow mapping is a partial genome, a
  # broad but shallow one is a genome the consensus masks in places.
  - id: depth_vs_breadth
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Depth against breadth
    roles: {x: mean_depth, y: cov_10x_pct, label: genome_id, color: reference, size: mapped_reads}
    config:
      x_title: Mean depth
      y_title: Genome covered at 10x (%)
      top_n_labels: 5
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample mapped to one constraint reference: its mean depth on the
      horizontal axis and the share of the genome covered at 10x or more on the
      vertical axis, sized by mapped reads and coloured by reference. It answers
      whether a deep mapping is also a complete one.

      How to read: points at the top right are deep and complete. A deep but narrow
      mapping is a partial genome, and a broad but shallow one is masked in places, so
      look at the other references of the same sample.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of the genome
      covered at 10x of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it
      follows the filters), not a cut-off of the pipeline.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: genome_id
    title: Constraint mappings table
    description: >-

      closest annotated reference, ambiguous bases, CheckV call, reads mapped and
      duplicated, depth, breadth and variant counts. It answers how each mapping
      performed and lets a row selection filter the other tiles.

      one sample to see which one fits its reads.

outputs.rawYaml:
id: viralmetagenome_samples_overview
name: Reads, host removal and assembly per sample
mode: per-sample/summary
description: >-
  One row per sample from the pipeline's samples overview table: read pairs
  before trimming, after trimming and after host removal, the host share,
  fastp's Q30 and duplication, the de novo assembly length and N50, the
  contig clusters kept and removed and the de novo consensus count. The share
  of raw read pairs left after preprocessing is derived alongside.
find:
  path_glob: "**/overview-tables/*samples_overview.tsv"
recipe: viralmetagenome/samples_overview.py
fixture: samples_overview.tsv
renders_as:
  - id: read_attrition
    component: card
    column: raw_read_pairs
    aggregation: sum
    aggregations: [median, max]
    secondary_layout: attrition
    attrition_cols: [trimmed_read_pairs, host_filtered_read_pairs]
    headline: true
    title: Read pairs through preprocessing
    caption: read pairs, at each step
    description: >-
      The hero number is the total of raw read pairs, and the bars show how many
      remain after trimming and after host removal. It answers how much sequencing
      reaches the assembly.

      How to read: a small loss at each step is normal. A large loss at trimming
      means poor read quality or adapters, and a large loss at host removal means a
      host-rich sample.
  - id: retained_share
    component: card
    column: retained_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Reads retained
    caption: reads retained (%), with their spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of raw read pairs left after
      preprocessing, and the box shows the quartiles over samples. It answers how
      much of each library survives.

      How to read: values near 100 are libraries with little loss. A long lower
      whisker marks samples that lost many reads and may be too shallow to assemble.
  # No sourced host-share cut-off: the pipeline publishes none, so the card shows
  # the spread across samples.
  - id: host_share
    component: card
    column: host_pct
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [max]
    secondary_layout: histogram
    title: Host reads
    caption: host share (%), per sample
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median share of reads removed as host, and the histogram
      shows it for every sample. It answers how host-rich the samples are.

      How to read: a high share means most sequencing went to the host, leaving less
      for the virus, and the highest samples are the ones to check first.

      Lines and annotations: none are drawn. Host removal uses a Kraken2 database and
      the pipeline publishes no cut-off for the host share.

      Source: https://github.com/nf-core/viralmetagenome/blob/1.2.0/docs/output.md
  - id: assembly_n50
    component: card
    column: assembly_n50
    aggregation: median
    aggregations: [box_plot_stats]
    secondary_layout: box_plot
    title: Assembly N50
    caption: N50 (bp), with its spread
    description: >-
      The hero number is the median N50 of the de novo assemblies, and the box shows
      the quartiles over samples. It answers how contiguous the assemblies are.

      How to read: for a virus with one genome segment, an N50 close to the genome
      length means a near-complete assembly. A low N50 means fragmented contigs that
      the clustering has to merge.
  # Reads left against the host share: a sample low on both lost its reads to
  # the host database, one low on reads alone was sequenced shallow.
  # C1 N/A: the recipe has no categorical column per sample (every column is a
  # numeric read count or percentage), so the points stay one colour and carry
  # the read depth in their size.
  - id: retained_vs_host
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: scatter_xy
    title: Reads retained against host share
    roles: {x: host_pct, y: retained_pct, label: sample, size: raw_read_pairs}
    config:
      x_title: Host reads (%)
      y_title: Read pairs retained (%)
      top_n_labels: 5
      reference_line: horizontal
      reference_stat: median
    description: >-
      Each point is a sample: its share of host reads on the horizontal axis and the
      share of raw read pairs retained on the vertical axis, sized by raw read pairs.
      It answers why a sample lost reads.

      How to read: a sample low on both axes lost its reads to the host database. A
      sample low on retained reads with little host lost them at trimming, so check
      its quality and adapter content. Large points that stay high are well sequenced.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median share of read pairs
      retained of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows
      the filters), not a cut-off of the pipeline.
  - id: host_filtered_bars
    component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    title: Read pairs after host removal
    dict_kwargs:
      x: sample
      y: host_filtered_read_pairs
      color: host_pct
      labels: {sample: Sample, host_filtered_read_pairs: Read pairs after host removal, host_pct: Host reads (%)}
    reference_lines:
      - {axis: y, stat: median, column: host_filtered_read_pairs}
    description: >-
      Each bar is a sample: the read pairs left after host removal, coloured by the
      share of reads removed as host. It answers how much usable sequencing each
      sample has.

      How to read: short bars are samples with little left to assemble, and the colour
      says whether the host removal or a shallow library is the cause.

      Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median number of read pairs
      after host removal of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show
      (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of the pipeline.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: RangeSlider
    column_name: host_pct
    title: Host reads (%)
    description: >-
      Keeps only samples whose host share falls in the chosen range.
  - component: table
    row_selection_enabled: true
    row_selection_column: sample
    title: Samples overview table
    description: >-

pb1	Fungi;Basidiomycota	0.37468566638725903	Fungi	Basidiomycota
pb1	Fungi;Mortierellomycota	0.005029337803855826	Fungi	Mortierellomycota
pb2	Fungi;Ascomycota	0.43139097744360905	Fungi	Ascomycota

outputs.name: SINTAX composition
outputs.rawYaml:
id: vsearch_sintax_abundance
name: SINTAX composition
mode: sintax
description: >-
  Per-sample Phylum-level relative abundance, built by joining the SINTAX
  per-ASV taxonomy to the DADA2 ASV count table written beside it. The
  classifier publishes taxonomy only, so the counts have to come from the
  denoiser's table.
# The reference-DB tag is part of the file name (`unite-fungi_8_2`), so the
# glob ends on the version digit. The `.raw.tsv` variant has `raw` immediately
# before the extension and is therefore never matched.
find:
  path_glob: "**/sintax/ASV_tax_sintax.*[0-9].tsv"
recipe: vsearch/sintax_abundance.py
fixture: sintax_abundance.tsv
renders_as:
  # Wide per-rank columns (Kingdom/Phylum), so the nested view is a sunburst;
  # `stacked_taxonomy` needs the single long rank column this table lacks, the
  # same reason `qiime2_rel_abundance` stops at a sunburst.
  # C1: arcs are coloured by phylum, the rank the reader compares.
  - id: sintax_sunburst
    component: advanced_viz
    kind: sunburst
    title: Kingdom and phylum composition
    roles: {ranks: [Kingdom, Phylum], abundance: rel_abundance}
    config:
      colour_by_rank: Phylum
    description: >-
      Each arc is a taxon: the inner ring is the kingdom and the outer ring the phylum,
      sized by relative abundance summed over the samples in view and coloured by
      phylum. It answers which groups dominate the community.

      How to read: a wide arc is a dominant phylum, and many thin arcs a diverse
      community. Click an arc to zoom into it, and filter the samples to see how the
      composition shifts. An Unclassified arc means the reference database could not
      place those sequences.

      Source: https://github.com/torognes/vsearch
  - component: figure
    visu_type: box
    title: Relative abundance by phylum
    dict_kwargs:
      x: Phylum
      y: rel_abundance
      color: Phylum
      labels: {Phylum: Phylum, rel_abundance: Relative abundance}
    description: >-
      Each box is a phylum: the spread of its relative abundance over the samples in
      view. It answers which phyla carry most of the community and how much that varies.

      How to read: a few high boxes and a long tail near zero is the usual shape of an
      amplicon community. A wide box is a phylum whose share changes between samples;
      filter by kingdom or sample to see which samples drive it.
  # How many samples were classified, how many phyla they resolve to, and how
  # unevenly the abundance sits across them.
  - component: card
    column: sample
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: Phylum
    top_n_count: 3
    caption: samples, by phylum
    title: Samples classified
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of samples with a classification, with the number of
      sample and phylum rows next to it, and the bars rank the phyla seen in the most
      samples. It answers how many samples the composition rests on.

      How to read: a phylum present in few samples is a sporadic taxon. The ranking
      shows which phyla are shared across the samples.
  - component: card
    column: Phylum
    aggregation: nunique
    aggregations: [count]
    secondary_layout: top_n
    breakdown_col: sample
    top_n_count: 3
    filter_expr: "col('Phylum') != 'Unclassified'"
    headline: true
    caption: phyla, by sample
    title: Phyla resolved
    description: >-
      The hero number is the count of distinct named phyla found, and the bars rank the
      samples by how many phyla they hold. It answers how diverse the community is at
      phylum level.

      How to read: a sample with few phyla is dominated by one lineage. Sequences the
      classifier could not place are left out of the count.
  - component: card
    column: rel_abundance
    aggregation: max
    aggregations: [median, q3]
    secondary_layout: compact
    caption: largest share, with the median and the upper quartile
    title: Dominant phylum share
    description: >-
      The hero number is the largest relative abundance any phylum reaches in a sample,
      with the median and the upper quartile of all phylum shares next to it. It
      answers how dominated the community is by one lineage.

      How to read: a maximum close to 1 means one phylum makes up nearly a whole
      sample. A median far below it is the usual long tail of minor phyla.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: Kingdom
    title: Kingdom
    description: >-
      Choose one or more kingdoms to restrict the tiles of this tab to them. It answers
      how a single domain of life contributes to the composition.

      How to read: pick a kingdom to see only its phyla in the sunburst and the boxes.
  - component: interactive
    interactive_type: MultiSelect
    column_name: Phylum
    title: Phylum
    description: >-
      Choose one or more phyla to restrict the tiles of this tab to them. It answers
      how a single phylum is distributed across the samples.

      How to read: pick a phylum to compare its relative abundance between samples.
  - component: table
    title: Relative abundance per sample and phylum
    description: >-
      Each row is a phylum in one sample: its taxonomy, the kingdom and the relative
      abundance. It answers exactly which taxa each sample holds and at what share.

      How to read: sort by relative abundance to find the dominant phylum of a sample.

tools.description: Illumina tool for large variant benchmarking.
tools.name: Wittyer

outputs.description: CNV/SV accuracy from Wittyer (precision/recall/F1) per callset, at the two levels Wittyer scores: per event and per base (`stats_type`). `caller` is the tool that made the calls and `truth_set` the truth set it was compared against. Event-type and size-bin strata are kept when a table carries them. Optional: not produced by the public megatest.
outputs.fixtureContent:
label	caller	truth_set	stats_type	precision	recall	f1
sampleA	manta	HG002	Event	0.62	0.41	0.494
sampleA	manta	HG002	Base	0.48	0.37	0.418
sampleB	delly	HG002	Event	0.43	0.29	0.346
sampleB	delly	HG002	Base	0.21	0.18	0.194
outputs.name: Wittyer CNV summary
outputs.rawYaml:
id: wittyer_summary
name: Wittyer CNV summary
mode: stratified
description: >-
  CNV/SV accuracy from Wittyer (precision/recall/F1) per callset, at the two
  levels Wittyer scores: per event and per base (`stats_type`). `caller` is the
  tool that made the calls and `truth_set` the truth set it was compared
  against. Event-type and size-bin strata are kept when a table carries them.
  Optional: not produced by the public megatest.
find: { path_glob: "**/summary/tables/wittyer/wittyer.summary.csv" }
recipe: wittyer/summary.py
fixture: summary.tsv
renders_as:
  # C1: the bars are coloured by the level Wittyer scores, per event or per base.
  # stats_type is in the recipe's OUTPUT_SCHEMA ("Not reported" on a table without it).
  - component: figure
    visu_type: bar
    dict_kwargs:
      x: label
      y: f1
      color: stats_type
      barmode: group
      labels: {label: Callset, f1: F1 score, stats_type: Scoring level}
    title: F1 per callset, event and base
    description: >-
      Each bar is the F1 score of one callset against the truth set, with the event
      level and the base level side by side. It answers how well the large variant
      calls match the truth, and whether they match in count or in the bases they cover.

      How to read: a high event bar means the callset finds the right events, and a high
      base bar means it covers the right bases. A callset good at one level and poor at
      the other has events that match in position but not in extent.

      Note: Wittyer counts an event as a match by percentage or base-pair distance and
      requires the genotype to match by default, and counts every overlapped base at
      the base level. The cited README states no cut-off for F1, so none is drawn.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/witty.er/master/README.md
  - component: table
    title: Large variant benchmark
    description: >-
      Each row is a callset at one scoring level with its precision, recall and F1, and
      the caller, the truth set and the strata when the table carries them. It answers
      the numbers behind the bars.

      How to read: compare recall and precision at each level to see whether a callset
      misses variants or adds false ones.

      Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Illumina/witty.er/master/README.md
